en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.

The Ancient Commentary on the *Abhidhammāvatāra* Chapter One 1. The First Chapter: The Exposition of the Aggregates, Bases, and Elements (*Khandhāyatanadhātuniddesa*) [The text continues with the formal definitions and classifications of the aggregates, bases, and elements.]

Commentary on the Exposition of Consciousness (Cittaniddesavaṇṇanā). 8. Therein, among those four kinds of ultimate meanings, this is the selection by genus (*jātiniddhāraṇa*). "Consciousness" means that which is called consciousness.
It is "cognizing" (*vijānana*) because it cognizes; the cognizing of objects is "object-cognizing. This is a definition of the essential nature of consciousness.

[This is] the statement. Now, what is the meaning of the word for that "consciousness" (citta), and what is its etymological sense? It is stated by the Teacher: "In the sense of encompassing all, that is, by the method of encompassing all consciousnesses;
it 'thinks' (cinteti) or knows the object, thus it is 'consciousness' (citta). In this case, all consciousness is intended.

"By way of the cognitive process (javana-vīthi), it 'accumulates' (cinoti) its own continuity, thus it is 'consciousness' (citta). In this case, [it refers to] wholesome, unwholesome, and great functional consciousness.

This is what is intended. The non-inclusion of other impulsion-moments (*javana*) is for the purpose of making it known that, as a general rule, only sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) impulsions impel seven times. 9.
That which has a variegated performance is "variegated-performance" (*vicittakaraṇa*); the state of being such is "variegated-performance-ness" (*vicittakaraṇā*). "Of this... [and so forth].
Having thought, "Let this part of the form be above, let this be below, and let this be on both sides," the production of the remaining mental forms occurs according to that intended sequence;
thus, whatever diverse craft exists in the world, all of it is performed by the mind alone.
Because it performs such diversity, it is called *citta*. At that time, because of its performing, it is said to "perform" (*karoti*).
"Citta. This is a derivative (taddhita) term. Or, there is this other method: by virtue of its own nature as consciousness (*cittatā*), that which is with lust (*sarāga*) is one thing;
that with hatred (*sadosa*) is another; that with delusion (*samoha*) is another. That belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) is one thing;

that divided into the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) and so forth is another. That having visible form as its object (*rūpārammaṇa*) is one thing; that having sound or other objects is another. Even among those with visible form as their object, that having blue as its object is one thing, and another...
The object is yellow and so forth. This same method applies to sound and other objects as well. Among all of them, one is inferior, another is intermediate, and another is sublime.

Even among the inferior and so forth, one is dominated by desire (*chandādhipateyya*), another by consciousness (*cittādhipateyya*), another by energy (*vīriyādhipateyya*), and another by investigation (*vīmaṃsādhipateyya*). Therefore, for whichever of these—concomitance, plane, object, inferior, intermediate, sublime, or dominance—[the conditions are met]...
It is "citta" because it is the state of one's own mind (*attano cittatāya*). It is "citta" because "citta exists in this. At that time, all [of these] are "citta.
Even in the case of a designation (*paññatti*), when consciousness (*viññāṇa*) is variegated, the "work of citta" is "cittakamma"; "cittakamma" itself is "cittakammaka.
In this context, within this specific section, the conventional term "citta"—the word "citta"—should be understood by the wise as referring to consciousness (*viññāṇa*) when it is variegated.

That consciousness, which has been described in the manner stated by the words "he reflects upon it by way of its all-inclusive nature," etc., is singlefold as having an object, by virtue of its state of possessing an object.

It is twofold as having result and not having result, by way of being with result and without result. Therein, among those two kinds of consciousness, that which is "with result" is wholesome or unwholesome;
that which is "without result" is indeterminate. By way of their state as wholesome or unwholesome...
The meaning is "unspoken. It is threefold according to the classification of its types: the wholesome type, the unwholesome type, and the indeterminate type.
Regarding that statement, what is the literal meaning of the word "wholesome" (*kusala*)?
It is so called because of the flowing away (*salanato*) of what is contemptible, because of the shaking off, or the destruction, of evil states; it is [so called] by way of a contemptible mode.
They are called *kusā* because they cut (*lavana*) or sever that which is reckoned as unwholesome (*akusala*). Or, it is *kusa* because it makes thin (*tanu*) what is contemptible (*kucchi*);
[it is so called] because it is to be taken up or grasped by means of *kusa*, which is knowledge (*ñāṇa*). Alternatively, there is this other method:
this word *kusala*—this word *kusala*—[is used] in the sense of skillfulness, in the sense of health, in the sense of blamelessness, and in the sense of desirable fruition.
The meaning has also been seen by us. Here, in this context, it is seen in the sense of being blameless (*anavajja*) and so forth.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the senses of health (*ārogya*), supremacy (*adhipati*), and fruition (*vipāka*) are to be understood. Since it has been seen, therefore the wholesome (*kusala*) is characterized by being blameless, supreme, and a fruition.

It is "blameless" (*anavajja*) because there is no blame (*avajja*)—that is, no defilement-blame (*kilesāvajja*), no fault of defilement (*kilesadosa*), and no distress of defilement (*kilesadaratha*)—in it.
It is called *vipāka* because it ripens through karma;

and because it is desirable by its own nature and by way of experiencing desirable and undesirable objects, it is "desirable fruition" (*iṭṭhavipāka*). Being exclusively blameless, it is "desirable fruition.

That which is to be characterized—the wholesome (*kusala*)—is characterized by this [fruition] while remaining unperceived; thus, it is the "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*). "Blameless desirable fruition" is the characteristic.
"Of this" refers to the characteristic of having blameless and most excellent fruition. Wholesome (kusala) is precisely that which has blameless and most excellent fruition.

One might raise the objection: "How can it be its own characteristic? This is because the relationship between the characteristic and the characterized is established through the nature of the words *viññāta* and *aviññāta*.
For, by way of the meaning of the word *kusala*, the wholesome is *aviññāta*, meaning unmanifest.
It is to be characterized. Through the sense of being known as having blameless, foremost, and ripening results, the wholesome characteristic is made manifest.
"Destruction of the unwholesome" (*akusalaviddhaṃsana*) means the destruction of unwholesome states;
that which has this as its function, its task, is "having the destruction of the unwholesome as its function. It manifests by way of its state of purification (*vodāna*).

It has purification as its manifestation, the mode of appearance of purification, and the mode of being grasped as purification. Or, this is another method: because it is the opposite of fault (*vajja*), the wholesome (*kusala*) has the characteristic of being faultless;

the meaning is that the wholesome has the characteristic of being the opposite of fault. It has the state of purification as its essence and the attainment of the state of purification as its fulfillment.
It has desirable ripening as its manifestation and the fruit of desirable ripening as its result. It has appropriate attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) as its proximate cause.
“Footing and place” is *padatthāna*; both terms are designations for the sense of cause. Therefore, the meaning is “the proximate cause.
Otherwise, there would be the fault of redundancy. Thus, *yonisomanasikārapadatthāna* means that wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) is its footing, its proximate cause.

The unwholesome (akusala) is characterized by being blameworthy and having an undesirable result. The indeterminate (abyākata) has a characteristic opposite to both of those; that is, it is the opposite of both the wholesome and the unwholesome, and its characteristic is the absence of a result.
Alternatively, there is another way: it is "unfit for a result" (avipākāraha), meaning it is unsuitable for a result.
Regarding the distinction between "having a basis" (*savaṭṭhuka*) and "lacking a basis" (*avaṭṭhuka*):

that which has a basis has the heart as its basis; that which lacks a basis is devoid of the heart as its basis. 12. By way of summary and in brief, there are two kinds of sensual desire (*kāma*): by way of defilement (*kilesa*) and by way of object (*vatthu*). Craving and lust (*chandārāga*) alone are the defilement. The "object" (*vatthu*) is that which proceeds within the three planes of existence together with the cycle of rebirth (*vaṭṭa*); it is called an "object" (*vatthu*) because the defilement dwells (*vasati*) therein.

13. Sensual desire as defilement desires—that is, seeks—the object; the object is desired—that is, sought—by sensual desire as defilement. Thus, through these two means of accomplishment—the agent (*kattukāraka*) and the object (*kammakāraka*)—this twofold sensual desire is established.

14–5. Thus, this twofold sensual desire (kāma) ranges over whatever region it possesses through its various attainments; for that reason, that region is of eleven kinds, according to the four types of beings—namely, the six classes of devas and humans.
16. Regarding the phrase "sensual desire ranges" (kāmavacara-ti): sensual desire ranges over these eleven kinds of regions;

for that reason, because that region is distinguished by this sensual desire, it is designated as "the sensual realm" (kāmāvacara). This is due to the application of the term "distinguished" (abhilakkhita).
Regarding the third sense, those learned in the science of grammar (saddasatthavidū) recite that "assā" is a genitive case. For "sasattha" means a place where people wander together with weapons;
it is called *sattha* because they shout at (*sasanti*) or injure (*hiṃsanti*) one another by means of them. Thus, "sasattha" means together with weapons.
A "sasatthāvacara" is a place where people wander together with weapons (*sasatthā purisā avacaranti ettha*). Just as in whatever place people wander together with weapons, [so too is this].
That region is called the "domain of weapons" (*sasatthāvacara*) because it is specifically characterized by those [beings] even while other two-footed and four-footed beings are also present there;

likewise, this region is called the "sensuous domain" (*kāmāvacara*) because it is specifically distinguished by those [states] even while other states such as the fine-material and immaterial domains (*rūpāvacarādīsu*) are also present there.

17. Just as *rūpabhava* (form-existence) is called simply *rūpa* by eliding the latter member of the compound, so too this [state] belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*)—which is designated as *kāma* by eliding the latter member—is proclaimed and spoken of by the wise as "kāma.
18. This consciousness always ranges within that kāma, within that sense-sphere; for that reason, it is called *kāmāvacara*.
Thus it was spoken by the Buddha, the destroyer of desires, the slayer of sensual pleasures. Although this [craving] operates even within the realms of form and formlessness,
just as an elephant who obtains the name "one who ranges in battle" because he mostly ranges there—

even when that elephant is wandering in the city— is still called "one who ranges in battle," so too living beings who range on land or in water are not [called such] when they are not on land or in water.

Just as those standing on dry land are nevertheless called "land-dwellers and water-dwellers," so too this [consciousness], although it ranges elsewhere, should be understood as "belonging to the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*).

Alternatively, it is called *kāmāvacara* because sense-desire (*kāma*) ranges within its objective domain (*avacara*) by way of being made an object. Granted, this [consciousness] also ranges within the fine-material and immaterial spheres;

however, just as one is called a "calf" (*vaccha*) because he walks (*vadati*), or a "deer" (*miga*) because he lies on the earth (*mahiyam seti*), so too is it called "sense-sphere" because it ranges in the sense-sphere.

When "earth-dweller" (*mahisa*) is said, it is not only those who say "earth" or those who lie upon the earth that receive that name; rather, it becomes the name for all [beings]. This should be understood as being of the same nature. 19.
Regarding "rebirth-linking in the sense-sphere existence": one applies the term "rebirth-linking" to the sense-desires known as "sense-sphere existence" (*kāmabhava*).
Therefore, it is called "belonging to the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*). Or alternatively, this is another method: therein, in that sense-sphere realm, it is included and contained within.
Thus, this is the sense-sphere [consciousness].
20. The eightfold consciousness designated as "sense-sphere" refers to these eight types of consciousness.

By way of the ten bases of meritorious action (*puññakiriyavatthu*), these are indeed meritorious actions; they are called "bases of meritorious action" because they are the foundations and causes for their respective fruits and benefits.
They are under their control; by them it proceeds.

21. Generosity, virtue, mental development, the dedication of merit, service, teaching the Dhamma, rejoicing in merit, rectification of views, hearing the Dhamma, and listening to the Dhamma, as well as honoring and paying respect—thus, in this manner described by me, are the merits.
These are the bases of merit; their classification, known as the "classification of the bases of merit," should be understood and known by the wise.
22–3. They are included within [the three types of merit]: giving, the transfer of merit, and rejoicing in merit are included within the category of giving;

service and honoring are included within the merit consisting of virtue (*sīlamaya*); teaching the Dhamma, hearing the Dhamma, rectification of views, and cultivation are included within the merit consisting of mental development (*bhāvanāmaya*).
They are included within merit; and even the ten meritorious deeds amount to only three. 24.

All the merits of the recollections (*anussati*), praise, the three refuges (*saraṇattaya*), and the praise of the qualities of the Triple Gem (*ratanattaya*)—these are included within the rectification of views (*diṭṭhijukamma*); there is no doubt or uncertainty regarding their inclusion therein. 25.
"Prior volition" (*purimā cetanā*) is the volition that occurred prior to that [moment]; "volition of release" (*muñcacetanā*) is the present volition.
Subsequent volition is the volition that occurs at a later time. Thus, just as there are three types of volition in merit consisting of giving,
so too should a wise person illuminate— that is, explain— the three types of volition in the remaining categories of merit consisting of virtue and meditation.
Indeed, it is true that when a person, depending upon and on account of the excellence of the recipient of the gift and so forth—
here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the place, time, virtuous friends, and others are included—

or on account of some other cause for joy, such as an abundance of faith, purity, right view, the performance of wholesome deeds, the perception of benefits, or being endowed with a joyful rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*)— [he gives]. By the inclusion of the term "other," [these qualities] are intended.
Inclusion. There is what is given; there is the fruit of giving. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), terms such as *atthi-huta* (the offering that exists) and others are included.
"Having placed before him" means having made it foremost. Without being urged or exhorted by others, he performs meritorious deeds such as giving.

By the expression "giving and so forth," the volition of giving (*dāna-cetanā*) arising in dependence upon the object to be given (*deyyadhamma*) is to be understood. At that time, for that person, there is the formation (*saṅkharaṇa*).
*Saṅkhāra* means volitional formation; that which has no such formation is *asaṅkhāra*, and that itself is *asaṅkhārika*. The meaning is "without effort.
By the "method already stated" is meant the statement: "the excellence of the gift, the recipient, and so forth.
However, in this context, *saṅkhāra*—meaning "it forms"—is a designation for one's own prior application (*pubbappayoga*) toward what is occurring.
Or it is a designation for another person’s previously initiated application. This is its intended meaning:

when someone, having generated the thought, "I shall perform acts of giving and so forth," does not do so [at that time], but later performs them impelled by his own prior volition, then it is "with effort" (*sasaṅkhārika*);
the meaning is that it occurs together with one's own previous application. By way of showing the practice...
*Paṭipatti* (practice) is so called because by means of it one practices through virtue and the other factors, knows, or goes toward *nibbāna*.
*Paṭipattidassanaṃ* (the demonstration of practice) is the seeing by means of that; [it is] by that. Those for whom familiarity has arisen are "those with arisen familiarity" (*jātaparicayā*).
"Suddenly" (*sahasā*) means with speed. One should demonstrate this in all four alternatives.

26. "And by way of the ten meritorious deeds (puññakriyā), these [mental states] become many. Indeed, these mental states become many even by way of the ten meritorious deeds and so forth; thus the Blessed One would explain. He should demonstrate:
"Seventeen thousand, two hundred and eighty;
such are the meritorious states of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara)."—
The teacher should explain and speak thus: "There are seventeen thousand two hundred and eighty meritorious deeds of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara-puñña).
These consist of: the ten bases of meritorious action (dasapuññakriyāvatthu); the six doors and their presiding deities;
the three [faculties] beginning with the body; and the three [levels of volition] beginning with the inferior."
In the two realms of existence—namely, the realm of sense-desire (*kāmadhātu*) and the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). According to the classification of the modes of progress (*paṭipadā*), there are:
painful progress with sluggish direct knowledge, painful progress with swift direct knowledge, pleasant progress with sluggish direct knowledge, and pleasant progress with swift direct knowledge.
That which proceeds by means of the merit of development belonging to the fine-material sphere is, by virtue of the merit of development proceeding in the fine-material sphere...
The active [kamma] produces a rebirth in the fine-material sphere; it brings about the rebirth-linking for an existence in the fine-material sphere.

Regarding the distinction between "having a physical basis" (savatthuka) and "lacking a physical basis" (avatthuka): when one born in the immaterial sphere is reborn in the sense-sphere or the fine-material sphere, then [the kamma] arises depending on the heart-basis;
thus, it is said to have arisen "with a physical basis. When one is reborn in the immaterial sphere, then [it arises] without the heart-basis...
It arises without depending [on anything], and therefore it is called "baseless.
The object of the base of infinite space is the space cleared by the removal of the kasiṇa. For the base of infinite consciousness, the object is the consciousness that occurs therein;
the mind—that is, the consciousness occurring in that space cleared by the removal of the kasiṇa—becomes the object. For the base of nothingness...

Its disappearance—that is, the disappearance, absence, conventional designation, and objective support of that base of infinite space—is the objective support for the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
For the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the base of nothingness is the objective support.
Perception of forms is "perception of form"; by this term "perception," consciousness is also included. "By transcending" means by transcending the space produced by the removal of the kasiṇa.
Perception occurring when there is a collision between the doors (the sense faculties) and their objects is "perception of resistance" (*paṭighasaññā*).

This is a designation for the two sets of fivefold consciousness. With the subsiding, through the subsiding, of those perceptions of resistance—that is, the two sets of fivefold consciousness—there occurs perception occurring upon diversity, that is, upon objects of diverse nature;
this is "perception of diversity" (*nānattasaññā*). It is called "diversity" (*nānatta*) because its own-nature (*sabhāva*) consists of various [objects].
Alternatively, *nānattā* means that its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is manifold; that very perception is *nānattasaññā*, meaning "perception pertaining to the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*).
By way of non-attention—that is, through not attending—to those various perceptions.
Regarding the distinction between those with fixed and unfixed bases: the stream-entry path has a fixed base. Why? Because it occurs only among [beings] in the sense and fine-material realms.
Because they arise depending upon the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*). However, the other three paths have indeterminate bases. Why?

Because in the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere they arise depending upon the heart-base, whereas in the immaterial sphere they arise without depending upon the heart-base; therefore, they have indeterminate bases.
"By means of the three doors to liberation" refers to the three doors to liberation known as emptiness (*suññata*), the signless (*animitta*), and the desireless (*appaṇihita*).

Those things which, when found in someone, yoke and bind that person to the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) are called fetters (*saṃyojana*). Only personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), and adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*) are the fetters;

thus they are the "fetters of personality-belief, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances. Their abandonment is the "abandonment of the fetters of personality-belief, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances.

That which effects this is "that which effects the abandonment of the fetters of personality-belief, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances," namely, the consciousness of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga-citta*).
Even conceit (māna), though it leads to states of deprivation in one part, is abandoned [by the path]; it is not abandoned in its entirety by the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga).
The same principle applies to the remaining defilements (kilesa). However, restlessness (uddhacca) is not abandoned even in that part which leads to states of deprivation.

The mind of the once-returner path (sakadāgāmi-magga-citta) effects the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion. [This refers to] those fetters (saṃyojana) already destroyed by the path of stream-entry.
If it is asked, "Why is abandonment not mentioned?"—it is because the second path is greater than the first path;

thus, since it is recognized that the fetters destroyed by the first path are also destroyed by the second path, it is therefore not mentioned. The same principle applies to the third and fourth paths as well.
Herein, "in this supramundane consciousness" (*lokuttara-citte*). "Each one" is stated in the sense of distributive repetition. "In accordance with the path" (*maggānurūpaṃ*).
This statement is for the purpose of making known that it is appropriate for the first path and the first fruit. 28.
Regarding sense-sphere states, there are exactly eight consciousnesses in the sense realm (*kāmāvacara*); five consciousnesses in the fine-material realm (*rūpa*);
four consciousnesses among the immaterial states (*arūpi*); and four unsurpassed supramundane consciousnesses (*lokuttara*). Thus, in this manner described by me—
Wholesome states of consciousness are twenty-one.
By the Sage who is mindful and free from both the wholesome and the unwholesome— by him who is endowed with mindfulness,
skilled in the wholesome, expert in the wholesome, and possessed of mastery through the five kinds of mastery— whatever wholesome consciousness pertains to the four planes [is to be understood].
All that has been spoken and uttered throughout the four planes— that wholesome consciousness has also been spoken and uttered by me, the teacher Buddhadatta.
"By way of the determined and undetermined bases" means that the two types of consciousness associated with aversion depend solely upon the heart-base within the sense-sphere.
It arises [only] in certain planes and does not arise in other planes; therefore, it has a fixed basis (*niyatavatthuka*).

The other unwholesome states, however, when arising in the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere, arise dependent upon the heart-basis (*hadayavatthu*); in the immaterial sphere, they arise without depending on the heart-basis.

Therefore, they have an unfixed basis (*aniyatavatthuka*). For that reason, and by way of whether or not they produce rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the state accompanied by restlessness (*uddhacca*)— [...]*
It does not produce rebirth-linking. If it were to produce rebirth-linking, it would produce it only in the states of misery (apāya). Why?

Because by means of the stream-entry path (sotāpatti-magga), even that portion leading to the states of misery has not been abandoned; the meaning is that it has not been abandoned in its entirety. Furthermore, that path itself does not lead to the states of misery.
However, other defilements leading to the states of misery have been abandoned by way of a partial portion; thus, by means of the first path—
Therefore, it does not produce [a rebirth-linking consciousness]. However, it produces eleven kinds of rebirth-linking;

by that [consciousness], one regards things such as "seen auspicious signs" (diṭṭha-maṅgala) and so forth—the word "etc. including "heard auspicious signs" (suta-maṅgala) and others—as essential and supreme. One believes (pacceti) them, meaning one has faith (saddahati). "Sabhāvatikkha" means that its intrinsic nature (sabhāva) is sharp (tikkha); thus, it is "sharp by nature.

By that "sharp by nature" [consciousness], it should be understood that when this [consciousness] associated with aversion (paṭigha-sampayutta) operates intensely during unwholesome kamma such as killing living beings, there is the arising of the "unprompted" (asaṅkhārika) type; when it operates weakly, there is the arising of the "prompted" (sasaṅkhārika) type.
Of that deluded one.
Of the specific kinds of suffering, of the various types of suffering.

30. By way of the root of greed, there are eight consciousnesses; by way of the root of hatred, two consciousnesses; by way of the root of delusion, two consciousnesses. Thus, in the manner described by me here, the unwholesome [states] would be of twelve types.

31. Whatever evil-mindedness, whatever unwholesome state of mind—whether among evils and non-evils, or among wholesome and unwholesome states—that which was spoken, uttered, and declared by one who does not engage in non-evil through non-evil, and who has abandoned both evil and non-evil:
that evil-mindedness, that unwholesome state of mind, has been fully set forth and explained by me.
However, whereas that wholesome [kamma]— by way of giving and so forth, or by way of the ten bases of meritorious action such as giving—
proceeds with respect to the six types of objects, this resultant consciousness does not proceed in that manner. For it is true that this resultant [consciousness] proceeds,
by way of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, death, and registration, only toward those states comprised within the limited (paritta) phenomena included among sense-sphere phenomena.

It occurs with respect to the six objects. And although there is no distinction among the associated states, this result—compared to the states associated with the wholesome—is, despite the difference in the associated states, devoid of effort, like the reflection of a face upon the surface of a mirror or similar material.
This is the intended meaning: just as the reflection of a face on the surface of a mirror...
When the mouth moves, it moves; when it does not move, it does not move. There is no cause for the mouth other than the mouth itself, as if there were no cause for the condition of the mouth.
Likewise, there is no other cause for the result (vipāka) than the wholesome cause (kusala-kāraṇa);

the result is effortless (nirussāha). 32. These eight great results (mahā-vipāka) serve as the rebirth-linkings (paṭisandhi) for sense-sphere devas and humans who possess two or three root-causes (duhetuka-tihetuka).
33–4. Thereafter, during the course of existence, they proceed as the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) for as long as the lifespan lasts;

when there is a powerful object—that is, an exceedingly great or manifest object—they proceed as the registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa); and thereafter, at the time of death, they proceed as the death-consciousness (cuti).
Thus, in the manner described by me, they ripen in these four places, being born as resultants (vipāka).

35. Together with the wholesome states of their own respective planes (*sabhūmikuśala*), they are equal; excluding the great results (*mahāvipāka*), the doors of action (*karmadvāra*), and the causes of action (*karmakāraṇa*).
And action (*karman*)—excluding the basis for functional [states] of those of great merit—is equal and similar only to the wholesome states occurring on one’s own plane.
The so-called "door of action" refers to the door of action consisting of bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) and the door of action consisting of vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*).
The mind-door, which is designated as the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), thus constitutes the threefold door of action and the instrument of action.
Here, "action" (*kamma*) refers specifically to the eight types of wholesome sense-sphere volition (*cetanā*). 36.
The results are wholesome resultant states; and because they do not produce intimation, both intimation and non-intimation are termed "intimation and non-intimation."

In what should have been said, the term "viññatti" was stated by applying the grammatical rule of *sarūpa-ekasesa* (retaining only one of identical forms). Those which produce these [expressions] are "viññattijana";
that which does not produce viññatti is "aviññattijana. The state of being such is "aviññattijanattaṃ.

Therefore, because of this lack of production of viññatti—due to the non-production of the doors of action known as bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*) and verbal intimation (*vacīviññatti*)—and because of its non-operation by way of the door of action known as the mind-door (*manodvāra*).

Because they lack the nature of ripening (*vipāka*), because they lack the nature of kamma, because they do not proceed, and because they do not proceed by way of the bases for meritorious action (*puññakiriyavatthu*),
they are not equal to, but rather unlike, merits. (37–9) For,
due to their having limited objects (*parittārammaṇa*), those results of ripening have exclusively limited objects.

Because those resultant states have sense-sphere objects, compassion and appreciative joy—which have the seven social designations as their objects—do not arise at any time whatsoever in relation to them.
Likewise, the three abstinences do not arise in these resultant states. For what reason do they not arise?
It is because the Teacher has stated that the five training precepts are wholesome; that is the reason why they are called "wholesome."
Therefore, they are not born. Likewise, in this case, there are no four predominants (adhipati) here either; it is exactly so.
Why? Because they do not exist, as they do not arise after having previously established the classes of phenomena such as desire (chanda) and so forth.
Thus the Teacher should explain, pointing out the statement.
40. Furthermore, regarding the classification of the non-determined (*asaṅkhāra*) and the determined (*saṅkhāra*) among the results of merit:
the classification of the non-determined and the determined among the results of merit should be understood by way of their origin from merit and from the wholesome (*kusala*).

In this regard, according to the opinion of certain teachers, just as the reflection of a face moves when the mouth moves upon the surface of a mirror, the result of a wholesome non-determined state is itself non-determined.

The result of wholesome [kamma] accompanied by volitional formations is itself accompanied by volitional formations; thus it should be known by way of its arrival. Furthermore, it should be known by way of its conditions:

according to the opinion of some teachers, that which arises through powerful and manifest conditions such as kamma and so forth is "without volitional formations" (asaṅkhāra), while that which arises through weak [conditions] is "with volitional formations" (sasaṅkhāra); thus it is to be understood and known by way of its conditions.
41–2. Because they are the results of inferior and other types of merit, these inferior and other results are elucidated by the Conqueror who teaches merit;

thus, in this manner, these eight kinds of consciousness that proceed in the stated way arise exclusively with a physical basis in the sense-sphere world (kāmaloka), but they do not arise elsewhere, that is, in other planes.
The pentad of consciousness has fixed objects: for eye-consciousness, visible form alone is the object, not sound and so forth.
As for the remaining three [mental consciousnesses], when they take as their object what was previously apprehended by eye-consciousness, then visible form is their object;
when they take what was apprehended by ear-consciousness, then sound is their object; when they take what was apprehended by nose-, tongue-, or body-consciousness...

When the apprehended objects become the objective fields, then their objective fields are odors, tastes, and tangibles. When the two types of mind-consciousness element have those as their objective fields, then they have all six objective fields;

thus, it has an indefinite objective field. "Apagamapadaṭṭhāna" means that the departure of the functional mind-element with visible forms as its objective field is its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*), its immediate condition.
The meaning is that when she has performed the act of adverting and stands ready, the function of seeing is carried out by the eye-consciousness.

It manifests as such a state (tathābhāvapaccupaṭṭhāna) through the mode of being grasped by way of receiving (sampaṭicchana). Its function is investigation and so forth. When associated with joy, it has the function of investigating and having that as its object via the mind-consciousness element;
but when associated with equanimity, it has the functions of investigating, having that as its object, rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death. It manifests as such a state.
The mode [of consciousness] that is grasped by way of investigating and so forth. 43. There are sixteen results of sense-sphere merit—that is, of wholesome sense-sphere [kamma].
Thus, as for the statement that was spoken, the Teacher explained it with reference to the highest grade of three-rooted merit. This is the meaning here.

—By way of the predominance of zeal (*chandādhipateyya*) and so forth, superior wholesome consciousness with three roots (*tihetuka-kusala*), having given a rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) with three roots in the fortunate realms of sense-sphere existence (*kāmasugati*), produces sixteen resultant states during the course of existence (*pavatta*):
eight rootless wholesome resultants (*ahetuka-kusala-vipāka*) and eight great wholesome resultants (*mahākusala-vipāka*).
44. Having been analyzed by following the wholesome, what sublime resultant consciousness is associated with the wholesome? What is wholesome?
Having made it conformable and having made it equal to a sublime wholesome state of mind, it was apportioned and taught by the Blessed One. Why?
For what reason? Because there is no [state] that does not have a fruit equal to sense-sphere merit, just like sense-sphere wholesome [kamma];
for that reason, having made the result conformable to the wholesome, it was apportioned and taught by the Blessed One. "Like sense-sphere merit" means...

Just as, among the eight types of sense-sphere wholesome states (*kāmāvacara-kusala*), the superior triple-rooted wholesome state, having bestowed a triple-rooted rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) within a fortunate sense-sphere existence,
produces sixteen wholesome resultant states during the course of existence; and the inferior triple-rooted and the superior double-rooted states,

having bestowed a double-rooted rebirth-linking within a fortunate sense-sphere existence, produce those [resultants] during the course of existence that are devoid of the triple root— namely, those reckoned as rootless (*ahetuka*) and double-rooted (*duhetuka*).

It produces [eight] resultant states; however, having given a weak, two-rooted rebirth-linking in a happy sense-sphere existence, it produces eight rootless resultants during the course of existence. Thus, sense-sphere merit has results that are not identical to itself.

Just as the shadows of elephants and other such beings resemble those beings themselves, so too sublime resultant states are in every way and in all respects identical to their own corresponding wholesome states.

46–7. Just as sense-sphere merit (*kāmāvacara-puñña*) is not to be experienced in subsequent lives, this sublime wholesome state (*mahaggata-kusala*)—unlike sense-sphere merit—is not one that yields fruit in a future existence.
Rather, for a being who has not fallen away from jhāna and is destined for a new existence, the fruit arises immediately after the wholesome state itself;
it is for the purpose of making this known [that this distinction is stated].
The Blessed One has established this conformity with the wholesome—the following after the wholesome—of this sublime resultant [consciousness]. 48.

Herein, regarding this sublime resultant, the sequence of the path and the distinction between the inferior and other types [of consciousness], as well as the manner of entering the jhānas, should be understood by a wise person through the way in which the sublime wholesome jhāna is attained. 49.

Herein, in the case of the resultant, there is an absence of predominance by zeal and the rest; this alone is the specific distinction from the wholesome, while everything else is considered and taught by the Blessed One to be identical to the wholesome in all respects without distinction.
50. "Emptiness," "signless," and likewise "wishless"—emptiness is non-self, the signless is impermanent, and the wishless is suffering;
these three names apply to the path and to the fourfold fruit that follows immediately after the fourfold path.

51. These three names are not obtained in the subsequent stage (*parabhāga*)—that is, at times other than when one is entering the fruition attainment (*phalasamāpatti*) among the fruits that function after the path has occurred.

These three names are obtained only by way of the fruits through the three types of insight (*vipassanā*) characterized as non-self, impermanence, and suffering, which occur by way of insight into the fruits; thus they are obtained by means of the fruits.

52. As for the supramundane fruits (*lokuttara-phala*), they possess predominance (*adhipati*) indeed; they possess predominance exclusively. Apart from the supramundane fruits, there is no predominance in any other kind of result-of-action (*vipāka*).

53. The Path is called "the Path" by the Blessed One by virtue of its own nature as a path. The Fruit is called "the Path" by the Blessed One by depending upon the Path—that is, by making the Eightfold Path its support.
54. These are the seven unwholesome results-of-action. A "pasture" (*gocara*) is so called because cattle graze therein; because it is similar to that, the object (*ārammaṇa*) is called a "pasture."
The desirable, the undesirable, and that which is neither-desirable-nor-undesirable—these very things constitute the range; thus, it is the "range of the neither-desirable-nor-undesirable.
They proceed, they move, within that range of the neither-desirable-nor-undesirable.

Those eight types of rootless wholesome-resultant [consciousness], associated with the triad of pleasure and so forth, are accompanied by the feelings of pleasure, mental joy, and equanimity. [The others] are associated with pain and equanimity.
These seven rootless unwholesome-resultant [consciousnesses] are accompanied by feelings of pain and equanimity.
Thus, in thirty-six ways, the Sugata—who is honored for his teaching of the result—is distinguished. What is this "result" (pāka)? It is the *asura* liquor;
he teaches it, thus he is the "Teacher of the Result" (*pākasāsana*). Alternatively, he instructs the gods by means of his own fruit of merit, which is the "result" (*pāka*); who is he? Sakka.

Honored by that teaching on ripening (*pākasāsana*), he who was skilled and expert in the ripened and unripened results of wholesome kamma-resultants and functional states—thus, in the manner described by me here, spoke of the thirty-six types of ripening consciousness. "In the inferior" means in the minor ones.

They have the manifestation of being such [as they are], and their mode is the grasping of the six objects. It has a range like the range of omniscient knowledge; thus it is "having the range of omniscient knowledge."

56. Regarding those associated with joy (*somanassayutta*): there are eight wholesome and unwholesome states associated with joy, and five functional (*kriya*) states; thus, according to the manner described by me, there are thirteen types of smiling consciousness (*hāsacitta*). 57.

As for ordinary persons (*puthujjana*), among these [thirteen], ordinary persons smile by means of eight types of consciousness. Learners (*sekha*)—the noble ones (*ariya*)—smile by means of seven types of consciousness. Those beyond training (*asekha*), whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), smile by means of five types of consciousness.

Furthermore, wholesome states—both material and immaterial wholesome states—arise in trainees (*sekha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*). These material and immaterial functional states (*kiriyā*) arise through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanākāra-vasa*);
that is, for those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), they arise solely as a mode of cultivation, and their occurrence is by way of that power of cultivation.
Those material and immaterial wholesome states arise through the power of merit consisting of cultivation; that is, they occur by way of wholesome states pertaining to cultivation. Of these...
This is precisely the distinction between those wholesome states of form and formlessness and those [wholesome] states of form and formlessness belonging to the practitioner.

58–9. As for that attainment of form and formlessness which was produced during the time of being an ordinary person—that attainment of form and formlessness produced by the yogi while established in the state of an ordinary person during the period of being an ordinary person—that attainment of form and formlessness belongs to that yogi who is one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava).
As long as that bhikkhu, having become a bhikkhu, does not attain those fine-material and immaterial meditative attainments (rūpārūpa-samāpatti),
for that length of time, for that bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava), there exists only the wholesome (kusala), namely, the wholesome fine-material and immaterial states.
If that fine-material and immaterial attainment is attained— that is, entered— by one whose taints are exhausted, it is functional (kriyā), namely, functional fine-material and immaterial.

60. In the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), there are eleven types of functional consciousness (kiriyacitta); in the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), five; and in the immaterial sphere (arūpa), four. Thus, all functional consciousnesses together amount to twenty. 61. Why, then, does supramundane functional consciousness not exist?

It does not exist because the Path (magga) lasts for only a single moment of consciousness. This is the intended meaning here: one who has reached the state of the four paths is not yet called an "Arahant" (khīṇāsava); it is only immediately after the Path that he becomes so.

The fruit arises; the path, too, lasts for only a single moment of consciousness. If the mind were to last for many moments of consciousness, then even for one who possesses the fruit and has destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*), there would still be a path-consciousness.
The intention [of this argument] is that if this were so, it would follow that there could be supramundane functional consciousness (*lokuttara-kiriya-citta*).
62. That which teaches the distinction between action and non-action is "karaṇa"; "action" (*kriya*) refers, according to the terminology of the Vinaya, to what ought not to be done.
"Doing" (*karaṇa*) means performing; "not doing" (*akaraṇa*) means non-performance. In the terminology of the Vinaya, "non-performance" refers to the failure to do what ought to be done.

"Offense" (*āpatti*) is the act of falling into [transgression]. An offense through the performance of an action is an "offense by performance" (*kriyāpatti*); an offense through the non-performance of an action is an "offense by non-performance" (*akriyāpatti*).
Both the offense by performance and the offense by non-performance are "offenses by performance and non-performance" (*kriyāpattyākriyāpattīyo*), with the word *āpatti* being elided once.

Having composed [this work], it is said: "The classification of actions, non-actions, and offenses. The analysis of these is the "classification of actions, non-actions, and offenses. One who teaches is a "teacher" (*desaka*);
thus, he is the "teacher of the classification of actions, non-actions, and offenses. They say that when the suffixes *ṇvu* or *tu* follow, the genitive case is used in the sense of the object.
What is the Victor distinguished by? He is the teacher of the classification of actions, non-actions, and offenses regarding the beneficial and the harmful.
One who delights in both action and non-action delights in the performance of what is beneficial and in the non-performance of what is harmful. Regarding "action and non-action":
some maintain that "action" refers to the active consciousness (*kriyacitta*), while "non-action" refers to wholesome, unwholesome, and resultant consciousnesses (*vipākacitta*). That is not so.
Why? Because in the section on the wholesome, it says, "The wholesome was spoken by the Sage," and in the section on the unwholesome, it says, "The evil mind [is overcome] by the non-evil of evils."

It has been stated: having said in the section on resultants (vipāka), “The Sugata spoke of the resultant,” there is no need to repeat the statement in the section on functional (kiriya) consciousness, “He spoke of the resultants of the wholesome and unwholesome.
Therefore, it is called *kriyākriya* because its nature is both functional and non-functional;

the meaning is that its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is functional and non-functional. This alone should be understood as the essential point. That which is the functional-non-functional consciousness is of the nature of functional-non-functionality.
He spoke and taught that which is "action-and-non-action," having been uttered by me with its nature as action-and-non-action; it was correctly uttered and explained.
64. All eighty-nine: Having set aside the eight supramundane states, all eighty-nine types of consciousness-arisings were briefly and concisely pointed out by the Great Sage, the Tathāgata.
65. In the Abhidhamma Piṭaka: For those monks who desire proficiency, [it is found] in the state of being expert in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.
*Pāṭava* means proficiency; *pāṭavattha* means the object of proficiency. Those who possess this are called *pāṭavatthino*—those monks who desire proficiency.
By those monks, this *Abhidhammāvatāra* should be mastered, studied, and reflected upon again and again. 66.

Those people who, by means of this *Abhidhammāvatāra*, which resembles and is similar to that [ocean], cross over the Great Ocean of Abhidhamma—which is like a vast sea—they cross over both this world and the world beyond. *Iti* signifies completion.
Thus ends the commentary on the Exposition of Consciousness in the *Abhidhammāvatāra-ṭīkā*.
This is the first chapter.
2. The Second Chapter:
Explanation of the Description of Mental Factors (Cetasika-niddesa-vaṇṇanā) 67.

Regarding those mental factors which have been enumerated by me immediately after consciousness: as for those mental factors that I have listed immediately following consciousness, hereafter I shall now provide an analysis of those mental factors.
Furthermore, in these cases, during the time of cultivation by way of compassion (*karuṇā*) and gladness (*muditā*), the meaning is as follows:

either the preliminary stage of compassion, or the preliminary stage to compassion that has reached absorption (*appanā*); in that preliminary stage, or in the sense of "prior to compassion," a single sense-sphere consciousness (*kāmāvacara-citta*) arises.
A single compassion arises. Or, in the preliminary stage of gladness, or in the preliminary stage to gladness that has reached absorption, a single gladness arises.

By means of this sense-sphere consciousness, the yogi abstains from such states as wrong action (micchākammanta). The verbal root *ram* signifies play (*kīḷā*), while the prefix *vi-* has the meaning of abstaining (*viramaṇa*). 68.

By means of the first great wholesome consciousness, which is an initial meritorious state of mind, thirty-three [types of consciousness] are considered to be fixed (*niyata*). By means of an initial meritorious state of mind...

Thirty-three mental factors are considered by the Blessed One to be fixed; alternatively, when compassion (*karuṇā*) or gladness (*muditā*) are unfixed, there are thirty-four factors together with one [other] state. 69.

But why are loving-kindness (*mettā*) and equanimity (*upekkhā*) not included here among these very "included" (*yevāpanaka*) factors? This is a selection: for what reason were loving-kindness and equanimity not included—that is, not mentioned—by the Teacher, the King of Dhamma?

70. Because loving-kindness (*mettā*) is included by way of non-ill-will (*abyāpāda*), and equanimity (*upekkhā*) is included by way of mental neutrality (*tatramajjhattatā*), therefore both of these were not separately mentioned by the Blessed One.

71. Why [are they called] "accessory factors" (*yevāpanaka*)? All those accessory factors, named as such, are found in their specific forms within the Canon (*pāḷi*) by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun (*Ādiccabandhu*).
It is called a "kinsman" (*bandhu*) because one binds [others] to oneself through affection; the kinsman of the Sun is the "Kinsman of the Sun."
These were neither extracted nor taught by that Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun.

For what reason? Because some of the *yevāpanaka* (miscellaneous) items are indeterminate; because for that reason they do not belong to or follow the category of the *Duka-vagga* and other such groups;
and because some of those miscellaneous items are weak—therefore, they were not spoken by the Blessed One in the *Pāḷi*.
73. Zeal, resolve, sympathetic joy, and mental attention;
equanimity, compassion, and the three abstinences;
by these, all meritorious deeds are either certain or uncertain.
The "inclusionary" (yevāpanaka) factors were not mentioned by the Sage.

Resolution through desire, gladness, attention, equanimity, compassion, and the three abstinences—these seven among the wholesome meritorious states are fixed; four are unfixed. All these inclusionary factors were not mentioned by that Sage. (Verses 74–80).
But why, among these mental concomitants, was contact alone mentioned first? Here, it is a specification by genus.

Contact (*phassa*) alone was mentioned first; it was spoken [first]. For what reason? It is said that I have heard: because it is the first striking down of the mind upon the object, contact was mentioned first.

But having touched the object by means of contact, the practitioner experiences the object through feeling (*vedanā*), perceives it through perception (*saññā*), and intends it through volition (*cetanā*).
One should attend to the object. Among the co-nascent mental factors, contact alone is mentioned first here in this consciousness by the Great Sage.
For what reason? Because it is the most powerful condition; therefore, it is mentioned first.
All of this [is not the primary cause]; rather, for all consciousnesses, it is because of "the first striking down" and "being the most powerful condition"—all of this [is the reason].
This statement is groundless, causeless, and illogical. Why?

Because mental factors—which are born of mind and arise simultaneously with the mind—proceed by way of having a common arising and so forth; that is, they proceed by way of having a common arising, a common cessation, a common object, and a common basis.
Therefore, it is groundless and illogical [to say] "this one has arisen first" or "this one is later," for such a distinction does not exist among these phenomena.
There is no such statement as "this phenomenon arose first" or "this phenomenon arose later.

Nor is any reason perceived for its having a stronger causal status. Because it was uttered first according to the sequence of the teaching, this fact—that contact was uttered first—should be understood by the wise and discerning in the manner just described by me.
"Especially" means particularly; it is not to be understood otherwise. Nor is this sequence of before and after to be sought;

therefore, because this sequence of before and after is not to be sought or searched for by the wise, only the phenomena (*dhammā*) themselves are to be sought by the learned person who understands them through their etymological meaning, characteristics, and so forth.
Its function is the experiencing of a desirable aspect; its role is the experiencing of a desirable object, like a king experiencing the flavor of fine food.

It is manifested as mental relish and has mental tranquility as its proximate cause. Its function is to provide a sign for recognition; its role is to acknowledge [the object], like a carpenter making a mark.
The intention is that it is like a carpenter’s marking line: even after he has once recognized the wood, he stretches the line across the timber. "By way of the sign as it was grasped" means:
By way of the sign as it has occurred, the act of fixing the mind is its mode of apprehension (*gahyākāra*).
Its function is exertion (*āyūhana-rasa*), and its purpose is to accomplish the process of occurrence. Like great carpenters and others:

just as a master carpenter both hews the wood himself and causes others to hew the wood, so too this consciousness itself applies itself to the object and causes the associated mental states to apply themselves as well.
*Āhananaṃ* means striking; *pariyāhananaṃ* means striking all around. That which has this as its essence is "having the essence of striking and all-around striking.
It has the characteristic of rubbing against the object (*ārammaṇa*) and the characteristic of massaging the object.

It "delights" (*pinayati*), thus it is "rapture" (*pīti*); the meaning is that it delights the co-nascent states and the object. Its essence is the pervading of body and mind. The state of a joyful mind is "elation" (*odagya*); that which has this as its manifestation is "manifesting as elation."

They have faith; they have faith in the Three Objects. It has the manifestation of non-turbidity and the manifestation of clarity. Its proximate cause is the object to be believed, and its immediate condition is the Three Objects that are to be believed.
It is like one who knows the way through a forest, or like one who knows the path once having gone into the forest.
"Of the states inseparable from itself" means of the mental factors that are not dissociated. "Of those" means of those mental factors.

Of mental factors (*dhammā*). Although there is a provision for those mental concomitants (*cetasika*) characterized by protection and so forth, that life-force protects those mental factors to be protected at the very moment they arise—that is, at the very moment those mental factors to be protected are occurring.
"Like water" means that just as water protects lotuses and other flowers within it, so too [does life-force].

The intention is that even though the functions characterized by preservation and so forth exist, it preserves [the object] precisely at the moment those [functions] exist; that is, it preserves it at the very moment it is present.

Furthermore, it preserves the phenomena that have arisen from conditions, just as a nurse (dhāti) protects a child born of another woman—she is called a "nurse" because she holds another's child on her lap and so forth. It is through its connection with the phenomena that have themselves come into operation...

It proceeds; it proceeds together with the phenomena that have proceeded by its own power. Like a pilot—just as a pilot proceeds together with the people aboard a single ship, yet after the moment of dissolution does not cause that life to proceed further because of his own absence and the absence of the mental factors (cetasika) that were to be established—he does not establish the mental factors at the moment of dissolution.
Because it is itself breaking up, just as the wick-oil, when diminishing, does not produce a flame;
"manifesting as gentleness" means manifesting as softness, or manifesting as coolness.
And here, by "body," the other three aggregates—namely, the feeling aggregate, the perception aggregate, and the formations aggregate—are included.
"Crushing function" means having the task of crushing. Because it is the opposite of defilements such as restlessness—which consist in the lack of tranquility of body and mind—the word "etc.
should be understood to include worry. Thus ends the commentary on the Description of Mental Factors in the *Abhidhammāvatāra-ṭīkā*.
The Second Chapter. 3.
The Third Chapter:
Commentary on the Exposition of the Classification of Mental Factors (Cetasika).
89. All mental factors have been taught by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun.
All those mental factors taught by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun, amount to fifty-two by way of the commonality of their names—that is, by virtue of having identical names.
They amount to fifty-two, ending with the absence of moral dread (*anottappa*).

90–92. Regarding the fifty-four [types of consciousness] in the sense-sphere, fifteen in the fine-material sphere, and twelve in the immaterial sphere: fifty-four types of consciousness are taught as belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).
Fifteen types of consciousness are taught as belonging to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara).
Twelve types of consciousness belong to the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara). Forty are the outflow-free supramundane states of consciousness (lokuttara-citta).
In brief, that is, in summary, there are one hundred and twenty-one types of consciousness in total. Hereafter, regarding these consciousnesses mentioned by me,

I shall explain— that is, I shall teach— the arising of those phenomena such as contact and so forth, by extracting them one by one from among the states of consciousness and mental factors, for the sake of the monks' proficiency.

93. One-pointedness (*ekaggatā*), mental one-pointedness (*cittekaggatā*), attention (*manakkāro*), mental application (*manasikāro*), vitality (*jīvita*), and the pentad of contact (*phassapañcaka*)—these eight mental factors (*cetasika*) are inseparable; they are not dissociated from one another, arise together, arise simultaneously, perish together, and undergo decay together. 94.

Contact (*phassa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saññā*), volition (*cetanā*), the faculty of vitality (*jīvitindriya*), one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*), and attention (*manakkāro*)—these mental factors are universal; they are common to all consciousnesses, or rather, they are shared by all states of consciousness.

95. Initial application (*vitakka*) is declared to exist in fifty-five types of consciousness. As for its range, the Blessed One has declared that initial application occurs in fifty-five types of consciousness:
namely, within the sense-sphere consciousnesses excluding the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness, as well as in the eleven types of first-jhāna consciousness.

Sustained application (*vicāra*) [is likewise declared] in the sense-sphere consciousnesses excluding the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness, and in the eleven types of first-jhāna consciousness.
And in the eleven second jhāna consciousnesses—thus it arises in sixty-six types of consciousness. There is no doubt regarding this statement. 96.

In fifty-one types of consciousness, zest (pīti) arises; in seventy-three types of consciousness, happiness (sukha) arises. Zest arises in fifty-one types of consciousness, excluding those accompanied by joy, grief, equanimity, and body-consciousness, as well as the fourth jhāna.
Happiness arises in seventy-three types of consciousness, excluding those accompanied by grief, pain, and equanimity.
It arises. Equanimity arises in fifty-five types of consciousness, excluding those accompanied by joy, pleasure, and pain.
Pain arises in three types of unwholesome resultant consciousness accompanied by body-consciousness and aversion.
(97) It exists in sixty-two types of consciousness; however, the faculty of joy exists in those excluding [the types] accompanied by grief, pain, pleasure, and equanimity.
The faculty of pain arises in sixty-two types of consciousness. However, the faculty of pleasure arises in only one: the unwholesome-resultant body-consciousness.
Likewise, the faculty of joy arises in one; likewise, it exists in one wholesome-resultant body-consciousness. 98.

The Leader, the Conqueror, stated that the faculty of energy is present in one hundred and five types of consciousness, excluding the five-door adverting consciousness, the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness, the receiving consciousnesses, and the investigating consciousnesses.
Regarding the one hundred and five types of consciousness, he spoke of the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*).

Regarding the one hundred and four types of consciousness, he spoke of the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*); that is, with the exception of the two types of consciousness accompanied by doubt, the fivefold sense-consciousnesses, the receiving consciousnesses, the investigating consciousnesses, and the five-door adverting consciousness, he stated that the faculty of concentration exists in those one hundred and four types of consciousness.

99. A wise person should declare the arising of *chanda* (desire-to-act) in one hundred and one types of consciousness: excluding all single-rooted consciousnesses, all eighteen rootless consciousnesses, and the two double-rooted consciousnesses;

that is, in the remaining one hundred and one types of consciousness. 100. The Blessed One has proclaimed *adhimokkha* (resolution) in one hundred and ten types of consciousness: excluding the ten types of consciousness beginning with eye-consciousness, and also excluding the consciousness associated with doubt; that is, in the remaining one hundred and ten types of consciousness.
101–2. Faith, mindfulness, moral shame, moral dread, non-greed, non-hatred, and equanimity—these nineteen states, being fixed, arise in ninety-one types of consciousness.
These nineteen states do not arise, nor will they arise, in the eighteen rootless [resultant] states, the unwholesome states, and the twelve unwholesome [functional] states.

103. Wisdom arises in seventy-nine types of consciousness. Wisdom arises in all instances, excluding the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses, the eighteen rootless great wholesome consciousnesses, the great resultant consciousnesses dissociated from knowledge, and the great functional consciousnesses dissociated from knowledge;
thus it arises in seventy-nine types of consciousness. Compassion and gladness may arise in twenty-eight types of consciousness:
in the eight great wholesome consciousnesses, the eight great functional consciousnesses, and the twelve fine-material-sphere consciousnesses, excluding the fifth jhāna.
...and thus they may exist in twenty-eight types of consciousness. 104.

In the forty kinds of consciousness—namely, all those in the sense-sphere wholesome states (*kāmāvacara-puñña*), all those that are supramundane (*lokuttara*), and all those in the great unwholesome states of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara-mahāakusala*)—there is the triad of abstinences (*viratittaya*). 105.

Faith, mindfulness, moral shame (*hiri*), moral dread (*ottappa*), the triad beginning with non-greed (*alobha*), the six pairs, equanimity (*majjhatta*), compassion (*karuṇā*), and gladness (*muditā*).

106. Thus, including the three abstinences, all those twenty-five factors associated with the great wholesome consciousness and the indeterminate consciousness have been clearly explained by the skillful one who has conquered the battlefield among all phenomena through his wholesomeness.

107. Shamelessness (*ahirika*), lack of moral dread (*anottappa*), delusion (*moha*), and restlessness (*uddhacca*)—these four factors, being fixed, arise only in the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses (*dvādasa-akusalacitta*).
108–9. Greed (*lobha*), hatred (*dosa*), and delusion (*moha*); conceit (*māna*), views (*diṭṭhi*), doubt (*saṃsaya*), perplexity (*vicikicchā*), torpor (*middha*), and restlessness (*uddhacca*).

Regret, sloth, stinginess, shamelessness, lack of moral dread, envy, and grief—these unwholesome states associated with unwholesome consciousness were spoken of by the Great Seer, who had conquered the battlefield and was free from stain.
(110) Greed was pointed out and shown by the Blessed One in the eight types of consciousness rooted in greed. View [is present] in four...

[These] are stated in relation to the consciousnesses associated with views (*diṭṭhi*). Conceit (*māna*) is stated in relation to the four [types of] consciousness dissociated from views, by way of grasping, disparaging, and breaking apart.
Hatred (*dosa*) was taught by the Lord of Sages (*muninda*) as occurring only in the two types of consciousness associated with aversion (*paṭigha*).
111. Envy (*issā*), avarice (*macchariya*), and remorse (*kukkucca*) arise in the two types of consciousness rooted in hatred; they do not arise together with one another.
The meaning is that each one arises individually. Doubt (*vicikicchā*), however, arises in a single [unwholesome] consciousness accompanied by doubt.
Sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*) arise in the five prompted unwholesome consciousnesses. 112–3.
Contact, feeling, perception, volition, life-faculty, mind, applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, and energy.
Concentration, zeal, resolve, and attention—these fourteen factors are both wholesome and wholesome mental concomitants;
they are also unwholesome and unwholesome mental concomitants, and indeterminate and indeterminate mental concomitants.
In twenty-nine types of consciousness, the jhāna is considered five-factored, [occurring] in the four unwholesome states accompanied by joy.
In twenty-nine types of consciousness— namely, the twelve great wholesome, great resultant, and great functional consciousnesses accompanied by joy (*somanassa-sahagata*),
the consciousnesses of pleasant investigation and the smile-producing consciousness, the three fine-material first-jhāna consciousnesses,

and the eight supramundane first-jhāna consciousnesses— the Blessed One considered the fivefold jhāna, which possesses five factors and consists of five constituents. There are four [types] accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*).
There are thirty-seven types of consciousness: two rooted in greed, two rooted in hatred, two rooted in delusion; the triad of mind-elements accompanied by equanimity;
the three rootless mind-consciousness elements accompanied by equanimity; twelve great wholesome, great resultant, and great functional consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity;
three fine-material second jhāna consciousnesses; and eight supramundane second jhāna consciousnesses.
One should describe them as "endowed with the four jhāna factors" or "endowed with the constituent parts of the four jhānas. 115.
Elevenfold consciousness is declared to be three-factored: the three fine-material-sphere third-jhāna consciousnesses and the eight supramundane third-jhāna consciousnesses;
thus, elevenfold consciousness is three-factored, being endowed with a three-constituent jhāna.
The thirty-four types of consciousness— consisting of the fourth and fifth jhāna consciousnesses of the six form-sphere (rūpāvacara) levels,

the twelve formless-sphere (arūpāvacara) consciousnesses, and the sixteen supramundane (lokuttara) fourth and fifth jhāna consciousnesses— are declared by the Victor to be associated with two factors (duvaṅgika), that is, endowed with a jhāna consisting of two constituents.
116. "In those states that are by nature without applied thought (*avitakka*), the Victor would not extract the factors of jhāna. This means:

in those two sets of fivefold sense-consciousnesses which are by nature, by their very essence, without applied thought—that is, devoid of *vitakka*—the Victor would not extract the factors of jhāna, the components of jhāna.

This is the intended meaning here: elsewhere, applied thought is said to be abandoned by the jhāna-consciousness; however, in these [sense-consciousnesses], it is not abandoned by the jhāna-consciousness, but is [absent] by their very nature.

The Victor would not extract nor teach the path-factors (magganga) as constituent parts of the path within the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousnesses, nor in any of the rootless consciousnesses (sabbāhetuka-citta).

117. The Buddha, the Victor, [does not teach them] in sixteen types of consciousness: namely, in the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness, in the threefold mind-element (manodhātu), and in the three types of investigating consciousness (santīraṇa).
One should speak of three faculties. However, in one case there are four;
in another case, in the consciousness accompanied by doubt, there are four faculties.

In thirteen types of consciousness—the eleven unwholesome consciousnesses excluding the consciousness associated with doubt, as well as the consciousness that arouses laughter and the investigating consciousness—the wise Blessed One would extract five faculties.

118. Regarding the twelve types of consciousness—namely, those classified as great unwholesome, great resultant, and great functional states dissociated from knowledge—the Victor, the Buddha, declared that there are seven faculties.
In the eleven [remaining] types of consciousness, there are eight.
And regarding the twelve types of consciousness classified as great wholesome, great resultant, and great functional states associated with knowledge, the Victor [declared the same].
In fifteen material phenomena and twelve immaterial phenomena—thus, in thirty-nine states—one finds exactly eight faculties.
(119) In the forty supramundane consciousnesses, the Leader spoke of, that is, taught, the "ninefold faculty-group.
Thus, the application of faculties should be understood by the discerning one in this manner, according to the method described by me regarding the faculties in consciousness.
One is called *vibhāvī* because it has the nature (*sīla*) of developing and manifesting wisdom (*paññā*) through specific discernment (*vibhāva*); thus it should be understood by that term. 120.
Regarding the "factors not on the path" (*amagganga*): among these [consciousnesses], there are eighteen rootless ones.

Because the path does not exist within these consciousnesses, they are called "factors not on the path. The factors of absorption (*jhānanga*) are not found in these two sets of fivefold consciousnesses.
The factors of jhāna are also not found in the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness.
(121) One type of consciousness—the consciousness accompanied by doubt—is a bad path factor, a constituent of a bad path;
and so too are the four types of unwholesome consciousness dissociated from views, the two types associated with aversion, and the type associated with restlessness.
In seven types of consciousness, the three path-factors are constituent parts of the path. In forty types of consciousness— namely,

in the twelve types consisting of the four unwholesome states associated with wrong view that are dissociated from knowledge, and the twelve types consisting of the great unwholesome, great resultant, and great functional states of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) comprising the second, third, fourth, and fifth jhānas— that path is fourfold.
In the forty consciousnesses—namely, those twelve of the fine-material sphere and those twelve of the immaterial sphere—the path consists of four factors;
it is a path with four constituents.
In fifteen consciousnesses—consisting of the great wholesome, great resultant, and great functional types associated with knowledge—the path is considered to be five-factored.

In fifteen types of consciousness—namely, in the twelve [types of consciousness associated with the first jhāna] and in the three types of consciousness of the first jhāna of the form realm—the Blessed One considers the Path to consist of five factors (pañcaṅgika), having five constituents.

Furthermore, in thirty-two types of consciousness, the Path is sevenfold; that is, in the thirty-two types of consciousness comprised within the second, third, fourth, and fifth supramundane jhānas, the Path consists of seven factors (sattāṅgika), having seven constituents.
123. Regarding the path: in the eight types of consciousness, by way of the paths and fruits, the path within the eight supramundane consciousnesses consists of eight factors;
thus it is complete. The word *iti* (thus) is used for the purpose of concluding. *Tu* is a particle used for filling out the meter.
Thus, in this manner as described by me, the wise one (*dhīra*) should extract—the meaning being that he should teach—the path-factors, the components of the path, in all states of consciousness.
124. Two powers in two types of consciousness: there are two powers in the two types of consciousness known as the arising of laughter and the supporting of the body.
A wise person should illuminate three in one: he should explain that in the consciousness associated with doubt, there are three powers.
In the remaining eleven unwholesome states, excluding that associated with doubt, there are four powers. There are six in twelve.

The wise one should point out and declare that in the twelve types of consciousness known as the great unwholesome, the great resultant, and the great functional— each dissociated from knowledge— there are six powers.
(125) In the seventy-nine [types of consciousness],
there are seven [powers] in the twelve types of consciousness known as the great wholesome, the great resultant, and the great functional— each associated with knowledge.

In twenty-seven sense-sphere consciousnesses, twenty-seven sublime consciousnesses, and forty supramundane consciousnesses—thus in seventy-nine types of consciousness—there are seven powers. However, only sixteen types of consciousness are powerless, being devoid of power;
these are the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness, the three mind-elements, and the three investigating consciousnesses.
Thus, in the manner described by me, the wise one should understand— that is, discern— the mind as being either "with power," accompanied by strength,
or even "weak," devoid of strength. For whichever factors of jhāna, path-factors, powers, and faculties arise in whichever minds, they are found in those very minds.
The factors of jhāna, the factors of the path, the powers, and the faculties arise;
having extracted them in brief and having extracted them without confusion, all those factors of jhāna, path-factors, powers,
and faculties have been stated— that is, spoken— in summary and in concise form by me, the teacher Buddhadatta.
Thus ends the commentary on the Exposition of the Classification of Mental Factors in the *Abhidhammāvatāra-ṭīkā*.
This is the third chapter.
4. The Fourth Chapter:
Commentary on the Exposition of the Singlefold, etc.
Henceforth I shall explain the method beginning with the singlefold.
"For the increase of the wisdom of the Abhidhamma bhikkhus.
From this point forward, beyond this section, I shall explain and teach the method beginning with the "singlefold" for the purpose of increasing the wisdom of the Abhidhamma bhikkhus.

128. All consciousness is singlefold because its intrinsic nature is that of cognizing; all consciousness is singlefold because its intrinsic nature is that of cognizing. Furthermore, consciousness may be twofold according to being rootless or having roots; this consciousness may be twofold in this way.

129. Indeed, the results of merit and demerit; and in the sense-sphere (kāma), the ten and five [resultants]—namely, the ten and five resultants of wholesome and unwholesome [kamma], and the three functional [states] in the sense-sphere—all these eighteen types of consciousness-arising are rootless (ahetuka).

130. Apart from these rootless consciousness-arisings, the remaining seventy-one types of consciousness-arising are with roots (sahetuka). Thus they were designated as "with roots" by the Great Sage (Mahesi)—the Tathāgata, who is such-like, whose nature is unerring, the proponent of causes, and the proponent of conditions.

131. By way of having a basis (*savatthuka*) and being without a basis (*avatthuka*), and likewise by way of both, as well as by way of having a basis and being without a basis, the mind is threefold in the manner already described.

132–4. All results of sensual desire (*kāmavipāka*), the fifteen types of consciousness-arising in the fine-material realm (*rūpa*), the first path, the initial path, the smile-producing consciousness, the functional mind-element (*manodhātu-kiriya*), and the two types of grief—these forty-three types of consciousness arise without a physical basis (*vatthu*).
Excluding those that arise without a physical basis (*vatthu*), all consciousnesses are necessarily "with-basis" (*savatthuka*).
