Furthermore, the resultant consciousnesses of the formless realm (*arūpāvacara*) are exclusively "without-basis" (*avatthuka*). Apart from these types of consciousness mentioned by me, the remaining forty-two types of consciousness may be of both kinds—either with-basis or without-basis. 135.
Consciousness may also be threefold according to the manner described by me: consciousness having a single object, consciousness having five objects, and consciousness having six objects.

136–8. There are two types of consciousness, five [sense-sphere] consciousnesses, and eight supramundane consciousnesses; excluding the mind-consciousness associated with direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), all are sublime (*mahaggata*).
Thus, forty-three types of consciousness-arising should be understood by the wise as having each a single object.

Among those, the Blessed One has declared that the triad of mind-elements (*manodhātu*) within the [eighteen] elements have five objects. The remaining forty-three [types of consciousness] are those mentioned by me.
The Teacher has declared that consciousnesses have six objects; likewise, consciousness is threefold according to its moral quality as wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the indeterminate (abyākata) should be understood.

Consciousness without root-cause (ahetuka), consciousness with one root-cause, consciousness with two root-causes, and consciousness with three root-causes—in this manner, consciousness should be known by the discerning person as fourfold.
140-2. The eighteen types of consciousness arising without roots (ahetuka) have already been indicated by me below.

The consciousness associated with doubt and restlessness is said by the Blessed One to have only one root. Thus, in the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), there are twelvefold arisings of consciousness—comprising the wholesome (kusala) by way of merit (puñña), result (vipāka), and functional (kiriya), as well as the unwholesome (akusala)—and tenfold [arisings of unwholesome consciousness].

Twenty-two types of consciousness arise with two roots. In the sense sphere—that is, in the sense-sphere realm—there are twelve types of consciousness arising as merit, ripening, and functional, according to their nature as merit, ripening, and the functional.
All sublime consciousness, measureless consciousness, and supramundane consciousness possess three roots.
143–50. Regarding the phrase "by way of producing or not producing matter, postures, and intimation," this refers to the capacity for producing matter, postures, and intimation.
All consciousness is fourfold by way of such modes as: producing the postures, producing material form, and producing the three functions, and so forth.

In that regard, within that consciousness, the twelve unwholesome states, the wholesome states of the sense-sphere, likewise the ten functional states of the sense-sphere, and the two types of direct-knowledge consciousness—these thirty-two types of consciousness originate material phenomena.

They assume postures and generate intimation. Wholesome states of exalted mind and functional states of exalted mind, as well as the eight types of taintless consciousness, give rise to twenty-six types of mental materiality and assume postures.
"They do not cause contact and do not generate intimation" is the meaning. These arisings of consciousness are fixed in their function of accomplishing what is to be done.

Excluding the ten consciousnesses, in the two planes [of existence], there are eighteen results—consisting of the two resultant mind-elements (*manodhātu*), the three investigating consciousnesses (*santīraṇa*), the great results, and the material-resultants—and the functional mind-element (*manodhātu-kiriya*). These nineteen types of consciousness produce material phenomena; the other two do not.
Furthermore, because the ten consciousnesses were mentioned first in the phrase "the ten consciousnesses," the term "again" (*puna*) refers to the two fivefold sense-consciousnesses.

Thus it was said. Among the formless (arūpī) resultant states, as well as the rebirth-linking consciousness of all beings and the death-consciousness of an Arahant—these sixteen types of mind do not perform the three functions.

(151) The Buddha, whose stainless eyes are fivefold, has declared and taught that the mind is fivefold, being divided into five types according to its single, double, triple, quadruple, and quintuple functions, categorized by the distinctions of having one, two, three, four, or five functions.
All wholesome and unwholesome states of consciousness,
the great functional states, the exalted functional states, and the four resultant types of mind—

these fifty-five states of consciousness in their entirety have been determined and taught by the Teacher in a single place and for a single purpose, through the function of impulsion alone at the stage of impulsion, by the Teacher who is free from the conceptual proliferation of craving, conceit, and views.
154. Furthermore, two sets of fivefold consciousnesses—arising at seeing, hearing, as well as smelling, tasting, and touching—were designated by the Teacher in their respective order.

155. The triad of mind-elements (*manodhātu*) occurs in adverting and receiving; these sixty-eight types of consciousness have reached, that is, attained, the state of having a single basis and a single function.
156–8. A pair of consciousnesses is declared by the Blessed One to have a double basis: the consciousness associated with joy (*somanassa*) in the five doors.
Investigation may occur; it occurs when there is a strong object or an excessively large object at the six doors, and likewise for determining.
Determining occurs at the five doors; however, at the mind door, there is adverting to all objects.
These two types of consciousness are called "two-staged."
159. By way of the station of rebirth-linking and by way of the function of rebirth-linking; by way of the station of the life-continuum and by way of the function of the life-continuum;
and by way of the station of death and by way of the function of death—these nine sublime resultants are considered by the Sage to have three stations and three functions.
160–3. Eight sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses are fourfold-consciousness states by way of rebirth-linking and the life-continuum, and by way of registration and the state of death;
thus the Wise One should point this out. At the five doors, there are two types accompanied by the indeterminate [resultants] of wholesome, unwholesome, and resultant [kamma].
There may be investigating [consciousness], and when there is a strong object even among the six doors, there may be registration.

Furthermore, by way of being the station for rebirth-linking and the life-continuum, and by way of being the station for death, these two types of consciousness are called "five-station consciousness" by the Sage.

164. Two types of consciousness have five functions; eight have four functions; nine have three functions; two types of consciousness-arising have two functions; and by means of these consciousness-arisings, the remainder has one function each.
The life-continuum, adverting, seeing,
receiving, investigating, determining, and the impulsion becomes the seventh.
(166) That consciousness is sixfold, being the sixfold consciousnesses of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
By way of division, it is sixfold; by way of the seven elements—the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind-element, and mind-consciousness-element—consciousness is sevenfold.

(167) There is a set of six with each object; and by way of the fivefold division of objects and the sixfold division of objects, consciousness is eightfold by way of the six types of consciousness with their respective objects.

168. In that regard, within that consciousness, two types of fivefold sense-consciousness have each a single object; two types of consciousness-arisings have visible form as their object; and two by two types of consciousness-arisings have sound and the other sense-objects as their respective objects. 169.
All sublime consciousness, excluding the five direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), and all supramundane consciousness—this consciousness would have a single object.
170. This group of six should be understood by the discerning one as having a single object; the triad of mind-elements (*manodhātu*) is said to have five objects.

171. The forty sense-sphere consciousnesses (*kāmāvacara-cittāni*) and likewise each of the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) have six objects; thus, the wise should understand that these are called "six-object" consciousnesses. 172.

Within the seven elements of consciousness (*viññāṇadhātu*), the final one—the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*)—is divided into three types according to the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; thus, it becomes ninefold. 173.

As for the classification of the mind-consciousness element, by way of the wholesome and unwholesome, and further by way of the distinction between resultant (*vipāka*) and functional (*kiriyā*), it is seventy-sixfold.

174. By dividing the mind-element (*manodhātu*) into two—namely, resultant and functional—the mental consciousness becomes tenfold when combined with the nine types of consciousness mentioned previously.

175. Regarding the final pair of elements—the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*)—if one divides the mind-element into three according to wholesome-resultant, unwholesome-resultant, and functional, and divides the mind-consciousness-element into three according to wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate, [then, in addition to] eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness...
"The mind becomes elevenfold"— thus should the wise person explain this statement.
(176) Having analyzed the mind-consciousness element into four types according to the wholesome, unwholesome, wholesome-resultant, and functional-resultant categories,
that mind [is further classified] together with the visual, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses, along with the three modes of the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
And the wise one should speak of it as twelvefold as well.
(177–9) Consciousness becomes fourteenfold through the division of fourteen bases:
by way of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, death, adverting, and the five functions of seeing and so forth.
And by way of the receiving consciousness, by way of the investigating consciousness, by way of the determining and impulsion consciousnesses,
and likewise by way of the registration consciousness— in this manner, according to the distinction of states and the distinction of functions,
consciousness is fourteenfold; thus a wise person should explain, or would explain, this statement.

180. By way of the diversity of planes and persons—that is, by way of the diversity of planes and the diversity of persons—the wise one should analyze and clarify this statement: "This consciousness becomes manifold according to its occurrence.

181. Here, in this Dispensation, whatever bhikkhu is intelligent and skillful in this method beginning with the "singlefold" and so forth, for that bhikkhu the meanings occurring in the Abhidhamma become as if they have come into his hand, entered his hand, like *āmalaka* fruits or pure gems.
Thus ends the commentary on the Exposition of the Singlefold, etc., in the Abhidhammāvatāra-ṭīkā.
The Fourth Chapter.
5. The Fifth Chapter:
An Exposition on the Arising of Minds in the Various Stages and Persons.
Hereafter, I shall explain the method that increases one's intelligence.
I shall hereafter explain and teach the method that increases wisdom and the method that enhances the intellect; namely,
the arising of consciousness upon the planes according to the types of persons (*puggala*), and the arising of consciousness upon the planes according to the types of persons.
I shall now explain the arising of consciousness within the planes according to these categories.

There are gods, humans, and the three planes of misery; thus, by way of the destinies of gods, humans, animals, ghosts, and hell-beings, five destinies have been pointed out and shown by the Teacher, the Blessed One.
Furthermore, there are three modes of existence (*bhava*) by way of the sensual, fine-material, and immaterial modes of existence.
Three [categories] were pointed out and shown by the Teacher.

184–5. Regarding the stages (*bhūmi*): there are exactly thirty stages therein; in those [stages], there are exactly thirty persons (*puggala*). Among those three existences (*bhava*), there are exactly thirty stages;
among those stages, there are exactly thirty persons who have arisen. Those who have arisen in these stages—
Furthermore, all individuals (puggala) are nineteenfold by way of rebirth-linking consciousnesses (paṭisandhi-citta).
This so-called rebirth-linking is declared by the Teacher to be twofold and of two kinds:

first, rebirth-linking without consciousness (acittaka-paṭisandhi), and second, rebirth-linking with consciousness (sacittaka-paṭisandhi). Thus, rebirth-linking is twofold, [the former] belonging to the non-percipient beings (asaññi) and the Brahmās.

The mindless rebirth-linking is material rebirth-linking. The remaining types of rebirth-linking, other than material rebirth-linking, are to be known by the wise as "mindful rebirth-linking" (sacittakapaṭisandhi). That mindful rebirth-linking, moreover, is of nineteen kinds.
By way of rebirth-linking—and specifically by way of mindful rebirth-linking alone—there are twenty persons. Herein...

In this section on consciousness, because it is a section on consciousness, rebirth-linking without consciousness (*acittaka-patisandhi*)—that is, material rebirth-linking (*rūpa-patisandhi*)—has neither been extracted nor mentioned by me.

(188) "With no cause and with two causes": there would be three types of persons; that is, persons would be of three kinds or three modes: those with no cause, those with two causes, and those with three causes.
However, as for noble persons (*ariya-puggala*), there are eight; thus, in the manner stated by me in this way.
All eleven types of persons have been proclaimed and described by the Blessed One.

Now, as I take up the arising of consciousness within these various levels—specifically the thirty levels according to the classification of all these persons—understand my words; you should know and listen.
190. How many types of consciousness arise in the three planes? Tell me, speak of those consciousnesses for me: in all planes there are exactly fourteen types of consciousness.

They are as follows: the determining consciousness, the meritorious consciousness of the sense sphere, those dissociated from views, and that accompanied by restlessness—these are the fourteen found everywhere.

191. "The twenty consciousnesses always exist only in the sense-sphere existence. This means that the twenty consciousnesses would always, at all times, exist only in the sense-sphere existence (*kāma-bhava*).

They are as follows: the eight great resultant [consciousnesses] in the sense-sphere, the two types of grief, and likewise the threefold nose-door and other [odor-]consciousnesses, which are results born of demerit.

"The triad of nose-consciousness and so forth" refers to the triad of wholesome-resultant [consciousness] beginning with the nose. The seven rootless resultants born of demerit arise from unwholesome [kamma].
Five [types of consciousness] exist only in the fine-material realm; these five types of consciousness occur only in the fine-material realm.
Four [types of consciousness] exist only in the immaterial realms; these four types of consciousness occur only in the immaterial realms. For example:
In the fine-material realm, there are results of fine-material kamma and results of immaterial kamma;
in the immaterial realms, there are nine sublime results. These results arise only in the fine-material and immaterial realms.
(192) There are eighteen types of consciousness only in the sense-sphere and fine-material existences.
It is as follows:
there are five material phenomena that are merit itself, the receiving consciousness born of merit,
the pair consisting of eye and ear, and the two types of investigating consciousness which are the fruition of merit.
The resultants of merit, the smile-producing [consciousness],
and the functional mind-element— these eighteen, along with the five material functionals,
always exist only within the sense-sphere and fine-material realms, and only in association with the first path.
There are forty-two types of consciousness even in the three realms of existence; there are forty-two types of consciousness. They are as follows:
The ten unwholesome [consciousnesses], excluding the two types with aversion;
the eight great wholesome [consciousnesses], and the functional [consciousnesses] of determining.

There are forty-two types of consciousness in the three realms of existence: the four formless wholesome states, the four formless functional states, and the seven supramundane states— excluding the lowest path.

193. However, setting aside all [of these], and excluding the four planes of the sense-sphere and the four planes of the woeful states—having excluded those from the woeful states—the remaining individuals in the twenty-six planes possess exactly thirteen consciousnesses.

As it is said: "The fourth form-sphere consciousness, the fruits beginning with that of the Non-Returner, and the Great Functional consciousness arise; these thirteen are excluded from the woeful states."
By the word "etc. in the phrase "the fruit of non-returning, etc.," the fruits of arahantship are included. 194.
Furthermore, in the remaining twenty-six planes—excluding the four formless planes (ārūpabhūmi)—another six types of consciousness arise. They are as follows:
the functional mind-element (manodhātu-kiriya), the receiving consciousness born of merit (puññaja-sampaṭicchana), and... [the rest of the verse continues].

The pair of eye and ear [resultants], the two merit-resultants, and the two investigating [consciousnesses]—these five types of consciousness arise in the same way when the higher planes are excluded.
(195) In the case of the gods of the Pure Abodes, excluding the five planes, in the twenty-five planes excluding those five, these five types of consciousness arise. They are as follows:
Associated with wrong view, as well as that conjoined with doubt—
these five arise everywhere except in the Pure Abodes.
There are two others that exist in the twenty-five planes.
Excluding the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the four planes of access, there are two other types of consciousness among the twenty-five planes. That is to say:
excluding the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the four planes of access.
In the remaining [planes], the third immaterial javana arises as a pair.

(197) Two types of consciousness arise in the twenty-four planes, excluding the four planes of misery and the two immaterial planes of nothingness and neither-perception-nor-non-perception. In those remaining twenty-four planes, both types of consciousness arise. That is to say:
excluding the fourth and third immaterial [attainments] and the planes of misery...
In the remaining [planes], two types of second-formless javana arise.
(198) Excluding the four planes of misery and excluding the three higher formless planes, in the remaining twenty-three planes there are only these two types of consciousness.
Namely: Excluding the planes of misery and the three formless planes...
In the remaining [planes], the first immaterial [consciousness] and two types of impulsion arise.
(199) Excluding the eight planes—the four immaterial planes and the four woeful planes—there are twenty-two planes in which eleven kinds of consciousness occur. They are as follows:
all resultant [consciousness], excluding the smile-producing mind, and all [types of] materiality.
Only eleven arise, excluding the states of woe and the formless realm.
(200) Excluding the Pure Abodes and the states of woe—setting aside these nine planes—the four mental states always occur in the remaining twenty-one planes. They are as follows:
the fruit of stream-entry and also the fruit of once-returning;
The path of once-returning, excluding those purified from the states of misery, and the path of non-returning—these indeed exist in twenty-one planes.

(201) One consciousness arises in seventeen planes alone: one consciousness arises in the remaining seventeen planes, excluding the Pure Abodes, the states of misery, and the formless planes. For example:
Excluding the Pure Abodes and the woeful states, as well as the formless planes,
there is only one initial path among the seventeen planes.
However, they arise in twelve [planes] within the eleven planes.
But setting aside all those [supramundane] planes, the remaining nineteen planes are "lofty" (*mahaggata*).
Excluding those nineteen planes, in the remaining eleven planes, twelve types of consciousness arise. They are as follows:
the two types of grief-consciousness, the seven unwholesome-resultant, and the wholesome-born.
Excluding the three beginning with the nose-consciousness, all the remaining [consciousnesses] are sublime (mahaggata).
In the seven sense-sphere planes—namely, by way of the gods of the sense sphere and by way of human beings—eight types of consciousness arise at all times. This is as follows:
"In the sense sphere, for gods and humans, the great resultants (mahāpāka) arise."
Always, having abandoned these twenty-three planes among the seven, [the remaining] exist.
(204) The single resultant consciousness of the fifth jhāna arises in six planes. The resultant of the fifth jhāna arises in the six planes beginning with the Vehapphala realm.
However, the four types of fine-material-sphere resultant consciousness arise in three planes each. This is the intended meaning here.
One first ripening of form arises in the three planes of the Brahma-parisajja, Brahma-purohita, and Mahābrahmā;
one second ripening of form, and one third ripening of form, arise in the three planes of the Parittābha, Appamāṇābha, and Ābhassara;
and one fourth ripening of form arises in the three planes of the Parittasubha, Appamāṇasubha, and Subhakiṇha.
205. Furthermore, there are four types of consciousness in each of the [lower] planes;
by way of the immaterial-sphere results, there are four types of consciousness in each respective plane.
Thus, in this manner described by me, the wise person should explain the arising of consciousness across all planes.
206–7. In the sense-sphere, there are twenty wholesome and unwholesome [consciousnesses].

Their results are the fifteen rootless (ahetuka) resultants and the two types of adverting consciousness; thus, in this manner described by me, thirty-seven mental states arise even in the four woeful states, such as hell. As for the remaining fifty-two consciousnesses, they never [arise there].
At no time do they arise. As it is said: "In the form realm, fifteen [factors] arise;
in the formless realm, twelve are reckoned;
in the supramundane, only eight; those with roots have the result of sense-sphere [kamma]."
The eight great functional consciousnesses (*mahākriyā*), the mind arising from laughter (*hasituppāda*), and the fifty-two [other types of] consciousness do not arise in the woeful states.

(208) In the sensual realm (*kāmāvacara*) of gods and humans, the nine sublime resultant consciousnesses (*mahaggata-pāka*) never arise; eighty mental consciousnesses (*mānasa*) always arise there. They are as follows:
There are twelve unwholesome [consciousnesses], twenty-one wholesome,
and twenty-seven resultants, excluding those of the sublime sphere.
Among gods and humans in the sense-sphere, there are twenty functional consciousnesses.
There are eighty consciousnesses to be understood by one who discerns them:
In the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), there are eight great resultant [consciousnesses], two accompanied by mental grief, and likewise the triad of nose-consciousness and so forth;

there are seven resultants born of demerit, and no resultants of the wholesome. Furthermore, there are no form-sphere (rūpāvacara) resultants and no formless-sphere (arūpa) resultants on the plane of the form-sphere.
And the four [resultants] do not exist on the fine-material-sphere plane (*rūpāvacarabhūmi*). This is the intended meaning here:

on the fine-material-sphere plane, the eight great resultants do not exist because they belong to the two types of resultant consciousness of beings in the sense-sphere happy realms; the two types of mental grief (*domanassa*) are also absent because they have been suppressed by meditative absorption (*jhāna*);
and the threefold nose-door, tongue-door, and body-door wholesome-resultants are absent because of the lack of the sensitive matter of the nose, tongue, and body.
There are none; because there is an absence of undesirable objects, there are no seven unwholesome-resultant [consciousnesses], nor are there any formless-resultants. Why?

Because the formless [realms] consist of resultant consciousnesses. Together with these [previously mentioned] consciousnesses, along with these twenty-four consciousnesses, there are three paths and two fruits:
the path of stream-entry, the path of once-returning, and the path of non-returning, as well as the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of once-returning.
And the four associated with views, as well as those associated with doubt—these four lower fetters—are not found, nor do they exist, in the Suddhāvāsa [heavens].

This is the intended meaning here: because they are not shared by ordinary persons (*puthujjana*), stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), or once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*), it is a "pure abode" (*suddhāvāsa*);
or alternatively, because they stand beyond the terrible [fetters], non-returners (*anāgāmin*) are "pure."

Because they have crossed over the four floods, those whose taints are destroyed are called "pure" (*suddha*). The "Pure Abode" (*suddhāvāsa*) is so named because it is the dwelling place of these two types of pure, supreme beings. This is the intended meaning here:
however, in the Pure Abodes, there are the path of stream-entry, the fruit of stream-entry, the path of once-returning, the fruit of once-returning, and the path of non-returning.

They do not exist. Why? Because they arise only at the stage of the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), and because the four unwholesome consciousnesses associated with views and the one associated with doubt have been destroyed by the stream-enterer (sotāpanna); for these reasons, they do not arise.
Furthermore, the four lower resultant [consciousnesses] do not exist, because they are the resultant consciousnesses of the lower form-brahmas.
The remaining fifty-one types of consciousness, however, are found in the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa).
They are as follows: those dissociated from wrong view, likewise that accompanied by restlessness, the eight sense-sphere wholesome states, and the five fine-material-sphere wholesome states.
The wholesome states of the formless realm, the Path, and those with taints exhausted;
the eye, ear, and mind elements born of merit; the two types of investigation;
the ripening of the fifth jhāna; and the fruits beginning with that of the Non-returner.
In the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa), twenty functional consciousnesses (kriya-citta) are found.
All those belonging to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara)—all fifteen fine-material-sphere consciousnesses—and all twenty-three resultant consciousnesses (vipāka) in the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu).

213. The path of the first [dhyāna] accompanied by grief (domanassa), the two paths of grief, the path of the first [dhyāna], the stream-entry path (sotāpatti-magga), and the functional (kriyā) [consciousness].

There are no forty-three types of consciousness in the formless plane (arūpabhūmi): namely, the two rootless (ahetuka) functional (kiriyā) five-door adverting consciousnesses and the smile-producing consciousness.

There are no five fine-material-sphere resultant (rūpāvacara-vipāka) consciousnesses because those are resultant consciousnesses belonging to beings with material bodies. There are no fine-material-sphere javanas because of the absence of desire for the lower jhānas.
There are no eye- and ear-consciousnesses because they are born of merit and are absent in those devoid of sense-faculties. As for nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness...

By its very nature, it does not exist. The wholesome-resultant mind-element (*manodhātu*) does not exist because its objects are the five sense-objects grasped by the eye and so forth, whereas [this element] has only non-material phenomena as its object.

Since the eye-consciousness and the others do not exist, that merit-born mind-element also does not exist; and because of its absence, the eye-consciousness and the others likewise do not exist at all.
The functional mind-element (*kriyā-manodhātu*) also does not exist precisely because its objects are the five sense-objects, as is the case with the smile-producing consciousness (*hasituppāda*).

Because of the absence of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and the absence of the white [kamma], there is none; for the Noble Ones (*ariya*) who have previously seen the Truths belong to the fine-material plane (*rūpabhūmi*), and therefore even the first path does not exist [there].
214. Thus, by way of the planes alone, one should discern the arising of consciousness (*cittuppatti*);

in this manner, by the method stated by me, the wise person should explain the arising of consciousness by way of the planes. Likewise, one should discern the arising of consciousness by way of the eleven types of persons (*puggala*).
The wise one should analyze and explain:
among the wholesome and unwholesome states of sensual desire,
their results are rootless (ahetuka).
"And two advertings"—
thus there are exactly thirty-seven mental factors.
This is the meaning of what was stated.
216. Thus, in the five planes—namely, the four woeful planes and the human plane—these [consciousnesses] arise and occur for a being who is without roots (ahetuka). As for the remaining fifty-two:
"the remaining fifty-two consciousnesses never arise" means that those fifty-two consciousnesses never arise or occur; they have already been stated according to their specific forms.

217. Together with the thirty-seven consciousnesses arising in a being without roots (ahetuka), forty consciousnesses arise for a being with two roots (duhetuka), namely the four great resultant [consciousnesses] and so forth; likewise, one [consciousness] arises for a being with two roots.

218–23. All sublime (mahaggata) states, all twenty-seven kinds of sublime states, all untainted (anāsava) states, all eight supramundane (lokuttara) states, the four three-rooted resultants, the smile-producing [consciousness] in the sense-sphere, and the great functional [consciousnesses] with roots.
Thus, for a being of two-rooted (duhetuka) nature, forty-nine types do not arise—namely, nine types of kiriya and forty-eight types of consciousness.

This is the intended meaning here: because of the incapacity to attain the fine-material and immaterial meditative absorptions (rūpa- and arūpa-samāpatti), the twenty-seven sublime (mahaggata) states do not arise;

because of the incapacity to realize the paths and fruits (maggaphala), the eight supramundane (lokuttara) states do not arise; and [the seven] resultant states of three-rooted (tihetuka) nature [also do not arise].

They do not arise because they are resultant consciousnesses for beings possessing three roots; nor do they arise because the nine functional consciousnesses occur only for those whose taints are exhausted (the *khīṇāsava*).
For a sense-sphere being—a worldling (*puthujjana*) with a rebirth-linking based on three roots—forty-four types of mind arise.
Which are they? The forty consciousnesses stated for those with two roots, as well as one [consciousness] in the desire realm.
Forty-four types of consciousness arise in the realms of form and the formless: the four resultant states associated with knowledge, and the nine meritorious states.
For an ordinary person (puthujjana) who possesses the three roots and is bound to the sense-sphere, thirty-five types of consciousness do not arise and will not arise. They are as follows:
excluding the two types of adverting consciousness, and the eighteen functional states.
The nine sublime resultant states and the eight supramundane states—
these thirty-five types of consciousness never arise at all for an ordinary person of the sense sphere who possesses a three-root rebirth-linking.

For a being who has become a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) born among the seven planes—namely, the four divine worlds and the human world—fifty types of consciousness arise. Thus the wise one should point out and explain that statement.
It is as follows: Those dissociated from views, the two types of mental grief, That accompanied by restlessness, and the eight wholesome states of the sense-sphere.
The nine sublime meritorious states, the two types of adverting consciousness,
all sense-sphere resultants, and the fruit of stream-entry—
these ninety-three types of consciousness do not arise for one who has attained stream-entry. Thus the wise man should illuminate and teach this statement, as follows:
Excluding the two types of adverting consciousness, there are eighteen functional consciousnesses;
nine sublime resultant consciousnesses; and seven supramundane consciousnesses.
Those associated with wrong view, as well as that associated with doubt;
Ninety-three do not arise for the embodied one who is a stream-enterer (sotāpanna).

(224) Excluding the first fruit, the states of consciousness described for the person who is a stream-enterer would, together with their own once-returner fruit (sakadāgāmiphala), belong to the person who is a once-returner.
(225) Excluding the two types of aversion and the second fruit—the once-returner fruit—the [remaining] states of consciousness described for the stream-enterer [belong to the non-returner].

Excluding those forty-eight consciousnesses stated for a stream-enterer that arise together with his own fruit of non-returning, the wise one should point out that these same [consciousnesses] arise for a non-returner being.
(226) How many consciousnesses arise for an Arahant? For an Arahant born in the seven sensual-sphere planes within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), [these arise].

How many types of consciousness arise for one whose taints are destroyed? Forty-four types of consciousness may and can arise for an Arahant born in the seven sensual-sphere planes of existence. They are as follows:
twenty-three resultants of the sensual sphere and twenty functional consciousnesses.
By means of the fruit of Arhatship alone, there would be [desires] for an Arhat.

(227) For all four of those persons standing on the path, their respective path-consciousnesses would exist; for they are indeed of a single moment of consciousness—this statement spoken by me is the truth. Those paths are of a single moment of consciousness.
(228) For an ordinary person, it is only in three; that is, for one born in the three levels of the first jhāna, only in those three levels of the first jhāna.
For an ordinary Brahmā, exactly thirty-five types of consciousness arise. Thus the wise one should explain and declare this. Namely:
having excluded the two kinds of mental pain, and the ten non-meritorious [states].
There are eight meritorious states pertaining to the sense-sphere, and nine sublime meritorious states.
The pair consisting of eye-consciousness and ear-consciousness, the two types of investigating consciousness,
the two types of adverting consciousness, and the receiving consciousness born of merit;
The ripening of the first jhāna consists of exactly thirty-five [types of consciousness]:
the three types of wholesome resultant consciousness occurring in the sensitive organs of the nose and so forth; the seven unwholesome resultants; the eight great resultants;
likewise, the resultants born of the higher jhāna planes; the four formless-sphere resultants; and also the two types of mental grief.

Furthermore, these fifty-four consciousnesses— namely, the eighteen functional (kiriya) consciousnesses excluding the two adverting consciousnesses, together with the eight supramundane (lokuttara) consciousnesses—

are not found, nor do they occur, in a person, a being, or a body of an ordinary worldling (puthujjana) born in the three planes of the first jhāna. Among those stated for a Brahmā who is an ordinary worldling born in those three planes...
Excluding the five non-meritorious states among the [thirty-six] consciousnesses,
thirty-one consciousnesses arise— arise together with the first fruit— for a *sotāpanna* Brahmā born there in the three planes of the first *jhāna*.
For a *sakadāgāmī* Brahmā born there in those same three planes of the first *jhāna*, the first fruit exists within those consciousnesses.
Excluding the fruit of once-returning and including it [in the count], exactly thirty-one consciousnesses arise.
For a non-returner born in those same three planes of the first jhāna, excluding the second fruit,
exactly thirty-one consciousnesses arise together with their own fruition-consciousness.
Consciousness of the eye and ear, the roots of merit, the receiving consciousness, the two types of investigating consciousness, and the functional consciousnesses—these are twenty.
(236–237) The fruit of Arahantship arises from the first jhāna; there are twenty-seven consciousnesses that constitute its maturation for an Arahant.

They arise for one whose taints are destroyed. For an ordinary person (puthujjana) born in the three levels of the second jhāna—namely, in the Brahma-world—the thirty-six types of consciousness arise simultaneously with the ripening of the second and third jhānas. This is as follows:
excluding the two types of grief, there are ten unwholesome states.
There are eight meritorious states pertaining to the sense-sphere and nine sublime meritorious states.
The pair consisting of eye-consciousness and ear-consciousness, the two types of investigating consciousness,
the two types of adverting consciousness, and the receiving consciousness are born of merit.
Through the ripening of the second jhāna, and through the ripening of the third jhāna,
there are exactly thirty-six types of consciousness for one possessing the second jhāna.
(238–241) Among those stated for an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), excluding the fivefold merit along with its own fruit, there are thirty-two.

Minds arise for one who has attained stream-entry (sotāpanna). Among those stated for the stream-enterer, excluding the first fruit—excluding the first fruit stated for the stream-enterer—there are thirty-two minds together with his own fruition-consciousness.
Among those stated for the once-returner (sakadāgāmin), excluding the second fruit, there are likewise thirty-two minds together with the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) for that non-returner.

They exist. For an Arahant, there are exactly three [planes]. For an Arahant born on his own three planes of the second jhāna, there are twenty-eight consciousnesses together with those matured by his own fruit—namely, the maturations of the second and third jhānas. They are as follows:
consciousness of the eye and ear, the merit-born, and the receiving consciousness.
The two types of investigating consciousness and the twenty functional consciousnesses,
the fruition of Arahantship, that which arises from the second jhāna, and the fruition of the third jhāna—
these are the twenty-eight classes of mind that are results (vipāka).
242–6. For the gods of the three planes beginning with the Parittasubha (Limited Beauty), thirty-five types of consciousness arise together with the result of the fourth jhāna.
For a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) there, thirty-one types of consciousness arise;

that is to say, in those three planes beginning with the Parittasubha, thirty-one types of consciousness arise for a stream-enterer. Just as it is thus for the stream-enterer, so it is for the once-returner (sakadāgāmin).

Thus, thirty-one [mental states] arise for a non-returner (*anāgāmin*). In those same three planes, there are twenty-seven mental states for one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*) who has been born there.

Likewise, in the Vehapphala [plane], there are the mental states of all five types of individuals—both worldlings (*puthujjana*) and trainees (*sekkha*)—who have been born in the Vehapphala plane. [This applies likewise] in the five Suddhāvāsa planes.
For a person born as a non-returner (anāgāmin), there are exactly thirty-one types of consciousness. Thus the Wise One would illuminate and teach this statement.
Likewise, for an Arahant born in those very Pure Abode (suddhāvāsa) planes, there are twenty-seven mental states.
In this manner, according to the method stated by me, for all persons born in the fifteen form-spheres (rūpibhūmi) among the realms possessing form—
The wise person, discerning, should understand and know these states of consciousness.

247. Twenty-four types of consciousness: twenty-four types of consciousness arise in an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) born on the plane of the first immaterial state (*paṭhamāruppabhūmi*). Thus the wise person should point this out. For example:
excluding the two types of mental pain (*domanassa*), there are ten unwholesome (*apuñña*) states.
The eight types of sense-sphere wholesome states, the wholesome states of the formless realm, the result of the first formless attainment,
functional consciousness, and the voṭṭhabbana consciousness—
these are the ten types [of consciousness] for a stream-enterer in that very same plane, excluding the five types of unwholesome states. (248–251) Therein, in that first formless plane...
Thus, for a person who has attained stream-entry (*sotāpanna*), having abandoned the fivefold set of demeritorious states, there are twenty consciousnesses together with their own respective fruits.

Likewise, in that same first immaterial sphere (*paṭhamāruppabhūmi*), for a person who is a once-returner (*sakadāgāmin*) or even a non-returner (*anāgāmin*), twenty consciousnesses arise together with their own respective fruits, excluding each preceding fruit. For one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*)...
In that very same first immaterial-sphere plane, ten and five mental [kamma-resultant] states arise for one whose taints are destroyed.
They are as follows:
the eight great functional states and the four lower functional states.

The fruit of arahantship, the ripening, and the mind of resolution—these are the twenty-three types of consciousness belonging to an ordinary person born on the plane of the second immaterial state. They are as follows:
excluding the two types of grief-consciousness, there are ten unwholesome states.

The eight sense-sphere wholesome states, the three wholesome form-sphere states, the resultant of the second immaterial state, and the investigating consciousness—thus, having spoken and explained in this manner, the wise and learned one should analyze and teach. Herein, for those born in this second immaterial plane, there are nineteen types of consciousness belonging even to the three types of trainees (sekkha). They are as follows:
Those dissociated from views, as well as that accompanied by restlessness—these eight are meritorious sense-sphere states;
three are meritorious fine-material and immaterial states;
and there is the resultant of the second immaterial state, as well as the investigating consciousness.
Just as by means of each respective fruit, there are nineteen types of consciousness.

(252) However, for one who has destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*) and is born in the second immaterial plane, there are exactly fourteen types of consciousness: twelve functional consciousnesses (*kiriyacitta*), one resultant consciousness, and the fruit of Arahantship (*arahattaphala*). These are as follows:
the eight great functionals (*mahākiriya*), three functionals pertaining to the higher formless states, and the fruit of Arahantship.
The act of adverting, its own fruition, and even the fruit of Arahantship.
(253) For an ordinary person born in the third immaterial plane—the third formless stage—there are twenty-two types of consciousness for that ordinary being. Thus the wise one should explain. Namely:
excluding the two types of mental grief, there are ten unwholesome states.

There are eight sense-sphere wholesome states, two wholesome states of the fine-material sphere and the immaterial sphere respectively, the resultant of the third immaterial sphere, and the mind-element of apprehension.
(254–5) There are eighteen types of consciousness; eighteen types of consciousness arise for a person who is a stream-enterer. They are as follows:
Those dissociated from views, likewise that accompanied by restlessness,
the eight great meritorious [consciousnesses], and the two meritorious [consciousnesses] of the fine-material and immaterial realms—
these eighteen, together with the fruition of stream-entry, [are the results of kamma].
The mind of one who has attained stream-entry (sotāpanna) arises as both resolved (voṭṭhabba) and sustained (mānasa).
For the once-returner (sakadāgāmin), excluding the first fruit, there are eighteen types of consciousness by way of their own fruit.
Among the types of consciousness stated for the once-returner, excluding the second fruit, there are eighteen together with their own fruit.
Only these [same] minds arise for a non-returner (anāgāmin).

256. And as for the thirteen minds: for one born in the third immaterial plane—the third formless stage—thirteen minds arise for the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava). Thus the wise man should point this out. It is as follows:
there are eight great functional (mahākriyā) minds, and two functional minds (kriyā) above the realm of form.
The fruit of arahantship, and the mind that has resolved [upon it].

(257) Twenty-one types of consciousness arise in the fourth immaterial plane. Twenty-one types of consciousness arise in a person who is an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*) born in the fourth immaterial plane. Thus the wise one should point this out. It is as follows:
Excluding the two kinds of mental grief and the ten unwholesome [consciousnesses];

The eight types of sense-sphere wholesome consciousness, the mind-element of determining, the fourth formless-sphere wholesome consciousness, and the ripening consciousness—these twenty-one [types of consciousness] should be declared by the wise one for a being who is a stream-enterer. They are as follows: [258–260]
Those dissociated from views, as well as that accompanied by restlessness—
these eight types of sensual merit, the fruit of stream-entry,
the merit of the fourth immaterial attainment, and the "throwing-out" consciousness, together with its ripening.
For a once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*), with the exception of the first fruit, those same consciousnesses are accompanied by their respective fruits.
Among the consciousnesses stated for a once-returner, with the exception of the second fruit, seventeen types of mind are accompanied by their own fruits for a non-returner (*anāgāmī*).
However, for an arahant born in the fourth immaterial plane, there are exactly twelve types of consciousness.
Minds arise. They are as follows:
the eight great functional minds, the determining mind, the fourth functional materiality, and the fruition of an Arahant.
Thus, in this manner, by way of these types of individuals as described by me, the wise and discerning one should analyze the movement of the mind within the planes.
(261–2) For those formless beings of the lower [planes], such as the Brahmās, both wholesome formless states and functional states arise in the successively higher [planes].
For those formless beings of the higher and higher sections, the lower and lower formless attainments [do not arise].
However, those belonging to the formless realm (*arūpāvacara*) that arise in the lower levels do not arise at all. For what reason? It is said that I have heard:
because of the danger seen in the lower meditations (*jhāna*), and because of the presence of the fault of wrong view (*diṭṭhadosa*), they do not arise at all. 263–5.
Excluding the first path—the stream-entry path (*sotāpattimagga*)—there are three and three wholesome and unsurpassed [paths] respectively.
The three supramundane wholesome paths, the eight sense-sphere wholesome states, likewise the ten unwholesome states of mind, and the four formless-sphere wholesome states—
all these are supramundane results (*lokuttara-phala*). Furthermore, the first formless-sphere result,
the nine sense-sphere functional states, all formless-sphere functional states, and these forty-three types of consciousness arise in the plane of the first formless attainment.
266–7. All twenty-three types of sense-sphere resultant consciousness, all fifteen kinds of sublime material phenomena,
the mind-element, the functional mind-element, the two types of grief-consciousness, the path of the first [jhāna], and likewise the three immaterial resultant states arising above that—
these forty-six types of consciousness do not exist here in this first immaterial plane.

268–9. Regarding the consciousnesses mentioned: among the consciousnesses mentioned in the first immaterial plane, excluding the three types of first immaterial consciousness—namely, the wholesome, the resultant, and the functional—forty consciousnesses, including their own resultants, arise in the second immaterial plane.

Thus, in this manner described by me, for the remaining two [planes], in the pair of planes consisting of the base of nothingness and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, which remain after the first and second immaterial planes...
Excluding the three formless [attainments] that have arisen in the lower portion by way of wholesome, resultant, and functional [consciousness],
each of their respective results should be known by the wise in the manner thus described by me.
(270–3) Furthermore, the four taintless [states]— the four supramundane resultant consciousnesses— are all of them [taintless].

They exist in the four formless planes (ārūppabhūmi). Together with the determining consciousness (voṭṭhabbana-citta), there are eight great functional (kiriya) consciousnesses regarding sense-sphere objects and four formless functional consciousnesses;
thus, exactly thirteen functionals arise for one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) born on the first formless plane.
For one whose taints are destroyed born on the second formless plane, there are exactly twelve functionals, having excluded the first formless functional.
They exist. For an Arahant born in the third immaterial plane, there are eleven functional consciousnesses, excluding the first and second immaterial functionals.
For an Arahant born in the fourth immaterial plane, it should be known that there are ten functional consciousnesses, excluding the first, second, and third immaterial functionals.
However, for an Arahant, there are nineteen types of consciousness:
all functional states of Arahantship, excluding the two types of adverting consciousness.
Excluding the two types of adverting consciousness, all functional states and the fruit of Arahantship constitute the nineteen types of consciousness of an Arahant.

However, there are two types of adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*). Although these two belong to one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), they likewise belong to others—both worldlings (*puthujjana*) and those in training (*sekkha*).

The statement "excluding the two types of adverting consciousness" was said for the purpose of making it known that nineteen types of consciousness belong exclusively to one whose taints are destroyed, and not to others.
(275–6) For the four persons established in the fruits and for the worldling with triple-rootedness (*tihetuka*), there are only thirteen types of consciousness.
Thus the wise one should explain this statement. For example: there are four great resultant consciousnesses associated with knowledge, and nine material and immaterial resultants;
these together constitute thirteen types of consciousness.
(277–9) For the four persons at the stage of fruition and for the twice-rooted worldling who is devoid of knowledge, there are four [types of consciousness] lacking knowledge.

Only resultant states arise. For the three types of worldlings (puthujjana), for the four noble beings, and for the seven noble individuals (ariyapuggala), there are exactly seventeen types of consciousness.
They are as follows: the two fivefold sense-consciousnesses, the triple mind-element (manodhātu) and investigation (santīraṇa), and the determining consciousness (voṭṭhabbana);
these constitute the seventeen.
280–5. For the three lower fruit-attainers, for a worldling possessing triple-rootedness, and for the four types of noble persons, only sublime wholesome states arise.
For the three types of worldlings and for the first three types of noble persons, thirteen consciousnesses arise from below among the noble ones.
Thus the Wise One has pointed out. There are eight meritorious states of the sense-sphere; as for demerit—

Including the four types of consciousness that are deficient in view due to unwholesomeness (*akusala*) and the one associated with restlessness (*uddhacca*), there are thirteen types of consciousness.

In the two lower fruit-attainers—the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) and the once-returner (*sakadāgāmin*)—and in all ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*), as well as in those ordinary worldlings with rootless (*ahetuka*), double-rooted (*duhetuka*), or triple-rooted (*tihetuka*) consciousness, only the two types of consciousness associated with mental grief (*domanassa*) arise. In the three...
And for worldlings, exactly five arise. They are as follows:
the four associated with views, that associated with doubt, and the respective path-consciousness for each of the four stages of the path.

For each of those four individuals standing at the stage of the path, there would be only one respective path-consciousness in each respective existence. Thus, in this manner and according to the method stated by me, the wise and learned person should discern and clarify the occurrence of consciousness.

(286–9) By means of existences and by means of individuals—by means of consciousnesses in all existences and by means of individuals—the occurrence of consciousness [is explained] for the sake of proficiency among the bhikkhus, the Abhidhamma bhikkhus.

It has been explained by me for the sake of easy comprehension. Thus, all this consciousness, according to the classification of planes and persons—in this manner as described by me through the classification of planes and persons—becomes manifold and of many types.
Thus, the grasping [of the subject] should be understood by one who discerns it, following what has been stated by me according to the sequence of my exposition.
The distinction—the differentiation of consciousness—can be known and understood by one who possesses analytical discernment (*vibhāvin*).

Fearing excessive prolixity, I have condensed these words that illuminate the occurrence of consciousness; however, this should be grasped by the discerning one after examining the preceding and following passages, reflecting upon them, and repeatedly investigating their meaning.
290. This *Abhidhammāvatāra*, which is well-substantiated, excellent, and a lamp for the darkness of the delusion of beings;

and this treatise, the *Abhidhammāvatāra-pakaraṇa*, which is well-substantiated, consisting of beautiful essence, and an excellent lamp, a radiant light, for the delusion resembling the darkness of beings—whatever person carefully contemplates or recites it, passion and hatred shall not approach or visit that person for a long, long time.
Thus ends the commentary on the Exposition of the Stages, Persons, and the Arising of Consciousness in the *Abhidhammāvatāra-ṭīkā*.
This is the fifth chapter.
6. The Sixth Chapter:
Explanation of the Classification of Objects (Ārammaṇavibhāgavaṇṇanā) But beyond this, the objects of these consciousnesses [will be explained].
"I shall show [the object] by means of that; for without that, there is no arising.
Beyond this, that is, beyond this section, I shall show the object of these consciousnesses. Why?
Because without that—that is, excluding that object—there is no arising of these consciousnesses. This is the reason.
For that reason, I shall demonstrate it.
Form, sound, smell, taste, tangible object, and mental phenomena—
these they call the sixfold objective field, according to those skilled in the six objects.
The clever and wise ones, regarding the six objects of cognition, have declared and explained the object as being sixfold and of six types. 293.

Therein, “derived from the primary elements” (*bhūte upādāya*): therein, among those objects, that which is derived from the primary elements means color-form (*vaṇṇa*) produced in dependence upon the primary elements, having arisen and been generated by four conditions reckoned as karma, consciousness, temperature, and nutriment.

That which occurs together with demonstration, that which occurs together with resistance, and that which is designated as having form as its object—these two kinds [of sound] have been pointed out by the Sage as arising from mind and ear.
Sound arising from mind is only that which possesses consciousness. How so? By means of a mind that effects vocal expression.

The state of transformation (*vikāratā*) of the earth element (*pathavīdhātu*), which has come to be and arisen from the ground, is called "transformation" because it possesses the characteristic of earth and the characteristic of being not excessively rigid.
That [transformation] is cognized as vocal intimation (*vacīviññatti*).

Thus, sound is the cause for the striking of the karma-born earth element by the striking of the intimated [element], and it is also the striking of the karma-born earth element by the mind-born earth element.
And it occurs neither before nor after. 295.

As for the sound devoid of consciousness (*aviññāṇaka-sadda*), that sound devoid of consciousness is produced by temperature (*utu-samuṭṭhita*). Both these two kinds of sound have reached the state of being an object of sound; they have attained the status of being an objective field of sound (*saddārammaṇatā*).
296. It is called "fragrance" (*gandha*) because it is "borne along" (*dharīyati*); as one goes and goes, it is borne along by people. [The root] *gamu* signifies going.
*Dhara* means "to hold. It is called *gandha* because it indicates (*sūcana*) its own common object, such as flowers, or because it makes manifest (*pakāsana*).
*Gandha* means "to indicate. This fragrance has four origins; thus, it is "four-origin" (*catusamuṭṭhāna*). It is recognized as having fragrance as its objective field (*gandhārammaṇa*).

297. "They taste, they relish," thus it is proclaimed by people as "taste" (*rasa*). Because people, while tasting, relish and experience that particular kind of phenomenon (*dhamma*), for that reason, for that cause, it is proclaimed by the wise as "taste"—that is, what is called "taste.
That taste is produced from four [elements] and is designated as the "object of taste" (*rasārammaṇa*).

298. It is called *phoṭṭhabba* (the tangible) because it is touched (*phusīyati*) by people; thus, that which is a class of phenomena (*dhammajāta*) touched by people is therefore *phoṭṭhabba*. These are earth, fire, and air. That tangible is produced from the four [great elements] and is considered the object of the tangible base (*phoṭṭhabbārammaṇa*).

299. Having abandoned all name and form—having abandoned the pentad beginning with form, as well as all name consisting of consciousness, mental factors, and Nibbāna, and form consisting of the five sensitive organs and subtle form—and having [considered] the characteristics, namely the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and non-self:
And conceptual designation (paññatti) is what is termed the mental-object (dhamma) object.
Six objects are found in the sense-sphere plane; in the sense-sphere plane, six objects are found.
Three are found in the fine-material sphere by way of visible forms, sounds, and mental objects. However, in the immaterial sphere, only one—the mental-object—is found.
301–3. Because of the brevity of their momentary existence and physical basis, those five objects—form and so forth—which do not enter the range [of the sense doors]:

because of the brevity of the moment of the five objects, because of their dullness, because of their short lifespan, because of the brevity of their physical basis, and because the physical bases of the five objects are too small, they do not enter the range—that is, they do not become manifest—at the five doors within the five sensitive organs (*pasāda*).
Those five objects, form and so forth, which do not perform the function of striking [the sense faculties], become the mental object (dhammārammaṇa).
Such is the opinion held by certain teachers. The particle *kira* is a particle used in the sense of hearsay.
Those teachers who speak thus must indeed be rejected; they are to be refuted by me. Why? Because of eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*).
One does not experience the sound that has become the domain of ear-consciousness, nor does ear-consciousness experience the visible form that has become the domain of eye-consciousness. Thus,
for those five consciousnesses beginning with eye-consciousness, which do not experience each other's domains, there is that domain known as the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element.
"But it experiences the impulsion (javana). Because this statement was spoken by the Blessed One, [the former view] must be rejected.
However, the objects such as visible forms are indeed the five objective supports (ārammaṇa) consisting of visible form and so forth.

304–6. Regarding the knowledges of the divine eye and so forth: visible forms and so forth alone are their spheres; those very visible forms and so forth are the spheres of the divine eye and other knowledges.
The statement that they have not even reached the state of being manifest to those [faculties] that have not come within their range is likewise untenable.
How, and in what manner, could that class of phenomena which has visible form as its object become a phenomenon with mental objects as its object?

This being so, if a phenomenon having visible form as its object were to become a phenomenon having mental objects as its object, then for these [phenomena] having visible form and mental objects as their respective objects—

How could there be a restriction? In what manner could it exist? All this object—this entire object—is declared by the Blessed One to be sixfold and of six types. It is considered to be of many kinds by way of the limited triad and so forth.

(307) And all karmic fruition of the sense-sphere, including all twenty-three types of sense-sphere fruition, as well as the two functional causes, [arise] by way of the mind-element and the smile-producing consciousness.

The twenty-five types of consciousness arising from these five—namely, the two functional-with-root states and the three rootless states—may have exclusively limited objects; that is, they may have objects belonging exclusively to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).

The fivefold division of desirable and so forth (iṭṭhādi) refers to visible forms, sounds, and the rest, which serve as the respective domains for the five pairs of consciousness in their sequential order.
However, the entire pentad of visible forms and the other sense objects serves as the domain for the triple mind-element (manodhātu).
However, while all five categories beginning with form (*rūpa*) serve as objects, for these thirteen types of consciousness, only the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) is their range and object.
They do not take non-form (*nārūpa*) or name (*nāma*) as an object. Nor do they take concepts (*paññatti*) as objects.
They do not take the past as an object, nor do they take the future as an object.

They do not take it as an object at all. For the object of these thirteen consciousnesses—namely, the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness and the three mind-elements—is only that which is currently occurring; it is only the present.
These thirteen consciousnesses arise in the sense-sphere realm; these thirteen consciousnesses arise in the sense-sphere realm.

In the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), four types of consciousness arise: the two merit-born [resultants] consisting of eye-consciousness and ear-consciousness and their respective receiving consciousnesses, and the functional mind-element (kiriyā-manodhātu). In the immaterial states (arūpi), that is, in the immaterial planes, not even a single type of consciousness arises at all.
312–3. During the occurrence of the eight great resultants and the eight great supermundane resultants, which perform the function of registration (tadārammaṇa) at the six doors:

Limited visible forms and so forth are the objects. During the occurrence of the three types of investigating consciousness (*santīraṇa*), limited visible forms and so forth are the objects both for the function of the three types of investigating consciousness in the five doors and for the function of taking that as an object in the six doors.

Limited visible forms and so forth—the six limited [objects]—are the objects of the smile-producing consciousness; for the smile-producing consciousness, the six limited [objects] consisting of visible forms and so forth are its objects. In the five doors, those that have arisen...

Those objects which are present at the five sense-doors, and those objects at the mind-door which belong to the three times—that is, those connected with the three periods of time—are fixed and have fixed objects.

(314–5) Furthermore, the second immaterial consciousness and the fourth immaterial consciousness—this sixfold consciousness, by way of the wholesome, resultant, and functional, has a sublime range; it is fixed and has a fixed object. That sixfold consciousness has a sublime range.
The objects of these two—the second and fourth immaterial resultant states—are the wholesome objects of the base of infinite space and the base of nothingness previously attained by oneself.

This is because of the statement: "Whichever wholesome jhāna one takes as an object, upon the attainment of rebirth-linking in the Brahma-world, that very object becomes the object of its respective resultant. Because they have Nibbāna as their object...
Indeed, for those whose minds are exclusively and uniquely free from taints (*anāsava*), the immeasurable states have only *nibbāna* as their domain and object.
Why is this? Because they have *nibbāna* as their object, and not any other object. 316–320.

Regarding the four deficient in knowledge: by way of wholesome states of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara-kusala*), there are four types that are deficient in knowledge compared to meritorious deeds of the sense sphere.

The four [consciousnesses] associated with knowledge through the aspect of action, the twelve unwholesome [states] associated with ignorance through the aspect of action, and those [four] associated with knowledge through the aspect of action—these are both limited in their objects and have the sublime as their domain, yet they are not to be so described. Why? Because their objects are conceptual designations (*paññatti*).

The four associated with knowledge through the aspect of merit, the four associated with knowledge through the aspect of the wholesome, and the four associated with knowledge through the aspect of action...

The objective range of these eleven types of consciousness—namely, those associated with knowledge (*ñāṇa*), the two kinds of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), and functional investigative consciousness (*kiriyā-voṭṭhabbana*)—is threefold according to whether it is limited (*paritta*), sublime (*mahaggata*), or immeasurable (*appamāṇa*). These eleven are also not to be described [as having a single type of object]. Why?

Because their objects are concepts (*paññatti*). As for those remaining after what has been stated—that is, those other than the aforementioned consciousnesses—[their objects are likewise to be understood].
Those consciousnesses should be understood by the discerning as having objects that cannot be described [as limited, etc.].
The triad of limited objects is finished.
Now, the second immaterial consciousness and the fourth immaterial mind;
However, sixfold [consciousness] may have an exclusively past object.

For the five pairs of consciousnesses—that is, the ten types consisting of the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness—and for thirteen types of consciousness including the three mind-elements (manodhātu), the five objects such as visible form are exclusively present.
This is because the eight great sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses function with respect to those [objects] by way of the registration function (*tadārammaṇa-kicca*).
They have as their domain the past, future, and present: by way of the function of death, they have the past as their object;

by way of the functions of rebirth-linking and the life-continuum, they have the present and past as their objects. The investigating consciousness accompanied by joy has the present as its object by way of the function of investigation;

it has the present, future, and past as its objects by way of the function of registration. The remaining two types of investigating consciousness [have the same] by way of the function of investigation.
It has a present object; by way of the function of registration (*tadārammaṇa*), it has a present, future, or past object;
by way of the function of death (*cuti*), it has a past object; and by way of the functions of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), it has a present or past object.

The smile-producing consciousness (*hasituppāda-citta*) has the present, past, and future as its range by way of the function of impulsion (*javana*). Thus, these twelve types of mind may have a past object.
They may have the past as their object. Those with the present and future as their domain may have the present as their object or the future as their object.
In the sense-sphere (kāma), there are twenty wholesome, unwholesome, and functional [consciousnesses]. By way of function, there are nine mental states in the sense-sphere:

the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*) has the present as its object by way of its determining function; it has all three times as its object by way of its adverting function. The great functional mental state has the impulsion function (*javanakicca*).

They have objects belonging to all three times; when they are designations (*paññatti*), however, their objects are not to be specified. The two types of consciousness associated with direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) may also have the past and so forth as their domain by way of the function of direct knowledge.

These [two] types of consciousness, even when they are designations, remain unspecifiable. Regarding the states of existence in the fine-material and immaterial realms, the wise person should understand that all remaining types of consciousness have objects of the past and so forth, according to the classification of having past objects and so on, as I have explained.
They are not to be said [as non-existent], nor are they simply not to be spoken of; the meaning is that they are indeed objects of wisdom (*paññā*). 327.
From the perspective of desire, there are five functional states (*kriyā*) by way of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*);

from the perspective of form, there is the fifth functional state, the consciousness of direct knowledge (*abhiññā-citta*), by way of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*). Among these six types of consciousness, there is not even one that does not have its own range (*agocara*).
"Objectless" means having all things as its object. The statement "the fifth is functional" (*kriyā*) is spoken with reference to the consciousness of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
It should be understood that for pure jhāna—the fifth type of form-sphere functional consciousness—there is only a conceptually designated object (*paññattārammaṇa*). 328.

And regarding Nibbāna, the fourfold fruit, the path, and form and the formless—which are called "name" (*nāma*) consisting of consciousness and mental factors—tell me, Teacher, which consciousnesses are capable of making these their objective range; tell those [consciousnesses] to me.
329–30. Four consciousnesses associated with knowledge (ñāṇa-saṃyutta) through the mode of merit (puñña) as merit;
likewise, four associated with knowledge through the mode of functional (kiriya); two with direct knowledge (abhiññā-mānasa);

and also the functional consciousness of adverting (kiriyā-voṭṭhapana)—these eleven types of consciousness are capable of taking Nibbāna, the fruit, the path, material form, the immaterial, and the mental object as their domain.
331-4. "But among all consciousnesses, tell me, how many are those consciousnesses capable of making the fruit of arhatship and the path of arhatship their object? Speak of them to me.
"Among all consciousnesses, listen to me regarding six consciousnesses, O gentle-faced one; listen to my words, for among all [consciousnesses]..."
Among the types of consciousness, six are capable of making the fruit of Arahantship and the path of Arahantship their object.

Six types of consciousness—namely, the four associated with knowledge, the functional consciousness of determining (*voṭṭhabbana*), and the functional consciousness of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*)—are capable of making them their object.
By way of merit, there are four associated with knowledge; and by way of merit, there is the consciousness of direct knowledge.
They are unable to take the fruit of arahantship or the path as their object. 335–8.
Ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) or those in training (*sekkha*) are unable to cognize the path-consciousness or the fruition-mind of an arahant whose taints are destroyed.
For what reason? An ordinary worldling does not know the mind of a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), and a stream-enterer [does not know] that of a once-returner (*sakadāgāmin*).
The stream-enterer does not know the mind of the once-returner; the once-returner does not know the mind of the non-returner; the non-returner does not know the mind of the arahant.
A lower person does not know the mind of a higher person, but a higher person knows the mind of a lower person.
339–342. Whatever state serves as the object for another state, I shall explain each such object individually hereafter. Regarding wholesome objects:
within the sense sphere, the eightfold wholesome state is the object for the eightfold wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere.
How so? The eightfold great wholesome [kamma] performed in the past...
Subsequently, during the moments of recollection and so forth, that object becomes the focus for that eightfold wholesome [consciousness] by way of the function of impulsion (javana),
through either the two types of consciousness associated with knowledge and accompanied by joy,

or the two types dissociated from knowledge and accompanied by joy, or the two types associated with knowledge and accompanied by equanimity, or the two types dissociated from knowledge and accompanied by equanimity.
It is the object of twelve kinds of unwholesome consciousness at such times as those of remorse; it is the object of wholesome supramundane consciousness and functional supramundane consciousness;
and it is the object of eleven kinds of sense-sphere resultant consciousness by way of registration (*tadārammaṇa*).
Likewise, it is the object of functional sense-sphere consciousness by way of the function of impulsion (*javana*), such as in the case of laughter.
It becomes the object of determining (voṭṭhabbana) by way of its function of adverting, and the object of great functional consciousness (mahākiriyā) by way of its function of impulsion;

it may be the object of these six groups. The five fine-material-sphere merits (rūpāvacara-puñña), excluding the resultant of the sense-sphere from those six groups, become the objects of the [remaining] five groups. At that time, by way of the roots of greed and delusion...
At the time of recollecting the jhānas attained by oneself, it becomes the object for those ten kinds of unwholesome states.
For a being of triple-rooted rebirth who has fallen away from jhāna while reviewing that jhāna, it becomes associated with grief and takes the jhāna as its object;
at that time, it becomes the object for the two types of aversion (*paṭigha*). As for "of one who acts according to desire," these are exclusively objects of the limited (*paritta*) category.

Excluding the functional mind-element and the smile-producing consciousness, it becomes the object of determining consciousness by way of the function of adverting, and of the great functional [consciousness] by way of the function of impulsion. (343) Furthermore, it is the object of the wholesome formless [consciousnesses],
of the wholesome of the three planes, of the great wholesome [consciousnesses], and of the fifth wholesome fine-material-sphere consciousness by way of the function of direct-knowledge.
It becomes the object of the second and fourth immaterial wholesome states, of the investigative consciousness (voṭṭhabbana) belonging to the three planes of existence,
of the great functional consciousness, of the fifth functional consciousness pertaining to the higher knowledges (abhiññā), and of the second and fourth functional immaterial states; furthermore,
the first functional immaterial state must be the object of the second functional immaterial state, and the fourth functional immaterial state [must be the object of the third].
Furthermore, there must be an object for the functional third immaterial attainment; and if that is so,

it must be explained how wholesome first immaterial attainment becomes the object for functional second immaterial attainment, and wholesome third immaterial attainment becomes the object for functional fourth immaterial attainment— namely,
when a worldling practitioner or a practitioner who is still in training enters the form-sphere attainments.
Having emerged from that [attainment], he entered the first formless attainment known as the base of infinite space;
having become free from lust and taking up the attainments he had previously realized,

he entered the second formless attainment— which he had not attained during his time as an ordinary person (puthujjana) or a trainee (sekha)— and this was the second formless functional (kiriya) attainment realized at the time when his taints were exhausted.
It takes the first immaterial wholesome state as its object; thus, the first immaterial wholesome state becomes the object for the second immaterial functional state.
