When the yogi, having entered the fine-material attainments and emerged from them, enters the first, second, and third immaterial wholesome states, and having become one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), takes up the attainments he has realized—

When one enters the fourth formless attainment not yet previously attained by oneself, then the functional (kiriya) fourth formless state takes the wholesome (kusala) third formless state as its object;
thus, for the functional fourth formless state, the wholesome third formless state becomes the object.
Later, at the time when the taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava), these become attainments of both the fine-material and the formless realms. Just as...
Just as [the fine-material sphere] is so for the wholesome, it is likewise an object for the unwholesome.
344–7. "Of the immaterial-sphere resultant states" is a specification by genus; it is also an object for the immaterial resultant states of the fourth and second [jhanas].
Although one should have said "of the fourth and second," the word *tiyānaṃ* has been elided, resulting in the form "catutthadū."
It has been stated that, at that time, the first and third immaterial-sphere javanas become the objects for the two immaterial-resultants;
for according to the statement, "Whatever wholesome jhāna is the object by grasping which rebirth occurs in the Brahma-world," the base of infinite space and the base of nothingness—
which serve as the respective objects for those wholesome states— become the objects for their second and fourth immaterial-sphere resultants.
They become objects; thus, immaterial wholesome states are the object-condition for these eighteen groups.

Furthermore, the supramundane wholesome states not included in the mundane, which are fourfold, are [the object-condition] for the wholesome consciousness associated with knowledge—namely, the great wholesome consciousnesses of the sense sphere—and for the functional consciousness of determining (voṭṭhabbana);
and for the functional consciousness associated with knowledge, they are [the object-condition] for the fine-material sphere consciousness by way of the fine-material sphere.

The object of the fifth sense-sphere wholesome consciousness (*rūpa-kusala*) and the fifth sense-sphere functional consciousness (*rūpa-kiriya*)—that is, of these four groups—is always supramundane merit.

This is the intended meaning here: for trainees (*sekkhā*), the threefold supramundane merit is the object of great wholesome consciousness associated with knowledge, of the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*), and of the fifth sense-sphere wholesome consciousness. For one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), [it is the object] of...

The merit of Arahantship is the object of the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*), the great functional consciousness associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta-mahākiriyā*), and the fifth functional consciousness of the fine-material sphere (*rūpakiriya*).

Just so, all unwholesome states from the sense-sphere are objects for wholesome and great wholesome states of the sense-sphere, as well as for the functional consciousnesses of laughter, determining, and the great functional consciousness; furthermore, [they are objects] from the fine-material sphere by way of the fine-material sphere.
It is the object of the fifth wholesome consciousness of the fine-material sphere and the fifth functional consciousness of the fine-material sphere;
likewise, it is the object of all unwholesome consciousnesses and of eleven types of sense-sphere resultant consciousness by way of the function of registration.
Thus, the Blessed One has declared it to be the object of six groups of consciousness.

348–352. Regarding the resultant object (*vipākārammaṇa*): all resultant objects in the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*)—both from the perspective of the sense-sphere itself and by way of the sense-sphere—are the objects of wholesome, great wholesome, functional, laughing, and the great functional [consciousnesses] of eructation;

as well as the fifth wholesome consciousness of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) and the fifth functional consciousness of the fine-material sphere, both from the perspective of the fine-material sphere itself and by way of the fine-material sphere.
It is the object of the eleven types of sense-sphere resultant (kāmāvacara-vipāka), as well as of the unwholesome (akusala) and the six groups [of consciousness] in exactly the same way.
In the fine-material sphere (rūpa), it is the resultant object for the wholesome (kusala), the great wholesome (mahākusala), the functional (kiriya),
and the great functional determining (voṭṭhapana-mahākiriya) consciousnesses, both from the sense-sphere and by way of the sense-sphere, and from the fine-material sphere.
And likewise, by way of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) and the wholesome (*kusala*) and unmeritorious (*apuñña*), it becomes the object of five groups;

this method regarding the immaterial-sphere results (*arūpāvacara-pāka*) is held by the Blessed One. Not included and not entered into the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) are the "unincluded" (*apariyāpanna*);

the results of those persons, according to their desire, are by way of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), [namely] of the wholesome and of the great wholesome associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta-mahākusala*).
Thus, it becomes the object for great functional consciousness associated with determining knowledge (*voṭṭhabbana-ñāṇa*),

for wholesome fifth-jhāna consciousness of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) from the perspective of both the form and the fine-material sphere, and likewise for functional fifth-jhāna consciousness of the fine-material sphere.
Herein, this intended meaning should be understood in the same manner as that stated regarding the non-encompassed merit (*apariyāpanna-puñña*).
353–6. In the sense-sphere (kāma), this entire class of functional consciousness belongs both to the sense-sphere realm and by way of the sense-sphere;

it pertains to the wholesome and the great wholesome, as well as to the functional—the laughing, the determining, and the great functional. In the fine-material sphere (rūpa), it belongs both to the fine-material realm and by way of the fine-material realm;
it pertains to the wholesome—the fifth wholesome of the fine-material sphere—as well as to the functional—the fifth functional of the fine-material sphere.
The object of these six groups—the eleven types of fruition in the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and likewise the unwholesome—is as follows:

that functional consciousness (*kiriyā-mānasa*) in the fine-material sphere (*rūpa-rūpāvacara*), and that functional consciousness which is the fruition of the sense sphere—excluding the fruition of the sense sphere from that group—it becomes the object of the remaining five groups. From the sense sphere...
By way of the sense-sphere, it becomes the object for functional investigating-consciousness and the great functional consciousness of determination;
because laughter has exclusively limited objects, it does not take material functional consciousness as its object. However, functional consciousness [takes] immaterial [consciousness];
and immaterial functional consciousness takes those same five groups [of consciousness], and the first immaterial functional consciousness [takes] the second immaterial functional consciousness.
It becomes an object; the functional third immaterial state becomes an object for the functional fourth immaterial state. Thus, it remains the range of the six groups.
Matter is of fourfold origination and is designated as having matter as its object.

It is the object-condition for these six groups: for the eleven types of sense-sphere functional consciousness—namely, the wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere, the two types of direct-knowledge consciousness, and the sense-sphere functional consciousness that results from kamma;

and for the great resultants of the sense sphere, which consist of the two eye-consciousnesses, the two mind-elements, the three investigating consciousnesses, and the sense-sphere functional resultants. Thus, it is the object-condition for these six groups comprising eleven types of sense-sphere functional consciousness.

359–360. Having Nibbāna as its object, [it] becomes the object of two types of consciousness: (1) for those in training (*sekkha*), it is the object of the great wholesome consciousness associated with knowledge belonging to the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere;

and (2) for those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), it is the object of both the great functional consciousness associated with the "determining" knowledge (*voṭṭhabbana-ñāṇa*) belonging to the fine-material sphere and the fifth functional consciousness of the fine-material sphere. Furthermore, because it is not included within the mundane realms (*apariyāpanna*), [it is the object of supramundane consciousness].
And likewise, by way of the supramundane, it is the object-condition for the fruit and for the wholesome among these six groups.

361–2. Furthermore, all that is of various kinds, being a conceptualized object (paññatti-ārammaṇa), is likewise [the object-condition] for the merit of the three planes, for the great wholesome, for the fivefold pure jhāna, for the wholesome of the fine-material sphere, and for the wholesome of the first and third immaterial attainments.
It serves as the object condition for nine groups: all unwholesome [states], all resultant states of form and the formless,

all resultant states of form, the resultants of the first and third immaterial attainments, the functional states of the three planes, the laughing, the effortful, and the great functional states— all functional states of form—
and the functionals of the first and third immaterial attainments.
363–4. Two sets of two types of consciousness arise with visible form as their object; two sets of two types of consciousness arise having sound and so forth as their domain;
and three types of consciousness reckoned as the mind-element are considered by the Blessed One to have the five [sensory] objects as their object.
Herein, in this context of the sense-sphere, exactly forty-one types of consciousness have the six objects as their object.
This is the sequence of objects for sense-sphere consciousnesses. 365–9.

Excluding the five direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), all these types of consciousness—whether pertaining to the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, or being untainted (*anāsava*)—have mental phenomena as their objective domain (*dhammārammaṇagocara*).
The wholesome first immaterial-sphere consciousness becomes the object of the wholesome second immaterial-sphere consciousness; [likewise] the second immaterial-sphere consciousness...
It is the object of resultant [consciousness], and it is also the object of the functional consciousness of the second immaterial realm.
The reason why the first immaterial wholesome state serves as the object for the functional consciousness of the second immaterial realm has already been stated below.

This is the result of the first immaterial wholesome state; it is the object of the wholesome consciousness of the second immaterial realm, of the resultant consciousness of the second immaterial realm, and of the functional consciousness of the second immaterial realm.
And it is not an object for them. Why? Because those wholesome, resultant, and functional states of the second immaterial realm have the wholesome state of the first immaterial realm as their object.
However, the first functional consciousness is not an object for the merit of the second immaterial consciousness;
nor is it an object for the resultant of the second immaterial consciousness. For in the fine-material and immaterial realms, those whose taints are exhausted—
The resultant consciousnesses take as their object the respective wholesome states by way of the death-consciousness (*cuti*).

However, the first functional consciousness (*kriyā-citta*) becomes the object for the second functional consciousness of the formless realm. Thus, in this manner, according to the method described by me, the wise one who discerns the arising of objects for these consciousnesses should understand it.
370-3. For an ordinary person (puthujjana) and for one in training (sekkha), the formless object (arūpārammaṇa) is twofold;
it is wholesome (kusala) and serves as the object for the second formless wholesome state. That first formless wholesome state may be the object for the result (vipāka) of the second formless state.
For a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), the first formless consciousness is a threefold object.

It is of three kinds. Thus was it spoken by the Great Sage. For functional [consciousness] as well as for the second immaterial functional [consciousness], the first immaterial functional [consciousness] serves as the object.
Wholesome [consciousness] and wholesome first immaterial consciousness also serve as objects for the second immaterial functional [consciousness].
Wholesome [consciousness] and wholesome first immaterial consciousness serve as objects for the second immaterial resultant [consciousness]. Thus, by this...
The object of the first immaterial-sphere consciousness described by me is threefold.
The third immaterial-sphere consciousness is the object for the wholesome fourth immaterial-sphere consciousness, and it is also the object for the resultant fourth immaterial-sphere consciousness.
Just as the object of the first immaterial-sphere consciousness is twofold, so too [is it here].
Likewise, the object of the third immaterial consciousness is twofold.
Just as the object of the first immaterial mind is threefold, so too the object of the third immaterial consciousness may likewise be threefold.

374. However, whatever sphere is taken as a basis here—in this context—whatever mental states arise depending upon that particular sphere, each such sphere becomes the object-condition for those respective mental states.

375. Furthermore, that person who crosses over to the far shore of this Abhidhammāvatāra—which is indeed difficult to cross here in this world—that person truly crosses over to the far shore, which is difficult to reach, across the great ocean of Abhidhamma.
Thus ends the commentary on the Analysis of Objects in the *Abhidhammāvatāra-ṭīkā*.
The Sixth Chapter. 7.
The Seventh Chapter:
Explanation of the Description of the Occurrence of Resultant Consciousness.
When the fruition [of kamma] had been explained by that compassionate one, who seeks virtues, who is free from passion, and whose knowledge is infinite—
for the sake of proficiency in understanding—
Listen to the origin of resultant consciousness. Listen, you all,
to the occurrence of resultant consciousness as it is being spoken by me— the origin of resultant consciousness— stated by that Conqueror of infinite wisdom,
free from defilements, a seeker of virtues, and compassionate, for the sake of proficiency in understanding resultants and for the sake of attaining excellence in intelligence.
377. Twenty-nine types of kamma and thirty-two types of resultants were shown by the Blessed One. Kamma is seen in three doors; resultants are seen in six doors. 378–9.
Wholesome [kamma] in the sense-sphere world: wholesome [kamma] occurs in the course of existence within the sense-sphere world, and also at rebirth-linking, depending upon this or that condition.
"This or that condition" means *so so paccayo*; where it should have been said "that condition" (*tatapaccayo*), the form is derived through the addition of the nasal stop (*niggahītāgama*).
"Each respective condition" is what was stated. This is a distributive *kammadhāraya* compound. It gives various fruits.
One rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is proclaimed by the Blessed One for a single volition (*cetanā*). However, through various karmas, various rebirth-linkings come to be.
380–1. As for that karma which possesses three roots (*tihetuka*), that karma known as belonging to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*) which possesses three roots—
It yields a result that has two roots and a result that has no root.
However, as for that karma which has two roots and that karma which has three roots, such karma does not yield a three-rooted result; it yields its own result with either two roots or no root.
(382–3) Through karma with three roots, rebirth-linking is three-rooted; rebirth-linking may also indeed be two-rooted.
The intention is this: there is no rootless rebirth-linking; by means of a superior triple-rooted kamma, there is a triple-rooted rebirth-linking;

by means of an inferior triple-rooted kamma, there is a double-rooted rebirth-linking. By means of a double-rooted kamma, there is a double-rooted rebirth-linking, and there is indeed also a rootless rebirth-linking, but there is never a triple-rooted rebirth-linking. By means of a superior double-rooted kamma, there is a double-rooted [rebirth-linking].
Rebirth-linking: the intention is that rebirth-linking occurs without roots (ahetuka) through a weak double-rooted (duhetuka) kamma.
384. Non-volitional kamma (asaṅkhārakamma) yields non-volitional fruition; it also yields volitional fruition (sasaṅkhāravipāka). Volitional kamma (sasaṅkhārakamma) yields a volitional fruit;

likewise, it yields a non-volitional fruit. 385. Regarding one volition: among these volitions, sixteen kinds of resultant consciousness arise from a single wholesome volition. Thus the Victor has declared.
386–92. The transformation of feeling occurs precisely through the object; the mind that takes that as its object (*tadārammaṇa-citta*) is also determined by the impulsion (*javana*).
The meaning is this: when a wholesome impulsion associated with joy has impelled, the *tadārammaṇa* [mind] is likewise associated with joy.
This same method applies to wholesome [impulsions] associated with equanimity. By means of the first wholesome [impulsion], which is a sense-sphere consciousness (*kāmāvacara-citta*), and so forth...
By means of a resultant consciousness that is similar [to the rebirth-linking consciousness]. This is the third qualification.

If the rebirth-linking [consciousness] has been grasped by a certain being, and if a desirable, powerful, agreeable, or excessively great object comes within the range of that being’s eye—that is, becomes manifest to the sensitivity of the eye—and the mind-element (manodhātu) turns toward it, thereby interrupting the stream of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), [then the process of adverting occurs].
When the process-consciousnesses beginning with eye-consciousness have arisen, first a wholesome sense-sphere javana arises.
After it has impelled seven times, when the first great wholesome [citta] has passed,
there arises a resultant consciousness taking that same desirable object and similar to that first great wholesome [citta], known as "registration" (tadārammaṇa).
By way of equality with the rebirth-linking [consciousness], through its state of being equal to the rebirth-linking, it is called the "root life-continuum" (*mūlabhavanga*) by the Blessed One.

And in this cognitive process (*vīthicitta*), the following consciousnesses enter into the count: the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*), the investigating consciousness (*santīraṇa*), the investigating consciousness associated with joy (*somanassayutta-santīraṇa*), the seeing consciousness (*dassana*), and the receiving consciousness (*sampaṭicchana*). These are the consciousnesses that have entered into the count within this cognitive process.
There are exactly four [results]. 393–4.

For when the second consciousness, a wholesome impulsion (javana), occurs—at whatever time a second wholesome consciousness becomes an impulsion for that same person who possesses the root-cause of joy—then at that time, by means of that impulsion, there is an equal result (vipāka).

Regarding that registration (tadārammaṇa): because it is not identical with the preceding link (sandhi), and because that registration-consciousness is not identical with the preceding link, this resultant consciousness receives two names;
by means of this resultant consciousness, two names are obtained: the name "adventitious bhavaṅga" and the name "registration. Thus, two names are obtained.
395–6. When that same person’s third impulsion (javana) of merit occurs, then a third resultant consciousness similar to that impulsion may arise as its object-receiving (tadārammaṇika).

This resultant consciousness is called "the adventitious life-continuum" (āgantuka-bhavanga) by the Blessed One; and together with this third resultant [consciousness], the preceding five resultant consciousnesses [constitute it].
However, there are six consciousnesses together [with the preceding ones]. 397–8.
When the fourth wholesome impulsion occurs, then the fourth resultant consciousness, which is equal to that impulsion, would proceed toward the state of registration (*tadārammaṇa*).
This fourth resultant consciousness is the adventitious life-continuum (*āgantuka-bhavanga*) known as registration.
There is; including this fourth ripening together with the previous six, there are seven consciousnesses.

399–403. When, at whatever time, a desirable-neutral object thus comes into the range of that eye-door, then, according to the method already stated, after the advertence, seeing, and receiving consciousnesses have arisen, here—in this [process]—
When the object is neutral, feeling turns according to the object; therefore, the investigating consciousness (santīraṇa) is accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā).
When four impulsion moments (javanas) accompanied by equanimity have occurred, four resultant consciousnesses arise that are equal to those impulsions.
By reason of the feeling of equanimity, which is absolutely and exclusively [present] as before...
Because they are not associated with the same mental factors as those accompanied by joy, these four consciousnesses are called "subsequent life-continuum" (*pīṭṭhibhavanga*) by name;
the meaning of "subsequent life-continuum" is that they are the life-continuums occurring subsequent to the results of joy.
These five resultant [consciousnesses] accompanied by equanimity, together with the seven previous resultants, constitute the twelve resultants.
Thus the wise one should explain. 404–6.
Just as there are twelve results in the door of the eye, so too there are twelve results in the doors of the ear and the others.
Thus the wise one should explain: these results mentioned by me amount to sixty in total.
Thus, when a single volition (*cetanā*) has been accumulated and set in motion by me in the manner described, sixty equal results (*vipāka*) arise;

there is no doubt regarding this statement. By the "non-inclusion of what was included" (*gahitāggahaṇena*), that is, by the non-inclusion of those results already mentioned among these results, there are twelve maturations at the eye-door, such as ear-consciousness and the rest.
"Four times four" makes sixteen results.
Just as it was when a wholesome kamma with three roots (*tihetuka*) was accumulated through effortless (*asaṅkhārika*) action, exactly so too,

when wholesome kamma is accumulated and set in motion through effortful (*sasaṅkhārika*) action with three roots, or through wholesome actions accompanied by effortless equanimity (*asaṅkhāra-upekkhā-sahagata*), for those three [types of kamma]...
This same method should be understood by the wise regarding the rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) bestowed by all three types of wholesome kamma-resultants (vipāka).
Herein, within this pair associated with equanimity, the arising of resultant consciousness is first shown by way of its desirable-neutral object;
thereafter, it should be shown that when the object is desirable, [the process] occurs later here. Thus, I have shown it later here.
But at a later time, following the previously described mental process, a wise person should demonstrate twelve results for each one of these desirable objects here.
By not including those results already included among those previously mentioned, there are sixteen resultant consciousnesses. All of this is according to the method stated by me at the earlier time.
This statement should be understood by the wise in its entirety and in its absolute completeness.
(412–4) By means of a three-rooted kamma, a rebirth-linking with three roots occurs; this section has been stated by me thus far, by this much of the discourse.
A single kamma produces a single rebirth-linking within a single existence; from that rebirth-linking...
Furthermore, it does not produce another second rebirth-linking, but it produces many results during the course of existence (*pavatti*).
Indeed, the statement beginning with “one kamma” and so forth is true. From a single seed—from one seed—one sprout is born;
from that seed, many fruits arise through the occurrence of causes, such as the production of water and other conditions.
415–21. Regarding the statement, "By a two-rooted kamma, rebirth-linking is two-rooted," this section has been presented in gradual and sequential order.

Here, in this context, when kamma is accumulated by means of a two-rooted meritorious deed performed with a mind associated with joy and without volitional effort (*asaṅkhārika*), then by means of that ripening which is equal to a wholesome [kamma] associated with joy and consisting of two roots—
If rebirth-linking is grasped by that being, then when a desirable object comes into the range of the eye-door for that being,
after a wholesome consciousness associated with joy and devoid of knowledge has impelled seven times with respect to that [object]— being double-rooted— and has passed away,
immediately following that impulsion, taking that same object, there arises a consciousness similar to it.
A consciousness that is entirely spontaneous (*asaṅkhārika*) arises similar to the impulsion (*javana*). "That" refers to that consciousness;

it is called the "root-life-continuum" (*mūlabhavaṅga*), and it is also called the "registration" (*tadārammaṇa*). Both names are names for that very same thing; they are the names of that specific consciousness.
Thus, in this manner, it has been elucidated by the Blessed One. [This applies] to those with two roots (*duhetuka*).

When wholesome impulsion with volitional effort has impelled, at that same time there arises a mind-objective-representing consciousness (tadārammaṇa-citta) known as "adventitious," which is similar to— that is, identical with— that [impulsive] consciousness.
And in exactly the same way, when two types of double-rooted consciousness associated with equanimity have a desirable-neutral object, [the same occurs].
Immediately after the javanas, two such mind-moments similar to those javanas arise as registration (tadārammaṇa);
these registration mind-moments have the name "post-bhavanga" and also the name "guest-bhavanga.
Together with the two types of investigation, seeing, and receiving, and these two types of bhavanga, there are eight [moments].

The resultants occur at the eye-door. Thus, by means of this method explained by me, making eight resultants for each of the five doors, there are forty resultants in the course of existence (*pavatti*).
By the "omission of what has been included" (*gahitāggahaṇena*), that is, by omitting from among these resultants those already included in the eye-door, there are eight [resultants] in the eye-door.
And including the resultants of the ear, nose, and so forth, there are exactly twelve resultants.
When a single volition has been accumulated and set in motion through action in the manner described by me, then indeed there are twelve resultants.
This statement was proclaimed and taught as if by one who has won a battle in a skillful war. Also by way of the three [types of consciousness] with two roots...

But by me, who am similar to those with two roots, this method has been stated—having been taught by the Stainless One—to be the same for a being who has taken a rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) through a ripening (*pāka*) that is similar even to the triad of two-rooted [kamma].
A rebirth-linking with two roots occurs through kamma with two roots. Thus, this section has been stated by me with this much of a statement.
430–8. By means of a double-rooted (duhetuka) kamma, a rootless (ahetuka) rebirth-linking occurs; thus this section has come down in regular succession.

Among those four double-rooted wholesome consciousnesses, when a kamma is accumulated and performed by any one of the roots, there arises a resultant rootless consciousness accompanied by equanimity, which is the fruition of that very same double-rooted wholesome javana.

For a being who has received rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) by means of the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*), that rebirth-linking should not be called "similar to the kamma" by the wise.
Indeed, the statement beginning with "rebirth-linking is not to be called [similar]" is true.
The kamma possesses two roots (*duhetuka*), whereas the rebirth-linking is rootless (*ahetuka*). For that embodied being who has attained growth—that is, who has reached maturity—...

However, when a desirable or neutral object enters the range of the eye-door, at the conclusion of any one of the four types of double-rooted wholesome javanas, this rootless mind arises as the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*).
There is no doubt or uncertainty regarding this statement; that rootless consciousness and the fundamental life-continuum (*mūlabhavanga*) are indeed the registration consciousness itself.
And it is accompanied by equanimity. Even when the process-minds beginning with eye-consciousness have arisen, the investigating mind (santīraṇa) is likewise accompanied only by equanimity.

Having set aside one among those two resultant states—the functions of investigating and registering—here, having excluded that single mind which performs the function of investigating or the function of registration from among the resultants already mentioned, [the remaining] resultants...
By excluding [the unpleasant], here there are only three types of consciousness that enter into the count regarding desirable and neutral objects. 439–41.

When a desirable object enters the range of the eye-door, at that time the investigation-consciousness is associated with joy alone, and the mind-consciousness with that same object is also associated with joy alone;
such is the case regarding those functions of investigating and registering.

Taking one or another resultant consciousness that performs the function of investigation (*santīraṇa*) or the function of registration (*tadārammaṇa*), there are only three or four preceding resultant states.
Thus, according to this method explained by me, there are four resultant consciousnesses at each of the five doors;
consequently, there are twenty resultant consciousnesses in the course of occurrence (*pavatti*).
442–8. Regarding the eye-door (*cakkhudvāra*): by excluding the resultant states that were included under the heading of "already grasped," there are four resultants in the eye-door here.

Thus, with these four resultants in this desirable object, together with the ear-, nose-, and other resultants, there is an eightfold set of rootless (*ahetuka*) consciousnesses. For a being with a rootless rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), there is the two-rooted and the three-rooted [resultants].
Or else, that object-of-apperception (tadārammaṇa) would not occur; for a being with a double-rooted rebirth-linking, there would be no triple-rooted object-of-apperception.

For those by whom rebirth-linking was produced in a happy destination—by whatever kamma that rebirth-linking was produced—even if the object-of-apperception were equal to or inferior to that resultant [kamma], it would occur for them in the human world.

Having intended this, it was said: "The group of eight born without roots" (*ahetukaṭṭhaka*) refers to those in the happy realms (*sugati*), and "the group of eight without roots" refers to those in the human world;

it was spoken by me with these as the basis and reason. However, in the four states of misery (*apāya*), they are called *apāya* because there is no going away (*apeta-ayo*)—that is, no firm footing—from them.

Within those [realms], during the course of existence (*pavatta*), the group of eight without roots is obtained by those bound for the miserable states. As for the Elder, he [said] regarding those in hell:
He teaches the Dhamma; he rains. One who possesses the quality of being steadfast (*thira-kāra-dhamma*) is called a *thera*.
The Elder Moggallāna, the second chief disciple, possessed of supernormal powers, teaches the Dhamma—that is, he makes it rain—to beings born in hell.
The meaning is that he causes the Dhamma to rain down, as in such passages as, "Sitting on my lap," and so forth. He creates fragrance and wind.
At that time, however, when those hell-beings see the Elder, hear the Dhamma, smell the fragrance,
drink the water, and are touched by the soft breeze, for those hell-beings who are drinking and being touched,
all five types of consciousness beginning with eye-consciousness are born of merit and are the result of wholesome karma.
Thus, there are two types of investigating consciousness born of merit and exclusively wholesome-resultant; and one mind-element born of merit. This makes eight.

(449–50) This discussion—beginning with the statement that "eye-consciousness and the rest are born of merit alone"—was spoken by me with reference to the impulsion-moments of merit within the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*) that have desirable, desirable-neutral, or neutral objects. [It refers to] the moments of consciousness that take those as their object (*tadārammaṇa-cetaso*).
That restriction which I stated by such words as, "The mind that takes that as its object is restricted by the impulsion," was stated with reference to wholesome [states].
When a sense-sphere wholesome state associated with joy has impelled, the registration [consciousness] is also associated with joy;
when a sense-sphere wholesome state associated with equanimity has impelled, the registration is also associated with equanimity.
The intention is this: even when unwholesome javanas such as doubt, which are associated with equanimity, have flashed forth, that object may still be accompanied by joy;
this is what is meant by the statement "it is so. Thus has it been elucidated by the Teacher.
451–7. Herein, according to this intention, in all four types of unwholesome consciousness associated with joy, when the object is desirable...

When those [unwholesome] consciousnesses have impelled, immediately following those unwholesome impulsions (javana), the rootless mind-consciousness element associated with joy arises as the registration (tadārammaṇa) of them.

When the six unwholesome consciousnesses associated with equanimity have impelled upon an object that is desirable-neutral, immediately following them, it is the rootless mind-consciousness element associated with equanimity born of merit that arises. Or else...
Immediately after those six unwholesome javanas accompanied by equanimity, there arises [a resultant consciousness] by way of being their object-registering (tadārammaṇa).
In the case of association with a desirable object— that is, association with a desirable object such as the form of the Buddha—
for a being who is doubting, thinking "Is he the Buddha or not?", or for a being who is agitated, the mind that registers that object is associated with joy.

The resultant life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is rootless. However, when a consciousness associated with joy has impelled a functional javana, five registration-minds associated with joy should be sought by the wise.
When a consciousness accompanied by equanimity has impelled a javana, six registration-minds accompanied by equanimity should be sought by the wise.
458–63. When a being who has taken rebirth with joy and gladness falls away from a jhāna and feels remorse, as he reviews that jhāna while reviewing it, his mind becomes associated with grief.
Immediately after that grief, what state of consciousness arises? Tell me, what is the mental state that follows a javana associated with grief?
Speak. For the arising of joy immediately after grief is prohibited in the *Paṭṭhāna*;
it has been forbidden by the Blessed One in the *Paṭṭhānapakaraṇa*. Likewise, the arising of grief immediately after that joy is prohibited in the *Paṭṭhāna*;
it has been forbidden by the Blessed One in the *Paṭṭhānapakaraṇa*. However, with reference to the sublime (*mahaggata*)...

Even when a sublime (mahaggata) state has been impelled by a functional (javana) consciousness, the mind that takes that as its object (tadārammaṇa-mānasa) is prohibited right there, in that very place, by the Blessed One;
it is warded off. For that reason, there is neither a lapse into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga-pāta) nor an object-taking [consciousness].
What indeed should be done? Regarding the absence of those two—the life-continuum and the object-taking consciousness—what is the reason that should be applied?
What indeed is that reason we ask you about? O Abhidhammika, for the sake of that matter, speak, speak that reason according to the nature of the Abhidhamma.
Could the rootless mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity have that [preceding state] as its object? 464–7.
Is there no adverting [consciousness] for this [state] having that as its object? How is that mind which has that as its object [established]?

In what manner does it arise? Is there merely adverting for the mind-moments of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and the adverting consciousness? Is there no adverting for the Path and for the Fruition that follows immediately after it?
And for the Fruition-consciousness of a monk emerging from cessation—thus have I heard—that in this manner, as described by me, there is no adverting. Without [adverting].
"Let it be, let the mind arise even with adverting; let it be, let it arise without adverting, having abandoned adverting.
O wise one, if you know what the object of that mind which has that as its object would be at such a time, tell me, speak of that object. Without an object, how can this mind [exist]?"
Without an object, or setting aside an object, [consciousness] does not arise. For this is true:

regarding the statement beginning with "without an object," when a sublime-object impulsion (javana) associated with mental grief (domanassa) impels, then at that very moment of the impulsion-consciousness, among the limited objects of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), any limited object whatsoever— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the logical flow of the preceding context.]
It arises conditioned by and dependent upon [these].

468–73. A wise person should understand five types of regularity (niyāmatā): the regularity of the season and the seed, the regularity of the season, the regularity of the seed, the regularity of karma and phenomena, the regularity of karma, and the regularity of the phenomena of the perfections such as virtue, as well as the regularity of the mind.
In this regard, among those five natural laws (*niyāma*), the simultaneous bearing of fruits, flowers, and so forth by all trees is the season;

this is the law of seasons (*utu-niyāmatā*). Furthermore, the arising of specific fruits corresponding to their respective seeds—even from crops that are similar to those various seeds—is the arising of fruits from those respective seeds; this is the law of seeds (*bīja-niyāmatā*).
The state of having a hole, the condition of being perforated, at the top of a coconut—that is, at the top of the coconut fruit—is the fixed order (*niyāma*) born of seed, arisen from a seed.

That a three-rooted kamma gives rise to a three-rooted result, a two-rooted result, or a rootless result—whatever kamma bestows what [result]—this is the fixed order of kamma (*kamma-niyāmatā*). Regarding the birth of the Bodhisatta, the sprout of the Conqueror...

The manifold distinctions such as the shaking of the earth at the moment of birth constitute the fixed law of phenomena regarding the perfections of virtue and so forth (*sīlādipāramīdhammaniyāmatā*).

When confidence is stirred by that object, the arising of the moments of consciousness beginning with adverting (*āvajjanā*) within this mental process (*cittavīthi*) constitutes the fixed law of consciousness (*cittaniyāmatā*).
474. Whatever wise person, endowed with wisdom and endowed with virtue, should desire the departure from the darkness of delusion—
relying not on darkness but seeking escape from ignorance— that wise one, if he should so desire, may [study] this treatise, the *Abhidhammāvatāra*,
which destroys the darkness of the hearts of blind people and of those fools who resemble the blind, and which [is for one] dependent upon darkness.
"A lamp that burns, blazing, which causes the destruction of the heart. "Diligent" (*payatta*) means one who exerts himself in a particular way, who makes effort;
thus, "one should train constantly, at all times," meaning one should train by means of recitation, memorization, and reflection.
Thus ends [the section from] the *Abhidhammāvatāra-ṭīkā*.
The commentary on the exposition of the occurrence of resultant consciousness is finished.
The seventh chapter.
8. The eighth chapter.
Commentary on the Exposition of Miscellaneous Topics (Pakiṇṇakaniddesavaṇṇanā):
Now, however, for the sake of proficiency in all these matters,
the miscellaneous topics (pakiṇṇaka) are being explained by me for the benefit of the bhikkhus.

Now, however, at this time, for the sake of the proficiency of the monks and for the sake of their skillfulness, I shall speak and explain the miscellaneous mental states of all these individuals—those with three roots, two roots, and those without roots. 476–85.
The Spider on the Path: A spider called the "spider on the path" spreads its thread in the five directions and lies in the middle of its web.
Regarding the first direction among these directions... [repeated] ...in the first direction.

When the thread extended in a particular direction is touched by an insect, a moth, or a fly, that spider-cobweb moves slightly and, after quivering, follows the thread from its place of rest along the length of the thread;
it then drinks the fluid—meaning the blood—of that creature. Having returned, it remains right there in the middle of that web.
Just as it lies down at ease, and just as it performs actions such as moving toward the first direction,
even so it performs actions such as moving toward the four directions beginning with the second; thus,
the wise person should regard the five faculties as being like the thread in the five directions, and the mind, moreover, as being like the spider in the center.

It should be seen as follows: the striking of the sensitive eye-organ (*pasāda*) by the object should be viewed by the wise as being like the jostling of that organ by small creatures such as insects.
Just as the movement of a spider lying in the middle of its web causes it to tremble, so too does the object strike the sensitive organ;
thus it is called "striking the sensitive organ" (*pasādaghaṭṭana*). What is that? It is the object. In this regard, within that cognitive process (*vīthi*):

The Blessed One considered the turning back of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅgāvaṭṭana*) to be the functional mind-element of the mind-consciousness (*manodhātu-kiriyā-citta*) which, having taken the object by striking the sensitivity (*pasāda*), causes the life-continuum to turn back.
A wise person should regard the arising of the process-minds (*vīthicitta*) as being like the monkey on the path following along the rope,
whereas the impulsion (*javana*) is like the drinking of the broth after having pierced that monkey on the head.
The wise person should see the mind’s movement among its objects.

Then, returning and lying down in the midst of the web of threads, the wise person should see the revolving of the mind as it depends solely upon the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*), just as [the spider] depends upon the substance itself. 486–93.
But what does this simile illustrate? Indeed, what meaning does this simile illuminate?

Does he explain it? First, when the sensitive matter (pasāda) is struck by an object, that which has the sensitive matter as its basis (vatthu) and support (nissaya) is "sensitive-matter-based" (pasādavatthu);
this refers to consciousness (citta). Then, from that sensitive-matter-based [consciousness], the mind termed *bhavaṅga* arises supported by that very basis;
such is the meaning illustrated by that simile. Each single object [is experienced] in two ways.
But when it comes within range in every way and in all its aspects through two doors, this meaning is also illustrated by that same simile with the words "through two and two doors.
The meaning is that a single visible object comes within range through two doors—at once through the eye-door and the mind-door. The same method applies to the ear-door and the others as well.
It should be understood thus. When a visible form strikes the sensitivity of the eye, it enters the range of the mind-door at that very moment;
the meaning is that it becomes a condition for the vibration of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).

There is no doubt regarding this statement; there is no uncertainty in these words. "Just as a bird" means just as a winged creature. "Truly" means the word spoken by me is the truth. [As for] "at the top of a tree":
While perched upon the tip of a tree, it brushes one branch against another; its shadow spreads across and strikes the ground, the earth.

Here, *idha* is a particle. The brushing of the branch by the bird and the spreading of the shadow upon the ground occur neither before nor after, but arise at one and the same moment (*ekakkhaṇe*). In the very same way, [it is with] matter and the sensitive faculty.

And likewise, the striking [of the object] and the arrival of the object at the mental door (manodvāra) by way of its meaning and purpose—as a condition for the movement of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga)—occur simultaneously, neither before nor after, but in one and the same moment. 494–7.
Following that, having interrupted the stream of the life-continuum, there occurs, in due order, adverting (āvajjana) toward the sensitive eye-faculty in the eye-door.

When the seeing has arisen, when the receiving has arisen, when the investigating has arisen, and likewise when the determining has arisen, a wholesome impulsion-consciousness (javana-citta) impels; likewise, an unwholesome consciousness alone impels.
This same method applies without distinction to the ear-door and so forth, when sounds and other objects strike the senses; it should be understood by the wise accordingly.
Having extracted the similes of the gatekeeper and others from that treatise to illustrate this meaning, they should be shown here by the wise in this section concerning the street (vīthi).
498–9. "The eye is undivided" means that even when life has ceased, that eye remains undivided.
That which is obstructed by bile, phlegm, or blood is called "obstructed" (*sambhinna*), being unable to serve as a condition for eye-consciousness;
that which is not so obstructed is called "unobstructed" (*asambhinna*).

By means of that unobstructed arrival of the visible object at the sensitive eye-organ, and also by dependence upon light—by these three kinds of conditions acting as the cause of mental attention (*samanakkāra*)—[eye-consciousness arises].
By way of occurring together with the condition of five-door adverting (*pañcadvārāvajjana*). Furthermore, these four conditions proceed together as one;

thus they are "assembled" (*sametā*). By means of those that are assembled—that is, come together into a state of unity—that eye-consciousness, which is consciousness dependent upon the sensitivity of the eye, arises together with its associated mental factors (*cetasika*).

500–1. By way of non-disruption: through the non-disruption of the ear and the sensitivity of the ear, and through the reaching of the sound-object by the ear and the reaching of the sound-object by the sound.
Even with space as its support, auditory consciousness does not arise for one whose ear-cavities are blocked.
Thus, it arises by means of these three conditions, together with the cause of equal attention, which functions as the five-door adverting condition.
When these four conditions are combined, accompanied, and brought together into a single state, that ear-consciousness arises together with its associated mental factors. 502–3.
Through the non-separation of the nose—that is, the sensitivity of the nose—and through the non-separate arrival of the odor-object, the odor [is perceived].
And by way of coming into the range [of the object]. "Also by means of the support of air" means by the air entering the nostril.

By these three conditions, together with the cause of the preliminary mental application (samanakkāra) which occurs as the condition for five-door adverting—when these four conditions are combined, accompanied, and brought into union, that nose-consciousness [arises].
It arises together with its associated mental factors.

(504–5) It does so without distinction, through the tongue and that which is not distinct from the tongue, and through the arrival of the taste at the range of the tongue and the arrival of the tongue at the range of the taste.
"Supported by the water-element" means it also arises having obtained the water-element within the tongue-base; for without that [water-element], there would be no arising in the case of dry food.
The meaning is that even when something is tasted by the tongue, tongue-consciousness does not arise.

By means of those three conditions—along with the condition of five-door adverting, which functions as the proximate cause—it arises together with these four conditions when they are combined, conjoined, and brought into a state of unity;
that is, it arises together with its associated mental factors.
506–7. By way of the non-disruption of the bodily sensitivity (*kāyapasāda*) and by the arrival of the tangible object (*phoṭṭhabba*) within its range.

"Even by means of the support of earth" means that even without that [earth], the door of the body strikes against the great elements which are the conditions for the sensitivity, having struck the internal bodily sensitivity whose external object is the great elements. By that threefold condition, and by the cause of mental attention (*samanakkāra*).
[It arises] together with that which occurs by way of the condition of five-door adverting.
Furthermore, when these four conditions are combined—meeting, coming together, and becoming one—that body-consciousness arises together with its associated mental factors.

508–9. “Because of the non-distinction of the mind”: *manas* refers to the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*). Even though that has ceased, it [serves as the basis] for the adverting consciousness.
Even when occurring at its weakest point, such that it is incapable of serving as a condition, it is called "mixed" (*sambhinna*).
That which is capable of serving as a condition for advertence (*āvajjana*) is called "unmixed" (*asambhinna*).

This occurs through the non-interruption of the mind, by way of the object entering the range of the mind, and by way of dependence on a physical basis—namely, dependence on the heart-basis. It is by means of these three kinds of conditions.
Together with the mind-door adverting consciousness that occurs by way of the cause of mere attention (*samanakkāra*), and when these four conditions are combined—
meaning they have come together into a single unity— that mental consciousness, which is the impulsion consciousness (*javana-citta*) designated as such,
arises along with its associated states.

510–11. That which is called the mind of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga-citta*) should be understood by one who discerns. The mind of the functional process of adverting (*āvajjana-kiriya-citta*) and the pair of minds of the functional process of adverting are designated as "equanimity" (*samanakkāra*) by one who discerns.
The reading "by way of dependence on a physical basis" (*vatthusannissayena*) does not apply in all cases or to all states of existence.

Because it is mixed with and separated from the five aggregates (*khandha*), it is called the "fivefold mode of existence" (*pañcavokāra*); [this refers to] the fivefold mode of existence (*pañcavokārabhava*).

Having intended a specific reason and made it the cause, I have stated this reading: “by way of dependence on a physical basis” (*vatthusannissayena*). However, the meaning is that this reading was not stated with reference to the fourfold existence of the formless realm (*arūpabhava*).

This is because, since the physical basis (*vatthu*) is material (*rūpa*), it does not exist in the formless realm; [therefore, the term refers only to the fivefold existence consisting of the sense-sphere and fine-material realms]. The fivefold existence (*pañcavokārabhava*) consists of the sense-sphere existence (*kāmadhātu-bhava*) and the fine-material existence (*rūpadhātu-bhava*); the formless existence (*arūpadhātu-bhava*) is called the fourfold existence (*catuvokārabhava*); and the non-percipient existence (*asaññībhava*) is called the singlefold existence (*ekavokārabhava*).
Thus, the meaning is that this reading was not spoken with reference to the fourfold existence of the formless realm.
The meaning is: "How could there be dependence on a physical basis? (512–4).

There are nineteen types of consciousness in total, beginning with rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*): ten in the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), five in the fine-material sphere (*rūpa*), and four in the immaterial sphere (*arūpa*).
All these nineteen types of consciousness are rebirth-linking consciousnesses. What is called "kamma" is wholesome and unwholesome volition (*cetanā*).
The "sign of kamma" (*kammanimitta*) consists of visible forms—the five sense objects—as well as concepts (*paññatti*) and exalted consciousness (*mahaggatacitta*).

Likewise, the "sign of destiny" (*gatinimitta*) includes such things as the wish-fulfilling tree (*kapparukkha*) and, on the side of the unwholesome, iron cauldrons and so forth, which serve as the objective supports for visible forms and other objects.
Thus, in this manner, according to the classification stated by me, the Blessed One has declared that the object of those consciousnesses, beginning with rebirth-linking, is threefold.

It has been stated: for the *saṃdhicitta* (rebirth-linking consciousness) of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), the Blessed One considers the object to be limited (*paritta*) and belonging to the sense-sphere.
The five objects such as visible form (*rūpa*) are present; likewise, the sign of destiny (*gatinimitta*) is both a fivefold object and present.
Past karma consists of wholesome or unwholesome volition (*cetanā*) which is past only, not present. There is no future object.
515–26. There are eight great resultants (*mahāvipāka*) and three investigating consciousnesses (*santīraṇa*); thus, eleven types of consciousness are designated as "registration" (*tadārammaṇa*).
Among these eleven types of registration consciousness, ten are wholesome resultants born of merit, while one is an unwholesome resultant born of demerit.
The great resultants do not arise in the two realms of existence—namely, the fine-material and immaterial realms—but [arise] in the sense-sphere and fine-material realms.
There are three types of investigating consciousness (*santīraṇa*). Regarding those registration-consciousnesses (*tadārammaṇa-citta*) spoken of by the Teacher, the Conqueror:

among those registration-consciousnesses, not even a single registration-consciousness ever occurs as a registration [of the object] within the two realms of existence, the fine-material and the immaterial.
For what reason? Because in that regard, concerning those two realms of existence—the fine-material and the immaterial—the challenger states: "There is no registration."
The resolution is that it would so occur, but because of the absence of the seed, it does not.
This mind which takes that as its object (*tadārammaṇa-mānasa*) does not follow after the sense-sphere phenomena when they are objects of the non-sense-sphere. For what reason?

Because its objects are limited (*paritta*), because the mind taking that as its object is invariably and necessarily restricted to sense-sphere objects, and because such [non-sense-sphere] objects have never been familiarized at all times.

It does not follow after that. For just as a young child, even when following a father or a relative similar to a father, follows only within familiar places such as the doors of houses, streets, or crossroads, and does not go to the forest or a battlefield;
so too, although it follows after the phenomena of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), it takes hold of the sublime and supramundane phenomena (*mahaggata-lokuttara-dhamma*).

It does not follow after a process that is currently occurring. And because all these states—the fruition of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), the functional mind-element (*kiriyā-manodhātu*), and the functional rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy (*somanassa-sahagata*)—are stated to have "limited objects" (*parittārammaṇa*), it follows that their object is exclusively limited;
therefore, this [mind] does not [arise] with respect to sublime (*mahaggata*) or supramundane (*lokuttara*) objects, nor even with respect to sense-sphere phenomena.
It should be understood that it does not follow [the object].

(527–32) What is the purpose of that discourse on reasoning (*yuttivāda*)? For it has been stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) by means of such [reasoning] as "it is similar to the producer" and so forth;
"discourse on reasoning" is a discourse based on reasoning. What is the use of such discourses on reasoning as "it is similar to the producer" and so forth?
Is it stated [there]? For in the *Aṭṭhakathās* (Commentaries), there is indeed the statement: "What is the use of that talk of reasoning?
Although one should say "atthakathāsu," it is written as "aṭṭhakathāsū" by changing the letter *ttha* to *ṭṭha* within the compound.

The teacher has stated this sentence to illustrate the state of being an object (*ārammaṇa*) for those [states] in dependence on states belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*). These are the resultant consciousnesses (*tadārammaṇacittāni*).

In all eleven ways, in every respect, the registration consciousnesses do not take registration even when the impulsion has occurred— namely, not by taking up the designation of name such as "Tissa" and so forth based on the name and clan,
nor by taking up the designation of clan such as "Kaccāyana" or "Kassapa"— nor do they take registration in the fine-material or immaterial realms.

When, with reference to a designation (*paññatti*), whether during the impulsion (*javana*) or even after it has impulsed, no registration (*tadārammaṇa*) is obtained by the teacher for that designation or for another designation mentioned by me;

likewise, when insight (*vipassanā*) has suffering, impermanence, and non-self as its object, no registration is obtained by the teacher. No registrations are obtained even in the case of those fixed in falsehood (*micchattaniyata*).

The four types of javanas associated with wrong view that are fixed in wrongness—due to their nature of wrongness and by way of [the thought] "there is no gift," etc.—are fixed in wrongness (*micchattaniyata*).
Regarding those fixed in wrongness as well, the teacher states that a registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) is not obtained.

Even when javanas proceed taking supramundane phenomena as their object, the teacher states that a registration consciousness is not obtained. Likewise, in the case of sublime phenomena (*mahaggata-dhamma*).
Even when a javana occurs with respect to an object, the subsequent registration (tadārammaṇa) is not obtained by the teacher;
even when a javana occurs with respect to the knowledge of the analytical insights (paṭisambhidāñāṇa), the subsequent registration is not obtained by the teacher.
Furthermore, in the mind-door as well, registration consciousnesses arise in succession immediately following all javanas.
533-4. At the mind-door (manodvāra), there is no striking against an object.

How and by what manner does the emergence of process-consciousness (vīthicitta) from the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) occur? Because even at the mind-door, consciousness arises as it enters the range of the senses even without a striking—precisely by avoiding a striking—therefore the occurrence of process-consciousness takes place.
535–6. The seventy-seven results of evil are the results of the twelve unwholesome (apuñña) consciousnesses, that is, the results of the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness.
These eighty-four occur during the course of existence (*pavatti*). For one unwholesome consciousness associated with joy and accompanied by wrong view, there are seven [resultants]:
eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness; receiving consciousness; and investigating consciousnesses associated with equanimity.
They are unwholesome resultants (*akusalavipāka*). Likewise, for each of the remaining eleven unwholesome states, there are seven resultants.
However, among the eleven types [of consciousness], excluding restlessness-accompanied mind, the rebirth-linkings (*paṭisandhi*) of those eleven types are likewise of eleven kinds. 537–8.
Among all functional consciousnesses (*kriyācitta*), that which is the two-fold adverting (*āvajjana*) and is not a javana—that two-fold adverting—[is the functional resultant].
Because it is merely an instrument (karaṇa-matta) or merely an activity (kiriyā-matta), it is considered by the Blessed One to be like a sky-flower, similar to a sky-flower.

This is the intended meaning here: when that twofold adverting consciousness arises in one whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava), it is appropriate for it to be an inoperative consciousness (kiriyacitta).
If it is asked, "How can it be an activity when it arises in all ordinary worldlings (puthujjana)?", the answer is: because it is merely an instrument.
The principle of fitness (*yutti-hāra*) is that a functional consciousness (*kiriyacitta*) ought to be fruitless, like a wind-flower (*vātapuppha*);

yet it is indeed functional. All functional consciousness, by accomplishing its task through the accomplishment of the function of impulsion (*javana*), attains the state of impulsion and the nature of impulsion.
Just as the flower of a tree whose roots have been cut is without fruit, so too [is the functional consciousness] for one whose roots of ignorance and craving have been severed.
For one who is free from lust (*vītarāga*), all that functional consciousness (*kiriyacitta*) would be fruitless and devoid of result (*vipāka*). 539–40.

However, because the fruit comes from this, it is a condition (*paccaya*); depending on a single phenomenon, the fruit comes—that is, it arises—from this phenomenon, therefore it is a condition. Whatever phenomenon [serves] for the stability or even the arising of another phenomenon...
That which is called "assistance" (upakāra)—that is, when one state is a condition for another state—is what is called a "condition" (paccaya) by the wise.
Arising, source, cause, reason, and condition are considered synonymous by the Blessed One; this statement is an explanatory expression used elsewhere.

Furthermore, as for greed and the other [roots]: that state such as greed which assists by way of being a root—that is, which assists the resultant state by way of its status as a root—that state of greed and so forth is to be understood by the discerning as the "cause" (hetu), meaning it is the cause of the resultant state.

542. Greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as their opposites—non-greed and so forth—are the six causes. By way of genus (*jāti*), according to the classification of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate genera, they may exist in nine ways through nine categories.

543–4. Regarding phenomena such as the wholesome and so forth: that phenomenon which establishes the state of being wholesome and so forth for phenomena such as the wholesome—that is, which establishes the quality of being wholesome and so forth—is called the "root-meaning" (*mūlaṭṭha*). Some say it is thus.

Some teachers say: "This being so, while the roots exist in the sense of being the root for establishing the wholesome and unwholesome nature of phenomena such as the wholesome and unwholesome, the status of the roots—namely greed and the other roots—as a root-condition (hetupaccaya) never actually occurs in relation to the material phenomena co-arisen with them, that is, the material phenomena originated by those consciousnesses (cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa) and the material phenomena born of mind (cittaja-rūpa). This is the intended meaning here.
If, when minds are producing material phenomena, greed and the other [mental factors] also produce those material phenomena because they arise simultaneously with the associated minds,
then according to their view, those mind-born material phenomena would possess the quality of being wholesome and so forth.

However, since material phenomena are never seen to be designated as "wholesome" or otherwise, therefore, for the purpose of making known the wholesome and other qualities of mind-born material phenomena:
It might be argued that those factors such as greed (*lobha*) are not the cause-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) for those types of mind-born materiality (*cittaja-rūpa*).

If this were the case, then mind-born materialities would exist at times even when dissociated [from the mind]; therefore, the sense of being a "root" (*mūlaṭṭha*), which establishes the state of being wholesome and so forth, would not apply to them.
Indeed, it is true that there is the statement beginning with, "But if this were so, of the causes... and so on. Those [factors] such as greed are the causes for those...
The roots do not establish or produce the state of being wholesome and so forth in material phenomena; nevertheless, they are indeed conditions for those material phenomena.

For that reason, any phenomenon that establishes the quality of being wholesome and so forth in wholesome and other states is called "the root-factor" (*mūlaṭṭha*), meaning it has the nature of a root, according to one who knows the conventions—that is, one whose character is to understand technical terminology.
It is to be understood and known by the wise.

547. That meaning which assists in accomplishing the state of being well-established through its accomplishment—that meaning is the "root-meaning" (mūlaṭṭha) and the "essential nature of the root" (mūlasabhāva) of the causes such as greed; this is how it should be grasped by one who discerns.

548–9. Wholesome and unwholesome roots—namely, wholesome roots, unwholesome roots, and functional roots—in every way and in all their modes, all functional roots have reached and attained the state of being a root-condition (*hetupaccaya*) by way of mutual conditionality (*aññamaññapaccayabhāva*) for associated states in the five-aggregate plane;
they have also reached and attained the state of being a root-condition for the mind-born material phenomena produced by them.
These causes have reached and attained the status of root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) for those mental states associated with the four planes of existence. 550–1.
In the sense-sphere realm (*kāma*), resultant roots (*vipāka-hetu*) also reach the status of root-condition for those states associated with themselves;

they also reach the status of root-condition for the kamma-born material phenomena (*kammaja-rūpa*) produced from the [kamma] that has already been performed at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). Therefore, it is precisely at the moment of the arising of the rebirth-linking consciousness— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
The arising of kamma-born material phenomena occurs because, during the course of existence, they have become root-conditions for mind-born material phenomena.

(552–5) In the realm of sense-sphere existence (*kāmāvacara-bhūmi*), resultant roots are root-conditions just like other roots; likewise, in the five-aggregate plane, supramundane resultant roots are root-conditions for mind-born material phenomena and for their associated mental states within the five-aggregate plane.
They exist. In the four-aggregate plane, the roots born of supramundane fruition become root-conditions for their associated states alone.

The other roots born of fruition in the four-aggregate plane and in the immaterial plane become root-conditions for their associated states within their own respective planes—that is, within the same plane or the immaterial plane.
The meaning of "root" (hetu) is the purpose of the roots; it refers both to the roots themselves and...
The causal condition itself, the arising of the causal condition, and the occurrence of the causal condition—in this very way, by this manner.
One for whom a cause of happiness has arisen is "one whose cause of happiness has arisen"; thus it is to be understood. 556–8.
Desire, consciousness, energy, and investigation—these are the four predominants taught by the Teacher, the Lord of the World.
It has been stated. At the time of the arising of consciousness when desire (*chanda*) is made the foremost, that which is the desire is called "desire-predominance" (*chandādhipati*).
The same method applies when concentration is produced by making desire the primary factor;
and this also applies to the remaining three predominances mentioned by me, other than desire-predominance. Whatever state (*dhamma*) is helpful in the sense of being preeminent—
"That Dhamma is the sovereign" means that sovereignty was pointed out by the Blessed One.
It is the awakening of the intelligence of those with good minds, a manifold exertion that is a fire for the fuel of the intelligence of those with evil minds.
Whoever experienced its exceedingly sweet flavor,
they each came to know the entire word of the Jina.

Whoever among the people [studies] this *Abhidhammāvatāra*, which awakens the intellect of those with good minds— that is, of the wise and those of beautiful intelligence— [shall likewise come to know it].

He who knows— that person knows the entire word of the Conqueror— knew that which awakens the intellect, which is manifold, which is a supreme fire for the fuel of the intellects of the foolish and the evil-minded, and which produces extreme sweetness.
Thus [ends] the *Abhidhammāvatāra-ṭīkā*.
The commentary on the Exposition of Miscellaneous Topics is finished.
The eighth chapter.
9. The ninth chapter.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Condition of Karmic Ripening:
There are thirty-two types of resultant consciousness, which are exclusively mundane.
Of these resultant consciousnesses, [there are those occurring] in rebirth-linking and in the course of existence.

Regarding those thirty-two types of resultant consciousness that are purely mundane: just as those formations—meritorious, non-meritorious, and so forth—are conditions for these resultant consciousnesses in the various ways they function within the states of existence, modes of birth, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings, during both rebirth-linking and the course of existence;
even so, those same formations [function] for these resultant consciousnesses within the states of existence, modes of birth, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings.
In the contexts of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and the course of existence (*pavatti*), these should be understood by the wise person who discerns them in that manner.

There are three realms of existence (*bhava*) and four modes of birth (*yoni*). The three realms of existence consist of the sense-sphere realm (*kāmabhava*), the fine-material realm (*rūpabhava*), and the immaterial realm (*arūpabhava*).

The four modes of birth consist of the egg-born (*aṇḍaja*), the womb-born (*jalābuja*), the moisture-born (*saṃsedaja*), and the spontaneously born (*opapātika*). The five destinations (*gati*) consist of the destination of hell-beings, the destination of animals, the destination of hungry ghosts, the destination of human beings, and the destination of devas.

Due to the diversity and manifoldness of the perception of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi-saññā*), and due to the diversity and manifoldness of the body—that is, the material body (*rūpakāya*)—there are the happy destinies of the sense-sphere (*kāmasugati*).
"Diversity" (*nānattā*) means that its self-nature (*sabhāva*) is manifold; those whose material bodies are manifold are "those of manifold bodies" (*nānattakāyā*);
"diversity" (*nānattā*) means that its self-nature is manifold; "perception of diversity" (*nānattasaññā*) is simply perception that is itself diverse.

Because they possess these [perceptions], they are called "possessors of diverse perception. The plane of the first jhāna and the planes of the four lower realms (apāya) are called "possessors of diverse bodies and unified perception.

The plane of the second jhāna is called "possessor of unified body and diverse perception. The plane of the third jhāna, the plane of the Vehapphala Brahmā-world, and the planes of the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa) are called "possessors of unified body and unified perception.
Together with the material forms existing below, the seven stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti) abide.
They are called "stations" (*ṭhitiyo*) because consciousnesses dwell therein; they are "stations of consciousness" (*viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo*) because they are stations for consciousnesses.

The plane of non-perception (*asaññībhūmi*) is not included because of the absence of consciousness there, and the fourth formless-plane is not included because of the absence of active consciousness.
However, if one includes the plane of non-perception and the fourth formless-plane by way of the abodes of beings (*sattāvāsa*), those abodes of beings become exactly nine.
563–8. In the sense-sphere (kāma), the eight volitions termed "meritorious formations" (puññābhisaṅkhāra) fulfill themselves and fulfill their agent;

they produce a desirable existence (bhava) in accordance with one's intention and are thus called "meritorious" (puñña). They form (abhisaṅkharonti) both the result (vipāka) and the matter born of karma (kammajarūpa), and are thus "formations" (abhisaṅkhāra).

These meritorious states themselves are the formations, hence "meritorious formations" (puññābhisaṅkhāra); these very things are what is termed [meritorious formations], hence "termed meritorious formations" (puññābhisaṅkhārasaññitā).

In the sense-sphere, there are eight volitions known as meritorious formations (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*). Regarding the nine resultant consciousnesses associated with equanimity and those nine great resultant consciousnesses that are rootless:

in the happy sense-sphere destinies, because it [the action] exists for a moment subsequent to the moment of the various volitions currently occurring, it is called "of different moments" (*nānākhaṇa*);
that itself is "belonging to different moments" (*nānakkhaṇika*), and that very action is "action belonging to different moments. From the volition currently occurring...

"Parā" means past volition. "Upanissaya-paccaya" is a strong supporting condition (*nissaya-paccaya*); here the prefix *upa-* signifies strength, thus the meaning is "strong condition. This refers both to the asynchronous kamma-condition and to the strong condition.
In two ways—that is, by two modes—these eight [conditions] become conditions for rebirth-linking.
The great wholesome volition (mahākusalacetanā) of the sense-sphere, when accompanied by equanimity,
acts as a condition during its occurrence for the mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity— excluding the mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity that is rootless—

and for the limited-resultant wholesome consciousnesses associated with joy that are rootless and arise in two ways (simultaneous and asynchronous), serving as both asynchronous kamma-condition and decisive support-condition. That same volition...

These same eight great wholesome volitions of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara-mahākusalacetanā) act as conditions during their occurrence for five resultant consciousnesses of the fine-material sphere (rūpabhava)—namely, the wholesome-resultant consciousnesses and the eye-door and ear-door receiving consciousnesses, the joyful and equanimous investigating consciousnesses—by way of two types of conditions: asynchronous kamma-condition and decisive support-condition (nānakkhaṇika-kammūpanissaya-paccaya).
However, they act as conditions for the eight limited [resultants] in the sense-sphere, and likewise for the eight [resultants] in the miserable destinies.
The limited wholesome-resultants— the eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-receiving consciousnesses, as well as the two investigating consciousnesses—
act as conditions during their occurrence at the moment of their arising, but they do not act as conditions at the moment of rebirth-linking.
In the sense-sphere happy realms, the eight great wholesome volitions of the sense-sphere are exactly of the types already described.

In the sense-sphere realm (*kāmasugati*), during the course of existence (*pavatta*), at the moment of occurrence, they act as conditions in two ways—as asynchronous kamma-condition (*kammūpanissaya*) and as decisive-support condition (*upanissaya*)—for sixteen wholesome resultant states;
during the course of existence, at the moment of occurrence, they act as conditions for seven wholesome resultant states.
At rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), at the moment of rebirth-linking, they act as conditions for nine wholesome resultant consciousnesses.

569–74. Regarding meritorious volitional formations (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) in the form realm: in the form-sphere plane, these serve as conditions at the moment of rebirth-linking for the five resultant consciousnesses during the process of rebirth-linking.
Regarding demeritorious volitional formations (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*) in the sense-sphere: in the miserable destinies (*duggati*), these demeritorious formations are of two kinds;

they consist of eleven types of volition (*cetanā*)—the opposites of the wholesome—with the exception of restlessness (*uddhacca*). These [formations] are conditions for the single rebirth-linking consciousness in the sense-sphere miserable destinies.
At rebirth-linking, at the moment of rebirth-linking, they act as conditions in two ways by way of asynchronous kamma and decisive support conditions.

The twelve unwholesome volitions, during the course of existence, at the very moment of their occurrence, act as conditions for the six unwholesome-resultant types of consciousness belonging to the eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-receiving classes;
however, at rebirth-linking, at the moment of rebirth-linking, they do not act as conditions.
During the course of existence, at the moment of occurrence, and at rebirth-linking, at the moment of rebirth-linking,
