the unwholesome-resultant [consciousnesses] become conditions for the seven— namely, the eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, receiving-,
and investigating-consciousnesses. Likewise, in the sense-sphere happy realms, the twelve unwholesome volitions are similarly [conditions] for those seven in the sense-sphere happy realms.

And these [twelve unwholesome volitions] act as conditions for those seven unwholesome resultant [consciousnesses] during their occurrence— that is, at the moment of occurrence— but they do not act as conditions for them at the moment of rebirth-linking during rebirth-linking.

For all four types of consciousness, likewise in the fine-material existence (rūpabhava), those same twelve unwholesome volitions act as conditions for those four unwholesome resultants known as eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, receiving-consciousness, and investigating-consciousness in that fine-material existence.
Thus, during the course of existence, these [formations] act as conditions at the moment of occurrence; however, at rebirth-linking, they do not act as conditions at the moment of rebirth-linking.

Furthermore, that unwholesome volitional formation acts as a condition for the perception of undesirable forms and so forth within the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), and for the perception of unpleasant forms and so forth as objects within that same sense-sphere existence.

It is the condition for the four types of unwholesome consciousness. For this is the truth, as stated in such passages as: "And that [consciousness] results in the attainment of undesirable form and so forth within the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava).
Unpleasant forms and other objects do not exist, nor are they found, in the Brahma-world.
Likewise, the immovable formation (āneñjasaṅkhāra) is called "immovable" (āneñja) because it does not move, does not quiver, and does not shake; and it is immovable...
That [condition] is "volitional formation" (*saṅkhāra*); thus it is immovable volitional formation (*āneñjasaṅkhāra*).

Likewise, during the occurrence of the four resultant consciousnesses in the formless realm, at the moment of their occurrence, and at rebirth-linking, at the moment of rebirth-linking, this immovable volitional formation acts as a condition.

In these states of existence, these aforementioned types of conditions function, in the manner described, for both rebirth-linking and the course of existence, according to how and by what means they do so.

And in whatever manner they serve as conditions through various asynchronous kamma and decisive-support conditions, in that very same way and by those respective modes should they be understood by a wise person who discerns them.
This same method is to be understood regarding the matrices and so forth; this same method applies to the matrices, destinies, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings.

The method stated by me regarding the states of existence (*bhava*) should be understood by the wise. Herein, this statement made concerning those states of existence from the beginning serves as a mere indication of the heading and a mere illustration of the means.

578–81. Meritorious volitional formations (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) are, without distinction, [present] in both states of existence by way of meritorious volitional formations pertaining to the sense-sphere (*kāma*) and meritorious volitional formations pertaining to the fine-material sphere (*rūpa*).

And the meritorious formation (puññābhisaṅkhāra), by way of non-distinction and equality, having granted rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) in the two types of existence—the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere—that formation produces and brings about every result.
Likewise, it is to be understood in the four modes of birth (yoni), such as the egg-born and so forth;
just as the meritorious formation [functions] in the two types of existence, so too does that meritorious formation [function] in the four modes of birth, such as the egg-born and so forth.
It should be understood by the wise. The statement "among those born from eggs, etc. was spoken with reference to the human state of the Paccekabuddhas Paduma and others.
Furthermore, by way of the many gods and humans, such a formation of merit should be understood by the wise as occurring only within the two [higher] realms of existence.

Likewise, regarding the stations of consciousness characterized by diversity of body and so forth—namely, those with diversity of body and diversity of perception, and those with diversity of body and unity of perception—it should be understood by the wise in that same manner.

By way of one who possesses a single body and diverse perceptions, and one who possesses a single body and a single perception, that formation of merit is to be known by the wise in relation to the four stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*).

Likewise, by way of those who possess diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, those who possess diverse bodies and a single perception, those who possess a single body and diverse perceptions, and those who possess a single body and a single perception— in relation to these fourfold abodes of beings as described, that formation of merit is to be known by the wise.

Thus, by this kind of meritorious formation (puññābhisaṅkhāra) described by me, there is a condition in two ways— by way of asynchronous kamma and decisive support (kammūpanissaya)— for the twenty-one types of results,
namely the sixteen results of wholesome sense-sphere kamma and the five results of form-sphere kamma, within existence (bhava), birth (yoni), destiny (gati),
stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), and abodes of beings (sattāvāsa), as appropriate.
582–3. In the sense-sphere realm, the formation of demerit leads to rebirth in the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) via the egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born, and spontaneous modes of birth;
within the destinies of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals; in one station of consciousness characterized by diversity of body and unity of perception;
and in one abode of beings characterized by diversity of body and unity of perception—thus it is twofold in one such abode.

At the moment of its occurrence, during the course of existence, and at rebirth-linking, during the moment of rebirth-linking, that unwholesome volitional formation (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*) serves as a condition by way of various non-simultaneous kamma and decisive-support conditions. 584–6.

Likewise for the immovable volitional formation (*āneñjasaṅkhāra*): in exactly the same manner, the immovable volitional formation [serves as a condition] in a single fine-material existence and in a single immaterial existence.
In one spontaneously born mode of birth (*opapātika-yoni*) and one divine destiny (*deva-gati*), within three mental abidings (*citta-ṭhiti*)— namely, the planes of the base of infinite space,
the base of infinite consciousness, and the base of nothingness— and within the fourfold abodes of beings (*sattāvāsa*) by way of the four immaterial planes,
there is a twofold relationship for the four immaterial resultant consciousnesses through the conditions of asynchronous kamma and decisive support (*upanissaya-paccaya*).
The immovable volitional formation (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*) is the condition. Thus, by way of rebirth-linking and the course of existence,
in the cases of existence and so forth, in this manner and according to the classification stated by me,
a wise person should understand exactly how those formations become the conditions for these resultant consciousnesses through the process of rebirth-linking and the course of existence.

587–90. There is no transmigration (*saṅkanti*) of material and immaterial phenomena; however, while transmigration exists for material phenomena, there is no transmigration or passing over for mental phenomena—those things termed mind and mental factors.

Since there is no such state of transmigration, and since there is no passing over of material phenomena from a past existence into this present existence, how and by what means does rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*) arise?
Could it be so in any way? There is no transference of consciousness; there is no transference or passing over of consciousness from a past existence into this present existence.

Therefore, apart from the past cause—that is, excluding the past—there is no manifestation of consciousness here in this present existence. It is merely a matter of form and name (nāmarūpa) that has obtained its conditions.
Only a mere designation of form and name arises when its conditions are well-obtained.
Thus, in the manner described by me, this mere matter and mere mentality arising after having obtained conditions is born as a mere designation of form and name.

In this same way, this mere matter and mere mentality arising after having obtained conditions in the manner described by me is [born as] another existence, a different becoming, a rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
"It approaches" means it goes toward. Thus, by way of conventional designation (*samaññā*), it is spoken of through worldly usage;
yet there is no "being" (*satta*), for "being" and "living soul" (*jīva*) are synonyms, nor does a "self" (*attā*) exist.
Having made this clear, [it is said]: "But as for the process of rebirth for that being, this is the process of rebirth."
"I shall demonstrate this process of rebirth-linking, which is very difficult to awaken to and extremely difficult to discern,
by making it manifest; understand this well and thoroughly, attend to it well and thoroughly, and—
without directing the mind toward various objects through the influence of greed— place it in the mind as if one were inserting a priceless jewel into a diamond casket."
The meaning is as follows: In his past existence, when he was near death,
while his faculties such as the eye-faculty were perishing like a green palm leaf placed in the heat and drying up within his body,
and while only the heart-base remained and the consciousness consisting of bodily sensitivity had ceased, at that moment [the mind] was dependent upon that base.

"Dependent on the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*). It should be understood that the term "consciousness" (*citta*) is stated with reference to the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), mind-door adverting (*manodvārāvajjana*), and impulsion (*javana*).

"Previously practiced" means that in a time prior to this present moment, one has practiced or habitually performed either meritorious karma or non-meritorious karma, or else the sign of the deed (*kammanimitta*) or the sign of the destination (*gatinimitta*) [arises] together with the fruit of that karma.
Having taken hold of that which is presented at the doors, the mind proceeds as a serviceable consciousness by way of mind-door adverting and impulsion.

Thus, this consciousness—that impulsion-citta—proceeding in the manner described by me, having obtained its conditions and having obtained the condition of an object, when it has impelled an unwholesome impulsion toward an object whose dangers are concealed by ignorance: of that...

In the case of a wholesome impulsion (*kusalajavana*), when that wholesome impulsion has impelled with respect to its object—such as karma—and the fault of that object is not concealed by ignorance (*avijjā*);

and [in the case of an unwholesome impulsion], when that unwholesome object—such as karma—is impelled by an impulsion and the fault of that object is concealed by ignorance that occurred prior to that cognitive process (*cittavīthi*).
"Craving" (*taṇhā*) refers to the greed co-arising with the unwholesome impulsion, or [the greed] when the unwholesome impulsion has impelled from that cognitive process.
Greed that has arisen in the prior stage is craving (*taṇhā*).

"It inclines" means that, without causing [the mind] to grasp another object, it causes that very object—known as the sign of the deed (*kamma-nimitta*) or the sign of destiny (*gati-nimitta*)—to be grasped by way of a firm grasp; this is the meaning.
As for the concomitant formations (*sahajā saṅkhārā*), they are the volitions (*cetanā*) born together with that consciousness, which impel—that is, set in motion—that very same object.

In this present existence, that consciousness—which has been led along by craving proceeding through a single continuum—leaves and abandons this former heart-base (hadayavatthu) which served as its support, just like a man crossing a stream who lets go of the rope he was holding from the near bank;
the meaning is that the death-consciousness arises and then ceases. Another [consciousness] born of karma...

Having obtained—or even without obtaining—the heart-base (hadayavatthu), which serves as its support and arises from a different kamma, that consciousness termed rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) proceeds by means of conditions such as objects.

The word "having obtained" is stated with reference to existence in the sense-sphere and fine-material realms; the word "without obtaining" is stated with reference to existence in the immaterial realm.
It has been stated. Herein, among these consciousnesses, the wise should understand that the preceding consciousness, mentioned by the word "abandons," is the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*),
and the subsequent consciousness, mentioned by the words "proceeds by way of conditions such as the object," is the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*).
600–6. Thus, this very rebirth-linking consciousness has not come here from a previous existence into this present final existence;
nor has it appeared as a rebirth-linking consciousness without excluding causes such as karma.
Furthermore, in this statement, there is no [transfer] of this rebirth-linking consciousness from a previous existence into this present existence.

Regarding its non-arrival from the past existence: when this rebirth-linking consciousness arises in the present existence due to causes in the past existence—namely, conditions such as karma—the examples of an echo, a lamp, a seal, and so forth, serve here as illustrations for that non-arrival from the past existence and its arising in the present due to causes in the past existence.
In this context, these examples of an echo, a lamp, a seal, and the like illustrate the meaning.
There are similes. Just as, apart from the actual location where echoes and the like occur, sounds and other causes—such as sounds and so forth—arise elsewhere by coming [to that place];

this is what is meant: in this place, objects such as sounds, lamps, and seals produced by people become the conditions for echoes, reflections, and seal-impressions occurring in other locations, such as on the other side of a mountain.

They are dependent on causes. Just as those echoes and so forth exist when those conditions such as sound are present, and do not exist when they are absent, even so should consciousness be understood by the discerning one as a consciousness that proceeds from past existence by way of the consciousness of present existence.
Through the continuity of the stream, there is a sense of unity by way of the binding of the stream.
There is no unification of consciousness as it occurs by way of past existence and present existence;
nor is there diversity, nor manifoldness, nor distinctness of that consciousness. However, if there were a binding of a continuum, there would necessarily be oneness;
if there were a binding of a continuum, there would necessarily be oneness—that is, unification—of that consciousness, due to its nature as milk.
The meaning is that what has arisen from milk—which has the nature of flowing—could never at any time whatsoever possess a solid nature;
it would always remain as milk, which has the nature of flowing. Furthermore, there is another way of explaining this:
if that absolute difference—that state of being absolutely distinct—were to exist for that consciousness, then the person who is the owner of the milk would [simultaneously] be the owner of the curd.
It would not be so. At the time of milk, the one who is the master and owner of the milk would, having abandoned its nature of oozing, no longer be the master of that curd when it arises;
consequently, the person who was the owner of the milk would become someone else who is neither the master nor the owner of that curd—this is the meaning.
Because of this reason, in this determination of the process of rebirth-linking...
Neither absolute identity nor absolute difference should be accepted by a wise person who understands the proper occasion.

Thus, when there is existence—devoid of the manifestation of transmigration and characterized by the mode of non-transmigratory manifestation as described by me in this way—there occurs in this human individuality an equality of the aggregates and so forth; whatever aggregates there are, [they arise in this state].
Because these [karmic formations] have ceased here in this human existence,
there is the arrival in another world— due to the fruit of that karma performed by people here in this human existence,
which serves as the condition for that fruit— and thus, from another being, from another karma, and from that other being, it is experienced by a different being.

If that fruit were to arise from an action performed by one [person] for another, then by the statement "of another being," it would follow that even the karma of a sectarian being could yield a fruit for someone else; therefore, for this reason, all this procedure stated by you is not correct.
"Regarding this, he says" means that standing in this position, the objector says:
—But surely, if this is so, does it not follow that statements such as "when there is existence characterized by manifestation without transmigration" imply determinism? It is said in reply:
That fruit which occurs within a single continuum (*saṃtāna*) is a fruit that belongs to no other being, nor does it arise from the karma of another;
rather, the volitional formation (*abhisankhāra*) of seeds is for the purpose of this meaning expressed by the phrase "in one continuum," and so forth.
It is the accomplisher and producer of this meaning.
Furthermore, the fruit occurring within a single continuum does not belong to another being, nor does that fruit arise from the karma of another.
The formative activity of seeds [establishes] this meaning: "Furthermore, within a single..."
It is the establisher and producer of this meaning, beginning with the words "in the continuity" (*santāne*). When a preparation of seeds is made by people using a substance such as honey,
that seed first obtains a condition— namely, the condition consisting of the honey and so forth— and subsequently,
due to the preparation of the seed with honey and so forth, it produces its fruit for that seed after a lapse of time.
At another time it becomes sweet. For this statement, beginning with "the processing of seeds," is indeed true.

For those very seeds first planted by people with honey and so forth do not, due to that processing, reach a state of sweetness at another time, nor even the fruit or the condition of bearing fruit. Thus, in this manner, this was [said] by me.
The statement beginning with “But in a single continuum,” etc., should be understood by the wise. Furthermore, there is another method:

by means of such actions as learning, missiles, or medicinal herbs performed during childhood or youth—that is, by that which is associated with youth—and which has the nature of yielding fruit in the time of old age, this meaning beginning with “But in a single continuum,” etc., should be illustrated by the wise.

616–20. The Opponent further says: Even if this is so—that is, even if that karma exists in the manner described by me, and even if that karma is present—does that karma, while existing at this very moment, become a condition for the fruit?
Or else, would it not be a condition if it were non-existent at this very moment? [If you say it is a condition,] then karma that is non-existent at this very moment...

Or it is a condition for the fruit. If it is the case that an existing [kamma] is a condition for the fruit, then at the moment of its occurrence—that is, at the moment when that kamma exists—it would have to be accompanied by its ripening (pāka) simultaneously with the causal kamma itself.
Alternatively, there is another way: an existing, ceased kamma is the condition for the ripening.

If there were a condition [for the fruit], it would mean that the fruit exists either at the time of the activity of that kamma, or before the time of its activity, or after the time of its activity—meaning at a time when that kamma is non-existent.
"It would be a permanent fruit" means that the fruit would exist at all times, devoid of the condition of kamma. The Teacher says: "Bhikkhus, greed..."
In such passages as, "Abandon [these], and I myself am the guarantor for the attainment of stream-entry," karma should be regarded as being like the guarantor.
The fruit arising from karma should be regarded as being like the fruit of stream-entry.
It is precisely because it has been performed by people that that karma becomes a condition for the fruit; yet its actual presence does not persist.
The existence of that non-existent karma, or its non-existence, does not occur.

This is the *Abhidhammāvatāra*; this *Abhidhammāvatāra* illuminates the ultimate truth (*paramattha*), reveals the true nature of things, increases joy and wisdom in the minds of listeners, and causes the wise to withdraw their minds from various sense objects.
It should be heard with careful attention.
Thus ends the commentary on the Exposition of the Conditions for Merit and its Ripening in the *Abhidhammāvatāratīkā*.
The Ninth Chapter.

An Exposition on the Analysis of Matter.

622. Regarding the matter stated at the beginning: that matter which arises immediately after consciousness, and that matter which follows immediately after consciousness and mental factors—stated by the Teacher at the outset of the treatise in such words as "consciousness, mental factors, and matter"—from this point forward, I shall now provide a brief exposition of that matter in summary.

623. "That which is disturbed is form" (*rūpyate iti rūpam*): that class of phenomena (*dhammajāta*) which is disturbed—that is, undergoes transformation—by adverse conditions such as cold and so forth.

Likewise, "that which makes manifest is form" (*rūpayatīti rūpam*): that class of phenomena which, by undergoing a transformation of color, manifests the state of mind and the underlying intention (*adhyāśaya*) present in the heart.
Thus it is called "form. What is it? It is the sense-sphere of visible form (*varṇāyatana*). [He is] one who has transcended existence in the realms of form and formlessness, and is beautiful.

The Blessed One, who has transcended existence in both form and formlessness, spoke of form; he, being well-formed, spoke of form—that is, he explained it. (625–6) "By the great element" (*mahābhūtena*):

that which has a great arising (*mahanto bhūto uppatti*) is a "great element" (*mahābhūta*); [the Buddha spoke] by means of that. Alternatively, because of his deceptive nature, he is equal to the great elements (*mahābhūtasama*).
(630) "With a mind free from clinging" (*nirupādānamānaso*): one whose consciousness is devoid of grasping.
633. *Tassa sampatti* means the successful accomplishment of that task.
634. *Upabrūhanarasā* means having the function of increasing.
637. Regarding *āsayānusaye ñāṇaṃ*: here, *āsaya* (disposition) means—
The views of eternalism and annihilationism, the inclination that accords with truth, and the knowledge of things as they really are—this is what is called the underlying tendency (*āsaya*).

"Existence," Kaccāna, is one extreme; "non-existence," Kaccāna, is another extreme. This "existence" is one extreme, this "non-existence" is another extreme, and these two parts constitute the extremes.
This is the view of eternalism (*sassatadṛṣṭi*). "It does not exist," Kaccāna, this is the second extreme; this is the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
"Acceptance in accordance with truth" means knowledge that conforms to the Four Truths; the meaning is the knowledge of equanimity toward formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa*).
And "knowledge as it really is" is the knowledge that sees name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) together with its conditions. This is called the "settling of the underlying tendency."

This is called "the underlying tendency" (*āsaya*). Knowledge regarding such an underlying tendency is what is meant by "knowledge of the underlying tendencies. As for "latent dispositions" (*anusaya*), there are seven latent dispositions, beginning with the latent disposition of views (*diṭṭhānusaya*).

"The higher and lower degrees of the faculties" (*indriyānaṃ paropara*) means that, according to whether they are superior (*para*) or inferior (*opara*) in intensity and power, this being possesses either a sharp faculty of faith (*tikkhasaddhindriya*), a weak faculty of faith (*mudusaddhindriya*), or a base faculty of faith (*hīnasaddhindriya*). The same applies to the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*) and the others.
The same method applies here. Thus is the knowledge of the higher and lower faculties of beings.

(638) Regarding "the knowledge of omniscience" (*sabbaññutā-ñāṇa*), the fourfold functional consciousness (*kriyā-cātukka*) of the sense-sphere accompanied by three roots (*tihetuka-kāmāvacara*) is to be understood.
(641) Internally, it is delimited by the frontal sinuses and the brain matter.
645. "The configuration of the arising of beings" refers to the sense-base of the appearance of beings as female or male.
647. These ten requisites, which arise from four [causes], become forty by way of the four conditions.
652. "Established" means firmly settled.
658. Of those exceeding [others], that is, exceeding the earth. 660–2. "When there is a distinction" means:

when there is a distinction among the four elements which serve as the basis, one should understand that the distinctness of the translucent elements (*pasāda*) arises through the specific nature of karma alone, having entirely abandoned the conceptualization of a distinction among all [other factors].
663. "It is sounded" means it is uttered. "They taste" means they relish.

668. From "after the first eon" (*parato*) onwards, it should be understood that two types of entities arise at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). The statement beginning with "they also arise during the course of existence" (*pavattepi samuṭṭhāyā*) was spoken with reference to Soṇa Kumāra and others.
672. "That is not the cause of the sex organ": that pair of faculties would not be the cause of the sex organ.
"Of that" refers to the sex organ. 674. "Carrying away" (*ubbāhana*) means removal.

676–7. Whatever material substance such as food and drink is produced by kamma, it carries away the fire; yet, being merely a single entity, that substance of food and drink is not able to sustain life alone. However, when combined, they are able to sustain life.

By means of this class of phenomena—characterized as a transformation of the air element—which is grasped through the apprehension of the body (kāya) and through the contemplation of the apprehension of the body, the wise understand the state of those who communicate their own existence by means of the body, that is, the physical body (rūpakāya).
Thus, therefore, it is bodily intimation.
681. In a cognitive process consisting of a single adverting moment, [the body] receives support from the air element produced by the six preceding consciousnesses. 684.
"Together with sound" means simultaneously with the sound.
690-1. Now, as for the manifestation of these three qualities—lightness and so forth—in due order: health is lightness (*lahutā*);
a massaged [metal] is plasticity (*mudutā*); and refined gold is wieldiness (*kammaññatā*).

Furthermore, because the triad of action cannot produce the triad of lightness and so forth, but rather the triad of nutriment alone produces the triad of lightness and so forth, that triad is called "the triad of manifestation" (*tijā*).

693. Regarding the phrase "stated by way of the diversity of modes": here, "diversity of modes" is stated by way of the mode of accumulation (*ācaya-ākāra*) and the mode of continuity (*anubandhatā-ākāra*).

"According to the disposition of those to be trained (*veneyya*)," according to some, means that some of those to be trained understand the nature of birth (*jātirūpa*) by way of accumulation, while others understand it by way of continuity.
Thus, the nature of birth is stated in two ways according to the manner of understanding of those to be trained.

694. When one's own nature has not departed—that is, when one's own nature remains—those teachers who assert that [the hindrances] are material form (*rūpa*) must be refuted. How so? "Surely you, O Sage, are a Perfectly Awakened One; there are no hindrances for you. This means:

since you are surely (*addhā*), that is, absolutely (*ekantena*), a Sage (*muni*) and a Perfectly Awakened One (*sambuddha*), there are no states that are hindrances (*nīvaraṇā dhammā*) for you, for yourself.

If, in the statement "there are none," the hindrance of torpor (*middha*) were to enter into the form-body (*rūpa*), then because the form-body exists, the Blessed One would have had to say, "There are no hindrances for you.

The hindrance of sloth-and-torpor (*thinamiddha-nīvaraṇa*), together with the hindrance of ignorance (*avijjā-nīvaraṇa*), is both a hindrance itself and associated with the hindrances. Thus, because of this statement regarding association—
Because of the absence of associated materiality (*rūpa*), that too should not be stated. "Not a pre-arising condition" means it is a mutuality condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*).
If dullness and drowsiness (*thinamiddha*) were material, how could they be mutual even in the immaterial realm? The meaning is that they could not be so. For it is said:
"In the immaterial realm as well, the hindrance of dullness and drowsiness arises dependent upon the hindrance of sensual desire. By this statement...
And it cannot be of the nature of torpor; the meaning is: how could it exist in the formless realm? Thus, the claim that "torpor itself is formless" must be rejected.
Furthermore, because there are statements proving the arising of this torpor even in the formless realm, the wise person should understand that the conclusion here is that it is "formless.
705–6. "Twenty kinds of matter by way of kamma": the eight faculties, the eight bases, the analysis of the aggregates, continuity, accumulation, and space are born of kamma.
Those produced by mind (*cittaja*) are sound, the triad beginning with lightness (*lahutā*), the inseparable [material qualities], continuity, accumulation, and space.

Those produced by temperature (*utujā*) are sound, the triad beginning with lightness, the inseparable [material qualities], continuity, accumulation, and space. Those produced by nutriment (*āhāraja*) are the triad beginning with lightness, the inseparable [material qualities], continuity, accumulation, and space.
707–17. "If those too were to be born": if even those [qualities] characterized by aging and impermanence were to be born, such being the case...

However, for those [elements], there would be aging, impermanence, and disintegration. Indeed, since it is true that speech does not cook, nor is it broken, therefore the statement that "for them there would be cooking and disintegration" is non-existent.

This pair—aging and impermanence—does not arise because they consist of the cooking and disintegration of what has been born, i.e., produced form. Someone might think: "Could this be understood here? Regarding this:

In the section concerning the determination of aging and impermanence, if anyone possessed the intelligence or knowledge [to discern this], then just as the statement "birth arises" is illustrated by the expression "accumulation in form," so too would there be such an understanding: "let decay also decay; let dissolution also dissolve.
Yet, birth does not arise. Thus it is by way of this method that one should discern it.
*Ñeyyā*. Birth (*jāti*) is explained as the manifestation (*nibbatti*) of that which is being born, namely, of produced form (*nipphanna-rūpa*).
In this regard, there may be understanding for those people who have such an expression.

For those produced phenomena (*nipphanna-rūpa-dhamma*) that possess birth, that birth is a conventional designation for their arising (*abhinibbatti-sammuti*), serving as the condition (*paccaya*) for the linguistic usage of "being conditioned by that" (*tappaccayatva-vohāra*) for those produced phenomena.

Just as that which has acquired the designation "kamma-born" and so forth indeed receives its conventional designation, so too these various modes of maturation of those produced material phenomena receive the conventional designation of "origination" (abhinibbatti-sammuti), namely, the conventional usage of their being conditions for that [continuity].
Such might be the thought of that person. To that person it should be said: "This pair—continuity and accumulation—is produced from kamma and other such causes."
Just so, these various results of maturation never receive the conventional designation of "arising from karma" and so forth.

For what reason? Because it is true that they do not receive such designations due to the absence of those various results of maturation at the momentary arising—which is termed the "potency" of the productive conditions such as karma.
This is because, in the momentary arising described above, there is an absence of a succession of births.

That birth receives [the designation]; for that reason, birth alone receives the conventional expression of "arising" (*abhinibbatti*) as its causal status, whereas the other two—aging and impermanence—do not.
It is not appropriate to say of that pair, aging and impermanence, "it ages" or "it breaks up. Why? Because at the moment when the conditions such as karma exert their influence, that...
Because of the absence of conditions for the pair consisting of aging and impermanence.
(718–23) This aging and death is both impermanent and conditioned; since the Blessed One has stated that it is called "the impermanent-conditioned," the pair of aging and impermanence arises.
If you think thus, then [you must admit] that it indeed arises.
The statement by the Blessed One should not be so expressed. Why? Because it was stated by way of a particular mode of teaching—by means of a figurative expression such as:

“This [aging and death] is impermanent and conditioned; indeed, aging and death are likewise. Thus, by this method of teaching, the Blessed One indicated that for impermanent, produced material phenomena, aging and death—which are designated as "aging and death"—are themselves impermanent and conditioned by their very nature. Furthermore, because they are modifications born of mind, the intimations (viññatti) are said to be "born of mind."

As if it were said, so indeed was it spoken by the Blessed One. If this were the case, and if this triad of characteristics of being affected by change (ruppanalakkhaṇa) did not exist in any way or in any manner because it had never been born—like a flower in the sky—and if one were to argue that it is therefore permanent like unconditioned Nibbāna, then the opponent might say:
"Both these statements—that 'it does not exist' and 'it is not permanent'—should not have been spoken by the Blessed One. Why?
Because it occurs by way of being dependent upon the supporting factors (nissayadhamma), such that when those supports—earth and so forth—are present, those three characteristics are also present;
therefore, like a flower in the sky, those three characteristics do not not exist—the meaning is that they do exist.
And because those three characteristics are not found in the absence of earth and so forth, [it follows that] Nibbāna...
Likewise, it is not permanent.

(724–5) Limitation and so forth are unproduced (*aniṣpanna*). Because they are modifications of those very same material phenomena—which are themselves produced—and because they are shown to be the differentiators of those [phenomena] described by way of the remaining conditioned factors, they are said to be both produced and conditioned. The rest has its meaning already explained.
This [work] was undertaken by that monk,
who desires the welfare of others and wishes to go forth into the Abhidhamma Piṭaka as fully mastered by the General of the Dhamma.
However, it must be studied thoroughly and correctly.
Any bhikkhu who wishes to attain and reach the true nature as fully expounded by the General of the Dhamma in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka—
that bhikkhu, seeking his own welfare, should study it with care, reverence, and correctness through investigation, reflection, and recitation.
This *Abhidhammāvatāra* should be studied.
Thus ends the commentary on the Analysis of Matter (*Rūpavibhāgavaṇṇanā*) within the *Abhidhammāvatāra-ṭīkā*.

The Eleventh Chapter:
Explanation of the Description of Nibbāna.
769. It is "small" because it weaves together existence and non-existence; it is "great" because it sews together existence.

"Relinquishment of all acquisitions" means the relinquishing of all conditioned acquisitions, defilement-acquisitions, and aggregate-acquisitions. "The taste of deathlessness" means possessing the attainment of deathlessness.
"Nibbāna was asked by the one who had asked" refers to the Elder Sāriputta, who had asked the Sugata about Nibbāna. "Of both suttas... [and so forth].
The meaning is: "of the two discourses spoken by the General of the Dhamma. Because it is the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for destruction means because it is the powerful cause for destruction.
At the moment of heedfulness, there would be only the destruction of lust and so forth regarding various phenomena; Nibbāna itself would be [merely] that.
All foolish worldlings (*puthujjana*) would have attained Nibbāna and realized cessation (*nirodha*). What more is there to say?

"What further reason is there? is the meaning. Because lust and the other [defilements] are conditioned (*saṅkhata*), Nibbāna would possess the characteristics of the conditioned for those conditioned things.
"But what is here? means: among these moments, which moment do you speak of? "Only when they are exhausted" means:
only when existence (*bhava*) and the rest have been exhausted. "Without superior" means: one whose task is accomplished.

771. "Lacking faith" (*assaddha*) means being devoid of external faith. "One who has vomited his hopes" (*vantāsa*) means one by whom hopes—that is, craving (*taṇhā*)—have been vomited out or cast away.
"Leading to escape" (*nissaraṇiya*) means connected with escape. That is to say, renunciation (*nekkhamma*); for this is the escape and the cessation of sensual pleasures.
It is the cessation and the escape from whatever has come to be, which is conditioned and of the nature of dependently arisen phenomena.

Thus, because of the fault of reaching non-existence (abhāva) in that which is called "escape" (nissaraṇa) when described in this manner, there would also be a non-existence of the first jhāna and the sphere of infinite space, which are themselves called "escapes. "There is escape" means there is Nibbāna.
"Of arising and so forth" refers to arising, persistence, and dissolution. "Due to the absence of proliferation" (papañca) means due to the absence of craving, conceit, and views.
772. "Apalokita" means that which has the nature of being invisible.
774. "Abyāpajjha" means free from suffering. "Akkhara" means indestructible. 777. It produces faith and wisdom;
it destroys delusion regarding the Tathāgata’s doctrine and the words of the Victor, and it gives rise to discernment (paññā).

It is the cause of wisdom and brings about serene confidence. Regarding the phrase "rich in meaning and phrasing" (*atthabyañjanasālinam*): it means possessing the essence of both meaning and phrasing;

it is exceedingly sweet. For that person who knows this *Abhidhammāvatāra*—described in such a manner—which is the essence of the Conqueror’s Dispensation for those who know its essence, which inspires wonder and is marvelous, that person reaches a firm conclusion regarding the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, which is profound, subtle, and the domain of subtle knowledge.
He attains, he reaches, the supreme consummation.
Thus ends the commentary on the Description of Nibbāna in the *Abhidhammāvatāra-ṭīkā*.

12. The Twelfth Chapter: Explanation of the Exposition of Designations (Paññatti-niddesa-vaṇṇanā)
It is called *saṅkhā* because it is reckoned (*saṅkhāyati*); the meaning is that it is spoken of (*kathīyati*). What is it that is spoken of? It is spoken of as "I" and "mine.
"Designation according to its kind" (*tajjāpaññatti*) means a designation arisen in accordance with that [basis], such as the eye, ear, and so forth.

"Of one" (*ekassava*) means having taken the name "deer" for a single named dhamma, and having taken the name "deer" for many named dhammas. "Only the collection" (*samūhameva*) means the collection of named dhammas itself.

"Previously grasped convention" (*gahitapubbasaṅketa*) means that by this [consciousness], a convention was previously grasped. What is it? It is the mind-door adverting consciousness and the javana-consciousness. By means of that, through a designation (*paññatti*) grasped by it, it is known as "sentient beings" (*sattā*) and is called "born of kamma" (*kammajā*).
"Woman and man" are *itthipurisā*; those of whom these are the first are "woman-and-man-beginning," and [the term refers] to them.
778. "The third point" (*tatiyā koṭī*) means the third section.
Thus ends the commentary on the Exposition of Designation in the *Abhidhammāvatāra-ṭīkā*.
This is the twelfth chapter.
Chapter Thirteen:
Explanation of the Penetration of the Agent "Of the experiencer" means of the one who experiences pleasure and pain. "Dependent on whom" means those for whom [the experience] is dependent and bound.
"Of those [results], their existence is dependent on that [kamma]; of them. Here, at this point, the Teacher states the resolution:

"Whence is this inclination of yours toward that?"—that is to say, whence, by what reason, is this inclination or partiality of yours toward that [result] here, in this case where there is no other agent, even though there exists one's own self designated as the "enemy"? (In the absence of an agent).
If wholesome states and so forth exist, how and for what reason could there be a contradiction with karma? Furthermore, "athāpi" (moreover) indicates another method of explanation.
"Kiñcettha" (what is there here? means that in this objection there is something yet to be said; first, state what remains, for your objection is not yet complete.
"Tassa" (of that) refers to oneself. "Kārakavedakattābhāvo" (the absence of being an agent and an experiencer) means that there would be an absence of the state of being an agent and an experiencer.
Now, "if it does not exist" means that if, when there is no destruction of the self, there is also no destruction of volition.

"The admission is inferior" means that the admission that "the self is not other than volition" is inferior. "In the manner stated" refers to the manner stated as: "when there is no destruction of the self, there is no destruction of volition.
"Contrary" would mean a contrary apprehension, such as: "when there is no destruction of the self, there is destruction of volition."
"Let the self perish, let volition remain; yet it does not exist in this way"—thus, let the self perish, let volition remain, but such a grasping does not occur.
Abandoning, repeatedly abandoning the position of non-otherness—that "the self is not other than volition"—his thesis is inferior, thus he is one whose thesis is inferior (*paṭiññā-hīna*).
There is no commonality or state of being a single part between the two consciousnesses.
And if you were to say, "Even if this is so, what fault is there in the absence of a single part for both?"—as for that statement of yours:
"Just as form, taste, smell, and so forth, though existing in a single location, are distinct by way of their characteristics."
What was said by her—that speech is improper; the meaning is that it is not suitable.
Your proposition is inferior because of the "difference in characteristic" of volitions (cetanā) existing in a single part [of the self].

And if this were so—if you were to ask, "What fault would there be if this [self] were distinct from volition?"—then there would be the statement, "The self is non-conscious," due to the fault previously mentioned: "It would be like a wall, a tree, a stone, or grass. This refers to the fault stated earlier.
780. "There are beings of spontaneous birth" means that there exist beings who are spontaneously born.
781. "The taking up of the burden" means the grasping of the burden. "The laying down of the burden" means the setting aside of the burden. 783.
The accumulation of the bones, the mass of bones, of a single person would, in one *kappa*, form a heap equal to a mountain.

785. O Māra, you conceive of a "being" (satta); on what do you base this? The apprehension of a "being" is merely your own adherence to a false view (diṭṭhigata). This is simply a heap of pure formations (saṅkhāra-puñja); in this world, no "being" is to be found. 787.
That bhikkhu who constantly and perpetually reflects upon this treatise attains for himself supreme wisdom (paññā) in its fullness and vastness.
788. That bhikkhu who studies this *Abhidhammāvatāra*—which transcends the mind, is most excellent, produces clear knowledge (abhiññā), and destroys doubt—[attains the highest goal].
The intelligence of that bhikkhu who always recites and hears [this work], which cuts through doubt and produces affection and love,
blossoms and fully blooms while he stands within this Teaching.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Abhidhammāvatāra*.

"Leading to welfare" (*hitānayanti*) means bringing about welfare. "And a well-gone mind" (*mānasañ ca sugataṃ*) means a mind that is proceeding excellently.

849. Regarding the "circle" (*vivaṭṭa*), however, for one desiring *micchattā*—that is, for one seeking *nibbāna*—it is appropriate to make that *kasiṇa* a circle measuring a span and four finger-breadths.

one should perform [the work] hand by hand. 868. "That" refers to that sign (nimitta). 871–4. "Of this" refers to the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta). "Of the former" refers to the learning sign (uggaha-nimitta). But what is this distinction?
It was like a bowl of water drawn out from its bag and polished until it resembles the surface of a mirror; or like a white crane against a dark rain-cloud.

884. *Ayanti* refers to the process of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

891–2. "The evenness of energy" means the state of equilibrium of energy. "Sinking" (*laya*) is the state of sluggishness; even when the mind—the advertence-consciousness (*āvajjana-citta*)—is moving or proceeding slightly toward that [state], [it is called sinking].

But having interrupted and cut off the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), that very earth-kasiṇa is made the object, and it arises in the mind-door of the yogi. "From that" means from the adverting consciousness;
in that same object—that object reckoned as the earth-kasiṇa—four or five impulsion (javana) moments arise for that yogi. At the end, one impulsion-moment [remains].

It belongs to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*); in that fine-material-sphere state, applied thought (*vitakka*) and the other factors are its constituent parts (*aṅga*). Because of these, they are stronger than the applied thought and other factors of other types of consciousness.

When these have not yet reached the state of absorption (*appanā*), they are called "preliminary" (*parikamma*) because they are the preparation for the mind of absorption—from the perspective of being the preparation, from the perspective of the state of preparation—and they are also called "access" (*upacāra*) because they are the state of access.
Those impulsion moments are called "conformities" (anuloma) precisely because they conform to absorption.
Among these conformities, that which is the very last impulsion is termed "change-of-lineage" (gotrabhū).
Thus, "change-of-lineage" has been pointed out as the view.

904–5. Having obtained, that is, having received, the repetition condition (*āsevana-paccaya*) from the preceding impulsions (*javana*), the sixth or seventh impulsion enters into absorption (*appeti*).
Thus it is said; regarding this doctrine, a teacher of the Abhidhamma named Godatta said:
"One whose mouth is at the edge of a precipice is called *chinnataṭamukha*."
908. That which has reflection as its cause is "reflection-caused" (*paccavekkhaṇa-hetuka*).
911–2. Concentration (*samādhi*) is the settling of the mind—which was previously distracted among various objects—upon a single object.
915. It is stated [that happiness] is itself tranquil because it is the antidote to the pair of restlessness and remorse, whose nature is unpeaceful.
917. “Dissociated from five factors” means dissociated from the five hindrances. “Endowed with five factors” means endowed with applied thought (*vitakka*) and the others.

920–1. “Vastness” refers to the expansive state of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). And that [vastness] is appropriate to increase after having investigated the access concentration (*upacāra*) of the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*).
928–31. “For one who possesses negligence”: for one who has become a practitioner through negligence, there are perceptions, mental orientations, and acts of attention accompanied by sensual desire.
As they proceed, that jhāna of the yogi becomes partaking of decline. When mindfulness is established in it, calm—meaning the state of being in accordance with that first jhāna—is found;
this calm, which is the state of conformity to that first jhāna, being present as a calm inclination, is established, it is firmly set. That jhāna belongs to a yogi of dull faculties.
It partakes of stability; it resorts to stability. It partakes of distinction;

the meaning is that it reaches the second and subsequent stages of development. Perception and attention associated with disenchantment are perception and attention associated with insight into disenchantment.
Partaking of penetration means partaking of the supramundane; the meaning is that it partakes of the supramundane path.

933. This attainment has proximate unwholesome states as its enemies; it has proximate unwholesome states as its enemies because of the grossness of the modes of reasoning. For that reason, this attainment is weak in its constituent factors (*aṅga*).
935. "Craving" (*nikanti*) means thirst (*taṇhā*). "Having exhausted" (*pariyādāya*) means having dried it up. 936.
"By the method" (*vidhinā*) means by the method previously stated. "Of one who is mindful" (*satassa*) means of one endowed with mindfulness.
938. "But that very sign" means that very first sign; for one who attends to it mentally as "earth, earth.
943. "Tranquillity" is faith (*saddhā*). "Equanimity" is equanimity regarding the object (*tatramajjhattatā*).
944. "Devoid of two factors" means devoid of applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
948. *Pīti* (rapture) means the gladdening of the mind, the state of being gladdened, from which cause it arises.
961–2. *Āsannapītidosā* means that rapture itself is the fault (*dosa*).

Here, in this third jhāna, whatever happiness there is—thus, such happiness—is the mental engagement (*ābhoga*) and attention (*manasikāra*) of the mind. In this manner, because of the magnitude of that happiness...
This attainment is weak in its factors. 974–5.

Furthermore, there is no cultivation of pleasure by means of equanimity; because there is no cultivation of equanimity, and because the impulsion-moments (javana) proceed accompanied by equanimity, therefore the fourth jhāna is described as being accompanied by equanimity. 976.
The second jhāna exists in two ways, established through two components.
979. This *Abhidhammāvatāra*, with its most sweet and excellent words—whose [words] are they?

Those of one whose range of intelligence is exceedingly sharp and clear—he, possessing such a range of exceedingly sharp and clear intelligence, is to be known by that person as one who can experience it.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Abhidhammāvatāra*.
The explanation of the description of the development of fine-material-sphere concentration is finished.
The fourteenth chapter. Fifteenth Chapter.
Commentary on the Description of the Development of Formless-Sphere Concentration (Arūpāvacara-samādhi-bhāvanā-niddesa):

982–3. "When form exists" (*rūpe kho vijjamānasmiṃ*) means when the body of form (*rūpa-kāya*) exists; "taking up sticks, etc. (*daṇḍādānādayo*) refers to seizing sticks and so forth. Thus, having seen the danger (*ādīnava*) in form—that is, in the body of form.
984. "Like a dog pursued by a pig" (*sūkarābhihatova sāti*): like that dog which is being chased by a pig.
985. "Vasī" means the yogi.
988–990. Regarding the phrase "the space touched by that": while mentally attending to that space touched by the mind as "infinite space," he breaks through [the confinement].
This is what is said; this is another method, namely, [attending to it] as "space."
One who practices that kasiṇa with the mind does not contract it.
998. "The enemy of fine-material-sphere jhāna" means the adversary to fine-material-sphere jhāna.
1004. Regarding "consciousness pervading space": consciousness that is indeed pervading is "pervading consciousness"; [it refers to] that pervading consciousness which has space as its object.
"This space is infinite"—thus, consciousness that proceeds having pervaded that very space is called by the term "consciousness-infinity. Consciousness itself is not actually infinite;
rather, because its object is infinite, it is said to be "infinite consciousness," and that consciousness is further described as infinite by virtue of the act of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
1010. The non-existence of the first immaterial-sphere consciousness is due to the emptiness—that is, the state of being empty—of that very first immaterial-sphere [consciousness].
1013. Mindfulness remains; mindfulness remains even more powerfully.
1015. In the absence, in the state of non-existence.

1017–8. *Dutiyāruppacakkhu*: This refers to the mental attention (*manasikāra*) by way of preliminary work (*parikamma*) through the eye, in the manner of "it is not, it is not," etc., regarding the second immaterial state.

It is the mere disappearance of that [second immaterial state], and the mere disappearance of that first immaterial state. 1029. As for this attainment which shall remain making even a mere non-existence its objective field—oh, how this attainment indeed appears as exclusively peaceful!
1033. By means of which perception one is neither percipient nor non-percipient—it is simply that such a perception does not exist at all.
Because it performs no function of clear perception, this attainment is designated as "neither-perception";
for just as heat arising from the fourth formless state is unable to perform the function of burning water because of the remaining conditioned phenomena, so too is this case.
1040. The palace floor and the cloth.

1041. But whichever bhikkhu knows this method for attaining the meditative absorptions (jhāna) of the form and formless realms as most essential—he, being a trainee (sekha) intent upon the attainment of the form and formless jhānas, having overcome and thoroughly mastered the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava), goes to and reaches the form and formless realms.
Thus ends the commentary on the exposition of the development of immaterial-sphere concentration in the *Abhidhammāvatāra-ṭīkā*.
This is the fifteenth chapter.
16. The Sixteenth Chapter:
Commentary on the Exposition of the Higher Knowledges (Abhiññāniddesa) 1045.
"Mindfulness" (sati) refers to one endowed with mindfulness. "Exertion" (anuyoga) refers to energy (vīriya).

1047. When the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) have been produced by the practitioner monk (*yogāvacara-bhikkhu*), the cultivation of concentration (*samādhi-bhāvanā*) for that practitioner monk may be said to have reached its fulfillment and completion.
1050. "Tamed" (*danta*) means established in taming. "Unshakable" (*acala*) means established in being unshakable. 1052–4.
If a yogi, having a basis of a hundred or even a thousand [beings], should [use] the basis for higher knowledge as the cause for higher knowledge...

If he so desires, having entered the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā), and then emerging from that jhāna which is the basis for direct knowledge, he performs the preliminary work of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) by thinking, "I am one hundred, I am one hundred.
Having thus performed this, he again resolves upon the jhāna that is the basis and cause for direct knowledge, enters it once more, and then emerges from that jhāna. Again...

He resolves. Together with that resolve—that is, together with the fourth jhāna consciousness termed "resolve"—that yogi becomes one who possesses the knowledge of the modes of psychic power (*iddhividhañāṇa*).

1067–8. This yogi, having attained direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), hears sounds occurring in the space touched by the object of the fourth jhāna—the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*)—whether they are past or present. This is the knowledge of the divine ear (*dibbasotañāṇa*).
1069. *Cetopariyaṃ* means that which encompasses and delimits another’s mind; that very same mental state is *cetopariyamānasaṃ*. 1070.
*Hadayaṃ pana nissāya* means depending upon the physical heart-base (*hadayavatthu*); the meaning is the blood circulating within the heart-cavity, the blood that flows in the heart-enclosure.
1075. *Kāmāvacaracittañca* means the sense-sphere consciousness of beings belonging to the sense sphere. *Rūpārūpesu* refers to the fine-material existence and the immaterial existence.

And the minds of beings. What kind [of mind]? He knows all the mind differentiated by passion and so forth through the knowledge of penetration of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*). This is the knowledge of penetration of others' minds.
1077–82. "Sitting is the last of all" means that among all postures (*iriyāpatha*), sitting is the one that arises last for a bhikkhu.
It should be brought to mind. From that point onward— starting from the very last sitting and taking that final sitting as the beginning—
one should bring to mind everything done by oneself in reverse order,
for as long as there has been rebirth and re-linking in this existence, and for whatever duration of time that may have been.
That bhikkhu should advert [to the object]. He should carefully advert to both the mind-and-matter that arose in his previous existence and that which arose at the moment of death.

When the bhikkhu has thus adverted to that very same mind-and-matter that arose at the moment of death, making that very mind-and-matter the object, there arises at the mind-door at the moment of death the mental application (manasikāra) and the mind-door adverting consciousness.
It arises: the knowledge of recollecting past lives.

(1086–96) Having made the jhāna based on a kasiṇa object—the foundation for direct knowledge—capable of being directed toward these three kasiṇas by those who have performed merit, therefore, "that or the other," meaning either the light-kasiṇa or one of the other two kasiṇas.
Having generated [the jhāna] in due order, one should place that light-kasiṇa while remaining on the access plane (upacāra-bhūmi) itself.
A wise person should not induce absorption (appanā); if he were to do so, that light-kasiṇa would become the object of the foundational jhāna (pādaka-jjhāna), supported by that foundational jhāna.
The form included within the expanded jhāna should be seen by that yogin.
It would be so. As that yogin continues to look at that form, the stage for the preliminary work (parikamma) passes away;
at that very moment, even the light of that yogin quickly disappears.
When that light has vanished, the visible form is no longer seen. Yet, if one sits and looks even for a whole day, the seeing of the form persists.

1100–1. *Taṃcittasaṃyutaṃ*: the mind associated with that fourth jhāna. It is the preliminary exercise for the knowledge of future existences (*anāgataṃsañāṇa*) and the preliminary exercise for the knowledge of the destiny according to deeds (*yathākammūpagañāṇa*). It is the divine eye knowledge (*dibbacakkhuñāṇa*). 1103.

Whatever bhikkhu here, in this teaching, hears this text and applies it to the mind, that bhikkhu, having crossed over by means of this raft of this text, goes to and reaches the further shore of the great ocean of the Abhidhamma; the meaning is that he understands it.
Thus ends the commentary on the Exposition of the Higher Knowledges in the *Abhidhammāvatāra-ṭīkā*.
This is the sixteenth chapter.
17. The Seventeenth Chapter:
Explanation of the Description of the Objects of Higher Knowledge (Abhiññārammaṇaniddesavaṇṇanā) 1104.
Regarding "knowledge of the future" (anāgataṃsañāṇa): it has not come, thus it is "future" (anāgata); the meaning is that it has not yet arrived. In the future, there are portions (aṃsa).
The knowledge of those divisions is the knowledge of the future. That which approaches and knows whatever karma according to its nature is "according-to-karma-going" (*yathākammūpaga*);
it is the knowledge that cognizes the volition of ripening. 1107–9.
In that context, among those triads of objects, "having made it dependent on consciousness" means having that body dependent on consciousness.
Having performed that very [act] by way of body, mind, and mental factors, one applies knowledge to the exalted consciousness; this is the knowledge of the modes of psychic power (*iddhividhañāṇa*).
Then, because the body—which is the object—is limited and belongs to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), the knowledge may have a limited object (*parittārammaṇa*).
1110–3. When a yogi, desiring to go with a visible body, wishes to go with a visible body...
When that yogi, having made the mind dependent upon the body and having made it dependent upon the material body,
applies that foundational jhāna-consciousness to the body by way of the body, then that knowledge— having shifted from the jhāna-object—
has a sublime sphere as its domain; that knowledge [takes] future categories of phenomena and past categories of phenomena as its object and focal point.
When he does so, that knowledge has the past as its object; when it takes the future as its object, at the time of making that object, it has the future as its range.
However, when that bhikkhu is walking with his body visible, the range of that yogi’s knowledge is called "present"; thus should it be defined.
1114. He places the body upon the mind by means of the mind, and he places the mind upon the body by means of the body;
thus, at the time of such transformation, the knowledge of that yogi may have an internal object.
It "proceeds among the seven" means among the seven categories consisting of limited, sublime, past, future, present, internal, and external objects.
It proceeds with respect to objects.
1120. "In the knowledge of the intermediate" means in the knowledge of the sublime (mahaggata). 1122.
The fact that this knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa) has the Path as its object is considered and known only in a figurative sense (pariyāyena).
1126–7. Therein, that which has reached the three moments is the present, beginning with the moment.
Therein, among those [three], that which is present and has reached the three moments—beginning with the moment—is that which has reached the moments of arising, presence, and dissolution;
such a present, consisting of a mere moment and a fraction of a moment, is called "present. It is included within one or two cycles of the mental continuum (*santati*).

That which is included within the course of one or two moments of consciousness in a single mental continuum is called "present by way of continuity" (*santatipaccuppanna*). "Present" means "subsequent," which is the meaning of "present by duration" (*addhāpaccuppanna*).

1131–2. Regarding those two—the adverting consciousness by which one adverts to phenomena and the impulsion consciousness by which one knows them—of these two, the adverting and impulsion consciousnesses...

Due to the absence of a simultaneous state (*sahaṭṭhāna*), the statement beginning with "the present consists of the triad of moments, etc. and ending with "a single consciousness necessarily pierces [its object] by one [moment]" is untenable.
Furthermore, it is untenable because it would result in advertence (*āvajjana*) and impulsion (*javana*) reaching different objects or occurring at different times.
However, if this undesirable position is not accepted, then those advertences and impulsions must share a single object.

If that [specific] place is not desired, it is not appropriate; however, in another place, such as along the path of the meditation track, the kasiṇa and so forth serve as the object for the advertence, preliminary work, and impulsion consciousnesses, while Nibbāna serves as the object for the change-of-lineage and supramundane consciousnesses.
In this context, the "single-object-ness" of the impulsions refers to their non-desire [for a specific location].
1134–41. Having stated, "That which is delimited by a single existence is the 'present' in its final sense," he speaks this [verse] to show that same present by another method.
This present, known as "duration" (addhā), should be illustrated by way of a cognitive series of impulsions (javana-vāra).
Thus the statement is explained. When a yogi possessing psychic power (iddhimā) adverts his mind to know another's consciousness, his adverting-consciousness (āvajjana-mano)—
Taking as its object the present mind-door adverting consciousness—which is called "present" because it belongs to the present moment—that [adverting] consciousness ceases along with it.
When those have ceased, four or five impulsion moments (*javana*) arise for that yogi.
That which is the final consciousness among these four or five impulsions is declared to be the supernormal power consciousness (*iddhicitta*). From the supernormal power consciousness...

The remaining [consciousnesses] are sense-sphere consciousnesses (*kāmāvacara-citta*). Since, among these sense-sphere [consciousnesses], that same [object] is the object for the supernormal powers (*iddhi*) and the impulsion-moments (*javana*), all those impulsions proceed with a single object. Otherwise, there would be no end to the diversity of objects for those impulsions;
for even though those impulsions have a single object due to having a present object, they are identical to the supernormal power mind itself.
And it knows the mind of another. However, other sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) minds do not know the mind of another.
Just as consciousness at the eye-door is called "eye-consciousness" and sees visible form, so too, the other [types of] mind do not see.
1161. Regarding "knowledge of the future": for knowledge of the future, a future phenomenon is not its objective range; the meaning is that it is simply not its domain.

1169. That which possesses various meanings and descriptive phrases is called "vividhatthavaṇṇapada. Who that is conscious would not listen to this supreme [teaching], which brings forth sweet meaning, delights the hearts of those who hear, and brings joy?
Thus ends the commentary on the Exposition of the Objects of Direct Knowledge (*abhiññārammaṇa*) in the *Abhidhammāvatāra-ṭīkā*.
The Seventeenth Chapter.
18. The Eighteenth Chapter:
Explanation of the Description of Purification of View.

1175. As for perception, which is merely the act of perceiving as "blue" and so forth—that perception performs merely the act of perceiving by way of blue and so on. "Penetration of characteristics" means the awakening to the characteristics such as impermanence. 1177.
That consciousness, having exerted itself and attempted to rise upward, is unable to lead beings to the path.
1178–9. However, the penetration of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena—the awakening to them by way of non-perversion—is the characteristic of wisdom (*paññā*).
1180. It is called "proximate cause of concentration" (*samādhāsannakāraṇā*) because it approaches concentration as its proximate cause.
1181. "In one way by means of its characteristic": wisdom alone is stated in one way by means of the characteristic of awakening to all phenomena.

1183. "By the one of vast wisdom" (*bhūripaññena*): it is "vast" (*bhūri*) because it delights in real objects—that is, in objects that are not perverted. One who possesses such vast wisdom is "one of vast wisdom" (*bhūripañño*); [it is] by him.
1186–91. Knowledge regarding the three—meaning, phenomena, and language—and knowledge regarding those meanings, phenomena, and languages that have arisen, is [knowledge of] knowledge.
Whatever fruit has arisen through conditions is a class of phenomenon (*dhammajāta*). "The meaning of what was spoken" refers to the meaning of the Pāḷi.
These five things are designated as "meaning" (*attha*) and named "meaning. A cause that produces a fruit is a generative condition. "What was spoken" [refers to the words].
*Pāḷi*: "Dhammasaññitā" means those named "dhamma. "Sabhāvanirutti" means unerring terminology. "Pariyatti" means training.
"By hearing and attainment through prior application" means by way of its previous occurrence. 1192.
"In those that have become the ground" means in those that have become the ground for insight (*vipassanā*).
1194. "From birth and so forth" means that wisdom should be developed by one who is afraid of birth and the rest.
1203. "By eighty-one types of consciousness" means by eighty-one types of consciousness, excluding supramundane consciousness, which constitute the plane of insight (vipassanā).
1208. "For the purpose of destroying delusion regarding beings" means for the purpose of eliminating the delusion concerning "beings."
1211. "Effortless" (*nirīhaka*) means devoid of striving, devoid of activity, as in the case of the conjunction of wood and rope.
1215. "Both conditions break apart" means due to the causal condition of mutual dependence. 1225. "The two extremes" refers to the pair:
devotion to the pursuit of sensual pleasure and devotion to the pursuit of self-mortification. "Cultivate" means one should increase the purification of view (*diṭṭhivisuddhi*).
Thus ends the commentary on the Exposition of Purification of View in the *Abhidhammāvatāra-ṭīkā*.
This is the eighteenth chapter.
19. The Nineteenth Chapter:
Explanation of the Description of Purification by Overcoming Doubt (Kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhiniddesa-vaṇṇanā) 1231.
Thus, with regard to the condition among these thirty-two groups [of conditions], the yogi first comprehends the root-condition (hetu-paccaya) mentally.
1233. The seed is the cause of the sprout; the seed is the producer of the cause of the sprout, while earth and so forth are the conditions for the sprout. 1234.
"Five phenomena" refers to ignorance, craving, clinging, karma, and nutriment—these are phenomena that function as causes and conditions. 1235.
Karma is the producer of name-and-form, just as a father who begets a son is the progenitor of his child.
1238. *Paccayā* means by means of a condition.
1240. *Yā sā* means that which is that doubt. *Pubbante* means in the prior limit, in the former portion.
1241. *Sabbathā* means from every aspect, from every portion; without exception, that doubt of that yogin is abandoned and eliminated.
1243. "Accomplishing a purpose" means that on the side of the wholesome, it accomplishes purposes such as giving, while on the side of the unwholesome, it accomplishes purposes such as killing.
"Its result" means that the result of that injurious kamma is said to have arisen. Thus, one yogi performs the discernment of the conditions for name-and-form by way of kamma and its result.

1246. "By way of the connection between cause and fruit": by way of the connection between cause and fruit, he correctly and non-erroneously contemplates (*sam-anupassati*) that this name-and-form proceeds solely and exclusively [in this manner].
1247. Beyond the occurrence of ripening, one does not see nor is it known that which brings about the realization of ripening. 1250–1.
What is called "non-occurrence" is not seen; rather, what has arisen is seen.

Not knowing this matter, the non-Buddhists (titthiyā), lacking self-mastery and failing to understand, have grasped the perception of a "being" (satta) as a perception of a self, and thus they hold views of eternalism and annihilationism.
Being mutually contradictory, they grasp at sixty-two views.
(Verse 1254) "Both" means that both karma and its result are empty of one another; yet, without karma there is no fruit—without karma, the fruit does not exist.
(Verse 1255) "By means of requisites" refers to the requisites such as the sun and so forth.
1257. That phenomenon of name-and-form is empty. 1258.
"By way of cause, equipment, and condition" means by way of both the cause and the conditions of equipment.
Thus ends [the section from] the Abhidhammāvatāra-ṭīkā.
The commentary on the description of purification by overcoming doubt is finished.
The nineteenth chapter.
20. The twentieth chapter.
Commentary on the Exposition of Purification by Knowledge and Vision of What Is and Is Not the Path (Maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhi-niddesa-vaṇṇanā) 1264.
“Of a present phenomenon” means of a present phenomenon consisting of mind-and-body (nāmarūpa).

1266–8. For a mind-and-body phenomenon that is arising or in the process of arising, there is no coming from a heap or a collection. “Going to a direction” means going toward a direction. Furthermore, for a mind-and-body phenomenon that has ceased, there is no accumulation in any single location.

With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form; with the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of form. With the arising of craving, there is the arising of form; with the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of form.
With the arising of kamma, there is the arising of form; with the cessation of kamma, there is the cessation of form. With the cessation of nutriment, there is the cessation of form.
"Phenomena" refers to the phenomena of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra-dhamma*).

1280. *Sampattapaṭivedhassa*: of one who has attained penetration—that is, of a person such as a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) who has realized the path and fruit known as supramundane (*lokuttara*). *Vippaṭipannassa*: of one who has failed to practice correctly, or who has practiced in a contrary manner.

1286. *Kāyacittāni*: "Body" (*kāya*) refers to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saññā*), and mental formations (*saṅkhāra*). "Mind" (*citta*) refers to consciousness (*viññāṇa*). 1290. *Yato yato paccayādito*: from whichever respective condition and so forth.
*Yaṃ amataṃ nibbānaṃ vijānataṃ*: for those who discern that deathless Nibbāna; *pītipāmojjaṃ*: the rapture and joy that they ought to obtain, or joy and rapture that are like the deathless itself.
1293. "Appatte" means not having attained the path and fruit within oneself. "Pattasaññī" means one who has the perception that "I have attained the path and fruit.

1297. "Sāravedino" means those whose nature is to know the essence. "Taṃ" refers to that knowledge and vision of the path and non-path. This knowledge is called "knowledge and vision of the path and non-path" (maggāmaggañāṇadassana).
Thus, in the *Abhidhammāvatāra-ṭīkā*.
The commentary on the description of purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path is finished.
The twentieth chapter.
21. The twenty-first chapter.
1299. "Knowledge that is free from fault and perfectly clear" is said with reference to the eightfold knowledge. 1302.
"Knowledge in conformity with the truths" is precisely what this is called.
1306. This very insight that has reached its peak is called the knowledge of conformity to the truths (*saccānuloma-ñāṇa*).

1309. "In the manner of having arrived at equanimity regarding formations immediately after the life-continuum" means by the method performed by the knowledge designated as equanimity regarding formations immediately after the life-continuum. 1314–16.
"And in conformity with the factors conducive to enlightenment as they proceed upwards" refers to the factors conducive to enlightenment that are occurring in an ascending order.
"In forward order": this knowledge of conformity (anuloma-ñāṇa) is called the "conclusion" of that which leads to emergence; it was spoken and taught by the Great Seer.
Having reached the knowledge of conformity to the truths (saccānuloma-ñāṇa), it arises with the change-of-lineage (gotrabhu) as its conclusion in every respect.
1318. "Therein": in insight (vipassanā).
Thus ends the commentary on the Exposition of Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Way in the *Abhidhammāvatāra-ṭīkā*.
This is the twenty-first chapter.
22. The Twenty-second Chapter:
Explanation of the Description of Purification by Knowledge and Vision (Ñāṇadassanavisuddhiniddesa). 1319–22.

That which is beneficial for adverting is "to-be-adverted-to" (āvajjaniya); that which has this as its object is the "object of what is to be adverted to" (āvajjaniyaṭṭhāna), namely, the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū).
This is the meaning. That *gotrabhū* consciousness is so called because it is the object to be adverted to (*āvajjanīya*) by the path-consciousness.
It never partakes in the "knowledge and vision of the way" (*paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana*); likewise, it never partakes in the "purity of knowledge and vision" (*ñāṇadassana-visuddhi*).

Between these two knowledges, there is one that is not included in conventional usage; it is "conventional" (*vohārika*) because it is connected with conventional expression (*vohāra*), and what is not conventional is "non-conventional" (*abbohārika*).

Because it has fallen into the stream of insight, it is conventionally designated as "insight" (*vipassanā*) due to its presence in the stream of insight. From that [state], [it proceeds] toward Nibbāna. (1325) "Sharp and keen insight":
this is said with reference to the change-of-lineage consciousness (*gotrabhū-citta*).

(1326–29) "Free from formations" (*visaṅkhāra*): meaning devoid of mental formations (*saṅkhāra*). "And like the first adverting" (*paṭhamāvajjanañceva*): meaning just as in the case of the first adverting [consciousness].

"And also by the first application" means like the first act of attention (*manasikāra*). "By conditions such as the immediate" refers to the conditions for the Path (*magga*). "Of that" refers to the Path.
"Upon the head" means at the very top of the head by means of that insight (*vipassanā*) which has reached its culmination. "Non-returning" means not turning back. 1330–3.

By a single adverting [consciousness], it occurs in one and the same cognitive sequence (*vīthi*). "The consciousnesses of conformity and change-of-lineage" refers to the minds of conformity (*anuloma*) and change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*).
