The state of having various objects has been stated. That change-of-lineage consciousness (gotrabhū-citta), although not itself an advertence (āvajjana), stands in the place of advertence for the Path;
it is as if it were giving a signal, meaning that its intention is: "I am making Nibbāna my object; you too, make that very same thing your object.
"Saññita" means a signal (saññā). The Path is something never before pierced.
This is that path, never before pierced. 1336.
"Ujjhati" means he cuts off. 1338.
It is connected with the initial path which bestows manifold benefits. This is the knowledge of the first path.
1341. There is no repetition for a single [cognition]; there is no condition of repetition (āsevanapaccaya) for a single arising of consciousness.

For that reason, two arisings of consciousness are conformable (anuloma). Having obtained—that is, having received—the condition of repetition by means of those arisings of consciousness, the third consciousness becomes change-of-lineage (gotrabhu).
1345–7. That which has the path as its object and has adverting as its mental function is "rooted in the reviewing of the path.
When that [adverting consciousness] has ceased, seven impulsion moments termed "reviewing of the path" arise in succession.
There are nineteen kinds of reviewing knowledge.
1351. Then, at that time, he enters the path of insight. This is the knowledge of the second path. 1361.
"Root-destroying" means the destruction of the root. This is the knowledge of the third path. 1363.
"By way of the nature of non-returning" means by way of not turning back. This is the knowledge of the fourth path.
Thus ends the commentary on the Exposition of Purification by Knowledge and Vision in the *Abhidhammāvatāra-ṭīkā*.
This is the twenty-second chapter.
23. The Twenty-third Chapter: Explanation of the Description of the Abandoning of Defilements (Kilesapahānaniddesavaṇṇanā) 1375.

Here, however, in this context, by way of figurative usage regarding the cause—that is, by way of designating the cause such as gain—the phrase "having gain and so forth as its basis" means that which has gain and so forth as its object (vatthu) for the underlying tendency (anunaya). Of that [tendency].
The subtle [defilements] are the subtle lust for sensual pleasures and aversion. 1376.

Whichever phenomenon, such as the fetters, is to be abandoned by whichever knowledge of the first path and so forth, and reaches destruction and ruin—that very phenomenon has been thus well demonstrated by me through that very same exhaustive knowledge. 1383.
"By means of the clear realization of full understanding" means by means of knowing through delimitation. "He clearly realizes suffering" means he penetrates suffering.
1394. The yogi who, having understood this, and having known and recognized that the forest of beneficial cultivation is exclusively conducive to happiness and welfare, approaches that benefit;

and having dispelled and destroyed the unsurpassed darkness of the mind—that which is base—he reaches and attains Nibbāna, the state to be entered and known, the state free from grasping, unshakable, and devoid of a physical body.
Thus ends the commentary on the Exposition of the Abandoning of Defilements in the *Abhidhammāvatāra-ṭīkā*.
This is the twenty-third chapter.
24. The Twenty-fourth Chapter: Commentary on the Exposition of Conditions (Paccayaniddesa-vaṇṇanā) 1395.
"Materiality is [a condition] for materiality" means that materiality is [a condition] for materiality. It is [a condition] for immaterial mental phenomena (nāma).
1396. *Missakassa* means "of that which is mixed," namely, of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
1397. *Tipañca ca* means "and fifteen.
1399. *Eko* refers to the kamma-condition. *Dvekāliko* means "belonging to two times" by way of the past and present periods. *Dassito* means "shown" or taught by the Blessed One.
Thus ends the commentary on the Exposition of Relations in the *Abhidhammāvatāra-ṭīkā*.
This is the twenty-fourth chapter.
Commentary on the Conclusion (Nigamanakathāvaṇṇanā) 1401.
"Awakening the investigation of the intellect of those of good mind" means awakening the investigative faculty of the intellect of poets who possess beautiful wisdom (*sumati*).
"Destroyer of the delusion of doubt in the ignorant" means the destroyer of the delusion of the foolish who harbor doubts. "Dispeller of the great darkness of the intellect of those of evil mind."
He is a destroyer of the dull-witted fools by means of an intellect resembling a great darkness; he is a maker of light for the keen-witted wise by means of his sharp wisdom.
Because the bhikkhu named Sumati has requested me for an incomparable honor, for that reason—
Therefore, for that reason, this is the *Abhidhammāvatāra*. From word to word, from section to section.
It was composed by me through the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) that clarifies benefit—that is, through the cultivation that reveals what is beneficial.
Alternatively, it is because I was requested by the monk Sumati, who was free from pride (*asamāna*) and devoid of conceit (*māna*). For that reason, therefore.

1405. For "the threefold course of expressions" (*byappathānaṃ gatiyo*): regarding expressions, that is, words, there are three courses by way of their connection with meaning, composition, and application.
1406. "By the tenets of other schools" (*nikāyantaraladdhīhi*): by means of the tenets found in other schools. "Dependent on the path of recitation" (*vācanāmagganissito*):

dependent on the continuity of the verbal expression. 1410. "Crowded with unmixed families" (*asaṃkiṇṇakulākule*): crowded with families that are not intermingled. "With very clear, cool water" (*supasannasitodake*): with sweet, cool water.
1411. *Saṅkaṭā* means in a narrow or crowded place.
1412. *Kelāsasikharākārapāsādapaṭimaṇḍitā* means adorned with palaces resembling the summit of the Silver Mountain (Sineru).
1413. *Vividhākāracārupākāragopurā* means possessing beautiful gate-towers and walls of various shapes.
1414. *Sallekhā* means a life of austerity (*sallekhavutti*). *Sākhalye* means in a state of friendliness (*sakhilabhāva*). *Satā* means by one endowed with mindfulness (*satisampanna*).
1415. *Vassavalāhakā devā* refers to the immortal deities who have become rain-clouds.
The commentary on the concluding discourse is finished.
The Ancient Commentary on the *Abhidhammāvatāra* is completed.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The New Commentary on the *Abhidhammāvatāra*.
(First Part) Introduction to the Composition (Ka) To the Buddha,
whose wisdom and compassion are purified, and who is honored by the Fully Enlightened Ones;
I pay homage to the Dhamma born of the True Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha free from defilements.
(Kha) I bow down to the Great Elder Sāriputta, who is proficient in the scriptures;
he is my teacher of peaceful conduct, a vessel for reverence.
(Ga) By me, while paying homage,
whatever perfection of merit has been gained—
by the power of that, having abandoned [suffering],...
(gha) By him who was an ornament to the lineage of the Elders dwelling at the Mahāvihāra— elders of steadfast virtue—
who acted for the benefit of living beings, [this work was composed] so that obstacles might be entirely eliminated.
(Ṅa) That which was composed by the Elder Buddhadatta,
being delightful because it serves as a means of entry into the Abhidhamma Piṭaka;
(Ca) renowned under the name *Abhidhammāvatāra* (The Entrance to the Abhidhamma).
I, a bhikkhunī well-versed in the Abhidhamma,
shall undertake, according to my ability, a commentary on the meaning of this supreme treatise—
which possesses various skillful and profound methods— for the purpose of generating joy.
Commentary on the Introduction to the Work:

1. As this master commences this treatise—which is endowed with most subtle and diverse methods, capable of penetrating the depths of both our own and other systems, and which generates a state of perfectly pure and expansive analytical wisdom—he first of all...
By means of making this homage to the Triple Gem, he prays for both the warding off of obstacles and the proficiency of wisdom.

For, in its essential meaning, homage to the Triple Gem is a wholesome volition (*kusalacetanā*) that brings about the act of paying homage. And because of the excellence of the field and the intention of both the one worthy of veneration and the one who venerates, this volition becomes something to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*), by way of providing reinforcement to the karma that has the attainment of whatever prosperity one has already gained as its result.
Having warded off obstructive and interrupting kamma that would hinder the continuity of the resultant consciousness produced by that [merit],
it brings about the non-occurrence of obstacles such as disease— which, being caused by that [kamma], would impede the attainment of one's intended goal—
and having purified the mental continuum by washing away the stains of lust and so forth, it effects the accomplishment of the intended goal through the wisdom dependent upon that [continuum].
It brings about a state of sharpness and clarity. It is a custom practiced by the wise that, at the commencement of a composition, one offers homage to the Triple Gem;
therefore, for the sake of preserving the conduct of the virtuous, the veneration of the Triple Gem is undertaken at the beginning.
In this way, many other purposes should also be discerned. These, however, are [to be found] therein...
Regarding the phrase "elaborated in many ways" there, we shall set aside that prolixity and explain [the text] exactly as it occurs.

And here, desiring to perform an homage to the Triple Gem, and because the remaining gems are rooted in the Tathāgata, he first begins the homage preceded by a praise of the Tathāgata, saying: "O you of infinite compassion and wisdom," and so forth.
For by bowing preceded by praise, the Teacher’s possession of preeminent qualities is shown; from that, his state of being unsurpassedly worthy of veneration;
by that, his status as the field for one’s own veneration; and by his being such a field, the fact that veneration is the cause for the accomplishment of whatever is intended is demonstrated.
In this context, *vanditvā* (having paid homage) is a designation for an action occurring at a prior time (*pubbakālakiriyā*).

Its connection, however, is with the expression of a subsequent action (*aparakālakiriyā*), namely “I shall speak” (*pavakkhāmi*), found in the concluding verse. *Buddham* is the designation of the object (*kamma*) of the act of homage.

The phrase beginning with “one of infinite compassion and wisdom” (*anantakaruṇāpaññam*) is its qualification (*visesana*). In that regard, it scatters (*kirati*) [suffering], thus it is *karuṇā*; [it is] the suffering of others...
It scatters or carries away; such is the meaning. Or, it is performed—that is, extended—toward those who are suffering; thus it is *karuṇā*. Alternatively, it acts;
thus it is *karuṇā*, meaning that when there is suffering in others, it produces a trembling and heartache in the virtuous. Or, it consumes;
thus it is *karuṇā*, meaning that it destroys the suffering of another by creating a deficiency in the conditions [for its persistence]. It understands; thus it is *paññā*.
The meaning is that he penetrates [things] according to their true nature through various modes. Compassion and wisdom are "compassion-and-wisdom" (*karuṇāpaññā*);

they are "infinite" (*anantā*) because there is no end to them. One who possesses infinite compassion and wisdom is "one of infinite compassion-and-wisdom" (*anantakaruṇāpañño*); [the text refers to] him, the one of infinite compassion-and-wisdom.
And here, although the Blessed One’s compassion and wisdom possess both an end in terms of arising and passing away, and an end in terms of the cessation of the continuum (*santati*),...
Its infinity should be understood from its occurrence with infinite objects within its limited scope.

For the Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of the Perfectly Enlightened One—which functions in the mode of removing suffering from all sentient beings and is not shared by others—occurs without exception toward all sentient beings, omitting no being whatsoever; likewise, it is capable of awakening to the true nature of all phenomena.
Wisdom, which is termed omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), also proceeds without remainder regarding all knowable phenomena;
therefore, because he possesses compassion and knowledge that proceed toward infinite objects, the Blessed One is "one whose wisdom is infinite compassion" (*anantakaruṇāpañño*).
By the mention of both compassion and wisdom here, the Blessed One’s perfection of all mundane and supramundane qualities is demonstrated. For, by the mention of compassion—
By illuminating the extraordinary qualities that have attained a sublime state among mundane things, the perfection of all mundane qualities is shown;
by the mention of wisdom (*paññā*), the perfection of all supramundane qualities is shown, as it illuminates the knowledge of the path which has the knowledge of omniscience as its proximate cause.
Furthermore, among all the qualities of a Buddha, compassion (*karuṇā*) is the beginning and wisdom is the end. One whose mind is impelled by great compassion...

For indeed, the Blessed One, having made the resolution to uplift beings from the mire of saṃsāra, gradually fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) and, through the attainment of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, acquired all the qualities of a Buddha.

Thus, because all the qualities of a Buddha have compassion as their cause, compassion is the beginning of all Buddha-qualities; furthermore, it is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for omniscient knowledge.
Wisdom is the culmination because there is nothing further to be done after the attainment of the knowledge of the Path.

By showing both the beginning and the end, the entirety of the Buddha’s qualities is demonstrated by way of method; for the grasp of the method alone is the means for seeing all the Buddha’s qualities.
Otherwise, even if one were to describe the qualities of the Tathāgata word by word—qualities that transcend the path of speech even for such an omniscient Buddha—[the task would never be completed].
"Who indeed would be able to bring it to its conclusion?
Having thus praised the Blessed One in brief by way of his compassion and wisdom through all his Buddha-qualities,
[the author] does so again because of his own lack of satiety in recounting the Buddha's qualities and for the purpose of generating abundant confidence in others.
Even though these distinguished qualities are included therein, he says "the Tathāgata" and so forth, extracting and showing them as the primary factors.
Therein, "Tathāgata" refers to the Tathāgata by way of eight reasons, beginning with "thus come. For it has been said:
"The Blessed One is a Tathāgata for eight reasons: he is a Tathāgata because he has come thus (tathā-āgata), he is a Tathāgata because he has gone thus (tathā-gata)..."
“He has come to the suchness-characteristic, thus he is a Tathāgata; he has perfectly awakened to the suchness of phenomena as they truly are, thus he is a Tathāgata;

because of his seeing suchness, he is a Tathāgata; because of his speaking suchness, he is a Tathāgata; because of his acting suchness, he is a Tathāgata; in the sense of overcoming, he is a Tathāgata.
“How, Blessed One, is the Blessed One a Tathāgata because he has come in such a way? Just as those of old who had applied themselves with zeal for the welfare of the whole world...”

"The Perfectly Enlightened Ones have arrived. What does this mean? It means that by the same aspiration with which those Blessed Ones arrived—being endowed with the eight factors beginning with human birth—this Blessed One has also arrived.
And just as those Blessed Ones arrived having fulfilled the thirty perfections and accomplished the five great renunciations, and just as those [thirty-seven]...

“Having developed and cultivated the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*), they have come; likewise, this Blessed One has also come—thus, first of all, he is ‘Thus-Come’ (*tathāgata*) because he has come thus.
(1) “How is it that he is ‘Thus-Gone’ (*tathāgata*) because he has gone thus? Just as those Blessed Ones, immediately upon birth, took seven steps...”

(2) "How is he a Tathāgata because he has come to the true characteristic (*tathalakkhaṇa*)? Because he has come to that which is the specific individual essence and intrinsic characteristic (*sabhāvasarasalakkhaṇa*) of those various phenomena;

just as they have gone by dispelling each respective side of unwholesomeness through the paths of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), so too has this Blessed One gone. Thus, he is a Tathāgata because he has gone thus."
It is suchness (*tathaṃ*), it is not otherwise; he has come to that characteristic of suchness (*tathalakkhaṇaṃ*) and has realized it as it truly is.
Therefore, because he has come to the characteristic of suchness, he is the "Tathāgata. This is because the sense of "going" (*gamana*) can also have the sense of "awakening" (*bujjhana*).
For they say: "Those things which have the sense of going have the sense of awakening; those things which have the sense of awakening have the sense of going. (3)

“How is it that he is a Tathāgata because he has fully awakened to the true nature of things (tathadhamma) as they really are? Because of such statements as, ‘Bhikkhus, this is suffering— this is true,
this is not false,’ and because of such statements as, ‘The conditionality of volitional formations in relation to ignorance,

and the fact that volitional formations have arisen and originated with ignorance as their condition, is true, not false, not otherwise,’ he is a Tathāgata in regard to what is designated as the true nature of things.”

He has fully awakened to dependent origination and the truths as they truly are; therefore, because he has fully awakened to the true nature of phenomena (*tathadhamma*) as they truly are, he is the Tathāgata.
(4) “How is he the Tathāgata by virtue of seeing things as they truly are? Because, in immeasurable world-systems, for immeasurable sentient beings...”
He sees and knows the object apprehended through the six doors exactly as it is;
and having known it, he analyzes and demonstrates it correctly in this way: "Which is that visible base (rūpāyatana) which is derived from the four great elements?
and so forth. Therefore, because he comes to, sees, and knows reality (tathatā), or because he causes that [reality] to come, shows it, or demonstrates it, he is called the Tathāgata.
Thus, he is the Tathāgata because of his seeing things as they truly are.

(5) “How is he the Tathāgata because of his speaking truthfully? Because from the time of his full enlightenment until his final nibbāna, he speaks only that which is uniform, true, and not false—having crushed out passion, pride, and the rest—he speaks what is real; he is the Real One, the Unmistaken One.”
Alternatively, by changing the letter *da* to *ta* in the word *āgatovacana*, it is said that he is the "Tathāgata" because his speech is thus;

in this way, he is the Tathāgata by virtue of speaking truthfully. (6) How is he the Tathāgata by virtue of acting accordingly? For the Blessed One acts exactly in accordance with his own words, as expressed in the phrase "one who acts as he speaks.
Therefore, since his body proceeds in the same manner as his speech, he is the Tathāgata because his body has gone (*gata*) in the same way (*tathā*) as his speech.
Thus, he is the Tathāgata by virtue of acting accordingly.

(7) “In what sense is he the Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming? Because he proceeds having overcome the world with its devas, being endowed with incomparable perfection of all mundane and supramundane qualities, therefore he is called the Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming.”
In this regard, the derivation of the word should be understood as follows: it is like a medicine (*agada*), namely, the splendor of his teaching and his store of merit.
For by means of these, he—possessing great majesty like a physician with a divine elixir—overcomes all proponents of opposing doctrines, as well as the world with its devas.
Thus, because he possesses such a medicine, which is true, unerring, and as described, for the purpose of overcoming the entire world, [he is called "Tathāgata"].
Having changed the letter *da* to the letter *ta*, he is called the Tathāgata; this is the summary here.
The detailed exposition, however, should be taken from the commentaries on the Dīgha Nikāya and other sources. And it is said in this regard:
"Just as in the world Vipassī and the others..."
The sages have attained omniscience here;
likewise this Sakyan sage has also arrived,
and for that reason the Visionary One is called the Tathāgata.
“Just as Vipassī and the other Great Seers, who possessed the splendor of light, departed after abandoning the stains of sensual desire and the rest through concentration and knowledge,
so too did the Sage of the Sakyas.”
Because he has thus gone, he is considered a Tathāgata. And that which is thus—
the characteristic of the elements, bases, and so forth, according to their specific nature, commonality, distinction, and division— [is what he has realized].
This Victor has arrived through self-born knowledge;
thus is the Bull of the Śākyas called the Tathāgata.
With his all-seeing eye, he [perceives] the truths as they truly are.
Likewise, because he has fully manifested this specific conditionality through its non-otherness and non-knowability,
the Victor is therefore the Tathāgata, in accordance with reality.
“Even in world-systems of infinite variety,
regarding the range of the Victor’s sense-sphere of visible forms and so forth,
his vision is exactly the same despite their diverse differences.”
Therefore the Tathāgata is Samantalocana.
And because he speaks the Dhamma exactly as it is,
he makes his speech conform to himself.
“He moves about having overcome the world with his qualities;
therefore the Tathāgata is the Leader of the World.
Because there is no one who excels him in any quality whatsoever, he has no superior; thus he is “unsurpassed” (*anuttara*).

For indeed, from the Avīci hell up to the peak of existence, and across immeasurable world-systems in the horizontal directions, there is no one equal to the Blessed One in any quality, much less anyone superior. As it is said:
“In form, in virtue, in concentration, and in wisdom, he is peerless.”
“Equal to liberation itself in the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma.
*Vinditvā* means having honored by means of the three types of salutation, through such states as being inclined toward it.
For there are three salutations according to the doors of body, speech, and mind. As it is said: “Bhikkhus, these are the three salutations: one salutes with the body, one salutes with speech...”

"...and worships with the mind. In this context, a volition (cetanā)—which is either a wholesome or functional (kiriyā) consciousness of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) having the qualities of the Buddha and so forth as its object—arises by way of proceeding through the door of the body after having originated a bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti); this is called "bodily worship" (kāyavandanā).
That same volition, when it arises by way of proceeding through the door of speech after having originated a vocal intimation (vacīviññatti), is called "verbal worship" (vacīvandanā).
But "mental homage" (manovandanā) is that which arises solely by way of the mental door’s activity, without having brought forth either of the two types of intimation (viññatti).
"With the head" (sirasā): by means of the head as the instrument. One who has awakened (abujjhi) or who awakens (bodheti) is a Buddha.
For he himself awakened to the Dhamma of the Four Truths and awakens others; therefore, in the sense of awakening and causing awakening, he is called "Buddha."
As it is said: "He is a Buddha because he has awakened to the truths; he is a Buddha because he awakens the world.

Alternatively, since the word *budha* also functions in the senses of "waking" and "blooming," he is a Buddha because he has awakened—having utterly departed from the sleep of delusion along with its latent tendencies—or because he has blossomed through wisdom (*buddhi*).
For the Blessed One [has destroyed] that which is called ignorance (*avijjā*), which acts as an obstruction to seeing the true nature of things.

Because it has been utterly removed from that [sleep] due to its being completely eradicated along with its latent tendencies by means of the noble path-knowledge (*ariyamagga-ñāṇa*), he is "awakened" (*buddha*).

Like a lotus flower blossomed through the attainment of supreme beauty, splendor, and excellence, he has blossomed—reached full bloom—through the attainment of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*) adorned by an immeasurable multitude of qualities;
therefore, he is called "Buddha" also in the sense of awakening and blossoming.
To this extent, the praise of the Blessed One has been performed in two aspects: by way of the attainment of his own welfare and by way of his practice for the welfare of others.

Among these, the attainment of his own welfare consists of the acquisition of unobstructed knowledge, the absolute abandonment of all defilements along with their latent tendencies, and the realization of Nibbāna without residue.
The practice for the welfare of others, however, is twofold, according to his disposition and his application.

The striving for the welfare of others. In this context, "aspiration" (*āsaya*) refers to the constant inclination toward their benefit even regarding those who are hostile beings, such as Devadatta and others who are unfit vessels for the teaching of the Dhamma, as well as the arrival of the time when the faculties of those whose faculties have not yet matured reach maturity.

Furthermore, it is the teaching of the Dhamma—which leads out of all suffering by way of the Three Vehicles—with a mind free from expectation of gain, honor, and the like, directed toward other beings.

This is the application of the terms. Among these two kinds of practice for the benefit of others and three kinds of attainment of one’s own welfare, the practice for the benefit of others is shown by the word *anantakaruṇā* (boundless compassion) in its sense of "having come thus" (*tathā-āgata*), and by the word *buddha* in its sense of "awakening" (*bodhana*), and by the word *tathāgata* in its sense of "seeing thus" (*tathā-dassana*) and "having come thus" (*tathā-āgata*). This is according to the underlying intention (*āsaya*).
It should be understood that by means of the term *payoga* (application), by the expression *anantapaññā* (infinite wisdom), by the word *tathāgata* which indicates the course of knowledge,

and by the word *buddha* in the sense of awakening, vigilance, and blossoming, the threefold attainment of one’s own welfare is revealed; and by the word *anuttara* (supreme), the attainment of both one’s own welfare and the welfare of others is revealed.
Furthermore, the praise of the Blessed One proceeds by way of three aspects through the perfection of cause, fruit, and assistance to beings;

thus, the praise here should also be understood according to those aspects. In this context, "perfection of cause" refers to the union with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and the accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*), because all the qualities of a Buddha have that as their root.
"Perfection of fruit," however, is fourfold: perfection of knowledge (*ñāṇasampadā*), perfection of abandonment (*pahānasampadā*), [perfection of power, and perfection of assistance].

[These are] the perfection of majesty and the perfection of the form-body. Among these, path-knowledge has omniscient knowledge as its proximate cause, and omniscient knowledge has path-knowledge as its proximate cause;
the ten powers and other knowledges rooted in those are called the perfection of knowledge.
The perfection of abandonment is the bringing about of the state of non-arising for all defilements, together with their latent tendencies, through the cultivation of the supreme path.

The perfection of the physical body (*rūpakāyasampadā*) consists in the excellence of majesty and sovereign power (*ādhipacca-ānubhāvasampadā*) in accomplishing the inconceivable and immeasurable welfare of all the world, and in overcoming the world including the devas;
furthermore, it is the attainment of a personal existence adorned with the primary marks and secondary characteristics, which serves as the consecration for the eyes of the entire world.
The benefit to sentient beings occurs precisely through the practice for the welfare of others described above.
This is to be understood. Furthermore, the perfection of the cause is shown by the term *anantakaruṇā* (boundless compassion) and by the word *tathāgata* in its sense as it has come (*tathā-āgata*).

Regarding the perfections of the fruit, the perfection of knowledge and the perfection of abandonment are shown by the term *anantapaññā* (boundless wisdom), by the word *tathāgata* which illuminates clear realization (*abhisamaya*), and by the word *buddha* in the senses of awakening, being awake, and blossoming.
It should be understood that the perfection of majesty is indicated by the word *tathāgata* in the sense of overcoming, and is further clarified by the term *anuttara* (supreme);
however, the perfection of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) is shown by the word *anuttara* in the sense of indicating the attainment of the pinnacle of form.
Having thus performed a salutation preceded by praise for the Buddha-jewel, he now begins the salutation to the remaining jewels:

He said: "The Dhamma and the assembly of the virtuous. By means of this praise of the Blessed One, the qualities of the Dhamma—such as its being well-expounded—and the qualities of the Saṅgha—such as its being well-practiced—are demonstrated;
because they arise from him and are not otherwise, no separate praise is made for them.
[It refers to] persons who have attained the path and realized cessation, according to the instruction.
And because it holds one who practices it, preventing one from falling into the sufferings of the states of woe and the sufferings of the cycle of existence, it is called *dhamma*.
It is tenfold by way of the four noble paths, the four fruits of recluseship, Nibbāna, and the Dhamma of the scriptures.
For this has been said in the *Chattavimāna*:
“The Dhamma free from passion, dispassionate, unshakable, sorrowless, unconditioned, and not repulsive—
sweet, skillful, and well-expounded.”
“Come to this Dhamma for refuge.
Herein, the path is called “the fading away of lust” (*rāgavirāga*) because all lust, including its divisions such as sensual lust, fades away by means of it.
This is because craving, which is reckoned as “wandering-on” (*ejā*), and sorrow, which is characterized by inward burning, have been entirely exhausted at the moment of its arising.
“Unagitated and sorrowless” refers to the fruit (phala). Because it is unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) by any condition whatsoever, “the unconditioned Dhamma” refers to Nibbāna.

However, because it illustrates non-opposition, possesses perfection in both meaning and phrasing, and is well-analyzed through the manifestation of its distinguished qualities, the term “not repulsive” and so forth refers to the entire Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti*). Therein:
The Noble Path and Nibbāna are, in the primary sense (nippariyāya), "Dhamma" because they hold one back from the states of misery;

however, the [other] attainments of the fruits are so only in a secondary sense (pariyāya). For here, "holding back" means the destruction of the defilements that produce rebirth in the states of misery and so forth.

Thus, it is by virtue of the Noble Path’s capacity to utterly eradicate the defilements, and by virtue of Nibbāna being its objective support—which serves as the cause for the accomplishment of that purpose—that they are so designated.

In the primary sense (nippariyāyato), both [the attainment of cessation and the fruit of arahantship] are applicable. However, in the other cases, because the defilements have been eradicated by the path of the noble fruit and its function has been pacified,
and because the teaching of the scriptures (pariyattidhamma) proceeds in conformity with that path and serves as the cause for its realization,
both are applicable only in a secondary sense (pariyāyato).
They are called *sādhū* because they accomplish their own welfare and the welfare of others; a group or assembly of them is a *sādhugaṇa*.

Alternatively, it is a *sādhugaṇa* because this is both excellent (*sādhu*) and a group (*gaṇa*). Or, it is a *sādhugaṇa* because the group is dependent upon the Excellent One (*sādhu*), the Fully Enlightened Buddha, being his legitimate sons.
Furthermore, it consists of those possessing the four noble paths and those possessing the four fruits.

The Noble Saṅgha is eightfold; that is the assembly of the virtuous (*sādhugaṇa*). *Picā* is a combination of particles, or it may be a single particle used for the purpose of joining together the act of paying homage to the Three Jewels.

Some explain that since the word "assembly" (*gaṇa*) here refers by context to the assembly of noble persons (*ariyagaṇapuggala*), they connect it with the word "having paid homage" (*vanditvā*) using the neuter form of the adjective "virtuous" (*sādhu*). In that case, however—
"Good" (*sādhu*) means they honor [it] thoroughly (*sakkaccaṃ*), being free from fear, gain, and so forth; such is the meaning.

2. Having thus performed the intended homage to the Triple Gem at the commencement of the treatise, he now elucidates that place where this treatise is set forth for the sake of proficiency, together with the excellence of the location and the recipient.
Showing this, he said: “On the stone named Paṇḍukambala,” and so forth. Therein, the connection is as follows:

seated upon the spotless, cool surface of the stone named Paṇḍukambala belonging to the king of gods, the God of Gods—possessing incomparable prowess, worshipped by the gods, and preceded by the gods—taught that Dhamma in the world of the gods among the deities.
The meaning here is as follows: because it has a color similar to a yellow blanket (*paṇḍukambala*), its name and designation is "yellow blanket"; thus, it is called *paṇḍukambalanāmā*.
For it was produced by the power of Sakka’s such merit, and it shines at all times with a color equal to a yellow blanket and a *jāsumana* flower;
as for its dimensions, it is sixty *yojanas* in length and fifty *yojanas* in width.
And it is fifteen yojanas in height. "Of stone" (*silāya*) is a genitive case used in connection with a part of a whole. "Equal to a balance" means measured by a balance;

"not equal" means incomparable; he whose stride and strength are incomparable is "one of incomparable stride and strength. For the Perfectly Enlightened One, by virtue of the power perfected through the supreme *pāramitās*, [his strength] is equal to a thousand million elephants when reckoned by the number of elephants, and to [a thousand million] men when reckoned by the number of men.
With bodily strength equal to the combined power of ten thousand million men, and with immeasurable power of knowledge, there is no one among the gods, Brahmās,
or others to whom he can be compared in terms of strength. Alternatively, because it is not shared by any other, his "incomparable" exertion—
consisting of right effort that brings about immeasurable and extraordinary qualities— is unique.
Alternatively, he is called *atulavikkamo* because this "unrivalled prowess"—consisting of the right exertions (*sammappadhāna*)—is possessed by him; thus he is one of unrivalled prowess.
While it would more properly be said "*atulyavikkamo*," the form "*atulavikkamo*" is used here due to the elision of the letter *y* for the sake of metrical composition in the verse.
Alternatively, since the suffix *-a* can also occur in the sense of "possessing" (*sammitattha*), it is stated "*atulavikkamo*" in the sense that his prowess is unrivalled (*atula*).
They are called *devas* because they play (*dibbanti*) with the five strands of sensual pleasure and so forth, or because they dwell among them;
because of their capacity for victory, they desire to conquer external and internal adversaries;

they conduct themselves by exercising lordship, wealth, and other honors, as well as by granting and receiving gifts and providing instruction on various matters; and they shine with the splendor attained through the power of merit and knowledge.
The meaning is that they proceed toward their intended object without resistance and are capable of accomplishing whatever is desired.
Alternatively, they are called *devā* because they are to be approached (*devanīyā*) as "refuge" and "final resort" by those seeking to overcome various calamities;

or they are *devā* because they are to be praised (*abhitthavanīyā*) due to their possession of exceptional beauty, or because they are desirable (*kamanīyā*). These are of three kinds: conventional deities (*sammutideva*), deities by birth (*upapattideva*), and... [text fragment].
"Pure devas. In this context, "conventional devas" refers to the Khattiyas such as Mahāsammata and others.

"Devas by birth" refers to the devas from the realm of the Four Great Kings upwards. "Pure devas" refers to those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsavā). However, here one should understand them as the devas by birth;
yet even among these, they are not taken without distinction, but rather specifically those dwelling in the realms of the Four Great Kings and Tāvatiṃsa, excluding the Yāma and other higher realms.
[The term] is intended [in this sense]. Because he delights them by means of the four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*), he is a king (*rājā*); the king of the gods, the lord, is the "Devarāja.
The intention is: "of that Devarāja," meaning "of Sakka, the King of the Gods. For the Blessed One did not teach the Abhidhamma Piṭaka while seated in other worlds of the gods.
3. This is an indefinite description; however, its restriction should be understood by means of the word “therein.
Among the three types of gods mentioned above, the supreme god is the Devadeva (God of Gods), the Blessed One, because he possesses play and other qualities to a greater degree than all of them.

For he [possesses] unsurpassed play of supernormal knowledge (*abhiññā*) through the supreme divine, brahma, and noble abidings (*vihāra*), which are accomplished within his own continuum as well as those of others.

Through his preeminent conduct—consisting of the correct practice of the seven treasures such as sovereignty of mind and faith based on conviction, as well as the giving and receiving of honors—and through his excellence in discourse characterized by instruction according to the offense, according to suitability, and according to the Dhamma;
and through his supreme wisdom and the splendor known as the radiance of his body;
and through his incomparable movement of the knowledge-body in the conquest of Māra, the attainment of omniscience, and the accomplishment of the welfare of others.

Because he is endowed with an irresistible spear, and because he is to be approached as a "refuge" by the world including the devas, because he is to be praised, and because he is desirable through his affectionate nature, he stands having overcome all those devas by means of their respective qualities;
thus he is the god more worthy of worship than all devas. Or rather, [he is so] because of the ornament of the quality of omniscience, which is designated as the state of a purified deva.
Because he has attained [this state] and is superior to other gods, he is called the God of Gods (*devadeva*).

"To the gods" refers here to those who received the Dhamma at that time—namely, the gods born by rebirth (*upapatti-deva*) dwelling within the ten thousand world-systems, headed by the Mother and the Son of the Gods.
Some say that the "purified gods" (*visuddhi-deva*) are also included here; however, they are subsumed within the gods born by rebirth, as human Arahants are not present there.

"By way of non-existence. "By the gods of gods" means by the purified gods (*visuddhideva*). For the purified gods, because they engage in play and other such activities to a far greater degree than other gods according to the method already stated, are intended here as "gods of gods";
[the Blessed One was] honored by them. "Worthy of worship" (*pūjito*) means he is to be worshipped, that he is worthy of being worshipped;
by this, he demonstrates the Blessed One's status as the supreme person even among the purified gods. "He taught" (*desesi*)—[with a voice] like the sweet sound of the *karavīka* bird.

He proclaimed [the teaching] while emitting the voice of Brahmā. "In the world of the gods" means in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven of the gods. That which bears the characteristic common to its own nature is *dhamma*;
the *Abhidhamma* is the classification into wholesome states and so forth; however, here it is the *Abhidhamma Piṭaka*, which elucidates that [Dhamma], that is called "Dhamma.
For he will say later, "in the supreme Piṭaka. "Surrounded by the gods" means by the deities and Brahmas residing in the ten thousandfold world-system.
"Preceded" means surrounded.
But is it not already established by the word "of the gods" (*devānam*) alone that he is preceded by the gods; what then is the purpose of the phrase "preceded by the gods" (*devapurakkhato*)?
This is not a fault. For the Blessed One is sometimes [honored] even when face-to-face, as was the case with the Elder Cūḷapanthaka and others.
Having sat down and emitted a radiance, he teaches the Dhamma as if appearing seated directly before the eyes of sentient beings;
sometimes, as in the case of the Pārāyanika Brahmins and others, he sits face-to-face with them and, surrounded by others, teaches the Dhamma to others as well.
But here it is not so; rather, this is for the purpose of showing that [the Buddha] is surrounded solely by devas and teaches the Dhamma to the devas.
“...should indeed be called ‘honored by the gods.

4. Thus, in this treatise, for the purpose of generating reverence, having elucidated the Abhidhamma Piṭaka—the subject matter regarding which proficiency must be achieved—along with its excellence in terms of the teacher and other factors, [the author] now sets forth the purpose, the subject matter, and the manner of inspiring the audience for the commencement of the intended treatise.

And in order to clarify this, the passage beginning with "In that regard, it is said" was stated. Therein, by the phrase "for the sake of proficiency," the purpose for undertaking the treatise is stated.
By the phrase "The Entrance to Abhidhamma," the title and the subject matter are indicated. By the words "Sweet," and so forth, the treatise is distinguished.
And by the word "In brief," it should be understood as the manner in which the author inspires the audience.
“*Aham*” (I) points to the self as the agent. For that which is not another is called the self (*attā*), designated as one’s own internal sphere, by the term “I.

The state of being proficient is proficiency (*pāṭava*); that very thing is the purpose (*attha*) in the sense of a motive, thus it is “for the sake of proficiency” (*pāṭavattha*); for that purpose. That...
The meaning is stated as: for the purpose of generating the knowledge consisting of what has been heard (*sutamayañāṇa*), which is capable of grasping various methods by means of [this teaching].
They are "bhikkhus" because they see fear in *saṃsāra*, or because they break (*bhindanti*) evil, unwholesome states.
It is both a "piṭaka" and "supreme" (*uttama*), thus "the supreme piṭaka" (*piṭakuttama*); the intention is that it refers to the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. For that indeed...

It is called a *piṭaka* because it has the sense of a "receptacle for the teachings" (*pariyatti-bhājana*), and it is called the "supreme *piṭaka*" (*piṭakuttama*) because it is preeminent among the three *piṭakas*.
In this context, "the sense of a receptacle for the teachings" means both by way of the sense of "teaching" (*pariyatti*) and by way of the sense of "receptacle" (*bhājana*).
For instance, in such passages as "Do not [be satisfied] with the mere handing over of the *piṭaka*," the teaching itself is called the *piṭaka*. Furthermore: "Then a man might come..."

In such phrases as "the hoe and the basket," it refers to any kind of vessel. Therefore, this [Abhidhamma] is called a *piṭaka* because it is a *pariyatti* in the sense of being something to be mastered, and a "vessel" (*bhājana*) in the sense of being a container for the meanings of the Abhidhamma;
thus it is called a *piṭaka* by way of being both a mastery and a vessel. For this very reason, they say: "The *piṭaka* is so called by those who know the meaning of *piṭaka*..."
"They say [it is so] from the perspective of the analysis of the scriptures (pariyatti);
having combined them accordingly,
all three— the Vinaya and the others— should be understood."

Its distinguished nature, however, should be understood from its teaching according to the actual mode of being (*yathāsabhāva*) beyond worldly convention (*lokavohāra*), and from its elucidation of the distinct aggregates of Dhamma (*dhammakkhandha*).

For here, having transcended worldly conventions such as "a being," "a person," or "monks," the teaching proceeds predominantly according to the actual nature of phenomena (*yathādhamma*) as "aggregates," "elements," and "bases," rather than according to the aforementioned conventions as is the case with other [teachings].

For this reason, it is called "the teaching according to the Dhamma. Herein, the aggregate of wisdom (*paññā-khandha*), which is distinguished from all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*), is specifically elucidated;

therefore, although all three Piṭakas are the word of the Buddha, it is appropriate that this [Abhidhamma] alone is distinguished among the three Piṭakas because its teaching does not transcend the true nature of things (*yathāsabhāva*). Furthermore, this is due to its state as a distinction that exceeds even the Dhamma itself.

The distinguished nature [of the Abhidhamma] should be understood. For, because the aggregates, bases, and other phenomena are analyzed in their entirety within the Abhidhamma, its textual tradition (pāḷi) is more extensive and more distinguished than the other two Piṭakas.

Therefore, it is appropriate to say that this alone is the most excellent among the three Piṭakas, by virtue of its more extensive and distinguished textual doctrine. Precisely because of its possession of the aforementioned distinguished nature...
This is called the "Abhidhamma Piṭaka" because the prefix *abhi-* denotes a distinguished or superior state.
Furthermore, it is the Abhidhamma Piṭaka because the qualities of growth and so forth are explained herein. As the ancients have said:
"That which is here possessed of growth, characterized, honored, and defined..."

“Furthermore, there are teachings that have been stated [in the Suttas] which are augmented; for that reason, they are called Abhidhamma. Thus, herein, teachings characterized by growth are also stated, such as:
“He develops the path for rebirth in the form realm; he dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness,” and so forth, as well as:
“Having a visible form as its object, or a sound as its object,” and so forth.
They are "characterized" because they are to be defined by their objects and so forth according to such methods as "states of training," "states beyond training," and "supramundane states";
they are "worthy of honor" because they are honored according to such methods as "there is contact," "there is feeling," and so on;
and they are "delimited" because their individual natures are circumscribed according to such methods as "lofty states," "immeasurable states," and "unexcelled states."

Because factors (dhammas) that are superior and distinguished by way of method have been taught, and because the prefix *abhi-* occurs in the sense of "increase" (*vuddhi*) and so forth, this Piṭaka is called "Abhidhamma" through such an etymological derivation as: "The factors that possess increase are herein.
The treatise named *Abhidhammāvatāra* is so called because one enters the Abhidhamma by means of it; furthermore, this is its designation which conforms to its meaning.

[The word] *dasseti* [is used]. The word *tu* is for the purpose of completing the metrical line (*padapūraṇa*). For the Teacher (Ācariya) generally employs particles (*nipāta*) here and there for the sake of completing the lines of the verses (*gāthāpada*).
However, where a specific purpose for them is seen, we shall explain that meaning in that very place.
As for *madhura*, this word *madhura* in its primary sense (*nippariyāyato*) refers to a particular kind of taste (*rasavisesa*) cognizable by the tongue.
Furthermore, here the perfection of both meaning and phrasing is expressed by the word *madhura* (sweet) due to the commonality of being "desirable.
For there is indeed the designation of something similar by means of the same word, as in the case of "the fire-boy" (*aggimāṇava*).

Moreover, because it is conjoined with that sweetness, this [text] is also called "sweet," just as a blue lotus is called "blue" due to its conjunction with the quality of blueness. This is owing to the perfection of phrasing, which is both skillful and profound.

It is called "increasing the intellect" (*mativaḍḍhana*) because it increases the understanding whose object is the Abhidhamma through both the perfection of its phrasing and the perfection of its meaning.
Alternatively, it is described as "sweet" due to the perfection of its phrasing, and as "increasing the intellect" due to the perfection of its meaning.
5. *Tāḷa* means a key; the sense is that it is like a key. It is called "delusion" (*moha*) because one is deluded by it; this is a designation for ignorance (*avijjā*).
Because it acts as a door-bolt (*kavāṭa*) by obstructing the entry of those entering the great city of the Abhidhamma, it is called the "delusion-door-bolt" (*mohakavāṭa*); [the text refers to] that.

It is an "opening" (*vighāṭana*) because it opens, or because it is opened by means of this. But is it not the case that the door-bolt of ignorance (*avijjā*) is struck open by wisdom (*paññā*), since the latter is its direct opposite? True; however, this [wisdom] is also [referred to here] by way of being its cause.

"It is called 'the opener of the door of delusion' (mohakavāṭavighāṭanakara). For even a cause of a cause is spoken of as a cause, just as one says, 'The village was burned by thieves,' or 'The meal was cooked by the grass.
6. "Difficult to cross" (suduttara) is said because it is associated with the fourfold profundity consisting of the Dhamma, the meaning, the teaching, and the penetration.
Because it cannot be crossed by those of dull intellect, it is "difficult to cross" (*atiduttara*).
For this very reason, because it is equal to the great ocean, it is called the "great ocean" (*mahodadhi*).

Indeed, even the great ocean, eighty-four thousand *yojanas* deep, cannot find a footing for anyone except for Sineru, the king of mountains; in the same way, this [Dhamma] is likewise connected with fourfold profundity.
"Except for the Tathāgata, no one else can provide a foothold. Regarding the phrase "of those crossing": this refers to those desiring to cross over, by way of grasping the meaning.
And here, it should be stated as "or crossing," either by virtue of the governing context or by bringing in what is to be said later to connect it.
"Of those crossing" means of those crossing over in order to reach the further shore. "Or crossing" refers to a raft.
"Like that," means "equal to that. Makaras are a species of fish; their mine, or place of residence, is the "makarākara" (the sea), that [is what is meant]. 7.
Those who are devoted to the Abhidhamma are the "ābhidhammikā"; for them. Like the essence of the hand (*hatthasāra*).
For just as, even though many jewels and such exist for people, in times of misfortune, for the sake of comfortable enjoyment, [they keep] in the hand—
Just as valuable items such as essential gems being carried are called "hand-treasures" (*hatthasāra*), so too, although the Abhidhamma Piṭaka is vast,
because it is impossible to carry it about in its entirety due to its total extent, this work— which is being composed by way of a compendium of the essence of its meaning—
serves for the easy maintenance of the Abhidhamma-versed bhikkhus; thus, because it is similar to a hand-treasure, it is so named.
“Hand-spirit” (hatthasāra) is what was stated. “I shall speak” (pavakkhāmi) means I shall explain in detail;

this is a future tense verb, yet because it is in proximity to the present, or because the present is used figuratively for the future, it functions as a present tense verb, meaning that he will speak immediately after his promise.
Although he speaks in detail according to the meaning, he says “in brief” (samāsena) to show that he will speak by condensing [the words] according to the terminology.

"Samāsa" means contraction or abbreviation; thus, it is said "by way of that summary," meaning not by way of detailed exposition. Having thus far demonstrated the manner of inspiring the audience by stating the purpose, the subject matter, and the title, [the author] now, since inspiring the audience consists in enjoining them to listen attentively, enjoins them to do so: ... He said, “Listen to that with concentrated minds. For right practice is dependent upon careful listening.
In this context, “that” refers to the *Abhidhammāvatāra* which I shall speak; “listen” means pay close attention. “With concentrated minds” means properly composed;
