Chapter One: The Description of Consciousness.
Commentary on Wholesome States of the Sense-Sphere (Kāmāvacara-kusala-vaṇṇanā). 8.

Having thus first shown the homage to the Triple Gem and so forth, the author now speaks the words beginning with “consciousness and mental factors,” briefly pointing out the Abhidhamma which constitutes the body of the meaning of this treatise as it has been commenced.
Regarding that, first, the literal meaning of the word *citta* (consciousness): [The text continues with the etymological analysis of *citta* and the definition of mental factors.]

He himself explains it immediately thereafter: "Mental concomitant" (*cetasika*) and so forth. It is called *cetasika* because it is connected to the mind (*cetasi citte*), that is, to consciousness, by way of being inseparable from it, or because it exists therein due to its dependence upon it;

this is a designation for the triad of aggregates beginning with feeling (*vedanā*). It is called *rūpa* because it is affected (*ruppati*) or it is made to appear (*rūpīyati*); it undergoes change through cold, heat, and so forth, and it is appropriated (*āpādīyati*).
"Meaning" (*attha*) is a designation for the aggregate of material form (*rūpakkhandha*), which is twenty-eightfold by way of the four great elements and the twenty-four derived forms.
"Craving" (*taṇhā*) is so called because it weaves together or binds one to existence after existence;
that craving does not exist here, or because it has emerged from that [craving], it is "Nirvana"—the deathless, unconditioned reality.
The word *iti* is used here in the sense of indication. He is "unsurpassed" (*niruttara*) because there is nothing superior to him.
Alternatively, he is "unsurpassed" because, due to his dwelling in the four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*), there is no opposing statement superior to his.

For in the world with its devas, among those who possess knowledge, those who have abandoned [defilements], and those who have attained the path of deliverance, there is no one capable of uttering a legitimate counter-argument against the Teacher.
In that regard, the Blessed One is indeed confident because there is no cause for fear. For this was said by the Blessed One:

"If anyone—in this world, whether a recluse, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else—should challenge me, who claims to be perfectly enlightened, on the grounds that 'these things have not been fully realized by you,' then [I would be shaken]."
“I do not perceive any ground for this, Sāriputta; not perceiving such a ground, Sāriputta, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, having attained self-confidence.
‘While you claim to be one whose taints are exhausted, these taints are not yet fully destroyed’—regarding that, indeed, I dwell [without fear]... [as before]... having attained self-confidence.”
“Those things which were spoken of as obstructive states, for one who indulges in them, are not sufficient to constitute an obstruction”—thus indeed do I dwell there... [as before] ...
“That purpose for which the Dhamma was taught by you does not lead the practitioner to the complete destruction of suffering”—thus indeed do I dwell there...
[as before]. He proclaims the four noble truths; thus he is the Proclaimer of the Four Truths. By way of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
For there are four noble truths. As it is said: “Bhikkhus, these four are the noble truths. Which four?
The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
Therein, the phenomena belonging to the three planes [of existence] are [included] because they are the locus of manifold calamities.
Suffering (*dukkha*) is so called because it is devoid of permanence, beauty, and so forth, and because it is contemptible and insignificant.

Craving (*taṇhā*) is called the origin (*samudaya*) because, through the convergence of specific conditions such as karma, it acts as the cause for the arising of suffering; that is, "suffering arises from this" by coming together.
Nibbāna is the cessation of suffering (*dukkhanirodha*), because it is the condition for the non-arising and cessation of suffering. Furthermore, that cessation of suffering—

It is called the "path leading to the cessation of suffering" because it proceeds by taking [cessation] as its object, because it reaches [that cessation], and because it exists as the practice for its realization;

thus, the supramundane path is so designated. As for their meaning as truths (*sacca*), they should be understood as such because of their state of being exact, non-erroneous, and real. For it has been said: "‘This is suffering,’ monks—this is true, this is not false, this is not otherwise."

This is the detailed explanation. Here, however, although the four noble fruits and those associated with the noble path are dissociated from the [ordinary] truths, it should be understood that they are included here by the very statement that explains the Path and Nibbāna;
for they share the same characteristic of being "without taints" (*anāsava*), and because they function as the respective causes and objects [of knowledge].

And here, by the words “unsurpassed, the proclaimer of the Four Truths,” he demonstrates the Blessed One’s specific excellence of qualities conducive to the fourfold teaching of the Dhamma beginning with consciousness, because one who is not such [as he] lacks the capacity for that teaching.
Alternatively, by the word “unsurpassed,” he illuminates the non-alterability of the fourfold Dhamma.
Furthermore, by the phrase “proclaimer of the Four Truths,” those...
The teachings taught by the Blessed One for the purpose of training and maturing [disciples] are not intended here.

Rather, he shows that it is those fourfold factors—suffering and so forth—which were spoken of as being to be fully realized by those who have been matured, that are intended here in the sense of being the subjects to be set forth.

Having thus briefly set forth the four factors, [the author now proceeds] because a "setting forth" (uddesa) exists for the sake of an "explanation" (niddesa); therefore, regarding the factors as they were set forth...

The passage beginning with “therein, consciousness” (*tattha cittaṃ*) was commenced in order to explain [the nature of these phenomena]. Therein, “therein” (*tattha*) means among those phenomena, namely consciousness and the rest.

“Consciousness is the cognizing of objects”: the meaning is that whatever cognizing or apprehending there is of an object termed a “sphere” (*visaya*), that is consciousness. By this, however, the dependence of consciousness upon an object, its impermanence, and its lack of agency are shown.
It illuminates. For by characterizing consciousness as "the cognizing of an object," it illuminates its dependence on that [object] since its occurrence is contingent upon it;

and by illustrating that, it illuminates its impermanent nature because it shows that consciousness arises only at the very moment it is directed toward that object. Furthermore, by the description of its mode of being, it illuminates its state of non-agency because it shows that it is merely the act of cognizing.
For this is nothing more than a mere occurrence according to conditions. This is what [is meant].

"‘A phenomenon by its own nature’ (sabhāvadhamma) means this. And having established it thus, for all mental states and mental factors (cittacetasika-dhammā), only the derivation based on their essential being (bhāvasādhana) is obtained in the primary sense (nippariyāyato).

However, that etymological explanation which is stated in terms of agent and instrument—such as "it thinks, therefore it is mind (citta)" or "by means of that, the mind ranges about, therefore it is investigation (vicāra)"—should be understood as a figurative statement (pariyāyakathana). Regarding their respective functions...
For indeed, the status of being an agent (*kattubhāva*) is obtained for mental phenomena (*dhammā*) only figuratively, by attributing to them the state of being the primary factor;

and the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatta*) is likewise obtained only figuratively, by attributing the status of being an agent to the collection of associated phenomena that are conducive to that [primary action].
Furthermore, such an illustration should be understood as intended to demonstrate the absence of any agent or other such factors distinct from the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena.
By the phrase "the cognizing of an object," it is stated that the characteristic of consciousness is the apprehension of an object;
its functions (rasa) and so forth are now explained. Consciousness has the function of being the precursor, it is manifested as the support [of continuity], and its proximate cause is name-and-form.
Having reached the sense-door, consciousness is the precursor and the forerunner in the sense of discerning that object. Likewise...

For it is by the mind alone that one knows the visible object to be seen through the eye-door... and so on... and by the mind alone that one knows the mental object to be cognized through the mind-door.

This should be understood as being just like a city guard who, sitting at a crossroads in the center of the city, observes every person as they arrive, thinking, "This one is a resident; this one is a newcomer."
Therefore, having reached the door, that object is "preceding" in the sense of being made clear; thus it has the function of a forerunner.
As each subsequent [moment] arises, it appears as if it were connecting with each preceding one by making them continuous, and it attains the state of grasping;
thus it has "connection" as its manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*). Furthermore, in the five-aggregate plane, its name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is invariably present.
In the fourfold existence, name alone is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*); thus, it is also the proximate cause for both name and form.
The diversity [of their characteristics] should be understood according to the method that will be explained below. For he will say in the section on the delimitation of matter:
“The commonality or the individual essence of phenomena is considered their characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*).”
"Function (kicca) or its accomplishment (sampatti) is explained as 'flavour' (rasa).
Alternatively, the fruit (phala), the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna),
or the mode of presentation (upatthānanaya)— whatever is the proximate cause— is designated as the 'proximate basis' (padaṭṭhāna)."
However, wherever the characteristics (lakkhaṇa) and so forth are mentioned, their diversity should be understood according to this very method.

Since the further analysis of the mind spoken of would shine forth for one who has already understood the commonality of the mind through knowing the meaning of the terms, knowing the meaning of the terms is more appropriate at the outset;
therefore, he asks first out of a desire to explain that.

“But what is the meaning of that statement? For there are five kinds of questions: the question for the illumination of the unknown (*adiṭṭhajotanā-pucchā*), the question for the verification of what is known (*diṭṭhasaṃsandana-pucchā*), the question for the cutting off of doubt (*vimaticchedanā-pucchā*), the question for assent (*anumati-pucchā*), and the question arising from a desire to speak (*kathetukamyatā-pucchā*).

Among these, the posing of a question for the sake of knowledge and vision of that which is not yet known or seen is called the question for the illumination of the unknown. However, that which is already known and seen...
The posing of a question for the purpose of comparing one's views with those of other wise persons is called a "question for the comparison of what has been seen" (*diṭṭhasaṃsandanā-pucchā*).

On the other hand, the posing of a question by one who is naturally prone to doubt, for the purpose of uprooting his own doubt, is called a "question for the cutting off of uncertainty" (*vimaticchedanā-pucchā*).
For example: "What do you think, monks, is form permanent or impermanent?"

“Does it blow? “It is impermanent, venerable sir. “And that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”—such posing of questions for the purpose of obtaining an affirmative answer is called an *anumati-pucchā* (a question for assent).
However, posing questions with the intention of teaching specific doctrines, such as “Bhikkhus, there are these four foundations of mindfulness. Which four?
and so forth, is called a *kathetukamyatā-pucchā* (a question from a desire to speak).
Of these, the first three do not apply to teachers.

For they did not begin by composing books and then illuminate what has never been seen, reconcile what has been seen, or resolve doubts; rather, their commitment to book composition was preceded precisely by the purification of those very matters.
The other two, however, are applicable. Among them, this is the inquiry arising from a desire to speak.
Furthermore, it should be understood that when the teachers formulate an inquiry (*codanā*), they do so by postulating another questioner and formulating it according to that person's words;
thus, in this context, even inquiries for the purpose of demonstrating what has not been seen or for cutting through doubt are indeed possible.
"Of that" refers to the word *citta*. For when the mind (*citta*) is attained, the word that denotes it is also attained due to their concomitance.
"He has indeed attained" means that here the word "his" (tassa) refers to the attainment. Some, however, state the meaning as "of that mind" (tassa cittassa);
but that does not agree with the question, "What is the referent of 'his'? For it is impossible for there to be a question regarding the mind such as, "What is the referent of [the word] 'mind'?
(cittassa ko vacanattho).

Now, in order to answer the matter as it was asked, he first makes the formal promise with the word "It is said," and then begins the answer with the words "By way of including everything," and so forth.

Therein, "by way of including everything" means by way of including all of them—starting from the very lowest, such as eye-consciousness and the rest—because they all have the essential nature of cognizing objects; it does not [mean]...
The meaning is: "according to what is available," as in the etymological explanations that will be stated later. It "thinks" (cinteti) means it cognizes (vijānāti).

Or, it is called "mind" (citta) because they think; that is, they take it as their objective range. For its status as an instrument (karaṇa-bhāva) is obtained by attributing the agency to the associated mental factors.
Having thus shown the meaning by way of a comprehensive inclusion, he now shows it also by way of what is available:
It has been stated: “Or, it is called ‘citta’ because it accumulates its own continuum,” and so forth.
Since the word *citta* is common to all states of consciousness, wherever and in whatever way a meaning is applicable, it should be understood accordingly.
However, in cases where the specific meanings already mentioned do not apply, that which is called *citta* should be understood by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhī*).
Just as something made from *kilañja* grass and other materials is called a "palm-leaf fan" (*tālavaṇṭa*) by way of conventional usage because it resembles a palm leaf;
so too, "one's own continuity" (*attasantāna*) means one's own mental continuity, that is to say, the continuity of impulsion (*javana*).
For since the word *atta* (self) denotes what is opposed to another, the phrase "the continuity of the self" refers to the continuity of impulsion arising in a similar manner.
"He piles it up" means he makes a heap; this meaning is to be understood by way of the impulsion-consciousnesses that perform repetition (*āsevanā*).
For those [preceding impulsions], having become a condition of repetition for the subsequent ones, "pile it up" by making their own stream of impulsion skillful and powerful.
The word *vā* is used in the sense of an alternative that does not include all possibilities. The word *pi* is used in the sense of combining the action.
Alternatively, since the phrase "by way of including everything" (sabbasaṅgāhakavasena) is connected here as well, when this too is understood as being stated by way of including everything,

the meaning of "mental continuum" (cittasantāna)— in the expression *atta-santāna*— is derived precisely because the word *atta* (self) is used in its own primary sense (*sakatthavutti*) for "consciousness" (*viññāṇa*).
For it is by way of that [consciousness] that the mental continuum is made to proceed without interruption through conditions such as contiguity (*anantara-paccaya*).

Every kind of mental state (*cittajāta*) is indeed called "accumulating" (*cinoti*) the mental continuum (*cittasantāna*). In this context, however, the particle *vā* should be understood as having the sense of an alternative formulation of the action.

The particle *pi* should be seen as serving the purpose of drawing in the term "mind" (*citta*). On the other hand, in the former position, "mind" (*citta*) is to be understood by virtue of its being the subject under discussion (*adhikāra*).
9. It makes variegated, or it is the making of what is variegated; thus, it is "variegated-making" (*vicittakaraṇa*).
From that "variegated-making," the meaning is: "because of the making of variegated works of art and so forth.

For whatever variety of variegated crafts exists in the world, such as works of art and the like, all of that is made only after being conceived by the mind. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, have you seen the footprint?"
“Is it called ‘mind’? “Yes, venerable sir. “That mind, monks, which is called ‘conduct,’ is thought by the mind alone.

This meaning is found in the thirty-two types of consciousness that possess intimation. Or, it is “mind” (*citta*) in the sense of making diverse, either through being associated with the wholesome or unwholesome accompanied by taints, or through performing diverse courses of action and so forth. But are not diverse courses of action and the like...
They are produced by way of karma. As it is said:
"Depending on the diversity of karma, the diversity of the destinies of beings is discerned: footless, two-footed, four-footed, many-footed;
material and immaterial; percipient, non-percipient, and neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient; depending on the diversity of karma..."
The differentiation of beings in their rebirth is discerned as high or low, inferior or superior, and well-faring or ill-faring;
depending on the differentiation of kamma, the differentiation of beings in their individual forms is discerned as beautiful or ugly, well-born or ill-born, and well-proportioned or ill-proportioned;
depending on the differentiation of kamma, [the differentiation of beings] in the worldly conditions...
"A distinction is perceived in gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, and pleasure and pain.

Therefore, because they are produced by the differentiation of karma, the states such as destiny (gati) and so forth possess diversity. And "karma" refers to volition (cetanā), which is a mental factor (cetasika-dhamma), and it is also said to include covetousness and the like;
it is not the mind (citta) itself. How, then, does the mind produce the diverse destinies and so forth? It is explained as follows:
— Because karma is dependent upon consciousness (*citta*), even that which is produced by it is said to be "done by consciousness" alone;

just as an enemy defeated by a king’s warrior is said to have been defeated by the king himself. Alternatively, it is called "variegated-action" (*vicittakaraṇa*) because its instrument is variegated.
For, with the exception of the single-pointed state, every consciousness possesses various functions such as rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and so forth.
Or rather, it is appropriate that the mind is "variegated" (*vicitta*) because it possesses various distinct functions such as adverting (*āvajjana*) and so forth.

In all these alternative analyses (*vikappa*), one should understand either that there is an elision of the final member of the compound—as in the case of "material existence is form" (*rūpabhavo rūpan*)—where the term *citta* is replaced by the word *vicitta*, or that there is an elision of the prefix *vi-*.
Alternatively, the phrase "making variegated" (*vicittakaraṇā*) refers to the state of being variegated by the mind.

This is an indication of the indicative reason (*ñāpakahetu*). Because this [mind] is a maker of diversity, it should therefore be understood that it produces that diversity while being diverse itself;
thus, the meaning is "citta" because it is diverse due to the diversity of its instruments (*karaṇa*).
Apart from that state of being diverse through the diversity of its instruments, [it is diverse] by way of its own genus, plane, association, and so forth.
Showing that it is called "citta" because of its variegated nature (*vicittatā*), he says: "or because of its own variegated state.

In this regard, since the wholesome is one thing, the unwholesome another, the indeterminate another, the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) another, the fine-material-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) and so forth another, that which is with lust another, that which is free from lust another, that which is with hatred another, that which is free from hatred another, and that which is with delusion another; [and so on].
It is free from delusion; it has one object of form and another object such as sound;
among objects of form, it has one blue object and another yellow or other-colored object. Likewise, this applies to objects of sound and so forth as far as possible.
Among all these, one is inferior, another is intermediate, and another is sublime; and among the inferior and the rest, one is dominated by desire (*chandādhipateyya*).
It is manifold and of many kinds, such as that which has mind as its dominant factor, that which has energy as its dominant factor, and that which has investigation as its dominant factor;
likewise, it is diverse according to its birth, plane, association, object, and its qualities of being inferior, medium, or superior, and so forth.
Therefore, it is called "citta" (mind) because of this variety of itself.
Now, while it is true that a single state of consciousness (*citta*) alone cannot be called "variegated" (*vicitta*), nevertheless, because it is included within variegated states,
it is permissible to call even one of these a "consciousness" by virtue of its variegation. This is because a part may be designated by the name of the whole,
just as when a portion of a mountain, a river, or the ocean is seen, one says, "the mountain has been seen," and so forth.

And just as feeling and the other [mental factors], though associated with each single moment of consciousness, are designated by the term "aggregate" in the sense of a "heap"—as in "the aggregate of feeling," "the aggregate of perception," and so forth—so too, here, resultant consciousness is called "consciousness" (*citta*) because it is accumulated (*cita*) by karma and defilements.

Furthermore, that [resultant consciousness] is said to be "accumulated" (*cita*) by those [karma and defilements] when it is produced as a fruit by means of karma accompanied by defilements. Let this be so for now.
This is said with reference to mundane resultants; but how is it so when the supramundane has been attained? It is replied:

because even for the volition of the Noble Path, the state of being supported by ignorance is made manifest by such passages as, "Which states are wholesome? At whatever time a wholesome supramundane consciousness has arisen...
at that time, with ignorance as condition, there are volitional formations," and so forth. Thus, [this applies] even to the wholesome supramundane.

The statement that "the underlying tendencies (anusaya) are the decisive support (upanissaya)" allows for the figurative expression that the resultant [consciousness] produced by them is accumulated by karma and the defilements (kilesa).

Alternatively, it is called *citta* because it "sustains what has been accumulated" (*citaṃ tāyati*). For even the personal existence (*attabhāva*) accumulated through karma and so forth is said to be "dead" when consciousness ceases. As it has been said:
“When life, heat, and consciousness abandon this body,
then it lies cast aside, like a useless log. Furthermore,
although this word *citta* is seen in various senses— as in the case of “Citta the householder,” and so forth— [it is used here in its primary sense].
It occurs in the sense of a designation (*paññatti*). In such passages as “The whole world is without mind by means of another’s mind,” it refers to consciousness (*viññāṇa*).
In such passages as “I do not see, monks, even a single class [of beings] that is so full of mind,” the meaning is “variegated” or “of diverse kinds.
In such passages as “What is called ‘conduct’ is mind,” it refers to the work of painting. But here, because of the exposition of the fourfold Dhamma, it is according to the context (*pakaraṇa*).
Showing that this meaning should be understood as being consistent with the sense of the words as they have been stated—namely, that it is like the word "consciousness" (viññāṇa)—he says:

“In the case of a designation (paññatti), too,” and so forth. It is called a *paññatti* because one designates by means of it; the meaning is “in that [designation], namely, the designation of a name. For “Citta” is the name of a certain householder.

The particle *pi* has the sense of including what is about to be mentioned. “In consciousness” (*viññāṇe*) refers to consciousness distinguished as having both resultant and non-resultant types. For that...
It is called "consciousness" (viññāṇa) in the sense of cognizing. As it has been said: "Monks, it cognizes; therefore it is called consciousness.
"Designation for mind" (cittasammutī) means the conventional expression "mind.
"Should be seen" means should be understood. "Here" refers to this context of the exposition of the fourfold dhamma. "By one who is wise" means by one who knows; that is, by an Abhidhammika.

Since the manifestation of the intrinsic nature of phenomena that possess differentiation cannot occur without analysis, the passage beginning with “because it has an object” (*sārammaṇato*) is undertaken in order to demonstrate the differentiation of consciousness.
In this context, that which they take as their support, depending upon which they arise, is the *ārammaṇa*—that is, the condition and the sphere of activity.
For instance, in such passages as “Māra finds an *ārammaṇa*; Māra finds an opening,” and so forth.
The condition is called the "object" (*ārammaṇa*). In such passages as, "The sign is the in-breath and out-breath;

it is without an object for a single state of consciousness," it refers to the domain (*gocara*). But here, both meanings are acceptable, because every state of consciousness possesses both a condition and a domain.

It is "with an object" (*sārammaṇa*) because it functions together with an object, being inseparable from it. And here, by way of a designation emphasizing the abstract state (*bhāva*), [it is understood as "the state of having an object"].

The state of having an object (*sārammaṇabhāva*) is expressed by the word "having an object" (*sārammaṇa*), just as in such passages as, "This too is the sublime jewel in the Buddha," and "The eye is empty of a self or of what belongs to a self," where the state of being a jewel or a self and so forth is expressed by the words "jewel" and so on;
therefore, the meaning is "because of the state of having an object. In other instances as well, it should be understood accordingly. "Of one kind" (*ekavidha*)...
"Of a single kind" means having a single portion.
"With and without result" refers to the existence or non-existence of the nature that produces a result (*vipāka*). For the word *vipāka* functions in two senses:
in some cases it refers to immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) that have reached the state of being matured, and in other cases...

In the sense of having the nature of producing result (vipāka). For thus, in such expressions as "resultant states" (*vipākā dhammā*), it applies to immaterial phenomena that have already reached the state of being matured (*vipakka*).

In such expressions as "states with the nature of resulting" (*vipākadhammadhammā*), it applies to the nature of producing result. But here, however, the nature of producing result is what should be understood.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that super-knowledges (*abhiññā*) and wholesome states (*kusalā*), etc., which possess results, would not be included under the term "with result" (*savi-pāka*).
For if only those states that have already reached the state of having ripened were included here, then for one who possesses them,

that [kamma] would be "with result" (savipāka) and the other "without result" (avipāka). However, this would lead to the inclusion of the term "without result" even for the wholesome kamma of direct knowledge— which is sometimes without result— such as that to be experienced in the present life,
and for unwholesome kamma to be abandoned by cultivation, because there is no arising of a result for them.
And this being the case, since it will later be stated that "the indeterminate is without fruition," it would follow that these [mental factors] possess the status of being indeterminate;
yet this is not desired, because they are already included in the exposition of the wholesome and unwholesome.

However, when their nature as producing fruition is taken into account, their very nature consists in a functional activity within a continuum where the underlying tendencies of craving have not been severed.
Since its inclusion among the "resultant" states is established by the fact that it exists in those [minds] even when no result is being produced,
no undesirable contradiction arises. As for the reason why super-knowledge (abhiññā), wholesome states, and so forth are non-resultant,
and whatever detailed analysis is to be made therein— all that we shall show in their respective places of occurrence.
In response to the inquiry, "But what herein is with result (savipāka), and what is without result (avipāka)?", he says, "Therein, that which is with result," and so forth.
"Indeterminate" (abyākata) is twofold, by way of resultant (vipāka) and functional (kiriyā).

Among these, first, resultant consciousness—because it is effortless—is incapable of producing a result, like the reflection of a face on the surface of a mirror. And among the functional consciousnesses, that which...
In the mental continuum of one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), eighteen kinds of consciousness necessarily arise;
however, because that continuum has its root of existence severed, it does not yield fruit—just as a flower on a creeper whose roots have been cut does not bear fruit.

As for the two types of adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*), although they arise in a continuum where the root of existence is not yet severed, they are like "vain flowers" because they are weak due to their lack of repetition (*anāsevana*).
If it lacks the capacity for the state of a seed, it is simply fruitless. Thus, all this is "indeterminate" (*abyākata*) because it is devoid of the nature of being subject to fruition;
it is called "non-fruition" (*avipāka*) and "indeterminate. Birth (*jāti*) refers to the arising of similar forms even from dissimilar causes; it is a common form.
The birth of the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate is "wholesome-unwholesome-indeterminate birth. According to its divisions, the wholesome is threefold.
“Unwholesome and indeterminate. The purpose of the inquiry regarding the meaning of the words has already been stated.
10. “Of the despicable,” etc., is the answer. Therein, “of the despicable” means of the censured; the meaning is:
of evil states that should be condemned by the wise, just as impurity is by citizens. “From salana” means from harming, or from removing.
For wholesome dhamma (kusala), by means of its appropriate factors such as "abandoning through substitution" (tadaṅga) and so forth, abandons unwholesome states;
thus it is said that it "injures" or "removes" them. Alternatively, its meaning is "flowing" (salana) and "restraining" (saṃvaraṇa), that is, "covering over.

For, by means of wholesome dhamma, through the prevention of the occurrence of unwholesome states and the induction of their state of non-occurrence, [it acts] upon the six sense-doors, including the mind-door.

They are restrained and closed off from non-occurrence. Regarding "kusā": they are called *kusā* because, through association with the impurities of lust and so forth, and by being the cause of various kinds of suffering, they lie and proceed within the mental continuum (*santāna*) in a contemptible manner due to their state of not having been abandoned; thus, they are evil qualities (*pāpadhamma*).
Alternatively, they are called *kusā* because they sharpen (*sāna*), whet (*nisāna*), and excite (*tejana*) contemptible, blameworthy states such as the destruction of life.
“Hatred, greed, and so forth. For it is through the influence of hatred and the rest that volition attains a state of sharpness, whereby acts such as the taking of life become greatly blameworthy.
The meaning is: by their “reaping,” that is, by their cutting off, or by abandoning them according to their respective natures. By “kusa”:

by means of knowledge (ñāṇa) which has received the name “kusa” because it is a source (sāna) for what is contemptible (kucchi), because it makes [defilements] thin (tanu-karaṇa), or because it brings them to an end (osāna-karaṇa). “Because they are to be taken” (lātabba-ttā) means because they are to be grasped (ādātabba-ttā).
Because it must proceed within the continuum by way of both co-nascence and decisive support conditions (*sahajāta-upanissaya-bhāva*).

For knowledge that is wholesome with three roots (*tihetuka-kusala*) proceeds in the continuum both by way of co-nascence and by way of decisive support, whereas wholesome [knowledge] with two roots (*duhetuka-kusala*) proceeds only by way of decisive support.
And having established this, the meaning of "wholesome" (*kusala*) as "produced by skill" (*kosalla-sambhūta*) is given as a common definition for all wholesome states.
It is so called. Alternatively, because it is a generic term (*jāti-sadda*), the singular number is used for *kusa*; however, the meaning is "by means of *kusa* grasses" (*kusehi*).

For the faculties such as faith (*saddhā*) that function by way of meritorious deeds are called "straws" (*kusāni*) according to the method already stated, since they are to be gathered by them and are to be set in motion according to the aforementioned method. Furthermore, in this context—
“Because it mows like kusa grass, or because it mows as kusa grass does;
because it scrapes away (saleti) what is wholesome (kusala), or because it mows away the very essence of kusa—it mows.
In this context, just as kusa grass, when grasped, mows the area of the hand on both sides, so too does this [wisdom] mow away [defilements] by way of those already arisen and those not yet arisen.
It mows and cuts away the faction of defilements belonging to both sides; it is the right effort (sammappadhāna) as it has been handed down thus:
"One generates desire, exerts oneself, for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states... [and so on] ...for the abandoning of arisen [evil, unwholesome states].
Therefore, because it mows like a sickle (kusa), it is *kusala*. Regarding the phrase "it mows like a sickle": here—
“Ku” is said to mean earth; because it resembles earth in its quality of being a foundation for phenomena, the aggregate of form and the aggregate of the formless are referred to here [by that term].
Because they burn away and destroy their own support—both now and in the future—they are called *kusā*, meaning lust and so forth.
That which cuts or severs its own support like those [weeds] is *kusala*. It is accomplished through application.

For wholesome states (kusala-dhammā) utterly eradicate both material and immaterial phenomena by preventing their further occurrence, thereby leading to the attainment of the Nibbāna-element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu).
Furthermore, according to the method already stated, it is called "wholesome" (kusala) because it moves away from and removes that which is named "ku"—namely, the aggregates of form and formlessness;

thus, "it moves away from the ku" (*kuṃ saleti*) is *kusala*. As for the expression "he mows the *kusa* grass," here *kusa* refers to that in which the loathsome things lie, namely, the body (*kāya*); it "mows" that [body].
"In the manner already stated" means it is wholesome (*kusala*).
Now, in order to show the extraction of the meanings of the word *kusala*, he says: "The word *kusala* [is used] in the sense of 'skilled' (*cheka*)," and so forth.
In this context, [it is seen] in such passages as: "You are skilled in the parts and sub-parts of the chariot; you are skilled in dance and song; the four women are well-trained."
The meaning is that "cheke" means "seen," and "chekapariyāya" means "a term for proficiency. In such passages as, "Is it well with you, sir?
Is it free from illness with you?", it refers to health. And in such passages as, "But what, venerable sir, is wholesome bodily conduct?
That bodily conduct which is blameless, Great King," and "Furthermore, venerable sir, this is unsurpassed, as the Blessed One... [it refers to excellence].
In such passages as, "He teaches the Dhamma regarding wholesome states," it refers to the blameless (*anavajja*).
In such passages as, "By reason of undertaking wholesome states, this merit increases; because wholesome kamma has been performed and accumulated," it refers to desirable ripening (*iṭṭhavipāka*).

Regarding the phrase "the blameless and so forth" (*anavajjādike*), it refers to the blameless and desirable ripening; and the term "the blameless and so forth" also refers to the characteristic that [the author] himself will explain later.

It is stated because of its suitability, but not because the attainment of health is impossible. For wholesome states (*kusala*) constitute health (*ārogya*) due to the absence of the disease of the defilements (*kilesa*).

Faults (*vajja*) are lust and the rest; that which does not possess these is "faultless" (*anavajja*). That which has a desirable ripening (*vipāka*) consisting of the four aggregates is "with desirable ripening" (*iṭṭhavipāka*).
And its state of having desirable ripening should be understood as possessing that very nature, not as something [external] to it.
Precisely because an agreeable result necessarily arises from it, it is called a "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*) since one is characterized by it;

and being both blameless (*anavajja*) and having an agreeable result (*iṭṭhavipāka*), it is "blameless-agreeable-result. That which has this characteristic is "characterized by blameless-agreeable-result.
Now, is it not the case that only the wholesome (*kusala*) is blameless-agreeable-result? However, according to the stated rule, [the term] "from the blameless-agreeable-result" [is used].
There may be another wholesome [state]. For is it not possible to say that a thing is its own characteristic?

This is not a fault, because even for a single entity, one can conceptually posit the state of being the characterized and the characteristic, depending on the distinction between the meanings of the terms "thoroughly understood" (*pariññāta*) and "not thoroughly understood.

For the term "faultless, desirable, and having a result" expresses the meaning of what is thoroughly understood; the term "wholesome" (*kusala*) expresses the meaning of what is not thoroughly understood.
And thus, by way of the distinction between the intrinsic natures (sabhāva) of those words whose referents are fully understood and those whose referents are not fully understood,
a distinction is even conceptually attributed to the single wholesome state possessing them— just as, for example,
a distinction is made based on a difference in quality when one says, "Formerly you were clever, but now you are even more clever."

And it is conceptualized by way of the distinction of its basis; therefore, since it is that which characterizes by virtue of having the meaning of a word not yet fully understood, and that which is to be characterized by virtue of having the meaning of a word not yet fully understood—when these conceptualized distinctions are thus grasped, no fault whatsoever arises.

Alternatively, it is called a "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*) because it is characterized (*lakkhīyati*); and since it is both blameless, desirable, and a result of kamma, and it is a characteristic, it is "that which has the characteristic of being blameless, desirable, and a result of kamma" (*anavajja-iṭṭha-vipāka-lakkhaṇa*).

The meaning is that it is "wholesome" (*kusala*) because it is characterized by being blameless and having a desirable ripening (*iṭṭhavipāka*). Alternatively, by the word "blameless" (*anavajja*), the state of being blameless is expressed;

by the word "desirable ripening," the state of having a desirable ripening is expressed. Therefore, "blameless and having a desirable ripening" refers to that which is both blameless and has a desirable ripening.

[The compound *anavajjaiṭṭhavipāka-lakkhaṇa*] is formed with the word "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*) in either the instrumental sense (meaning "that which is characterized by this") or the accusative sense (meaning "this is its characteristic").

“Characterized by blameless, excellent fruition” means possessing the nature of blameless, excellent fruition, or it means that which is to be characterized by the state of blameless, excellent fruition.
What, then, is the reason for employing two terms? Could not the intended meaning be established by a single term alone?
For even if one were to say “characterized by the blameless,” [the following would apply: “Furthermore...”

In passages such as, "Venerable sir, this is unsurpassed, namely, how the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding wholesome states," there might be the possibility of including the indeterminate (abyākata) as well, because it is free from censure.

Therefore, the phrase "having desirable ripening" must certainly be stated. But if one says "having the characteristic of desirable ripening," should the other [phrase] not be stated? For since the indeterminate possesses the quality of being capable of ripening, there would be the possibility of it having desirable ripening.

This is true. Two phrases were spoken in order to show the happiness of the wholesome’s occurrence through the phrase "blameless" (anavajja), and the happiness of its result through the phrase "desirable ripening" (iṭṭhavipāka).

For the blameless phrase is a statement of characteristic by way of the nature of its own occurrence, while the other is by way of its capacity to produce a ripening at a later time. Alternatively, [it shows] the purity of the purpose of the wholesome.
The first phrase was stated to show this, and the latter to show its pure ripening.
Alternatively, the former indicates the wholesome’s exclusion from the nature of the unwholesome, while the latter indicates its nature as indeterminate; enough of this excessive elaboration.
And here, by the expression “blameless... characteristic,” the general characteristic of the wholesome is stated, as it has the nature of blameless desirable ripening.

Because wholesome states share a commonality of genus. It should be understood that the characteristic of intrinsic nature is expressed by way of the unique (asādhāraṇa) status of unwholesome states and so forth.

"The function of destroying the unwholesome" refers to the task of abandoning the unwholesome in its appropriate manner. For the wholesome—divided into the categories of limited, exalted, and supramundane—abandons the side of the unwholesome respectively by means of substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga*), suppression (*vikkhambhana*), and eradication (*samuccheda*). Then...
What is the distinction between the various types of abandonment, such as abandonment by way of the factor itself (*tadaṅga*) and so forth? It is said:

Abandonment by way of the factor itself (*tadaṅgappahāna*) is the abandonment of each respective unwholesome factor, such as stinginess, by means of each respective wholesome factor contained within the bases for the performance of merit, such as giving.
This should be regarded as being like the destruction of darkness by the light of a lamp; for the wholesome states of the sense sphere possess only limited power.
Because, when those unwholesome states have been destroyed at their own moment of existence and have ceased, they are overcome by their non-return upon that cessation.
The abandonment of each respective hindering state by way of obstructing its occurrence—known as suppression—is called "abandonment by suppression.
This should be understood as being like the clearing away of moss from the surface of water by striking it with a jar.
Just as when moss has been swept away by a powerful blow from a water-jar, even after that blow has ceased, the moss does not suddenly spread back over it due to the force of that blow;

in the same way, sensual desire and the other hindrances, which have been suppressed by jhāna—distinguished here as access (upacāra) and absorption (appanā)—do not suddenly surge back at the time when they are no longer active, owing to the power of that jhāna.
This is what is meant by "the state of being subject to non-arising" (anuppattidhammatā).

Abandonment by way of right eradication is "abandonment by complete cutting off" (*samucchedappahāna*). This, however, should be regarded as like the total destruction of trees and the like by a stroke of lightning, which uproots them.
For once the defilements have been completely cut off by the Noble Path, they do not arise in the continuum even in the form of a mere latent tendency (*anusaya*).
Just as things destroyed along with their roots by the fire of Indra, even after a single occurrence, [do not grow again].

Just as trees and the like do not grow again, even so, by that single moment of consciousness through its mere arising, the defilements—even those persisting as latent tendencies—are utterly destroyed in every way.

"Vodāna" means purification; the meaning is freedom from the stains of defilement. Having become thus, it is its manifestation; thus it is said to be "manifested as purification," meaning it appears to the meditator’s knowledge in the form of complete purity.
Thus, having described the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) of the wholesome by way of its nature as the fruition of what is free from faults,

and its functions (*rasa*), manifestations (*paccupaṭṭhāna*), and modes (*ākāra*), the passage beginning with “Because it is the opposite of faults” is stated in order to further show its characteristic by way of being the antidote to faults,
and its function and so forth by way of the fruit of attainment. In that context, the state of being the opposite of faults is...

Because it is the opposite of fault (*vajja*). By this, he shows that in the phrase "the characteristic of being faultless" (*anavajjalakkhaṇa*), the prefix *a-* has the sense of opposition; thereby, its exclusion from the indeterminate (*abyākata*) is established.

For otherwise, since the indeterminate is neither "faulty" nor "other than faulty," there would be the undesirable consequence (*atiprasaṅga*) that it too possesses that characteristic. "Because it is the opposite of fault" (*vajjapaṭipakkhattā*).

However, when this has been stated, since it is only the wholesome and the unwholesome that stand in a state of direct opposition to one another—as light and darkness do—by way of being the abandoner and the abandoned, it follows as a proven fact that the wholesome alone has the characteristic of being blameless because it is the opposite of what is blameworthy, and nothing else.
Its function is the state of purification (*vodānabhāva*); that is, it brings about the attainment of the state of purification from the stains of the defilements.

The meaning is "accomplished through being undefiled. It is called *paccupaṭṭhāna* because it is presented or brought forward by a cause, or because it stands facing [the result] in dependence on its own cause due to being bound to that;
thus, having a desirable ripening as its presentation is "having a desirable ripening as its presentation" (*iṭṭhavipākapaccupaṭṭhāna*).
Because the wholesome does not arise in the absence of wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*), and because it does arise when that [wise attention] is present, wise attention is its proximate cause;
thus he said, "it has wise attention as its proximate basis" (*yonisomanasikāra-padaṭṭhāna*). In this context, wise attention is attention by way of the proper method or means.
In terms of its meaning, however, for one whose mental continuum possesses underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), when objects have come into the range of the six sense-doors—

Attention that arises by turning back the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) through its functioning as a condition for wholesome states—by means of the perfection of dwelling in a suitable locality and so forth—is called "wise attention" (yonisomanasikāra).
By way of the opposites of what has been stated, "unwise attention" (ayonisomanasikāra) is also to be understood.

However, setting aside that which arises as a condition for functional consciousnesses (kiriyacitta) in one whose mental continuum is free from underlying tendencies (niranusaya), [the rest is wise attention].
Because the faultless dhamma does not become a condition for any faulty dhamma, it may belong to the side of wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*).

Since it exists within the mental continuum of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), it does not serve as a condition for any state of either the wholesome or the unwholesome—apart from its mere arising toward objects that have come into range—without regard for whether they are wisely attended or unwisely attended; thus, by way of both these aspects...
Or it might be designated as "indeterminate attention" because it is not to be expressed [in terms of fault].

Regarding the definition of the unwholesome (*akusala*) as having the characteristic of being blameworthy and having an undesirable result (*aniṭṭhavipāka*): here too, the application of the opposite [terms] is to be understood according to the method already stated, such as: "Faults (*vajja*) are lust and so forth;
that which possesses these is 'blameworthy' (*sāvajja*); that which has an undesirable result is 'having an undesirable result' (*aniṭṭhavipāka*)," and so on.
It should be seen as follows: by way of its function (*rasa*), it has the function of producing what is harmful;

by way of its manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*), it manifests as defilement (*saṃkilesa*). Alternatively, because it is censurable, it has the characteristic of being blameworthy (*sāvajja-lakkhaṇa*); its function is the state of defilement; it manifests as an undesirable result (*aniṭṭha-vipāka*);

and its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) is improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*). As for the etymological meaning (*vacanattha*), it is "unwholesome" (*akusala*) because it is not wholesome (*kusala*), that is, the opposite of the wholesome.
This is the meaning. For this negative particle *a-* has the sense of "opposition" (*paṭipakkha*), and not any other sense, nor the sense of "non-existence. Otherwise, there would not be a triad;

rather, it would result in a dyad or a tetrad. For if that which is other than the wholesome were unwholesome, then the indeterminate (*abyākata*)—by virtue of being other than that [wholesome]—would also be included under the term "unwholesome" due to the distinction between the classes of wholesome and unwholesome.
It should be stated as a dyad (duka) consisting of two types. If non-existence of the wholesome were unwholesome, then no specific category would be grasped;
therefore, it should be stated as a dyad based on the distinction between the wholesome and the indeterminate categories.

If it were argued that "non-existence too should be grasped separately," then, because it lacks a category, there could be no connection with the word "category" (*jāti*). [This applies only] to that which exists.
For there is indeed such a thing as "birth" (jāti). Or else, just as there is an absence of the wholesome, so too there is an absence of the indeterminate;

thus, one might speak of an "indeterminate birth," and a fourfold classification would result. But this is not desired, because birth is intended to be only threefold—by way of the wholesome and so forth—and because in the Canon it is presented as a triad:
"wholesome states, unwholesome states, and indeterminate states."

However, when it is stated as "the opposite of the wholesome" (*kusalapaṭipakkha*), then—just as the opposite of a friend is a non-friend (*amitta*) and the opposite of greed is non-greed (*alobha*)—whatever class of phenomena constitutes a direct antithesis to the wholesome is "unwholesome. On this basis, the triad [of the unwholesome roots] is established;
and its status as a direct antithesis is due to its being blameworthy and having an undesirable result. By means of that...
It should be understood as something to be abandoned because of its very nature of being abandonable, but not because of the destruction of the wholesome.
For the unwholesome does not abandon the wholesome; rather, it is the wholesome itself that abandons it due to its great strength. Indeed, the wholesome is powerful, while the unwholesome is weak.
Therefore it was said: "The weak are overcome by the strong; dangers crush them. Thus, it is the wholesome itself [that abandons].
It should be understood that, according to the method already stated, the unwholesome is abandoned by the wholesome, and the wholesome is not [abandoned] by the other.

As for those two... [etc. ...the indeterminate (*avyākata*): that class of phenomena which, unlike the wholesome, does not have the characteristic of blameless and desirable ripening (*vipāka*), nor, like the unwholesome, has the characteristic of blameworthy and undesirable ripening, but rather, because it lacks ripening, possesses characteristics opposite to both of those.

The meaning is that it is "indeterminate" (abyākata). But would it not follow that something is indeterminate if it possesses some other result that is the opposite of desirable and undesirable results—just as the feeling of equanimity is the opposite of pleasant and painful feelings—when it is stated that its characteristic is "the opposite of both of those"?
It does not so follow, because such a thing is impossible. For just as light and darkness...
There is nothing else that is the opposite; thus, there is no result whatsoever that is the opposite of desirable and undesirable results.
Alternatively, the word *taṃ* here refers solely to the wholesome and unwholesome, independent of desirable and undesirable results.

Since the wholesome and unwholesome possess results, their opposite characteristic—that is, the characteristic of being without result—is the meaning of "the characteristic of non-result" (*avipākalakkhaṇa*).
Enough with further inquiry here. It is called "indeterminate" (*abyākata*) because it is not defined by way of being either wholesome (*kusala*) or unwholesome (*akusala*).

For, having mentioned the wholesome and the unwholesome, the fact that the indeterminate is stated [separately] implies that it is not stated by way of being either wholesome or unwholesome; this is understood, and not through any other mode of expression.
And its non-statement in that manner is precisely because its characteristic is the opposite of both those, and not merely because it is something that cannot be stated at all.
It should be understood thus. Alternatively, the prefix *vi-* signifies opposition (*virodha*), while the prefix *ā-* indicates the state of being directed toward (*abhimukhabhāva*).

Therefore, it is explained that wholesome and unwholesome states are "opposed" because they are mutually opposed by their own conditions, and because they stand in opposition to one another as that which abandons and that which is to be abandoned. That which is other than these is the indeterminate (*abyākata*). For that [indeterminate] is neither wholesome nor unwholesome in terms of its characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*).

It is not contradictory to that [the indeterminate], for the state of being non-resultant does not conflict with either the state of having a desirable result—just as it does not conflict with the state of having an undesirable result—nor with the state of having an undesirable result—just as it does not conflict with the state of having a desirable result.

Furthermore, the indeterminate does not abandon anything among the wholesome or unwholesome, nor is it something to be abandoned by anyone. Thus, "the indeterminate has a characteristic opposite to both of those."
When it is being cognized, there was karma, but there was no fruition of karma; there is no fruition of karma;

there will be no fruition of karma—by means of this triad, because of the absence of the arising of fruition for that karma which is to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*) and so forth, which is comprised by the failure of destiny, basis, time, and effort, as well as for unwholesome states to be abandoned through cultivation and for wholesome states of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), [the view] "it might be... [is held].
Thinking, "Could it perhaps be that this is an indeterminate state? someone might occasionally wonder;

therefore, to prevent such a thought, he says, "or it is incapable of producing a result. It is "incapable of producing a result" because it lacks the capacity to give rise to a ripening (vipāka). This is what is meant:
first, those [karmas] to be experienced in the present life and so forth may fail to produce a result due to causes such as the deficiency of conditions; however, if these...
If they were far removed, then, by virtue of their incapacity to yield a result, they would indeed be "not fit for fruition"; however, that is not the case.
Rather, it is precisely because of their incapacity to yield a result in any way whatsoever that they are "not fit for fruition," and thus they are called "indeterminate" (*abyākata*).
Now, among the wholesome and so forth thus defined by way of the triad, first analyzing the wholesome consciousness:
By the passage beginning with “therein, wholesome consciousness,” he shows its numerical limit. It is of twenty-one kinds:
briefly, it is of twenty-one kinds as follows—eight sense-sphere [consciousnesses], five fine-material-sphere, four immaterial-sphere, and four supramundane.
As for its being fourfold according to plane, this refers to those known as the planes of the sense-sphere, the fine-material-sphere, the immaterial-sphere, and the supramundane.
By way of four planes, the consciousness occurring therein is also fourfold.
In this context, "plane" (*bhūmi*) means a place (*ṭhāna*) or a state (*avatthā*). For a state is understood as the locus of occurrence for those things that possess it;
thus, their comprehension is easily achieved. And here, "state" refers to the states of phenomena through sensual craving and so forth.

The state of being delimited and undelimited. In this regard, the first three planes should be understood by way of both [delimitation and non-delimitation], while the others are to be understood only by way of their specific states.
For no location other than the sense-sphere existence (*kāma-bhava*) and so forth is found for supramundane phenomena (*lokuttara-dhamma*).
Even when they occur elsewhere, because they are included within the sense-sphere plane according to the method that will be explained, they are "of one kind by way of plane."
Regarding the distinction between "having a basis" (*savaṭṭhuka*) and "lacking a basis" (*avaṭṭhuka*): there are six bases, namely the five beginning with the eye and the heart.
However, because wholesome consciousness lacks dependence on the eye and so forth, it is the heart-base that is intended here as the "basis.
That which is accompanied by this [heart-base] and necessarily proceeds dependent upon it is "with a basis," referring to the consciousness occurring in the sense-sphere and fine-material realms.

For there, the immaterial [consciousness] occurs in dependence upon the material; however, in the immaterial realm, because of the absence of matter, it occurs entirely devoid of a physical basis (*vatthu*).
Thus, as it occurs there, it is "without a basis" (*avatthuka*). Regarding the passage beginning with "inferior... threefold":

here, it is "inferior" (*hīna*) because it is inferior to the intermediate and sublime [states] in terms of its conditions and its fruit, or because it is deficient in their qualities. By its own conditions...
"Exalted" (*paṇīta*) means brought to a state of excellence; "middling" (*majjhima*) means existing between the two.

Therein, that which is set in motion by inferior desire (*chanda*), mind (*citta*), energy (*vīriya*), or investigation (*vīmaṃsā*) is inferior; that set in motion by middling desire and so forth is middling;

and that set in motion by exalted [desire and so forth] is exalted. Furthermore, the inferiority and other qualities of desire and the rest should be understood by way of their respective inclinations (*adhimutti*).
For their inferiority is due to an inferior inclination, their excellence due to a superior inclination, and their mediocrity due to an inclination that lies between those two.
Or else, wholesome action performed out of a desire for fame is inferior; that performed out of a desire for the fruits of merit is mediocre;

Regarding "from the distinction of joy...": the word *bheda* (distinction) should be connected with each term individually, as in "from the distinction of joy and equanimity, from the distinction of knowledge, and from the distinction of application.
In this context, "from the distinction of application" means "from the distinction of formations" (*saṅkhāra*). Is it not so?

First, the distinction between joy (*somanassa*) and equanimity (*upekkhā*) is appropriate, because their intrinsic natures (*sabhāva*) are different. But how is the distinction between knowledge (*ñāṇa*) and application (*payoga*) [to be understood]?
It is said: the distinction between knowledge and application is "the distinction of knowledge and application," because it occurs by depending on the presence or absence of those two.
Now, in order to show that very distinction of joy, equanimity, and so forth through analysis, [the text says]: "That is to say" (*seyyathidaṃ*).
Having asked, he answers with the words beginning, "accompanied by joy" (*somanassasahagata*). Therein, *seyyathidaṃ* means "what is that? or "how is that?
*Sumana* means a beautiful mind, or one whose mind is beautiful; the state of being such is *somanassa*, which refers to mental pleasant feeling.
"Adhivacana" means that from its arising through to its cessation, it occurs accompanied by joy—this is the sense of being "conjoined" (*saṃsaṭṭha*) and "associated" (*sampayutta*).
Alternatively, it is "accompanied by joy" (*somanassasahagata*) because it has attained the state of simultaneous arising and so forth with joy.

It is "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) because it knows and penetrates according to the true nature of things; it is "associated with knowledge" (*ñāṇasampayutta*) because it is joined with that knowledge in ways such as simultaneous arising.

It is "without volitional effort" (*asaṅkhāra*) because it has no volitional effort; that which is simply without volitional effort is "spontaneous" (*asaṅkhārika*). That which proceeds together with volitional effort is "with volitional effort" (*sasaṅkhāra*);
that itself is "prompted" (*sasaṅkhārika*). And here, "volitional effort" (*saṅkhāra*) refers to one's own or another's prior application, [expressed as]:
"he prepares [it] by means of a particular adornment known as sharpness," or "it is prepared, it is made ready."

"Having made the mind [firm] by this. In that context, when the mind is sinking due to defilements such as the stain of stinginess (*macchara-mala*) or lethargy-and-drowsiness (*thinamiddha*) at the time of performing meritorious deeds like giving, right effort (*sammāvāyāma*)—which operates through the three doors by way of pacifying those defilements and generating energy in the mind—is called "one's own application.
However, for one who lacks energy in performing what is wholesome, [it is said]: "O good man!..."
The performance of wholesome deeds is the path cultivated by the wise; it is fitting for you, too, to practice therein.
Therefore, give gifts and guard your virtue, for that will lead to your welfare, benefit, and happiness.

Such an instruction, proceeding through the doors of the body and speech toward others in order to generate enthusiasm for the performance of wholesome deeds, is called "instigation by another" (*parappayoga*). Among these:
However, while the former arises in one’s own mental continuum during its prior stage of development, the latter arises only in the mental continua of others;
therefore, the specific excellence of the mind characterized by sharpness produced by that [latter] should be understood here as "formation" in a figurative sense. Thus the teachers have said:
“The excellence arising from the mind, Produced by previous application...”
“Volitional formation (saṅkhāra) is so designated by those who know the intrinsic nature of volitional formations.

Alternatively, the terms “prompted” (sasaṅkhārika) and “unprompted” (asaṅkhārika) are stated solely with reference to the presence or absence of the factor of volition itself, and not with reference to the presence or absence of its simultaneous occurrence;
for even a volitional formation that occurs within a different mental continuum [may be so classified].

Because that [volition] exists, the consciousness produced by its power possesses volitional activity (*saṅkhāra*); thus it is "with volitional activity" (*sasaṅkhārika*), since the prefix *sa-* indicates the sense of existing, as in expressions such as "having hair" (*salomaka*) or "having wings" (*sapakkhaka*).
Conversely, that which is the opposite of this is "without volitional activity" (*asaṅkhārika*) precisely because of the absence of that [volition], according to the aforementioned principle.
Alternatively, it is so called because of the act of preparing (*saṅkharaṇa*) or because it is prepared (*saṅkharīyati*) by means of this adventitious factor that has arisen.
It is called *saṅkhāra* because it prepares or constructs that [wholesome state] by means of removing the nature of mental despondency, precisely in the manner already described;
thus, the term refers directly to the state of sharpness produced by prior application. That which lacks this is *asaṅkhārika*;

the meaning is "sharp by its own nature. That which is accompanied by such [application] is *sasaṅkhārika*. Alternatively, it is so called because it is constructed (*saṅkharīyati*) by the stains of stinginess and the like.
*Saṅkhāra* is the nature of the mind’s sinking; that which lacks this is *asaṅkhārika* (spontaneous), while the other is *sasaṅkhārika* (prompted).

Alternatively, a powerful condition such as excellent weather or food is called *saṅkhāra*, because it is understood as "it conditions the mind to a state of sharpness" (*saṅkharoti cittaṃ tikkhabhāvena*) or "the mind is conditioned by this" (*saṅkharīyati vā taṃ etena*).
Since the vowel *a-* has the sense of increase (*vuḍḍha*), it is a *saṅkhāra* that has reached a state of growth.
"Assā" means "unprompted" (*asaṅkhārika*), the sense being that it possesses powerful conditions.
However, because it is not distinguished by the vowel "a"—which indicates growth—the intention is that it is "prompted" (*sasaṅkhārika*), possessing conditions, and having weak conditions.
"Dissociated from knowledge" (*ñāṇavippayutta*) means devoid of, or separated from, knowledge.
It is called *upekkhā* because it looks on with equanimity (*upekkhati*). Even while feeling, it looks on at the object with impartiality;

this is the meaning of its being established in a neutral mode. Alternatively, it is *upekkhā* because it looks upon (*ikkhati*) and experiences the desirable and undesirable object by way of arising or logical fitness, through the absence of partiality.
Or else, it is the looking upon and experiencing that has approached (*upetā*) and is not opposed to pleasure and pain.
Equanimity (*upekkhā*). Because it is non-opposed, it can indeed arise immediately after those two.
However, pleasant and painful feelings (*sukha-vedanā* and *dukkha-vedanā*), having mutually opposed natures, do not arise one after the other.
For this very reason, in the *Paṭṭhāna*, the arising of displeasure (*domanassa*) immediately after joy (*somanassa*), and the arising of joy immediately after displeasure, is taught.
[These feelings] are excluded. Furthermore, this meaning applies even to the feeling associated with greed-accompanied consciousness, whereas the previous two do not.
For there is no "looking on with equanimity" (ajjhupekkhana) in a neutral mode toward states such as those accompanied by greed, nor is there any "seeing" (ikkhana) arising from birth.
"Accompanied by equanimity" (upekkhāsahagata) is entirely according to the method explained below.
But surely there are other associated states such as contact (phassa) and so forth; why then is the eightfold nature [of consciousness] grasped specifically by way of joy (somanassa) and the rest?

Because they possess a differentiating character. For since contact and the others are common to all consciousness, and since faith and the others are common to all wholesome states, no differentiation of consciousness is made by them.
Joy and the rest, however, exist only in certain types of consciousness.
Since they exist in some consciousnesses and do not exist in others, the differentiation of consciousness by means of them is indeed evident.
But why is it that these [mental factors] exist in some consciousnesses and do not exist in others? It is because of the presence or absence of their respective causes.
What, then, is their cause? It is said: in this regard, the state of being accompanied by joy (*somanassa*) occurs by way of the object. For when there is a desirable object...
A consciousness accompanied by joy arises. But surely, since a desirable object is the basis for greed and is something to be relished, how can wholesome consciousness arise with respect to it?
This is not an absolute rule, because wholesome consciousness arises even toward a desirable object when it is determined by such factors as restraint.
For one whose mind is fixed solely on performing what is wholesome, thinking, "Only the wholesome must be done by me," [wholesome consciousness arises].
It has been restrained; having turned away from unwholesome activity, it has been directed solely toward performing wholesome deeds.

Furthermore, through constant practice, the wholesome has become habitual by way of the fourfold supporting conditions—namely, dwelling in a suitable locality, hearing the true Dhamma, relying upon virtuous friends, and having performed merit in the past—and through the application of wise attention (*yoniso ābhoga*), even when a desirable object arises, only a consciousness associated with non-greed (*alobha*) arises in him.
It is not associated with greed. And in this regard, there is this [verse]:

“Due to the certainty [of the result], due to transformation, And due to habitual practice, When preceded by knowledge and accompanied by volition, Even toward a desirable object, it may be wholesome.”
Furthermore, the mind’s association with joy (*somanassasahagatā*) should be understood through causes such as an abundance of faith (*saddhābahulatā*).

For even upon seeing the form of a Tathāgata—which is exclusively desirable to those who lack faith and hold wrong views—joy does not arise. And for those who do not perceive the benefit in the occurrence of wholesome states, even when encouraged by others, joy does not arise.
Even when performing wholesome deeds, joy does not arise; therefore, through these reasons—abundance of faith, purity of view, and seeing the benefits—the mind becomes accompanied by joy.
Furthermore, there are those eleven factors that lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of rapture (*pītisambojjhaṅga*). Namely:

—The state of the mind being accompanied by joy is to be understood through these causes as well: recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of virtue, recollection of generosity, recollection of the deities, recollection of peace, avoiding persons who are harsh, associating with persons who are gentle, reflecting on discourses that inspire confidence, and devotion to those [qualities]. Regarding the qualities of the Buddha and so forth...
For one who recollects [the virtues], joy arises that pervades the entire body from the moment of access concentration (upacāra).
Likewise, for one reflecting upon the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla) protected by oneself through its integrity and other qualities over a long period;
or for a layperson reflecting upon the ten precepts or the five precepts; or reflecting upon fine food during times of famine, fear, and so forth.
For one who, having given to fellow practitioners of the holy life, reviews their own generosity, thinking, "I have given such a gift";
for a householder as well, at such a time, reviewing a gift given to those possessed of virtue;
for one reviewing the presence within oneself of those qualities endowed with which the devas attained the state of devas; and through serenity and insight—
Seeing that even for sixty or seventy years his defilements did not manifest after they had been suppressed,
he thought, "Oh, my defilements do not manifest! Yet, because of his lack of reverence in visiting shrines and seeing elder monks— which manifested his harsh nature—
and because of his lack of serene confidence and affection toward the Buddha and others, he avoided coarse persons who were like dust upon the back of a donkey.
For one who attends upon affectionate persons whose minds are softened by abundant confidence in the Buddha and so forth;

for one who reflects upon inspiring discourses that illuminate the virtues of the Triple Gem; and for one who, even while standing or sitting, applies himself to those same inclinations and so on in order to generate joy—joy generally arises.
And because joy is invariably concomitant with mental happiness (*somanassa*), [mental happiness arises as well].
Since the arising of that [joy] is necessarily preceded by the arising of the former [pleasure], thus even the causes of joy should be regarded as causes of mental happiness (*somanassa*).
Furthermore, the state of being accompanied by mental happiness occurs through these two reasons:

having a non-profound temperament and having a rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) characterized by mental happiness. For one who has a non-profound temperament is satisfied even with a slight beneficial resource, and one whose rebirth-linking is characterized by mental happiness—
Even when the objects are unattractive, one who views them as not repulsive will for the most part give rise to a consciousness accompanied by joy.
However, due to the absence of the aforementioned causes for joy and because the object is neutral,
it should be understood that the state is accompanied by equanimity.
However, it arises from these causes: from karma associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta*), from rebirth, from the ripening of the faculties, and from the distancing of the defilements.
For one who teaches the Dhamma to others out of a desire for their welfare, or [teaches] crafts such as weaving, sealing, and arithmetic;
occupations such as carpentry, smithing, and trade; and sciences such as the neutralizing of poisons—[for such a person, this knowledge arises].
In this way, he causes others to train in blameless crafts, fields of knowledge, and so forth, or trains in them himself;
having honored a preacher of the Dhamma, he causes the Dhamma to be preached; and having formed the aspiration, "May I be wise in the future," he performs various kinds of meritorious deeds.
As he thus accomplishes such various kinds of kamma conducive to wisdom, for him—
Wholesome consciousness accompanied by knowledge arises dependent upon that kamma.
Likewise, when one has arisen in a world free from affliction, the wholesome consciousness that arises is associated with knowledge. For this has been said:
“For him, being happy there, the words of the Dhamma flow forth; slow, O monks, is the arising of his mindfulness, yet that being quickly becomes a partaker of distinction.”
Likewise, for one who has attained the group of fifteen factors, the wholesome consciousness arising in dependence on the maturation of the faculties is associated with knowledge.

Furthermore, for one by whom the defilements have been suppressed through the cultivation of serenity and insight, the consciousness arising in dependence on the removal of those defilements arises associated with knowledge. As it has been said:
“Indeed, through yoga much is born; through non-yoga there is the destruction of much.
Furthermore, those qualities that lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena (dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga) are as follows:
being inquisitive, keeping the basis pure, balancing the faculties, and avoiding persons of poor wisdom.
The state of being associated with knowledge arises through these causes: associating with wise persons, reflecting on the practice of profound knowledge, and being intent upon that.

For instance, when one approaches those possessed of wisdom and frequently inquires about the aggregates, elements, bases, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, path-factors, jhāna-factors, serenity, insight, and so forth, there arises—beginning with the knowledge consisting of what has been heard (sutamaya-ñāṇa) produced by means of that [association]—[further knowledge].
The mind is accompanied by knowledge. However, for one who has previously made internal and external objects—
such as the nails, hair, robes, and lodgings— clear by means of clipping, cleaning away stains, and so forth,
there arises clear knowledge regarding the arisen states of consciousness and mental factors, just as [clarity arises] depending on lamps, mirrors, and the like that have been made pure.
It is like the radiance from the flame of a lamp that has been lit.
