Now, for one whose faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) or any other among the faculties is strong while the others are weak, those [weaker] ones are unable to perform their respective functions; therefore, he brings them to a state of balance through various modes according to the method set forth in the *Bodhipakkhiyā Dhammā Vibhaṅga*. As he thus brings the faculties to a state of balance...

Through the power of insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) and so forth, the mind becomes accompanied by knowledge (*ñāṇasahagata*). Furthermore, for one who avoids persons lacking wisdom, attends upon persons possessed of wisdom,
reflects upon the Blessed One’s profound course of knowledge as it penetrates into the aggregates (*khandha*) and so on,
or dwells with a mind intent upon that during standing, sitting, and other postures— for these [persons] as well, [this knowledge] arises.
It is wholesome and associated with knowledge. Furthermore, by recollecting the qualities of the Buddha and so forth, the mind becomes accompanied by knowledge. As it is said:
"Mahānāma, at whatever time a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor by hatred... nor by delusion; his mind is indeed straight."

At that time, the mind is directed toward the Tathāgata. Now, Mahānāma, a noble disciple whose mind is upright gains knowledge of the meaning, gains knowledge of the Dhamma, and gains joy connected with the Dhamma.
In one who is joyful, rapture arises; in one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; one whose body is tranquil feels happiness; and the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated.
“He becomes concentrated; being concentrated, he understands things as they truly are,” and so forth.

In this way, it should be understood that the recollections of the Buddha and the others also serve solely as causes for the arising of knowledge by means of purifying the stains of lust and the like.
Furthermore, rebirth with three roots (*tihetuka-paṭisandhika*) is a cause for the arising of knowledge; for the wisdom of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi-paññā*) exists from the very beginning.

When it occurs frequently by way of the continuity of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), it becomes a particularly distinguished proximate cause for the arising of knowledge through the cultivation of that continuum.
However, its state of being unprompted (*asaṅkhārikatta*) arises from favorable conditions such as climate, food, and dwelling.
And on this point there are these verses: “Desirable objects, abundance of faith, and purity of view;”
The visibility of the fruit, the causes for the joy factor of enlightenment,
the eleven factors likewise, the nature of being not deep,
and the connection associated with gladness— these are the causes of happiness.
“The absence of causes for pleasure, the neutral object,
and the cause for the arising of equanimity— thus should it be understood by one who discerns.
Likewise, from kamma and rebirth, and from the ripening of the faculties.”
Through the subsiding of defilements and by means of the causes for the investigation of phenomena—
by recollecting the qualities of the Buddha and others through seven factors,
and by being sustained by wisdom— the mind becomes endowed with knowledge.
“By means of such causes as season, nutriment, abode, and suitability, the state of being unprompted (asaṅkhārika) should also be understood by one who is discerning.

Having thus demonstrated the eightfold sense-sphere consciousness according to the distinctions in the application of knowledge regarding feeling, he now concludes it, saying: “This... [is] called...”
12. Now, in order to show the sense in which this is called "belonging to the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*), the passage beginning with "In brief" (*uddānato*) is commenced.

Therein, "in brief" means by way of enumeration; that is, in summary. Although the defilement-desire (*kilesakāma*)—like the remaining defilements and so forth—is included within the object-desire (*vatthukāma*) because it is something to be relished, it is nevertheless included [separately] in summary, just as knowledge is included within the knowable.

There may be only one kind of desire; nevertheless, when *kilesakāma* (defilement-desire) takes on the state of *vatthukāma* (object-desire), it does so by way of being desirable (*kāmanīyatthena*), not by way of being desired (*kāmanavasena*).
And yet, by way of being desired, it is indeed *kilesakāma* and not *vatthukāma*. With this in mind, he said, "By way of defilement and object," and so forth.
Keeping in mind the objection, "But what here is *vatthukāma*, and what is *kilesakāma*? [the author proceeds].

“Desire is sensual pleasure (kāma), lust is sensual pleasure, desire-and-lust is sensual pleasure; intention is sensual pleasure, passion is sensual pleasure, intention-and-passion is sensual pleasure”—it is precisely this craving for sensual pleasure (*kāmataṇhā*), as it appears and is defined in the explanatory text (*niddesapāḷi*), that is here meant by "defilement-sensual-pleasure" (*kilesakāma*). As for "object-sensual-pleasure" (*vatthukāma*), it refers to:
"agreeable forms... agreeable tangibles... all phenomena belonging to the sense sphere... all... [and so forth].

Having pointed out right there that all phenomena of the three planes—including those of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), and so forth, as well as all those of the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*), and so forth, down to "the sensual realm" (*kāma*)—are distinguished by the categories of consciousness and non-consciousness, he says: "Defilement... [and so forth]... the round.

By the restrictive phrase "or lustful desire" (*chandarāgo vā*), he excludes the nine defilements such as hatred and delusion from among the ten—greed, hatred, delusion, and so on—which are established as being of the nature of defilement.
The basis for craving for sense-desires, fine-materiality, and immateriality is the "foundation" (*vatthu*);
or rather, it is the foundation because it serves as the cause. 13. But what is called "defilement-desire" (*kilesakāma*), and what is "object-desire" (*vatthukāma*)?

He says, "defilement-desire," and so forth. "It desires" means it longs for an object-desire. "It is desired" means it is longed for by defilement-desire. The word *iti* [here] signifies the meaning of "therefore."

The particle *ca* has the sense of *eva* (only/itself). Therefore, because *kilesakāma* (defilement-desire) desires, it is called *kāma*; and because *vatthukāma* (object-desire) is desired, it is also called *kāma*.
Consequently, both these two kinds of *kāma*—namely, defilement-desire and object-desire—are established in the two grammatical roles of agent (*kattṛ*) and object (*karman*).
The meaning is that they experience the state of being the agent and the state of being the object. Now...
"Or it is twofold" means it is twofold by way of expressing two types of objects. The word "kāma" (desire) is established in two grammatical roles;
that is to say, the formation of the word "kāma" occurs in both the agent (*kattari*) and the object (*kammani*), as in the aforementioned pair of grammatical relations.
The particle *vo*, however, is merely an expletive, as in such phrases as "evam vo kālāmā. Alternatively, it refers to the two grammatical roles [expressed by] the syllable *vo*.

The meaning is "in two aggregates. For sensual desire as defilement (kilesakāma), because its intrinsic nature is that of volitional formations (saṅkhāra), is included in the aggregate of volitional formations;

and sensual desire as objects (vatthukāma), being composed of the five strands of sense pleasure according to the method to be explained, is included in the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) because its intrinsic nature is that of form.
Thus, this twofold desire is established—that is, it is accomplished and finds its place—within these two aggregates.
14. *Sampajjanāni sampattiyo*: by way of these [accomplishments], the meaning is: through their mutual convergence as object and subject, and through their attainment.

By this, however, he illustrates the following: wherever both kinds of sensual desire (*kāma*) occur together in the relation of object and subject, that very elevenfold region is designated as the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*). But where, in the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpadhātu*),...
Only sensual desire for the physical basis (*vatthukāma*) occurs; that sphere is not called "belonging to the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*).

But is it not the case that both types [of desire] together occur in the fine-material and immaterial realms, because the phenomena belonging to the fine-material and immaterial realms are themselves sensual objects (*vatthukāma*), and because the craving for the fine-material and immaterial—which serve as the objects of those [phenomena]—is established as "defilement-desire" (*kilesakāma*) through its connection with them? This is not so, because [the latter] is a lower-fetter (*orambhāgiya*).
Because here it is specifically the intense defilement of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) that is intended by the term "defiled sense-desire" (*kilesakāma*).

For although all sense-desires were indicated by the summary statement, “In brief, there are two kinds of sense-desires,” yet by defining the scope through such phrases as “a portion of the four nutriments,” the sensual lust mentioned here in the state of being an hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*)—
which constitutes a part of sense-desire— is described by way of its nature as a defiled sense-desire.
It is understood that only those phenomena which serve as the basis for them are grasped as sensual objects (*vatthukāma*),

and not craving for the fine-material and immaterial realms, nor the phenomena that serve as their basis. By taking it in this way, the simile involving the range of weapons mentioned below becomes appropriate,

because only the types of sensual pleasures already described are intended here, [whereas] in the fine-material and immaterial realms there exist celestial palaces, wish-fulfilling trees, dwellings, ornaments, protective spells, wholesome deeds, and so forth.

It is established that the desire and lust proceeding toward phenomena belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) is not called "defilement-desire" (kilesakāma), nor is the collection of limited phenomena (parittadhammajāta) that serve as their basis—such as celestial palaces, wish-fulfilling trees, and so forth—called "object-desire" (vatthukāma). For this very reason it was said:

"Neither desire nor the perception of desire exists in the Brahma-world. [This refers to] when [these objects] function as the objective field for the craving residing within the mental continuum of beings belonging to the sense-sphere.

However, it should be understood that even when a limited state (*parittadhamma*) occurs in the fine-material and immaterial realms by way of association with that [sensual desire], it is indeed sensual desire for the objective base (*vatthukāma*).

Alternatively, according to the method presented in the *Niddesa*, here there occurs in its entirety sensual desire as defilement (*kilesakāma*), comprising the divisions of craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*), craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*), craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*), and craving for cessation (*nirodhataṇhā*).
Even regarding sensual desires as objective bases, everything except for a small portion consisting solely of the resultant states of the fine-material and immaterial realms is included here.
It is said, "this desire, though twofold, proceeds," with reference to its proceeding without remainder.

Although this is what was stated, it is said "by way of success" (*sampattīnaṃ vasena*) in order to show that among those two, it is the sensual desire consisting of abundant defilements (*bahala-kilesa-kāma*), as well as the abundant passion for sense-pleasures (*kāmarāga*) and the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇā*) which have that as their basis, that are intended here. By way of attainment...
The meaning is "by way of succeeding. "It ranges" means it occurs. The word *iti* is used in the sense of a reason;
because both these kinds of desire range there, therefore it is called "the realm of desire" (*kāmāvacara*), meaning that desire ranges therein.

15. The *apāyas* are so called because the paths (*ayā*) generally recognized as merit—which are the causes for heaven and liberation—are mostly absent from them. [They are classified] by way of hell and so forth.
The four *apāyas* are the four states of misery. "Six" refers to the six celestial worlds consisting of the Cātumahārājika, Tāvatiṃsa, Yāma, Tusita, Nimmānaratī, and Paranimmita-vasavatti.
However, since the *asuras* who dwell at the base of Mount Meru are included within the Tāvatiṃsa realm itself, it is not stated that there are seven [realms] including them.
They are called "humans" (*manussa*) because of the abundance of mind (*manasa*), by virtue of qualities such as mindfulness, courage, and fitness for the holy life (*brahmacariya*).

The meaning is: "due to the state of having cultivated the mind" and "due to the state of a mind possessing superior qualities. However, in the primary sense, these should be understood as the inhabitants of Jambudīpa. As it is said:

"Bhikkhus, by three factors do the humans of Jambudīpa surpass the humans of Uttarakuru and the devas of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. By which three? They are brave, they possess mindfulness, and here there is the living of the holy life (*brahmacariya*)."

Furthermore, because they shared the same physical form and other characteristics with the inhabitants of the minor islands, those dwelling on the other great continents were also designated as "human beings" (*manussa*).
However, worldly people say they are "human beings" specifically because they are the descendants of Manu.

Regarding the phrase "of eleven kinds": although there is no separate, delimited space for the animal and hungry ghost realms within the four states of misery (*apāya*), wherever [they may be found]...
They dwell in fixed residence in places such as forests, oceans, and the foothills of mountains; because such a location has been taken up, it is elevenfold. [Objection:
But since the occurrence of other phenomena is also possible here, how is it that the name is obtained specifically by way of being the range (*avacara*) of sensual desire (*kāma*) alone?
[In response,] he says: "Because it is distinguished by that," and so forth. Therein, "of that" refers to this twofold sensual desire.
"Abhilakkhitattā" means because it is manifest in eleven types of locations. Alternatively, "assa" is used in the sense of the instrumental case;
therefore, the meaning is: because by means of these two kinds of desire, the eleven types of location are distinguished (*abhilakkhita*) or made known (*paññāpita*).
Alternatively, by way of the genitive case in the sense of the accusative, [it means] by that twofold [desire] of those eleven types of location.
The meaning is "because of being conspicuous. *Sasatthā* means "together with weapons. That place where they move about is *sasatthāvacaro*, a location.

It is like that; for just as in whatever place men with weapons move about, even though other bipeds, quadrupeds, and so forth are also moving there, that place is distinguished because of their prominence there, or because they are conspicuous due to those [weapons].

“It is known as ‘the sense-sphere realm’ (kāmāvacara) alone,” meaning that even though other realms such as the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) and so forth exist and operate there, this particular region is designated specifically as the “sense-sphere realm” by way of its distinctive characteristic. This same method applies to the fine-material and immaterial spheres.
But has it not been stated that “consciousness is of the sense-sphere”? [The answer is: Yes, but because the region was taken according to the manner already explained.

"How is it that what moves within that [sphere] is called 'belonging to the sense-sphere' (kāmāvacara)? To this he says: "This very... and so forth. The connection is: "This very sense-sphere is designated as 'desire' (kāma).

Just as the existence in the form realm (rūpabhava) is "form" (rūpa)—that is, just as the existence in the form realm is form—the word *yathā* (just as), though not explicitly stated, is obtained from the determination provided by the word *evaṃ* (thus). For example: "He develops the path for rebirth in the form realm."

Here, although one should say "rebirth in the fine-material existence" (*rūpabhavūpapatti*), the term "fine-material existence" (*rūpabhava*) is designated as "form" (*rūpa*); this is the meaning here.
But how is it designated in this way? He says: "of the subsequent [term]," and so forth.

Alternatively, just as this "fine-material existence" is uttered by omitting the subsequent word and is thus designated as "form," so too this sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*) is [designated] as "sense-desire" (*kāma*).
The connection [is as follows]: "In that sense of desire" means in that place designated as "desire" (kāma), by way of eliding the latter member of the compound.

"This" refers to this eightfold consciousness. However, even though it is mentioned specifically here, this meaning applies to all limited (paritta) states of consciousness, because all of them range within the realm of desire (kāmāvacara).
"Always" means at all times; the intention is "for the most part. By this—

This, however, illustrates the following: just as an elephant who is generally active in battle and thus receives the name "battle-active" (saṅgāmāvacara) is still designated as "battle-active" even when moving elsewhere— due to the predominance of its activity in that state—
so too this [consciousness], although active elsewhere, is called "sense-sphere" (kāmāvacara) because it occurs predominantly in the sense-world (kāmaloka).

However, this raises the following objection: "Since this [consciousness] also operates within the realms of form and formlessness, would it not also receive the names 'form-sphere' (rūpāvacara) and so forth? To resolve this, it is said:
"It moves within the sense-sphere (kāma); thus it is designated as 'sense-sphere-bound' (kāmāvacara)."
“Just as one who moves within a battle is called a ‘battle-mover’ (saṅgāmāvacaro).
Here, the word *iti* indicates a reason. The word *ca* serves to collect other things that ought to be stated.

Therefore, because the term *kāmāvacaro* is designated as “kāma” through the elision of its latter member (*uttarapadalopa*), and because this consciousness always moves within that *kāma*, it is therefore called simply “kāmāvacara.”
The intention is that it was spoken [as such], but not as pertaining to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), nor as pertaining to the fine-material or immaterial spheres (*rūpārūpāvacara*).

"By the Destroyer of Desire" means by the Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*) who, by means of his knowledge of teaching (*desanāñāṇa*), has the nature of destroying the defilement-desire (*kilesakāma*) existing within the mental continuum of those to be trained. 19.
"He does not direct a rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*)... or alternatively, because even if it has arisen anywhere...

It causes rebirth-linking only in the sense-sphere (kāma-bhava); therefore, because it operates within the sense-sphere, it is called "sense-sphere-bound" (*kāmāvacara*), with the meaning being that the long vowel of the word *cāra* has been shortened.

Having thus shown the derivation of the term by means of the elision of the latter member (*uttarapadalopa*), he now shows the derivation of the word *kāmāvacara* even without such elision, [beginning with] "Included... (*pariyāpanna*).
"Or there," it is said. "There" means in that sensual existence (*kāmabhava*). "Included" (*pariyāpanna*) means contained within. Now, this is the intended meaning here:

"Which phenomena are of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*)? Taking the Avīci hell as the lower limit and including the Paranimmitavasavatti devas as the upper limit, whatever aggregates (*khandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) exist within this interval, and are operative here and included herein..."
"Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— these phenomena belong to the sense-sphere. Because it has been stated thus,
just as even a being of the animal realm who is reborn in the womb of a human woman is called simply "an animal" because he is included within the animal birth-realm,
so too this [consciousness], although arisen in the fine-material or immaterial realms, is [included here] because it is comprised within the sense-sphere existence.

It is stated as "belonging to the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*). Its inclusion therein should be understood as being due to its status as an object for sensual craving (*kāmataṇhā*) which is directed toward the delimited locations of Avīci and the Paranimmita [heavens]. For it has likewise been said by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla in the *Nikkhepakaṇḍa*:
"'Moving within this'—this expression refers to sensual craving whose delimited locations are Avīci and the Paranimmita [heavens]."
"It was said with reference to the state of being an object. Furthermore, the derivation of the terms here should be understood as follows: craving for sensual pleasures is "kāma";

because it moves within this [realm] by way of making it its objective support (ārammaṇa), it is called "kāmāvacara" (belonging to the sense-sphere). Now, one might ask: what here is "craving for sensual pleasures"?

It is that craving which has phenomena belonging to the sense-sphere as its object. And what are the "phenomena belonging to the sense-sphere"? They are those things which are the objects of craving for sensual pleasures.

Does this not result in the fault of mutual dependence? It does not result in that fault, because—due to the eleven types of bases such as the Avīci hell and so forth—any kind of craving is taken as "craving for sensual pleasures" (kāmataṇhā), and thus sense-sphere phenomena (kāmāvacara-dhammā) are characterized by being the objects of that craving which has that same nature.
Alternatively, both kinds of sensual pleasure (kāma)—namely, the defilement and the basis—are [included] according to their respective suitability by way of co-nascence.

It is called *kāmāvacara* because it moves within (*avacarati*) desire (*kāma*). Alternatively, it is called *kāmāvacara* because it moves within both kinds of desire by way of making them its object.

Or else, just as when people sitting on a bed shout, one says "the beds are shouting" by applying the designation of the support to those supported—since the intellect grasps the non-difference between the support and the supported—it is so called here by way of such metaphorical usage.

In this way, because it proceeds within the existence of the sense sphere and is dependent upon it, it is called "belonging to the sense sphere" (*kāmāvacara*) by way of the conventional designation of its support. And there is a verse on this point:
"It belongs to the sense sphere" (*kāmovacara*) means "it moves within the sense sphere" (*kāmevacarati*), or "it moves among the sense objects" (*kāmeṣu carati*).
"Or else, by way of metaphorical designation of the place, that [kamma] would belong to the sense-sphere.

Because they produce the fruit of what is worthy of praise (*pujja*), because they nourish one's own continuum (*attasantāna*), they are "meritorious deeds" (*puñña*). Because they are things to be done, they are "actions" (*kiriyā*);

and because they serve as the basis for various benefits, they are "bases" (*vatthu*). Thus, they are "bases of meritorious action" (*puññakiriyavatthu*). As for their number, they are so called because they are ten in measure.

The ten bases of meritorious action (*puññakiriyavatthu*) are those ten; "by means of them" means by means of the ten bases of meritorious action. The sense is: having become composed of that, by way of the state of being the ten bases of meritorious action.

By the particle *eva*, however, he shows that it is not only by way of meditation (*bhāvanā*), as in the case of the form, formless, and supramundane [realms]. Alternatively, it is "only by way of the ten bases of meritorious action."
It occurs, but not by way of the bases for meritorious action such as praising others as imagined by others;
this is the restriction indicated by the word "eva" (only). For he will say later:
"And all the merit of the recollections," and so forth. 21. But what are those ten bases for meritorious action, by way of which these eight types of consciousness [arise]?
With reference to the inquiry, "It is said that [the path] proceeds," the passage beginning with "Generosity (dāna), virtue (sīla)," etc., was stated in order to show those factors in their own form.

Therein, "generosity" (dāna) is that by which something is given; it is the volition of relinquishment (*pariccāga-cetanā*). However, in this context, because the focus is on the mind, that which is associated with it must be understood.
The same applies to "virtue" (*sīla*) and the others. "Virtue" (*sīla*) is so called because one cools down (*sīlati*); it means that one composes the bodily and verbal actions.
This is the meaning. For by means of virtue (*sīla*), bodily actions and so forth are not scattered;

they are properly established and concentrated, bringing welfare and happiness both now and in the future. Alternatively, it is called *sīla* because one cools down (*sīlayati*) or upholds (*upadhāreti*).

Here, "upholding" refers to the state of being a firm foundation for wholesome states. It is called "development" (*bhāvanā*) because one develops, cultivates, or increases wholesome phenomena by means of it.
*Pattidāna* (the giving of merit) is that by which the merit produced within one’s own continuum is given away.

*Veyyāvacca* (service) is the state of being occupied with the performance of various duties. *Desanā* (teaching) is that by which one teaches. *Pattānumoda* (rejoicing in merit) is that by which one rejoices in the merit;

however, it is called simply "anumoda" through the elision of the first member of the compound. *Diṭṭhujjukataṃ* (straightening of view) is the straightness of one's view, meaning the making straight of right view.
Meaning (*attha*): Because by means of this one listens rightly through an inclination toward the welfare of oneself or others, it is called *saṃsuti*.

Because by means of this one honors through acts of worship and performs proper conduct (*sāmīci*), it is called *apacāya*. The classification of the bases for meritorious action is *puññakiriyavatthuppabheda*.

However, by eliding the middle term (*majjhapadalopa*), it is stated as "classification of the bases of merit" (*puññavatthuppabheda*), just as a chariot yoked with thoroughbreds is called an *ājaññaratha*.
“A chariot that can be directed at will. This, first, is the analysis of the words here.

As for the detailed exposition: therein, the volition occurring in those still in training (*sekha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*), consisting in the relinquishing of existing material things out of a desire to honor or assist another, is the basis for meritorious action consisting in giving (*dānamaya-puññakiriyavatthu*).
It is called *nāma*. Even for those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), giving that occurs in such a manner exists;

however, because it is not a "meritorious deed" (*puññakiriyā*), it is not intended here. For merit (*puñña*) is so called because it produces a fruit of honor and because it refreshes one's own continuity (*santāna*);

yet that which occurs in the continuity of one whose taints are destroyed does not produce a fruit, nor does it refresh [the mind], as it proceeds from a purified continuity. The same applies to the remaining cases.

Furthermore, it is the restraint of one who undertakes the five precepts, the eight precepts, or the ten precepts by way of the perpetual precepts (*niccasīla*), the Uposatha precepts (*uposathasīla*), and so forth;

or even of one who does not undertake them, but refrains from bodily misconduct and the like as it occurs through the influence of family custom; or of one undertaking restraint in the ordination hall (*upasampadamāḷaka*);
or of one fulfilling the *Pātimokkha*; or [the restraint] of the eyes and other faculties regarding objects that have come into their range.

The volition occurring in one who restrains the sense faculties, reflects upon the requisites such as robes, and purifies one’s livelihood from the basis of hypocrisy and so forth—this is called the basis for meritorious action consisting in virtue (*sīlamaya-puññakiriyavatthu*). Here it is said:
"This giving is my family lineage and family custom"—thus, for one who gives while standing firm in the virtue of conduct (*cārittasīla*).
Is this basis for meritorious action consisting in giving (*dānamaya-puññakiriyavatthu*) that which proceeds [as such], or is it that which consists in virtue (*sīlamaya*)?

It consists in virtue alone, because it has the nature of the virtue of conduct (*cārittasīla*). For even though this proceeds by way of the relinquishing of things to be given, it is a basis for meritorious action consisting in virtue alone—not one consisting in giving—because it proceeds in that manner through volition (*cetanā*) subsequent to a prior formative impulse (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra*), and because it arises from a desire to honor and assist.
For it is said that "this is a gift consisting of giving.

However, for one who contemplates by applying the three characteristics—impermanence and so forth—to the eye and other sense bases, there arises volition of insight (vipassanā-cetanā) beginning with the stage of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) and culminating in purification (vodāna).
When directed toward objects such as the kasiṇas, this volition does not reach absorption (appanā), but culminates in the stage of change-of-lineage.
And the volition of preliminary work (*parikamma-cetanā*)—this is what is called a basis for meritorious action consisting in cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya-puññakiriyavatthu*).
Even that which has reached absorption (*appanā*) is indeed cultivation; however, because it does not belong to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), it is not included here.

The teachers maintain that even the volition involved in training in the blameless spheres of knowledge (*vijjāyatana*), the spheres of craft (*kammāyatana*), and the spheres of art (*sippāyatana*) is comprised within what consists in cultivation. And as for the gift-object (*deyyadhamma*) herein...

Having comprehended [the body] through its dissolution and disappearance, when one gives while it is occurring, that too—because volitions proceed in both ways just as before—should be understood as a basis for meritorious action consisting in development (*bhāvanāmaya-puññakiriyavatthu*).
Having performed any kind of well-done deed such as giving, [one should dedicate it thus: "May there be merit for so-and-so; may it be for all beings..."

Or let it be for the Teacher”—thus, the basis for performing meritorious deeds consisting of the giving of merit (*pattidāna*) is so called because it proceeds by way of aspiring for one’s own deed to be shared with others.
But does the merit of one who gives merit in this way diminish? It does not.
However, just as when one has lit a single lamp and then lights a thousand lamps from it, one cannot say that the first lamp is exhausted; for the previous light—
However, when combined with the light of the western world, it becomes exceedingly vast;
in the same way, it should be understood that for one giving a gift, there is no such thing as loss, but rather only increase. But how is it that this [gift] is said to be "given"?
It is by saying, either before or after: "May this meritorious deed of mine ripen for all beings, or for such-and-such a person."
It is called "given" when it is bestowed either by one who utters a verbal expression or by one who merely intends it with the mind. However, some say:
"Even if one says, 'I give the fruit of whatever good conduct has been performed by me,' the merit is indeed given.
But because the subject matter concerns wholesome karma (*kusala-kamma*) and because others must likewise rejoice in that very karma, it is the karma itself that must be given.
The teachers' conclusion on this point is that even when one rejoices, it is indeed the *kamma* itself that is being rejoiced in.

The basis for the performance of meritorious deeds consisting of service (*veyyāvaccamaya-puññakiriyavatthu*) refers to the practice of performing duties and counter-duties toward ascetics and brahmins with an undefiled intention by one who has no expectation of receiving robes or other requisites, as well as through the act of nursing the sick.
Standing at the head of the bases of liberation (*vimuttāyatana*), with a mind free from any expectation of material gain, one [teaches] the Dhamma in which one is proficient.

The teaching that proceeds when one is descending [from a mountain] and likewise instructing others on the blameless bases of psychic power (*vijjā-āyatana*) and so forth, is called the basis of meritorious action consisting of teaching (*desanāmaya-puññakiriyavatthu*).

The basis of meritorious action consisting of rejoicing (*anumodanā-puññakiriyavatthu*) is that which proceeds when one, having abandoned the stains of envy and stinginess, rejoices with the words "Well done! Excellent! over whatever wholesome deed has been performed by others, whether it was given or not given. "There is..."

The "basis for performing meritorious deeds through the straightening of views" refers to that which occurs in one who straightens their view by means of the knowledge of the ownership of kamma, starting with the words "It has been given," and so forth.
If this is so, does it not follow that a state of performing meritorious deeds through the straightening of views cannot be obtained for a consciousness dissociated from knowledge?
It is not that it cannot be obtained; for even the preceding and succeeding volitions are included within those very same acts of merit. For he will say accordingly:
“The former act of relinquishing, and the three subsequent volitions—this constitutes merit consisting in giving.
In the same way, this should be illustrated for the remaining [perfections].

Therefore, although at the moment of straightening [the mind] the consciousness is associated with knowledge, in its preceding and succeeding phases it may also be dissociated from knowledge; thus, even that [dissociated state] arises as a meritorious deed consisting in the straightening of views.
Others, however, say: "Vision" (*diṭṭhi*) consists of consciousness (*viññāṇa*) and wisdom (*paññā*). "Straightness of view" (*diṭṭhi-ujubhāva*) is that which is associated with right view.
What is it? It is wholesome consciousness and the right vision consisting of the knowledge of the ownership of one's actions (*kammassakatāñāṇa*), and so forth.

In that context, even when knowledge arises through wholesome consciousness, there are [instances such as] the recollection of one's own good conduct, the praising of the virtues of others, and going for refuge.

Inclusion consists in right view regarding the path of action through the knowledge that one is the owner of one’s own deeds (*kammassakatā-ñāṇa*). Furthermore, it should be understood that the knowledge associated with giving and so forth is itself included within giving and the rest.
"Having heard this Dhamma in this way, by practicing according to the method taught therein, I shall attain the distinction of mundane and supramundane qualities;
or, having become learned, [I shall benefit others] through the teaching of the Dhamma."

“I shall favor them. Thus, for one listening to the true Dhamma under the heading of the "bases of liberation" (vimuttāyatana), whether for oneself or others, there occurs what is called the basis of meritorious action consisting in hearing.
The volition of hearing the blameless bases of knowledge (vijjāyatana) and so forth is also included herein.

Furthermore, for one who rises from their seat upon seeing those worthy of honor, those in a position of respect, or elders; and who offers them a bowl and robes, gives way on the path, performs prostrations and the gesture of joining palms (añjali), and presents seats, flowers, perfumes, and other offerings—[this is also included].
And the volition of great respect that arises while performing such acts is called a "basis for meritorious action accompanied by reverence.

Now, this is the distinction between service (*veyyāvacca*) and reverence (*apacāyanā*): service consists in performing the respective duties for those who are senior in age or virtue, as well as for the sick;
whereas reverence is the performance of respectful conduct.

22–3. Having thus shown the ten bases of meritorious action according to the method found in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, [the author] now says, "They go into inclusion," and so forth, in order to show that—according to the method found in the Sutta—there are only three:
giving (*dāna*), virtue (*sīla*), and development (*bhāvanā*). In doing so, he demonstrates that the others are included within those three.
Therein, the transference of merit (*pattidāna*) and rejoicing in merit (*anumodanā*) go into inclusion within giving, because they share its essential nature.

For generosity (*dāna*) is the opposite of envy and avarice; since these [latter two] are its opposites, they share the same characteristic as generosity and thus are included within the basis of meritorious action consisting in generosity.

Service and reverence are included within the merit consisting in virtue (*sīla*), because their nature is that of conduct-virtue (*cāritta-sīla*). The straightening of view through teaching and hearing is...

However, because they consist in the cultivation of wholesome states through practice and development, they are included within that which consists of development (*bhāvanāmaya*). Some, however, maintain:
"When teaching and when listening, one penetrates the characteristics by directing knowledge according to the teaching; thus, one teaches and listens.
Since both that teaching and that listening bring about penetration itself, teaching and listening are included within that which consists of development."
They say this. Because it is a gift of the Dhamma, one may also rightly say that "the teaching is included within the category of giving.
Likewise, the rectification of views (diṭṭhijukamma) is so called because it possesses the characteristic of determining everything for everyone in all respects.
For among the perfections such as giving, whatever is purified by right view—proceeding in the manner of "there is what is given," and so forth—becomes of great fruit.

"It has great benefit. Having established this, it is stated in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*: "The rectification of views (*diṭṭhijukamma*), moreover, is characterized by the settling of all [matters].
However, the Mahāsaṅghikas and those dwelling at Abhayagiri do not include the rectification of views as a distinct category of meritorious action (*puññakiriyā*).
For they hold that giving, virtue, meditation, listening to the Dhamma, teaching, recollection, and rejoicing [in merit] [constitute such actions].

By adding these three— recollection of one’s own performed merit, taking refuge in the Buddha and the others, and praising the virtues of others— to the nine, they establish twelve bases of meritorious action (*puññakiriyavatthu*),
excluding the rectification of views (*diṭṭhijukamma*). "Again, there are only three" means that although there were originally ten, they once again amount to only three when condensed.

24. Now, in order to show that the recollection of merit (*puññānussati*) and so forth, which are pointed out by others, are actually subsumed within those [qualities] pointed out by oneself, it is said: “And all the merit of recollection,” and so forth.

Therein, the recollection of every single wholesome deed (*sucarita*) performed by oneself is called “all the merit of recollection. “Praise” refers to [the recollection of] meritorious deeds and right practice performed by others.
And "praising with a serene mind" means being satisfied. Regarding the "Three Refuges": here, they are called *saraṇāni* because they "injure" (*saranti*) [fear];

these are the three jewels beginning with the Buddha. For they injure—that is, destroy—the fear, terror, and the defilement of miserable rebirths for those who have gone to them for refuge by that very act of going for refuge. That which has three parts (*avayava*) is a "triad" (*tayaṃ*).
This is a designation for a composite whole consisting of three parts. "The triad of refuges" (*saraṇattaya*) means the three refuges; what is meant is "the three refuges.
For there is no such thing as a "whole" that exists apart from its constituent parts.

However, here, by the mention of the "triad of refuges," what is intended is the act of going for refuge, either through figurative usage (*upacāra*) or by the elision of the latter member of the compound (*uttarapadalopa*). It is not...
Indeed, the Three Refuges are called the bases for meritorious action (*puññakiriyavatthu*).

As for their meaning, they are comprised within the rectification of view (*diṭṭhijukamma*), because volition (*cetanā*)—arising by way of obtaining confidence (*pasāda*) in the Buddha and the others through such [thoughts] as, “The Blessed One is indeed a perfectly enlightened one; the Dhamma is well-expounded;
the Saṅgha is practicing rightly”—is effective precisely through that [rectification]. For it is not otherwise.

These three can occur for one who holds wrong view; therefore, they are included exclusively within the basis for meritorious action consisting in the straightening of views, and should not be understood as being meritorious actions in their own right.
This is the intended meaning. Hence he said, "There is no doubt.
Although the straightening of views is included within that which consists in development, by way of summary, these [three] are included within what consists in development.

However, according to the method of detailed exposition (*vitthāranaya*), since there might be doubt as to where [these] belong, their inclusion within those consisting of development (*bhāvanāmaya*) was not stated.

Alternatively, it is said that they are included separately therein to show their preeminence, because they constitute the root by determining the great fruitfulness of the rectification of views (*diṭṭhijukamma*). Others, however, say: "While including..."
They say: "Because it is stated that 'one who grasps does not let go,' the act of taking refuge is possible as a form of grasping, similar to the undertaking of moral discipline (sīla);

therefore, it is included within the category of what consists of moral discipline. Some say: "Taking refuge is included within that which is accompanied by reverence, because it is a state of prostration.
25. Now, although these aforementioned bases for meritorious action occur according to their prior and subsequent sequence, [the following applies...]
In order to show that volition (cetanā) is included within each of those respective stages, it is said: "The prior relinquishing," and so forth.
Therein, "prior" refers to everything from the time one righteously and equitably acquires the object to be given for the purpose of giving;

and while the object has been acquired, from the time one thinks, "I shall relinquish it," and seeks out a recipient worthy of offerings, up until the moment the object is placed into the hand of the receiver.

The volition that occurs up until that point is the preliminary-stage volition (*pubbabhāga-cetanā*). However, the volition at the moment of relinquishing [the object] into the hand of the recipient, or the volition of dedication (*pariṇāmana-cetanā*), is called the volition of releasing (*muñcana-cetanā*).
That same [volition] is referred to as "mucanā" by means of the elision of the nasalized vowel (*niggahīta*).
Alternatively, the reading is simply "muñcanā. "Parā" means not forming an attachment (*ālaya*) toward the object already relinquished by oneself, thinking: "Excellent..."
The volition that arises at a later stage in one who reviews with a joyful mind, thinking, "I have given a truly excellent gift"—these three types of volition:

namely, this prior volition, this volition of relinquishing, and this subsequent volition—these three volitions together constitute the merit consisting in giving; it is called the "basis for the performance of meritorious action consisting in giving."
The meaning is "it becomes. With reference to the word "merit" (*puñña*), the singular designation "becomes" (*hoti*) is used.
Now, extending the aforementioned meaning to the remaining [bases of meritorious action], he says: "In this way, one should illuminate the rest. Regarding "the rest":

among the bases of meritorious action such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth, in the same manner as described above, for one who thinks, "I shall guard my virtue," or "I shall go forth to the monastery,"...

"One should explain and clarify [this] as follows: 'The prior volition that arises while one is walking; the intermediate volition that arises when one is undertaking the precepts, when one is going forth, or when one is fulfilling the precepts;

and the subsequent volition that arises when one reflects, "I have fulfilled them"—thus these three types of volition, being unified, constitute what is called the basis for meritorious action consisting in virtue. So it should be shown and explained.
[The answer is: It has that purpose. But surely, the volition of recollecting merit performed by oneself is included within the purification of view (*diṭṭhijukamma*);
and since this other volition is that very same thing, how can it be included therein? This is not a fault, because there is a distinction between the two due to the difference in their objects.

For the recollection of merit has as its object only the merit performed by oneself; however, this [other] one has as its object the basis for that [merit]. Thus, the distinction between the two is indeed evident.

And to this extent, regarding what was stated—that [the mind] "proceeds by way of the ten bases of meritorious action" (dasapuññakiriyavatthu)—having demonstrated those ten bases of meritorious action both in their specific forms and by way of their classification, the passage beginning with "Now" (idāni) is commenced in order to show the individual modes and objects of its proceeding in that manner.
In this context, "this" (ayaṃ) is a demonstrative referring to what is about to be explained. "The dhamma to be given" (dātabbo dhammo)...
The object to be given consists of ten kinds of things. For it is said:
“Food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, beds, dwellings, and lamps—these are the ten bases for giving.”

Those beginning with the recipient—namely, the place, time, friend, and so forth—are "the recipients and others. The excellence of both the object to be given and the recipients and others is "the excellence of the object to be given, the recipient, and so forth.

In this context, the excellence of the object to be given consists in its being refined and pleasing, and its having been acquired through righteous and equitable means. The excellence of the recipients consists in their being the most worthy of offerings (*aggadakkhiṇeyya*).

The excellence of the recipient (*paṭiggāhakasampatti*). The excellence of the place (*desasampatti*) refers to a location where food and drink are difficult to obtain. The excellence of the time (*kālasampatti*) refers to a similar [time].
For a gift given in such a place or at such a time—where food and drink are difficult to find—is of great fruit due to the strength of the donor's intention (*ajjhāsaya*), and it is rooted in joy;
therefore, these are described as excellences of giving. As for the excellence of the friend (*mittasampatti*), however...
The state of having virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamittatā*). For by relying on a virtuous friend, the mind becomes filled with joy regarding generosity and the other perfections.
Furthermore, "perfection of attendants" refers to the acquisition of a retinue who, even without being commanded, are diligent in performing their respective duties.
Or, "another cause for gladness" refers to other causes for joy, such as an abundance of faith, purity, right view, and so forth.

“Having approached” (*āgamma*) means having drawn near; the meaning is “dependent upon. “Exultant and overjoyed” (*haṭṭhapahaṭṭho*) means both exultant and overjoyed by way of mental gladness (*somanassa*);
by both terms, excessive gladness is expressed. “There is... [etc. ...they proceed”:
“There is what is given, there is what is sacrificed, there is what is offered, there is the fruit and result of deeds well done and ill done, there is...”
"This world exists; the other world exists; there is mother and father; there are beings of spontaneous birth;

there are in the world ascetics and brahmins who have fared rightly and practiced rightly, who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves through direct knowledge, enter and abide therein"—thus it proceeds by way of the ten bases of right view.
And it occurs by way of the factors conducive to the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena (*dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga*) and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), not only the nine bases of right view are included, but also those things conducive to the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena are comprised.
Right view is that which proceeds by way of the correct method (*ñāya*), or it is "right view" because it is a praiseworthy view; that [view]. "Placing before" means...

Having made it the forerunner. And this is by way of being a co-nascent forerunner, because association is intended—as in such passages as "states have mind as their forerunner" (*manopubbaṅgamā dhammā*).
"Unprompted" means by oneself, due to not falling into contraction regarding the performance of meritorious deeds through greed, stinginess, and so forth.
Or having been urged by someone else. For this is a demonstration of the occurrence of merit according to its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

However, the phrase "by others" is stated by way of showing the urging of others who are well-known. "First" means first either in the order of the teaching (*desanā-krama*) or in the order indicated here.
"Great wholesome consciousness" (*mahā-kusala-citta*) refers to a great wholesome consciousness due to the fulfillment of factors such as being accompanied by joy (*somanassa-sahagata*).

Alternatively, it is called a "great wholesome consciousness" (*mahākusalacitta*) because it is a great, honored wholesome state of mind that draws forth the rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) of Bodhisattvas in their final existence.

For it is stated that the rebirth-linking of all omniscient Bodhisattvas is the result of a spontaneous (*asaṅkhārika*) three-rooted joyful consciousness preceded by loving-kindness (*mettā*). In this context: "The object to be given... [etc.]..."

By the phrase "exultant with joy," it should be understood that he expresses the state of being accompanied by mental happiness (*somanassa*); by "placing right view foremost," the state of being associated with knowledge (*ñāṇa-sampayutta*);
and by "without being urged," the state of being unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*). "In the manner already stated" means:
"by way of the excellence of the gift, the recipient, and so forth, or by resorting to some other cause for joy."

"In the manner thus stated": "Encouraged" means that because of being concerned with the object to be given, and because of falling into a contraction regarding meritorious deeds due to a lack of resolve toward the perfection of virtue (*sīla-sampadā*) and so forth, one is encouraged by oneself or by someone else. "By others," however, is exactly as stated in the previous method.
The connection is: "one performs meritorious deeds such as giving. "That very [state]" refers to that which is accompanied by joy (*somanassa*) and so forth.

It is stated thus because of its similarity to that. For the designation of one thing is applied even to what is similar to it, as in the expressions, "That very same partridge," or "Those very same medicinal herbs.
Here, however, by the word "urged" (*ussāhito*), he shows its state of being prompted by volitional effort (*sasaṅkhārikata*). The remainder is exactly according to the method already explained.
Regarding the phrase "in this meaning": in this meaning denoted by the term *sasaṅkhārika*, which consists of the mental formation (*citta-saṅkhāra*) that is to be urged.

The meaning is "having that as its object. "Of the prior application" refers to the mental application that occurs by way of encouragement, having diverted [the mind] from the contraction of meritorious action that was arising.
However, the inclusion of the word "prior" (*pubba*) here is stated on the grounds that that application arises by way of a prior volitional formation (*abhisaṅkhāra*) occurring in such a manner;
it is not stated because of its being temporally prior. This is the meaning already explained.
"By showing right practice" means by showing such practices as the relinquishing of things to be given and paying homage upon seeing monks.

"Fools" (bālā): they are called fools because they do not possess wisdom; the intention is that they live merely by inhaling and exhaling, not by the life of wisdom. "Foolish ones" (bālakā) refers to those very same fools.
Furthermore, in this context, they are so called due to the absence of right view—which functions according to the method beginning with "there is what is given"—and so forth.
"Children whose intelligence has not yet arisen. Here, the term "infant" (*bālaka*) is used in its literal sense;

however, at times such as when acting impulsively, even others possess a state of consciousness dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇavippayutta*). "Those in whom joy has arisen" means those for whom joy has been produced;
the sense is "those who have experienced joy. "Impulsively" means very quickly, at the very moment the desire to give arises.
And here, by the phrase “by demonstrating the practice,” he states the absence of effort on the part of others; by “having become familiar,” he states the absence of effort on his own part.
By both together, he illustrates the unprompted (asaṅkhārika) nature of this [act]. By the words “children, suddenly,” he states the state of being dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇavippayutta);
by “the bhikkhus... were born,” he states the state of being accompanied by joy (somanassasahagata). Alternatively, “the practice... [etc. [is explained as follows:]...

By the word "familiarity" (*paricayā*), the state of being unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*) is indicated; and by the words "the young bhikkhus... have become," the state of being accompanied by joy dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇavippayutta-somanassasahagata*) is shown.
Thus, by the expression "suddenly" (*sahasā*), it reveals that very same state of being unprompted and dissociated from knowledge as previously described.
This being so, the state of being accompanied by joy and so forth is shown in reverse order. In direct order (*anuloma*), however, it is "born of joy" (*somanassajāta*).

By this, he indicates that it is accompanied by joy (*somanassasahagata*); by the inclusion of the word "suddenly" (*sahasā*), he indicates that it is unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*) and dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇavippayutta*).
However, up to the point where it says, “Having seen the practice...,” the cause for its being accompanied by joy and so forth has been stated.
“Those” means those relatives, or the meaning is “those children. “On account of the absence of causes for joy”—this is merely an illustration.

It should be understood that even mental formations (*cetobhisaṅkhāra*) and so forth, when directed toward a neutral object (*majjhattārammaṇa*), are indeed causes for being accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhāsahagata*).
Because the absence of joy (*somanassa*) in the mind implies the person is also devoid of joy, it is stated—referring to the person—that "in all four [types of persons]...
they exist," with the intention that those performing merit are devoid of joy.
“Thus,” and so forth, is the conclusion.
Among these eight types of consciousness, however, that accompanied by equanimity is stronger than that accompanied by joy;

that associated with knowledge is stronger than that dissociated from knowledge; and that which is spontaneous (asaṅkhārika) is equally stronger than that which is prompted (sasaṅkhārika). But as for those of a different kind—
It becomes strong or weak by way of the application of knowledge regarding feeling.
For, compared to the unprompted triple-rooted consciousness accompanied by joy, the prompted triple-rooted consciousness accompanied by equanimity is stronger;

and compared to the unprompted double-rooted consciousness accompanied by equanimity, the unprompted triple-rooted consciousness accompanied by joy is stronger. Thus, the third consciousness is stronger than the fourth consciousness.
The eighth consciousness is stronger than that; the seventh than that; the second than that; the first than that; the sixth than that;
and the fifth than that. In this way, the relative strength and weakness of these [consciousnesses] should be understood.
Having thus demonstrated their eightfold nature according to the method found in the Pāḷi—by way of the distinctions in feeling, knowledge, and application—now...
In order to show the classification by way of the meritorious deeds and so forth mentioned in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is said: "The ten types of meritorious deeds, etc.

By the word "etc.," the inclusion of the six objects, the four predominants, the three kinds of kamma, and the classification into inferior and so forth should be understood. For this very reason, they say:

“By way of the bases of merit in due order, by way of the predominance of the objective field, and also by way of inferior karma and so forth—the one skilled in method should calculate [the results]. 27.
Now, regarding that [consciousness] proceeding in such a manner, whatever numerical limit is obtainable for each of those [types], [that shall be explained].
To show these [consciousnesses] collectively, it is said: "seventeen thousand," and so forth. The calculation therein should be understood as follows:

first, these eight consciousnesses, because they proceed by way of the ten bases of meritorious action, amount to eighty consciousnesses (ten for each). And since those proceed with respect to six objects, they are multiplied by six.
There are four hundred and eighty; these, when multiplied by four through association with the four predominants, become one thousand nine hundred and twenty.
These, in turn, when multiplied by three through the three types of action—namely body, speech, and mind—become five thousand six hundred and sixty. And these...
When multiplied by three according to the division into inferior, medium, and superior, they amount to seventeen thousand two hundred and eighty.

But is it not the case that, because consciousness dissociated from knowledge lacks the concomitant of the predominance of investigation (*vīmaṃsādhipati*), there would be one thousand six hundred and eighty [states] by way of predominance?
[If so,] when those are combined with the categories of karma and so forth, they total twenty-one hundred and eighty.

"Are there fifteen thousand [types of consciousness]? Yes, this is true; however, it should be understood that while those [fifteen thousand] are included by way of falling within the stream [of consciousness], they were not taken into account here because the calculation was undertaken according to the primary factors (*adhipati*), and thus no reduction in the number was made on their account.
But has it not been stated that "the wholesome is with result"? How is that so, where does it occur, and what is its fruit? Such is the objection.

Having intended this, he said: “But that,” and so forth. Because wholesome [kamma] with three roots gives either a rebirth-linking with three roots or one with two roots, but it does not give a rootless rebirth-linking.
And when it produces a rebirth-linking with three roots, then during the course of existence it brings about sixteen resultant states;
when it is with two roots, then twelve. But [kamma] with two roots [produces] those with two roots and those without roots.
It produces rebirth-linking, but not with three roots. And when it produces [kamma] with two roots, then there are twelve [resultants] during the course of existence (pavatti);

when it is rootless, then there are eight. However, according to those who maintain that there is a distinction in the types of formations (saṅkhāra) based on the arrival [of the kamma], in their opinion, when [the kamma] has three roots, twelve or ten [resultants] ripen; when it has two roots, ten or eight [ripen]. Therefore, it was said:

"Accordingly": it is "beautiful" (*sugata*) because it is the locus of various kinds of prosperity; it is a "destination" (*gati*) because one must go there; thus, it is a "good destination" (*sugati*).
The "good destination of the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara-sugati*) is simply the existence of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara-bhava*). Regarding the phrase "the excellence of existence and enjoyments":

here, "existence" (*bhava*) refers to that which comes into being; it is a designation for the resultant aggregates and the kamma-formations (*kaṭattārūpa*) comprised within the existence of rebirth (*upapatti-bhava*).

"Grasping" (gahaṇaṃ) means that which is to be enjoyed; "possession" (bhoga) is the prosperity to be obtained during the course of existence (pavatti), or alternatively, "existence" (bhava) refers to rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).

"Possession" (bhoga) is the prosperity to be obtained during the course of existence together with the remaining resultant [aggregates] and kamma-produced matter. Both "existence" and "possession" constitute "existence-and-possession" (bhavabhoga);
these very things, by virtue of their perfected state, are "prosperity" (sampatti), or the prosperity of those two is "prosperity of existence-and-possession" (bhavabhogasampatti).
It brings that about; the meaning is that it accomplishes it both by way of being a producer (*janaka*) and by way of being a decisive support (*upanissaya*).
And here, with reference to the place where the attainment of existence and enjoyments is obtained without remainder, it is said: "in the happy destinies of the sense-sphere.
However, [it also produces] the attainment of existence, which consists in the nature of resultant-process and kamma-produced matter, excluding the root-cause-resultants (*sahetuka-vipāka*).

Whether it be the attainment of some degree of wealth or the perfection of wealth itself, it invariably brings about results both in the happy destinies (*sugati*) and even in the miserable destinies (*duggati*).

For even for beings such as *nāgas* and *supaṇṇas*, their delightful variety of enjoyments—which are similar to the prosperity of the gods—and the resultant consciousnesses pertaining to those objects, as well as their golden complexion, sweet voices, and so forth—all of this is the fruit of sense-sphere wholesome action (*kāmāvacara-kusala*) alone. Not...
For there is no desirable fruit for the unwholesome. Indeed, this has been said: "It is impossible, it is out of the question, that a desirable and pleasing result should exist for the unwholesome.
The commentary on wholesome states of the sense-sphere is finished.
Commentary on the Wholesome States of the Fine-Material Sphere (Rūpāvacara-kusala-vaṇṇanā):

Now, since the opportunity for the exposition of the wholesome states of the fine-material sphere—which were listed immediately after the wholesome states of the sense-sphere—has arrived, the passage beginning with "In the others" is commenced in order to demonstrate them.
Therein, "in the others" refers to [states] other than the aforementioned wholesome states of the sense-sphere.
"In the others" means in those belonging to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) and so forth. It is "of one kind with a physical basis" because it is exclusively dependent upon a physical basis.

For the fine-material-sphere phenomena are not found in the immaterial realm (*arūpadhātu*), because they are produced through the cultivation of dispassion toward form, and because there is no further attainment of fine-material-sphere jhāna therein.

Regarding the classification into inferior, medium, and superior: here, as before, the inferior and other qualities of the jhāna should be applied according to the inferior and other states of the dominant factors (*adhipati*).
Alternatively, that which is merely attained but not cultivated is "inferior" due to its extreme weakness;
that which is not well-cultivated and lacks complete mastery is "medium"; whereas that which is exceedingly well-cultivated and possesses mastery in every respect is [superior].
It is "excellent" (paṇīta). Likewise, that which is undertaken out of a desire for the fruits of sublime merit is "inferior";

that which is undertaken for the sake of mundane higher knowledge (abhiññā) is "middling"; and that which is undertaken by one established in the state of a Noble One (ariya) out of a desire for seclusion is "excellent.

Alternatively, that which is undertaken for one's own benefit is "inferior"; that which is undertaken solely with a disposition of non-greed (alobha) is "middling"; and that which is undertaken for the benefit of others is "excellent."
That which is set in motion by an inclination toward the round (*vaṭṭa*) is inferior; that set in motion by an inclination toward seclusion (*viveka*) is middling;
and that set in motion by an inclination toward turning away (*vivaṭṭa*), having the supramundane as its proximate cause, is sublime.

"By way of the distinction of the path and so forth" means by way of the distinction between the paths and direct knowledges such as the painful path with sluggish direct knowledge, and so on. By the very mention of the "path," [the distinction is understood].
Or, because of its inseparable connection with that, even direct knowledge (abhiññā) is obtained. Thus, since they here refer to it as the "fourfold way" (paṭipadā-catukka), the word "etc.
(ādi) should be understood as including the dominant factors (adhipati) and so forth. Therefore, "by way of the classification of the way, etc.

means by way of the classification of the way, the classification of the dominant factor, the classification of the object (ārammaṇa), and the classification of the parts conducive to decline (hānabhāgiya) and so forth. Among these, "by way of the classification of the way":

Thus it is fourfold: that which is painful in practice and slow in direct knowledge, that which is painful in practice and quick in direct knowledge, that which is pleasant in practice and slow in direct knowledge, and that which is pleasant in practice and quick in direct knowledge. In this context, "that which has a painful practice" is *dukkhapaṭipadaṃ*.
"That which has slow direct knowledge" is *dandhābhiññaṃ*. The same method applies to "painful in practice... [and so forth].

[This is also the case] in such passages as "quick direct knowledge" (*khippābhiñña*). Therein, for one whose hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) have not been abandoned and who has not suppressed the inclination toward jhāna, because the function of knowledge (*ñāṇakicca*) is not yet manifest,
[the process begins] from the first act of attention (*paṭhamasamannāhāra*) that occurs in the form "earth, earth" or "water, water," once all prior duties have been completed.

The preliminary development that occurs from the beginning until the abandonment of the hindrances and the suppression of attachment through the attainment of the access concentration (upacāra) of each respective jhāna is called the "way" (*paṭipadā*), because one proceeds toward jhāna by means of it.
However, for one whose hindrances have been abandoned and whose attachment to jhāna has been suppressed, the function of knowledge becomes fully manifest.
The wisdom that occurs from the beginning of access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*) until the arising of absorption (*appanā*) is called "direct knowledge" (*abhiññā*),
because it is distinguished from preliminary wisdom (*pubbabhāga-paññā*). Therefore, when one initially suppresses the defilements and attachment to meditation,
suppressing them with difficulty, with effort, and with exertion while becoming fatigued, [this is the case of] suppressed defilements and attachment to meditation.
And for one who dwells in the preparatory stage (parivāsa), the manifestation of the factors [of absorption] occurs only after a long time;

his jhāna is of difficult progress and slow direct knowledge (dandhābhiñña). However, for one who suppresses the defilements and so forth with effort (sasaṅkhāra) and attains the manifestation of the factors without delay, his jhāna is of difficult progress but quick direct knowledge (khippābhiñña). For one who, while suppressing the defilements and so forth...

One who suppresses [the hindrances] with ease but takes a long time for the preliminary stage (*parivāsa*) of absorption attains the path of easy practice with sluggish direct knowledge (*dandhābhiññā*).

However, one who suppresses the defilements and so forth with ease and reaches absorption quickly should be understood as having the path of easy practice with swift direct knowledge (*khippābhiññā*).

Furthermore, this distinction between the modes of practice (*paṭipadā*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) should be understood by way of the predominance of defilements (*kilesa*) and faculties (*indriya*).

For one whose defilements such as lust are intense and whose five faculties beginning with faith are dull, and who has not performed work in serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), his occurring jhāna is of difficult progress (*dukkha-paṭipadā*) and slow direct knowledge (*dandhābhiññā*). This is because for him—
Because the suppression of the hindrances is accomplished only with difficulty and great effort due to the intensity of the active defilements, the practice is painful and unpleasant;
likewise, because of the dullness of his faculties such as faith, even his direct knowledge is sluggish, weak, and slow to arise.
Alternatively, because he has not performed the preliminary work for serenity (samatha) in another life, the practice is painful.
Because one has not performed the preliminary work for insight (*vipassanā*), even the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) are sluggish.

However, for one who is the opposite of what was described, because of the excessive manifestation of defilements, the sharpness of the faculties, and the fact that they have performed the preliminary work for both serenity (*samatha*) and insight, there is, respectively, an easy path of practice and swift higher knowledge.
For just as in the case of one who has cultivated familiarity in another existence...
Having mastered [the texts] and released the burden of the books, one becomes fluent and proficient through even a slight application;

thus, meditation succeeds with ease. Now, this practice—both unperformed and performed—is said to be based on serenity (*samatha*) within the path because the path has concentration as its primary factor.
That which is based on insight (*vipassanā*) is [said to be] based on direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) because it has wisdom (*ñāṇa*) as its primary factor.
It should be understood as "in absorption.

However, for one whose defilements are sharp, whose faculties are keen, and who has performed the preliminary work specifically in insight (vipassanā), the way of practice is painful according to the method already stated, yet direct knowledge is swift;
for one who is the opposite of that, the way of practice is pleasant and direct knowledge is sluggish.

Therefore, the distinction between these [jhānas] should be understood by way of the predominance of defilements and faculties— according to whether the defilements are intense or mild, the faculties are sharp or dull,
and whether there has been previous practice or not— and furthermore, by way of the subsequent favorable and unfavorable conditions,
the preliminary duties such as the severing of impediments, and the skillfulness regarding absorption.

And there will be those who come; among them, for one who indulges in what is unsuitable both before and after attaining the access [concentration], the practice is painful and direct knowledge is slow.
For one who indulges in what is suitable in both instances, the practice is pleasant and direct knowledge is swift.
But for one who, having indulged in what is unsuitable prior to that, later becomes an indulger in what is suitable—
For him, the practice is painful and direct higher knowledge is swift. For one who is the opposite of that, the practice should be understood as pleasant and direct higher knowledge slow.
Likewise, for one who applies himself to meditation without having first performed the preliminary tasks such as severing impediments, it is obstructed.
The way of practice is painful; conversely, it is pleasant when there is no obstruction.
For one who does not achieve skill in absorption, direct knowledge is sluggish due to the lack of clarity of his knowledge; for one who does achieve it, direct knowledge is swift by contrast.
Furthermore, their distinction should be understood by way of craving, ignorance, birth, and becoming. For the way of practice is painful for one who is overcome by craving.
The way of practice is "pleasant" because that concentration is directly opposed to it and acts as an obstacle to the way of serenity (*samatha*);

for one who is not overcome [by ignorance], that [obstacle] is absent, hence it is pleasant. Furthermore, for one overcome by ignorance, direct higher knowledge (*abhiññā*) is sluggish because wisdom (*paññā*) is directly opposed to that [ignorance]; for the other, it is swift. Moreover, this distinction of ways of practice occurs solely by way of the cultivation of serenity.
However, for one who has attained jhāna by way of the realization of the Path, there is no distinction such as "difficult practice" and so forth.

Some, however, describe its distinction of practice and so on by way of the Path alone, saying: "For when the Path possesses the state of difficult practice and so forth, that [jhāna] is likewise characterized as 'difficult practice' and so on."

Regarding the classification by predominance (*adhipati*) and so forth: there is that which has desire as its predominant factor, that which has consciousness as its predominant factor, that which has energy as its predominant factor, and that which has investigation as its predominant factor—thus it is according to the classification by predominance.

There is the limited with a limited object, the limited with an immeasurable object, the immeasurable with a limited object, and the immeasurable with an immeasurable object—thus it is according to the classification by object. [There is also] that which partakes of decline (*hānabhāgiya*).

The fourfold classification should be understood according to the divisions beginning with "conducive to decline" (*hānabhāgiya*), namely: conducive to stability (*ṭhitibhāgiya*), conducive to distinction (*visesabhāgiya*), and conducive to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*).

Among these, that which arises having made zeal (*chanda*) the primary factor—thinking, "If jhāna will be produced for one who possesses zeal, it will be produced for me too"—is called "dominated by zeal" (*chandādhipateyya*). The same method applies to those [jhānas] dominated by consciousness (*citta*) and so forth.
However, that which lacks abundance and is unable to serve as a condition for a higher jhāna is "limited" (paritta).

That which is produced with objects that have not increased beyond the measure of a mere trickle of water is "limited-object" (parittārammaṇa). The "immeasurable-object" (appamāṇārammaṇa) and so forth should be understood respectively as the opposites of what has been stated.
The distinctions such as "conducive to decline" (hānabhāgiya) and so on, he will explain himself.

"By way of the distinction in the association of jhāna factors": in some places there are five jhāna factors, in some four, in some three, in some two, and in others yet another two; thus it is by way of the distinction in the association of the jhāna factors.

Now, why is the distinction of the formations (*saṅkhāra*) not included here, as it is in the case of wholesome states of the sense sphere? For this [distinction] also occurs solely by way of application to serenity (*samatha*).

Is it therefore to be said that "it is tenfold according to the distinction of association with the volitional formations of the jhāna factors," namely, that which is acquired with volitional formation and that which is acquired without volitional formation by way of the attainment of the Path? This is not so;

for even that which is acquired from the moment of the attainment of the Path arises subsequently only through the process of preliminary work (*parikamma*). Therefore, all jhāna is [to be understood] by means of the prior volitional formation known as preliminary work.
Since it does not arise solely by the force of its specific application (*adhikāra*), one cannot say it is "without effort" (*asaṅkhāra*);
and since it does not arise solely through preparatory effort (*parikammābhisaṅkhāra*) without that application, one cannot say it is "with effort" (*sasaṅkhāra*).
Thus, its fivefold nature is stated according to the distinction between the factors of absorption (*jhānaṅga*) and their application (*yoga*).
He has abandoned these five hindrances—sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt—thus he is one "by whom sensual desire...

[and so on]... has been abandoned. Here, the word *vippahīna* (abandoned) should be understood as having the same case-ending as the word *āhita* (placed) in the phrase *agyāhito*. Alternatively, it means "one by whom sensual desire and the rest have been abandoned."
It is dissociated from them by way of their abandonment; thus, sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*)... [etc] ...is abandoned.

In this context, it is called "sensual desire" (*kāma*) because one desires (*kāmeti*), and "desire" (*chanda*) in the sense of longing; thus, *kāmacchanda* is a designation for intense lustful passion. He will explain the meaning of ill-will (*byāpāda*) and so forth later.
Since meditative absorption (*jhāna*) does not arise as long as sensual desire and the other hindrances have not been abandoned, they are therefore its factors of abandonment.
They should be understood. But surely other unwholesome states (*akusala-dhammā*) are also abandoned by this jhāna;
why then are only five mentioned as factors of abandonment? Because they specifically create obstacles to jhāna.
