For a mind enticed by various objects through sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) does not become concentrated on a single object. Or rather, a mind overcome by sensual desire is [distracted] by the multitude of various objects.
One does not practice the way of abandoning the sense-sphere realm; being struck by ill will against the object, one's mind does not proceed in a concentrated state;
overcome by sloth and torpor, it becomes unwieldy; possessed by restlessness and remorse, it wanders about without becoming tranquil;
and afflicted by doubt, it does not ascend the path to the attainment of jhāna.
Because for one who doubts—thinking, "Is it a Perfectly Enlightened One or not? Is earth earth or not?
through such modes of attention, or "Could there be jhāna or not?"—the path to the attainment of jhāna does not become confused. As he will say:
"I shall certainly be a partaker of this practice..."
“Having made supreme effort for the bliss of seclusion.

Therefore, because these [five hindrances] specifically create obstacles to the attainment of jhāna by being direct opposites to concentration and the other factors, they are called the factors to be abandoned. And there is this verse here:
“Since there are five opposites here, Of concentration and the rest...”
"Therefore, those things which obstruct jhāna are restricted to the factors of abandoning.
Having thus shown this by way of the factors of abandoning, it is now said, "applied thought... associated," in order to show it by way of the factors of association.
Therein, applied thought and the others will be explained further on according to their etymological meaning, characteristics, and so forth.
Since, however, when these have arisen, it is called "jhāna" has arisen, they should be understood as its factors of association;
therefore, one should not take it that there is some other thing called "jhāna" apart from those [factors].
Just as the designation "chariot" and so forth occurs for a collection of parts such as the wheels and so on, so too the designation "jhāna" occurs for a collection of jhāna-factors.
For this is said in the Vibhaṅga: “Jhāna is applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind.
But why, when other associated states such as contact and so forth are also present, are only these five stated as the factors of jhāna?
It is said: because they possess the function of closely contemplating (upanijjhāna), and because they are the direct opposites of sensual desire and the other hindrances.
For initial application (*vitakka*) applies the mind to the object, while sustained application (*vicāra*) follows after it.

Thus, through these two—which serve as specific conditions for the attainment of *jhāna*—the joy (*pīti*) arising from the perfection of the mental effort that has been concentrated for the sake of non-distraction brings about exhilaration, and pleasure (*sukha*) brings about nourishment.
Then, together with its associated states, this [consciousness] is characterized by these [four factors]: applying, following, exhilarating, and nourishing.
Supported by its function of concentration, it causes the mind to follow after itself; it places [the mind] evenly and correctly upon the single object.
It places [it] "evenly" by way of the balancing of the faculties, and "correctly" by way of the removal of opposing states through the absence of lethargy and agitation.
Thus, this very act of close contemplation (*upanijjhāna*) is their unique function. This is because it serves as the antidote to sensual desire and the other hindrances.

But he himself will explain this later. Thus, because they possess the function of close contemplation (*upanijjhāna*) and because they are the direct opposites of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and the other hindrances, only these five are established as the factors of absorption (*jhānaṅga*). As it has been said:
"Because of their function of close contemplation, And because they are the opposites of sensual desire and the rest..."
"And even when there are other [attainments], only these five are designated as jhānas.

Regarding this, some say it is called "first" because it comes first in the order of teaching, because it is the first among the exalted states (mahaggata-dhamma) to be attained, and because it is the first to be entered upon.
However, that is not an absolute definition, since it is impossible [to call it "first"] when entering [jhāna] in reverse order and so forth.

Because initial application (*vitakka*) does not arise at the moment of absorption (*appanā*), even though it arises during the preceding and succeeding moments of consciousness, it has been abandoned by him;
or, because he has abandoned it, it is "one who has abandoned initial application" (*vitakkavippahīna*).

Indeed, because it has been abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā*), initial application does not arise at the moment of jhāna. However, because its intrinsic nature is undefiled (*asaṃkiliṭṭha-sabhāva*), it can be abandoned through access cultivation (*upacāra-bhāvanā*).
Because it lacks the capacity [to arise] in the preceding stage and because it arises only from a non-opposing state of mind in the subsequent stage, it simply does not arise.
But was it not stated that "it is by virtue of its undefiled nature"? If so, how is it abandoned by means of jhāna?
For there is no abandoning of an undefiled dhamma by wholesome states; rather, this [jhāna] is for the purpose of abandoning evil dhammas such as greed and other defilements.
"Because it is the direct opposite"? It is said: although this [pleasure] is by nature undefiled, because of its grossness and weakness, it is incapable of arising at the moment of jhāna;
therefore, for the purpose of ensuring its non-arising at that moment, the cultivation of the second jhāna occurs by way of suppressing attachment to it.
By the power of that [second jhāna], that [pleasure] does not arise at the moment of jhāna, or it is suppressed by way of the suppression of attachment.

It is called "abandoned. If that were so, then since attachment is suppressed even by the access concentration (*upacāra*), its abandonment would occur there as well—just as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are abandoned in the access to the first jhāna? This is not the case;
for, unlike the abandonment of the hindrances, the suppression of attachment directed toward the object of thought is not achieved to such an exceptional degree by access concentration.
For it is only through absorption (*appanā*) that the abandonment of attachment (*nikanti*) therein occurs to a superior degree;
therefore, what we said—that "it is impossible to abandon that by means of access development (*upacāra-bhāvanā*)"—should be understood as having been stated after careful examination.

The meaning in such passages as "wherein investigation (*vicāra*) has been abandoned" should also be understood according to the method already explained. [This refers to] that which is abandoned specifically in the second jhāna.

The mention of "thought" (*vitakka*) is made here for the purpose of showing the mere non-occurrence of thought; thus it is also in such expressions as "having abandoned thought and examination" (*vitakkavicāra*) and "having abandoned thought, examination, and rapture" (*vitakkavicārapīti*), and so forth.
"According to possibility" means not exceeding whatever object is possible for whichever [meditative stage], such as the earth-kasina and others.
For in the case of the kasiṇas and the breaths, only five jhānas occur; in the foul objects (asubha) and mindfulness occupied with the body (kāyagatāsati), the first jhāna occurs;
in the divine abidings (brahmavihāra) excluding equanimity, the jhānas occur except for the fifth; and in the divine abiding of equanimity, the fifth jhāna occurs.
Regarding the phrase "in the earth-kasiṇa and so forth," here the inclusion of "and so forth" (ādi) refers not only to the water-kasiṇa and the rest, but also to the foul objects and so on.
It should be understood that this is a compendium of meditation subjects that lead to absorption (*appanā*).
Herein, although the bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) and the liberations (*vimokkha*) differ from the jhānas merely in their mode of occurrence, they have the same objects as the kasiṇa-bases;
thus, they are included within the jhānas of the kasiṇa-bases. Furthermore, by the expression “as far as possible... manifold,” [the inclusion] of the fine-material-sphere jhānas is indicated.
Since every existing variety is included [within this], the bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) and the liberations (*vimokkha*) are not mentioned separately;
however, they should be understood according to their specific nature as follows.
In that regard, for a practitioner whose excellence is knowledge (*ñāṇuttara*), having mastered the objects such as the earth-kasiṇa and so forth, [he thinks]: "There is nothing here for me..."

For one who has entered the practice with the thought, "The burden lies in the production of absorption," the jhāna obtained from the second or third cognitive process (vīthi) onwards—after the arising of the sign (nimitta), or in the fourth or fifth process—is called an "overcoming base" (abhibhāyatana). For it overcomes the object;

thus it is "overcoming" (abhibhū). This is because it serves as the foundation for the yogi’s specific excellences of happiness and because it is included within the sense-base of mind (manāyatana) and the base of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana).

Or, "base of mastery" (*abhibhāyatana*) means a base of mastery; or, that which is to be mastered is the "master" (*abhibhū*), which is the object (*ālambana*); since that is the base (*āyatana*) of this [consciousness], it is a "base of mastery.
Alternatively, because of the very mastery over the object, the preliminary practice (*parikamma*) or the knowledge (*ñāṇa*) is the "master";
since that is the base—that is, the cause—of this, it is a "base of mastery. Having mastered the object through either the preliminary practice or the knowledge...
While occurring, it produces absorption without exceeding the fifth cognitive process from the moment of access.
However, that which is produced beyond the fifth process—even if produced with the desire to master [the object]—is not called an "abhibhāyatana" (sphere of mastery).
Rather, by way of its general nature, it is merely a *kasiṇāyatana* (totality-sphere). It is precisely with reference to this more rapid occurrence that [this was said].
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: “Having mastered those [objects], one attains absorption; here, one produces absorption simultaneously with the arising of the sign.

Now, why is the meaning not accepted according to the literal sense of the *Aṭṭhakathā*? For, since it is said “simultaneously with the arising of the sign,” is it not understood that the jhāna arisen together with the arising of the sign is the base of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*)? This is not so.
Because absorption cannot arise simultaneously with the arising of the sign.
For "the arising of the sign" here refers either to the appearance of the counterpart sign or to access concentration which has that as its object.

First of all, absorption does not arise simultaneously with the appearance of the counterpart sign, because that is impossible in the absence of access concentration. Nor does it arise simultaneously with access concentration.
It was not reborn in a single street because, at that time, it was impossible for it to be cultivated through the continuous practice of access concentration;

therefore, it should be understood that it is stated thus in the Commentary by using the term "nearby" (*samīpa*) in the sense of proximity, in order to show that its occurrence does not last very long. If the base of mastery occurs not long after the arising of the sign, [then...]
How is the distinction between slow direct knowledge (*dandhābhiññā*) and quick direct knowledge (*khippābhiññā*) stated in the Canon? It is said:

that which arises in the fourth or fifth cognitive process (*javana-vīthi*) is "slow direct knowledge" because it is produced after a long time; that which arises in the second or third process is "quick direct knowledge" because its characteristic is the opposite of that.
Some, however, say: "The so-called 'base of mastery' (*abhibhāyatana*) refers only to that which has attained mastery (*vasibhāva*), not to any other."

That is merely their opinion; for it contradicts the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā*—“In this case, one produces absorption simultaneously with the arising of the sign”—because [the arising of the sign] is far removed from the attainment of mastery.
Furthermore, jhāna that has attained mastery does not depend on the cause of suppression, but rather, by the power of mastery itself, it is thoroughly...

Because it is not possible to attain [it], that is not called an "abhibhāyatana" (sphere of mastery); therefore, one must conclude that the first [sphere] is an abhibhāyatana precisely because mastery has not yet been attained.
If this is so, how is it stated in the teaching on the abhibhāyatanas: "The immeasurable with a limited object;
the immeasurable with an immeasurable object"? For it is only when jhāna has attained mastery...
It is called "immeasurable. But is this [state] merely limited because it has only just arisen? This is not a fault.

The jhāna first acquired by way of the bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana) retains the name "base of mastery" even when it later attains mastery; thus, the base of mastery that has attained mastery is immeasurable, while the other is limited.
Alternatively, it is called "immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*) by way of including the highest stage of mastery when one has attained mastery.
However, they say that this is stated as an illustration for the meaning that "whatever is more powerful is immeasurable. The state of being immeasurable is based on the state of being powerful;
and the state of being powerful exists because of the increasing power of the successive stages of absorption (*appanā*) following the first stage of absorption.

Since the state of being "immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*) is possible even in a jhāna that has reached its conclusion, while the other is "limited" (*paritta*), one should understand that the status of being immeasurable and so forth applies to a jhāna even when it has reached its conclusion.
Alternatively, what is called the "powerful state" of absorption (*appanā*) occurs only when there is a powerful access concentration (*upacāra*).
And that access concentration is powerful which is capable of producing absorption immediately; therefore—
For those with quick direct knowledge (*khippābhiññā*), the two *abhibhāyatana* jhānas arise in the second cognitive process immediately following the access-process of the first;
because of the strength of the access-jhāna, they themselves are even stronger and are thus called "immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*).

Having transcended the second process, those arising in the third process are "limited" (*paritta*) due to their other inherent nature. Likewise, for those with sluggish direct knowledge (*dandhābhiññā*), [they arise] in the fourth process.
That which arises in the fifth cognitive process is "limited" (paritta). Alternatively,
since the fourth [consciousness] arising in any appanā-process sequence possesses a state of greater strength than the fifth appanā that is to arise,
it is by way of this [relative strength] that the states of "limited" and "immeasurable" (appamāṇa) should be understood here.
Furthermore, this consists of eight types by way of enumeration, as it is said:
"Not perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally that are limited; having mastered them, one perceives: 'I know, I see.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally that are limited..."
Beautiful and ugly. Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are immeasurable.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are immeasurable, beautiful and ugly;
having mastered them, one knows and sees them. Blue, blue-colored, blue-appearing, blue-luminous; having mastered them...
“I know, I see. Yellow things—yellow in color, yellow in appearance, yellow in luster.
Red things—red in color, red in appearance, red in luster. White things—white in color, white in appearance, white in luster.
Having mastered these, one has the perception: ‘I know, I see.’”

In this context, "not perceiving forms internally" means that, either due to lack of attainment or lack of interest, one is devoid of the preliminary and absorption perceptions regarding internal things such as head hair and so forth.
"One sees forms externally" means that one sees forms externally within the eight *kasiṇas*,
or specifically within the four primary element *kasiṇas*, by way of both the preliminary stage and absorption, through having performed the preliminary work upon them.
And externally, he sees those eight or four kasiṇa-forms as limited—that is, not large. "Having mastered" means:
just as a gluttonous man with a great appetite, having received a mere spoonful of food, gathers it together thinking, "What is there to eat here?
Is this all the food? and makes it into a single mouthful; so too does he master them.
In the same way, a person of supreme knowledge, possessing clear wisdom, thinks: "What need is there to attain anything upon such a limited object?
This is no burden for me. Having mastered those forms through preliminary work or through knowledge, he enters attainment.
By the method explained above, he quickly produces absorption (*appanā*). Furthermore, his prior mental application is expressed by the thought: "I know, I see."
It was stated [in this way] because of that arrival and because of the mental formation (*cittābhisaṅkhāra*) within the attainment (*samāpatti*).

Otherwise, if only the mere application of attention (*ābhoga*) had been mentioned by him, the jhāna to be accomplished by him would not have been described; for in the sequence of the teaching on the bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*), it refers to the objects of jhāna.

However, in the commentaries on the scriptures (*āgama-aṭṭhakathā*), it is said that at the moment of jhāna, by way of the preliminary development (*pubbabhāga-bhāvanā*) of one who has emerged from attainment...
Having taken up the mode of activity that overcomes what is occurring, and referring to the mental application (*ābhoga*) as it occurs, it is said:
"But by this, his mental application is described. And that is for one who has emerged from attainment, not while within the attainment.

In the second [case], "beautiful and ugly colors" refers to pure and impure colors. For here, those blue and other colors that are pure are intended as "beautiful," while those that are impure are intended as "ugly."
In the third [kammaṭṭhāna], "immeasurables" (*appamāṇāni*) refers to vast and extensive threshing-floors and so forth, which possess the dimension of growth.

However, "immeasurability" is not taken here in the sense of expansion, because the expansion of the *kasiṇa* is impossible in this context. For there are only two stages for the expansion of a *kasiṇa*:
the stage of access (*upacāra-bhūmi*) or the stage of absorption (*appanā-bhūmi*). Of these, expansion is not possible here at the stage of access.
Since jhāna arises simultaneously with the appearance of the sign (*nimitta*), where would there be room for that [expansion]? Nor is there room in the stage of absorption (*appanā*).

It is not logical for that which has been expanded to have as its object the jhāna that first arose; therefore, it is intended here that the objects are called "immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*) precisely because of their greatness by nature.
However, some, taking them to be immeasurable solely by virtue of being expanded, first...
They say: "Because there was no desire to master [the object] at the time of expansion, but later, when the desire to master it arose, it proceeded in the mode of mastery;
thus, having attained absorption (appanā), this 'base of mastery' (abhibhāyatana) is said to be among the expanded signs.
Regarding the fourth [base], "having mastered" (abhibhuyya) means having overcome. It is like a man who is a voracious eater and has a great appetite.
Just as one who has received an extra portion of food does not regard it as something great, thinking, "Let there be more for others too;
what will this do for me?", so too a person of superior knowledge and clear wisdom overcomes [the thought], "What need is there to enter this?
This is not immeasurable; the burden lies with me to achieve one-pointedness of mind," and thus enters into attainment.
In the same manner as previously described, one brings about absorption (*appanā*).
Regarding the fifth [meditation object]: "blue... pe ...having a blue appearance"—these are synonyms. Therein, "blue" is stated by way of including everything.

However, if only that much were said, there might be the undesirable consequence of applying that designation to something possessing a quality (*guṇa*) through association with it; therefore, in order to prevent that:
“Blue-colored” is stated by way of color (*vaṇṇa*). For even in this case, by way of a *bahubbīhi* compound, there would be the possibility of including a quality (*guṇa*) as well;
therefore, it is stated as “blue-appearing” (*nīlanidassanāni*) by way of appearance (*nidassana*). For that which is to be pointed out is an appearance, namely, a form (*rūpa*) visible to the eye.
Thus, the compound is formed with the word “blue” in order to exclude white and other colors; [this refers to] robes whose color is not clearly discernible.

"Of unmixed colors" means they are seen as being entirely blue; this is what is intended. "Blue-appearing" (nīlanibhāsāni), however, is stated by way of their radiance; the meaning is that they have a blue appearance and are endowed with a blue luster.
By this, he shows their extreme purity. The meaning in the cases of "yellow" and so forth should be understood in this same manner. Among the eight...

Regarding the first [of these], it is said with reference to that which has arisen by taking all eight kasinas as its object in a limited way, in the mode of overcoming, and devoid of attention to color. The third is likewise [limited].
The second and fourth alone have arisen in relation to those accompanied by attention to color; however, they do not arise by way of the color-kasina, because that will be explained separately.
However, with reference to those who have already performed the preliminary work (*katādhikāra*), the fifth and subsequent bases are taught solely by way of their perfectly pure color.
For the cause of their mastery is neither their limited nature nor their immeasurable nature, but rather the state of being perfectly pure blue and so forth;
for it is therein that they have performed the preliminary work. But is it not said in the commentaries on the scriptures (*āgama-aṭṭhakathā*) that "whether they be beautiful or ugly..."?
Or is it said that these bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) were taught solely by way of the limited (*paritta*) and the measureless (*appamāṇa*)? That is true;
however, it was stated because the bases of mastery are recorded differently in the *Āgama*. For there, it says:
"One who is percipient of forms internally sees forms externally, limited, beautiful or ugly; [one who is percipient of forms internally sees forms externally] measureless..."
“Beautiful and ugly forms; one who is percipient of the formless internally sees forms externally, limited, beautiful and ugly;

and immeasurable, beautiful and ugly”—thus only four spheres of mastery (abhibhāyatana) are mentioned. Therefore, since the description of their colors exists in the commentaries on those [spheres],...
The fact that these [meditations] were taught by way of both the limited (*paritta*) and the measureless (*appamāṇa*), even when the color is not actually present, has been stated.
For the limited and the measureless are the causes for mastery (*abhibhavana*) in these four, whether the apprehension of color (*vaṇṇābhoga*) is present or absent.
But is it not the case that, because the expression "beautiful and ugly" (*suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni*) occurs everywhere, they are taken there as being necessarily accompanied by the apprehension of color?

That is not so; for all the limited [realms]—both those devoid of attention to color and those that are combined—are grouped together and described as "limited, beautiful and ugly," and likewise "immeasurable, beautiful and ugly.

If this is so, how can there be a single-pointed mental attention toward those distinguished [realms] which are devoid of attention to color and are combined? It is not single-pointed; rather, it is distinct for each.
Their attention is [on that]. If this is so, how is it that "oneness" (*ekatta*) is mentioned separately?

Because of the commonality of their limited nature (*parittabhāva*). If this is so, does the mention of "beautiful color" and "ugly color" exceed [the scope], being redundant? It is not redundant, because it is a teaching given by way of a method (*pariyāyadesanā*).

For there is this method: namely, without taking into account the distinction between what is produced and what is not produced by the application of attention to color, [they are included] by way of the commonality of their limited nature.
Having brought them to a state of unity and stated, "having overcome the limited," he then shows their internal differentiation according to the mode of training:
sometimes they are adverted to by way of color; because of the need to say, "having overcome the beautiful and ugly," they are devoid of the mental application to color;
and having attended to them both together and separately, in both cases there is the overcoming of the limited while being devoid of the mental application to color.
And in the case of the "conjoined with limited" and "overcoming limited," having taken the commonality of "overcoming limited," they were made into one.
However, in the Abhidhamma, because the teaching is given in its definitive sense (*nippariyāya*), those [bases] devoid of attention to color and those conjoined [with it] are stated separately.
For there is indeed a distinction in the overcoming in both cases. Let it be so for now, according to this difference in the textual readings of the Sutta and the Abhidhamma.
But as for the difference in the reading of the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), what is the intended meaning? It is said:
In the Sutta, having divided the first liberation into two, the first and second bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) were taught.

Since the teaching is given by way of a figurative method (*pariyāyadesanā*), there exists a figurative application of "mastery" even to the liberations; thus, the two bases of mastery are stated as "perceiving forms internally."
In the third and fourth bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*), the second liberation (*vimokkha*) is included because it functions as a mastery;
likewise, in the bases of mastery over color-forms, the third liberation is included for the same reason.

However, here, because the teaching is given in its definitive sense (*nippariyāya*), the bases of mastery are explained separately from the liberations in order to show them without confusion, and thus the liberations are omitted. Furthermore, all the functions of the liberations [are present here].

It is understood that this definition was established because the two *abhibhāyatana*s (bases of mastery) mentioned in the sutta as "perceiving forms internally" are not explicitly stated in the Abhidhamma, and because expressions such as "possessing form, he sees forms" are common to the functions of all the liberations (*vimokkha*).
This must certainly be accepted; it cannot be accepted by those who do not so accept it.
Another reason must be stated for the difference between the readings in the Suttas and the Abhidhamma. Now, what is there to say?

Is it not already stated in the Aṭṭhakathā: "But why, when in the Suttanta it is said, 'One percipient of forms internally sees forms externally as limited,' and so forth, is it not the case that here, in all four bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana), only the state of being 'percipient of the formless internally' is mentioned?"
Having said this, is it stated that "because internal forms are not to be overcome" is the reason? That is not a statement of the reason for that;
rather, it is a statement of the reason for that which is said everywhere—"one sees external forms"—without saying in some instances "one sees internal forms.
For it is precisely for that reason that, whether there [in that context] or here, it says "externally..."
It is stated right there [in the Sutta] that "only forms are to be overcome.

And the reason internal forms are not to be overcome is because, unlike external forms, they are not clearly manifest. For it is impossible for those with superior knowledge to overcome an object without that object being clearly manifest.
But is it not the case that the distinction between these two readings in the Commentary is merely a display of the Teacher’s pedagogical skill?
Is it stated as being by way of its causal nature? It is true that it is so stated, and it should be understood precisely according to the aforementioned analysis.

For what is called the "elegance of teaching" (desanāvilāsa) is the elucidation of an existing method in accordance with the disposition of those to be trained, not just any arbitrary method whatsoever.
Thus, first of all, the base of mastery (abhibhāyatana) should be understood.
In this context, "liberation" (vimokkha) means that immediately after the impulsion-series (javana-vīthi) has proceeded with the desire to attain the jhāna already acquired,
one enters the object without hesitation— just like a child whose limbs and members have been cast upon its father's lap—
and without emerging quickly, as in the first mental construction (paṭhamakappanā), remaining for at least four or five mind-moments without wavering through delight in the object.
This is a designation for jhāna that has proceeded and attained mastery.

For when it has arisen by way of the kasiṇa bases or the bases of mastery, it is called "liberation" (vimokkha) because it is well-freed from opposing states and because of its resolute intent toward the object.
This has also been stated in the Commentary:
“In what sense, then, should liberation (vimokkha) be understood? In the sense of resolving (adhimuccana). What is this so-called sense of resolving?
It is the sense of being thoroughly liberated from opposing states (paccanīkadhamma), and the sense of being thoroughly resolved through delighting in the object.
If liberation is only that which has attained mastery (vasibhāva), how is it that its limited nature (parittatā) is stated in the Canon within the tetrad of objects?
Is it not the case that jhāna which has attained mastery is called "limited" (paritta)? This is not a fault;
for it refers to that which has attained full mastery, since the state of being "limited" is intended there for that which has not attained full mastery.
Therefore, only jhāna that has attained mastery is called "liberation" (vimokkha), and not the other. As for the other, if it has arisen by way of the kasiṇa-bases, it is a kasiṇa-base.
Then, by way of the bases of mastery, they are simply the bases of mastery. However, some say:

"With the exception of the first absorption—which arises by way of the kasiṇa-bases and the bases of mastery because it is thoroughly liberated from its respective opposites starting from the first absorption onwards—all the rest are indeed liberations."
This, moreover, is threefold by way of counting, as it is said:
"One possessing form sees forms; one not percipient of form internally sees forms externally; one is intent upon the beautiful.
Therein, "possessing form" means that the jhāna of form produced internally with respect to the head-hairs and so forth is "form," and because he has that, he is "one possessing form."
"He sees forms" means that he sees external forms, such as the blue kasiṇa and so forth, with the eye of jhāna.
By this, the attainment of jhāna regarding kasiṇas that have both internal and external objects is shown. "Perceiving no form internally" means not perceiving form internally;

the meaning is that he has not yet produced fine-material-sphere jhāna with respect to his own hair and so forth. By this, it is shown that having performed the preliminary work externally, [he perceives] only externally...
The attainment of jhāna is demonstrated. By the word "beautiful" (*subha*), the jhānas based on the color-kasinas (*vaṇṇakasiṇa*) such as blue and so forth, which are perfectly pure, are shown.

Although there is no mental application (*ābhoga*) as "beautiful" within the actual absorption (*appanā*), one who dwells having made a perfectly pure beautiful kasina the object does so by way of resolving upon it as "beautiful."
Having attained the first jhāna, he dwells therein; likewise for the second and so forth. Therefore, the teaching was given in this manner.

However, in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, the beautiful liberation is described by way of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), beginning with: "Here, a bhikkhu dwells having pervaded one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness," and so on. In the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, however, the divine abodes are treated separately.

Having rejected that method on account of its being [contrary to] what has come down [in the tradition], it is stated in the Commentary that the beautiful liberation occurs precisely by way of the "beautiful blue" and so forth;
thus, here too, the definition is made according to the method stated therein. In this way, first of all, the jhāna of liberation should be understood.

"According to what is appropriate" means according to what is suitable for the inferior and so forth. For the first jhāna is inferior when one is reborn among the Brahmā-pārisajja gods, whose lifespan is a third of an eon.

It produces rebirth that is inferior among the Brahmā-purohitas with a lifespan of half an eon, middling among those with a lifespan of one eon, and superior among the Mahābrahmās with a lifespan of two eons.

Likewise, the second jhāna is inferior among the Parittābhas with a lifespan of two eons, middling among the Appamāṇābhas with a lifespan of four eons, and superior among the Ābhassarās with a lifespan of eight eons. The fourth jhāna is inferior... [among the Subhakinhās].

The minor degree of the "Beautiful" (parittāsubha) leads to rebirth among the gods with a lifespan of sixteen eons; the medium degree of the "Immeasurable Beautiful" (appamāṇasubha) leads to rebirth among the gods with a lifespan of thirty-two eons;

and the superior degree of the "Wholly Beautiful" (subhakiṇha) leads to rebirth among the gods with a lifespan of sixty-four eons. Furthermore, all three grades of the fifth jhāna produce rebirth among the Vehapphala gods with a lifespan of five hundred eons.
That same jhāna, when cultivated by the followers of other sects through the fading away of perception (saññāvirāga), results in a lifespan of exactly five hundred eons.

Regarding non-percipient beings: however, for those who are non-returners (*anāgāmī*), beginning from the time they were worldlings (*puthujjana*) and continuing thereafter, by developing themselves through the sequence of being inclined toward the faculties such as faith (*saddhādi-indriya*), they bring about rebirth in the five pure abodes (*suddhāvāsa*) known as Avihā, Atappa, Sudassa, Sudassī, and Akaniṭṭha—where the lifespans are respectively one thousand, two thousand, four thousand, eight thousand, and sixteen thousand eons—according to their respective order.
Thus, this [development] accordingly brings about rebirth in the sixteen realms of the fine-material Brahma-worlds (*rūpāvacara-brahmaloka*).
He said: “It occurs according to its correspondence...

[etc]...”. However, because even in the fine-material realm (rūpabhava), the excellence of enjoyment obtainable during the course of existence is the fruit of the sense-sphere realm (kāmāvacara) alone, therefore, instead of saying here that it "produces the excellence of existence and enjoyment," it is stated only that it "produces rebirth."
It should be understood that here, with respect to all [levels] from the plane of the second jhāna upwards, the limit is to be seen by way of a complete great aeon (*mahākappa*);
however, on the plane of the first jhāna, it is by way of an incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeyyakappa*).
For in that case, a limit by way of the other [measure] is not possible, because even within a single aeon there is no destruction of the world-system.
Because it subsists at only the fourth stage.
The commentary on the wholesome of the fine-material sphere is finished.
The commentary on the wholesome of the immaterial sphere.
Now, since the opportunity for the exposition of wholesome states of the formless realm has arrived, he says “But as for the rest,” etc., in order to explain that.
Space obtained by the removal of any kasiṇa whatsoever—excepting the space-kasiṇa—is called “space obtained by the removal of the kasiṇa.
Consciousness occurring therein is what is meant by the base of infinite space; for that indeed serves as the object of the second formless attainment.
"In every way" (*sabbaso*) means: in every aspect—by seeing the taking up of the staff, the arising of the sign of form, and so forth, regarding all material phenomena;
by the aspect of seeing the flaws in the signs of form such as the earth-kasiṇa and the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) that have them as their object;
or by the aspect of abandoning attachment to those very same signs of form, the lack of desire to enter [absorption], and so forth. Alternatively, "in every way" (*sabbaso*)...

The meaning is: "of all," that is, without exception, according to their divisions such as wholesome (*kusala*) and so forth. "Of perceptions of form" refers both to the fine-material-sphere jhānas expressed by way of the term "perception" (*saññā*) and to their objects.
For the fine-material-sphere jhāna itself is called "form" by eliding the latter member of the compound, as in the passage, "one possessing form sees forms.
Its object—the kasiṇa-form—is also [called "form"] by eliding the first member of the compound, as in the phrase, "by the deva..."

As in the passages, “He has given,” and “he sees external forms,” etc., here too, in the context of form and form-jhāna, the perception associated with that is taken as “perception of form” (*rūpasaññā*).
This is a designation for the fine-material-sphere jhānas spoken of under the heading of “perception. It is called “perception of form” because it has “form” as its perception;
the meaning is that it possesses the name “form. By including that [perception], there is the inclusion of the various types such as the earth-kasiṇa and so forth.

It should be understood that this is the name for that which has those as its object. For the designation "perceptions of form" (*rūpasaññānaṃ*) is made by way of a collective singular (*sarūpekasesa*).
"By transcending" means by way of dispassion (*virāga*) and cessation (*nirodha*). What is meant?
By these fifteen perceptions of form—reckoned as jhānas—which are wholesome, resultant, and functional, and by these nine [perceptions] based on the earth-kasiṇa and so forth...
It is the wholesome consciousness of the formless sphere accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite space,
which has arisen through the fading away and cessation— by way of disgust and by way of the suppression of the desire and lust that obstruct it— of all perceptions of form known as objects,
either in their entirety or by way of abandoning attachment to them, such as through the lack of desire to enter [into them]. For it is not possible...
"By one who has completely not transcended the perception of form, this is produced.
This is produced not only by the transcending of these [perceptions], but also by the subsiding of perceptions of resistance and so forth;
thus he said, "of perceptions of resistance," and so on. In that context, there are the bases such as the eye, and the objects such as visible forms.
Perception arisen through striking—that is, through the mutual impact known as "striking"—is "perception of resistance" (*paṭighasaññā*).
This is a designation for the five types of perception beginning with the perception of forms. As it is said:

"In this context, what is perception of resistance? Perception of forms, perception of sounds, perception of odors, perception of tastes, and perception of tangibles—these are called perceptions of resistance."
This means by their disappearance, abandonment, non-arising, and causing them not to occur—referring to those states that are wholesome, unwholesome, and resultant.

But are these not absent even for one who has attained the fine-material-sphere jhānas? For indeed, at the time of attaining the first jhāna and so forth, consciousness does not proceed by way of the five sense doors.
This is true; however, just as [it is said], "With the abandoning of pleasure and pain... [the same principle applies].
And in the passage, “With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna,

which possesses neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness through equanimity,” although pleasure and pain have already been abandoned elsewhere, they are mentioned here in the context of the fourth jhāna by way of praise.

Similarly, in the passage, “With the abandoning of identity view and doubt, and with the thinning of lust, hatred, and delusion, he enters and dwells in the path of the once-returner,” although these factors have already been abandoned at the first path, they are mentioned there as well.
Just as there is mention of personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and so forth in the context of the second path because they have been abandoned, even so,
it should be understood that these [fetters] are mentioned here by way of praising this jhāna for the purpose of generating enthusiasm in those practicing this jhāna.
Alternatively, although they do not exist even for one attained to the fine-material-sphere absorption, they do not fail to exist merely because they have been abandoned.

Why? Because of the absence of conditions. For the development of the fine-material sphere does not lead to dispassion for the fine-material realm, since its occurrence is dependent upon the fine-material realm itself.
However, the development of the immaterial sphere does lead to dispassion for the fine-material realm; therefore, it is appropriate to say, "These are abandoned here.
Indeed, because these had not been abandoned prior to this, [it is said that they are abandoned] for one who has attained the first jhāna.

“Sound is a thorn,” so it was said by the Blessed One. And here, because the formless attainments have been abandoned, their immovability (*āneñjatā*) and state of peaceful liberation (*santavimokkhatā*) are expressed through such terms as “imperturbable volitional formations” (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*) and “those peaceful liberations which, transcending forms, are formless,” and so forth.

“Of perceptions of diversity” (*nānattasaññānam*) means of those perceptions that occur with diversity as their object, or of diverse perceptions; the meaning is of the remaining forty-four perceptions belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*). For these alone—

“In this context, what are perceptions of diversity? The perception, perceiving, and state of having perceived in one who has not attained [jhāna] and possesses either the mind-element or the mind-consciousness-element—these are called perceptions of diversity.

Thus they are explained in the *Vibhaṅga*. Furthermore, because they occur with respect to objects that are diverse—that is, of various natures—such as the distinctions of visible forms, sounds, and so forth;
and because there are eight wholesome perceptions of the sense sphere and twelve unwholesome perceptions...
There are eleven types of perception that are wholesome-resultants of the sense-sphere, two types of unwholesome-resultant perceptions, and eleven types of functional perceptions of the sense-sphere;
thus, they are divided into forty-four kinds, possessing diverse intrinsic natures, dissimilar from one another. Therefore, they are called "perceptions of diversity.
"Non-attention" means the complete absence of adverting, lack of mental application, and non-reviewing, by which [the mind] is led toward the impulsion stage.

Or, it is said that it is "due to non-attention to perceptions of diversity" because of the mind’s non-discrimination among various objects, setting aside the space cleared by the kasiṇa within the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*).
By this, the surmounting of material phenomena—which are the causes for the attention to perceptions of diversity—is also stated;
however, since those are absent in the form-sphere jhāna, it is said: "due to non-attention to perceptions of diversity."

It was not stated. Now, what is the distinction between "surmounting" (samatikkama) and the others? It is said: because the perception of form (rūpasaññā) and the perception of resistance (paṭighasaññā) do not exist even in the existence produced by this jhāna, and because through the absence of the cultivation of the perception of the formless (arūpasaññā), there is the state of non-arising for those perceptions of form and resistance—which would otherwise lead to rebirth after death—until their own fruition arises.
Because they are not being attained, let alone at the time of having entered this jhāna; therefore, by both expressions—“having surmounted” and “having disappeared”—their mere absence is shown.

As for the perceptions of diversity, those which do not arise in that state because they depend exclusively on form do not arise simply due to the lack of opportunity, not because they have been excluded by the development of the formless.

And because some [mental states] arise unavoidably, non-attention toward them—meaning non-orientation, non-reviewing, or not allowing them to enter within the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) by means of the impulsion-mind—is what is intended.
For even while those [states] are occurring, there is simply non-attention toward them for one who has attained jhāna; otherwise, there would be no attainment of jhāna at all.
Thus, in brief, by the phrase "with the surmounting of perceptions of form" (rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā), the abandoning of all phenomena pertaining to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) is stated;

by "with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity" (paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā), the abandoning of all mind and mental factors pertaining to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) is stated, as well as non-attention (amanasikāra). Furthermore, by these three [phrases], the stability of concentration (samādhi) is described.
Regarding the phrase "accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite space": here, that which has no end is "infinite" (*ananta*);

infinite space is "space-infinity" (*ākāsānanta*), which is the space revealed by the removal of the kasiṇa. Furthermore, its infinity should be understood either through the absence of the limits of arising and passing away, or by way of infinite attention;
for neither a limit of arising nor a limit of passing away is discerned in this, because it is a non-substantial phenomenon (*asabhāva-dhamma*). A substantial phenomenon...
For it is delimited by arising and passing away because it comes into being without having previously existed and perishes after having existed; it is not otherwise.
Furthermore, the practitioner of yoga does not grasp its limit, which is defined as this delimitation, while attending to it;
rather, he directs his attention in a manner that pervades infinitely by grasping merely the isolation of form. Therefore...
This should be understood as "infinite" (ananta) either by way of its being devoid of arising and passing away, or by way of its mental attention (manasikāra).
And although it should be called "infinite space" (anantākāsa), it is called "space-infinity" (ākāsānanta) due to the inversion of the word "ananta.

"Space-infinity" itself is "the base of infinite space" (ākāsānañcaṃ); having changed the *t*-sound of the latter member of the compound to a *c*-sound, that very thing is the base (āyatana) together with its associated states (sasampayutta-dhamma).
Because it serves as the object of jhāna, it is like a divine abode (devāyatana) in the sense of being a foundation; thus, it is the "base of infinite space" (ākāsānañcāyatana).

The perception that has reached absorption (appanā) regarding that is "perception of the base of infinite space. Consciousness accompanied by that is "accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite space.
Alternatively, it is called "base of infinite space" because this perception, together with its associated states, has infinite space as its base (āyatana).
That same perception; because the jhāna is accompanied by that, it is "accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite space.

… "Accompanied by consciousness" … [etc. … Because it has the nature of a phenomenon of the same essence as that first immaterial-sphere consciousness, even though it is limited by its beginning and end in terms of its arising and so forth, it is nevertheless—by way of making it its object and by not grasping a limit with respect to itself—pervasive throughout infinite space.
Alternatively, because consciousness is infinite due to the occurrence of mental attention (*pavattamanasikāra*), it is "infinite consciousness" (*viññāṇānanta*).

Although one might expect the phrase to be "and of infinite consciousness" (*viññāṇānañca*), the word *viññāṇañca* is used instead; this is because the term *viññāṇañca* is conventionally established in that sense, or because the vowel *ā* and the consonant *n* have been elided.
Having explained it in this way, he will say:
“‘Infinite consciousness’—this indeed should be said.

Alternatively, it is called *viññāṇañca* because it is to be reached (*añcita*) by means of the consciousness of the second formless attainment as its object; it is to be attained. The rest is exactly as before.
Regarding *akiñcaññā...* and so on: there is no *kiñcana* (anything) belonging to this first formless consciousness, even in the slightest degree; thus it is *akiñcana*.
The meaning is that not even a mere fragment remains. For if even a mere fragment were to remain, there would still be "something belonging" (*sakiñcana*) for him.
The state of being without anything is *ākiñcañña*; this is a designation for the absence of consciousness pertaining to the base of infinite space.
The rest is exactly as previously explained.

"Neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*nevasaññānāsañña*) refers to the fourth immaterial jhāna. It is called "neither-perception" because, as in the lower jhānas, there is an absence of gross perception;
it is called "nor-non-perception" because there is still the presence of subtle perception.
Thus, being neither perception nor non-perception, it is "neither-perception-nor-non-perception. If this is so—
“Should it be called ‘neither-perception-nor-non-perception’?”—this is true. However, it is stated with a long vowel for the sake of euphony.
Alternatively, it is stated as “nevasaññānāsaññaṃ” by way of a collective *bahubbīhi* compound, meaning “it has neither perception nor non-perception.
And that base (āyatana) is so called because it is included within the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and the mental-object-base (*dhammāyatana*).

The base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*); that which is associated with it is "accompanied by perception" (*saññāsahagata*), meaning it is accompanied by the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Alternatively, because perception itself is incapable of performing the function of clear perception, it is "not perception" (*nevasaññā*);

yet, because it has reached a state of extreme subtlety through the remaining residual formations—like the heat-element in hot water—it is "not non-perception" (*nāsaññā*). That very [perception] is the [condition] for the remaining phenomena...

It is the "base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*) because it is a base by way of being a condition of dependence, or simply because it is included within the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*) in the sense of being a foundation.

It is "accompanied by the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasaññāsahagata*) because it is accompanied by the perception that constitutes the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

[The phrase] "accordingly... and so forth... [refers to] "productive" (*nipphādaka*), meaning: first, in relation to the first immaterial plane; second, in relation to the second immaterial plane... [and so on].
By the passage beginning with "the second," etc., the attainment of rebirth in the four formless planes (ārūpabhūmi) according to one's own suitability is established.
It should be understood that among those, the first has a lifespan of twenty thousand eons, the second forty thousand eons, the third sixty thousand eons, and the fourth eighty-four thousand eons.
The commentary on wholesome states of the formless sphere is finished.
Now, having thus demonstrated the threefold mundane wholesome state, he spoke as follows while demonstrating the supramundane wholesome state: "The other..."

"Panā" and so forth. It is called "the world" (*loka*) in the sense of breaking up and disintegrating; it is threefold: the world of formations (*saṅkhāra-loka*), the world of beings (*satta-loka*), and the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).

That which transcends this is "supramundane" (*lokuttara*). For all four paths transcend the world of formations—consisting of the aggregates of clinging—by virtue of being free from taints (*anāsava*).
And among the worlds of beings, the path of stream-entry transcends the world of the ignoble (*anariya-loka*), while the path of once-returning...
The stream-entry path transcends the world of stream-enterers; the once-return path transcends the world of once-returners; and the arahant path transcends the world of non-returners.
Furthermore, among the receptacle worlds, the first path transcends the world of the woeful states; the once-return path transcends a portion of the sense-sphere world;
the non-return path transcends the entire sense-sphere world; and the arahant path transcends the form and formless worlds. Thus, it is fourfold.

The path-consciousness is "supramundane" (lokuttara) because it transcends the threefold world; it is "wholesome" (kusala) because of its faultless movement and so forth, and "consciousness" (citta) because of its nature of cognizing and so forth—thus it is supramundane wholesome consciousness.
The fruit, however, is supramundane because it has crossed over from the world;

or alternatively, both [the path and the fruit], together with Nibbāna, are "superior" (uttara) because they transcend and are more distinguished than the world comprised of the aggregates of clinging.
It is supramundane. As it is said: "Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared to be the foremost among those phenomena.
[The distinction] is according to the division between those with fixed and unfixed bases, because the path of stream-entry does not arise without the condition of another's voice.
Because there is no arising in the formless realm (*arūpabhava*), that [concentration] has a fixed basis;

however, the other sevenfold [concentration] can arise even there, because it is accomplished through the power of insight (*vipassanā*) alone even without the voice of another. Therefore, it has an unfixed basis.

"By three... [and so on] ...threefold" refers to emptiness-contemplation (*suññatānupassanā*) and the others, which are termed "gateways to liberation" (*vimokkhamukha*) because they serve as the doors to the supramundane liberations (*lokuttaravimokkha*).
Because it is to be attained by means of the three kinds of insight leading to emergence, this supramundane wholesome state is threefold:
emptiness (*suññatā*), the signless (*animitta*), and the desireless (*appaṇihita*). But what are those supramundane liberations? They are the nine supramundane states.
As it is said: "The four noble paths, the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna—this is the untainted (*anāsava*)."
“Liberation. For these are called liberations because they are thoroughly liberated from defiled states. Furthermore, each of them is threefold:

the void liberation, the signless liberation, and the desireless liberation. As it is said: “Bhikkhus, there are these three liberations: the void liberation, the signless liberation, and the desireless liberation.”
However, here, because the context concerns the wholesome (*kusala*), only supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*)—comprising the four paths—are intended.
Their acquisition of the names "emptiness" (*suññatā*) and so forth should be understood by way of their arrival (*āgamana*), their qualities (*saguṇa*), and their object (*ārammaṇa*).
For thus, it is called "arrival" (*āgamana*) because the path arrives and the fruit comes by means of it. That [arrival] is twofold: the arrival of the path and the arrival of the fruit.

Among these, insight leading to emergence is the approach to the path, and the noble path is the arrival at the fruit. Therein, where the path has arrived, the "approach to the path" is to be understood;
where the fruit has arrived, it is the "arrival at the fruit. But here, because the path has arrived, the "approach to the path" is taken.
[The terms are explained as follows: "From that arrival," from its coming; "by way of qualities," by way of its intrinsic nature; "by way of object," by way of the phenomena that serve as its object.
For one who attains the path by means of the contemplation of non-self— which proceeds through the penetration of the characteristic of non-self in all conditioned phenomena—
that contemplation, by way of suppressing those defilements associated with views that are the conditions for the adherence to a self and which render things non-empty,
[realizes] the emptiness of self in the phenomena of the three planes according to reality.

From the perspective of its apprehension, it is called "contemplation of emptiness. However, the path attained by means of that [contemplation] is called "the void" because it has arrived at emptiness.
Therefore, he said: "One who attends to [phenomena] as non-self is liberated by the void liberation.
Furthermore, regarding one who, through the contemplation of impermanence—which proceeds by way of penetrating the characteristic of impermanence in all conditioned formations—

He attains the path; for him, that contemplation is called "contemplation of the signless" because the defilements that grasp at signs such as permanence have been suppressed, and thus he does not grasp at signs such as permanence, which are defined as the appearance of a state of stability.

Furthermore, the path attained by means of that [contemplation] is called "signless" because it has come about through the signless. Therefore, he said: "While attending to [the object] as impermanent..."
“He is liberated by the signless liberation. Furthermore,
for one who attains the path by means of the contemplation of suffering— which proceeds through the penetration of the characteristic of suffering in all conditioned formations—
that contemplation, by way of suppressing the aspiration of craving, is devoid of aspiration.

This is called the contemplation of the wishless (*appaṇihitānupassanā*). Furthermore, the path attained by means of that [contemplation] is called "wishless" because it has come about through the wishless.
Therefore he said: "One who attends to [the object] as suffering is liberated by the wishless liberation.
This, first of all, is its acquisition of the name by way of its arrival.
Furthermore, because it is empty of lust and the other [defilements] within itself, because it is devoid of the sign of permanence and so forth, and because it lacks craving and aspiration—

thus being endowed with its own qualities— and because it takes as its object Nibbāna, which is likewise empty of lust and the rest, devoid of the sign of permanence and so forth, and liberated from aspiration,
it is called the "emptiness liberation" and so on both by way of its intrinsic quality and by way of its object. Thus it is for him.

The acquisition of the name [“mind”] by way of objects possessing qualities (saguṇa) is to be understood; however, this is only according to the method of the Suttantas, not according to the method of the Abhidhamma.
For the discourse of the Suttantas is a teaching by way of a figurative method (pariyāya-desanā), whereas the other is a non-figurative teaching (nippariyāya-desanā).

Therefore, because the name is not established as being common to all [objects] when considered from the perspective of objects possessing qualities, its acquisition occurs only according to the method of the Suttantas due to its figurative nature.
Furthermore, according to the method of the Abhidhamma, it is [threefold] because it is the primary way of defining [the path], being non-figurative (nippariyāya).

For this very reason, that same teacher stated, "It is threefold because it is to be attained through the three doors of liberation (vimokkhamukha)," making the door of liberation itself the primary factor, rather than saying, "It is threefold by way of the names 'emptiness' (suññatā) and so forth. As for the name "signless" (animitta), it is [also established] here by way of its source (āgamana).
It is obtained only by way of the Suttanta method, because in the Abhidhamma, the name "signless" (animitta) is not mentioned in relation to the path.
However, its non-mention is not merely due to its not being included; rather, it is because it is not found in the path in the direct, primary sense.
For although this insight proceeds by removing the sign of permanence, it does not remove the sign of formations (*saṅkhāra-nimitta*).
However, because it is not relinquished, it does not receive the name "signless" (animitta) in the absolute sense. But as for that which is stated in the Sutta:
"Cultivate the signless and abandon the underlying tendency to conceit;
then, through the full comprehension of conceit, you shall live at peace."
The statement regarding the signless nature (*animittabhāva*) of the Path is made by taking that which is applicable according to the manner already explained.
However, in the Abhidhamma, since that [Nibbāna] does not even itself receive the name "signless" in the direct, non-figurative sense (*nippariyāyato*), how could it bestow that name upon the Path?
Therefore, the name "signless" is not mentioned for the Path. If this is so, then as for the name "emptiness" (*suññatā*)—this...
It is the same. For although the contemplation of non-self (*anattānupassanā*) grasps the emptiness of the person (*puggala-suññatā*), it does not grasp the emptiness of phenomena (*dhamma-suññatā*);
thus, in the ultimate sense, it is not itself called "contemplation of emptiness" (*suññatānupassanā*). Consequently, it would not even bestow the name "emptiness" upon the Path.
If, however, by the mere fact of grasping the emptiness of the person it were itself to become the contemplation of emptiness, [then it would bestow that name upon the Path].

Could it be that the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*), by uprooting the sign of permanence and so forth even while the sign of formations (*saṅkhāranimitta*) is still being apprehended, would itself become the contemplation of the signless (*animittānupassanā*) and thus bestow the name "signless" upon the Path? This is not so;

for the state of being signless is not obtained in the Path in its primary sense through the mere uprooting of the signs of permanence and so forth, since the uprooting of the signs of permanence and so forth is itself only a figurative designation.

But is this not the same in all cases? For even the state of emptiness (*suññatā*) and the wishless (*appaṇihita*) are not found in what is not the path in an absolute sense, because the apprehension of the emptiness of the person and the drying up of desire (*paṇidhi*) are accomplished directly only by means of the path.
Therefore, both the contemplation of emptiness and the contemplation of the wishless receive their respective names only in a figurative sense.

Is it not the case that they do not give a non-figurative name to the Path? No; because for one who has obtained the Noble Path through that [insight], the names "emptiness" (suññatā) and "wishlessness" (appaṇihita) can occur only by way of the associated states in a non-figurative sense. How so?

Because, even in times such as those of the teachers Sarabhaṅga and Satthar when no Buddha had appeared, the subtle characteristic of non-self (anattalakkhaṇa) is difficult to discern by means of wisdom.
Thus, by way of its objective field and by way of contemplating [phenomena] as non-self, the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*) becomes predominant at the moment of the Path.
As it has been said: "For one who attends to things as non-self, the faculty of wisdom becomes predominant.
And that [predominance] is indeed in the absolute sense, because it uproots the inherent adherence to a self and because it is comprised within the Noble Path.

It receives the name "emptiness. Because it dries up the lust termed "aspiration," which is opposed to concentration during the contemplation of suffering, the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*) becomes predominant for one who contemplates by way of that [emptiness] at the moment of the Path.
As it is said: "For one who attends to [things] as suffering, the faculty of concentration becomes predominant. And that, moreover, is itself...
It receives the name "wishless" (appaṇihita) in the primary sense because it withers away all wishes and because it is included within the Noble Path.

Furthermore, having heard of the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena and subsequently seeing it for oneself through direct experience, one gains an abundance of faith in the Blessed One, thinking:
"Truly, that Blessed One said 'impermanent' because it is indeed impermanent. It is on account of this that [the concentration] receives its name.
For one who attends to the contemplation of impermanence, the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) becomes preeminent at the moment of the Path. As it is said:

"For one attending to [things] as impermanent, the faculty of faith becomes preeminent. However, although that [faculty] itself emerges from the sign of formations (*saṅkhāranimitta*), it does not yet include the Noble Path;
therefore, in the ultimate sense (*nippariyāyato*), it does not receive the name "signless" (*animitta*).

Therefore, just as the mind that is predominant in bodily action is called "bodily action," so too the path that is predominant in the faculty of wisdom—designated as emptiness—receives the name "emptiness";
that which is predominant in the faculty of concentration—designated as the wishless—receives the name "wishless";
but that which is predominant in the faculty of faith does not receive that [name] itself, because faith receives the name "signless. If...

The acquisition of names such as "emptiness" (suññatā) and so forth occurs by way of the associated states (sampayuttadhamma). Now, how is it that it is said [to be acquired] "by way of its arrival"? True;
however, even when a name is acquired by way of a predominant faculty (indriya), it is nonetheless acquired by way of its arrival.

Alternatively, even according to the Abhidhamma method, what is called the state of emptiness is indeed the emptiness of the person (puggala-suññatā); thus, because of the grasping of the emptiness of the person—
The name "emptiness" (*suññatā*) is obtained for the contemplation of non-self (*anattā*) in the absolute sense alone.

Since what is called "aspiration" (*paṇidhi*) is nothing other than lust and so forth, the name "the wishless" (*appaṇihita*) is also obtained for the contemplation of suffering (*dukkha*), which is dried up by lust and the like, in the absolute sense alone.
However, setting aside the Sutta method, according to the Abhidhamma method, "sign" (*nimitta*) refers to the sign of formations (*saṅkhāra-nimitta*).
The name "signless" (*animitta*) is not obtained in the direct sense for the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*), because it grasps the sign of formations (*saṅkhāra-nimitta*).

Therefore, the path—obtained by way of the contemplations of non-self (*anattā*) and suffering (*dukkha*), which are named "emptiness" (*suññatā*) and "wishless" (*appaṇihita*) in the direct sense—is given the name "emptiness" and "wishless" from the perspective of its arrival; however, the name "signless" is...
It is obtained only by way of a figurative expression (pariyāya). Therefore it was said:
“But here, the name ‘signless’ is obtained only by way of the Suttanta method, because in the Abhidhamma, when dealing with the path, the name ‘signless’ is not mentioned.

Thus, because these three liberations serve as the doors of entry, there are three [insight knowledges] named the contemplation of emptiness and so forth, and the contemplation of non-self and so forth.
Having gradually attained the state of strength, they should be understood as the three gateways to liberation, which constitute insight leading to emergence. For it has been said:
"These three gateways to liberation lead to the escape from the world; by way of delimitation and circumscription of all formations..."
These three are: the leaping of the mind into the signless element through the contemplation of all formations as impermanent;
the leaping of the mind into the desireless element through the arousal of the mind toward all conditioned phenomena;
and the leaping of the mind into the void element through the contemplation of all phenomena as other.
“The doors to liberation lead to the world’s transcendence.
For here, “delimited and circumscribed” means both by way of delimitation and by way of circumscription through the process of arising and passing away.
Indeed, the contemplation of impermanence, having delimited them by the thought, “Before their arising, formations did not exist,” [discerns] their course...
"Searching from the beginning, they do not go beyond; they vanish right here"—thus he perceives them as enclosed and bounded.
"By way of perception" (*samanupassanatāya*) is connected [to the phrase] "they lead to correct perception.

"By way of mental agitation" (*manosamuttejanatāya*) means by way of the arousal of the mind. For by means of the contemplation of suffering, the mind [is turned away] from conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
"It exists. "By way of viewing from another" means by way of viewing as non-self, thinking: "I am not, this is not mine.
Thus, it should be understood that these three terms are stated by way of the three [contemplations], beginning with the contemplation of impermanence.
And for that very reason, in the answer to the question immediately following:

“It is said: ‘When one attends to things as impermanent, formations appear as destruction; when one attends to them as suffering, formations appear as terror; when one attends to them as non-self, formations appear as void.
Now, since the *Abhidhammāvatāra* is being recited here, is it not more appropriate to define the doors of liberation according to the Abhidhamma method?
True; however, the emergence of the path occurs even through the contemplation of impermanence.”

For the sake of clarification, one definition has been given according to the Sutta method; however, it should be understood that the Path thus emerged is included within the "pure practice" (*suddhika-paṭipadā*) alone according to the Abhidhamma method.
"By way of the distinction of the fourfold conjunction with the Paths" means by way of the classification of association with the four Noble Paths, beginning with Stream-entry. Of the Noble Paths...
However, because they possess the nature of the eight factors beginning with right view, and because these exist in all supramundane states, there is no difference in terms of their dissolution;

nevertheless, due to the distinction in the realization [of the path] through the degrees of the faculties’ lack of proficiency, proficiency, and extreme proficiency, there is a distinction in the abandoning of the defilements.
It is on account of this that their fourfold nature should be understood. For this very reason, it was said: "personality-belief, doubt," and so forth.
When the body, which is comprised of the five aggregates, exists, the view [regarding it] is *sakkāyadiṭṭhi*; or, when there is a view directed toward that very [body], it is *sakkāyadiṭṭhi*.
This is a designation for the wrong view that proceeds by way of the adherence to a self or what belongs to a self within the five aggregates.
Furthermore, because it adheres to each individual aggregate in four ways, it is of twenty types.
It is so; for someone regards form as self, thinking: "Whatever is form, that is self;
whatever is self, that is form—just as the color of a lamp is the flame, and the flame is the color. Or one regards self as possessing form, like a tree possessing shadow.
Or form in self, like fragrance in a flower. Or self in form.
Like a gem in a casket. In the same way, for feeling and the other aggregates as well, one should apply the formula beginning with, “One regards feeling as self.

In this context, it should be understood that the fivefold adherence to a non-distinct self is the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi), whereas the fifteenfold adherence to a distinct self is the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi).

It is called *vicikicchā* because one who investigates its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) finds it difficult and exhausting; or else, it is *vicikicchā* because the remedy of knowledge (*ñāṇa-paṭikāra*) has departed from it due to its difficulty of being cured. Furthermore, it consists of eight bases according to the manner of doubting regarding the Buddha and so forth, as stated:

"One doubts and is perplexed regarding the Teacher, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the training, the past, the future, both the past and the future, and regarding things that have arisen dependently through specific conditions.
Thus, it is characterized by doubt toward the Buddha and the rest.
“Did I exist in the past? Or did I not exist? What was I in the past? How was I in the past?
Having been what, what did I become in the past? Shall I exist in the future? Or shall I not exist?
What shall I be in the future? How shall I be in the future? Having been what, what shall I become?”
"One wonders: 'What shall I become in the future? Or what am I now in the present? Thus one is inwardly full of doubt: 'Do I exist? Do I not exist?
What am I? How am I? From where has this being come, and to where will it go?'"
Thus, by way of their occurrence with reference to the past and so forth, they are demonstrated as having sixteen bases.
Among these, one who doubts the Teacher doubts whether his physical body (rūpakāya) and mental body (dhammakāya) exist or do not exist;
one who doubts the Dhamma doubts whether it is well-expounded or ill-expounded; one who doubts the Saṅgha...
He doubts regarding the state of having practiced well or having practiced wrongly; doubting regarding the training, he doubts whether it is well-proclaimed or ill-proclaimed.
Doubting regarding the past, relying on the mode of eternalism and the mode of fortuitous origination, he doubts the existence and non-existence of himself in the past.
Doubting regarding the future, [he doubts] through the mode of eternalism and the mode of annihilation.
Relying on this, one doubts one’s own future arising and non-arising;

doubting regarding the past and the future, one doubts one’s own existence and non-existence in the present. For the present time-period (addhā), by virtue of possessing divisions of prior and subsequent parts, is called the "past and future" (pubbantāparanta).
But is it appropriate to generate doubt concerning that? It is appropriate; it is not inappropriate.
What need for deliberation here? For the foolish worldling is like one who is mad; therefore, he doubts whatever he encounters.
It is for this very reason that, in the exposition of doubt based on the sixteen grounds, it is said: "Or else, regarding the present," and so forth. The teachers, however, explain:
"The past and future" means taking the past and the future together as one, and doubting with reference to both of them.

Some say, “He doubts about the past and the future. However, one who doubts regarding phenomena that have arisen dependently through specific conditionality (idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppanna) doubts whether the conditions such as ignorance and the conditionally arisen states such as volitional formations actually possess the nature of cause and effect, or whether they lack it.
In this way, first of all, the occurrence of doubt consisting of eight bases should be understood.

But one who has the sixteen bases, doubting whether "did I exist... or did I not exist," doubts, according to the method already stated, regarding the existence or non-existence of oneself in the past. When one asks, "What indeed was I?"—referring to birth, gender, and rebirth—one wonders:
"Was I a khattiya? Or was I a brahmin and so forth, or a householder and so forth, or one among the devas and so forth?"
He doubts. How so? Relying on the mode of physical configuration, he doubts: "Was I long in the past, or was I short, fair, black, or one of the other [complexions]?
They say that relying on such factors as the creation by a Supreme Lord (Issaranimmāna), he doubts from the perspective of the mode of origination: "In what manner indeed did I come to be?
Relying on birth and so forth, he wonders: "Having been what, have I become what?"—namely, "Having been a Khattiya..."
He doubts his own successive states of existence, wondering, "Was I a brahmin... or, having been a deva, was I a human?
He doubts whether he will exist or not in the future, according to the method explained below, concerning his own future presence or absence. "What shall I become?
and so forth, is according to the same method already stated. "Am I indeed, or am I not indeed? [he wonders].
Now, he doubts regarding his own existence and non-existence. The reason for this has already been stated.
"What indeed am I?"—being a kṣatriya or the like, he doubts his own status as a kṣatriya and so forth. The same method applies to the remaining cases.
"How indeed am I?"—having grasped that there is something called a "life-principle" (jīva) within, he doubts its nature as being long and so forth.
However, there is no one who does not know the present configuration of their own body.
