It should be understood that one "doubts" regarding the places from which the personal existence has come and to which it will go, thinking: "From where has it come? Where will it go?

Regarding "virtue and observance" (*sīlabbata*): therein, the path of purification such as the "cow-virtue" (*gosīla*) and so forth is "virtue" (*sīla*) by way of undertaking; it is [also] by way of non-transgression.
Vata. Or, alternatively, both are *sīla*. It is called *vata* because it is undertaken as an act of ascetic toil (*tapokamma*).

*Sīla* is the undertaking of one’s own nature as a cow or the like, based on the natural state of cows and so forth; whereas *vata* is the performance of the actions of cows and the like, such as "eating while walking" or "urinating while standing.
Alternatively, *sīla* is the abstention from various improper acts through right reflection, while for one who has undertaken that [abstention], it is [called *vata*].

Vow (*vata*) is the specific practice consisting of eating at a particular time, performing certain duties, and so forth. Clinging (*parāmāsa*) is the grasping or seizing of something beyond its own nature;

thus, clinging to rules and observances is "clinging to rules and observances" (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*). It is the notion that purity comes through the morality, the observance, or the combination of both morality and observance of ascetics and brahmins outside this [teaching]—thus, regarding what is not a path to purity as "the path to purity."
This is a designation for the active adherence to what is false. "Personality-belief, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances" refers to personality-belief...
[and so on] ...adherence. These very things are called "fetterings" (*saṃyojanāni*) because they fetter and bind beings to kamma and its results, or to the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
By means of the purification of view and the other [stages], through their abandonment by way of "overcoming the factor" (*tadaṅga*), these fetters are brought to a state of non-arising.
It is called "that which effects abandonment" because it brings about the ultimate eradication [of defilements].
The Noble Eightfold Path is called a "stream" (sota) because it flows toward and leads to Nibbāna;

the initial entry into that stream is "stream-entry" (sotāpatti). It is called a "path" (magga) because it seeks Nibbāna, it is sought by those who desire Nibbāna, and it proceeds while slaying the defilements.
Or, the path itself is stream-entry; thus, "stream-entry path" means the path to stream-entry.

Alternatively, one who attains or reaches the stream for the first time is a "stream-enterer," the first noble person; his path is the "stream-entry path," consisting of the eight factors beginning with right view.
The consciousness associated with that is "stream-entry path-consciousness."

It is called *rāga* because one is attached (*rajjati*) and becomes resentful (*abhisajjati*); here it refers to craving (*taṇhā*) directed toward the objects of the five sensual pleasures and the objects of sensual existence.

It is called *dosa* because one hates (*dussati*); its proximate cause is malice (*byāpāda*), which is based on the ten grounds for resentment. It is called *moha* because one is deluded (*muyhati*); it is ignorance regarding the eight [truths] such as suffering.
Because it makes these defilements thin—that is, brings about their attenuation—it is called "that which effects attenuation" (*tanuttakara*). In this context:
It is thin due to two reasons: because of its infrequent arising, and because of the weakness of its obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).
For in the case of a once-returner, the defilements do not arise frequently as they do for the common crowd who follow the round of existence;
rather, they arise only occasionally and in a sparse manner. Even when they do arise, they do not arise crushing, covering, or creating darkness.
However, because they have been abandoned by two paths, they arise very faintly and extremely attenuated.

Some, however, say that the defilements of a once-returner arise only after a long time, yet when they do arise, they arise thickly; for instance, they point to the fact that he is seen with sons and daughters.
That is not a valid reason, because conception can occur even without the pursuit of sensual objects; therefore, it is according to the method already stated.
Their attenuation should be understood by way of two reasons. But why is the attenuation of delusion mentioned here?

Should it not rather be stated that its attenuation is achieved only by what is to be abandoned by the third path? Otherwise, since all defilements to be abandoned by the higher paths are being abandoned—whether in their state of being thick or thin—by the three lower paths as well, [it would follow that] here [all of them]...
The attenuation of the higher fetters (uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana) should be stated; for that very reason, it is said in the Pāḷi:

"For the attenuation of sensual lust and ill-will, and for the attainment of the second stage. This is true; however, in the Sutta, by taking the figurative expression of the attenuation of those [defilements] to be abandoned by the higher paths, it says:
"Because of the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, one is a once-returner (sakadāgāmī)," thus referring to the attenuation of the triad of causes.
Because he has come [to this state], it is stated here as well in accordance with that. Alternatively, the reading is simply “kāmarāgabyāpādānaṃ.
For it is said in this very work, later in the description of the knowledge of the second path: “But one effects the attenuation of ill-will and sensual lust.
One who comes to this human world only once by way of rebirth-linking is a *sakadāgāmī* (once-returner); of him...

The path is the once-returning path. Although it is only one who stands in the fruit who is called a "once-returner"—since it is impossible for one standing on the path to come [back] by way of rebirth-linking—nevertheless, the path that constitutes his coming is called the "once-returning path" in order to delimit it from other paths, by bringing it into a state of dependence upon that [fruit].
The consciousness associated with that is the "once-returning path-consciousness."
Sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) is attachment to the five strands of sensual pleasure and to sensual existence (*kāmabhava*). Ill will (*byāpāda*) is that by which the mind becomes corrupted.

One who does not come back to this sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*) by way of rebirth-linking is a non-returner (*anāgāmī*). Lust for form (*rūparāga*) is desire and attachment toward existence in the fine-material realm (*rūpabhava*).

Lust for the formless (*arūparāga*) is desire and attachment toward existence in the immaterial realm (*arūpabhava*). Here, conceit (*māna*) refers merely to a state of loftiness based on the attainment of arahantship.
Restlessness (*uddhacca*) is merely the lack of tranquility in the mind, occurring in such a mode as thinking, "What burden is there for me in the total eradication of the defilements?
Ignorance (*avijjā*) is the perversion of perceiving what is not happiness as happiness. It is called "Arahant" because it is far removed from defilements or those who have entered wrong practice;

because it has destroyed the enemies such as lust and so forth, as well as the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra; because it is worthy (*arahat*) of requisites and so on; and because even in secret, one does not commit evil deeds.

Because of the absence of evil states—which are called "raha" because they are to be hidden (*rahitabba*), because they are to be abandoned (*jahitabba*), or because they are not to be resorted to (*arahitabba*) by the virtuous—or because of the absence of wandering through the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), which is reckoned as "going" (*raha*), he is an *arahant*, the eighth type of noble person (*ariyapuggala*).
His state is *arahatta*; this is a designation for the highest fruit (*aggaphala*).

For it is called "arahantship" (arahatta) because it is the state (bhāva) of one who is an arahant, being the basis for the application of the designation "arahant" and for the occurrence of the corresponding cognition.
The path that leads to this is the "path to arahantship" (arahattamagga), and the consciousness associated with that is "consciousness of the path to arahantship" (arahattamaggacitta).

"By way of the distinction in the association with jhāna factors": this means by way of the distinction in association with the five jhāna factors, as in the case of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara).
How, then, is there a distinction in this? Herein, first, there are four positions: the commentary position (*aṭṭhakathāvāda*) and the three Elder-monk positions (*theravāda*).
For instance, in the commentary, it is said: "Having reached the state of equanimity regarding formations, [the path] of insight leading to emergence..."

"...it determines the jhāna factor," so it is said. However, the Elder Cūḷanāga of the Tipiṭaka said, "It determines the foundational jhāna, which serves as the proximate cause for the insight that is close to the path.

The Elder Mahādatta, resident of Moravāpi, said, "The aggregates that serve as the object of insight determine [the jhāna]. For whatever jhāna one emerges from after having reflected upon it, the insight becomes similar to that."
He said: "But the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷābhaya said, 'The inclination of the individual determines it;
according as his inclination is—such as, "O, may I reach the fivefold path" or "the fourfold path"—so indeed does the path become.
Since the commentary's doctrine is authoritative and these three elders are wise and competent, all four [views] are thus."
These arguments should be understood as being non-oppositional to one another. How so? First, regarding the phenomena of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*):

for one who has attained the path by contemplating these phenomena through dry insight (*sukkhavipassaka*), or for one who has attained the path without making a meditative absorption (*jhāna*) the basis, their factors are still of the first jhāna according to the method of insight. However, if [they attain] any jhāna...
Having made that the basis, it is produced; by way of that, there is a transformation of the factors (*aṅga-pariṇāma*), and thus it becomes similar to the respective jhāna.

However, because in this case insight (*vipassanā*) proceeds by taking the sense-sphere aggregates as its object, and because—unlike in the case of sublime states (*mahaggata-dhamma*)—there is no distinction in the jhāna-factors due to a specific mode of development regarding sense-sphere phenomena, therefore [it is said]: "In insight..."
The second Elder’s position—that “the aggregates which have become the object determine [the result]”—does not enter into this argument.

When one has developed the path after having comprehended the dhammas of jhāna, if there is no foundational jhāna, one becomes a possessor of that specific jhāna according to the rule of the jhāna that was comprehended.
If, for instance, one emerges from the first jhāna, comprehends the second jhāna or others, and develops the path, [one becomes a possessor of that specific jhāna].
According to the inclination of the individual, it resembles one or another of the two jhānas. But if the person lacks such an inclination, how does it proceed then?

In this regard, some say: "In the single-advertence cognitive process (*ekāvajjana-vīthi*), having reached the state of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*) from the basic jhāna that was returning within the multiple-advertence process (*nānāvajjana-vīthi*), the aggregates themselves—which serve as the object for the insight (*vipassanā*) that is returning—[become the object]."
"Because they are powerful, the path is similar to that [insight] according to the method of the aggregates as they were comprehended," so they say.
And this being the case, the first Elder’s statement— which proceeds thus, "It occurs according to the method of the foundational jhāna"—
stands as referring specifically to the path produced after emerging from the foundational jhāna and comprehending the aggregates of the sense-sphere.
Others, however, say: "The foundational jhāna is a condition for the path both by way of being its root cause and by way of being its proximate cause;
whereas the aggregates being comprehended are conditions only by way of being the root cause.
Therefore, the foundational jhāna is stronger than the aggregates being comprehended, and thus the path becomes similar to the foundational jhāna. This being so:

However, the second Elder’s position, which proceeds thus: “by way of the aggregates as they were rightly contemplated,” stands with reference only to the path produced by contemplating merely the states of jhāna without making attainment the basis.
For it is because each successive jhāna becomes more powerful than the preceding one that [the path arises] from each preceding jhāna.

When one emerges from successive higher jhānas and develops insight into their constituent states, the path that arises becomes associated with whichever specific jhāna was being contemplated, regardless of the foundational jhāna.

However, when one emerges from a higher jhāna, contemplates the states of the successively lower jhānas, and develops the path, that path becomes similar to the foundational jhāna, regardless of the jhāna that was being contemplated; this is the essential point here.
For this being so, the arguments of both elders are complete in their scope and equal in their result.
Furthermore, in the case of the third elder’s argument, the foundational jhāna or the jhāna of comprehension does not succeed by mere intention alone.
In all three arguments, apart from the transformation of the remaining jhāna factors, the transformation of feeling occurs solely through the process of insight (vipassanā).
It exists. It should be understood that even the three elder-disciple traditions do not exist without the method of insight (vipassanā).
[Objection: But surely feeling (*vedanā*) is also a factor of jhāna; therefore, should it not also follow the method of the foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*)?

[Response: That is not so. For when feeling is transformed according to the method of the foundational jhāna, it occurs by the method of the foundational jhāna itself, without depending on the method of insight.

At the moment of the Path, although the remaining jhāna factors would involve a transformation of feeling as well— since they occupy the same position for transformation— it does not happen that way; rather,

because of the determination of feeling through insight (vipassanā), which occurs in close proximity to the path-exit cognitive process by virtue of being transformed from the very beginning of a single adverting consciousness-series, the determination of feeling takes place.

Alternatively, it cannot be said that when access jhānas based on the jhāna-factors (*pādakajjhāna*) and jhānas based on insight (*sammasitajjhāna*) are possible, feelings not yet arisen therein do not exist for insight, or that they necessarily transform according to the pattern of the jhāna-factors and insight-jhānas.
Here it might be argued: "Insofar as the jhāna-factors are present, they determine that [insight]; however, where there is a threefold or fourfold jhāna-factors..."
In that formless existence, what determines [the level]? There too, it is the foundational jhāna alone that determines it.

For a bhikkhu who has attained the eight meditative attainments, having made the first jhāna the foundation, and having realized the path and fruit of stream-entry, dies without falling away from that jhāna and is reborn in a formless existence, [he does so] by means of the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry based on the first jhāna.
Having emerged [from the preliminary concentration] and established insight, one brings forth the three higher paths and fruits; for such a person, these possess the factors of the first jhāna alone.
The same method applies to those consisting of the second jhāna and so forth. For even in the formless realm, supramundane jhānas of the triad and tetrad arise.
Thus, in this context, the distinction regarding the association with jhāna factors for each type of supramundane wholesome consciousness should be understood.

"...The paths... 'Produces' means that, although they do not ripen during rebirth-linking or the course of existence—unlike the wholesome states of the three planes—they produce their respective fruits by bringing about the attainment of those various fruits.
Thus, in a general sense, they produce the four noble persons: the stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, and the arahant.
Specifically, however, [they produce] the state of being one who has at most seven more births, and so forth."
He also brings about the attainment of many stream-enterers and others.
The commentary on supramundane wholesome states is concluded.
The commentary on wholesome states of the four planes.

28. Having thus demonstrated the wholesome consciousness of the four planes according to its nature, he now concludes that section by saying, "In the sense-sphere there are eight," and so forth. Therein, "in the sense-sphere" (*kāme*) means in the sense-world (*kāmabhava*).

The same applies to "in the fine-material sphere" (*rūpe*), and so on. 29. "By that which is devoid of wholesome and unwholesome [kamma]" means by that which is free from wholesome and unwholesome kamma.
For, from the moment the supreme path (*agga-magga*) arises, all wholesome and unwholesome kamma of an Arahant are said to be abandoned due to the deficiency of conditions (*paccaya-vekalla*).

Because it is incapable of giving rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). And since noble path-knowledge (*ariyamaggañāṇa*) is said to "bring about the destruction of karma," [the wholesome is] by means of the wholesome—that is, by the wholesome path that cuts off the defilements (*kilesa*), which is devoid of unwholesome states because there is no purification through the absence of causes and conditions.
Regarding "in the wholesome by means of the wholesome": it refers to the practice designated as "wholesome" (*kusala*) because it flows away from what is contemptible (*kucchita*).

By one skilled in the production of the [noble] path and so forth. "By the Sage" means by one who is a sage because he is endowed with the knowledge of the fruit of the highest path (*aggaphala-ñāṇa*) or with omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*). Thus it is said:
"He who understands both worlds is therefore called a sage."

"By one who has mastery" means by one endowed with the supreme state of mental mastery through the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*), and because of the presence of the fivefold mastery over the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and so forth; that is, by one whose faculties have attained mastery, having become masterful.
The commentary on the wholesome states of the four planes is finished. [Now begins] the commentary on the unwholesome states.

Having thus demonstrated in its specific form the wholesome (kusala) mentioned here as being "threefold according to the classification by way of the types of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate," he now says "But the unwholesome... and so forth, while demonstrating the unwholesome (akusala) that was listed immediately after it.
To define the meaning stated as "of one kind according to plane," he says "only of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara)."
However, since other schools (nikāyantarika) maintain that unwholesome states exist even in the fine-material and immaterial spheres, this restriction was made in order to refute their view.

For even though this [unwholesome state] arises in the sublime plane (mahaggatabhūmi), and even though it yields its result as a process-result (pavattivipāka) there in the fine-material element, it is nevertheless exclusively of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).
But from what source is this rule established? From the fact that it is the object of craving for sense-pleasures (kāmataṇhā).

For the state of having craving for sense-desires as its object is the cause of existence in the sense-sphere realm, just as the state of having craving for the fine-material and immaterial realms as its object is the cause of existence in those respective realms.
This must be accepted unreservedly; otherwise, the characteristic of pervasiveness would not hold.

For if the determination of the planes were made on the basis of the dhammas that can be taken as objects, then in that case, there would be no inclusion of those [dhammas] that are without an object.
It could not be so. Now, if it were by way of giving rise to kamma-result (vipāka), then likewise there would be no inclusion of those things that are resultless;

therefore, the inclusion of the mundane (pariyāpanna) states must be made solely by way of their objects (ālambana-dhamma). However, the supramundane (lokuttara) nature of the non-mundane states should be understood as being due to their having transcended the world, and their unsurpassed (anuttara) nature as being due to the absence of anything superior to them.
Because there is an absence of the state of being an obstruction for displeasure (*domanassa*), the arising of consciousness associated with it occurs only on the sense-sphere plane (*kāmabhūmi*);
thus, it has a fixed basis (*niyatavatthuka*). Since the others also occur on the formless plane (*arūpabhūmi*), they have an unfixed basis (*aniyatavatthuka*). Therefore, he said:

"Fixed... [and] twofold. Because those accompanied by doubt (*vicikicchā*) and restlessness (*uddhacca*) have delusion as their sole root-cause, while the others likewise have greed-and-delusion or hatred-and-delusion as their roots...

Because it possesses two roots, he says, "from those with one root and two roots. Because eleven unwholesome consciousnesses produce rebirth-linking from the beginning, whereas that is absent for the restlessness-accompanied consciousness, he says, "from those that produce rebirth-linking and those that do not.
For even when the restlessness-accompanied consciousness gives its result during the course of existence (*pavatti*), it does not draw forth rebirth-linking. As he will say:
“Excluding the elevenfold mind characterized by restlessness,
there are likewise eleven kinds of rebirth-linking.
As for the reason why that [restless consciousness] does not draw forth that rebirth-linking, it is [explained] through the discourses on the determination of rebirth-linking in this [work].
We shall explain this by way of a commentary on the verse itself.

"By means of the three feelings" means by means of the three feelings known as pleasure (*sukha*), pain (*dukkha*), and equanimity (*upekkhā*). As it is said: "Bhikkhus, there are these three feelings. Which three? Pleasure, pain, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
However, as for the statement found in some suttas, "Bhikkhus, there are these two feelings: pleasure and pain," that refers to the side of the wholesome (*kusalapakkhika*).

It should be understood that equanimity has been mentioned by way of a figurative expression (pariyāya) by including it within the category of pleasure and unwholesome states within the category of pain.
It is called a "root" (mūla) because it is like a root insofar as it is the cause for being well-established; thus, "greed-rooted" (lobhamūla) means that greed is its root.
Although delusion (moha) is also present among the greed-roots, it does not serve as a defining factor because it is common to all unwholesome states.
It is described specifically as "rooted in greed" by way of its unique characteristic (asādhāraṇadhamma), just as one says "the sound of a drum" or "a barley sprout.
The same applies to the phrase "rooted in hatred. Because it lacks any other root, delusion alone is its root and nothing else; thus, it is "rooted in delusion" (mohamūla).
Seeing in a wrong manner is "view" (diṭṭhi); view itself is "gone to view" (diṭṭhigata), just as one says "gone to space" or "gone to a firm foundation" (thāmagata).
Alternatively, it is "gone" (gata) by means of a view that grasps things erroneously;

it is called "gone to views" (diṭṭhigata) because there is no further object to be gone to here as being of such a nature, or because it is included within the sixty-two views. It is "associated with what is gone to views" (diṭṭhigatasampayutta) because it is conjoined with that [view] in various ways.
“*Yadā hi*,” etc., is a demonstration of the mode of occurrence of minds rooted in greed.

“Wrong view” (*micchādiṭṭhi*) refers to wrong views such as annihilationism (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*). For it is by means of that [view] that those whose minds are perverted reject the next world—ranging from the object of anger up to the range of the sense faculties—and grasp at the notion:
“There is no danger in sensual pleasures. By the word “etcetera” (*ādi*),—
“That path by which those with children go, free from sorrow, is a wrong way on the journey to the gods;
that path is seen by beasts and birds alike.”

By such means as "Therefore, even with one's mother they engage in sexual intercourse," he includes wrong views such as the notion that "beholding the face of a son is the path to heaven and liberation.

In the phrase "or in sensual pleasures" (*kāme vā*), the word *vā* has the sense of indefiniteness; by this, [it is implied] that for Brahmins, the seizing of gold is indeed [an example of] taking what is not given.
Regarding such false graspings as: "Lying is blameworthy; however, lying for the sake of one's teachers, cattle, one's own life, or marriage is blameless, while other lying is blameworthy";
"Slandering for the sake of one's teachers and so forth is blameless, while other slandering is blameworthy";
and "The stories of the Bhārata war, the abduction of Sītā, and so on, serve to pacify evil."
He clings. "The seen as an auspicious sign, etc. refers to the seen, heard, and sensed as auspicious signs.
"He conceives of it as essential" means that, rather than taking it as a mere precursor to prosperity, he grasps it by way of its essence, thinking, "This alone is the cause of prosperity.
"By its very nature sharp" means by way of greed or wrong adherence—by its own inherent quality—that which is sharp and cruel.
“Slowly” means with what is sluggish and not sharp. However, such [sluggishness] occurs through one’s own or another’s encouragement;
thus he says, “by being encouraged. By the word “or,” it should be understood that stealing another’s property includes lying and other such acts occurring in that manner.
“Of sensual pleasures” refers to the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) being experienced. By the word “or,” [it includes] that which belongs to another.
Because it is not as intended, that which is obtained must be accepted; thus, it includes the grasping and so forth.

Due to the absence of differentiation based on associated states (*sampayutta-dhamma*), it is a root of hatred (*dosamūla*). It is twofold, by way of the distinction between the unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*) and the prompted (*sasaṅkhārika*).
If this is so, why is it said to be "accompanied by mental displeasure (*domanassa*) and associated with aversion (*paṭigha*)"? [It is because] by means of specific (non-common) factors...
For the purpose of characterizing that state of mind: *pāṇātipāta* is the striking down (*pātana*) of a living being (*pāṇa*), either excessively or by transgressing [the limit].
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), it includes taking what is not given, false speech, slander, harsh speech, idle chatter, and ill will.
For among the ten unwholesome courses of action (*akusalakammapatha*), these three—namely, sexual misconduct, covetousness, and wrong view—are not established by this [term].
The intention is that a consciousness occurring with sharp intensity is indeed without effort (*asaṅkhāra*), whereas the other is with effort (*sasaṅkhāra*);

thus he says, "at the time of sharp or dull occurrence. However, it cannot be definitively known that what occurs with dull intensity is necessarily with effort. That which proceeds with effort and application— [End of excerpt]
It should be understood that it is stated thus because it is indeed weak.
Since the mind rooted in delusion is extremely deluded due to the absence of other roots, and is restless due to its association with doubt and restlessness, it is accompanied by equanimity alone;
it never possesses natural sharpness. This is because, by way of crawling over the object—
Furthermore, regarding the two types of consciousness occurring by way of distraction, must they possess an inherent sharpness or a state of being incited in such a function?
Therefore, there is no differentiation of formations (*saṅkhāra*) therein. But is not restlessness (*uddhacca*) common to all unwholesome states;
why then is it specifically mentioned as qualifying that [consciousness] by saying "accompanied by restlessness"?
"Especially because of its powerful nature. For this [restlessness] is powerful in this consciousness; therefore, it proceeds as the preeminent factor among the associated states.

Thus, this alone is what should be distinguished by it. For that very reason, in the Canon, restlessness is mentioned among the remaining unwholesome states merely as a "minor defilement" (*yevāpanaka*), whereas here it is specified by its own essential form. In this way, [the consciousness is defined] by way of its unique and preeminent factor.
It should be understood that it is stated to be twofold: rooted in delusion and associated with doubt, and associated with restlessness.
"Non-conclusion" means uncertainty; "distraction" means lack of tranquility; the meaning is "wavering.
In this context, the occurrence of the [state] accompanied by doubt should be understood at the time of non-conclusion, and that of the state accompanied by restlessness at the time of distraction.

"According to what is appropriate" means according to whether [the action] produces rebirth-linking or does not produce it, and according to whether it has attained the status of a path of kamma or not.

Alternatively, "according to what is appropriate" means according to whatever is the cause for a particular state. For generally, those rooted in greed arise in the realm of hungry ghosts (*petas*), where hunger, thirst, and so forth are constant;
those rooted in hatred, like hatred itself, arise in a hell similar to that [of the angry], due to their fierce nature; and those rooted in delusion—
Because one is perpetually deluded regarding the animal realm, it brings about rebirth in various states of woe corresponding to causes such as greed;
thus he said, "according to its correspondence... for rebirth. Because unwholesome karmic results are characterized primarily by suffering, it is stated, "of specific types of suffering."
31. The connection is as follows: among minds that are non-evil, free from evil, and have abandoned both evil and non-evil, whatever evil mind has been spoken of;

or, among persons who are non-evil, free from evil, and have abandoned both evil and non-evil, whatever evil mind has been spoken of by one who is non-evil, free from evil, and has abandoned both evil and non-evil.

Alternatively, it refers to that which was spoken with an evil mind—by means of an evil mind, through the influence of evil—among minds that are non-evil, free from evil, and have abandoned both evil and non-evil.
The construction is: "it was spoken with a wicked mind. However, the intended meaning here is this:

since the true nature of phenomena is difficult to discern, even what is wholesome might be called unwholesome by one who is not a Perfectly Enlightened One, and even what is unwholesome might be called wholesome;

but for the Blessed One, whose unwholesome [states] have been destroyed along with their latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) by the knowledge that brings about the destruction of karma, and whose wholesome karma has been destroyed due to the deficiency of its conditions.
And because he is a perfectly enlightened Buddha, the teaching on the unwholesome is exclusively by way of unwholesome phenomena alone.
The commentary on the unwholesome is finished.
The commentary on the indeterminate.

“Result” (*vipāka*) means the ripening (*pāka*) of wholesome and unwholesome states that are distinguished from one another; this is a designation for immaterial phenomena that have reached the state of having ripened.

Just as in the world, the fruits produced from rice seeds and the like—which resemble those [seeds]—are said to be “ripened” and receive the linguistic term “result,” whereas the roots, sprouts, leaves, stalks, and stalk-reeds do not, so too it is with the fruits of the wholesome and unwholesome.

Because they possess the nature of non-material phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) and the quality of having an object (*sārammaṇa*), those [states] which have reached the state of fruition (*vipakka*) receive the designation "resultant" (*vipāka*), on account of their similarity to it.
However, material phenomena produced by kamma do not receive this designation, because they are dissimilar to kamma. Resultant consciousness alone is called "resultant consciousness.
Merely performing an action is "functional" (*kiriya*), because it lacks the capacity to yield a fruit. But for whatever reason that consciousness yields a fruit, [it is termed resultant].
That it does not occur has already been stated above. "Functional consciousness" (*kiriyacitta*) means consciousness that is merely functional.
The status of the result as belonging to the sense-sphere and so forth should be understood according to its possibility, following the method explained under the wholesome [consciousness].

It is "with root-cause" (*sahetuka*) because it proceeds together with root-causes such as non-greed; it is "without root-cause" (*ahetuka*) due to the absence of those. Although this [resultant consciousness] is established by way of the producing cause, it is [classified] precisely by way of the associated root-causes.
It is called “with cause” and “without cause,” for otherwise there would be no distinction.

“Like one’s own wholesome [kamma]” means like the sense-sphere wholesome kamma that produces it. For each respective wholesome state is called the “own” (sakam) of its respective result by virtue of the relationship between the producer and the produced.
Since it is stated as “like one’s own wholesome [kamma],” it might follow that it is similar to that [wholesome kamma] in terms of its mode of occurrence, object, and so forth.

To prevent that [misunderstanding], he said: “But as...,” and so forth. “In the six objects” means in the six objects such as visible form, etc., which are divided into categories such as limited (*paritta*), past (*atīta*), internal (*ajjhatta*), and so on.
It is called *paṭisandhi* (rebirth-linking) because it links one to another existence (*bhava*).

It is called *bhavaṅga* (life-continuum) because it is a constituent part of existence by virtue of being the cause for its uninterrupted occurrence. It is called *cuti* (death) because it exhausts the existence already produced and because it is the cause of death. “Included among limited phenomena” means...

[Included] among those phenomena included within the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). For sense-sphere phenomena are called "limited" (paritta) because they possess limited power due to their inability to suppress defilements and so forth, or because they are grasped by coarse sensual craving and the like.
Because there is no grasping of an object through volitional intention (saṅkappa) regarding the result, it proceeds strictly in accordance with the karma; thus, it is "limited karmic fruition."

It is said that [this consciousness] is capable of occurring only with a limited object (*parittārammaṇa*), and not with a sublime (*mahaggata*) or immeasurable (*appamāṇa*) object; thus it is stated: "among those included within limited phenomena" (*parittadhammapariyāpannesu*).
If this is so, does it follow that even a sublime resultant (*mahaggatavipāka*) must have only a sublime object?

It does not follow, because the result of an action (*kamma*)—which depends on perception (*saññā*) for its object and is dominated by concentration (*samādhi*)—must be of a corresponding nature when it reaches absorption (*appanā*). For [the object of such an action], such as the characteristic of color (*vaṇṇalakkhaṇa*) and so forth, is...
Having grasped earth and so forth merely in accordance with worldly perception, the object known as the counterpart sign— which has been produced by the preliminary perception—
is under the influence of perception and dependent upon perception. Therefore, because it is an object dependent on perception,

there is no distinction [between this state] and that which has reached absorption (appanā) through the predominance of concentration, being the result of karma that has reached absorption through the predominance of concentration.
It must be so. However, there is also kamma that produces a limited result even when it has as its object a sublime or immeasurable designation;
this will be discussed later.
"Like the sign of a face" means like a sign that arises dependent upon a face. For just as that [face] is inactive and not another...
Just as one is unable to produce a facial expression or perform any other action by one's own power, so too this [kamma] lacks the capacity to produce a result (vipāka) and so forth.

Therefore, it is called "devoid of effort" (*nirussāha*). Herein, "effort" (*ussāha*) refers to the capacity to produce a result within a mental continuum where the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) of ignorance, craving, and conceit have not been severed;
it refers to the state of being a condition through repetition (*āsevana-paccaya*); and it refers to the quality of generating intimation (*viññatti*).
And there is no activity [in it]. That [activity] is absent in the resultant [consciousness] because, having been cast forth by the momentum of karma, it proceeds as if fallen;
since its state is exclusively weak, it is devoid of effort (*nirussāha*).
"The place of ripening" means the place where it proceeds by way of ripening, namely, by way of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, death, and the object of that [death-moment].

The meaning is that this is the occasion for the occurrence of these four functions. Therein, the interval between the death-consciousness (*cuti*) and the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) is the place for the function of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

The interval between the rebirth-linking and the adverting [consciousness], between the registration and the adverting, between the impulsion and the adverting, and between the determining and the adverting, is the place for the functions of the life-continuum.
[Also included are] the intervals between registration and rebirth-linking, and between impulsion and rebirth-linking.
The interval between the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) should be seen as the occasion for the function of death;
likewise, the interval between the impulsion (javana) and the life-continuum should be seen as the occasion for the function of registration (tadārammaṇa).

Since this "occasion" (ṭhāna) becomes manifest through the respective functions of these mental states, it is therefore said that "the occasion should be understood," and having extracted the term "occasion," it is explained solely by way of its manifest function.

The passage beginning with "For these" was stated in order to reveal [the bases]. Alternatively, since even a function (kicca) is understood as a state of occurrence for those possessing functions, it is also designated as a "base" (ṭhāna);
thus, the passage beginning with "For these" was stated to show that very thing according to its specific form.
32. For humans born from egg-born and womb-born matrices, and for the Asuras of the states of misery, there is also rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) without a root-cause (ahetuka).

Because they exist, he says: "Of those with two roots and three roots. Those for whom the two roots, such as non-greed, etc., are associated with the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*) are "those with two roots" (*duhetuka*).
This same method applies to those with three roots (*tihetuka*) as well.

In that regard, there are four rebirth-linkings dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇavippayutta*) for those with two roots, and four associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta*) for those with three roots; likewise for the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and the death-moment (*cuti*).
For by whichever mind rebirth-linking occurs, that very same [mind] proceeds also as the life-continuum and as death.
However, its being an object-of-attainment (*tadārammaṇa*) should be understood without distinction, because an object-of-attainment with three roots is admitted even for those with two roots.
But is this not a statement made without due consideration? No, because it has been refuted by the Teacher himself. For he will say:
“For one with rootless rebirth-linking, there is no registration [consciousness];
nor for one with two-rooted or three-rooted rebirth-linking.
This is not a statement made without due consideration, because it is prohibited therein with reference to the kamma that produces rebirth-linking.
For that kamma by which a rebirth-linking has been taken does not produce, during the course of existence, a registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa) stronger than itself.
However, it is possible that some other kamma, having found no opportunity [to ripen] there, might not produce even a result stronger than that [rebirth-linking].
Thus, the bhavaṅga with root-cause [can be] for one without root-cause...

For by the statement in the *Paṭṭhāna*, "It is a condition for the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) by way of proximity-condition," it is admitted that even for one who is rootless (*ahetuka*), there can be a resultant state with roots (*sahetuka*) having that same object (*tadārammaṇa*) in a happy destination (*sugati*) due to various kamma. Therefore, the teachers have said:
"There is a state with roots [arising] through another kamma, even for one who is rootless."

Just as they accept that what is with-root (sahetuka) follows from what is rootless (ahetuka), so too they maintain that what is with-three-roots (tihetuka) follows from what is with-two-roots (duhetuka).

However, the Elder Master Jotipāla, because the term "with-root" was stated without qualification, maintains that even for those [minds] that are rootless, there can be a registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa) with-three-roots. For he said:
"By the unqualified teaching of 'with-root,' both the two-rooted and the three-rooted should be understood. Likewise...
For in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: “Even for that which is rootless, a three-rooted object-of-reference (*tadārammaṇa*) is mentioned;
and as for what was said in the *Atthasamāsa*—that ‘it gives three-rooted fruits to those who are rootless’—how is that so? One must ask this very question of the author of that [text].
However, others say: “Because of the dullness of its fundamental connection (*mūlasandhi*), a three-rooted object-of-reference is simply not obtained for it.”
33–4. "After that" means after the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), starting from the second consciousness.

Although there may be the intermittent arising of process-consciousness (vīthicitta) in between, it is said to be "for as long as life lasts" because it does not turn back until the end of that lifespan. "With a powerful object" means with an extremely great and manifest object.
For in the case of the five doors, this refers to an extremely great object, and in the case of the mind door, to a manifest object.

The registration consciousness arises [only] with that as its object, and not with others. In the summary list (uddesa), the registration consciousness is placed at the end for the purpose of showing that rebirth-linking and the other two [processes]—though they all occur with a single object—share one and the same location.
However, here it should be understood that death is placed at the end according to the sequence of the course of existence (pavatti).
35–6. "The doors of action" means that they do not proceed by way of generating the doors of bodily and vocal action;

this is what is meant. In this context, "body" refers to bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*). "Action" refers to the volition (*cetanā*) that originates it; action performed by the body is "bodily action" (*kāyakamma*).
For although the body is not a condition for action by any of the twenty-four conditions, [it is still so designated].
Nevertheless, because that [volition] which originates from it exists, there is the conventional designation "bodily action" (kāyakamma) and so forth;
thus, it is said that "it was done by that. The door that serves as the locus for the occurrence of bodily action is the "door of bodily action" (kāyakammadvāra).

If this were the case, the definition of the doors of action would not be possible. For an action established by means of the body-door is called "bodily action"; however, that [action] operates within the door.
If it were argued that because of the statement "actions" (*kammāni*), [kamma] is established even at the door of speech, then there would be no definition of kamma by way of its door;
likewise, since verbal kamma is also established at the door of the body, there would be no definition of the door by way of the kamma.

This is not so, because [the doors and kamma] are defined by way of their predominant occurrence and their general mode of operation. For bodily kamma occurs predominantly only at the door of the body.

It is slight at the door of speech; therefore, because it occurs frequently at the door of the body, its status as bodily action (*kāyakamma*) is established, just as the status of "forest-dweller" and so forth is established for those who dwell in the forest.
Likewise, bodily action itself occurs mostly at the door of the body, not the other [types of action];
therefore, because bodily action occurs mostly right here, its status as the "door of bodily action" is established.
It is established that the status of a "brahmin village" and so forth belongs to the brahmin village itself; thus, there is no obstacle here in defining the doors of action (*kamma-dvāra*).
This same principle should be understood as applicable to the door of verbal action (*vacī-kamma-dvāra*) as far as possible.

As for the door of mental action (*mano-kamma-dvāra*), since it is the mind itself, it serves as the basis for the volitions (*cetanā*) associated with it, such as non-covetousness (*anabhijjhā*) and other karmic factors.
It receives the designation "mind-door" (manodvāra) by way of being the door for the occurrence [of consciousness];
thus, one does not take it as the door for the arising of consciousness itself. For it does not occur by its own self-nature.

However, if those associated with consciousness are intended by way of being the "door of action" (kammadvāra), then their status as the door of action is not metaphorically attributed to the mind; therefore, [the term applies] to the associated states.
Because the mind exercises sovereignty over itself within the mind, the mind is called the "door of mental action" (*manokamma-dvāra*).

However, in terms of its intrinsic nature, the door of action consists only of the associated states; thus, because it proceeds from that [mind], the mind proceeds by way of the door of mental action.
But as for the state of being the door of mental action belonging to that which serves as the immediately preceding condition (*anantara-paccaya*), there is simply nothing further to be said.

Furthermore, here, because non-occurrence is established by the statement "due to not being produced by intimation" specifically through the doors of bodily and vocal action, the door of mental action is certainly not included.
For the reason "due to not being produced by intimation" does not establish non-occurrence even with respect to the door of mental action.
Alternatively, by the statement "because its nature is non-resultant," [non-occurrence is established] even with respect to the door of mental action.

Non-arising (appavatti) is thus established. Regarding the term "door of action" (kammadvāra), since "action" (kamma) here is intended to include both simultaneous and asynchronous (nānakkhaṇika) actions, that [asynchronous action] should also be understood as being included.

Thus, it is not the case that resultant (vipāka) states arise in the same way as wholesome (kusala) states do within these two doors—namely, those designated as the doors of bodily and verbal action—or within all three doors when including the door of mental action (manokammadvāra).

And whereas wholesome [kamma] proceeds by way of the accumulation of bodily, verbal, and mental action, and by way of the bases for meritorious deeds such as giving, this [unwholesome kamma] does not do so.
Furthermore, it does not proceed through the doors of bodily and verbal action because it lacks the capacity to originate intimation (*viññatti*);

nor does it proceed by way of [actual] action, because it lacks the capacity to produce a result (*vipāka*); and it does not proceed even by way of the door of mental action, because it lacks the capacity to produce a result.

It is said, “The doors of kamma... are not equal,” in order to show that [the path] proceeds by way of meritorious action (*puññakiriyā*)—that is, by way of giving and so forth—and does not proceed in that manner [through the doors].
“In this way” means by way of giving and so forth. 37.

The passage beginning with “Because they have limited objects” (*parittārammaṇattā*) is a demonstration of the distinction [of these paths] by way of their associated states (*sampayuttadhamma*). Since these have limited objects, [they are thus distinguished].
Compassion (*karuṇā*) and gladness (*muditā*) have the concept (*paññatti*) as their object, because they proceed with respect to the concept of a being (*satta-paññatti*).
Therefore, since two objects cannot simultaneously become the domain of a single consciousness, compassion and gladness never arise with respect to those [two] objects.
This is the intended meaning of the first verse here.
38. Furthermore, in the second verse, the word *hi* has the sense of *yasmā* (because). The meaning is:
because it was stated that "the five training rules (*sikkhāpada*) are wholesome" (*kusala*), therefore [it follows]. This is what is meant:
for in the *Sikkhāpadavibhaṅga*, the Blessed One stated that the five training rules—beginning with "abstention from taking life"—are wholesome by saying, "The five training rules are wholesome."
And these [factors] are by nature abstinences from the very beginning: in the case of the first three training rules, and in the case of the last one, right action;
and in the case of the other, right speech. This is because they are included within right livelihood, which functions as the refraining from the five types of misconduct rooted in wrong livelihood.
Therefore, while they are exclusively wholesome, they are at times indeterminate.
Otherwise, like faith, mindfulness, and so forth, they would have been stated as "sometimes wholesome, sometimes indeterminate.
If this is so, do the eight or seven path-factors not obtain in the supramundane fruits? They are not non-obtainable;
for while it is stated that only the mundane abstinences (*virati*) possess an exclusively wholesome nature therein, the supramundane abstinences belong to the fruit.
Because it is a reflection of the Path, resembling the Path by way of its eightfold or sevenfold nature,
it is not appropriate to define it as being exclusively wholesome. And having established this,
the distinction of the Path into eightfold and so forth is also mentioned in relation to the supramundane fruits above.
39. “*Tathādhipatino*” and so forth is a demonstration of the distinction by way of predominance (*adhipati*).

For among all the wholesome states of the three planes, the time of their accumulation (*āyūhana*) is one thing, and the time of their ripening (*vipaccana*) is another; therefore, they are unable to cause their own results to take them as a predominance.
Consequently, they do not proceed with desire (*chanda*) and the other [mental factors] as their primary focus. However, as for supramundane wholesome states, at the time of their accumulation...
Because there is no interval between the time of maturation and the moment when one's own desire and so forth have not yet subsided, they produce the result at that very time;
thus, acting as an immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*), they are able to cause the dominant influence (*adhipati*) to be grasped by the results.
And having established this, he will later explain the connection with the dominant influence for supramundane results.

40. Since the Elder Mahādatta, resident at Moravāpi, maintains that the distinction between the spontaneous (*asaṅkhārika*) and the prompted (*sasaṅkhārika*) arises from the arrival of the results of kamma, while the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷanāga maintains it arises from conditions, [the author] says "the classification of the spontaneous and the prompted" and so forth in order to demonstrate the views of both.
For the former Elder [explains it] as follows: just as when the mouth moves, [the reflection appears] on the surface of a mirror...
It moves for the sake of the face; thus he said that the result of a spontaneous (asaṅkhārika) wholesome state is spontaneous, and the result of a prompted (sasaṅkhārika) state is prompted.
Therefore, in order to demonstrate his understanding, it was stated: "Spontaneous... from merit.
But as for the second Elder, when any kind of action—whether spontaneous or otherwise—has been accumulated by the mind of one who is near to death, [the result arises].

Rebirth-linking that arises without one's own or another’s volitional effort, without prompting, and without application—when the kamma, the sign of kamma, or the sign of the destination presents itself—is "unprompted" (*asaṅkhārika*).
That which arises for anyone with volitional effort, with application, when the kamma or other signs present themselves, is "prompted" (*sasaṅkhārika*).

The same applies to the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and the death-moment (*cuti*). Furthermore, the object of that [rebirth-linking] depends on conditions such as superior or inferior weather, food, and so forth.

Or, by way of wholesome and unwholesome [states] that have ceased immediately prior, it is "without effort" (*asaṅkhāra*) or "with effort" (*sasaṅkhāra*); thus he states the classification of the "effortless" and so forth according to their conditions.
Therefore, in order to demonstrate his understanding of this, it is said: "The knowable is to be understood both by way of condition...

And this very point is what the teachers praise. 41–2. "Because they are the result of inferior and so forth": even in the absence of a dominant influence (*adhipati*), because they are the results of wholesome [states] that are inferior, middling, or superior.
By this, he clarifies the state of being inferior and so forth from the perspective of its arrival.

Because it dispels the stains of the defilements existing within the mental continuum of those being trained and causes them to arise again, it has "meritorious speech" (*puññavāda*)—that is, vocal sound—as its nature; or, according to the method already stated, it is "one who speaks merit" (*puññavādī*). Thus, by that "speaker of merit.
Although it was said, "exclusively with a basis," the occurrence [of merit] in the realm of form (*rūpaloka*) is not excluded; hence he says:
“In the sense-sphere world. By the phrase “but it is not born elsewhere,” however, he shows the meaning obtained through the method of exclusion (*vyatireka*).
Having thus demonstrated the result with roots (*sahetuka-vipāka*), he now says “But as for the rootless resultant consciousness,” and so forth, in order to demonstrate the rootless [result].
Why, then, does a rootless result arise from karma that possesses roots? It is said:
—First, because the five [consciousnesses] beginning with eye-consciousness consist merely in the impingement upon an object, association with non-greed and so forth is impossible;

likewise, it is impossible in the reception and investigation consciousnesses, whose functions are weaker. Thus, their lack of roots (ahetukatā) should be understood from the impossibility of the arising of roots.
As for their association with equanimity and so forth, first, in the case of the eye-consciousness and the rest...

Because the contact with the physical basis (vatthu) and the object is weak when the [five-door] consciousnesses are occurring even toward four desirable objects, they are accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā);
whereas body-consciousness is accompanied by pleasure because it is strong due to that [contact].
However, the receiving consciousness (sampaṭicchana) is gross because it is capable of striking the object, and because it has arisen long ago by way of having passed through four mind-moments.

Furthermore, because it arises in dependence on a weak basis such as the eye-faculty and so forth—which are of a different nature [from itself]—and because it has obtained the condition of immediate antecedent (anantara-paccaya) from the eye-consciousness and the rest that have arisen, and because its basis is unprecedented, it is weak in its enjoyment of the flavor of the object;
thus, with respect to desirable and other objects, it is accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*) alone. Investigation (*santīraṇa*), however, is the opposite of what was stated.
It should be understood that [mental consciousness] is accompanied by pleasure when the object is desirable, and accompanied by equanimity when the object is desirable-neutral.

Like mental-consciousness-element, it is called "mind-element" (*manodhātu*) because it is merely mind (*manomatta*) due to the absence of the specific function of reflecting (*visiṭṭhamanana*), and it is called an "element" (*dhātu*) in the sense of being devoid of a sentient being and devoid of a soul.
For although it possesses the nature of consciousness, it does not perform the specific function of reflecting, which is the source of mental-consciousness.
It consists of mere mental reflection (*mananamatta*). However, because it is the mind (*mano*) and that consciousness (*viññāṇa*), it is "mind-consciousness" (*manoviññāṇa*);
and in the sense already stated, that itself is an "element" (*dhātu*), thus "mind-consciousness-element" (*manoviññāṇadhātu*).

The pentad of consciousnesses has a restricted object (*niyatārammaṇa*), because they take as their respective objects only one thing at a time, such as visible form and so forth. The remaining triad has an unrestricted object (*aniyatārammaṇa*), because they can have either five objects or six objects.
The visible object base (*rūpāyatana*) is "seen" because it is to be seen. The sound base (*saddāyatana*) is "heard" because it is to be heard.
The smell and so forth—the triad of odor, taste, and tangible objects—is called "sensed" (*muta*) because it is to be apprehended only when [the object] has arrived; this is the meaning of "sensed.

The mental object base (*dhammāyatana*) is "cognized" (*viññāta*) because it is to be known by the mind alone, apart from the eye and the other [senses]. This is stated because it does not specify a particular time.
Furthermore, even past and future forms and so forth are designated by the terms "seen" and so on.

For this very reason, their derivation is stated by way of the commonality of time in the phrase "by way of being seen," and so forth. That which has a seen object as its objective support is "diṭṭhārammaṇaṃ. The same applies to "sutārammaṇaṃ" and the others.
“Proceeding from the eye” means proceeding solely through the eye-door, because all [the following] statements have the function of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
By this, the status of being eye-consciousness is excluded for the mind-element and so forth, since those can also proceed through other doors.
Alternatively, the phrase “proceeding from the eye” is stated with reference to the proceeding of its arising (*sañjāti-pavatti*), not the proceeding of its movement (*sañcaraṇa-pavatti*).
Therefore, it is not the case that what occurs here is taken as occurring by way of flowing out from the opening of a vessel, like water from a bowl;
rather, it is taken as occurring by way of being produced [from within], just as water issues forth from a moonstone (*candakanta-pāsāṇa*).
And how is this so? Just as bile, phlegm, blood, and so forth, which have arisen from within the belly, [issue] from the mouth...
Even though it flows from the mouth, it is not called "mouth-saliva"; rather, it is called "mouth-saliva" only when it originates from the mouth itself and flows from there.

Likewise, visual consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*) does not exist as that which originates from the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*) and proceeds from the eye; rather, it is that which originates from the eye itself and proceeds from there.

"Eye-consciousness" (cakkhuviññāṇaṃ) means "name. However, one who, failing to discern this meaning and adhering merely to the literal expression, might imagine that all other consciousnesses occurring through that same door also possess the nature of eye-consciousness—in order to prevent such a misconception, he provides an analysis by another method, saying:
"Dependent upon the eye" (cakkhumhi sannissitaṃ). Just as it proceeds from the eye, it is "dependent upon the eye."

Or, regarding consciousness as "eye-consciousness," he says "likewise ear-consciousness and so forth" while extending the application by way of such formulations as: "consciousness that has proceeded from the ear, or consciousness supported upon the ear, is ear-consciousness.
That which has the characteristic of cognizing visible form by being supported by the eye is "that which has the characteristic of cognizing visible form supported by the eye."
In this context, by the expression "dependent on the eye," other consciousnesses that have visible form as their object—such as the divine eye (dibbacakkhu) and so forth—are excluded.
By the inclusion of the term "cognizing" (vijānana), mental factors such as contact (phassa) and others that depend on the eye are excluded.
By the inclusion of the terms "eye" and "visible form," the mind is distinguished in terms of its support and its object, because its existence is dependent upon both. For if the eye...
It would not be so; even the blind would see visible forms, yet they do not see them.
Furthermore, if there were no such thing as a visible form such as blue and so forth, there could be no restriction by way of location and the like, yet such a restriction certainly exists.

Moreover, since it has been stated that consciousness has an exclusive object, the doctrine that consciousness proceeds with the appearance of blue and so forth even without an external object must be understood as a false doctrine.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises," and so forth. Here it may be asked:
when the eye and forms act as conditions for consciousness, do they function as a single condition or as multiple ones?
The eye, at least, is a single [condition], but the forms are multiple when combined. What is the reason? Because of the distinction in their mode of being conditions.

For the eye, in being a condition for eye-consciousness by way of the conditions of support (*nissaya*), pre-existence (*purejāta*), faculty (*indriya*), and dissociation (*vippayutta*), does so precisely through its state of existence; for when that [eye] exists, the [consciousness] comes to be, and when it is absent, it does not. Therefore, it is said that it is a condition for it by way of the conditions of presence (*atthi*) and non-disappearance (*avigata*).
This state of being a condition is not impossible in a single [factor]; thus, even a single [eye] is [a condition] for eye-consciousness.

It serves as a condition. As for material form (*rūpa*), although—like the eye—it serves as a condition by way of the pre-arising, presence, and disappearance conditions because it assists while existing at the very moment [of the consciousness] having already arisen earlier, nevertheless, it serves as a condition only when combined in multiplicity, by virtue of its being an object (*ārammaṇa*). For that which is the object, in whatever manner...

The state of being an object-condition exists precisely by way of being apprehendable; and for consciousness, which functions in dependence upon the sense-faculties, the perception of the essential nature of an object does not occur by way of a color contained in one or two *kalāpas*, nor even by way of a color contained in a few *kalāpas*, but rather by way of a color that has entered the range of the senses in accordance with attention (*ābhoga*).
Thus, multiple material phenomena (*rūpa*) act in combination as a condition for consciousness.
"It is a condition" means that it is precisely to clarify this distinction that the variation in phrasing "dependent on the eye and forms" was employed in the Canon.

The same should be stated accordingly for ear-consciousness as well. However, because olfactory consciousness and the others grasp what is present, they apprehend only that which is conjoined with their own support;
thus, even a scent and so forth belonging to the same momentary group (*kalāpa*) [is apprehended].
It is the condition for their arising.
"Having the mere form as its objective flavor" means having the act of making the sense-base of form alone its object as its function.
By the word "mere" (*matta*), just as it excludes other objects, it likewise excludes certain specific qualities that might otherwise be found within the sense-base of form. Not...
For visual consciousness is not able to apprehend any specific quality such as blue or the like there, other than mere color.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "By means of the five types of consciousness one does not cognize any phenomenon other than the mere impact.
Since visual consciousness arises only with respect to a visible-form object when it arises, it apprehends it by being directed toward that very object.
It is said: "Its manifestation is the state of being directed toward visible forms (*rūpa*).

To show that the immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) which arise immediately after themselves are proximate causes—acting as immediate, contiguity, absence, and disappearance conditions by providing the opportunity for the occurrence of those immaterial phenomena, just like the supporting and objective conditions—he said: "having visible forms as its object..."
"...the basis for the disappearance of the functional mind-element (kiriyā-manodhātu). The meaning should be understood in the same manner as stated regarding ear-consciousness and the others.
Because the functional mind-element possesses a distinct nature due to the diversity of its objects, he says "of the functional mind-elements.
It receives and grasps the object—such as visible form and so forth—previously apprehended by eye-consciousness and the rest, immediately thereafter, without allowing it to fall away.

It is said to "be as it were" (*viya hoti*), meaning its function (*rasa*) is the reception of visible forms and so forth. It "manifests through that state of being," that is, through the state of receiving; thus, it has "that state of being as its manifestation" (*tathābhāvapaccupaṭṭhāna*).
Among the six objects, at times five [are received] by those such as the blind from birth, or even fewer than that, and in the Brahma-world...

Although they have the nature of cognizing only two [objects], they are said to have the characteristic of cognizing six objects because they do not transcend that nature, or because the other five objects are included within those very six.
"Having investigation and so forth as their function" means they perform the functions of investigating, registering, and so on, as appropriate;
the intended meaning is that they perform the functions of investigating, registration, rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death. "With the heart-base as their proximate cause."
This was stated to show the fixed cause for these two mind-consciousness elements (manoviññāṇadhātu) because they lack a fixed location.

However, according to the method already explained, it is also appropriate to say that their "footing" (padaṭṭhāna) is the departure of the respective consciousness that has immediately preceded them.
Since the individual characteristics and so forth of rootless (ahetuka) cittas have been shown separately, [the following] applies by way of elimination to cittas with roots (sahetuka).
It is understood that the characteristics (lakkhaṇa) and so forth are exactly the same; however, that has already been explained below.
Now, in order to show the distinction between these [three knowledges] by way of their objects (ārammaṇa) and other factors, it is said: "Therein, the first," and so on.

"In an exclusively desirable object" means in an object that is exclusively desirable—that is, in an extremely desirable object. "In five places" refers to the five types of root-cause-accompanied resultant consciousness (sahetuka-vipāka).

The meaning is that [it arises] in five places— namely, in the four mentioned [previously] and in the position of investigation (santīraṇa), which is reckoned as the interval between reception (sampaṭicchana) and determining (voṭṭhabbana)—
or, alternatively, in five functions. Although, for one whose rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) was accompanied by joy,

there may be no registration (tadārammaṇa) following the conclusion of a javana of grief, nevertheless, a registration accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā-sahagata-santīraṇa) arises taking as its object some limited (paritta) object previously familiarized.

Although it is intended [to include more], since that which arises in such a way occurs only at certain times, the five locations were stated instead of the six by taking its predominant occurrence into account.

Alternatively, it should be understood that because that which arises is produced precisely in the location of its object (tadārammaṇa), the location of that [object] is also taken as the location for it. This is due to its being produced by kamma conducive to non-visual form.
"Blind from birth" (*jaccandha*) means one who is blind by way of birth (*jātiyā*). For although at the moment of birth the eye is absent in all those born from eggs or from a womb—
such that there could be no consideration of being blind or not blind based on its presence or absence— nevertheless, even at the time when the eye ought to arise,
[the person is so called] because of the other [kamma], namely the rebirth-giving kamma whose capacity has been obstructed by kamma that acts as a hindrance to the impairment of the eye.
Or, because it is not grasped by that kamma, a being is called "blind from birth.
Alternatively, "blind from birth" means blind even at the moment of delivery; the sense is that he emerged having been blind already within the mother's womb.

By this, it is established that for those with two roots or three roots, the eye faculty does not fail even while they are in the mother's womb. The same applies accordingly to those who are deaf from birth and so forth.

It should be stated. "Born-blind" (*jaccajaḷo*) means one who is ignorant by birth. Although even one with a two-root rebirth-linking is ignorant by birth, wisdom (*paññā*) can arise during his course of existence (*pavatti*);
however, according to the method already explained, because wisdom generally does not arise even during the course of existence, he is to be understood as "born-blind.

"Born-intoxicated" (*jaccummattako*) refers to one whose state of intoxication is conditioned by karma conducive to the state of intoxication through the drinking of fermented and distilled liquors and so forth.
"One who has taken rebirth through karma" means one who has taken rebirth through karma conditioned by such acts as adultery with another's wife.

That [eunuch] is of five kinds: the drenched eunuch (*āsitta-paṇḍaka*), the envious eunuch (*ussuyā-paṇḍaka*), the periodic eunuch (*pakkha-paṇḍaka*), the accidental eunuch (*opakkamika-paṇḍaka*), and the neuter eunuch (*napuṃsaka-paṇḍaka*).
However, in this context, because even the accidental eunuch possesses the presence of a root-cause (*sa-hetuka*), [the term refers to] the neuter.
And by taking them separately, three types of *paṇḍaka* (eunuchs) are intended. By the word "etc.

(*ādi*), there is an inclusion of those who are blind from birth, mute from birth, lame from birth, mentally deficient, and so forth. However, some say: "Certain individuals with rootless rebirth-linking (*ahetuka-paṭisandhi*), though possessing unimpaired faculties, are also of a nature to engage in a small amount of investigation;
therefore, such persons are also included here by the word 'etc. And in this context, it refers specifically to those who are blind from birth and so on.
"This is the rebirth-linking" should not be grasped [as a literal fact]. However, it should be understood that those such as the blind from birth take rebirth-linking by means of this [volition].
43. "Of three-rooted merit": this refers to the highest grade of merit even among those with three roots.

Since the sixteen results are in no way possible for karma with two roots, the volition is stated without qualification as "of three-rooted merit" because its purpose is to exclude that [two-rooted karma].
The commentary on the sense-sphere resultant [consciousness] is finished.
Regarding the commentary on the fine-material and immaterial sphere resultants:

because the loss of jhāna factors in the sublime resultants occurs solely through the departure from their respective wholesome states and not through a specific distinction in meditation (*bhāvanā*), their factors of abandoning have not been mentioned. "In rebirth" means in the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*).
The connection is that they are called "resultant consciousnesses of the formless sphere" (arūpāvacara-vipāka-cittāni).
44. "Having made it conformable to the wholesome" means having made it similar to the wholesome, corresponding to the wholesome.

The meaning is: not having analyzed it as the sense-sphere resultant was analyzed—which, though dissimilar to the wholesome, was treated as such—but rather having made it exactly similar to the wholesome.

They say this. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, having placed [the resultant consciousness] immediately after the wholesome, it is stated that "it was divided by following the order of the wholesome," with reference to the portion of the text (*pāḷi*) where the sublime resultants (*mahaggata-vipāka*) are analyzed. For in the text it says:

"Which states are indeterminate (*abyākata*)? At whatever time, as a result of having performed and accumulated wholesome karma of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), the resultant eye-consciousness has arisen," and so forth.
Having analyzed the resultant consciousness of the sense sphere, one analyzing the sublime resultant [consciousness] [states]:
"Which states are indeterminate? At whatever time one develops the path for the attainment of form, secluded from sensual pleasures...
[as before] ...and dwells having attained the first jhāna with the earth-kasiṇa, at that time there is contact... [as before] ..."
“Non-distraction occurs; these states are wholesome. As the result of that same wholesome kamma of the fine-material sphere having been performed and accumulated, secluded from sensual pleasures...
[as before] ...one enters and dwells in the first jhāna with the earth-kasiṇa...
[as before] ...these states are indeterminate.”
Having thus pointed out the wholesome (kusala) and immediately following it, the sublime (mahaggata) resultant (vipāka) was analyzed.

Therefore, in order to illuminate this meaning—that unlike the sense-sphere resultant, which was not so analyzed, this [sublime resultant] was analyzed immediately after the wholesome—the commentary states:
"having placed it in sequence with the wholesome. And by this very teacher, through the method of providing a solution...
An objection was raised there according to the method already stated, due to the desire for a specific meaning that will be explained later.
For if this were so, the clarification that "the fruit arises immediately after the wholesome [state]" would be well-established; this is our teacher’s approach in this matter.

"Lofty" (*mahaggata*) means the lofty resultant (*vipāka*). For that is what is attained here. "Sensual... [etc. "...because" (*yata*) means because the sense-sphere wholesome (*kāmāvacara-kusala*)...
It has a non-equal fruit because it produces the two-rooted and rootless results of a three-rooted [kamma], as well as the rootless results of a two-rooted [kamma];
this, however, is not so, for since it produces a result that is strictly similar, it has an equal fruit—this is the meaning.
And here, although "wholesome" (kusala) is not explicitly stated, because it is compared to sense-sphere merit, the object of comparison is also [implied].
The state of being wholesome (kusalabhāva) is understood. But why is this [wholesome state] of similar fruition, and not of dissimilar fruition like that of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara)?

It is said: for one accumulating sense-sphere merit, one accumulates it by means of the underlying tendency toward craving for sense-pleasures (kāmataṇhā) directed toward various bases such as craving for form (rūpataṇhā).
Therefore, the wholesome state supported by that [craving] produces a fruition of various bases in accordance with it. As for the sublime (mahaggata) [merit]...
Furthermore, when one accumulates [kamma], one does so by means of craving for existence (*bhava-taṇhā*) alone;
thus, in accordance with that, rather than producing various bases (*vatthu*), it produces only a single base. 45–6.

"In all respects" means according to their nature (*dhamma*), their objects (*ārammaṇa*), their modes of practice (*paṭipadā*), and so forth. For instance, those contacts (*phassa*) and other factors that exist in wholesome states...

And just as those [factors] are obtained in the wholesome, they are also obtained in its result (*vipāka*). Furthermore, whatever object the wholesome arises upon, upon that very same object this result also arises.
As long as the path and so forth are obtainable for the wholesome, so too are they obtainable for this result.
Granted, the shadow of anything whatsoever resembles its respective base; however, for a great wholesome result, there are only great [bases].

"It must be by way of a simile" refers to the statement beginning with "of elephants, etc. Others explain that it is *aparāpariyavedanaṃ* because its feeling (*vedanā*) occurs in various successive states of existence (*attabhāva*).
If there were no *aparāpariyavedanaṃ*, how then could this fruit arise?
To this he says: "For one who has not fallen away from jhāna," and so forth.
