47. "Immediately after the wholesome" means immediately after a wholesome existence (*bhava*).

For that existence in which that wholesome deed was performed is here taken by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) by the term "wholesome," because a fruit cannot arise immediately after a mere action (*kamma*).
Indeed, unlike supramundane wholesome states, that [mundane wholesome state] does not produce its fruit immediately; rather, it is certain types of sense-sphere wholesome states [that do so].

Without being experienced either in this life or in subsequent lives, even though there are many kamma-formations belonging to the sense-sphere, it— like a great flood overwhelming a small amount of water—
uniquely produces its fruit in the immediately following existence alone by giving its own result.
But is it not the case that for someone who has not fallen away from jhāna, rebirth-linking in the sense-sphere existence occurs through the influence of craving?

It is so; for it is said that the Great Brahmā Tissa, having developed the path for rebirth in the higher brahma-world, when requested by the bhikkhus, passed away from there and took rebirth in the house of the brahmin Moggallī. How then is this to be explained?
They say that jhāna is lost solely through the power of craving, and thus one who has fallen away from jhāna is reborn there. Others [say...]
However, the teachers, having stated that "the decline of jhāna must be understood after investigating the attachment that exists when there is no state of non-obstruction," say:
"Even though there is an absence of limited kamma capable of obstructing the ripening of sublime kamma, the mental aspiration for the sense-sphere existence succeeds, because of the statement:
'Bhikkhus, the mental aspiration of one who is virtuous succeeds because of its purity.'"
They say that it obstructs the fruition of a sublime (mahaggata) kamma and creates space for the fruition of a limited (paritta) kamma;
this is correct. "Of this" (etassa) is connected with "for the purpose of making known this meaning. 48–9.
Having thus extended [the description] by way of similarity to the wholesome (kusala) without distinction, he now shows the difference, beginning with "the sequence of the path" (paṭipadākkamo).

Thus it was said, beginning with “...and so forth. For just as when one has produced a jhāna that is difficult of practice and slow in direct knowledge and enters into it again and again, that jhāna remains of that same mode of practice;

even so, when the respective resultants are being produced while those [causes] have not been lost, they ought to be of that same respective mode of practice. This is the state of having desire as the dominant factor, and so on.
However, at that moment, it exists by way of being the dominant condition (*adhipatipaccaya*) for the desire and other factors present at that time, not by way of their arrival.

For indeed, a single jhāna becomes dominated by different factors at different moments; therefore, the state of being dominated by desire and so forth is not attributed to the fruition (*vipāka*) by way of its arrival.
Thus he said: "of those lacking a dominant factor. Precisely because of their absence, [the fruition] is [so called] by its own nature (*sarasato*).
Since inferiority and so forth are not possible for that [resultant consciousness], it too is described as arising solely from the attainment of jhāna.
The commentary on the fine-material-sphere and immaterial-sphere resultant consciousnesses is concluded. The commentary on the supramundane resultant consciousnesses.

Just as with the path-consciousness, because there is no distinction in the fruit-consciousness due to its connection with the path, it is not stated as "due to connection with the four paths," but rather as "because it is the fruit of consciousness associated with the four paths.

The meaning is: because it is the fruit of wholesome consciousness associated with the four noble paths, that is, because it has the nature of consciousness associated with the fourfold fruition of stream-entry and so forth. [This refers to] the stream-entry path...
The "fruit-consciousness" is the consciousness of the fruit of the stream-entry path; the same applies to the remaining [paths].

Although the attainment of the fruit occurs an unlimited number of times—either twice or thrice—within the course of the path, it is said to be "twofold according to its occurrence by way of the path-course and the attainment of the fruit" because it occurs in only two instances.
50–1. The intention is that the fruits are obtained immediately after the path because they follow the path.

For the path, having received the name "void" (*suññata*) by way of its arrival, also receives the names "signless" (*animitta*) and "desireless" (*appaṇihita*) through its objective support consisting of specific qualities; thus, it bestows these three names upon the fruit as well.
Likewise, the desireless path, by way of its arrival, is named "signless," "void," and "desireless" through its objective support consisting of specific qualities.
It gives even three names to a single fruit. Having done so, three names are stated for each individual fruit in the Abhidhamma.
But was it not stated in the Abhidhamma that "a name is not intended when the object possesses a quality"? True, it was stated;
however, that was with reference to the acquisition of a name, not to the giving of a name. For in that context, there is an absence of the capacity to provide a definitive distinction.

Likewise, it is not unintended because it is not unobtainable. However, in this case, since each fruit receives even three names, and because there is no purpose for such a fixed distinction, one gives all three names to that which has received its name from the objects possessing qualities (saguṇārammaṇa).
This must certainly be accepted in this way; otherwise, even insight (vipassanā) would [be called by those names] for one who is practicing insight.
"One should not give that to one who has attained the path" means: "In the subsequent stage" (*parabhāgasmiṃ*) means in the later stage.
"Regarding the fruits of utilization" (*vaḷañjanaphalesu*) means regarding the fruits to be experienced by way of actualizing [the attainment].

He said, "By way of insight alone," etc., because the attainment of the path was rejected with the words "not regarding the fruits of utilization. For the fruit of utilization is distinct and occurs only by way of insight.
"It is produced" means that it acquires its name by virtue of that [signless state]. If this were so, would it not follow that it cannot acquire the name "signless" in the same way as the Path does?

That is not the case; for just as the Fruition that immediately follows the Path and the attainment of the fruition-exercise both possess a distinction in their meditative procedure (*jhāna-paṭipadā*) due to having proceeded from the Path, so too does it receive the name "signless."

52–3. “They exist as having a dominant influence” (*sādhipati*): the reason for this has already been stated. Regarding the phrase “by way of being the Path” (*maggabhāvena*): it means by way of being the Path that penetrates the Four Truths through sixteen aspects;

or by way of being the Path in the sense of “going,” which is defined as the destruction of the defilements (*kilesa*); or by way of being the Path in the sense of being that which is to be sought after (*maggita*) by those who desire Nibbāna.
“The fruit... is called”: although it is itself the state of being the fruit (*phalabhāva*), [it is so called].

The intention is that because it is the fruit of the path, or because it resembles it, it is called "the path" by way of depending upon that [path], as in such expressions as "a factor of the path" (maggaṅga) or "included in the path" (maggapariyāpanna).
The commentary on supramundane resultant [consciousness] is finished.
Now begins the commentary on unwholesome resultant [consciousness].

Just as the wholesome resultant mind-consciousness element is twofold— accompanied by joy and accompanied by equanimity— due to the possibility of different feelings arising toward extremely desirable and moderately desirable objects,
so too, since there is no differentiation of feeling toward extremely undesirable and moderately undesirable objects,
the unwholesome resultant mind-consciousness element is of one kind; thus it is said, "seven unwholesome resultants."

It has been stated: for if there were a division of feeling there that was undesirable, it would have to be associated with mental grief (*domanassa*), and mental grief does not arise without resistance (*paṭigha*). The bodily consciousness accompanied by suffering should be understood through the reverse of what was said regarding the wholesome resultant.
And here, just like the suffering found in unwholesome resultants, equanimity (*upekkhā*)—though not extremely bitter—is exclusively inferior.

Because they are the result (*vipāka*) of the unwholesome (*akusala*) and are of the nature of suffering (*dukkha*), they are indeed inferior. For the result of the unwholesome is never non-suffering;

rather, its state of equanimity (*upekkhā*) should be understood as being like the indifference of a weak man who, being oppressed by a powerful person and unable to strike back, merely endures the affliction inflicted upon him. These... [as above] ...are the seven types of consciousness.

There are resultant consciousnesses for each individual unwholesome state, but unlike the wholesome resultants, they do not differ according to distinctions such as being "three-rooted" (tihetuka) due to specific merit.
For even in the case of that accompanied by restlessness, only five resultants are found during its occurrence.

Why, then, is the unwholesome resultant not extracted here in the same way as the wholesome resultant, which was shown to be with roots? Because of the impossibility of [unwholesome] roots [functioning in the resultant stage].
For greed and the other [unwholesome roots], because they are exclusively blameworthy and have improper attention as their cause, there is no state of kamma-result.

Likewise, for non-greed and the others, because they are by nature exclusively blameless and because their cause is remote from those [unwholesome roots], there is likewise no state of unwholesome result.

For greed and the others, which are the opposites of non-greed and so forth, do not produce those [unwholesome roots]. Therefore, this [explanation] pertains entirely to the occurrence of that which has a cause.
Because it is impossible [for them to arise], it is indeed causeless.
Regarding the phrase "in the case of kamma, the sign of kamma, and the sign of the destination":

here, "kamma" refers to kamma performed in a past existence that is to be experienced either in a subsequent life (*aparāpariyavedanīya*) or upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*). The "sign of kamma" is the object grasped by volition (*cetanā*) at the time of performing that kamma.

The "sign of the deed" (*kammanimitta*) is as follows. The "sign of the destination" (*gatinimitta*) refers to the appearance of flames and so forth in hells and other realms, which is included within the state of existence one is to be reborn in.

54. These are the unwholesome resultants (*akusalavipāka*). By stating that they occur with respect to undesirable, desirable, and neutral objects, it follows by implication that wholesome resultants (*kusalavipāka*) occur with respect to desirable, desirable-neutral, and neutral objects; therefore, they are not treated separately.
“Are said. “Associated with the triad of pleasure,” etc., means associated with pleasure (*sukha*), mental joy (*somanassa*), and equanimity (*upekkhā*).
“Thus,” and so forth, is the conclusion regarding the aforementioned results.
The commentary on the unwholesome results is finished.
Commentary on Resultant Consciousness (Vipākacittavaṇṇanā): 55. He is called Pākasāsana because he instructs (sāsana) and destroys (vināsana) the ripening (pāka) of the wombs of the Asura maidens;
or alternatively, because he destroys the Asura known as Pāka, he is called Pākasāsana. Sakka, the king of the gods, is "honored by Pākasāsana" (Pākasāsanapūjita) because he is honored by him.
"Those for whom the teaching has ripened or is fully matured" are the *pākasāsanā*; those who have exhausted the taints (*khīṇāsava*). He is "honored by them," thus he is the *pākasāsanapūjita*.
The commentary on the resultant consciousnesses is finished.

Regarding the phrase "by way of giving and so forth": it means by way of giving and so forth merely as the mode of occurrence, and not by way of the bases of meritorious action (*puññakiriyavatthu*), because the state of performing meritorious action does not exist within the continuum of one whose taints are exhausted. This is the meaning already stated.
"It adverts" means adverting (*āvajjana*); the sense is that it "faces toward," "inclines toward," "turns toward," or "restrains. For it first faces toward the object that has come into its range;
it inclines the stream-cognitions, such as eye-consciousness and the rest, toward the object that has entered the path of the senses;
or it turns the continuum of consciousness away from its previous mode and toward another; it is that which causes the process to proceed by way of continuous succession.
It prevents the life-continuum consciousness from proceeding further, or it prevents the object that has entered the avenue of cognition from departing elsewhere.
It is called "arising with laughter" (*hasituppāda*) because laughter arises by means of it or is produced by it;
that very consciousness is thus "the consciousness arising with laughter. It discerns, thus it is "discernment" (*voṭṭhabbana*). But why are advertence and discernment mentioned here?
Are they accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*), and is the consciousness arising from laughter accompanied by joy (*somanassa*)? It is said:

First, advertence (*āvajjana*), because it occurs for a new object and functions by interrupting the continuity of the stream of consciousness all at once, is in every respect unable to experience the flavor of the object;
thus, in all cases regarding desirable objects and so forth, it is necessarily associated with equanimity.
As for determining (voṭṭhabbana), although it is likewise capable of being classified according to the different types of feeling as described above,
because its function consists specifically in the transformation of the continuity— by cutting off the stream of resultant consciousness and giving rise to a stream of dissimilar consciousness—
it is incapable of relishing the flavor of the object, just like the resultant consciousness; therefore, in all cases, it is accompanied by equanimity alone.

As for the smile-producing [consciousness], because it arises only in the mental continuum of those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) and who are free from the aforementioned deficiencies and perversions, and because it arises only toward a desirable object, it is in every respect accompanied by joy.
As for their characteristics and so forth: among these, the first has the characteristic of cognizing visible forms and so on as the precursor to eye-consciousness and the rest.

The first [advertence] has the function of adverting; it manifests as suchness (tathābhāva) and has the state of interrupting the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) as its proximate cause. The second has the characteristic of cognizing the six objects;
for Arahants, it has the function of producing a smile regarding non-repulsive objects; it manifests as suchness and has the heart-base exclusively as its proximate cause.
The third also has the characteristic of cognizing the six objects, occurring in the five doors and the mind door.
Its function is determining and adverting; its manifestation is the state of being such [i.e., the state of having turned toward the object];

its proximate cause is the departure of any one of the rootless resultant mind-consciousness elements or the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). "Turning back the life-continuum" means as if turning back the stream of the life-continuum. "Common" means shared by those in training (sekkha), those beyond training (asekha), and worldlings (puthujjana).
“Common. “Uncommon” means exclusive to those who have nothing further to learn (asekkha). Therefore he said, “of one whose taints are destroyed.

“In the six doors... in regard to objects”: in the six doors, namely the eye and so forth; and in the six objects, namely visible forms and so forth, located in places suitable for striving and so on.
For, having seen a place suitable for striving, for the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very life, [one thinks], “This place is suitable.”
When one is satisfied thinking, "I have obtained it," regarding a visible object at the eye-door;
when one hears a great noise at the place where goods or vessels are kept and is satisfied thinking, "Such greedy craving has been abandoned by me," regarding an audible object at the ear-door;
or at the time of worshipping a cetiya with perfumes or flowers, [one is satisfied] thinking, "Indeed, with such a sweet fragrance I worship the Blessed One."

When one is content with the object of fragrance at the nose-door; when, having shared a meal of excellent flavor with one's fellow celibates, one is content at the tongue-door with the object of taste, thinking, "I have fulfilled the duty of endearing service";
and when, at the time of fulfilling the duties of proper conduct, one is content, thinking, "I fulfill the duties and counter-duties with my body."
In the door of the body, with tangible objects as its object—in this way it proceeds in the five doors with respect to the five objects.
In the mind-door, however, it proceeds with respect to the same five present objects as mentioned above;
or with respect to past objects fully known by the Blessed One’s knowledge of past lives, such as in the Ghaṭīkāra Sutta and others, for example: “The Paccekabuddha named Aṭṭhissara...”

It should be understood that laughter arises only with respect to these six objects—namely, those delimited by the knowledge of the future (*anāgataṃsañāṇa*) regarding places where [the Buddha] will go, and so forth, as well as future objects.
But is it not the case that, after speaking of the unimpeded knowledge regarding the past and so forth, it was said:
"For the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is endowed with these three qualities, everything..."?

Since it is said, "Bodily action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge," how could the arising of this smile of the Blessed One be appropriate if it were devoid of the wisdom of investigation?
Even though the Blessed One’s act of smiling occurs through a mind that produces a smile,
because it conforms to his knowledge of past lives, his future-faring knowledge, and his omniscience, it indeed follows after knowledge.
But when there is this state of revolving in accordance with knowledge (*ñāṇānuparivatti*), there is no contradiction with the Canon. And having established it thus, the Commentary states:
"When those knowledges have reached their limit through practice, this consciousness arises. This must necessarily be accepted in this way;
otherwise, even for another rootless consciousness (*ahetuka-citta*) that originates intimation (*viññatti*), [the same would apply] to the Blessed One...

Otherwise, its arising would not be logical. For there is no obstruction to the state of one who originates intimation (viññatti) from becoming a performer of bodily action and so forth by means of the intimation originated by that [volition].

And this being the case, in the five sense-doors, it should be understood that this consciousness merely produces mental joy (somanassa), not physical happiness (ābhoga), because the consciousnesses of the five doors do not generate intimation. However, in the mind-door—
The production of laughter. For this very reason, in the Commentary, regarding the five sense doors, only this much is stated: "he becomes joyful";

and regarding the mind door, it says "causing laughter. Here, however, the expression "having the function of producing laughter" is a general statement that includes both that which operates in the five doors by way of producing joy and that which acts as a condition for generating laughter in the mind door.
It should be understood that this was said with a specific intention (*sandhāya*). "Having the function of producing a smile" means having the function of producing a smile itself.
For that very reason, it is called "smile-producing," not because other types of smile-producing consciousnesses do not exist.
Indeed, he will say later: "from the wholesome, by four," and so forth.

The six unique knowledges (*asādhāraṇañāṇāni*) are: the knowledge of the underlying tendencies and latent dispositions (*āsayānusayañāṇa*), the knowledge of the superiority and inferiority of the faculties (*indriyaparopariyañāṇa*), the knowledge of the twin miracle (*yamakapāṭihāriyañāṇa*), the knowledge of the attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇāsamāpattiñāṇa*), omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), and unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*).

These six are knowledges not shared by Paccekabuddhas and others. But is it not the case that omniscience itself is unobstructed knowledge? Otherwise, [there would be] a distinction between omniscience and unobstructed knowledge.

And there would result a state of knowledge that is obstructed by non-omniscience; for if there were a knowledge other than omniscient knowledge that were unobstructed, then because that [other] knowledge is obstructed, and because there would be an absence of penetration into the true nature of objects that are obstructed, the state of being omniscient could not be established.
Furthermore, since unobstructed knowledge would have only all phenomena as its object, wherever that [knowledge] does not occur—
"In that case, would it not follow that because an obstruction is possible, there could also be a state of non-obstruction? True, this is so;

yet that single knowledge is called 'omniscience' (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) because its object comprises all conditioned and unconditioned conventional phenomena without exception. And because there is no obstruction therein, it is called 'unobstructed knowledge' (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*) by way of its freedom from attachment.
Thus, [these names are used] to show its uniqueness compared to others, through the distinction between its objects and its modes of activity."
"It is stated in two ways":

as it was said—"The knowledge that knows all the conditioned and the unconditioned without exception is 'omniscience' (sabbaññutaññāṇa); because there is no obstruction therein, it is 'unobstructed knowledge' (anāvaraṇañāṇa)," and so forth.
"Standing here" refers to the place where the consciousness described as "the arising of a smile" arrives, from the perspective of the production of a smile.
"Having stood. "To be grasped" means to be taken up after having delimited [them].

Although, because the abandonment of the jhāna factors in the functional states of the fine-material sphere does not exist as a distinct entity—as it does in the case of the resultants—there being only a mode of occurrence produced by a specific cultivation similar to that in wholesome states, nevertheless, because the first jhāna possesses the possibility of factors for abandonment, the others are also described by way of one [factor] alone.
It is because the factor of abandoning (*pahānaṅga*) was not mentioned, and only the factor of association (*sampayogaṅga*) was shown among them.

Furthermore, since there is no duty to be performed through cultivation—such as the abandoning of the hindrances—without at least the mode of occurrence (*ākāramatta*) that functions by way of cultivation, there is no such thing as "cultivation" in a direct sense;
therefore, the term "mode" (*ākāra*) was included [in the compound] as "those occurring by way of the modes of cultivation."
58–9. It does not destroy that aforementioned attainment of the form and formless realms.

Regarding the phrase "if one who has attained [it] acts," although it is impossible to enter that very same attainment again because those [factors] have ceased and have not yet arisen, and because one enters [an attainment] only together with the desire to enter it once the attainment has already been acquired, [one enters] having first acquired the first jhāna and so forth.

And because it is impossible to attain the second jhāna and so forth, and because one attains it again in a manner similar to the attainment previously acquired—rather than like the attainment produced during the time of being an ordinary person (puthujjana)—that very attainment is described here in that way. 61.
"In a single moment of consciousness" means because it occurs in only a single moment of consciousness. For if it were to arise repeatedly, [it would not be so].
In that case, one would have to admit that for an Arahant there is the state of being a functional consciousness (kiriyabhāva) at the moment of its arising.

However, it occurs only once, because the task of penetrating the Four Truths is completed in a single instance, and because that [consciousness] cannot be found apart from its specific function. Therefore he said:
"They do not go to the further shore twice. Thus, the intended meaning here is that there is no supramundane functional consciousness (lokuttara-kiriyacitta).
62. *Kriyā*... [as before] ... *desaka*: those offenses which one incurs by doing what should not be done with body and speech are *kriyā* (actions);
however, those offenses which one incurs by not doing what should be done with body and speech are *akriyā* (non-actions). Both action and non-action constitute *kriyākiriyā* (action-and-non-action);
and because these are offenses to be incurred, they are called *kriyākiriyāpattiyo* (offenses of action-and-non-action).

"He teaches their classification" refers to the action... [etc. ...the teacher. Alternatively, the attainments that consist of functional consciousness (*kriyā-jhāna*) are "functional attainments" (*kriyā-patti*);

however, the attainments that consist of the wholesome (*kusala*) are "non-functional attainments" (*akriyā-patti*). "He teaches their classification" refers to the action... [etc. ...the teacher. The connection is:
"that which is functional and non-functional consciousness. He is the "Conqueror" (*jina*) because he has conquered the five Māras. Of the beneficial and the harmful...

"Of what is beneficial and what is not beneficial. "He" refers to that Conqueror (*jina*). "Delighting in doing and not doing" means he is devoted to performing what is beneficial for all beings and to refraining from what is harmful.
Alternatively, because its ripening is exclusively desirable, "beneficial" is a designation for wholesome states (*kusala*);
because it is the opposite of that, "harmful" is a designation for unwholesome states (*akusala*). [The phrase refers to] their performance in due order.
"Delighting in non-action regarding what is beneficial and harmful... [and so forth]... "delighting. Alternatively, "beneficial and harmful" refers specifically to the wholesome and unwholesome;
he wishes to effect their mere state of being action or non-action, and their lack of karmic result, thus "delighting in what is beneficial and harmful... [and so forth].

Or else, it refers to the performance or non-performance of their respective functions by individuals who are beneficial or harmful, which brings about their respective results in this world and the next.
"Delighting in the instrument" means being devoted to it; [this refers to] delighting in what is beneficial and what is harmful...

[etc. ...delighting. 64–6. The connection is as follows: "Having established all the supramundane [factors], those eighty-nine types of consciousness that have been mentioned—those consciousnesses have been explained by me.
They seek or aspire for proficiency (*pāṭava*); or, proficiency is their goal (*attha*).
"For one desiring proficiency. "It should be mastered" means it should be mastered by way of hearing and interrogation;

however, having mastered it, one should not remain at the mere level of mastery—showing this, he said, "it should be reflected upon again and again," for the intention is that it is not possible to reach full certainty here through mastery alone. "The Great Ocean of Abhidhamma."
The great ocean of the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, established by way of the seven treatises beginning with the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*;
or the ocean of ultimate reality, established by way of the aggregates, bases, and so forth. "They cross over" means they go across by way of grasping the meaning;

or the meaning is that they descend [into it] by means of the knowledge of development rooted in the knowledge consisting of what has been heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*). "This world" refers to the present existence. "The other world" refers to...
"Future existence. "They cross over" means they transcend. For in this world, they cross over this world by means of abandoning desire and lust;
they cross over the next world because they destroy future rebirth-producing karma through the knowledge that brings about the exhaustion of karma;
and they attain final nibbāna by means of non-clinging—this is the meaning.
Thus ends the commentary on the Exposition of Consciousness within the *Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanā*, titled *Abhidhammatthavikāsinī*.
2. The Second Chapter:
Explanation of the Description of Mental Factors (Cetasika-niddesa-vannanā) 67.
And at this point, regarding the four categories of phenomena thus enumerated—consciousness, mental factors, matter, and Nibbāna—

Having first demonstrated the mind through its classifications—such as by way of its genus, plane, association, occurrence, and mode—it is now begun with the words "enumerated immediately after the mind" and so forth, in order to demonstrate the mental factors (cetasika-dhamma) that were listed immediately following it.

"Classification" means classification by way of genus, plane, and so forth; and it also means the individual distribution [of those factors] according to their respective associations within each particular state of consciousness as appropriate.
Now, as for those mental factors whose classification is being stated, in order to show them according to their own forms together with their etymologies, it is said:
"In this context, those associated with consciousness," and so forth. Therein, "associated with consciousness" is a demonstration of the characteristic of a mental factor (*cetasika*).
By that, he shows that only those things which are conjoined with consciousness by way of the characteristic of association are indeed mental factors. But what [are they]?
Is that the characteristic of association? It consists of the modes known as arising together, ceasing together, having a common basis, and having a common object.
For they are "associated" (sampayutta) because they are joined (yutta) equally (samaṃ) by these modes.

In this context, if association were intended merely by way of arising together, it would follow that material and immaterial phenomena arising simultaneously would be mutually associated; therefore, the inclusion of "ceasing together" is made.
In this way too, it would follow that inseparable material phenomena (avinibbhoga-rūpa) possess mutual association; therefore, the term "having a single basis" (ekavatthuka) is included.
Furthermore, among inseparable material phenomena, one great primary (mahābhūta) serves as the support-condition (nissaya-paccaya) for the remaining great primaries and derived matter;
thus, they are said to have a single basis. Alternatively, the primary elements that serve as the support for the eye and so forth constitute a single basis.

For one who might conceive that "dependent on these" means they have the same physical basis (*ekavatthuka*), there could arise the fallacy that they are associated (*sampayutta*); therefore, the inclusion of the term "same object" (*ekārammaṇa*) is for the purpose of preventing that.

Alternatively, when it is said "having the same object" in reverse order, [it excludes] the fivefold sense-consciousnesses, the receiving consciousnesses, and so forth, within a single cognitive process (*ekavīthi*), as well as those in different processes (*nānāvīthi*).
Furthermore, if they were to arise in another person’s mental continuum with respect to the same object, they would fall into the error of being associated despite having different bases;

therefore, the term “having a single basis” (*ekavatthuka*) is included. Even so, if they were to arise in the cognitive process immediately preceding death, they would fall into the error of being associated despite having different cessations (i.e., occurring at different moments);
therefore, the term “having a single cessation” (*ekanirodha*) is included. But do not these [mental states] possess these three characteristics even when they do not arise simultaneously?

Now, in order to show that they arise together and thus possess these three characteristics, the term "arising together" (*ekuppādā*) was stated for the purpose of investigating whether they indeed arise simultaneously.
Thus, by means of these four characteristics of association, those factors which are associated with consciousness are called mental concomitants (*cetasika*);
in this way, the characteristic of a mental concomitant is established. But how are these called "mental concomitants"?

He said: "They exist in the mind. Although it should have been stated as "mental factors (cetasika) are those existing in the consciousness (cetasi)," the expression "they exist in the mind (citte)" was used to show the mere meaning, since the word *citta* has the same referent as the word *ceto*.
"Fixed" means having a fixed arising; like compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and so forth, they do not arise at all times, but rather whenever [their conditions are met].
The meaning is that consciousness arises, and at each such moment it arises inseparable from them.

"They are mentioned by their own specific form" means that, unlike desire and the rest which are included under the catch-all phrase, "or whatever other immaterial, dependently arisen states exist at that time," they are not mentioned as mere inclusions;
rather, they are mentioned by their own specific forms, such as "there is contact," "there is feeling," and so forth.
These are found in the Pāli. "Yevāpanakā" means those for whom such is the teaching; thus they are called *yevāpanaka*.
"Twenty-nine states" refers to twenty-nine states by way of distinct, unmixed phenomena alone, without taking into account the differentiation of their functions.
However, in the Pāli, having taken thirty states together with consciousness, fifty-six states are mentioned by way of grasping their differentiated functions. "Seyyathidaṃ" (namely):
"Questions with identical form": this refers to the explicit presentation of the factors as they were asked about—namely, contact (*phassa*)... up to ... rectitude of mind (*cittujukatā*).
The word "iti" indicates either completion or illustration. The connection is: "there are again thirty-three.
"There are thirty-three" means that those same twenty-nine factors [plus four more] are intended.

It was said, “They arise at times”; how is that to be understood? He says, “In these,” and so forth. “By way of compassion and gladness” means by way of the preliminary work (*parikamma*) consisting of compassion and gladness that proceeds from the first mental application (*samannāhāra*) up to the end of the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*).

“The preliminary stage of compassion” means the preliminary stage of compassion; it refers to the cultivation of compassion that proceeds by way of both the preliminary work and the absorption (*appanā*).

From the perspective of the stages leading to absorption (*appanā*), it means that starting from the first act of attention, it constitutes the stage of preliminary work (*parikamma*) occurring up to the end of the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*).
This is also the meaning in the phrase "the prior stage of sympathetic joy" (*muditā-pubbabhāgo*).

Because the word *bhāga* denotes a substance and because a *tappurisa* compound has the final member as its predominant referent, it is expressed in the masculine gender in such phrases as "the prior stage of compassion" (*karuṇā-pubbabhāgo*).
However, because the word *eta* functions as a quality-term (*guṇavutti*), when it refers to that which possesses a specific quality, it conforms to the gender of that [quality].
Thus, in reference to compassion (*karuṇā*) and appreciative joy (*muditā*), it is stated as “these two” (*etā*) in the feminine gender. But they do not arise simultaneously;

rather, the meaning is that they arise separately, one after the other. For this very reason, there is the alternative formulation: “either the preliminary stage of compassion, or the preliminary stage of appreciative joy.”

"Thus it is said. But why do these two not arise together? Because their objects are distinct. For compassion (*karuṇā*) proceeds by taking suffering beings as its object, with the desire to remove their suffering;
whereas sympathetic joy (*muditā*) proceeds by taking happy beings as its object, with the rejoicing in their happiness.
Therefore, because the spheres of both are distinct, their simultaneous arising in a single consciousness is impossible.
"By wrong action, etc."—by the word "etc.," there is the inclusion of wrong speech and wrong livelihood. "They fulfill right action, etc.
means they fulfill right action, right speech, and right livelihood. Regarding "which one of the abstinences": among the three, one abstinence arises;
that which fulfills right action is the first, that which fulfills right speech is the second, and [that which fulfills] right livelihood...
The meaning is that the third abstinence arises as they fulfill [their respective functions].

They do not arise together with compassion (*karuṇā*) and sympathetic joy (*muditā*), because those two have concepts as their objects, whereas abstinence has exclusively limited objects. Furthermore, they do not arise with one another because even for each other, their spheres of activity are distinct.
For the objects of wrong action and so forth are, respectively, the very objects of right action and so forth.
"Objects" [are so called] because of the state of abstaining from them. "In these" means in these five.

(68) Although one should have said "in compassion, sympathetic joy, and so forth" (*karuṇāmuditādīsu*) for the sake of including the other forms of abstinence as well, it is stated as "in compassion and sympathetic joy" (*karuṇāmuditāsu*) by the elision of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) for the sake of the meter of the verse. And having done so, it is stated "by one," otherwise—
“‘Of one’ should be said. 69–71.
What, then, is the reason here that two of the four divine abodes (brahmavihāras) are specified here, and not the others?

One who raises this objection says, “But why,” and so forth. The connection is: “And equanimity (upekkhā) has not been extracted [from the list]. By means of the nine supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma)...

He is a *dhammarāja* (Dharma King) because he delights the people. He is the Teacher (*satthā*) because he instructs the world with its devas in matters pertaining to both the present life and the future life.
By "non-ill will" (*abyāpāda*), loving-kindness (*mettā*) is included, since at the time it functions as a mode of promoting the welfare of others, it takes on the nature of loving-kindness;
for this very reason, it is defined as "loving-kindness, the act of loving-kindness," and so forth. By "equanimity" (*upekkhā*), equanimity based on neutrality (*tatramajjhattatā*) is included.
Because it functions with an attitude of equanimity toward beings, it constitutes the divine abode (brahmavihāra) of equanimity.
He is called "Kinsman of the Sun" (Ādiccabandhu) because he shares the same lineage as the Sun, or because he is the son of that Blessed One by virtue of being a noble disciple;
thus, the Sun is his kinsman, or he is the kinsman of the Sun.
72. "Pile up" means to heap together the seventeenfold collection beginning with the fivefold contact.

By way of the first great arising of consciousness: "There is contact, there is feeling, there is perception, there is volition, there is consciousness, there is applied thought, there is sustained thought, there is rapture, there is pleasure, there is one-pointedness of mind, there is the faculty of faith, there is the faculty of energy..."
There is the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of wisdom, the faculty of mind, the faculty of mental pleasure, the faculty of life;
there is right view, right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration; there is the power of faith, the power of energy... [and so forth].
There is the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, the power of wisdom, the power of moral shame, and the power of moral dread;
there is non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion; there is absence of covetousness, absence of ill will, and right view;
there is moral shame, moral dread, tranquility of body, tranquility of mind, and lightness of body.
“There is lightness of mind, lightness of body; malleability of mind, malleability of body; wieldiness of mind, wieldiness of body;
proficiency of mind, proficiency of body; rectitude of mind, rectitude of body;
mindfulness, clear comprehension, serenity, insight, exertion, and non-distraction.”
Thus, while extracting the Dhamma, the Blessed One took thirty phenomena— beginning with contact— and made them fifty-six, [grouping them as follows]: the heap of the fivefold contact,
the heap of the fivefold jhāna, the heap of the eightfold faculty, the heap of the fivefold path, the heap of the sevenfold power,
the heap of the threefold root-cause, the heap of the threefold course of action, the heap of the two-fold world-guardian, the heap of the six pairs, and the heap of the two-fold assistance.

The classification is made by way of seventeen groups, beginning with the group of the two difficult-to-master factors of coupling (yuganaddha) and the group of the two difficult-to-master factors of energy and serenity (vīriya-samatha). How so?
Even among these, first, having reached the pentad of contact, consciousness is called "consciousness" (citta); having reached the faculties, it is called the "mind-faculty" (manindriya).
Having reached the jhāna factors, applied thought (vitakka) is called "applied thought"; [having reached] the path factors...

Having reached the [category of] right intention, it is called "right intention. Faith, having reached the faculties, is called "the faculty of faith," and having reached the powers, "the power of faith.
Shame, having reached the powers, is called "the power of shame," and having reached the dyad of world-protectors, it is called "shame.
The same method applies to fear of wrongdoing as well. Non-greed, having reached the roots, is called "non-greed," and having reached the path of action—

Having reached the path of action, it is called "non-covetousness. Having reached non-hatred as its root, it is described as "there is non-hatred," and having reached the path of action, it is "non-ill will.
These seven are analyzed in two places. Feeling, however, having reached the pentad of contact, is described as "feeling";
having reached the factors of jhāna, it is "bliss"; and having reached the faculties, it is "the faculty of mental joy. Thus this...
A single dhamma is analyzed into three states. However, when *vīriya* (energy) reaches the faculties (*indriya*), it is called "the faculty of energy" (*vīriyindriya*);

when it reaches the path-factors (*maggaṅga*), it is called "right effort" (*sammāvāyāma*); when it reaches the powers (*bala*), it is called "the power of energy" (*vīriyabala*); and when it reaches the factor of energy-tranquility (*vīriyasamatha*), it is called "exertion" (*paggāha*).
Likewise, when mindfulness (*sati*) reaches the faculties, it is called "the faculty of mindfulness" (*satindriya*); when it reaches the path-factors... [text truncated]
Having reached the [set of] right mindfulness, it is called "right mindfulness"; having reached the [set of] powers, it is called "the power of mindfulness";

and having reached the pair of beneficial factors, it is called "mindfulness. Thus these two states are analyzed in four contexts. Concentration, however, when reaching the jhāna factors, is called "one-pointedness of mind";
when reaching the faculties, it is called "the faculty of concentration"; and when reaching the path factors, it is called "right concentration."
Having reached the powers, it is called "the power of concentration"; having reached the pair of the twin method, it is called "tranquility";
and having reached energy and tranquility, it is said that "there is non-distraction. Thus, this single state is analyzed in six ways.
Wisdom, however, when reaching the faculties, is called "the faculty of wisdom"; when reaching the path factors, it is called "right view"; and [when reaching] the powers...
When it reaches the stage of "the power of wisdom" (*paññābala*), it is called "non-delusion" (*amoha*); when it reaches the path of action (*kammapatha*), it is called "right view" (*sammādiṭṭhi*);

when it reaches the dyad of assistance (*upakāraduka*), it is called "clear comprehension" (*sampajañña*); and when it reaches the dyad of the twin [practice] (*yuganandhaduka*), it is called "insight" (*vipassanā*).

Thus, this single dhamma is analyzed into seven places. In this way, these twelve dhammas, by virtue of possessing their respective functions such as that of the faculties (*indriya*) and so forth, [are established].

They are classified into seventeen groups by way of the division into those with two bases (*dviṭṭhānika*), and so forth. As for the other eighteen, because they lack such divisions according to their functions, they are all "single-based" (*ekaṭṭhānika*).

Therefore, it is said that "they do not belong to a group," considering that among these seventeen groups, the "included states" (*yevāpanaka-dhamma*) do not even belong to a single group, as they exist according to their respective functions.
[Objection: "But surely, although these [remaining] groups do not include them, they are established by way of a collective inclusion of similar functions.

However, since the group of the five beginning with contact is established specifically by way of the aggregate-inclusion (*khandha-saṅgaha*), it is logical that they be included therein, as they are comprised within the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) just like volition (*cetanā*).
[Reply: That is not so; for even though the group of the five beginning with contact is established by way of the aggregate-inclusion,"

It is established by including those factors common to all consciousness, because desire (*chanda*) and the other two [volition and contact] arise only occasionally and thus lack the quality of being common to all consciousness;
and although attention (*manasikāra*) is indeed common to all consciousness, it is not included in the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) in the primary sense,
and therefore these three do not even share the same classification as the pentad of contact (*phassapañcaka*).
"Appropriate. But why is it that, in the ultimate sense (*nippariyāyato*), attention (*manasikāra*) is not included within the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*)?
It is said: because, with the exception of volition (*cetanā*), all other phenomena proceed in dependence upon others even in the performance of their own respective functions;

therefore, the characteristic of "forming" (*abhisaṅkharaṇalakkhaṇa*) is not found [in them] in the ultimate sense. If it were so found, then [it would apply to] one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
Because they are common to all consciousness, those [mental factors] should have been mentioned within the pentad of contact (phassapañcaka), just like feeling and consciousness;

however, they were not so mentioned. Therefore, apart from volition (cetanā), the characteristic of "volitionally constructing" (abhisaṅkharaṇa) does not exist in a non-figurative sense for the remaining phenomena;

thus, their inclusion in the aggregates (khandhasaṅgaha) is not obtained in a non-figurative sense. But it is only in the case of volition that—by way of accomplishing its own function and the functions of others—[the characteristic of constructing is found].

Because it exists as a process and because it possesses, in the ultimate sense, the characteristic of volitional formation (*abhisaṅkharaṇa*), its inclusion within the aggregates (*khandha*) is obtained.
If this is so, how is it that contact (*phassa*) is mentioned among the fivefold set of contact? Because of such statements as, "With contact as condition, feeling arises; being touched, one feels;
being touched, one perceives," [contact is the basis] for these immaterial aggregates, namely: feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness.
Contact (phassa) is mentioned there because, while standing at the stage of the summary (uddesa), it also desires to summarize their respective conditions.

They are "weak" because they function even within their own domain only by being dependent on others. For resolution (adhimokkha) functions dependently on concentration (samādhi), since its manifestation depends on the manifestation of concentration;
likewise, attention (manasikāra) functions dependently on volition (cetanā), since its manifestation depends on the manifestation of volition.
They are indeed dependent on others. 73.

*Manasīkāra* is both *manasi* and *kāra*. For the term *manasikāra*, there is an analysis into separate members (*asamāsa*) for the sake of ease in composing the verse, as well as the lengthening of the vowel and the inclusion of the word *ca* in the middle; these serve to indicate merely the meaning of the word.
The connection is with the phrase "by that best of sages.
(74–80) "From the first impact" means from the very first striking [of the object] by way of contacting the objective field (*ārammaṇa*).

Since all mental factors (*cetasika*) are dependent on the mind and are spoken of as being the activity of the mind, it is said "of the mind" (*cittassa*). The particle *kira* indicates a lack of approval.
Having thus shown the opinion of the Mahāsaṅghikas, the following passage beginning with “But having touched” is now stated in order to elaborate upon that very point.
For the Mahāsaṅghikas maintain: “First, contact touches the object; then, secondly, feeling feels what has been touched by that [contact];
thus, thirdly, perception perceives what has been touched and felt by these two; but by those [three], what has been touched, felt, and perceived...”
They say, "The fourth [mental factor] unites the phenomena associated with volition," and so forth.

"Because it is a powerful condition" means that just as pillars are a powerful condition for the remaining building materials once the palace has been reached, so too is this [volition] a powerful condition for the remaining associated factors;
such is the meaning. "Therefore" is the conclusion based on the reason.
In the phrase *saheva ca*, the particle *ca* is used in the sense of *aṭṭhāna* (impropriety); it should be understood as following the word *cittajānaṃ*. Why?
Because it should be understood here that the connection between the words is: "It occurs together with the mind and the mind-born [phenomena] by way of simultaneous arising and so forth.
*Idaṃ* refers to this aforementioned method; thus, having set aside the reason "because of the first impact," etc.
Now, while resolving the objection that [the mind-consciousness-element] is "due to its being a powerful condition," he says:
"The powerful... is not seen. The word *ca* is used for emphasis; the meaning is "it is certainly not seen.

For since the state of being a co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*) is common to all other factors as well, no reason whatsoever is seen for its alone having the status of a powerful condition. If all this is without reason, how then...
Since contact was mentioned first, he said, "According to the order of the teaching," and so forth.

One might also cite such passages as, "There is feeling, there is contact, there is perception, there is contact, there is volition, there is contact, there is consciousness, there is contact, there is feeling, there is perception, there is volition, there is applied thought," and so on; however, according to the section of the teaching [in question],...
It should be understood that contact (*phassa*) is mentioned first. And just as it is here, so too in the case of the remaining phenomena, one need not search for a sequence of priority.
"By way of the meaning of the words and by way of characteristics" means both from the perspective of the etymological meaning and from the perspective of the defining characteristics.
"It touches" (*phusati*) is a designation of the agent. The reason for this has already been stated below; or else, "that by which they touch" is contact (*phassa*).
For the associated states (sampayutta-dhammā), while occurring with respect to an object, are as if touching it by means of contact (phassa) characterized by touching;
or, contact is simply the mere touching of the object—thus the threefold proof is indeed appropriate.
"That which has touching as its characteristic" is *phusanalakkhaṇo*; in the sense of being a condition for feeling (*vedanā*), it is "that which has the characteristic of touching the object."
Meaning: Its function (*rasa*) is impact. It has the task of impacting because it impacts the mind-object (*ārammaṇa*) at the mind-door (*manodvāra*).
For even though it does not adhere to the object, it causes the mind to strike against the object, just as the eye strikes against visible form or the ear strikes against sound.

Or, in the case of the five doors, it is called "accomplished through impact" (*saṃghaṭṭana-sampattika*) because it is accomplished by the impact between the physical bases (*vatthu*) and the objects.

Contact (phassa) is said to have "impact" as its essence. Just as in such expressions as "two hands might strike each other," the striking occurs in the hand and consists of material phenomena (rūpadhamma) that are specific to it, so too the impact of consciousness upon its object should be understood as a single mental factor (cetasikadhamma) that is specific to it.
This is because it is made known by way of its own cause, namely, the conjunction of the three.
It has the manifestation of a collocation (*sannipāta*). For, according to the statement, “Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises;

the meeting of the three is contact,” it is to be understood by way of the collocation of the three—the eye, the form, and the consciousness—and because it manifests as such, it is called "manifestation" in the sense of being the manifestation of that cause termed "collocation. In this sense of manifestation, it is [contact].
By way of its manifestation, it is said to have the manifestation of a meeting. Because of the statement, “With contact as condition, feeling arises,” feeling is its fruit;

thus, it has feeling as its manifestation. Since it arises immediately and without obstruction when the object has been prepared by the corresponding attention and the sense faculty, it has the object that has come into the range [of the senses] as its proximate cause (*padatthāna*). For this [feeling] is the result of that contact.

The "appropriate attention" (samannāhāra) is that which serves as the cause and conforms to it; because it arises exclusively with respect to an object that has already entered the range of the senses—
having been prepared and conditioned by the advertence (āvajjana) known as "attention born thereof" and by the eye-faculty and so forth, respectively,
through the processes of making the object its focus and turning toward it— the object that has entered the range of the senses is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna).
"Of this" means its proximate cause; thus, its proximate basis (*padaṭṭhāna*) is the object that has come into the range of the senses.

Now, one might raise an internal objection: "Is this not a mental factor (*cetasika*)? Since it is a non-material phenomenon (*arūpadhamma*), how can it have the characteristic of touching (*phusanalakkhaṇa*)?
Bearing this in mind, the passage beginning with "Even though it is a non-material phenomenon" was stated in order to resolve that objection.
In this context, by the phrase "it occurs in the mode of touching," he shows that this is the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of that phenomenon, even though it is immaterial (*arūpa*).
And that occurrence of its mode of touching is like the salivation of another person upon seeing someone eating sour mangoes and the like;
or like the trembling of the body of a compassionate person upon seeing one being tormented; or [like the movement] at the tip of a tree branch...

It should be understood as being like the trembling of the shanks of a man standing on the ground when he sees another man who is deformed, or the stiffening of the thighs when he sees something to be feared, such as a *pisāca* demon, and so forth. "That" (*so*) refers to that contact characterized by the aforementioned features and so on.
"Beautiful" (*sundaraṃ*) means praiseworthy because it is associated with pleasant feeling. "Mind" (*mano*) is consciousness (*viññāṇa*). "The state of one who is well-minded" (*sumanassa bhāvo*)...
It is the state of consciousness known as *sumanas*. That object which serves as the basis for the arising of the word (*sadda*) is *somanassa*.

For it is because it is associated with the feeling of joy (*somanassavedanā*) that the word *sumanas* applies to that consciousness. It is called "that which is felt" (*vedayita*) because it has been brought about and occurred in the manner of experiencing through feeling;
it has this as its characteristic, thus it is "characterized by being felt" (*vedayitalakkhaṇā*). [It arises] from the desirable aspect of what is desirable...

"Experiencing is its function" means that its essence (*rasa*) is the experiencing of a desirable aspect. For, by its very nature, it experiences a desirable object as desirable, and it also experiences other [objects] precisely as a desirable aspect. In this context, the experiencing of a desirable aspect is found in feeling associated with wholesome and unwholesome consciousness, because even an undesirable [object] is grasped there as a desirable aspect through the power of conceptualization (*kappanā*). However, the experiencing of what is desirable by way of its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*)— [The text continues: ...is found only in wholesome consciousness. As for the experiencing of an undesirable aspect, it is found in unwholesome consciousness; for even a desirable object is grasped there as an undesirable aspect through the power of conceptualization. But the experiencing of what is undesirable by way of its own intrinsic nature is found only in unwholesome consciousness. The experiencing of what is neither-desirable-nor-undesirable by way of its own intrinsic nature is found in resultant indeterminate (*vipāka-abyākata*) and functional indeterminate (*kiriyā-abyākata*) consciousness. The experiencing of the desirable aspect in both [the desirable and the undesirable] is found in wholesome-resultant consciousness. The experiencing of the undesirable aspect in both is found in unwholesome-resultant consciousness. The experiencing of the neutral aspect in both is found in functional indeterminate consciousness. Thus, the experiencing of the desirable aspect in both is found in wholesome-resultant consciousness; the experiencing of the undesirable aspect in both is found in unwholesome-resultant consciousness; and the experiencing of the neutral aspect in both is found in functional indeterminate consciousness. This is the detailed analysis. In this context, "desirable" refers to the five cords of sensual pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇā*); "undesirable" refers to the opposite of those five cords of sensual pleasure; and "neutral" refers to the remaining states. "By way of its own intrinsic nature" means according to the actual mode of being of the object. "Through the power of conceptualization" means by way of mental construction. "Grasping" means apprehending. "By way of its own intrinsic nature" means according to the actual mode of being of the object. "Wholesome-resultant consciousness" refers to the eight types of sense-sphere wholesome-resultant consciousness. "Unwholesome-resultant consciousness" refers to the two types of unwholesome-resultant consciousness. "Functional indeterminate consciousness" refers to the nine types of sense-sphere functional indeterminate consciousness. "This is the detailed analysis" concludes the explanation of the meaning of the term "experiencing. Furthermore, "experiencing" is a synonym for feeling (*vedanā*). Feeling is the experiencing of the desirable aspect, the experiencing of the undesirable aspect, and the experiencing of the neutral aspect. It is the experiencing of the desirable aspect in both [the desirable and the undesirable], the experiencing of the undesirable aspect in both, and the experiencing of the neutral aspect in both. It is also obtained when associated with an indeterminate (abyākata) state of mind, because that [indeterminate state] lacks the grasping of perversions (vipallāsa). By the phrase "like a king to the taste of fine food," this is illustrated:
there is for contact (phassa) merely the act of touching; for perception (saññā), merely the act of perceiving; for volition (cetanā), merely the act of intending;
and for consciousness (viññāṇa), merely the act of cognizing. However, [the king's role] is solely by virtue of his sovereignty.
Feeling experiences the flavor of the object through its own nature, just as a king [experiences] the flavor of fine food prepared by a cook.
That which is relished is "gratification" (*assāda*); it is pleasant feeling. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Bhikkhus, whatever pleasure and joy arise dependent upon the five aggregates of clinging—this, bhikkhus, is called the gratification in the five aggregates of clinging."

“...the gratification. Because it is dependent on the mind, its existence in the mind is the gratification of mental factors; thus, it is said to have the manifestation of the gratification of mental factors (*cetasika-assāda-paccupaṭṭhāna*).
It is said to have “tranquillity as its proximate cause” because one who has a tranquil body experiences happiness.
This, however, should be understood by way of spiritual joy (*nirāmisa-somanassa*).
It has the characteristic of perceiving; that is, having made the perception of the object—such as blue and so forth—the very act of perceiving, it knows [it].
Thus, it is "characterized by perceiving" (*sañjānanalakkhaṇā*). Its function is to effect recognition (*paccābhiññāṇakaraṇa-rasa*);

for "recognition" (*paccābhiññāṇa*) is that by which one recognizes again (*pati abhiññāyati*), and its "sign" (*nimitta*) is the aspect such as shape and so forth, which serves as the basis for recognizing it again as "that very same thing. Its function is the performance of that [recognition]; this is its task.
Its function is to provide a basis for subsequent recognition. For when it arises, it does so by grasping the configuration or other features that serve as the cause for later identification.

This [function] should be applied to all types of common perception—both that which produces a sign and that which recognizes by means of a sign—for even that which recognizes by means of a sign [serves as a basis] for further recognition by another perception.

“He makes a sign”: this should be understood as taking the perception of wholesome, unwholesome, or functional impulsion (*javana*) as the primary factor. As for how this making of a sign is to be regarded, he says: “like a carpenter’s making of a mark.
Just as a carpenter [identifies] in pieces of wood, “this is the top, this is the bottom,” so too [it is] the condition for subsequent recognition.
The making of a sign means, in this context, the making of a cause for future recognition.

Because one forms an adherence based on the sign as it was grasped through the perception that "this alone is the truth," like a blind man who has seen an elephant, [perception] has the manifestation of such adherence.
By this, it is shown that view and the other [defilements] arise in one who stands having performed the grasping of the mode [of the object] by means of perception.

The manifestation of the fruit is shown by way of its conformity with unwholesome perception (*akusalasaññā*). Alternatively, "the making of a fixed adherence" refers merely to the adherence to a perception, thinking, "This alone is the truth.

Therefore, because it manifests in the mode of adherence according to the sign as it was grasped through the state of investigation, it is said to have "adherence as its manifestation" (*ākārapaccupaṭṭhāna*). [As in the case of] young deer [seeing] grass-men.
“Persons”: because their intrinsic nature is non-conceptualizing, like a perception that has already arisen, they have as their proximate cause the object exactly as it presents itself.
And here, at the time of arising by way of grasping the mode of appearance through a perception dissociated from knowledge, the consciousness is indeterminate and follows the lead of the perception.

But in the case of a consciousness associated with knowledge, both perception and consciousness follow one another, just as the remaining elements follow the element of earth when it is accompanied by its constituent parts.
It is expressed as "it is" (atthi) and follows after knowledge.
"It binds together" (abhisandahati) means it connects, it causes to proceed; the meaning is that, as if saying "Seize!
Seize!", it applies the associated mental states toward the object and establishes them in their respective functions. It has the characteristic of volition for one who has fallen asleep...
At the moment of awakening, it has the characteristic of the mind’s exertion, like the onset of agitation.

Alternatively, because it is said to "connect" (*abhisandahati*), its meaning is precisely that it has the characteristic of application. Its function is "striving" (*āyūhana*); that is to say, its function is the mental effort (*iriyanā*) of the mental factors;

it is said to have the function of "exertion. However, this [mental factor] is obtained only when associated with wholesome, unwholesome, functional, or javana consciousness. It is manifested as "connecting" (*saṃvidahana*).
It has "investigation" as its manifestation because it is, as it were, deliberating, "Do this!

For when this [mental factor] is active, all associated states become intent upon their respective functions; for that very reason, it is said to accomplish both its own function and the functions of others.
It is like an elder student who, while urging others toward recitation, recites himself as well; for while they are reciting...
When the eldest pupil has begun, the other pupils also begin their recitation; when the chief carpenter has begun his work, the others likewise do so.
Thus he said, "like the eldest pupil, the chief carpenter, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the inclusion of the eldest resident disciples and others is intended.
This is for the purpose of precluding the notion of mastery over phenomena that proceed according to their own conditions, as there is no such thing as exercising control over them.

“It is the thinking of thought (vitakkana) that is called ‘thought’ (vitakka),” it is said. This means the striking against an object, the imagining of it, or rather, the directing [of the mind] toward it.
Because the mind, through the power of thought, becomes as if it has mounted upon the object, it is therefore said:
“It has the characteristic of directing the mind onto the object. For example, just like some man living in a village...

Just as one ascends to or enters the royal palace by relying on a favorite of the king or a friend connected to him, so too does consciousness ascend to its object by relying on initial application (vitakka).
If this is so, how does consciousness devoid of initial application (avitakkacitta) ascend to its object?
For initial application is not found in the two types of fivefold sense-consciousness, nor in the second jhāna and those that follow, yet it is by the power of which [consciousness] [ascends].
It ascends to that object; therefore, does it not arise there by its own nature through the power of meditation? True, yet even that ascends by the power of applied thought (*vitakka*).

For just as that man, through familiarity, enters the royal palace without apprehension even without [the king's] presence, so too, through familiarity, the thought-free mind (*avitakkacitta*) ascends to the object even without applied thought.
In this context, "familiarity" refers to the cultivation of the mind that occurs frequently within the mental continuum.
For, through the influence of applied thought (vitakka) occurring repeatedly in the continuum, the mind's mounting upon its object becomes long-practiced;
consequently, that mind sometimes proceeds toward that object even without applied thought. This is just as it does when accompanied by knowledge (ñāṇa).
Just as that which was long familiar through the practice of comprehension may at times proceed even without knowledge by way of comprehension,
or just as that which proceeded accompanied by defilements may proceed entirely free from defilements yet still function by way of the latent tendencies of defilement due to past habituation—
so too should this case be understood.

Alternatively, although the two sets of fivefold consciousness are without applied thought (*avitakka*), they "strike" the object because of the strength of the impact between the physical base and the object;
and the second jhāna and those above it "ascend" to the object because of the strength of the preceding lower-stage cultivation.
"Striking" (*āhanana*) means either an initial, direct striking or a mere blow; "striking thoroughly" (*parāhanana*) means striking all around or striking with particular distinction.
"Striking" (*pariyāhanana*) means that this is its function; thus it has "striking and repeated striking" as its function.
For it is said that by means of this, the practitioner strikes the object with thought and repeatedly strikes it with thought.
"Leading on" (*ānayana*) is the bringing of the mind toward the object or its drawing [toward it]; since it is manifested as being thus, it has "leading on" as its manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*).
"By that" means by that sustained thought (*vicāra*), acting as an instrument or as a cause, the mind ranges over and explores the object.
However, the mode of occurrence for a mind devoid of sustained thought should be understood according to what was stated regarding the mind devoid of applied thought (*avitakka*).

Ranging, exploring, and traversing [the object]—this specific distinction, while obtainable within a continuum (*santāna*), should be seen as becoming manifest in the continuum of impulsion (*javana*).
This same method applies to the others as well. "Anumāsanā" (investigation) means the rubbing over of the object;

its characteristic is the complete rubbing over of the object, thus it is said to have the characteristic of rubbing over the object (*ārammaṇānumajjanalakkhaṇo*). For in this way, sustained application (*vicāra*) is spoken of as being like a hand that rubs all around, or like a hand that moves about.
"Therein" (*tattha*) means in the object. It is the application to co-nascent states by way of the rubbing over (*anumajjana*) defined as the repeated moving about in the object.
This should be understood. For there is no such thing as an activity that is divorced from the intrinsic nature (sabhāva) of phenomena.

Thus, although a phenomenon possessing an intrinsic nature is in the ultimate sense of a single nature, it is nevertheless manifested in many ways through figurative expressions and through various forms superimposed upon its object, in accordance with the needs of those who are to be enlightened. For in this way, it is thoroughly elucidated.
"Manifestation as uninterrupted continuity" means it manifests as the occurrence of the mind upon an object as if without interruption.
For it is described as "linking together.
And here, in comparison to investigation (vicāra), by virtue of its grossness and its role as its precursor, it is like the sound of the first stroke of a gong.
Initial application (*vitakka*) is the first impact of the mind; sustained application (*vicāra*) is the subsequent wandering, like an after-resonance.

For just as the first sound produced by striking a bell is grosser than the after-resonance and acts as its precursor, so too initial application is gross in the sense of directing the mind toward the object and acts as its precursor.
Subsequently, sustained application is subtle in its nature of continuous touching.
And sustained thought (*vicāra*) is without continuous succession, like the resonance of a bell. Furthermore, initial application (*vitakka*) is expansive;

at the moment of the mind’s first arising, it constitutes a surging forth of the mind, like the flapping of the wings of a bird wishing to fly into the sky, or like the bee’s rush toward a lotus when its mind is drawn by the fragrance. Sustained thought (*vicāra*), however, is a peaceful movement of the mind.
The state of not being excessively agitated is like the spreading of wings by a bird that has flown into the air, or like the hovering above a lotus by a bee that has fallen toward it.
However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary), this is presented in reverse order. And so it is stated in the commentary on the *Dukanipāta*:
“Vitakka is like the flight of a great bird traveling through the sky, which proceeds by catching the wind with both wings and bringing them to rest;
vicāra is like the flight of one who proceeds while fluttering the wings for the purpose of catching the wind.”
This too is applicable to its occurrence in a continuous flow.

For, whether in access concentration or in absorption, during its occurrence as a continuum, applied thought (vitakka) proceeds as if it has entered the object after becoming steady; it is not as manifest as it was at the initial impact.
"It gladdens" means it causes the body and mind to enter into absorption, or it causes them to increase. "Characterized by endearing" means [endearing] the object because of its pleasantness.
Its characteristic is grasping. Its function is to refresh, meaning its task is to nourish both body and mind. Its function is pervasion:

it has the function of pervading the body with sublime material qualities; what is meant is that it causes the entire material body to be pervaded by the material qualities originated by the consciousness associated with itself.
For otherwise there would be no such pervasion by this [pleasure], since phenomena (dhammas) are devoid of agency.
Because there is not even a hair’s breadth of wavering. *Udaggabhāva* (exultation) is the state of being uplifted.

That which has a single object as its peak is *ekagga*; this refers to the mind (*citta*). Furthermore, that quality through association with which the mind becomes "one-pointed" is the state of one-pointedness (*ekaggabhāva*).
And since this belongs to the mind alone and not to anything else, he said: "of the mind."
"One-pointedness" means the stability of the mind like the steadiness of a lamp-flame in a windless place; this is what is meant.

Non-distraction (*avisāra*) is the natural state that is the opposite of the scattered or wavering state; it is not merely the absence of scattering. He said "characterized by non-distraction" because this is its defining mark.
Non-agitation (*avikkhepa*) is the state of being undistracted among associated mental factors; [this refers to] non-distraction and non-agitation.
It should be understood that although there is no difference in meaning due to their state of being concentrated (*samādhāna*), both are stated by way of direct presence and by way of association.

It is "manifested as tranquility" (*upasama-paccupaṭṭhāna*) because it presents itself in the mode of calming the mind, being the antidote to distraction (*vikkhepa*) which has the characteristic of non-tranquility.
"By way of distinction" means for the most part; for there is [concentration] even when devoid of pleasure (*sukha*).
Regarding "concentration": for the most part, that has happiness as its proximate cause. Alternatively, "distinguished" means preeminent.

For according to the statement, "The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated," happiness is the specific cause of concentration; this is because concentration succeeds even for one devoid of happiness solely through the support of that [previous] happiness.

"By means of this they have faith" (saddahanti etāya) indicates that faith is the condition for those phenomena occurring as the act of believing in the results of karma and so forth, by virtue of its sovereignty over them.
For when faith functions as such a condition for those phenomena, the person possessing it is conventionally described as "one who has faith.
Faith is the act of believing, which is the acceptance of an object worthy of belief.

Its characteristic is that of this [faith]: it has the characteristic of believing. Its function is that of clarifying: its task is to cause the clarity of associated states, or of the person themselves, by dispelling the stain of turbidity.
To the question "In what way?", he says: "Like a water-clearing gem. It is manifested as non-turbidity, meaning it is manifested as the state of being unclouded.
The Triple Gem, kamma, and the fruit of kamma are the objects of faith; these constitute its proximate cause.
Indeed, faith does not arise toward those such as the followers of other sects who do not serve as the objective basis for it.
Furthermore, this faith is like a hand in taking up wholesome states, like wealth in bestowing all forms of prosperity, and like a seed in producing the fruit of the deathless.
And it should be viewed as being like that. For here, the supporting evidence is such statements as: "The noble disciple has faith as his hand, Mahānāma; faith is the supreme wealth of a person here;
faith is the seed, austerity is the rain," and so forth.
It is called *saraṇa* because by means of it one remembers (*saranti*); thus, it is so named by virtue of its sovereignty over those phenomena that proceed as the act of going for refuge.
It shows that mindfulness is a condition. For when there is such a state of being a condition for phenomena, the person possessing it is conventionally designated as "one who remembers.
