Non-floating (*apilāpana*) is the placing of the object in a state of immobility—like a stone—and not allowing it to drift away like a gourd in water;
it is the making of non-forgetfulness. Since this is its characteristic, it is called "having non-floating as its characteristic" (*apilāpanalakkhaṇā*).
For it is called a "pillar" because it is firmly established upon its object. Its function is to counteract confusion;

its essence is non-confusion, not merely the absence of confusion. Because it is said, "He dwells with a mind guarded by mindfulness," it is described as "manifesting as protection," since it wards off the thieves of the defilements that steal the jewels of the qualities of the mind. For it likewise protects the doors of the eye and so forth.
The "gatekeeper" is so called because, first, perception establishes firmness in the arising [of the object], and subsequently, mindfulness becomes established there;
thus it is said, "having firm perception as its proximate cause. Now, what is the difference between mindfulness and perception? First, perception perceives an object that has not yet been grasped;
then, regarding the object already grasped, it acts as the condition for subsequent recognition.
However, when it has not been grasped first, the function of perception (*saññā*) is secondary, whereas mindfulness (*sati*) remembers both the sign already grasped and even a sign not yet grasped;
thus, when the sign has been grasped, the function of mindfulness becomes the primary factor—this alone is the distinction between them.
"Heroic state" (*vīrabhāva*) refers to that quality by which one becomes known as a hero through energy (*vīriya*). Or, "the work of heroes" (*vīrānaṃ kamma*) refers to that action by which...
It is called "heroic" (*vīra*); that is what is meant by the "deed of heroes. However, it is described as such because energy (*vīriya*) is its accomplishing factor.
Alternatively, since there is no deed whatsoever apart from mental states (*dhamma*), it should be understood that energy itself is spoken of in the sense of being the deed.
Or, energy is that which is to be impelled or set in motion according to the proper method. It is effort, the undertaking of various tasks, and exertion.
Or rather: support (*upatthambhana*) is the sustaining and providing of reinforcement for associated states, preventing them from falling into the side of indolence.
It is the state that prevents the sinking of associated states; it is not merely the absence of sinking, but it manifests as the state of non-sinking;
thus, it is "manifested as the state of non-sinking. "One who is moved by spiritual urgency (*saṃvigga*) [should] apply [the mind] fundamentally..."
Because of the statement, "He is struck by his own foot," it is the basis for the state of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). Here, "spiritual urgency" refers to knowledge consisting of that urgency.
However, for wholesome activity not preceded by such urgency, it is the basis for the undertaking of energy (*vīriyārambha*). In this context, the bases for the undertaking of energy are as follows:
"A path must be traveled; the path has been traveled. A task must be done; the task has been done. It is but a trifle... [and so forth].
An affliction has arisen; he has recovered from illness, having recently emerged from sickness.

While wandering for alms in a village or town, he does not obtain, to his heart’s content and full satisfaction, either coarse or refined food… [as before] …“to his heart’s content and full satisfaction.”—Thus it was said.
Thus have been stated these eight bases for the arousal of energy, accompanied by their appropriate reflections, or the reflections rooted therein.
Herein, thought (vitakka) directs the associated states toward the object; volition (cetanā) enjoins them to their respective functions;
but energy (vīriya), not allowing them to sink, instigates them. This is the distinction between thought, volition, and energy.
"Characterized by cognizing" means characterized by specific knowing; the meaning is that it has the characteristic of penetrating the true nature (yathāsabhāva) [of things].

"Illumination of the object" means the shining upon or making manifest of the objective field (visaya), which is the illumination of the objective support (ārammaṇa) through the dispelling of the darkness of delusion that conceals it;
since this is its function (rasa), it is "having the illumination of the object as its function. By way of not being deluded regarding any given object...
It is "manifested as non-delusion" because it is manifested as the opposite of delusion, or because it is manifested as the absence of delusion.
The function of life is the preservation of the co-nascent states that must be preserved by itself;
and since that is their "living," it is said with reference to its status as their cause: "they live by means of it. [This applies to] the material and immaterial life-faculties.
In order to show the characteristics and so forth according to their respective types, it is said: "of those inseparable from itself.
For if it were stated as "associated," there would be no inclusion of the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*), because material phenomena lack association.
However, because it is stated as "inseparable," those inseparable material phenomena, together with the material life-faculty...
They are inseparable and non-disjoined. This constitutes the inclusion of all those immaterial phenomena that are associated with the immaterial life-faculty (*arūpa-jīvitindriya*).

"Having the function of making them proceed" means their activity of proceeding from arising until dissolution, by way of maintaining them and accomplishing their nature of not turning back in the interim.
However, some [hold that] the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*) [is what maintains] them...
The claim that "from the moment of its stationing, it is a condition for the occurrence of the immaterial life-faculty from the moment of its arising" is not correct.

For in the *Paṭṭhāna*, regarding the faculty-condition for non-percipient beings, it is stated: "In dependence on an indeterminate state—in dependence on one great primary element of non-percipient beings—it is like the kamma-condition. Thus, the faculty-condition for non-percipient beings [is established].
It is stated as being similar to the condition of kamma; therefore, it should be understood that the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*) is also a condition from the moment of its arising.
From arising until its dissolution, it is the "establishment" (*ṭhapanā*) by way of establishing.

Its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) consists of those phenomena that must be maintained and kept in operation by means of preservation; thus, it is the "proximate cause of phenomena to be maintained. If...

Thus, having explained that which accomplishes their preservation and so forth, he asks: how does their cessation come about? For it must be maintained at all times; thus he says, "And even though," and so on.
In the phrase "in [the state] characterized by preservation, etc.," the word "etc. includes its function of maintaining and so forth.

"At the very moment of its existence" means either at the very moment when those things to be preserved by oneself exist, or at the very moment of one's own existence. "Water" refers to the water contained within a reservoir.
Or [it is like] water held in a staff. In that regard, by taking up the water in a pond, one accomplishes the preservation of those things that must be preserved by oneself when they are present;
but by taking up the water in a staff, one preserves them when they are not yet present.
To the question, "How does one preserve things not yet produced by oneself? he says: "Like a nurse for a child. If...
There must be some cause for the occurrence of other phenomena; but what is the cause for the occurrence of life itself?
To this he says: "It occurs by itself... [etc. ...it occurs. How is it like? He says: "Like a pilot.
That too occurs through its connection with the ship set in motion by itself. If the occurrence of phenomena were dependent upon the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), [then...]
He says, "Not after its dissolution," in response to the question, "Does it also cause [the mind] to proceed even beyond dissolution? He asks, "Why?

and replies, "Because of the absence of both itself and those things to be proceeded with. But what about at the moment of dissolution? He says, "It does not establish [it] at the moment of dissolution.
Furthermore, since non-greed (*alobha*) is the opposite of greed (*lobha*), and those phenomena which are associated with it, or the possessor of that [non-greed], [are established].
Beings do not become greedy for them, nor does one oneself ever become greedy; in its true sense, it is simply the mode of non-greed. Therefore, it is said:
"They do not become greedy because of that," and so forth. This same method applies to the phrases "they do not become corrupt because of that," and so on.
Non-adherence is the state of being unattached even while proceeding in dependence upon an object. Thus he said: "Like a lotus petal..."
"A drop of water," it is said. "Without attachment" means not grasping at any object by way of the sense of "mine.
"Like a monk who has cast off [defilements]" means like a monk whose taints are exhausted; for he, because he has abandoned lust, is devoid of the sense of "mine" toward anything.
"One whose disposition is unattached" means one whose intention is such. Thus, by the simile, "like a man fallen into filth," [the meaning is shown].

It is so. For just as that person’s state is "unattached" despite his physical clinging, even so non-greed (alobha), although it takes an object by way of making it its objective support, occurs only in the mode of being unattached due to its lack of stickiness toward the object.
Such indeed is the nature of that dhamma.
The state of being *caṇḍika* is *caṇḍikka*; it is the state of harshness. In meaning, however, it is simply anger (*kopa*). Its opposite, the state of non-harshness, is *acaṇḍikka*.
Non-opposition, non-conflict, and the absence of a contrary side is its natural state (*sabhāva*). Regarding the phrase "having the function of removing resentment" (*āghātavinayanarasa*):
here, "resentment" (*āghāta*) refers to malice (*upanāha*) directed toward another for their own sake, or toward oneself for the sake of another, or toward another for the sake of yet another.
It is strong anger. Its function is to discipline, its function is to remove. Its nature is gentleness by way of immersion, its nature is coolness by way of being delightful.
Therefore he said, "like the full moon.

"By bodily misconduct, etc."—this is an instrumental expression used in the sense of a cause. One feels shame (*hirīyati*) in the manner of being ashamed; one is disgusted by those very things. By those very same [things]...
[It arises] precisely from bodily misconduct and so forth. "Ottappa" means one is terrified. Since *hirī* (shame) looks upon evil as if it were excrement and feels disgust, it is said:
“*Hirī* has the characteristic of disgust for evil. Since *ottappa* (fear of wrongdoing) looks upon that [evil] as if it were heat and recoils from it, it is stated:
“*Ottappa* has the characteristic of trepidation. Both have the function of non-performance of evil; they [act] by way of a sense of shame toward evils.
Moral shame (*hirī*) has the essence of non-doing; moral dread (*ottappa*) has the aspect of being terrified.

They have "the shrinking away from evil" as their manifestation, in the sense that they manifest by way of shrinking away from evil in the manner already described. They have "respect for oneself and respect for others" as their proximate cause:

moral shame has respect for oneself as its proximate cause because it originates within oneself and has oneself as its dominant influence; moral dread has respect for others as its proximate cause because it originates externally.
And [they differ] by way of being the lord of the world. For one abandons evil through shame (*hirī*) by holding oneself in high esteem, like a noble lady;
one abandons evil through dread of blame (*ottappa*) by holding others in high esteem, like a courtesan.

Their status as originating internally and so forth should be understood according to how they are manifest in various instances, but not because of any mutual dissociation between them at any time. Not...
For there is shame that is fearless, or fear of evil that is shameless. However, when shame is predominant, moral dread (*ottappa*) becomes negligible;
when moral dread is predominant, shame becomes negligible. And these two qualities are called "the guardians of the world.
As it has been said:
“Bhikkhus, these two bright qualities protect the world. Which two? Moral shame and moral dread.
Bhikkhus, if these two bright qualities did not protect the world, the designation ‘mother,’ ‘maternal aunt,’ or ‘uncle’s wife’ would not be known here. And so forth.
*Passambhanaṃ* means the subsiding of agitation. The word *kāya* is a term denoting a collection. And here, that [collection] refers to the triad of aggregates beginning with feeling (*vedanā*).
For the word has a specialized application according to the speaker's intention; thus he said, "And here, 'body' (*kāyo*)... and so forth. "Feeling and the rest" refers to the three aggregates:
the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception (*saññā*), and the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhāra*). And it has been stated therein accordingly:
“What, at that time, is bodily tranquility? It is that which, at that time, belongs to the aggregate of feeling,” and so forth.
*Daratha* (distress) is a synonym for the agitation and strife of the defilements such as restlessness which are conditioned by displeasure, or for the four aggregates as they occur in that manner.
That which has the subsiding of this [distress] as its characteristic is “characterized by the subsiding of distress of body and mind.”
The "taste" (*rasa*) of body and mind... [etc. ...is the taste of overcoming those very opposing states previously mentioned.

The state of coolness (*sītibhāva*), free from the burning heat and agitation caused by the crushing of distress, is the "coolness of non-agitation. Agitation (*avūpasama*) is the state of being agitated, a lack of peaceful dwelling.
The "defilements such as restlessness" (*uddhaccādi-kilesa*) refers to mental states associated with restlessness as their predominant factor, or those in which restlessness is excessive.

The defilements (*kilesa*). For these too, by way of restlessness (*uddhacca*), are makers of non-tranquillity. Or, taking restlessness as the first, all defilements whatsoever are "defilements beginning with restlessness.
The same applies to the remaining [terms]. Heaviness (*garubhāva*) is sluggishness (*dandhatā*);

it is a designation for the four aggregates that occur in such a manner when dominated by sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*). Non-sluggishness (*adandhatā*) is the opposite of sluggishness; it is lightness (*agarubhāva*).
Stiffness (*thambha*) is the state of being rigid. This is the name for the four aggregates that are dominated by views and conceit, or those in which these are predominant.
Because they crush out stiffness, they manifest toward certain objects in an unobstructed manner;
or, because they cause their associated mental states to manifest there without obstruction, they are said to have "non-obstruction as their manifestation" (*appaṭighāta-paccupaṭṭhāna*).

"Workable" (*kammañña*) means suitable for action; "unworkable" (*akammañña*) means unsuitable for action. The state of being unworkable is "unworkability" (*akammaññabhāva*), which is the incapacity for performing meritorious deeds such as giving and virtue.
In terms of meaning, it consists of the defiled states beginning with sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), or alternatively, the four unwholesome aggregates dominated by those [defilements].
The perfection of making an object one's focus (*ārammaṇakaraṇasampatti*) is the grasping of an object in a perfected manner precisely through the crushing of that unworkability.
The remaining factors, such as sensual desire and so forth, along with the defilements associated with them, such as the other hindrances and so on,

have already been mentioned. These two, however, should be understood as bringing about clarity regarding objects that inspire confidence through the crushing of the shackles, and as bringing about a state of fitness for application in beneficial activities, like the purification of gold.

Illness consists of lack of faith and so forth, as well as those evil states associated with them; their characteristic is the state of health, which is the opposite of that, hence they are "characterized by the state of health.
Because they crush illness, they have no disadvantage, fault, or affliction, nor do they proceed toward any misery; thus they are "without disadvantage," and they manifest in that manner.
Or, because it presents itself among the associated states as being free from defect, it has "manifestation as faultless" (*nirādīnavapaccupaṭṭhāna*).
Because it is characterized by the state of rectitude belonging to both body and mind, it has "the characteristic of straightness of body and mind.

In its actual sense, it is the opposite of the crookedness of body and mind, which consists of the curvatures known as the curve of a ploughshare, the tip of a crescent moon, and the bend of a cow's tail.
Its function is to crush the crookedness of body and mind by crushing deceit, guile, and so forth.
Precisely for that reason, it manifests itself in every way as straightness, or it causes its associated states to manifest as straight;
thus, it has "manifestation as straightness."

But surely, since each pair of factors—such as bodily tranquility (*kāyapassaddhi*) and so forth—acts as the antidote to one specific opposite, each performs its function, such as crushing resistance, individually.

Why, then, are they taught in pairs? One should not think thus; for even the Blessed One taught them in that very way. Why did the Blessed One teach them in that manner? Because they possess the nature of phenomena with intrinsic characteristics (*sabhāvadhamma*). For it is not...

These phenomena, which did not exist previously, were brought forth by the Blessed One through the power of his teaching; rather, they already existed by way of their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
Having correctly realized them through his self-enlightened knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇa*), he taught them according to their true nature.

Therefore, how could it be possible for the Blessed One to diminish that which exists by way of its own intrinsic nature? And because they exist by way of their own intrinsic nature, [the Blessed One... in this regard...
The word itself is the authority. For the Blessed One would not speak contrary to the Dhamma when it comes to the teaching of the Dhamma.
However, that which is not mentioned despite being present must have another cause;
and no such cause is found here by which there would be a non-mention of each individual factor among these. Just as, for example, between two men, only one is an enemy.
When those men, seeing an opportunity, strike him down together as one, even so do these pairs of states, acting together, strike down a single opposing state.
However, whereas they might strike down that enemy even when seen separately, these do not strike it down separately because of their mutual inseparability; therefore, these...
Although each of the opposing states exists individually, they are spoken of as pairs;

furthermore, through mental serenity (*cittapassaddhi*) and so forth, the mind itself becomes serene, light, malleable, wieldy, and straight. However, through bodily serenity (*kāyapassaddhi*) and so forth, the material body also [becomes so].

It is for the purpose of demonstrating this meaning that the Blessed One has stated this twofold nature specifically in this context, and not in the case of concentration (*samādhi*) and the other factors.
*Chanda* is desire; it is the state of being desirous of an object. However, in such passages as "desire is lust" (*chando kāmo*), craving (*taṇhā*) is also called *chanda*.

In such passages as "he generates desire and exerts effort" (*chandaṃ janeti vāyamatī*), energy (*vīriya*) is also referred to as *chanda*. Therefore, in order to exclude those [other meanings], it is stated:
"This is a designation for the wish-to-do (*kattukamyatā*). The wish-to-do is said to be the desire to act. [It is] a mental factor (*cetasika-dhamma*).
Because it has an object, the desire to act arises specifically through the desire to take an object as its support;
thus, zeal, which has the characteristic of desiring to act upon an object, is described as having the characteristic of "the desire to do. For this very reason, it is said:

"Its function is the seeking of an object, and it is manifested as a need for an object. Furthermore, to the extent that this [zeal] has the function of seeking an object for itself, to that same extent...
The associated states (sampayuttadhammā) likewise possess the quality of having a single object (ekārammaṇatā).
Therefore, it is said that in the grasping of an object, they are like the stretching out of the hand of consciousness.

But how is it that the desire (chanda) associated with volition (cetanā), which proceeds by way of relinquishing the basis for giving, is "desirous of the object"? Have we not already stated that its characteristic is "the wish to make something an object"? Therefore—

Just as one who has entered a battle has need for the grasping of arrows that have been shot, so too, the desire that proceeds by way of relinquishing objects of giving has need precisely for that which is to be relinquished.

This desire arising in relation to wholesome states is called "wholesome desire" because it originates from wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*). Conversely, that which arises in relation to unwholesome states is "unwholesome desire."

Adhimuccana (resolute conviction) should be understood by way of certainty regarding the object, not by way of serene confidence (*pasāda*). Therefore it is said: "It has the characteristic of certainty.

For resolute conviction is the determination of the object in whatever way it may be; for one who lacks such conviction, there is no engagement in acts such as killing living beings or in acts such as giving.
Faith, however, is the conviction of serene confidence toward things that inspire confidence; this is the distinction between these two.
This is the distinction. However, determining (*voṭṭhabbana*) occurs by way of deciding upon the meaning as it has been investigated;
it serves as a condition for subsequent states to arise in that same manner. If this is so, how is it with regard to states associated with doubt?
In their case too, it should be understood that they function as a condition for the mode of wavering (*saṃsappanākāra*) in an absolute sense, just as in the case of a child...
Non-wavering (*asaṃsappana*) is the act of counteracting indecision—such as thinking "I shall do it" or "I shall not do it"—which involves crawling here and there like a snake.
In those mental arisings where this resolution (*adhimokkha*), characterized by decisiveness, occurs, the object-dhamma itself is what is to be decided;

thus, it is the "dhamma to be decided upon" (*sanniṭṭheyyadhamma*). Since that [object] is its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*), it is called "having the dhamma to be decided upon as its proximate cause" (*sanniṭṭheyyadhammapadaṭṭhāna*).
“Indakhīla” means a boundary pillar.
“In those various states” refers to those states which have arisen in oneself—that is, the mental states (citta) and mental factors (cetasika) associated with oneself.
For even when these states are proceeding equally, the state of neutrality toward them is called “equanimity regarding those states” (tatramajjhattatā).

Its characteristic is even carrying (*samavāhitalakkhaṇā*), meaning that it carries evenly or without unevenness, or that its function is to cause those mental factors associated with itself to proceed in their respective duties.

In this context, "having a characteristic of proceeding evenly" expresses a state of not falling into partiality; "having a characteristic of proceeding without unevenness" expresses the prevention of deficiency or excess.
For even though this [equanimity] proceeds in a state of indifference, it causes the associated states to proceed equally in their respective functions;
just as a king, though sitting in silence, causes those engaged in legal affairs to proceed equally and attentively in their respective duties.
It is due to the deficiency or excess of those states that serve as conditions for proceeding in a non-sluggish and non-agitated manner that the states of sluggishness and agitation arise.
It is said that its function is warding off; thus it is stated: "Its essence is the warding off of deficiency and excess.

If this is so, how can there be the status of predominance (*ādhipacca*) for co-nascent predominant factors (*sahajātādhipati*)? For is not their predominance simply their state of being superior by virtue of their function? This is not a fault. That too is merely its function:
namely, the causing of co-nascent phenomena to proceed in a state of predominance. Just as, for example, a wrestling arena...

Just as a master actor arranges his various actors on the stage each according to their own appropriate role, so too does this [volition] establish its associated states in their respective positions of predominance when they are in a state of predominance, and in their state of faculty-ness when they are in a state of faculty-ness;
it does not, however, allow them to fall short of or exceed their own individual functions. [It does not think: "Let this one have a diminished function..."
"This is an additional duty"—such an occurrence, as if through partiality, is "partiality" (pakkhapāta). It acts as if cutting that off;

thus, it has the function of severing partiality. It should be regarded like a charioteer toward well-bred horses that are proceeding evenly through his impartial supervision of the mind and mental factors.
"Kiriyā kāro" (action is *kāra*) expresses that the word *kāra* has the sense of an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*).
By this, it is shown that what is called "*kāra*" is nothing other than action itself. "Making in the mind" (*manasi kāro*) means the making of an object within the mind.

For by that [mental state] through which the mind is made to act upon an object—because of its conjunction with that object—the object itself is thereby "made in the mind" (*manasi karīyati*). Thus, it is called "attention" (*manasikāra*).
And here, a compound without elision (*aluttasamāsa*) is to be understood. "From the preceding mind" means from the life-continuum mind (*bhavaṅgamana*).

A "mind dissimilar [to that]" is the cognitive process mind (*vīthijavanamana*); that which performs this is "attention" (*manasikāra*). By means of the commonality of the term "attention," he indicates that which introduces the cognitive process and the impulsion.
Furthermore, in this case, a compound with the locative case expressing the sense of the accusative is to be understood. [It is attention] which directs the associated states toward the object.
Because it acts as if recollecting and impelling, attention is said to have the characteristic of recollection (*sāraṇa*). Its function (*rasa*) is that of impelling (*payojana*).
Initial application (*vitakka*), because its nature is to direct associated states toward the object, acts as if throwing the mind onto the object.
Volition (*cetanā*), while grasping its own object, [causes] the associated states also to perform their respective functions.
"Causes to act" means that by its own acting, it is like a powerful leader who employs strength.
"Directs the associated states toward the object" means it is like a charioteer who directs a noble steed; this is the distinction between them.
"Manifestation as being directed toward the object" means its manifestation is the state of being directed toward that object by way of connecting with it.

In this context, the distinction between these two is that mindfulness has as its domain the desire not to forget and its manifestation as being directed toward the object, whereas attention functions by way of conjunction.

The statement that the factor which leads to the object is included in the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) shows that other types of attention are included in the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha). However, the Mahīśāsakas [hold that] "of advertence..."
They say: "If it were of the nature of consciousness, the omniscient knowledge would lose its quality of having all things as its object;
therefore, it is included within the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) associated with the impulsion (javana). For their intention is this:

if it were a distinct mental state, then for the impulsions arising immediately after it—which function by taking a present mind as their object—it would follow that those impulsions have a present object.

It would not exist; rather, it would simply have the past as its object. And this being the case, since even the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa) would lack an object consisting of present consciousness, it would follow that it does not have all things as its domain.
And to the extent that it does not have all things as its domain, to that same extent it would be obstructed, because an obstruction is possible in that which it does not operate.
Therefore, its status as an omniscient one, established for the entire world, [would be lost].

Furthermore, its state of being unobstructed would be lost; however, when it is associated with the impulsion (javana), this undesirable consequence for the adverting consciousness (āvajjana) does not arise.

This [objection] is merely their own dogmatic insistence, because of the statement: "Adverting is a condition, by way of proximity-condition (anantara-paccaya), for wholesome aggregates and unwholesome aggregates," which establishes that wholesome and unwholesome states arise immediately after it.
Because it has been explained. Furthermore, the fact that the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa) has present consciousness as its object should be understood in this way:

when advertence (āvajjana) occurs with the thought, "I know this person's mind," without making a distinction such as past and so forth, it adverts generally to whatever consciousness has come into focus;
thereafter, the impulsion moments (javana) also [take] whatever has come into focus for each of them.

They proceed by taking consciousness as their object; nor should it be suspected here that the impulsions (javana) have different objects, because the object is not differentiated due to the commonality of the consciousness.
Therefore, depending on the fact that the knowledge of omniscience has present consciousness as its object, no suffering whatsoever need be experienced.
What is the use of this line of reasoning? Has it not been said by the Blessed One:

—“The domain of the Buddha is inconceivable. Therefore, because the fruit of the accumulation of immeasurable merit is of an inconceivable nature, there is no obstruction to the grasping of an object even without adverting; thus, its occurrence anywhere at all is entirely unimpeded.
However, some here [hold that] “adverting ceases having made a future consciousness its object, but it is the impulsion itself...”

They say that it grasps a present object. However, since there is no textual authority (pāḷi) stating, "Adverting with a future object is a condition, by way of proximity-condition, for aggregates with a present object," therefore that [assertion] is not authoritative.
It acts; thus it is compassion (karuṇā). What does it do, for whom, and for what reason? To this he says: "When there is suffering in others, it causes the hearts of the virtuous to tremble."
"Compassion" (*kampana*) refers to a transformation of the mind characterized by an inability to endure the suffering of others upon seeing it;

this belongs only to virtuous persons (*sappurisa*), hence he says "of the good" (*sādhūnam*). For virtuous persons are called "good" because they accomplish their own welfare and the welfare of others.
Regarding the word "destroys" (*kiṇāti*), he states its meaning as "annihilates," which means he causes [the suffering] to go out of sight or removes it.
This is the meaning. Therefore he said: “It has the characteristic of proceeding in the mode of removing the suffering of others.

Whether or not there is actually the removal of the suffering of others, that mode of removing the suffering of others exists; thus it is “having the characteristic of proceeding in such a way,” i.e., having the characteristic of...

[removing the suffering of others]. The inability to endure or the non-acceptance of the suffering of others due to the desire to remove it is “intolerance of the suffering of others” (*paradukkhāsahana*). It is not violence (*avihiṃsā*).
Non-cruelty (*avihiṃsā*) means not harming living beings; it manifests as that, or it manifests as the opposite of cruelty, thus it is "manifesting as non-cruelty" (*avihiṃsā-paccupaṭṭhānā*).

It has the characteristic of rejoicing (*pamodana-lakkhaṇā*), meaning it has the characteristic of rejoicing in the success of others. It has the function of non-enviousness (*anissāyana-rasā*), [meaning] of the absence of envy...
[Discontent] has the function of being the opposite of envy (*ussuyana*). Discontent (*arati*) is the lack of delight in secluded lodgings and in superior wholesome states.

In terms of its actual nature, it should be understood as follows: the former [discontent] is associated with grief and characterized by excessive envy, while the latter is characterized by excessive sloth-and-torpor and restlessness;
therein, the former has the excellence of others as its object, whereas the latter has secluded lodgings and so forth as its object. Of discontent...
It manifests in the manner of striking down; it manifests as the removal of that [striking down] or its pacification—thus, it is "manifesting as the removal of aversion.
By the phrase "desiring what is undetermined," he shows that she desires [it] by way of being a distinct mental factor (*cetasika*).
"From bodily misconduct" means from misconduct consisting of transgression regarding the object. "The bases of bodily misconduct, etc."...
The objects are precisely those things that serve as the basis for bodily misconduct and so forth, such as the lives, wealth, and wives of others.

"Characterized by non-transgression" means characterized by non-oppression. It should be understood that by way of the term "the act of shrinking away from the bases of bodily misconduct and so forth," it is actually the act of shrinking away from the bodily misconduct itself that is being described.
For the abstinences do not [arise] from the bases of misconduct; rather, they arise from the misconduct itself.

They are appropriate as manifestations of non-action; however, the distinction between them is this: there is a contraction of misconduct itself through the absence of shame (*hirī*) and fear of blame (*ottappa*), and a contraction of the abstentions through the presence of moral dread (*soracca*); furthermore, there is non-action through the influence of disgust and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "faith... the proximate cause" (*padaṭṭhāna*): some maintain that all these factors, beginning with faith, are the proximate causes for bodily good conduct and the rest.
Others, however, say: "Faith and the other [three] qualities are, respectively, the proximate causes (padaṭṭhāna) for three things:
because one who has faith in karma and its fruit refrains from bodily misconduct and so forth; because one endowed with moral shame and dread of blame does not speak falsehoods and so forth;
and because one possessed of the qualities of fewness of wishes, contentment, and effacement avoids wrong livelihood. "Some" refers to the inhabitants of Abhayagiri.
"In these" means "in these three abstinences. "They desire one definite abstinence" means they desire another fourth definite abstinence distinct from these.
Alternatively, by virtue of the locative case used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*), the meaning is: "among these, they desire one definite abstinence.
In either case, however, their position is untenable, for even the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) did not [recognize] another abstinence.
Because they have not been specifically prescribed, and because there is no fixed single [occasion] due to the absence of the constant presence of their respective objects.
For this very reason, some residents of Abhayagiri themselves maintain that these [three] are threefold and indeterminate. Indeed, it has been said by them:
"Compassion and sympathetic joy are right speech, right action, and right livelihood;"
“For the most part they are undetermined, due to the diversity of their objective spheres.
Here, the expression “for the most part” is stated with reference to the fact that [these factors] are always found together as one within supramundane consciousnesses.
The grammatical connection is: “they enter into association with the second consciousness. And just as it is with the consciousness, so too it is with the states associated with it.
Regarding the second [jhāna], he said, "They are with volitional formations (sasaṅkhāra) alone," meaning that "the distinction here consists merely in the state of being with volitional formations.

"In the same way" means as in the third; likewise in the fourth, because joy (pīti) is the proximate cause for happiness (sukha). And because of the absence of happiness here, he said, "excluding joy.
But do they not say that compassion (karuṇā) and gladness (muditā) do not arise in association with equanimity (upekkhā)?
Therefore, should the rejection of these [two] be made in the same way as that of *pīti* (rapture)?
It should not be so made, because prior to reaching absorption (*appanā*), both compassion (*karuṇā*) and sympathetic joy (*muditā*)—even when accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*)—are possible.

For at the time of developing compassion and sympathetic joy, the preliminary work (*parikamma*) is performed with a mind accompanied by equanimity prior to the absorption process; however, within the absorption process itself...

Because there is no turning back of the feeling within a single-advertence cognitive process (*ekāvajjana-vīthi*) by means of a consciousness accompanied by joy (*somanassa-sahagata-citta*), the teachers maintain that compassion (*karuṇā*) and gladness (*muditā*) can only arise in association with states accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā-sahagata*) by way of their preliminary stages (*pubbabhāga*).
However, others do not accept that these two ever arise in association with states accompanied by equanimity; they hold that "the remaining [two] associate with the fifth [consciousness]."
Because it was stated without distinction, he now says, "and in the place of joy," and so forth, for the purpose of showing the specific details.
(81) "Compassion, gladness, and so forth" refers to compassion, gladness, and the three types of abstinence. Therefore, he says, "five.
Having thus shown those associated with wholesome sense-sphere consciousness, he now [shows] the states associated with wholesome fine-material-sphere consciousness.
In order to demonstrate this, he said, "But as for the remainder," and so forth. Therein, "excluding the three abstinences" means setting aside the three abstinences.

Why, however, are the three abstinences excluded here? It is said: the occurrence of wholesome states pertaining to the fine-material and immaterial spheres proceeds by way of the concentration of the mind in one whose bodily action and so forth are thoroughly purified;
it does not proceed by way of the purification of bodily action and so forth, nor by way of [the avoidance of] misconduct and wrong livelihood.
By way of cutting off. For indeed, there are three stages for phenomena such as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*):

the stage of transgression (*vītikkamāvasthā*), the stage of obsession (*pariyuṭṭhānāvasthā*), and the stage of latent tendency (*anusayāvasthā*). Among these, wholesome states of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*) are the antidote to the stage of transgression;

those of the fine-material and immaterial spheres (*rūpārūpāvacara*) are the antidote to the stage of obsession; and supramundane wholesome states (*lokuttarakusala*) are the antidote to the stage of latent tendency. [This applies likewise] to misconduct and wrong livelihood.

However, setting aside the state of transgression and the state of latent tendency (*anusaya*), a separate state of manifest obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) is not found apart from the state of transgression.
Since its counteragent would be the wholesome states of the fine-material and immaterial spheres, it neither purifies their state of transgression like the wholesome states of the sense-sphere,
nor does it eradicate the state of latent tendency like the supramundane path.

Or it subsides. In the purification of virtue (*sīlavisuddhi*), because it proceeds by way of the concentration of the mind for a practitioner whose bodily action and so forth are purified—having become free from transgression through the cleansing of virtue by means of sense-sphere wholesome states (*kāmāvacara-kusala*) alone—the non-arising of abstinences (*virati*) in the arising of exalted consciousness (*mahaggata-citta*) is indeed certain.
It is precisely to establish this point that the passage beginning with "But the abstinences... has been undertaken.

Or thirty-three [mental factors] at the time of occurrence by way of the jhānas of compassion (*karuṇā*) and so forth. "From that" means from the aforementioned mental factor mentioned in the third [jhāna].

Because compassion and appreciative joy (*muditā*), when they have reached absorption (*appanā*), are exclusively accompanied by mental pleasure (*somanassa*), he said: "By the fifth... excluding compassion and appreciative joy.

The intention is that there are thirty [factors], according to the method stated for the fifth fine-material-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) jhāna. If this is so, what is the distinction from the fine-material-sphere?

He said: "In this case, the distinction is the state of the formless realm (*arūpāvacarabhāva*). This means that because of the absence of perception of form (*rūpasaññā*) in the fifth [attainment], it is the state of the fine-material realm (*rūpāvacarabhāva*);
however, since it is to be attained here by the complete surmounting of the perception of form, it is the state of the formless realm, and this alone is its distinction from that [fifth attainment].

"Possessing the first jhāna" (*paṭhamajjhānika*) means having the first jhāna. "In the path-consciousness" (*maggacitte*) refers to all fourfold types of path-knowledge. "Distinguished as possessing the second jhāna, etc. (*dutiyajjhānikādibheda*).
“In the second, third, fourth, and fifth jhānas. By the method stated means by the method stated as “in the second [jhāna], with the exception of applied thought,” and so forth.
If it is asked, “Is this without distinction? he says, “No; [it applies] to compassion and sympathetic joy,” and so on.

Among the path-factors, there might at times be an absence of right intention due to the basis-jhāna and so forth, but there is no absence of the abstinences, because bodily misconduct and the rest have been completely eradicated.

Because it sets the noble path in motion, it is said: "the state of fixed abstinence. The supramundane state is the condition of transcending the world, as it is to be attained through the succession of the six purifications.
Having thus shown the meanings of association, function, and characteristics for the wholesome mental factors, [he now treats] the unwholesome mental factors.
The passage beginning with “But the unwholesome” is commenced in order to demonstrate this. Regarding the phrase “only the evaṃyevāpanaka states”:

although the *aniyata-yevāpanaka* states are not found in the first [unwholesome consciousness], nevertheless, in order to show together in one place the *yevāpanaka* factors that are actually obtainable among the unwholesome states, their mention here should be understood.
And having done so, immediately after the enumeration of the factors above, the passage beginning with “Thus the *yevāpanaka*” follows.

It has been stated. Because of the absence of desire (*chanda*) and resolve (*adhimokkha*) in the consciousness accompanied by doubt (*vicikicchā*), and the absence of desire in the consciousness accompanied by restlessness (*uddhacca*), it is said:
"In the ten types of consciousness in their respective order.

(82) "Shown" (*niddiṭṭhā*) means demonstrated exhaustively. They are "struck down," "dispelled," and "scattered" because they lead to evil, such as the suffering of the states of deprivation (*apāya*).
"By him who has destroyed evil" means by that Blessed One through whom unwholesome states— designated as "evil"— have been eliminated. By the Perfectly Enlightened One,
who is "such-like" (tādi) in the sense of being unshakable amidst these eight worldly conditions— gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, pleasure and pain—
he is indeed called "such-like" because he remains exactly the same whether in gain and so forth, or in loss and so forth.
“Does not feel shame” means he does not feel abashed. *Ahirika* refers to a person or a collection of phenomena.
Although it should be called *ahirikka*, by eliding one *ka*-sound, it is stated as *ahirika*. “Does not feel dread” refers to the state that is the opposite of moral dread (*ottappa*).
Non-disgust is non-reproach. Non-embarrassment is lack of bashfulness. “Characterized by non-disgust” is said by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
It is stated that its characteristic is "lack of shame" (*alajjana*) by way of being the opposite of *hiri*, which is common to both the wholesome and the indeterminate.
"By those very things" means by bodily misconduct and so forth. Lack of dread (*asārajjana*) is fearlessness (*nibbhayatā*). Fearlessness (*anuttāsa*) is the absence of agitation (*asambhama*).

The "flavor" (*rasa*) and other qualities should be understood by way of the opposites of what was stated for *hiri* and *ottappa*; therefore, they are not mentioned here. For among those [qualities], it is in the mode of lack of shame (*alajjanākārena*)...
Lack of shame (*ahirika*) is the relish for committing evil deeds. Lack of dread (*anottappa*) is the state of being unafraid.
Both have the non-retraction from evil as their manifestation, in the manner already described. They have the absence of reverence toward oneself and others as their proximate cause.

Through lack of shame, one feels no disgust for the impurities of the defilements, just as a village pig feels no disgust for filth. Through lack of dread, one has no fear of evil, just as a moth has no fear of fire.
It occurs through lack of moral dread. As the ancients have said:
"The shameless man does not feel disgust for evil, like a pig for dung;
lacking moral dread, he has no fear, like a moth for a flame."

And here, some say that just as when shame (*hirī*) is predominant, fear of wrongdoing (*ottappa*) becomes indeterminate (*abbohārika*), and when fear of wrongdoing is predominant, shame becomes indeterminate, so too when lack of shame (*ahirika*) is predominant, lack of fear of wrongdoing (*anottappa*) is indeterminate, and when lack of fear of wrongdoing is predominant, lack of shame is indeterminate;
however, that is not tenable. For just as one who defiles oneself with impurity...
Just as a foolish child, while smearing [something on] his hand and thrusting it into the mouth of a snake, feels neither disgust nor fear because he does not investigate its repulsiveness or danger;
even so, through ignorance of the true nature of phenomena (dhammasabhāva), delusion (moha) feels neither disgust nor fear toward evil.
Therefore, in the arising of consciousness associated with that [delusion], both [ignorance and delusion] are exceedingly powerful.
“They lust” means they crave; it is said that they cling. “Having the characteristic of grasping an object” (ārammaṇaggahaṇalakkhaṇo):

here, “grasping an object” does not mean merely making something an object, but rather the non-relinquishing of an object that has been adhered to by way of the adherence of craving, thinking “this is mine.
“Attachment” (abhisaṅgo) is the state of being difficult to release due to an excessive degree of clinging.
“Non-renunciation” means not letting go. It is like the stain of oil and collyrium; even after washing, it cannot be relinquished, just like the stain of oil and collyrium smeared on the skin.
It is called “having the perception of gratification as its proximate cause” because of the statement: “For one who contemplates gratification, craving increases.

In this context, “perception of gratification” (*assādadassana*) is the act of seeing by way of gratification. But is it not the case that the perception of gratification is, in actual fact, nothing other than greed?

How is it that truth itself is its own proximate cause (*padatthāna*)? Truth is stated to be its proximate cause because, first, through the influence of not very strong greed one perceives gratification (*assāda*), and subsequently strong greed arises;
thus, truth is said to be the basis for that [greed]. For this very reason it is said: "Craving increases. Others, however, say:
"Gratification is pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*); 'perceiving gratification' means the view of gratification (*assādadiṭṭhi*)."

Some say that the "delight" (assāda) is the sign of beauty which serves as the cause for pleasant feeling, while the "viewing of delight" (assādadassana) refers to the three perversions that occur by perceiving the foul as "beautiful. "They are deluded" means they do not understand.
The blindness of the mind is the failure to see the true nature of phenomena (dhammasabhāva) as it actually is.

Ignorance (*aññāṇa*) is a state that is the opposite of knowledge (*ñāṇa*). In this context, the former characteristic is stated by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), while the latter is stated by way of its opposite.
Alternatively, "characterized by ignorance" is stated by way of its function (*kicca*);

for it is described as having non-penetration (*asampaṭivedha*) as its essence. The inability to penetrate the intrinsic nature of phenomena is non-penetration. Its essence is the obscuring of the intrinsic nature of the object (*ārammaṇa*).

Just as ignorance, or a person possessed of delusion, is unable to penetrate the true nature of an object, so too the occurrence of delusion consists in the obscuring of that object's true nature. In this context, knowledge knows the object according to its true nature;
view, having abandoned the true nature, grasps it as not being what it truly is; but delusion does not cognize it in any way at all.
If this is so, how does it know the object at the time of grasping the object? Even then, it does not know.

However, just as contact and the other [mental factors] grasp the object merely by way of the mode of touching and so forth, and not by way of knowing, so too this [consciousness], arising while grasping the object, grasps it only by way of the mode of concealing, and not by way of the mode of knowing.

That which arises for someone is a "darkness" (*andhakāra*) because it creates blindness; it manifests itself in that way, or it causes that [blindness] to manifest, thus it is "manifesting as darkness.
"Seeing wrongly" means they see the impermanent and so forth as permanent and so forth, by way of perverting the true nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*).

Improper adherence (*ayoniso abhiniveso*) is adherence to a wrong path. Misapprehension (*parāmāso*) is the grasping of things as permanent and so forth, or as having an external cause, by overstepping their true nature (*dhammasabhāva*).
Wrong adherence (*micchābhiniveso*) is the insistence, through a distorted grasp, that "only this is true, everything else is false.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "not wishing to see the Noble Ones, etc.," one includes such factors as not wishing to hear the True Dhamma.
That state by virtue of which the mind becomes agitated, or the states associated with it—that state is restlessness (*uddhacca*).
Therefore he said, "the state of being agitated. "Non-settling" means the state of not being composed. "Like a banner... [and so on]... like a flag":
just as a flag, though not letting go of the flagpole due to the strength of its rope, is unable to remain fixed there because of the impact of the wind; so too is the mind.

In this way, even though it does not let go of the object due to the power of resolve (*adhimokkha*), it is unable to remain steady and fixed upon that object because of the power of improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*).
Thus, like a banner or flag fluttering in the force of the wind, its function is non-stability.
Its state of wavering is the mode of roaming about. Because restlessness (*uddhacca*) is common to all unwholesome states, as are other factors common to the unwholesome—
Because it is found as a separate proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*), it is stated: "Improper attention... [is] the proximate cause.
Alternatively, improper attention here is the act of attending in whatever manner that agitation arises;
or else, improper attention here is the act of attending to an object that is a sign of agitation.

"Maññati" means he conceives (abhimaññati); the meaning is that he forms an "I-making" (ahaṃkāra). "Uṇṇati" is the lifting up of oneself by way of being superior, such as through [the pride of] being better and so forth.
"Sampaggaharaso" means having the function of grasping firmly either oneself or the associated mental states by way of such elevation;
it is not like energy (vīriya), which functions by accomplishing its respective task. Through the power of overcoming, one makes oneself low compared to what is inferior.

It should be understood that even "grasping" (*gahaṇa*) is by way of "exerting" (*paggaṇhana*). Regarding the phrase "the banner... the manifestation": here, "banner" (*ketu*) refers to a raised flag;
however, in this context, it is "like a banner," thus a "banner. It is the state of being most excellent and so forth.

That which desires such a state—designated as the "banner-state"—is "desirous of the banner" (*ketukamyatā*). That phenomenon by virtue of which one is desirous of the banner is "desire for the banner" (*ketukamyatā*).
Because it proceeds with the thought “I am,” conceit operates in a manner similar to views;
thus, view and conceit do not arise together in a single moment of consciousness, like two maned lions in a single cave.

Therefore, although conceit never arises at all within a consciousness dissociated from views, because it necessarily does not arise within a consciousness associated with views, it has greed dissociated from views as its proximate cause (*padatthāna*).

Conceit (māna) operates by way of self-exaltation, having become powerful in grasping a collection of phenomena; view (diṭṭhi), however, operates by grasping even a single phenomenon in such modes as permanence and so forth.
Alternatively, conceit is based on attachment to a self, while view is based on devotion to self-mortification;
this is the distinction between them.

“Issati” means he envies. “Tattheva” means precisely regarding the excellences of others. Because one does not rejoice in the excellences of others due to envy, it is said that its “taste is dissatisfaction. For this very reason it is said:
“Those in whose hearts the flame-tips of the fire of envy burn here, They find no joy, which is cultivated by the Fully Awakened Ones and the rest.”
Taking the word *macchara* as it occurs in the sense of being stingy through the application of the term "stinginess" (*macchara*), he said: "The state of being stingy is stinginess (*macchariya*).
According to the method of etymology (*nirutti*), however, the ancients say: "May this wonder (*acchariya*) not belong to others, but to me alone"—thus it is *macchariya*.
Concealment is the non-showing of one's own prosperity to others; shrinking back is [the withholding] of one's own accomplishments.
It is the shrinking back by way of disliking the making of one's state of being common to others.

Some say that because one makes what belongs to oneself an object [of thought] by repelling it from others with the thought, "Let this not belong to another," stinginess (*macchariya*) is found only among the types of consciousness associated with aversion (*paṭighacitta*);
however, that is not correct, because it would follow that a single mental factor, having been repelled elsewhere, could then become an object for something else.

However, it is logical that stinginess arises among the states of repulsion because it proceeds by way of resistance toward that commonality with others. "Success in oneself" refers to success in one's dwelling and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "made contemptible": here, even that which has been done and that which has not been done is called "made contemptible" because it is to be censured.
For thus people say: "That which was not done by me is a misdeed (kukata). Accordingly, it will be said: "Its flavor is the grieving over what has been done and what has not been done.
In this way, both misconduct and even good conduct are called "badly done" (kucchitaṃ kataṃ) when they have been performed [with regret].
For even for one who censures his own good conduct, it becomes "badly done. Just as the jhāna that has the earth-kasiṇa as its object is called the "earth-kasiṇa," so too...
The mind that arises through remorse concerning a misdeed (*kukata*) should be understood here as "misdeed" itself, by virtue of its association with that [object].

Alternatively, the very mind of remorse arising in relation to what has been done or not done is called "misdeed" (*kukata*) because it is blameworthy—[that is,] "a contemptible thing done" (*kucchitaṃ kataṃ*). It is by means of this state that the mind is termed a "misdeed."
That which exists is the state of *kukkucca*. Therefore, he said: "The state of what was badly done. *Pacchānutāpa* is subsequent regret;

it is a vexation consisting of repentance. It is the grieving over what has been done or not done—that is, grieving over good conduct or misconduct performed—repenting by thinking, "Alas, a wholesome deed was not done by me," and so forth, [thinking], "Previously, a wholesome action was not performed by me; now, from this..."
However, the energy that belongs to the side of the wholesome—which proceeds with the thought, "I shall do it"—is indeed *vīriya*; it is not *vippaṭisāra*.
*Vippaṭisāra* is a deformed refuge consisting in the remorse for good and bad conduct distinguished by what has been done and what has not been done.
For such remorse regarding what was done and left undone is a deformed refuge because it fails to bring about progress; it is so because it is caused by a state of dependence on others.
It should be regarded as like slavery. For just as when one is in a state of slavery, the slave is dependent on another, so too is the person who possesses remorse (kukkucca).
Indeed, he is unable to engage in wholesome states by his own nature.

Alternatively, because of the dependence [on others] through the grieving over what has been done and not done, whether wholesome or unwholesome, the person who possesses it [is bound] by that remorse (kukkucca) in both respects.
"It becomes" means it becomes like slavery.
*Thina* is the state of being bound together by way of lack of exertion and despondency; because the mind is conjoined with that, it is "stiff" (*thina*), and its state is "stiffness" (*thinatā*).
Therefore he said: "the state of being bound together through lack of exertion. *Middha* is unworkability due to incapacity and distress.

Therefore, he said: "the frustration of effort. Because by means of *middha* (torpor) itself, the associated states become torpid and their capacity is destroyed, it is therefore called "torpidity" (*middhatā*) or "torpor" (*middha*).
That which has no effort is "lack of effort" (*anussāha*); the state of being that is also "lack of effort.
The state of being unable to exert oneself, characterized as lack of effort, is "languor due to lack of effort" (*anussāhasaṃsīdanatā*), which is to say, the state of being indolent (*kusītabhāva*).

It exists. Regarding "the affliction of incapacity" (*asattivighāta*): since that drowsiness arises precisely by way of destroying capacity (*satti*), that associated consciousness is "incapable" (*asatti*) because it lacks capacity;
the state of being so is also "incapacity," and the affliction consisting of that very incapacity is "the affliction of incapacity."
“Characterized by discouragement” means characterized by the opposite of enthusiasm. “Dispelling energy” (vīriyavinodana) means the removal or casting off of energy.
It manifests itself through the mode of sinking of the associated mental states, or it causes their sinking; thus, it is “manifested as sinking.
Regarding the phrase “characterized by unwieldiness”: although lethargy (thina) indeed has the very same nature of unwieldiness, [the two are distinguished here].

However, the distinction here is that lethargy (*thīna*) is the unserviceability of the mind, while drowsiness (*middha*) is the unserviceability of the triad of aggregates beginning with feeling (*vedanā*).
For thus does their definition proceed in the Canon: "In this context, what is lethargy? That which is the lack of fitness, the unserviceability of the mind.
What is drowsiness? That which is the lack of fitness, the unserviceability of the body," and so forth. [The term *oṇahanam* means] covering over.
It is the closing of the doors of consciousness, or the binding together of the associated mental factors. *Līnatā* is a state of sluggishness, a contraction in the grasping of the object.

Since through *thina* there is a stiffening of the mind alone, whereas through *middha* there is a stiffening of the entire triad of aggregates—feeling and so forth—as well as the physical body, it manifests as drowsiness and sleep;
thus it is also said to have "drowsiness and sleep" as its manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*).
It is appropriate. Delusion (moha) is that which obscures the intrinsic nature of the object, like a cloth covering a book.
Sloth (middha) is that which does not allow associated states to expand, like a cloth tied over the mouth; this is the distinction between them.

"The rest" refers here to the remaining factors beginning with contact (phassa), as described by way of their characteristics and so forth. "In the manner stated for the wholesome" means by way of their characteristics and so forth.
If it is asked whether there is no distinction here from what has been stated above, he says “But here,” etc., to show that it is not so;

the meaning is that for the three beginning with applied thought (*vitakka*), the distinction consists merely in their names, namely wrong intention (*micchā-saṅkappa*) and so forth. Regarding the nineteen:

setting aside the six indeterminate factors such as conceit (*māna*) and the rest included in the *yevāpanaka* category, the remaining fifteen mentioned by their specific names, together with those beginning with desire (*chanda*), [make up the nineteen].
The four "invariably included" factors—these, together with the previously mentioned ones, constitute nineteen mental factors (cetasika).
As for the "indeterminately included" factors, the reason why some are not found here has already been stated.
Regarding the phrase "the indeterminacy of sloth and torpor" (*thinamiddhassa aniyatabhāvo*), it refers to the fact that the indeterminate state of sloth and torpor arises here [in this context].
But it is not [included] in the first [category] because its state of being fixed does not arise there at all;

for a mind that is naturally sharp does not possess sloth and torpor. In the third [category], although pride (*māna*) is possible as something unfixed, the statement "eighteen" was made with reference to those factors that are fixed.
Therefore he said: "Pride, however, is unfixed here. It is not [counted] together with wrong view (*diṭṭhi*).
The reason for the phrase "it arises" has already been stated. In the fourth [jhāna], there are eighteen remaining;

in the fifth, excluding *pīti*, there are eighteen along with *diṭṭhi*; likewise in the sixth. In the seventh, because of the absence of both *pīti* and *diṭṭhi*, there are seventeen; likewise in the eighth.

"These three as well" means that not only compassion (*karuṇā*) and gladness (*muditā*), but these three as well do not arise together, precisely because their respective objects (*visaya*) are mutually distinct.
For envy (*issā*) has the success of others as its object; avarice (*macchariya*) has the non-sharing with others of one's own success as its object;
and worry (*kukkucca*) has what has been done and left undone as its object. Therefore, as for what the inhabitants of Abhayagiri say:
As for the statement, “Envy and avarice arise from one or the other according to desire,” that should not be accepted.

Rather, the experience or enjoyment of an undesirable object, or the experience of an undesirable aspect of an object—whether by way of its intrinsic nature or through conceptualization—is the "experience of an undesirable object.
That which has this as its characteristic is "characterized by the experience of an undesirable object."

Therefore he said: "Its function is the enjoyment of an undesirable aspect. This means that its function is the experiencing of an object in an undesirable aspect, whether it be according to reality or not according to reality; that is, its role is subsequent relishing.

For even when objects such as the Buddha—which are desirable by their very nature—arise for sectarians and others, mental grief (domanassa) arises through the mode of grasping them as undesirable. Of this mental grief...
Because it functions exclusively within the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu) alone, it is said to have "the heart-base as its proximate cause" (hadayavatthupadaṭṭhāna).
For, due to the absence of the state of being free from hindrances (anīvaraṇa), it cannot exist in the fine-material or immaterial realms (rūpārūpadhātu).
Its "spreading in various ways" (visappana)—meaning its improper movement—occurs either by way of its own mode of occurrence or by way of producing undesirable forms.
Alternatively, "spreading" (*visappana*) refers to the trembling of the body by way of producing undesirable forms; that is its flavor (*rasa*) or function (*kicca*).
Or, it has the quality of spreading (*visappanarasa*). Because it brings about a state of being burnt in the heart-basis, which is its support, or in the entire body, he says:
"or it has the flavor of burning its own support. And "bringing about a state of being burnt" means bringing about a state of withering.
The meaning [is as follows]. To the question "In what way?", he says: "Like a forest fire.
For that [fire] arises only within a forest thicket and burns that very same thing. It is manifested in the manner of defiling oneself and others.
For it, having arisen in the continuum of someone, certainly defiles that [continuum], even by bringing about deformity; and [it defiles] another...
Or else, whether it defiles him or not, it is like impurity held in the hand.

Its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) is the nine grounds for resentment (*āghātavatthu*), such as "He has done me harm," and so forth; thus it is called "having the grounds for resentment as its proximate cause.

It should be regarded as like urine mixed with poison because it is undesirable at the times of application and fruition. "Or eighteen" means eighteen when combined with one of the indeterminate factors, such as envy (*issā*) and the rest.

“Mere persistence of occurrence” means the mere persistence of the mind’s occurrence; the meaning is that it does not attain the status of path-factors and so forth because it lacks resolute confidence (*adhimokkha*).
Alternatively, “mere persistence of occurrence” means mere persistence for a moment.

For it has been said: “Like the persistence of the flame of a lamp in a windless place. It is able to become a condition for the persistence of the continuum, just as it is for the persistence of the mind.

Because it is incapable, because there is an absence of certainty, and because it does not persist due to being merely a condition for the occurrence of consciousness, it is called "stability" (*ṭhiti*) in the sense that it is merely the occurrence, merely the stability at a moment, and merely a condition for occurrence; thus, "stability-occurrence" (*pavatti-ṭhiti*) is formed.

"Vigata-cikicchā" is a word in the nominative case used in the sense of the ablative, as in "abstaining from malicious speech" (*pisuṇā vācā paṭivirato*), meaning "from which healing has departed. Alternatively, it means "healing has departed."
*Attha*. Or rather, this is the reading itself. It is said that "the treatment has departed" because it is difficult to treat, not because of a total absence of treatment.
"Doubt" (*saṃsayo*) is so called because one lies down by way of wavering, thinking "Is it thus?
Is it not thus?", or because one lies down all around [in indecision]. Its function is to cause trembling; for restlessness (*uddhacca*) is the mental function of causing trembling.
It "wanders" by remaining in the very mode it has grasped; thus, it proceeds by way of fluctuation within a single object alone.
However, although doubt arises with respect to a single object, it nevertheless depends upon another mode to be grasped—such as "Is it thus?
Or is it not?"—and thus there is a wavering toward multiple objects. It does so in the mode of non-ascertainment and the mode of indecision.
It is called "manifesting as non-resolution" because it either manifests itself as non-resolution or brings about non-resolution.
It is said, "by the absence of doubt," because resolution and doubt have mutually opposite functions.
Concentration (*samādhi*) is one-pointedness of mind; for it is called "concentration" because it places the mind correctly (*sammā-ādhānato*) upon the object.
"He becomes strong" means that he becomes strong like a man who has been given the strength of his back by a powerful friend; the intention is that he attains a state of strength and so forth.

"Because it has beings as its object" means because it has the conceptual designation of a being (*sattapaññatti*) as its object. [Objection: But are not resultant states also objects of conceptual designations?

With reference to this objection, he said: "Because the results (vipāka) of the sense-sphere are exclusively of limited objects. But from what [source] is it established that the abstinences (virati) are exclusively wholesome (kusala)?
To answer this, he said: "For it is stated that the five training precepts (sikkhāpada) are wholesome.

If this is so, would it not follow that the abstinences are not found among supramundane (lokuttara) results? No, they are not absent; for in the Vibhaṅga on the training precepts, only mundane (lokiya) abstinences are mentioned.

Because it was spoken with a specific underlying intention (*sandhāya*). Therefore, it should be understood that abstinences (*virati*) do not occur in mundane resultant states (*lokika-vipāka*) alone.

Because it is based upon the physical sensitivity (*kāyapasāda*), its existence in the body is characterized by a state of pleasure; thus, it is "characterized by bodily pleasure" (*kāyikasātalakkhaṇā*). The manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*) and other factors should be understood according to the method explained for mental happiness (*cetasika-sukha*); hence he says, "The rest are exactly as described.

But is it not the case that pleasant feeling arises toward a desirable object, painful feeling toward an undesirable one, and [neutral feeling] toward an object that is neither desirable nor undesirable?
Equanimous feeling and the wholesome-resultant eye-consciousnesses and so forth arise with respect to an agreeable or agreeable-neutral object.
In that regard, the association with equanimous feeling applies first to the agreeable-neutral object, but not to an agreeable object;
nor can it be said that one takes even an agreeable object as agreeable-neutral by way of mere conceptualization.
Just as [the term] "kamma-consciousness" is used because it is not deceptive regarding its results (vipāka), so too, one might raise this objection:

"How is it that when eye-, ear-, nose-, and tongue-consciousness arise in relation to desirable or desirable-neutral objects, only equanimous feeling (upekkhā-vedanā) occurs and not pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā), since equanimous feeling is said to occur in them?
To show this objection briefly, [the author states]: "In connection with a desirable object," and so forth.
Having said this, it was further stated—"and by means of derived matter" (*upādāya ca rūpena*)—for the purpose of clarifying that [matter].

Derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) is matter that arises depending upon and supported by primary matter (*bhūtarūpa*). The phrase "and by means of derived matter" follows the same method as that explained for the term "mental attention" (*manasikāra*).
Alternatively, the reading is "by means of the matter that is the derivative" (*upādāyakarūpena*), referring to that which serves as the physical basis (*vatthu*) for eye-consciousness.
The meaning is: by means of the sensitive eye-faculty (*cakkhupasāda*), and likewise by means of the sensitive ear-faculty and so forth, which serve as the bases for ear-consciousness and the rest;

that is, by means of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*). As for the phrase "but in the case of derived matter" (*upādārūpake pana*), this is an expression formed by the elision of the letter *ya*, as in the case of such phrases as "reflecting wisely" (*paṭisaṅkhā yoniso*);

the meaning is: in derived matter such as visible forms and sounds, which respectively serve as the objects of eye-consciousness and the rest. Regarding the phrase "of the sound produced by impact" (*saṃghaṭṭanānighaṃsassā*):
[This refers] to "striking" (*nighaṃsa*), which is designated as "impact" (*saṃghaṭṭana*).
Impact itself is called "striking" because it is like a friction characterized by the arising in a suitable location for the mutual relationship of object and subject.

Alternatively, the meaning is that there is both impact and striking by way of grasping what has been reached and what has not been reached; for the eye, visible form, ear, and sound do not reach one another.
Through their arising in suitable locations, they are said to "strike against" one another.
Consequently, by way of those [elements], the state of being directed toward one another—which constitutes the manner of striking—is called "impact" (*saṅghaṭṭanā*).
However, the nose and odors, as well as the tongue and tastes, having met one another, arise in an even more proximate location; they rub against one another and remain in contact. Then...

"By way of those [two], rubbing is spoken of. "Because of weakness" means that it is weak by virtue of its mere state of being touched, like when a lump of cotton is placed on the surface of a bowl and struck by that very lump of cotton. "He should illuminate":

because rubbing through such contact is weak, he should explain the connection with equanimity (*upekkhā*), showing that feeling stands in the position of neutrality. If this is so, then in body-consciousness (*kāyaviññāṇa*) as well...
They raise this objection, but he says, "But the sensitivity," and so forth. For just as when one places a ball of cotton-wool on the surface of an anvil and strikes it with a hammer,
the hammer passes through the ball of cotton-wool and strikes the anvil,
even so, at the door of the body, the external object consisting of the great elements strikes the internal bodily sensitivity and, passing beyond it, [impinges upon the consciousness].
It strikes against the great primary elements (mahābhūta) that serve as conditions for clarity;

the impact is powerful, and therefore, when the object is desirable, there is pleasant feeling associated with body-consciousness, whereas when the object is undesirable, there is painful feeling according to the method already stated. Regarding the term "mind-element" (manodhātu):
although here the word *dhātu* appears only in the feminine gender, by this very [usage]...
By the word of the Teacher, it is established that the masculine gender exists. However, some say, "This was stated according to the Pāli (Sakkata) convention.
The connection is: "the ten states associated [with it]. Therefore, in the phrase *tasmā vettha*, the syllable *va* serves merely to facilitate the euphonic junction (*padasandhi*) of the words.
Regarding the statement "painful feeling in body-consciousness," although there is pleasure and so forth—by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the unwholesome resultant body-consciousness is included.

The association with painful feeling has already been mentioned; however, here, for the purpose of showing its characteristic and other features, the addition "painful feeling in body-consciousness" is made. As for its flavor and so forth, they should be applied by way of the opposite of what was stated for pleasant feeling in the case of wholesome resultant [consciousness], and thus they are not mentioned here.
"The rest" refers to the remaining mental factors (*cetasika*).

"Attained to strength" means that this [concentration] has reached a state of power through its association with the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*), compared to the remaining types of concentration associated with rootless consciousness;

however, the meaning is not that it has attained the "heap of strength" (*balarāsi*). If this is so, why is it stated in the *Cetasikavibhāga-niddesa* that "the strengths (*balāni*) are two in two types of consciousness"?
It is because that statement was made with reference to the pair of functional rootless mind-consciousnesses (*kiriyāhetuka-manoviññāṇa-yugala*).
In the analysis of one-pointedness of mind (*cittass’ekaggatā*) among all remaining rootless consciousnesses, only this much is stated:
“What at that time is one-pointedness of mind? It is the stability of mind at that time.
However, in the analysis of one-pointedness associated with the functional rootless mind-consciousness element (*kiriya-ahetuka-manoviññāṇadhātu*), it is stated as follows:

“What, at that time, is one-pointedness of mind? It is, at that time, the stability, steadfastness, stability, non-wavering, non-distraction, unperturbed state of mind, serenity, the faculty of concentration, and the power of concentration”—thus it is analyzed by concluding with the "Power Section.
