And in the *Vīriyavibhaṅga*: “What, at that time, is the faculty of energy? It is, at that time, the arousal of mental energy...”
"Exertion, striving, endeavor, effort, enthusiasm, perseverance, fortitude, steadfastness, unfaltering exertion,
non-abandonment of desire, non-abandonment of the burden, the grasping of the burden, energy, the faculty of energy, and the power of energy"—
having thus concluded with the "End of Powers," the power of concentration and the power of energy are presented because they have been analyzed in the section on the Vibhaṅga.
Having in mind [the statement], "The two powers are in two types of consciousness," it was so said;

however, this does not refer to the power included in the "group of powers" (*balarāsi*) in the section on the enumeration of factors (*dhammuddesa*), because that enumeration of factors has been omitted starting from the "group of paths" (*maggarāsi*) in all rootless (*ahetuka*) consciousnesses. 87.

"By resultant, functional, and heart [consciousnesses]" means by resultant and functional consciousnesses. For "heart" (*hadaya*), "mind" (*mano*), "mentality" (*mānasa*), and "consciousness" (*citta*) are synonyms.

This is a term of synonymy. He whose going (*gata*)—that is, his movement—is beautiful (*sobhana*), thus he is the *Sugata*. For the Blessed One’s approaching of those to be trained is beautiful because it invariably accomplishes their welfare and happiness.

Likewise, his bodily movement is beautiful due to his physical form being adorned with the primary marks (*lakkhaṇa*) and secondary characteristics (*anubyañjana*), and because it is free from defects such as shakiness or slowness; it surpasses the gait of royal swans, bulls, elephants, and lions.

Furthermore, his progression of knowledge—endowed with the distinguished qualities of stainless, vast compassion, mindfulness, energy, and so forth—is truly beautiful in its faultlessness from the initial resolve (*abhinīhāra*) up until Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).

Alternatively, he is the "Well-Gone One" (*sugata*) because, through the realization of full comprehension (*pariññābhisamaya*), he has rightly gone to and understood the entire world by means of his self-born knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇa*);
likewise, through the realization of abandonment (*pahānābhisamaya*), [he has rightly gone to and understood] the origin of the world.
He is the "Well-Gone" (Sugata) because, having abandoned [defilements] and brought about the state of non-arising, he has gone rightly and transcended;
he is the Well-Gone because he has rightly gone to and attained Nibbāna—which is defined as the cessation of the world—by means of the clear realization through direct experience;

he is the Well-Gone because he has rightly gone to and reached the path—which is defined as the practice leading to the cessation of the world—by means of the clear realization through cultivation. Alternatively, he is the Well-Gone because he goes rightly.
For the Blessed One speaks the Dhamma that is real, true, and beneficial to those to be trained, at the appropriate time and as is fitting;
therefore, because he speaks well, the letter *da* is changed to *ta*, and he is called "Sugata.
Alternatively, he is Sugata because he has gone (*gata*) to a beautiful state—namely, perfect enlightenment or Nibbāna itself; thus, by that Sugata.

88. Regarding the phrase “avagacchati” and so forth: that bhikkhu who understands, comprehends, and—by means of correctly grasping, retaining, and so on—penetrates this treatise called the *Abhidhammāvatāra*, which is complete in both meaning and phrasing, and is therefore supreme and distinguished;
or alternatively, because it illuminates the supreme method (*paramanaya*).

This is the supreme treatise; whoever understands and knows it without omission—for one who thus understands according to its true nature through reflection—the wisdom termed *matisaṅkhātā* (wisdom consisting of understanding) stands in a place far more difficult to reach than even Mount Sineru, the king of mountains, when compared to that which is difficult to approach and difficult to attain by means of worldly knowledge, such as the subtle atom (*paramāṇu*) perceived by the fleshly eye. It is established in a realm of extreme profundity.
Just as it is impossible for even those with massive bodies, such as Rāhu and others, to plunge entirely into the great ocean, so too,
with the exception of the Perfectly Enlightened One, it is impossible for disciples— even those of great wisdom like Sāriputta— to plunge entirely into the method of the Abhidhamma;
yet, like a row of sal trees in winter, it unfolds and expands face-to-face before them.
Or, the meaning is "it proceeds in accordance with the Dhamma.
Thus [ends] the commentary on the *Abhidhammāvatāra* named *Abhidhammatthavikāsinī*.
The commentary on the Exposition of Mental Factors is finished. 3.
The Third Chapter:
Commentary on the Exposition of the Classification of Mental Factors.
89. "By the commonality of name alone" means that there are fifty-two by virtue of the commonality of names such as "contact" (phassa) and so forth—being fifty plus two;

however, by way of the distinction between associated states, contact associated with eighty-nine types of consciousness is of eighty-nine kinds, and thus they become manifold in this manner. This is the meaning.
But surely, contact and the others were shown above according to the sequence of the text; why then are they not stated in that same way here?
It is because [the author] wishes to point them out in a single place by means of their respective general characteristics (*sāmañña*), as each possesses its own individual nature (*sabhāva*).

For the thirteen factors beginning with contact and ending with attention are stated together due to their commonality as wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate; whereas those beginning with equanimity...

The twenty-five [mental factors] ending with *muditā* (altruistic joy) are stated together because they share the common characteristic of being either wholesome or indeterminate; whereas those beginning with greed (*lobha*) and ending with lack of moral dread (*anottappa*) are stated together because they share the common characteristic of being unwholesome.
Thus, these factors of similar nature have been mentioned collectively by virtue of their respective commonalities. 90.
Having thus enumerated the factors such as contact (*phassa*), he now explains: "In how many of these is this particular factor found?"
In order to show their application among the arising of states of consciousness (*cittuppāda*), he first shows the counting of the types of consciousness, saying “in fifty-four ways,” and so forth.
“In the sense-sphere” (*kāme*) means in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*). The same applies to “in the fine-material and immaterial [realms]” (*rūpe arūpe*).
They are called “without taints” (*anāsava*) because taints (*āsava*) do not exist within them, owing to the absence of being objects for the taints.
91–2. It is stated "in brief" with the intention of providing a detailed exposition, not because there is no further condensation possible.
However, in extreme brevity, there are eighty-nine types of consciousness-arising (*cittuppāda*).

Regarding these—meaning within these consciousness-arisings—I shall explain the arising of those factors such as contact (*phassa*) and so forth, extracting them one by one from among the consciousnesses and mental concomitants (*cetasika*), for the sake of the monks' proficiency.
[This is] the connection. "Each one" (*ekakaṃ*) means one by one; the elision of the vowel *e* occurs due to the requirements of metrical composition (*gāthābandhavasena*).

93. Although wishing to explain the classification of mental factors (*cetasika*), [the author] speaks of them as the "fivefold contact" (*phassapañcaka*), grouping them together with consciousness (*citta*) because they are phenomena that cannot be separated.
Those whose arising is simultaneous are "simultaneously arisen" (*ekuppādā*); those that perish together are "perishing together" (*sahakkhayā*).
The meaning is: "arising from one [side] and ceasing from the same [side].
(94) They are "common to all" because they are found in all the one hundred and twenty-one types of consciousness.
Although their status as common to all was already stated by the mention of their simultaneous arising and so forth with consciousness in the immediately preceding verse, nevertheless, therein—
Only the statement regarding their simultaneous arising and so forth is intended, not their universal commonality.
Or rather, although this matter was already stated there, it is stated here again after being made explicit because it was not clear there.

95–100. Among the forty-four sense-sphere consciousnesses (kāmāvacara-citta), excluding the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness, according to the distinction between mundane (lokiya) and supramundane (lokuttara):
Because applied thought (vitakka) is taught in fifty-five types of consciousness—namely, in the eleven types of consciousness associated with the first jhāna—it is said: “Applied thought...

is proclaimed. Sustained thought (vicāra) arises in sixty-six types of consciousness—namely, in those same fifty-five types of consciousness accompanied by applied thought plus the eleven types of consciousness associated with the second jhāna—it is said: “Sustained thought... is born.”

Regarding "joy (pīti) in fifty-one types of consciousness": joy arises in fifty-one types of consciousness, namely, in the eighteen sense-sphere consciousnesses accompanied by mental pleasure (somanassa), excluding body-consciousness, and in the thirty-three fine-material-sphere jhāna consciousnesses, excluding those of the fourth and fifth jhānas.
Regarding "pleasure (sukha) in sixty-three": pleasure arises in the fifty-one types of consciousness accompanied by joy and in the eleven types of fourth-jhāna consciousness.
And in the wholesome-resultant body-consciousness—thus, pleasure arises in these sixty-three types of consciousness.

Having excluded the sixty-six types of consciousness consisting of the sixty-three accompanied by pleasure and the three accompanied by pain, equanimity arises in the remaining fifty-five types of consciousness;
thus it is said: "Equanimity in fifty-five types of consciousness. Pain [arises] in three—in the two types of consciousness accompanied by aversion.
And in the three types of consciousness—namely, the two types of unwholesome-resultant mind-consciousness and the wholesome-resultant body-consciousness—suffering arises.

Regarding the phrase "there is the faculty of mental joy (*somanassindriya*)," in the sixty-three types of consciousness accompanied by pleasure, the faculty of mental joy exists in all except for that single instance of body-consciousness.

By way of the unwholesome-resultant body-consciousness, there is exactly one type accompanied by the faculty of suffering (*dukkhindriya*); likewise, it is only the wholesome-resultant body-consciousness [that is accompanied by the faculty of pleasure].
He said, "associated with the pleasure faculty," because he stated, "the pain faculty... [and so on] ...the pleasure faculty. He said, "five more than...

[and so on] ...he stated," because energy is taught among the wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional consciousnesses—excluding the rootless resultant and functional mind-elements—which number one hundred and five according to the intermediate calculation.
[This applies to] beings regarding goals pertaining to the present life and the future life.
"Vināyaka" means one who leads away (*vineti*), or one from whom the leader (*nāyaka*) has departed; or one who is a distinguished leader and master of the entire world;

or one who specifically leads the beings to be trained to the city of Nibbāna—thus he is a "Vināyaka. Since the faculty of concentration is said to exist in minds accompanied by energy that is free from doubt, he says "one hundred and four," and so forth.
In order to show that desire arises in the remaining one hundred and one types of consciousness, excluding the eighteen rootless consciousnesses and the two single-rooted consciousnesses, it is said:

"all rootless consciousnesses," and so forth. "The ten consciousnesses" refers to the fivefold sense-consciousnesses, such as eye-consciousness and the rest, each doubled by way of being wholesome, unwholesome, or resultant.
102–6. "Niyatā" means that they do not arise occasionally, as is the case with the *neyyāvapaṇaka* (indeterminate) states.
But how is it that these arise only within the ninety-one types of consciousness? He says, "In the rootless," and so forth. "Seventy-nine" refers to:

twelve sense-sphere consciousnesses associated with knowledge, fifteen fine-material-sphere consciousnesses, twelve immaterial-sphere consciousnesses, and forty worldly supramundane consciousnesses; thus...

In the seventy-nine types of three-rooted consciousness; in twenty-eight types of consciousness—namely, in the sixteen sense-sphere wholesome and functional great consciousnesses, and in the twelve mundane fourth-jhāna consciousnesses—thus in these twenty-eight types of consciousness;

in the forty-eightfold [set] together with the eight, that is to say, in the forty-eightfold set including the eight; and the six pairs—namely, the bodily tranquility and mental tranquility, and so forth.

There are six pairs. "Wholesome and indeterminate" means: they are wholesome because of association with wholesome consciousness, and indeterminate because of association with indeterminate consciousness;
thus, they were "proclaimed and taught" (pakāsitā desitā) by the Teacher, who is skilled in the methods of proclaiming and teaching the wholesome.
108–111. "Doubt" (saṃsayo) is doubt (vicikicchā). For it "doubts" (saṃseti), meaning it lies all around; [it thinks], "Is it thus? Or is it not?"...
*Kho* means "to wander about"; thus, there is doubt. One who seeks and searches for the great aggregates of virtue and so forth is a *mahesi*.
By that *mahesi*, the Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*). "In eight" refers to the eight consciousnesses accompanied by greed (*lobha*).

"In four" refers to those same [eight] when accompanied by views (*diṭṭhi*). The connection is: "in four [consciousnesses] dissociated from views. "In two only" refers to the two consciousnesses rooted in hatred (*dosa*).
"They arise together in two" means they arise only in those two [states] rooted in hatred; however, they do not arise simultaneously.

For instance, envy (*issā*) arises at the time of envying, while stinginess (*macchariya*) arises at the time of being stingy; thus, they arise as distinct states. "In five" refers to the five types of prompted consciousness (*sasaṅkhārika-citta*).

112. Although the mind (citta) lacks the quality of being a mental concomitant (cetasika), it is also called "mind" (mano) because it serves as the locus for counting wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states. 114–15.

Having thus far shown the classification of mental concomitants, the passage beginning with "In twenty-nine types of consciousness" is now stated in order to show the analysis of the factors within the groups found in each individual arising of consciousness.
But is it not the case that there is a group consisting of contact as the fifth [factor]?
Why is it that she who arrived first of all was not mentioned? Because she is common to all. For there is no arising of consciousness that is devoid of contact as its fifth factor.

There are eleven types of consciousness belonging to the first jhāna accompanied by joy, twelve types of wholesome sense-sphere consciousness accompanied by roots, and likewise four types of unwholesome consciousness—namely, the investigating consciousness accompanied by pleasure, the investigating consciousness accompanied by equanimity, and the smiling consciousness.

Regarding "two": among the twenty-nine types of consciousness, the five-factored jhāna is considered to be comprised of five groups. Regarding "four"... [and so on]... "should be pointed out": there are eleven types of second-jhāna consciousness;
twelve types of sense-sphere consciousness accompanied by equanimity and associated with roots—by way of the wholesome, resultant, and functional;
eight unwholesome types accompanied by equanimity or by mental grief; and those accompanied by equanimity, excluding the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness.
These thirty-seven consciousnesses, including the six rootless consciousnesses, are associated with the four jhāna factors as appropriate.
For herein, the eleven second-jhāna types are accompanied by vicāra, pīti, sukha, and samādhi;
the others are associated with four factors—vitakka, vicāra, samādhi, and either upekkhā or domanassa—as appropriate.
"Of eleven kinds" means that the third-jhāna consciousness is declared to have three factors due to its association with zest, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind.

"Thirty-four... [etc. ...are declared" refers to the twelve formless-sphere consciousnesses and the twenty-two fourth- and fifth-jhāna consciousnesses—both with and without taints—which, as appropriate, consist of thirty-four consciousnesses through their association with equanimity and one-pointedness, and bliss and one-pointedness.
And it is said to have two factors. For the eleven [jhānas] belonging to the fourth jhāna are accompanied by happiness and one-pointedness;
the remaining twenty-three are accompanied by equanimity and one-pointedness.

(116) "By their very nature in those without initial application" means that, unlike the second jhāna and so on, these are without initial application by their very nature, without the power of meditative development.

In the two fivefold consciousnesses, even though the remaining jhāna factors are present, they are incapable of performing the function of close contemplation (*upanijjhāna*) due to the absence of applied thought (*vitakka*).
For this very reason, it is said in the Commentary: "The final factor of jhāna is indeed applied thought.

However, those [factors] which have attained a state free from applied thought through meditation become more acute in performing the function of close contemplation by the power of that very meditation.

Therefore, one should not extract the jhāna factors from those states that are by their very nature without applied thought (*avitakka*). Alternatively, the reading is "not extracted" (*na uddhaṭā*), which means they have not been extracted.
If this is so, why is one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*) mentioned in its own form among the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousnesses?

Is it not more appropriate to speak of it as a "mere inclusion" (*yevāpanaka*), since—due to its lack of applied thought—it is incapable of performing the function of a jhāna factor and thus lacks a specific place within the group?

It is said: Because a state that does not exist among the wholesome and unwholesome is not found even among their results, and because it does not perform the function of a jhāna-factor, it is mentioned here in its own form according to the very order taught for the wholesome and unwholesome. Let this be so;
but why is feeling (vedanā) mentioned in the section on jhānas? For it is common to all consciousness, and thus [is included] in the group of the fivefold contact.

Is it not true that because they possess the nature of faculties such as equanimity (*upekkhā*), they should be mentioned only within the category of faculties (*indriya-rāsi*) and not elsewhere, since those [other categories] lack that nature?

True; however, feeling (*vedanā*) is included in the pentad of contact (*phassa-pañcaka*) by way of its general characteristic common to all feelings, and it is specified there by another particular term.
It is not for the purpose of subsuming it within that [pentad] that it is placed there. For this very reason, in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*...

In the section on inclusion regarding the two sets of fivefold consciousness, the aggregate of jhāna factors is not mentioned; for although the three great primary elements in the fine-material sphere are non-reactive (appaṭigha), they share the same nature as the reactive great primary elements in the sense-sphere. Thus, even there, they are treated as if they were reactive.

Similarly, in the two sets of fivefold consciousness, although feeling and one-pointedness of mind do not perform the function of jhāna due to their dissociation from applied thought (vitakka), they are nonetheless included among the states associated with applied thought.
Because they are identical with the feeling and other factors associated with the jhāna-consciousness, it is indeed appropriate to speak of them as jhāna-factors.

For this very reason, in the summary of mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa-samāsa), it is stated: "The aggregate of the fivefold contact, the aggregate of the two jhānas, and the aggregate of the three faculties.

Alternatively, what is the use of such deliberation on logical consistency? The Tathāgata, who knows the intrinsic nature of phenomena (dhammasabhāva), has spoken without deviating from that intrinsic nature.

"Taught" means that no further inquiry need be made here. Because mind-moments without roots (ahetuka-citta) lack the quality of being well-established upon their object and thus do not lead to liberation, it was said:
"All... [do] not transcend... This is indeed stated in the Commentary as well: "The path has the root as its final limit. 117.
"Three among the sixteen consciousnesses" refers to the fifteen rootless resultant consciousnesses and the functional mind-element (kiriyā-manodhātu).

Thus, among the sixteen types of consciousness, there are three faculties: the mind-faculty (*manindriya*), the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), and one from among the feeling-faculties (*vedanindriya*) as it occurs [in each case].
Within these as well, in the wholesome resultant body-consciousness element, there are three faculties by way of the mind-faculty, the pleasure-faculty (*sukhindriya*), and the life-faculty;
in the unwholesome resultant body-consciousness element, there are three including the pain-faculty (*dukkhindriya*); and in the pleasant investigating consciousness...

In three [types of consciousness] together with the faculty of mental joy (*somanassindriya*), and in the remaining thirteen types of consciousness together with the faculty of equanimity (*upekkhindriya*).

Here, since "consciousness" (*citta*) is intended as a cognitive arising together with its associated states (*sampayutta-dhamma*), it is logical that the faculty of mind (*manindriya*) also serves as its basis.
Otherwise, if "the faculty of mind" were taken as referring to consciousness alone, it would follow that it is the basis for itself.

"It is not applicable. However, "in one, four" means that in a consciousness accompanied by doubt, there are four [faculties]: the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*), the faculty of mind (*manindriya*), the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekkhindriya*).

"In thirteen, five" refers to the thirteen types of consciousness: the eleven unwholesome consciousnesses excluding the one accompanied by doubt, and the two functional root-cause mind-consciousness elements (*kiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu*);
in these thirteen consciousnesses, there are the three beginning with the faculty of energy, as well as the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*).

The "one" found among the feeling faculties refers to the five faculties. For here, within the two roots of hatred, there are five by way of the faculty of energy, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of mind, the faculty of life, and the faculty of mental grief;
within the five accompanied by joy, there are five consisting of the first four together with the faculty of joy;
and in the remaining [states], there are five consisting of those same four together with the faculty of equanimity.

118. "Seven in twelve consciousnesses": In the twelve types of consciousness dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇa*), there are seven faculties—namely, the faculties of faith, mindfulness, concentration, energy, life, and mind—and one among the feeling-faculties that is obtained. For therein, in the six types accompanied by joy (*somanassa*), there are seven:
the six beginning with the faculty of faith together with the faculty of joy; in the other six, [there are seven] with the faculty of equanimity (*upekkhā*).

Together there are seven. When [the mental factors] are deficient by one... pe ...and in the case of the mind-faculties (manas), there are twelve consciousnesses associated with knowledge belonging to the sense-sphere, and twenty-seven mundane jhāna-consciousnesses;
thus, among the thirty-nine types of mundane consciousness, there are exactly eight faculties:
the aforementioned seven and the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya). For here, within the six sense-sphere consciousnesses accompanied by joy (somanassa-sahagata):

In the eighteen types of consciousness—namely, the twelve fine-material-sphere (rūpāvacara) fourfold jhānas and the six [sensuous-sphere] ones—one should understand that eight faculties are present: by associating the faculty of mental joy (somanassindriya) with those [twelve], and the faculty of equanimity (upekkhindriya) with the remaining [six].
119. Regarding the phrase "nine in forty": in the forty-nine types of supramundane (lokuttara) consciousness, the first nine [faculties] are present in each type.

There are eight faculties—the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of knowing, and the faculty of one who has known—which, when occurring together among these, constitute a set of nine faculties.
For the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" is found in the paths of stream-entry;
from the fruit of stream-entry up to the conclusion of the path of arahantship, it is not found there. In its place is the faculty of knowing. [In the fruit of arahantship...]
Even that is not obtained. In its place, the faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya) remains.

Thus, because of the absence of association with six faculties, there is a conjunction of faculties in six ways: in some cases three, in some cases four, in some cases five, in some cases seven, in some cases eight, and in some cases nine faculties.
It should be understood that not only is there the conjunction with the factors of jhāna, but also the association of the arising of consciousness with the faculties.

Now, showing the association with the factors of the path, [the author] first points out those states of consciousness in which the path-factors are not found, and subsequently, in order to show the states of consciousness associated with the path-factors, he says: "Those without path-factors," and so forth.
"In this" means in this consciousness consisting of one hundred and twenty-one varieties, or in this section concerning the path factors (*maggaṅga*).
"In the two and five consciousnesses" refers to the two and fivefold consciousnesses, such as eye-consciousness and so forth, which are by nature devoid of initial application (*avitakka*).

Although it was already stated below that the jhāna factors are absent in the two and fivefold consciousnesses, and that the path factors are absent in those without roots (*ahetuka*), the non-jhāna factors are nevertheless mentioned there by virtue of the present context.

These have been stated here by way of incidental context. As for the non-path factors, they were mentioned there by way of incidental context, whereas here they are mentioned by way of the primary subject matter; thus, there is no fault of redundancy.
"One" refers to the consciousness associated with doubt. For that [consciousness] possesses two path-factors due to its association with wrong intention and wrong effort.

"Herein": in the case of the two paths of the sense-sphere (*dumaggaṅga*). "Three path-factors in seven" means: four [types of consciousness] dissociated from views, two rooted in hatred, and the consciousness accompanied by restlessness;
thus, in these seven, there are three path-factors due to their association with wrong intention, wrong effort, and wrong concentration.
"Forty... pe ...fourfold" means: twelve dissociated from knowledge, four associated with views, and so forth.
Excluding those associated with the first jhāna, there are twenty-four sublime consciousnesses;

thus, among these forty consciousnesses, whichever path is obtained is considered fourfold according to its association with right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration, as well as its dissociation from wrong view, wrong intention, wrong effort, and wrong concentration, and its association with right view, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. Among these, in the cases dissociated from knowledge...
Among the twelve [types of consciousness], the first four are found; among those associated with wrong view, the middle four; and in the remaining types, the last four are obtained.

Regarding the fifteen [types]... [as follows]: "five-factored" refers to the fifteen types of consciousness consisting of the twelve sense-sphere consciousnesses associated with knowledge (*ñāṇa*) and the three mundane first jhāna consciousnesses, by way of right view, right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
The five-factored path. [Objection: But are not right speech and the others found among those belonging to the sense-sphere? [Reply: True, they are found there;

however, because they do not appear in the [specific] textual recitation, they are excluded here. "In thirty-two types of consciousness" means in the thirty-two supramundane consciousnesses, excluding those of the first jhāna.
It is called "seven-factored" because right intention is not obtained due to the absence of applied thought (vitakka). Thus, that [intention] is omitted.
Having relinquished [the first three], it is called "seven-factored" by way of the remaining seven path factors.
However, where right intention (*sammāsaṅkappa*) is obtained, it is eight-factored along with that; thus he said, "The path in eight," and so forth.
Therein, "in eight consciousnesses" means in the eight supramundane (*lokuttara*) consciousnesses belonging to the first jhāna. "Thus" refers to the six...

Because there is no association with all the path-factors simultaneously, in some cases there are two path-factors, in some three, in some four, in some five, in some seven, and in some eight; thus, it occurs in six ways.
Now, showing the association with the powers (*bala*), he says: "Two powers," and so forth. Therein, by way of the power of energy (*vīriya-bala*) and the power of concentration (*samādhi-bala*)...

Regarding the statement "two in two types of consciousness," it is said that in the two types of functional mind-consciousness elements (*kiriya-manoviññāṇadhātu*) mentioned in the *Vibhaṅga* section, the two powers—the power of energy (*vīriyabala*) and the power of concentration (*samādhibala*)—are each found individually.

Regarding "three in one," in the single type of consciousness associated with doubt, there are three powers by way of the power of energy, the power of moral shame (*ahirika*), and the power of moral dread (*anottappa*). Regarding "four in eleven," this refers to [the remaining] eleven types of consciousness, excluding those associated with doubt.
In the eleven unwholesome consciousnesses, there are four powers: the power of concentration and the three previously mentioned [powers].
"Six in twelve" means that in the twelve types of consciousness dissociated from knowledge, there are six powers by way of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, moral shame, and moral dread.
"Seventy-seven in eighty-nine" refers to the twelve sense-sphere consciousnesses associated with knowledge and the twenty-seven sublime consciousnesses.

And among the forty types of supramundane consciousness—thus, within these seventy-nine kinds of consciousness, there are seven powers (bala) consisting of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, serenity, and moral dread.
"Sixteen are indeed powerless" means that fifteen are resultants (vipāka) without roots (ahetuka), and the functional mind-element (kiriyā-manodhātu) as an adverting consciousness;
these sixteen are "powerless consciousnesses" due to their dissociation from power. Thus, because of the absence of association with the five powers [in these cases].
In some cases there are two, in some three, in some four, in some six, and in some seven;

thus it should be understood as "possessing strength" (*sabala*) by way of these five modes, and as "lacking strength" (*abala*) due to the absence of even one of these. The meaning is that it is "to be known" (*viññeyya*), i.e., to be discerned.

It should be understood that the "heap of causes" (*heturāsi*) and so forth are not mentioned because they constitute the state of analytical determination (*vinicchaya*). Regarding those consciousnesses in which the factors of jhāna, the factors of the path, the powers, and the faculties [are present]...
The connection is "they are born. The conclusion regarding the faculties is for the sake of the ease of the verse composition.
Thus ends [the section] from the *Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanā*, titled *Abhidhammatthavikāsinī*.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Classification of Mental Factors is finished. 4.
The Fourth Chapter:
Commentary on the Exposition of the Singlefold, etc.
128–30. "By way of having the nature of cognizing" means by way of having the nature of cognizing an object (*ārammaṇa*).
But was it not already stated above that they are of one kind because they possess an object? True, it was stated;

however, since that [quality of having an object] is common to mental factors (*cetasika*) as well, it is here stated specifically as "having the characteristic of cognizing" in order to exclude them. And by way of concise enumeration, those with roots are of seventy-one kinds.
It is said: "By one who speaks of causes" means by one skilled in explaining the roots (hetu) of the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate;

or alternatively, by one who maintains that specific conditions for each respective phenomenon arise from those specific conditions, based on the statement: "Of those phenomena that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has declared their cause."
131–4. "With a basis and without a basis" means, respectively, because they are entirely dependent on a physical basis and because they lack such a basis.
Some, however, explain "with a basis and without a basis" by way of the heart-basis (*hadayavatthu*);

that is not correct, because in the description of "with a basis," the phrase "all resultants of sensual desire" includes those [mental factors] dependent on clarity (*pasāda*) as well. "By way of both" means by way of being with a basis and without a basis.
For some consciousnesses are exclusively with a physical basis (*savatthuka*), some are without a basis (*avatthuka*), and some possess both natures.
It is described accordingly as "all resultant [consciousness] of the sense sphere" (*sabbaṃ kāmavipākaṃ ca*) and so forth.

"All resultant [consciousness] of the sense sphere" refers to all twenty-three types of sense-sphere resultant consciousness, distinguished by those that are with roots (*sahetuka*) and those that are without roots (*ahetuka*).

"The first path" refers to the stream-entry path (*sotāpatti-magga*). It is called the "first path" because it arises first among all supramundane paths, or because it belongs to the first of the eight noble persons (*ariya-puggala*).
"Without a physical basis" means that they do not arise without their respective physical bases (*vatthu*).
For this very reason, these [consciousnesses] do not arise in the formless realm (*arūpa-bhava*), due to the absence of physical bases there.
And the statement, “They do not arise without a basis,” is said with the purpose of including the internal cause.
Therefore, because they do not arise without a basis, it is implied that they are invariably accompanied by a basis.

They are invariably without a basis only in the formless realm (*arūpabhava*), because they proceed there by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and so forth. But how [do they exist] in dependence on the material?
If the formless (arūpa) proceeds there without that [materiality], why does it not proceed as the fivefold plane (pañcavokāra)? Because it is not seen to do so.
If this is so, then in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), materiality should also proceed even without edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra); what is the reason for this?

Because it is not seen to do so in the realm of sense-desire (kāmadhātu). Nevertheless, for whatever continuum of consciousness the cause of its proceeding is craving that has not departed from materiality...

Its occurrence is simultaneous with matter. However, for one whose craving for matter—the cause of its production—is absent, its occurrence takes place without matter because the cause is turned away from it;
thus, the immaterial (arūpa) occurs there without dependence on matter.
"The remaining forty-two" refers to the mind-door adverting consciousness and the sixteen sense-sphere wholesome functional states, as well as the same [sixteen] unwholesome states.
The forty-two remaining types of consciousness mentioned are: the eight formless-sphere consciousnesses; the seven supramundane consciousnesses excluding the first path-consciousness;
and the ten unwholesome consciousnesses excluding the two types involving aversion.
135–7. That which has only one object among visible forms and so forth is "single-object. Of each respective object...
At the time of encountering [an object], because one recognizes each respective [object], there are five objects for this; thus it is "five-object" (*pañcārammaṇa*).
"In this way too" means not only by way of having a basis (*savatthuka*) and so forth, but also by way of having a single object (*ekārammaṇa*) and so on.

Since all sublime states (*mahaggata*), excluding the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), have a single object by virtue of having the Dhamma as their object, he said "all sublime. It is "single-object" by reason of having a conceptual designation (*paṇṇatti*) as its object.
Some [say]: "That [number] is not applicable when one has attained the second and fourth jhānas of the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara), because their objects are sublime (mahaggata).

Since the two types of direct knowledge (abhiññā) have sixfold objects, and since that [fifth jhāna] is not distinct from the fifth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), excluding it, 'forty-three' is stated."

141. The connection is: "In the sense of meritorious, resultant, and functional, there are twelve in the sense-sphere. *Dhā* is a mere particle. "From meritorious, resultant, and functional" means from the wholesome, resultant, and functional [consciousness] dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
143–9. It is called a "posture" (*iriyāpatha*) because it is the path of occurrence for bodily activity—that is, for physical action—such as walking and so forth.
In terms of its actual meaning, it is the occurrence of matter (*rūpa*) in that particular state. Granted, in this context, there is no posture or intimation (*viññatti*) apart from matter.
Nevertheless, every consciousness that originates matter supports the postures and produces intimation and transformation.
However, that consciousness which generates intimation invariably generates the other two as well, because they are inseparable; likewise for the matter that supports the postures.
It is for the purpose of showing this distinction that [the text] says: "from that which generates or does not generate the material postures and intimations," and so forth.
The separate mention of the postures (*iriyāpatha*) and the intimations (*viññatti*). "From that which produces, that which does not produce, and so forth" means:
from that which produces all three; from that which produces none at all; and from that which produces two or one.
For some states of consciousness originate matter, fashion the postures, and generate intimation; others originate matter and fashion the postures.
They do not produce intimation (*viññatti*). Some produce matter alone and do not perform the other two;
others do not perform all three at all. He shows this very point in the passage beginning with “twelve unwholesome [states],” and so forth.

And thus, that consciousness is fourfold not only from the standpoint of being rootless and so on, but also from the standpoint of producing matter and so forth. It is also said: “And thus, at the beginning, that.”
They write [thus]. Furthermore, they explain the meaning as follows: "And the mind placed at the beginning of that [process] is fourfold.

Regarding the phrase "therein" (*tattha*), it means among those [types of consciousness], such as the producers of material form (*rūpajanaka*). "Ten functional [consciousnesses]" (*dasa kiriyā*) refers to the ten functional consciousnesses excluding the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
"They originate material forms" (*samuṭṭhāpenti rūpāni*) means that at the very moment of their own arising, they originate the material forms that are to be produced by themselves.
“They brace” means they steady them; they support the postures as they occur.

For just as when the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) is proceeding uninterrupted by the path-consciousnesses (*vīthicitta*) arising from time to time, the limbs sink down and become as if trembling, it is not so with the thirty-two kinds of consciousness that will be mentioned, nor with the twenty-six kinds of wakefulness-consciousness.
While these [mental states] are occurring, the factors then proceed with their postures firmly established, precisely as they were proceeding before.

Furthermore, regarding the production of intimation (*viññatti*): it should be understood that only those [states] occurring at the mind-door produce intimation, whereas those occurring at the five doors do not.
Because the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness lack the application of the factors of jhāna and thus do not produce material form, it says "the two sets of fivefold consciousness.
For the factors of jhāna, together with the mind, are the originators of material form;

as for the path-factors and so forth, they provide them with supporting power, since it is observed that when these are present, the occurrence of material form is especially distinguished. However, the immaterial resultant states arise through the cultivation of detachment from material form.
Because it is averse to that cause, it does not arouse matter; thus he said, "And the resultants in the immaterial [plane].
(150) "The rebirth-linking consciousness of all" means the rebirth-linking consciousness of all sentient beings.
For that, due to the weakness of its physical basis (*vatthu*), its lack of support, the deficiency of conditions, and its adventitious nature, does not arouse matter. Likewise...

For the physical basis (vatthu) that arises simultaneously with the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhiviññāṇa) is devoid of the condition of post-nascence (pacchājātapaccaya) and is weak because it is not supported by nutriment and so forth;
and because of its weakness, the consciousness dependent upon it is also weak.

And just as one who has fallen into a precipice cannot serve as a support for another, so too that [basis]—due to being projected by kamma within a broken continuity—cannot serve as a support for another consciousness.
Like something fallen from a precipice, it lacks a foundation and is unable to produce a material form;
this is because, since it arises neither after nor before itself, it cannot obtain the condition of pre-existence (*purejāta-paccaya*).
Just as a stranger who has gone to a region never visited before might say to others, "Come, sirs, within the village there are food, drink, perfumes, garlands, and so forth..."
Just as one cannot say, "I shall give," because it is outside of one's own domain and due to a lack of resources, so too the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*) is adventitious.
Thus, due to reasons such as the weakness of the physical basis (*vatthu*), it does not originate matter.

Furthermore, by whatever modes—such as through nutriment or the faculties—the mind and mental factors are conditions for mind-originated matter, all of those [conditions] are absent in the case of rebirth-linking.
Mind and mental factors are conditions, as appropriate, for the thirty types of kamma-born material phenomena. For this has been stated in the *Paṭṭhāna*:

"At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant indeterminate nutriments are a condition by way of nutriment-condition for the associated aggregates and for the kamma-born material phenomena," and so forth.

Therefore, it should be understood that because the thirty types of kamma-born material phenomena occupy the positions of the mind-originated material phenomena, the rebirth-linking consciousness does not originate material phenomena [at that moment].

Regarding the phrase "the death-consciousness of one who has attained arahantship": here they say that the death-consciousness of one whose taints are destroyed does not produce matter because it possesses an exceedingly peaceful mode of existence within a continuum whose roots of the round have been stilled; for such [peaceful existence] is absent in the case of non-returners and others.
However, the commentator Ānanda-ācariya says:

“At the moment of arising of the final consciousness of those in the sense sphere; for those whose consciousness immediately following it will give rise to the final consciousness of the sense sphere;

for those in the fine-material sphere and the immaterial sphere who are in their final existence; and for those who, having been reborn in the fine-material or immaterial sphere, will attain final Nibbāna at the time of death—for these, verbal formation [does not exist].”
"Because of the statement, 'It will cease, but for them bodily formation will not cease,' the death-consciousness of others also does not produce matter.
For this is the teacher's intention: by the phrase "of the final consciousness of those in the sense-sphere realm," without distinction...

Regarding the death-consciousness of beings in the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), by the phrase "and those [consciousnesses] belonging to the fine-material sphere... will cease," it is stated that for those who, having passed away from the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), are reborn in the fine-material or immaterial spheres, the verbal formation (*vacīsaṅkhāra*) ceases from the moment after the arising-phase of the sense-sphere death-consciousness;
since it is stated that the bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) does not exist at that time, it follows that the death-consciousness does not originate a bodily formation.
This is established. Furthermore, to the same extent that it does not arouse that bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*), it does not produce that remaining materiality (*rūpa*) either.
For there is no reason why the bodily formation should fail to arise—given the absence of obstructions such as being in the womb—for one who is capable of arousing materiality.
Nor is it logical that mind-originated materiality should continue to occur after death.

Nor is there any textual authority stating that "the death-consciousness produces matter. Furthermore, the non-cessation of the root of the round of existence is not the cause for the production of matter by the death-consciousness;

for even if matter were produced by the death-consciousness, it would not arise in the next life, just as matter produced by those preceding it does not. Therefore, the death-consciousness of all beings does not produce matter. If...
If it is argued that only the production of bodily formations establishes the state of being capable of generating material form, then how is this possible in the fourth jhāna?

This is not a fault; because of its exceedingly peaceful mode of existence through the power of cultivation, although bodily formations are not produced, there is no obstruction to the generation of material form, as there is an absence of weakness—unlike the consciousnesses at the moment of death.
But from what point onward does mind-born materiality (*cittajarūpa*) no longer arise? It is from the point onward when the bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) does not arise.
And when does the bodily formation not arise? It does not arise from thirty-two mind-moments prior to death;
having arisen in the thirty-third mind-moment, it ceases even before the final sixteen moments.

They say: regarding the question, “For one whose bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) does not cease, will their mental formation (*cittasaṅkhāra*) not cease?”—the answer, “At the moment of the dissolution of the final consciousness (*pacchimacitta*), for them both the bodily formation does not cease and the mental formation will not cease,” is given because the final consciousness itself is excluded;
thus, even by means of the second or third consciousness after death (*cuti*).

Others say: "It ceases together [with the body]. Regarding the statement, "That consciousness immediately after which the final consciousness of the sense-sphere arises," the word "whose" (*yassa*) refers to the consciousness that serves as the immediate condition for the death-consciousness of the sense sphere.

Since it is stated that the bodily formations are absent even after the arising of that [death-consciousness], [the cessation occurs] by means of the third consciousness itself from the point of death at the lower limit.
It ceases simultaneously. Some say it does not reach a second moment of consciousness.
151–7. "Of this one, there are one, two, three, or four positions" is *ekadviticatutthānaṃ*; the meaning is "the state of having one, two, three, or four positions.
And here, "position" (*ṭhāna*) is intended in the sense of a function (*kicca*), for it is therein that phenomena abide and remain established.
Because they appear as if [present], it is called a "basis" (*ṭhāna*).
He possesses five stainless eyes—namely, the flesh-eye, the divine eye, the wisdom-eye, the Buddha-eye, and the universal eye—thus he is "one with five stainless eyes.

By "without proliferation" (*nippapañca*) is meant being free from the proliferation (*papañca*) of passion and so forth; for passion and the like are called "proliferations" because they cause proliferation within saṃsāra.

The connection is: "In advertence, reception, and stationing, there is the triad of mind-element. The meaning is: the functional mind-element (*kiriyā-manodhātu*) is in the place of advertence, and the two types of resultant [mind-elements] are in the place of reception.

Although it should have been stated, "Investigation associated with joy may be investigation in the five doors," only the words "associated with joy" were mentioned for the sake of metrical convenience in the verse, as the term "investigation" is already understood from the context.
The phrase "when there is a strong object" is stated because the function of registration (*tadārammaṇa*) occurs only when the object is strong; it is not [the case otherwise].
Because, due to its unique nature, it arises only for all those objects of registration when the object is strong.
"Determining" (*voṭṭhabbana*) refers to the consciousness characterized by the function of determining, which is comprised within the functional mind-consciousness element.
(158–9) "Of all" means of all beings belonging to the realms of sense-sphere existence, fine-material existence, and immaterial existence. By this, he shows that [this occurs] at the five doors.

The function of determining (*voṭṭhabbanakicca*) occurs only for certain beings because of the total absence of five-door consciousness activity in the formless realm (*arūpabhava*), and the absence of activity in three doors in the fine-material realm (*rūpabhava*). However, the function of adverting (*āvajjanakicca*) in the mind door occurs for all sentient beings possessing a mind.
It is called "possessing two locations" (*dviṭṭhānika*) because it possesses the two aforementioned locations.

It is called a consciousness with two bases. Some, however, say: "The investigating consciousness accompanied by joy draws forth rebirth-linking in the sense-sphere happy destinies; therefore, it has five bases.
That is merely their own opinion, because it is not so explained in the *Paṭṭhāna*. For therein—
Regarding the statement, “Dependent on a state accompanied by equanimity, a state accompanied by equanimity arises by way of the non-root condition”:
here, dependent on one rootless aggregate accompanied by equanimity, three aggregates arise; dependent on three aggregates, one aggregate arises;
dependent on two aggregates, two aggregates arise; [and so on] at the moment of rootless rebirth-linking accompanied by equanimity.
“Dependent on one aggregate, three aggregates [arise]; dependent on three aggregates, one aggregate [arises];

dependent on two aggregates, two aggregates [arise]”—thus the method of dependence for the term “accompanied by equanimity” has been set forth by way of both occurrence and rebirth-linking. However, for the terms “accompanied by rapture” and “accompanied by pleasure”:
“Dependent on a state accompanied by rapture, a state accompanied by rapture arises by way of the not-root condition (*nahetupaccaya*).
Dependent on one rootless aggregate accompanied by rapture, three aggregates arise; dependent on three aggregates, one aggregate arises;
dependent on two aggregates, two aggregates arise. Dependent on a state accompanied by pleasure, a state accompanied by pleasure [arises]...”
“...arises by way of the non-root condition (*nahetupaccaya*). In dependence on one rootless aggregate accompanied by pleasure (*sukhasahagata*), three aggregates [arise];
in dependence on three aggregates, one aggregate; in dependence on two aggregates, two aggregates.
Thus it is extracted solely by way of the process of occurrence (*pavatti*), and not by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) such as “at the moment of rootless rebirth-linking,” and so forth.

Therefore, since even non-statement in the teaching according to the Dhamma indicates non-existence, it is said that there is no giving of rebirth-linking for that [non-percipient being], and thus its status as having two locations is stated.
"Those nine sublime resultant [consciousnesses]" is the connection. 162.
"Six-door" means those belonging to the six doors (*chadvārikā*). Alternatively, "among the six-door" means "among the six-door consciousnesses."
“Five functions,” and so forth, is the conclusion for those [consciousnesses] already mentioned. “The rest” refers to the sixty-eight types of consciousness.
It is called “one” because it possesses a single function, or because its function is one; thus it is singular (*ekaka*).
In order to show the sequence of functions as well, at the very point where all consciousnesses are described by way of their functions, it is said: “Life-continuum, adverting,” and so forth. If...
Should it not be stated that [the process] begins from rebirth-linking and ends with death? True;
however, it was not stated in that way because death and rebirth-linking are well known. For it is indeed well known that rebirth-linking is the beginning of existence (bhava) and death is its end.
Therefore, setting aside the well-known points, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) itself was mentioned at the outset in order to show [the process] starting from the less well-known point.

Although that registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) is not manifest, it is nonetheless not invariable because it is not obtained in every instance of the impulsion process (*javana-vīthi*) within any given existence;
thus, it was not mentioned here for the purpose of illustrating that which is invariably obtained.
Alternatively, since the registration consciousness is for the most part designated as "life-continuum" (*bhavaṅga*), the registration [consciousness] in the preceding impulsion process—
Because the adverting consciousness that precedes the final javana-process is already included by the mention of the "life-continuum" (bhavaṅga), it is not mentioned separately.
However, some say: "The phrase 'adverting from the life-continuum' and so forth was stated in order to show the fivefold nature [of adverting] according to its occurrence in the five sense-doors.
But in that case, since there is the presence of certain [types of adverting] that do not occur [in all instances], [the specific terminology is necessary].
That is not appropriate; rather, it is correct to say that it is for the purpose of demonstrating the sixfold method by way of the activity of the six doors.

And just as it was stated here regarding the eye-door in the sequence beginning with "life-continuum and adverting," so too should the occurrence of functions be applied to the ear-door and the others, omitting seeing and so forth and inserting hearing and so forth. But in the case of the mind-door—
“First there is the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), then adverting (āvajjana) is considered the second;
having transcended that, the third may be the impulsion (javana).
Thus should the construction be understood. “Of the six consciousnesses” refers to the five beginning with eye-consciousness and mind-consciousness (manoviññāṇa).

"And the seven consciousness-elements" refers to the seven consciousness-elements: the five beginning with the eye-consciousness-element, and the two consisting of the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element.
(169–71) "Excluding the five direct knowledges" means—
“Supernormal power, the divine ear, knowledge of others’ minds,
recollection of past lives, and the divine eye— thus it is fivefold.

This excludes the fifth jhāna consciousness of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) associated with these five supernormal knowledges (abhiññā) that have thus been described, such as the divine ear and the rest.

Even though each [higher knowledge] has its own specific object, it is stated as "excluding the five higher knowledges" because there is no difference in the state of the single consciousness [in which they arise].

Some, however, say: "Since here only those states of consciousness that have mental phenomena (dhamma) as their object are mentioned, this is a rejection of the five higher knowledges together with the knowledge of the future, excluding the knowledge of others' minds."
By excluding the two sets of fivefold consciousness and the three mind-elements (manodhātu), there are forty-one; thus he said, "Forty and likewise one.
Regarding the word *ca* in the phrase "and the direct knowledges" (*abhiññāni ca*), it is used out of its proper place;
it should be understood as following immediately after "forty and likewise one," and by it, the two types of direct-knowledge consciousness are included. Alternatively, *abhiññā*...

It should be understood that because the fifth jhāna mentioned previously—among those with a single object—is merely a specific state (*avatthāviseso*) of that same jhāna, the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) are not included among the six types of objects. 172–3.
"Having divided into three" means for the purpose of dividing into three; for this particle *tvā* has the sense of a causal suffix (*hetvattho*), as in the expression "having seen a lion."
“Fear and trepidation arise; yet, having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed.

By the passage beginning with “By way of merit and demerit,” it should be understood that the method (naya) has been provided in order to demonstrate the classification of consciousness by way of the mental-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu), having analyzed it into as many as seventy-six varieties according to birth, plane, cause, feeling, and so forth.

175. “Having made threefold” means: first, by dividing [each element] into the two types of resultant and the functional; second, by dividing them into the wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth—thus having made each of the two elements threefold.
180. “The thirtyfold earth... explain” means: it is thirtyfold because it occurs according to the diversity of the thirty planes;
and it is also thirtyfold because it occurs according to the diversity of the thirty types of persons therein, and so on. This refers to the consciousness as it has been described.
"And he discerns them in many ways" means that he should analyze them.

"Here" means in this teaching. "They become as if they were myrobalan fruits in the palm of one's hand" means that just as a myrobalan fruit held in the palm is very clearly visible to one with good eyesight, so too are the meanings contained within the Abhidhamma Piṭaka to this wise bhikkhu.
They are well-manifested; the meaning is that they appear very clearly at every moment of adverting.
Thus ends [the section] from the *Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanā*, titled *Abhidhammatthavikāsinī*.
The commentary on the exposition of the singlefold and so forth is finished. 5.
Fifth Chapter:
Commentary on the Exposition of the Levels, Persons, and Arisings of Consciousness.
182–8. It is called "producing growth of intelligence" (*buddhibuddhikara*) because it brings about the increase, expansion, and development of wisdom.
Having stated that he will demonstrate each specific method of exposition as it was promised, he says, "The arising of the planes of consciousness.

Having said that, in order to show—by way of the planes being the support—the various types of destinies (*gatibheda*) and the various types of existence (*bhavabheda*) that arise incidentally, he says, "And the gods," and so forth.

It has been stated thus: having said, "There are four planes of means," they claim that because the destiny of the asuras is included within the destiny of the petas, it was therefore said, "There are five destinies.
However, we think that the reading should rather be, "Three are the planes of the states of misery (apāya).
For this teacher, whose speech is unconfused, would not have spoken in such a way—contradictory from beginning to end and productive of confusion.
He speaks these words.

For in the Pāḷi as well—“Sāriputta, there are these five destinations. Which five? Hell, the animal realm, the sphere of hungry ghosts, humans, and devas”—it is stated thus by way of only the three woeful states (apāya).
There are three realms of existence (bhava) by way of the sensual, fine-material, and immaterial [realms]. “Therein” means among those.

"In the three realms of existence. "In thirty" means: the four planes of misery, the sevenfold plane of happy destinies in the sense-sphere, the sixteen Brahma-worlds of the fine-material sphere, and the four immaterial planes—these constitute thirty-one planes. However, because the subject matter concerns the occurrence of consciousness, the non-percipient plane is excluded;
thus, the meaning is that there are only thirty remaining planes. "In those very thirty, persons" refers to those [persons] within those [thirty].
The individuals who arise in the planes are exactly thirty according to the enumeration of the planes.
However, showing that even these thirty types, when reckoned by way of the number of rebirth-linking consciousnesses (*paṭisandhicitta*), amount to nineteen, he says:
"In these planes," and so forth. Regarding "rebirth-linking consciousnesses": there are ten sense-sphere rebirth-linking consciousnesses and five fine-material-sphere rebirth-linking consciousnesses.
Regarding the phrase "the four immaterial-sphere rebirth-linking consciousnesses," this refers to the nineteen types of rebirth-linking consciousnesses.
"The non-percipient beings are without consciousness" means that the rebirth-linking of non-percipient beings is without consciousness. For it has been said:
"The gods who are non-percipient beings appear without root-cause, without nutriment, without contact, without feeling, without perception, without volition, and without consciousness."

If there are twenty persons by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), how is it said that there are thirty by way of plane? To the objection that "thirty-one" should be stated, he says "here," and so forth.
Those for whom no cause exists are "causeless" (*ahetu*); there are two. Those for whom two or three causes exist are "two-cause" or "three-cause" (*dviti-hetu*). The meaning is:

those who are causeless, those with two causes, and those with three causes by way of rebirth-linking. Among them, the causeless ones are those bound for the states of misery (*āpāyika*) and certain earth-deities.

Among humans, there are those who are blind from birth, deaf from birth, insane from birth, eunuchs, hermaphrodites, and so forth. Those remaining as mentioned are inhabitants of the happy realms of the sense-sphere who possess only two roots.
However, those possessing three roots are exclusively inhabitants of the happy realms of the sense-sphere.
As for the "eight noble ones," this refers to the eight types of noble persons by way of the four who possess the noble paths and the four who possess the noble fruits.

"But are not even the Noble Ones possessed of only three roots? True; however, it should be understood that they are mentioned separately because there exists a specific distinction among them when it comes to the arising of consciousness.
Having heard [the author] say, "Listen as I speak of the arising in the planes," the opponent replies with the words, "In thirty planes," and so forth.
He asks about the universal consciousnesses of all planes, and the other replies, "Only fourteen.

In this regard, there are exactly fourteen—namely, the eight limited wholesome states, the four dissociated from views, the [consciousness] accompanied by restlessness, and the mind-door adverting consciousness;
they are neither fewer nor more. They exist in all thirty planes; the meaning is that they are common to all planes.

"Always... may they be": these two roots of unwholesomeness [are excluded]. The eighteen sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses—excluding the wholesome-resultant eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, receiving consciousness, and the two types of investigating consciousness—make twenty consciousnesses that "may always exist only in the sense-sphere realm";
the meaning is that they never arise elsewhere. But do not unwholesome-resultant [consciousnesses] also arise among the Brahmās?
Truths arise; they arise by taking undesirable forms and so forth as their object in the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava), because of the absence of such objects in the Brahma-world.

Therefore, they are restricted to the sense-sphere existence alone. The five fine-material-sphere resultant consciousnesses would exist only in the fine-material-sphere existence, and the four immaterial-sphere resultants in the immaterial realms; thus he said, "five in the fine-material existence," and so forth.

“Kāma …pe… they come to be”: eighteen types of consciousness—namely, the wholesome and functional consciousnesses of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), the wholesome-resultants, the eye-, ear-, receiving-, and investigating-consciousnesses, and the two rootless functional consciousnesses excluding the determining-consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*), as well as the consciousness of the first path—exist only in the sense-sphere and fine-material spheres, not in the immaterial sphere (*arūpabhava*).
For there, because all perceptions of form have been completely transcended.
Wholesome and functional states of the fine-material sphere do not arise. Eye-consciousness and the others do not arise because they lack a physical base (vatthu) and a door (dvāra);

the smile-producing consciousness does not arise because it is exclusively dependent on a physical base; and the stream-entry path does not arise because it is produced solely through the condition of another’s voice.
"Forty-two" refers to the eight limited wholesome states, the four formless-sphere wholesome states, and those excluding the first path.

There are forty-two types of consciousness in the three realms of existence: the seven supramundane consciousnesses; the ten unwholesome consciousnesses, excluding the two types associated with aversion;
the nine sense-sphere functional consciousnesses, excluding the two previously mentioned rootless functionals; and the four formless-sphere functional consciousnesses.
Thus, there are forty-two types of consciousness in the three realms.
193–204. Having thus shown the arising of consciousness by way of existence (*bhava*), he now says “But setting aside,” etc., showing it by way of time (*kāla*).
The genitive case in *sabbāsanti* is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). There are thirteen types of consciousness that are free from the states of misery (*apāya*):

the eight great functional (*mahākiriyā*) consciousnesses, the consciousnesses of the path and fruit of Arahatship, the fruit of Non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), and the wholesome functional consciousness of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*).
They exist in twenty-six planes because they do not arise when there is the presence of the obstruction of karmic result (*vipākāvaraṇa*) in the woeful states.

This connects with the phrase "the other six consciousnesses. These, moreover, should be understood by way of the five limited resultant [consciousnesses] common to the fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*) and the functional mind-element (*kiriyamanodhātu*).
"Five types of consciousness" refers to the five types of consciousness associated with wrong view and doubt. These are not found in the five Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsabhūmi),
because those realms are inhabited exclusively by non-returners (anāgāmin) whose taints are exhausted,
and because even by the first path these [beings] have brought about the state of being non-arising for these five kinds of consciousness.

"Two others" refers to the third immaterial wholesome and functional consciousnesses. Indeed, these do not arise because their objects transcend the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and because they lack root-cause rebirth-linking in the woeful states.
"Two in twenty-four planes" refers to two types of consciousness by way of the wholesome and functional consciousnesses of the base of infinite consciousness.
"Only two in twenty-three planes" refers to the wholesome and functional consciousnesses of the base of infinite space.

"Of eleven kinds" means that there are eleven [types of consciousness], namely the wholesome and functional states of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) and the smile-producing consciousness (*hasituppāda*).
From the fruit of stream-entry up to the path of non-returning, these four types of consciousness occur in twenty-one planes, excluding the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*) and the woeful states (*apāya*).
The single consciousness of the stream-entry path arises in seventeen planes, excluding the Pure Abodes, the woeful states, and the immaterial planes (*arūpabhūmi*).

The two types of consciousness rooted in hatred, the four wholesome-resultant consciousnesses of the nose, tongue, and body, and the seven unwholesome-resultant consciousnesses—these twelve types of consciousness arise in the eleven sense-sphere planes (kāmabhūmi), excluding the sublime planes (mahaggatabhūmi). The eight great resultant consciousnesses arise in seven planes according to the realms of devas and humans within the sense sphere.
"In six planes" refers to those reckoned as the Vehapphala heaven and the Suddhāvāsa heavens.
In the six planes of the fifth jhāna. "Four...
[etc. ...in the planes" means that the fruition of the fourth jhāna arises in three planes by way of the Parittasubha, Appamāṇasubha, and Subhakiṇha realms;
and the fruition of the second jhāna and the fruition of the third jhāna arise by way of the Parittābha, Appamāṇābha, and Ābhassara realms.
In the three planes, the resultant of the first jhāna occurs in the three planes by way of the Brahma-pārisajja, Brahma-purohita, and Mahābrahmā [realms].
Thus, four types of consciousness arise in each of the three planes respectively.
206–9. In this way, only so many types of consciousness arise in so many planes; such is their arising according to the fixed determination of consciousness.

Having thus shown [the general classification], he now begins the passage beginning with "Wholesome and unwholesome in the sense-sphere" (*kusalākusalā kāme*) in order to demonstrate, by way of the restriction of planes (*bhūmi-niyama*), that only so many types of consciousness arise in each of these specific planes.
Therein, in the sense-sphere (*kāma*), there are twenty wholesome and unwholesome states;

fifteen of these are rootless resultants (*ahetuka-vipāka*), and together with the two types of adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*), there are exactly thirty-seven mental states even in all four realms, such as the hells and so forth.

They are born in the woeful states (*apāya*). However, the remaining fifty-two types of consciousness—namely, the seventeen sense-sphere resultant and functional consciousnesses (*kāmāvacara-vipāka-kiriya-citta*) and the thirty-five sublime and supramundane consciousnesses (*mahaggata-lokuttara*)—never arise among those [beings], because they are not the appropriate plane for them; this is the meaning.

"Eighty in the heart" refers to the eighty types of consciousness remaining after those have been stated. "The triad of nose-consciousness and so forth" refers to the triad of wholesome and resultant nose-consciousness and so forth.

Regarding the phrase “the ripening of demerit”: because all unwholesome (akusala) ripenings are included therein, even though the triad of nose-consciousness and so forth is not specifically mentioned, it is understood through the method of elimination (pārisesa-naya) to be exclusively wholesome ripening. 213.

“Dissatisfaction” (domanassa) means accompanied by dissatisfaction. “And two functionals” (kriyā) refers to the two rootless functionals (ahetuka-kiriya), excluding the determining consciousness (voṭṭhabbana).

214. *Bhūmivaseneva* means "solely by way of the planes," without referring to individuals (*puggala*). The connection is: "one should analyze the arising of consciousness by way of individuals and by way of the planes.

216–8. *Pañcabhūmisu* means "in the five planes" by way of the four woeful states and the human realm. It is stated as "seventy-seven" by way of the rootless (*ahetuka*) rebirth-linking and its similar object-moment (*tadārammaṇa*);
however, because other types of kamma can also produce a two-rooted (*dvihetuka*) object-moment, there are forty-one [additional moments].

[They] exist. According to the intention of the Elder Ācariya Jotipāla, it should be understood that there are forty-five [consciousnesses], including those with triple-rooted (tihetuka) resultant states.
"Together with those stated for the rootless" means together with the thirty-seven mental states stated for a rootless being.
"Nine functional states" refers to these nine uncommon functional consciousnesses: the eight great functionals and the smile-producing (hasituppāda).

220–1. Having stated, "Fifty-four types of consciousness," he says, "Of the two-rooted," and so forth, in order to show their specific forms. Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Fifty-four" is the conclusion. 223–4. "His fifty-five types of consciousness":
among the fifty-four types of consciousness mentioned for a worldling (*puthujjana*) possessing three roots, there are forty-nine excluding those accompanied by wrong view and doubt;
adding the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*), these constitute his fifty-five types of sense-sphere consciousness (*kāmāvacara*). This refers to one who is a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*).
They arise. "Serving ninety" refers to thirty-nine consciousnesses. "The first fruit bears fruit" means the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).

"And having abandoned the second fruit" means having abandoned the fruit of once-returning (*sakadāgāmi-phala*). By the word "and" (*ca*), the meaning is that the fruit of stream-entry is also abandoned.
Those forty-eight consciousnesses which, together with their own respective fruits, belong to the being who is a non-returner (*anāgāmi*).
They arise. There are forty-four consciousnesses: twenty-three sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses, twenty functional consciousnesses, and the fruit of Arahantship.

Each one’s own [path-consciousness] refers to the path-consciousness of each respective individual, such as "the stream-enterer’s path-consciousness of stream-entry" or "the once-returner’s path-consciousness of once-returning," and so forth. But why?
He said, "They have only one consciousness at a time," meaning "by means of a single moment of consciousness. There are thirty-five [types of consciousness]:
seventeen wholesome consciousnesses of the sense-sphere, fine-material, and immaterial realms; ten unwholesome consciousnesses, excluding the two types of aversion;

five rootless resultant consciousnesses obtainable in the fine-material realm; the two types of adverting consciousness; and the resultant consciousness of the first jhāna. Thus, there are thirty-five consciousnesses.
[These states] arise in an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) on the three levels of the first *jhāna*.
Regarding the phrase "having abandoned" (*hitvā ca*): here, by the word "and" (*ca*), the inclusion of the first fruit (*phala*) is indicated.

Thus, the meaning is: "having abandoned the fivefold non-meritorious [states] and having taken up the first fruit. The "fivefold non-meritorious [states]" refers to those associated with wrong view and accompanied by doubt.
There are five unwholesome consciousnesses. "Therein" means among those stated for the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*). "Right there" means among those stated for the once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*).
The connection is: "the merit-born, the receiving, and the two types of investigating.
(237) Having thus shown the arising of consciousness on the plane of the first jhāna by way of the worldling, the stream-enterer, and so forth, [the text continues].
Now, in order to show [the results] on the plane of the second jhāna by means of those very same [beings], the passage beginning with “of the worldling” (puthujjanassa) is commenced.

Although it is impossible for the single being to possess the fruition of both the second and third jhānas simultaneously, those worldlings and others who have been reborn in the realm of the second jhāna are taken together under the commonality of their status as worldlings and so forth; thus it is said: “fruition of the second and third jhānas.”

242. From the *Parittasubha* realm up to the Akaniṭṭha realm, the occurrence of consciousness in the planes of the third and fourth jhānas should be understood according to the enumeration given for the plane of the first jhāna. Therefore, he said: "of the *Parittakasubha* and so forth. 247.
"Twenty-four types of consciousness" refers to: the eight limited wholesome consciousnesses; the four formless-sphere wholesome consciousnesses;
