the ten unwholesome consciousnesses excluding the two with aversion; the resultant of the first formless attainment; and the mind-door adverting consciousness—thus making twenty-four types of consciousness.
Fifteen types of consciousness arise for a worldling in the first immaterial plane:
the eight great functional consciousnesses, the four immaterial functional consciousnesses, mind-door adverting, the resultant of the first immaterial attainment, and the fruit of arahantship.

Twenty-three types of consciousness [arise] for a worldling in the first immaterial plane; that is, from among the twenty-four consciousnesses stated for that plane, excluding the wholesome and resultant of the base of infinite space.
The twenty-two [types of consciousness] and the resultant of the second immaterial state—thus, twenty-three types of consciousness belong to the worldling on the plane of the second immaterial state.

On that same plane, for the three who have attained the fruits and the trainees, there are nineteen types of consciousness: eighteen from among those mentioned for the worldling, excluding the five unwholesome types, plus the respective fruit-consciousness.
There are twelve functional consciousnesses (*kriyā-citta*): the eight great functionals, the three formless functionals excluding the base of infinite space, and mind-door adverting.

There is one resultant consciousness of the formless realm (*arūpa-vipāka*). In the second formless plane, twenty-two consciousnesses arise for a worldling (*puthujjana*): twenty-one—excluding the wholesome and resultant consciousnesses of the base of infinite consciousness—from among those mentioned for the second formless plane, plus the resultant consciousness of the base of nothingness. In the third formless plane, these same twenty-two consciousnesses arise for a worldling.

254–60. Among those stated for the worldling (*puthujjana*), seventeen—excluding the five non-meritorious [consciousnesses]—and the first fruit (*paṭhamaphala*) make eighteen that arise in a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) on the plane of the third immaterial attainment (*tatiyāruppabhūmi*). "Those" refers to those same eighteen consciousnesses.
For, by the statement "excluding the first fruit," the meaning that the second fruit is included is established even though it was not explicitly mentioned.
For it is not the case that the fruit of once-returning does not arise for one who is a once-returner. And having made this point, it was said: "excluding the second fruit.
Here too, it should be understood that the fruit of non-returning is established by the context itself. [The consciousnesses are:

the eight great functional consciousnesses, the two functional consciousnesses of the third and fourth immaterial spheres, mind-door adverting, the resultant of the base of nothingness, and the fruit of arahantship.
Thirteen types of consciousness arise for one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) in the third immaterial plane.

Among the twenty-two types of consciousness stated for a worldling (puthujjana) in the third immaterial plane, twenty—excluding the wholesome and resultant [consciousness] of the base of nothingness—along with the resultant consciousness of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, these twenty-one types of consciousness arise for a worldling in the fourth immaterial plane. Among those stated for a worldling...

There, seventeen types of consciousness arise for one who has attained stream-entry (*sotāpanna*): the sixteen excluding the five unwholesome (*apuñña*) classes, together with the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*).

There, twelve types of consciousness arise for an Arhat (*arahant*): the eight great functional (*mahākiriyā*), the two functional-resultants (*vipākakiriyā*) of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*), mind-door adverting (*manodvārāvajjana*), and the fruit of arhatship (*arahattaphala*).

261–3. The intention is that immaterial wholesome states (*arūpa-kusala*) and functional states (*kiriyā*) arise, but not resultant states (*vipāka*). Regarding the phrase "higher and higher immaterial realms" (*uddhamuddham-arūpīnaṃ*):

this refers to those in the immaterial realms, such as the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*), and so forth. Regarding the phrase "those below": for those belonging to the base of infinite consciousness, the wholesome and resultant states of the base of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatana*) do not arise; for those belonging to the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*), the wholesome and resultant states of both the base of infinite space and the base of infinite consciousness do not arise.
By such means as these, each successive lower immaterial state does not arise. Why? He says: "Because of the perceived danger," where *kira* indicates tradition.

"Because of the perceived danger" means because of the faults seen in both the object and the jhāna. "Wholesome supramundane" refers to the wholesome states of the supramundane (lokuttara). 266. "All sublime form" refers to every arising of sublime consciousness belonging to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*).

"Mind-element" (*manodhātu*) is used because the functional mind-element (*kiriya-manodhātu*) and the resultant mind-element (*vipāka-manodhātu*) have already been included by the mention of the sense-sphere resultants (*kāmavipāka*).

269–73. Thus... [and so on]... excluding the threefold set of the second immaterial sphere from among those stated in the second immaterial sphere, thirty-nine consciousnesses arise in the third immaterial sphere along with their own maturation;

and excluding the threefold set of the third immaterial sphere from among those stated therein, thirty-seven arise along with their own maturation. In this way, for the remaining two as well, each lower stage is excluded.

The reckoning of consciousness should be understood as follows: "one's own, one's own" refers to the fruition of the first immaterial sphere in the first immaterial plane, and the fruition of the second immaterial sphere in the second immaterial plane;

thus, for each of the four immaterial planes, five fruitions arise—namely, the four respective immaterial fruitions and the taintless supramundane fruition. As for the functional [consciousness], there are thirteen.
If there are [such], they arise for one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) in the first immaterial plane; this is the connection.
In the second immaterial plane, for one whose taints are destroyed, there are twelve functional consciousnesses (kriyā), excluding the first immaterial functional consciousness.

In the third immaterial plane, there are eleven, excluding the second immaterial functional consciousness. In the fourth immaterial plane, [there are ten, excluding] the third immaterial functional consciousness...
Excluding these ten, [the remaining] eleven are to be understood.

274–5. Now, in order to show the unique consciousness of those very persons solely by way of the individual, [the author], having first shown the consciousness arising only for an Arahant with the words "But for an Arahant," etc., [proceeds to] show the individual [consciousness] for the Non-returners and others.
The state of mind associated with its respective fruit is indeed evident; thus it is stated concisely. "Of the Arahant" means of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).

The state of being an Arahant is *arahatta*; the meaning is the fruit of arahantship. For that is called "arahantship" by virtue of being the ground for the application of the term "Arahant" through such definitions as "one who is an Arahant because of having slain the enemies.
Now, [the author sets forth] the common types of consciousness for those various individuals.
In order to show this, it was said: “And of the four who stand in the fruit,” and so forth. 290. *Susāraṃ*:
because of the absence of any softwood (*pheggu*) that ought to be discarded in terms of either meaning or phrasing, it is “well-essenced” (*suṭṭhu sāraṃ*);

the sense is that it is entirely solid essence (*sabbaso sāraṃ*). *Paraṃ*: precisely because of its being well-essenced, it is supreme (*paraṃ*). [It is] for sentient beings, [acting as] a coverer of the welfare of this world and the world beyond...
Because it dispels the darkness of ignorance, it is "a lamp for the darkness of delusion. "He reflects" means he reflects by way of the meaning (*attha*).
"He recites" means he rehearses by way of the phrasing (*byañjana*). Since greed and hatred are inseparable from delusion, their non-approaching [of the person] is already established by implication;
thus, although it says "a lamp for the darkness of delusion," the phrase "greed and hatred do not approach the man... refers specifically to their non-approaching.
It has been said: by the very expression “a lamp in the darkness of delusion,” the non-approaching of delusion is stated; thus, the non-approaching of greed and hatred alone is stated.

However, it should be understood that by the statement regarding the non-approaching of the three [defilements] which constitute the root, the non-approaching of all remaining defilements is also stated.
Thus ends the commentary on the Exposition of the Bases,
Persons, and the Arising of Consciousness,
within the *Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanā* titled *Abhidhammatthavikāsinī*.
The first part is finished.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
*Abhidhammāvatāra-abhinavaṭīkā* (A New Commentary on the Entrance to the Abhidhamma).
(Second Part) 6.
The Sixth Chapter:
Commentary on the Exposition of the Classification of Objects (Ārammaṇa)

291–3. [The phrase] "of these" refers to those classified as previously stated. Now, one might raise this objection: "Since consciousness and mental factors were already enumerated by the statement 'consciousness, mental factors,' and so forth, it is precisely those that should be explained; however, the object has not been mentioned there, so why is it spoken of here?
Having taken this objection to heart, he says: "For without that, there is no occurrence. This is because, without an object...
There is no such thing as a consciousness that has arisen without an object; for there is no such thing as a consciousness called "objectless. Therefore, the meaning is:
"In order to dispel the doubt, 'Upon what, then, does this consciousness arise?', I shall hereafter show its object. To the questions, "In how many ways is that object?
And what is its specific nature? he says: "Visible form, sound," and so forth. [Now, the] etymological meaning...
But he himself will explain this later. "Skilled in the six objects" refers to the Buddhas and others who are expert in explaining the six types of objects.

"The primary elements" (bhūta) refers to the four great elements. "Derived from" (upādāya) means depending upon. "Arising from the four" (catusamuṭṭhita) means arisen from the four conditions, such as kamma and so forth.
"Illustration" (nidassana) is that which should be illustrated. What is it? It is the state of being visible, the state of being the objective domain of eye-consciousness.

"With demonstration" means "with visibility" (*sanidassana*). "Resistance" (*paṭigha*) refers to that which strikes back or the act of striking back; it is the occurrence of a modification in the bases such as the eye when they are accompanied by other conditions for modification, such as mental activity.

Its meaning is: resistance (*paṭigha*) is the state of being turned toward one another and the mutual impact between those [bases] themselves, both those that have come into contact and those that have not, by way of their own support. In this context, the contact of the tangible object itself...

By way of dependence, there is success (sampatti) for the nose, tongue, and body in relation to odors, tastes, and tangible objects respectively. For the others, however, there is non-success (asampatti) in both ways;
therefore, here, the state of being opposed to those things that are not successful is called "resistance" (*paṭigha*). That which is "with resistance" is *sappaṭigha*;
and that which is "visible" and also "with resistance" is "visible-with-resistance" (*sanidassana-sappaṭigha*). Here it is asked: for that which has the state of being visible...
There is such a thing as "being visible" (*sanidassana*); it should be understood as the very state of being an object of visual consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*).
Since that [state] is not other than the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), how is it appropriate to say it is "with visibility" (*saha nidassanena*)? It is said:
although it is not other than that, it is spoken of as if it were something else in order to distinguish the sense-sphere of form from other phenomena; thus it is said, "together with visibility."

"Visible. For when phenomena have become unified through their commonality of intrinsic nature (*dhammasabhāva*), that specific distinction which creates differentiation is fit to be treated as if it were something else by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).
In this way, there is an understanding of the specific meaning. "Known as the perception of the visible object of form":
this kind of color is known as the "visible object of form. This is what is meant: depending upon the four great elements (*mahābhūta*)...
That which, not abandoning its occurrence, arises from kamma, arises from consciousness, arises from temperature, and arises from nutriment;
which is seen by way of blue and so forth, and which strikes the sense faculties—that is called the visible-object base (rūpārammaṇa). As for "cittotu-sambhava":

"citta" and "utu" constitute "cittotu"; that which originates from these is "cittotu-sambhava. Alternatively, it is so called because these two are the originating conditions (sambhavā paccayā) for this [visible object].
"Born from mind and temperature. Sound that occurs together with consciousness that originates intimation is "sound with consciousness.
However, sound with consciousness does not arise solely from within a conscious continuum;
for it can also be produced by temperature, as in the case of sounds such as those from the womb.
"It sustains" means it is maintained by a succession of groups [of atoms]. "By indicating" means by making its own basis clearly manifest.
For fragrance makes known, "This is sweet-smelling; this is foul-smelling";
it is like a backbiter who, regarding hidden flowers, fruits, and so forth, reports, "There is this here."

*Rasamānā* means being satisfied by way of relishing (*assāda*). *Rasanti* means they taste; the meaning is that they experience. Here, the letter *ra* is used for euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*).
For in this way, the etymological method (*niruttinaya*)—“*rasamānā naṃ asantīti raso*” (that which they taste while tasting is *rasa*)—becomes elegant.
Otherwise, if it were said “*rasanti assādentī*” (they taste, i.e., they relish), the term "*rasamānā*" would be redundant. Alternatively, "*rasamānā*" [is explained as follows]:...
Taking the letter *ra* from *rasantī* and the letter *sa* from *rasantī*, the etymological method (*niruttinaya*) for the term "taste" (*raso*) should be understood. 298.
"It is touched" means it is struck. To the question, "What is that which is called the tangible? he says: "earth, fire, and air.
By this, it is shown that only these three elements constitute what is called the tangible—defined as being cognizable by body-consciousness—and nothing else.
[The author] shows this. But why is the water element (*āpodhātu*) not included here? Is it not the case that coolness is perceived through touch, and that is indeed the water element?
True, it is perceived; however, it is not the water element, but rather the fire element (*tejodhātu*) itself. For when the state of heat is dull, there is the perception of coolness;
there is no such quality as "coolness" existing in itself. Rather, it is merely due to the dullness of the state of heat that there arises the misconception of coolness.
If it is asked, "How, then, is this to be understood? It is because the increase of cold is unstable, like [the shifting] of the near and far shores.
For instance, in the summer season, for those who stand in the heat and enter the shade, there is an increase of cold;

yet for those who emerge from the earth's interior at that very same spot, there is an increase of heat. Furthermore, this is because we observe that cold acts as a ripener during times such as the onset of snowfall.
And it should be understood that coolness is indeed the fire element (*tejodhātu*).
If coolness were the water element (*āpodhātu*), it would be perceived within a single group (*kalāpa*) together with heat, because the two elements function inseparably; yet it is not so perceived.
Therefore, it is known that "coolness is not the water element. This is the inseparable functioning of the four great elements.

This is the superior argument for those who desire it; however, even for those who do not accept it, this very same argument is the superior one, since the uniformity of function has been established by showing that the four great elements perform their respective functions within a single group (kalāpa). Some, however, claim that "the air element is coldness";
for them as well, this very same argument is the superior one. If the air element were coldness, then within a single group, [coldness] would coexist with heat.
If it were to be perceived, it would not be perceived in this way; therefore, it is understood that "the air element is not coldness.
As for those who say, "The water element is fluidity, and that is apprehended by touch," they should be told:
"To say that even the state of fluidity is touched is merely a matter of the venerable ones' overestimation, just as in the case of shape. For this was said by the ancients:
“Touching the three elements that function as the manifestation of fluidity,
this world conceives the thought, ‘I am touching fluidity.
Just as, having touched the elements, a shape is grasped by the mind;”
"I touch it through direct experience"—in this way, fluidity should be understood.
(299) "All that is called 'name'" means all that is recognized as mind, mental factors, and Nibbāna. For mind and mental factors are called "name" because they bend toward an object;
Nibbāna, however, is called "name" because it bends toward the self of mind and mental factors.
"Form" (*rūpa*) refers to produced form (*nipphannarūpa*). If it is asked, "Is this without distinction? he says, "no," adding, "having excluded the pentad beginning with visible form.
"Characteristics" (*lakkhaṇa*) refers to the characteristics of impermanence and so forth. "Designation" (*paññatti*) is twofold, by way of name and by way of dependence. 300.
Now, are all these six kinds of objects found everywhere, or only in some places?

Regarding the phrase "some," he says: "six objects," and so forth. In the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara-bhūmi*), three objects are obtained by way of visible form, sound, and mental phenomena (*dhamma*).
However, because the triad of the nose and the other [senses] is absent there, objects such as odors are not obtained separately from the object of mental phenomena.
In the immaterial realm (*arūpa-bhava*), however, because of the total absence of material forms, there is only one [object].
"Only a mental object (dhammārammaṇa) is obtained, and no other," thus he said: "In the formless realm, there is only the single [consciousness] with a mental object.

But is it not the case that for those who, having passed away from the formless existence, are reborn in the sense-sphere existence, a visible-form object appears precisely in the formless existence as the sign of their destination (gatinimitta)?
True, it does appear; however, that is an object only within the sense-sphere existence. For in the existence in which one is to be reborn—
Color appears by way of its characteristic of movement.
Having thus shown the six objects according to their essential nature and the distinctions in their occurrence, [the author] now states,
"Because of the brevity of the momentary basis," etc., in order to demonstrate a certain deviation on the part of the inhabitants of Abhayagiri regarding those [objects] and to refute it.
In that context, "due to the brevity of the moment and the object" means because of the brevity of both the moment (*khaṇa*) and the object (*vatthu*).
The connection is with the words "those [factors] beginning with form" (*ye rūpādayo*). "Of whom" (*yesam*) refers to those teachers whose doctrine it is.

Alternatively, "of whom" is used because of their state of being connected with the mental object (*dhammārammaṇa*), and because they are the determiners (*vavatthāpaka*). For they, while determining the mental object, connect it with themselves.
Therefore, because it requires a relationship with the object of the Dhamma, the word "yesaṃ" (of which) is used in the genitive case.
By this, the following is meant: those five objects, beginning with visible form, are momentary for only a brief duration—like a drop of water falling upon a red-hot iron ball;
they have minute bases, like atoms, being impossible to grasp even by the divine eye.

Furthermore, for those who hold the view that "those things which do not come within the range of their respective consciousnesses, but are exclusively the domain of mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*) alone,
are called 'dhamma-objects' (*dhammārammaṇa*)," or for those who hold the view that "those [others] are what are called 'dhamma-objects'"—
by this very fact of being past or future, by being too distant or too near, and by being obstructed by walls and so forth, they do not come within the range [of the senses].
"The inclusion of even those forms and so forth that do not come [into contact] has been made. However, those who hold such a view should be refuted by citing this sutta:

"Friends, for these five faculties which have different domains and different ranges, and which do not experience each other's domain and range, the mind is their resort, and the mind experiences their domain and range.
Demonstrating this, he said, "They should be refuted," and so forth.
In this context, "to be rejected" means they are not to be followed. Regarding the phrase "mutually...

becoming," it refers to those who do not experience one another's objective domain—such as the eye-faculty not experiencing the range of the ear-faculty, and likewise the ear-faculty not [experiencing] the eye-faculty—and so forth;
that is, those who do not experience, do not undergo, and do not grasp one another's objects. Of them...
Of those five faculties.

303. The connection is: "And the mind experiences that range. The mind experiences—that is, takes as its object—that fivefold range of visible forms and so forth, and by the word "and" (ca), it also experiences mental objects (dhammārammaṇa). The meaning is that the consciousness makes them its object. This...

The intended meaning here is this: if, when the objects of the eye and so forth have passed away, the remaining mental states (dhammārammaṇa) arise, then at that time the consciousness having those as its object is not said to be experiencing the objects of the five faculties;
rather, it is said to be experiencing only its own object. And this being so, it is the mind alone that experiences their range of objects.
It would be difficult to maintain [otherwise], and it is not possible to override the words of the Sutta;

therefore, according to the method already stated, even when forms and so forth that are objects of the mind have not come within the range of the eye and other senses, they are still exclusively objects of form and so forth, and not objects of mental phenomena (dhamma).
If a consciousness whose object is form does not experience its own objective domain, but experiences only the objective domain of another, how [is this to be understood]?
Why does it not perform functions such as seeing? Because it is not supported by the physical bases (*vatthu*) that serve as the supports for those respective functions.

How, then, is it said to experience the objects of the five faculties? Even though it does not perform functions such as seeing, it is said to experience the objects of the five faculties because the aspects of what is seen and so forth are apprehended by eye-consciousness and the rest. For if [the object were not apprehended] by eye-consciousness and the rest...

It does not apprehend aspects such as "seen" and so forth; rather, it is mental consciousness alone that knows visible forms and the rest by way of their blueness and other qualities, and not the fivefold sensory consciousnesses.
Thus, there is no knowing in that manner [by the five senses]. However, this must be understood precisely because of its existence:
a mind whose object is a visible form or other sense-object that has not come into the range of the senses does not experience its own domain. Rather, indeed...
"It experiences only the objects of the five faculties. Now, it might be argued: "We do not deny that the mind experiences the objects of the five faculties;
however, its experience occurs solely by way of mental objects (dhammārammaṇa), because it is devoid of the functions of seeing and so forth.
That too is not correct, because there is no such passage in the Sutta. For if the mind were indeed devoid of the functions of seeing and so forth...
One experiences the objects of the five sense-faculties solely by way of mental objects (*dhammārammaṇa*);

and while experiencing the objects of the five sense-faculties, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) would also have only mental objects as their objects.

This being the case, it follows that "the sphere of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*) is a condition for the mind-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and the mental states associated with them, by way of object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*)."
In the *Paṭṭhāna*, it could have been stated thus; however, instead of saying that, it says:

“The visible-object base, the sound base, the odor base, the flavor base, and the tangible-object base are conditions by way of object-condition for the mind-element and for the states associated with it,” and: “The visible-object base...
[and so on] ...the mental-object base is a condition by way of object-condition for the mind-consciousness element and for the states associated with it.”

Because the five faculties have been mentioned, one must reach the conclusion here that the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) experience the objects of those five faculties by way of those five faculties themselves, and not by way of the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*).
Having thus shown the method of refutation in one manner, he says "the divine eye, etc. in order to show it again by another reason;
by the inclusion of "etc.," the knowledge of the divine ear is included. Thus, it is not tenable either.
It is not only for the reason stated previously, but for this reason as well that [the position] is untenable; this is what is meant.

Even if visible forms and so forth that have not come within the range of the eye and other faculties are called "mental objects" (dhammārammaṇa), then the divine eye and other such powers would not have visible forms and so forth as their objects, because they would be apprehending only those visible forms and sounds that are the domain of the sensitive organs (pasāda). And thus...
In the Suttas, it must be stated that the divine eye and divine ear have only mental phenomena (*dhamma*) as their object, not visible forms (*rūpa*) and so forth;

and this has indeed been stated. Therefore, since visible forms and the rest are not the objects of the [physical] eye and other [senses], they are exclusively objects of the [divine] eye and so forth, and not objects of mental phenomena.
For this very reason, it is also said in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*:
“At whatever time a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen, accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge,
having as its object a visible form, a sound, a smell, a taste, a tangible, or a mental phenomenon—
or whatever it may be directed toward— at that time there is contact... [and so on] ...there is non-distraction.”
It has been stated. But how does it follow that, since [the objects] have not come within range, the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) would not have form and so forth as its object?

If this were the case—that is, if sometimes it has form and so forth as its object and sometimes it has mental phenomena (*dhamma*) as its object, and sometimes it has mental phenomena as its object and sometimes it has form and so forth as its object—then, in regard to those instances where it has form and so forth as its object...
How could there be a restriction? There would be no restriction such as "this has visible form, etc., as its object" and "this has mental phenomena (dhamma) as its object";
the meaning is that there would be a confusion of objects.
Having thus shown the sixfold object, he now shows its immediate classification by way of the triad beginning with "limited object."
Showing this, he says: “All objects,” and so forth. The connection is: “all that [consisting of] the sixfold limited triad and so on is the object.

Regarding “the limited triad and so on”: this refers to the limited-object triad and the rest. Here, the limited-object triad is called the “limited triad” by means of eliding the middle term (*majjhapadalopa*).
By the inclusion of the word “and so on” (*ādi*), the path-object triad is included.
This is the inclusion of these three triads: the triad of past objects and the triad of internal objects. Among them, the triad of limited objects is presented as follows:
"states with limited objects, states with exalted objects, states with immeasurable objects. By way of the first term, [the triad of path objects is presented as]:
"states with the Path as object, states caused by the Path, states dominated by the Path."
The triad of objects of the path is introduced thus: "States with past objects, states with future objects, states with present objects.
The triad of past objects should be understood as introduced thus: "States with internal objects, states with external objects, states with both internal and external objects."

307–9. "The two functional causes" refers to the two types of causeless functional consciousness: the smile-producing mind-element (*hasituppāda-manodhātu*) and the other [mind-element], because the latter will also be explained by way of having sublime and so forth as its object.
The phrase "divided into desirable and so forth," etc., is an elucidation of their state of having limited objects. "Divided into desirable and so forth" means divided into:
desirable, desirable-neutral, undesirable, and undesirable-neutral. "In succession": "Visible form is [the object] of eye-consciousness... [and so on].
"Sound is the object of ear-consciousness," and so forth, in successive order. For the triad beginning with visible form... [and so on]...

the entire fivefold objective sphere of visible forms and the rest belongs to the functional mind-element (*kriyā-manodhātu*) and the two types of mind-elements distinguished as wholesome, unwholesome, and resultant.

These, depending upon the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*), occur in a fixed sequence—either preceding or following the eye-consciousness and the others—and they proceed by taking only visible forms and the other objects as their basis.
311. "In the sense-sphere realm" (*kāmadhātu*) means in the existence of sensual desire (*kāmabhava*). For it is there that the bases and objects of all these [consciousnesses] are found.

"Four" refers to these four types of consciousness: the functional mind-element (*kiriyā-manodhātu*), the wholesome-resultant eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, and likewise the receiving consciousness (*sampaṭicchana*).
The remaining [types of consciousness], however, do not arise there due to the absence of their respective bases and objects. Neither...
“Nothing” (*kiñci*): because of the total absence of both the physical basis (*vatthu*) and the object (*ārammaṇa*), nothing whatsoever arises within these [bases].
312–3. The phrase “of great results” (*mahāpākānaṃ*) and so forth has the same meaning as that explained in the first chapter. “Manifest” (*paṭuppannā*) means present (*paccuppannā*). 314.
Having thus shown [the states] with limited objects, he now shows those with exalted objects (*mahaggatārammaṇa*) and immeasurable objects (*appamāṇārammaṇa*).
“‘And the second immaterial consciousness,’ and so forth, was said. Therein, the second immaterial consciousness has a sublime object because its object is the first immaterial state;

the fourth immaterial consciousness has a sublime object because its object is the third immaterial state. ‘Sixfold’ means it is of six types due to being threefold each according to the wholesome, resultant, and functional categories.”
316–20. Their knowledge has declined; or, because they have declined from knowledge, they are "devoid of knowledge" (*ñāṇahīna*).

They have limited objects... [as before] ...these eight types of consciousness dissociated from knowledge belong to trainees (*sekha*), worldlings (*puthujjana*), and those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) when, due to occasional lack of enthusiasm or a failure to act with reverence, there is either unfitness of the body or preoccupation with other matters during such acts as giving, reflection, or listening to the Dhamma performed without careful attention.
When extremely proficient insight (vipassanā) occurs taking sense-sphere phenomena as its object, it has a limited object (parittārammaṇa).

When there is the reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa) of the first jhāna and so forth that have become highly proficient, it has a sublime object (mahaggatārammaṇa). When there is the reviewing of designations (paññatti) such as the kasiṇa-signs, it cannot be defined in terms of having a limited object and so forth.
Among the unwholesome states, the four types of consciousness associated with views take the fifty-four sense-sphere phenomena as their objects.
When there is misapprehension, relishing, and delighting in form as "self" or "a being," they have a limited object.

In that same manner, when they occur taking the twenty-seven sublime states as their object, they have a sublime object. When they occur taking a concept (paññatti) as their object, they may be described as having a limited object and so forth, or they may be "not to be defined. Those same [states] dissociated from views—[take the aforementioned objects].

With reference to their occurrence through the relishing and delighting [of an object] without misapprehension; with reference to their occurrence through association with aversion and the state of mental grief;
with reference to the state of doubt when associated with uncertainty; with reference to the state of distraction when accompanied by restlessness;
and with reference to their occurrence as non-quiescent—[these states have respectively] limited, sublime, and indeterminable objects.
They should be understood. "And likewise from the functional" means that there are four associated with knowledge from the functional consciousness as well.
"Functional registration" is a statement of its specific nature; it is not, however, because of the non-existence of wholesome, unwholesome, and resultant registration.
"The range is threefold" means that the range is indeed threefold by way of limited, sublime, and measureless. How so?

By way of wholesome functional consciousness, the eight types of consciousness associated with knowledge— occurring at the time when trainees (*sekha*), worldlings (*puthujjana*), and those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) attentively review their acts of giving,

listen to the Dhamma, practice insight (*vipassanā*), and so forth, taking sense-sphere phenomena as their object— and during the stages of preliminary work (*parikamma*) and conformity (*anuloma*) for the superknowledge (*abhiññā*) having a sense-sphere object,

have limited objects (*parittārammaṇa*). At the time of reviewing the first jhāna and so forth, and during the preliminary work for jhānas and the like that have exalted objects (*mahaggatārammaṇa*), [they have exalted objects].
When comprehending sublime states, they have a sublime object. At the moments of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) and purification (vodāna), according to what is obtained;
at the moment of reviewing supramundane states; and at the moment of the preliminary work for superknowledge (abhiññā) having Nibbāna as its object, they have an immeasurable object.
At the moment of reviewing concepts (paṇṇatti) and at the moment of the preliminary work for jhānas and superknowledges having concepts as their objects, [they have a concept-object].

And they should not be spoken of [as such]. The fact that the two types of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) have limited objects (*parittārammaṇa*) and so forth will be explained in the seventeenth chapter.
Functional registration consciousness (*kriyā-voṭṭhabbana*) also functions by preceding those aforementioned states as they proceed toward their respective objects, advertising to each of them;
thus, it has limited objects and so forth. By way of registration in the five doors...
In the course of occurrence, it has only a limited object.

"The remaining ones mentioned" refers to the fifteen remaining fine-material-sphere consciousnesses—namely, the first and third [of each triad]—and the six immaterial-sphere wholesome, resultant, and functional consciousnesses;
thus, twenty-one types of consciousness. These have objects that cannot be specified.
Because they take as their object the non-designatable— namely, the seven designations of signs such as the kasiṇa, space, and the absence of consciousness—
which cannot be defined by way of the limited and so forth,
these are the "non-designatable objects. The triad of limited objects is completed.

321-2. Having thus shown the classification of the subject by way of the triad of limited objects, now—since the classification of the subject is also demonstrated by the description of the immeasurable object itself as being included within the triad of path objects—it is said, "And the second immaterial consciousness," etc., in order to show it by way of the triad of past objects instead of that [previous one].
Therein, the second immaterial consciousness [is the object] of the first past immaterial consciousness.
By way of taking an object, the fourth immaterial state has exclusively a past object because it takes the third immaterial state as its object.
"The present alone is their domain" means that the five-door consciousnesses arise only when visible forms and so forth are actually present.
However, there is no fixed consciousness with a future object, because even the knowledge of the future portion is not distinct from the fifth jhāna.

324–6. “It may be... [as before] ... not having the future as its object”: first, the eight great resultants (*mahāvipāka*) have the past as their object during the course of existence (*pavatti*) when they arise by taking either kamma or the sign of kamma (*kammanimitta*) as their object at the time of seizing rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) for gods and humans. The same principle applies at the time of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and at the moment of death (*cuti*).

However, at the time of seizing rebirth-linking, they may sometimes take the sign of the destination (*gatinimitta*) or both the sign of the destination and the sign of kamma as their object; immediately thereafter—
At the time of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), it has a present object; likewise during its occurrence as registration (tadārammaṇa) in the five doors.
However, in the mind door, when it occurs having taken the object of impulsions (javana) that have past, future, or present objects, it has past, future, or present objects.
This is also the case in the two types of mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) which are resultant, wholesome, unwholesome, or rootless, and are accompanied by equanimity.

The same method applies. The only difference is that these [types of consciousness] occur respectively as the rebirth-linking for those born blind among humans and for all beings in the woeful states;
furthermore, at the time of investigating (santīraṇa) within the five sense doors, they have only present objects—this is their distinction.
However, when accompanied by joy, they occur in the five sense doors by way of investigation and by way of registration (tadārammaṇa) at the time of occurrence.

It should be understood that [these consciousnesses] have present objects; however, at the door of the mind (manodvāra) during the stage of registration (tadārammaṇa), they may have past, future, or present objects.
Furthermore, the consciousness arising from laughter (hasituppāda-citta) in those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava)—which produces a state of extreme joy in the five doors—has a present object;
whereas at the door of the mind, it arises by way of laughter directed toward phenomena belonging to the past and other time periods.
In its occurrence, it has as its object the past, future, and present. Regarding the terms “wholesome and unwholesome” and so forth:

first, among the wholesome states, the four types of consciousness-arising associated with knowledge—occurring in trainees (sekhā) and worldlings (puthujjana)—have as their objects the past, future, and present when they are comprehending the aggregates, elements, and bases according to their divisions into past and so forth;
when they are engaged in reviewing; and when they are performing the preliminary work for the supernormal knowledges (abhiññā) that have the past, future, and present as their objects.

At the time of reviewing Nibbāna as a concept (paññatti), at the time of the purification of the change-of-lineage (gotrabhu-vodāna), and at the time of the preliminary stages (parikamma) and so forth for super-knowledges (abhiññā) having Nibbāna as a concept as their object, they have an inexpressible object.
For here, Nibbāna and its concepts are inexpressible by way of time such as the past and so forth;
therefore, the objects having them as their focus are also inexpressible by way of being past-objects and so forth. Hence he said: "Even at the time of the peaceful concept."
The meaning is: "at the time of making existent Nibbāna and its conceptual designation (paññatti) the object [of consciousness], according to what is possible.
However, in the manuscripts they write, "in the presence of [Nibbāna] and at the times of designation"; that is not the correct reading.

Not recognizing that it is not the correct reading and failing to observe even the loss of the sense, they write the meaning based on a distortion of the words as: "when there is designation at the time."
Those dissociated from knowledge should be understood in the same manner already described.
The only difference is this: because they lack knowledge, they are incapable of taking supramundane phenomena as their object; thus, they lack the reviewing of the Path, the Fruit, and Nibbāna.

Among the unwholesome states, there are four types of consciousness associated with views, which arise at the time of relishing, delighting in, and adhering to the phenomena of the three planes, categorized by way of the past and so forth.
[These consciousnesses] have past objects, etc., as their object. Likewise, at the time they arise by taking a conceptual designation (paññatti) as their object, they have an "indeterminable" object.

The same method applies to those [consciousnesses] dissociated from views; for in that case, there is simply no grasping through misapprehension (parāmāsa). As for the two types of consciousness associated with aversion:

when they arise in a state of hating phenomena classified as past, etc., they have past objects, etc., as their object; when they arise in a state of hating a conceptual designation, [they have an indeterminable object].

They have an indeterminable object. Those associated with doubt and restlessness, by virtue of having reached an undesirable state regarding those phenomena and by way of non-quiescence and distraction, have an indeterminable object—past, future, or present—during their occurrence.

Among the functional consciousnesses, the eight types of root-cause-accompanied consciousness belong to the same category as the wholesome consciousnesses; for therein, those associated with knowledge...
Among the wholesome [states], those associated with knowledge are similar to those dissociated from knowledge in being dissociated from knowledge. However, the distinction here is this:
the former arise in trainees (*sekha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*), while these arise in those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*).

Furthermore, the functional mind-consciousness element accompanied by the root of cause and accompanied by equanimity has a present object during its occurrence as the "determining" (*voṭṭhabbana*) process in the five doors.

At the mind-door, during the preliminary stage of impulsions (javana) that have as their objects past, future, and present phenomena, as well as designations (paññatti) and Nibbāna, [the consciousness] has past, future, present, or indeterminable (navattabba) objects.
The fact that the two types of direct knowledge (abhiññā) have past and so forth as their objects will be stated later. Regarding “indeterminable...
etc.”: because they have as their objects designations such as the sign of the kasiṇa (kasiṇanimitta), they cannot be defined by way of having past objects and so forth.
327. There are five functional [consciousnesses]: the four associated with knowledge, and the rootless mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity—these are the five functionals.
"The fifth functional from the perspective of form" refers to the functional direct-knowledge (abhiññā) consisting of the fifth jhāna of the fine-material sphere.
"There is nothing that is not its domain" means that among the divisions such as the past and so forth, and those liberated from time, there is nothing whatsoever that is not its domain.
There is none; the meaning is that everything is their objective field.
This concludes the triad of past objects.
Following the same method already stated, it is possible to understand the classification of the subjects (visayī) as included within the triad of internal objects.

Therefore, it has not been extracted separately. However, it should be understood according to its own nature as follows: first, the six types of consciousness-arising—namely, the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*) and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*)—in their modes of wholesome, resultant, and functional, have internal objects because they proceed by taking as their object the lower attainment connected to one's own continuity. The fine-material-sphere jhānas (the fourfold set), the first and third immaterial attainments, [the second and fourth immaterial attainments, and the fivefold set of fine-material-sphere jhānas]... The supramundane wholesome and its resultant states have external objects because they arise by taking as their object the earth-kasiṇa and so forth, which exist externally to one's own internal self.

All sense-sphere wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states, as well as the fifth jhāna of the fine-material sphere, have both internal and external objects. Among these, from the sense-sphere wholesome states, four...
In the case of consciousness-arising associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta*), when one reviews one's own aggregates and so forth, it has an internal object;
when reviewing the aggregates and so forth of others, or when reviewing concepts (*paṇṇatti*) and Nibbāna, it has an external object;

and by way of both, it has an internal-external object. The same method applies to those [consciousnesses] dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇavippayutta*). For in their case, however, there is no reviewing of Nibbāna.
There is none. Unwholesome states are also internal objects at the time of relishing, delighting in, or misapprehending one's own aggregates and so forth;
they are external objects at the time of occurring in the same way toward the aggregates of another person, as well as toward non-sensory-bound matter, the kasiṇas, and so on;
and they are both internal and external objects by virtue of both these ways. As for the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness and the three mind-elements:
These thirteen types of consciousness have internal objects when they arise taking one's own visible forms and so forth as their object;
they have external objects when they arise with respect to another person's visible forms and so forth; and they have both internal and external objects by way of both.

Furthermore, the investigation-consciousness accompanied by joy functions as investigation and registration in the five sense-doors regarding one's own fivefold phenomena such as visible forms, and in the mind-door.

By way of having that as their object, other internal sense-sphere phenomena (*kāmāvacara-dhamma*) are also taken as objects; thus, when they occur with reference to internal states, they have an internal object (*ajjhattārammaṇa*);
when occurring with reference to the phenomena of others, they have an external object (*bahiddhārammaṇa*); and by way of both, they have an internal-external object (*ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇa*).
This same method applies to the two types of investigation (*santīraṇa*) accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*).

Furthermore, that [consciousness] occurs solely by way of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death in the realms of happy and miserable destinies; and it occurs with respect to internal and other such categories among kamma and so forth.

Because the eight great resultants occur with respect to phenomena categorized as internal and so forth by way of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, death, and their objects, they have internal and other such objects.
The smile-producing consciousness also takes its own material qualities and so forth as its object.
In its occurrence by way of producing a joyful expression, it has an internal object; when occurring toward another’s visible forms and so forth, it has an external object.
In the mind-door as well, the arising of a smile through reflecting on an action performed by oneself has an internal object;
through reflecting on an action performed by others, it has an external object; and through both, it has an internal-external object.
Mind-door adverting consciousness, however, functions by way of adverting at the mind-door and by way of determining at the five doors, taking internal and other objects during its occurrence.
The eight great functional (kiriya) consciousnesses belong exclusively to the wholesome category;

for they arise only in those whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava), whereas the wholesome types arise in trainees (sekha) and worldlings (puthujjana)—this alone is the difference. [This concludes the section on] the fifth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara).
He will explain their status as having internal and other types of objects.
(329) Because the question was asked in general terms as "the fruit" and "the path," he said: "The four... [etc. ...from the perspective of merit.
(332–4) However, they are unable to know the path and fruit of Arahantship, nor likewise the wholesome direct knowledges (*abhiññā*). Therefore, he said:

“‘But in all’ and so forth. With reference to the moment when determining (voṭṭhabbana) performs the function of adverting, it was stated as “determining also” for the sake of metrical convenience in the verse composition.

The statement “The four... [omission] ...from merit” is merely an illustration of the inability—even of a consciousness associated with knowledge occurring in the mental continuum of a trainee (sekha) or an ordinary person (puthujjana)—to know the supreme path and fruit.
However, that wholesome direct-knowledge consciousness (kusalābhiññācitta) also...
It is simply incapable of making [that] its object. And having established it thus, it was stated below that "the functional direct knowledges (*kriyā-abhiññā*) are mind-elements (*manodhātu*).
(335–8) "Why? is the question regarding the reason. "Of the Arahant," etc., is the answer. The word *hi* has the sense of "because" (*yasmā*).
Because neither ordinary persons (*puthujjana*) nor those in training (*sekha*) are able to know the path-consciousness or the fruition-mind of an Arahant...

The meaning is: "they are able. And this incapacity of theirs is stated in the passage beginning with "The worldling does not know" in order to show that because [the truth] has not been attained, and because delusion exists regarding an unattained object for everyone, [this applies to all].
"The mind of a stream-enterer" refers to the supramundane mind of a stream-enterer, consisting of the path and fruit specific to that individual. Likewise, "of a once-returner... [and so on].
[This applies] also to the mind (*mānasa*) and so forth. However, the mundane mind (*lokiya-mānasa*) even an *arahant* knows. For it has been said:
"Then Māra the Evil One, having known with his own mind the reflection in the Blessed One’s mind...
Showing this same point in brief, he says: "The lower, the lower," and so forth. Just as each lower person [knows] each higher one...
If it is asked: "Does one mind not know [the mind of another], and likewise, does each subsequent mind not know the mind of each preceding one?"—[the answer is] no, it does not fail to know.
However, because it has attained its own object, it certainly knows. Demonstrating this, he said "uparūpari" (successively) and so forth.
Just as it was stated as "uparūpari," so too, although one would have to say "heṭṭhimassa heṭṭhimassa" (of each preceding one), he omits one instance of the word *heṭṭhima*.
Having included it by means of the word *ca*, it is stated as "and the conceit of the lower [person].

(339–41) Thus, having shown the classification by way of emphasizing the subject (*visayī*), he now says "that state which... and so forth, in order to show it by way of emphasizing the object (*visaya*).
"Wholesome object" (*kusalārammaṇa*) means that the object is exclusively wholesome. The word "in the sense of desire" (*kāme*) applies in both instances.

It should be connected [with the phrase] "in the sense-sphere (kāme) a wholesome object for the wholesome and unwholesome. For although there is no need to specify this [unwholesome state] because it belongs exclusively to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), the wholesome [state] must indeed be specified;
therefore, with reference to that, the upper term "in the sense-sphere" must necessarily be connected. Alternatively, [this is said] because of its association with the unwholesome.

Since only the wholesome [kamma] pertaining to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) is intended here, the term "in the sense-sphere" (*kāme*) should be understood as a qualification of the preceding word alone. Regarding "of the resultants of the sense-sphere":

because the fivefold sense-consciousness and the two types of receiving consciousness (*sampaṭicchana*) have exclusively the aggregate of material form (*rūpakkhandha*) as their object, this refers to the remaining eleven kinds of sense-sphere resultant.
Regarding "of the functional of the sense-sphere": by the same method already stated, this refers to that which excludes the mind-element (*manodhātu*).

Of the tenfold functional consciousness of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara-kiriyacitta*). Regarding the phrase "their object may be," first, in the case of the wholesome [consciousness], it is at the time of recollecting with a confident mind one's own sense-sphere wholesome deeds such as giving; likewise, at the time of rejoicing in those performed by others;
and at the time of reviewing that same twofold [wholesome deed] by way of its impermanence and so forth; and for the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*) and the rest.
It serves as the object during the preparatory stages (*parikamma*) and so forth for the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) that have limited wholesome states as their object.
Among the unwholesome states, it is the object at the time of relishing, delighting in, and misapprehending (*parāmasana*) sense-sphere wholesome states associated with the four types of wrong view;
and at the time of mere relishing and so forth for those dissociated from wrong view; and for the two types associated with aversion, it is the object by way of oneself.
It serves as an object at times when there is remorse and dissatisfaction regarding wholesome deeds performed by others; at times when the mind is characterized by doubt and lacks resolution;

and at times when the mind is accompanied by restlessness and is unsettled and distracted. In the two types of direct-knowledge consciousness (*abhiññā-citta*), it is an object for trainees (*sekha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*) at times when they themselves or others recollect wholesome deeds performed by themselves or others, and at times when they know the minds of others.

At the time of knowing, "By this meritorious deed, one is reborn among humans and among the deities of the sense-sphere," and at the time of knowing, "In the future, I shall perform meritorious deeds such as giving," it becomes an object for functional consciousness;

and likewise for those whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava), it becomes an object at times such as when they themselves or others recollect deeds performed. Among the nine sense-sphere resultant states...
It becomes the object at the time of rebirth-linking for those with a fortunate rebirth when that rebirth-linking has the kamma, the sign of kamma, or the object as its condition;
and it becomes the object at the time of registration for all those who have registration, immediately after a javana having a sense-sphere wholesome state as its object.

Furthermore, among the ten types of sense-sphere functional consciousness, it becomes the object for the eight great functional consciousnesses of those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) at the time of reviewing or reflecting upon sense-sphere wholesome states.
At the time of the preliminary (parikamma) and subsequent stages of functional direct-knowledge (abhiññā) with limited objects,
at the time of the arising of a smile after reflecting on giving and so forth, and at the time when mind-door adverting (manodvārāvajjana) precedes sense-sphere wholesome javanas,
it becomes the object; thus, sense-sphere wholesome consciousness has the six groups as its object.

342. Therefore, it is as stated above. Thus he said, "But of the five groups. And herein, among the functional consciousnesses (*kiriyacitta*), the smile-producing consciousness (*hasituppāda*) is not possible because its object is exclusively limited (*paritta*).

Among those, first, for the *sekhas* (trainees) and *puthujjanas* (worldlings), at the time of reviewing or investigating a fine-material-sphere wholesome state, there is the wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara-kusala*) having a fine-material-sphere wholesome state as its object;
and [there is] the superknowledge (*abhiññā*) which has a fine-material-sphere wholesome state as its object.
At the time of preliminary work (*parikamma*) and so forth; at the time of grasping (*parāmasana*) and so forth by way of the unwholesome (*akusala*) according to the method already stated;

among the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), at the time when those in training (*sekha*) or worldlings (*puthujjana*) recollect jhānas produced by themselves or others in a past existence through wholesome higher knowledge;
at the time of discerning the fine-material-sphere consciousness (*rūpāvacaracitta*) of others; and [when thinking], "By this kamma, one will be reborn in this Brahma-world."

At the time of knowing, or at the time of knowing "one will develop jhāna in the future," and at the time of the occurrence of functional direct-knowledge (kiriyā-abhiññā) for those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) according to the manner previously stated,
as well as at the time of the reviewing of fine-material-sphere wholesome states (rūpāvacara-kusala-paccavekkhaṇa) by those whose taints are destroyed according to the method explained below—
thus, fine-material-sphere wholesome consciousness is the cause for five [types of consciousness].

It is the object for those [states] that abide [in the immaterial sphere]. 343–7. The connection is: "The wholesome of the immaterial sphere is also an object-condition. Regarding "of the wholesome of the three planes":

this refers to all wholesome states of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), among the wholesome states of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) it refers to the wholesome direct-knowledge (abhiññā), and among the wholesome states of the immaterial sphere, it refers to the second and fourth wholesome states.
And this refers to wholesome [consciousness] of the three planes. This same method applies to the phrase “of the functional [consciousness] of the three planes.

Alternatively, where one should say “of the fourth and second,” it is stated as “of the fourth and [the first]” (catutthadū) by eliding the case ending due to the requirements of the verse meter, or by eliding the case ending of the word *tiya* itself.
“The condition for these... [etc. refers to wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*).

Just as for one skilled in direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) regarding the objects of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), by way of the second and fourth immaterial attainments (*āruppa*) according to the method already stated, and by way of the first and third; so too, at the time of understanding wholesome states of the three planes (*tebhūmaka-kusala*),

or likewise at the time of understanding wholesome immaterial states (*āruppa-kusala*) occurring within one’s own continuum or the continuum of another during the stage of a trainee (*sekha*) or an ordinary person (*puthujjana*),
there occurs the functional consciousness of the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere precisely at that time of being a trainee or an ordinary person.
Taking as its object the first and third immaterial attainments produced by oneself at the time when the taints are exhausted during the production of the second and fourth immaterial attainments—
thus, for the immaterial functional consciousness (arūpakiriyacitta), and likewise for the unwholesome consciousness of the three planes according to the method explained below,
and for the two types of immaterial-sphere resultant consciousness, namely the fourth and the second— the immaterial wholesome state serves as the object for these eight groups.
"Included" (*pariyāpanna*) means having fallen into craving that grasps by way of delimitation; it refers to the class of phenomena belonging to the three planes.

"Not included" (*apariyāpanna*) means not so fallen; this very thing is "merit not included" (*apariyāpanna-puñña*). There is a connection between "even from the wholesome and functional [kamma] of the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara-kusala-kiriya*) and the following.

"From the fine-material sphere" (*rūpato*) means from the fine-material realm (*rūpāvacara*). Regarding the phrase "of the four... pe... moments": this refers to the time when those in training (*sekha*) are reviewing the path.

At the time of the preliminary (parikamma) and subsequent stages of wholesome direct knowledge (abhiññā) having the Path as its object, there is the wholesome consciousness associated with knowledge; at the time of the Path-reviewing of those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), there is the functional consciousness associated with knowledge belonging to functional direct knowledge having the Path as its object during its preliminary stage;

at the time of the occurrence of the mind-door adverting consciousness (manodvārāvajjana) by way of being the precursor to those respective impulsion-moments (javana); and for those in training (sekkhā), their own [adverting consciousness].
Or at the time of knowing the paths of others, there is the two-fold direct knowledge (*abhiññā*). Thus, for these four groups, the object is the unconditioned wholesome.

Likewise for the unwholesome... [and so on]... up to "bodily intimation" (*īrita*): this occurs at the time of reviewing the defilements remaining after they have been abandoned by those in training (*sekha*), or at the time when trainees and worldlings comprehend the unwholesome states occurring in their own or others' continuums, or through the wholesome direct knowledge that has the unwholesome as its object.
At the time of the preliminary work (*parikamma*) and so forth, it belongs to wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara-kusala*);

at the time of recollecting one’s own or others’ unwholesome states as they occurred, it belongs to wholesome consciousness of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara-kusala*); at the time when those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) review their abandoned defilements or contemplate the unwholesome states occurring in the mental continuum of another;
at the time of being satisfied by reviewing the abandoned defilements; and at the time preceding all those respective impulsion moments (*javana*).

And [it is the object] of the functional consciousness (kiriyacitta) of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara); of the functional consciousness of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) according to the method stated for wholesome direct knowledge (abhiññā);

of the unwholesome [consciousness] when it occurs by way of misapprehension, relishing, and delighting; of the investigating consciousness (santīraṇa) that is the result of the unwholesome, when it has as its object a kamma devoid of restlessness (uddhacca);
and of all eleven results (vipāka) that have those [preceding states] as their object at the time of recollecting the impulsions (javana) of the sense-sphere.
"Thus, [the object] of the results of the sense-sphere" means that in this way, the unwholesome is the object for these six groups. 348–56. "The result as object...

condition": for trainees (sekkha) and worldlings (puthujjana), at the time of reflecting on results and so forth, it is the wholesome of the sense-sphere; at the time of recollecting the resultant aggregates and so forth, it is the wholesome of the fine-material sphere;
and for those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), in the same manner described above, at the time of reflecting on results and so forth.

At the time when one is satisfied regarding the absence of undesirable results during the stage of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), at the time preceding the aforementioned javanas of a sense-sphere functional consciousness (*kāmāvacara-kiriyacitta*),
and likewise for a fine-material-sphere functional consciousness (*rūpāvacara-kiriyacitta*) according to the method stated for the wholesome [states],

when one takes rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) through kamma that has a resultant object during the occurrence of the "registering" (*tadārammaṇa*) phase directed toward that result, it occurs by way of the sign of the kamma (*kammanimitta*).
And during its occurrence as the result of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*); and during the occurrence of the unwholesome through the modes of relishing, delighting in, and misapprehending [it].
Thus, for these six groups, the sense-sphere resultant serves as the object condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*).

The application should be made in this same manner even regarding the fine-material-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) resultant as an object. For that [fine-material-sphere resultant] [serves as an object] for the sense-sphere resultants and for the functional consciousnesses (*kiriyacitta*).

"The object of the smile-producing consciousness does not exist"—this is the distinction here. The sequence of objects for supramundane fruition and for sense-sphere wholesome and functional consciousnesses should be understood according to the method stated in the "Description of the Immeasurable Object.

As for the sequence of objects for sense-sphere functional consciousness with respect to the six groups beginning with the sense-sphere wholesome, [the order] regarding wholesome objects is as follows: [The sequence of objects for sense-sphere functional consciousness with respect to the six groups beginning with the sense-sphere wholesome is as follows: regarding wholesome objects...

It is similar to what was said before. For here, the ninefold functional consciousness (kiriyacitta) which is fixed exclusively to the mental continuum of one whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) becomes the object of the wholesome and unwholesome states occurring in the continua of others, as well as the object of the wholesome states occurring during the preliminary stages (parikamma, etc. of supernormal knowledge (abhiññā) directed toward future objects while one is still a trainee (sekha) or an ordinary person (puthujjana). And among the resultant states, those designated as rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and death (cuti)— [The text continues: ...are the objects of the wholesome and unwholesome states occurring in the continua of others, and of the wholesome states occurring during the preliminary stages of supernormal knowledge directed toward future objects while one is still a trainee or an ordinary person.

Furthermore, the resultant states—namely, those termed rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death—are the objects of the wholesome and unwholesome states occurring in the continua of others, and of the wholesome states occurring during the preliminary stages of supernormal knowledge directed toward future objects while one is still a trainee or an ordinary person. Moreover, these same [resultants] are the objects of the functional consciousness occurring in the continua of others, and of the wholesome states occurring during the preliminary stages of supernormal knowledge directed toward future objects while one is still a trainee or an ordinary person. And finally, they are the objects of the wholesome and unwholesome states occurring in one's own continuum during the time of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death. Thus it is said. This is the section on the objects of consciousness. Now follows the section on the doors. Therein, the five doors are the eye-door, the ear-door, the nose-door, the tongue-door, and the body-door. The mind-door is the heart-base (hadayavatthu). These six doors are the bases for the occurrence of consciousness. Among them, the five doors are the bases for the occurrence of the fivefold sense-consciousness; the mind-door is the basis for the occurrence of the remaining types of consciousness. As for their functions: the eye-door is the door for the occurrence of eye-consciousness; the ear-door, for ear-consciousness; the nose-door, for nose-consciousness; the tongue-door, for tongue-consciousness; the body-door, for body-consciousness; and the mind-door, for the occurrence of all the remaining types of consciousness. Thus it is said. This is the section on the doors. Now follows the section on the objects. Therein, the objects are visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangible objects, and mental objects (dhammārammaṇa). Of these, visible forms are the objects of eye-consciousness; sounds, of ear-consciousness; odors, of nose-consciousness; tastes, of tongue-consciousness; tangible objects, of body-consciousness; and mental objects, of the remaining types of consciousness. Thus it is said. This is the section on the objects. Now follows the section on the adverting of consciousness. Therein, the adverting of consciousness is the turning of the mind toward an object. It is of two kinds: sense-sphere adverting (pañcadvārāvajjana) and mind-door adverting (manodvārāvajjana). Of these, sense-sphere adverting occurs in the five doors; mind-door adverting occurs in the mind-door. Their functions are as follows: sense-sphere adverting is the adverting of the mind toward an object in the five doors; mind-door adverting is the adverting of the mind toward an object in the mind-door. Thus it is said. This is the section on the adverting of consciousness. Now follows the section on the impulsion of consciousness. Therein, impulsion (javana) is the rapid movement of the mind toward an object. It is of many kinds: wholesome, unwholesome, and functional. Its function is the grasping of an object with intensity. Thus it is said. This is the section on the impulsion of consciousness. Now follows the section on registration. Therein, registration (tadārammaṇa) is the fixing of the mind upon an object after it has been experienced. It is of two kinds: wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant. Its function is the retention of the object. Thus it is said. This is the section on registration. Now follows the section on the life-continuum. Therein, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is the stream of consciousness that flows on uninterrupted in the absence of active cognitive processes. Its function is the maintenance of personal continuity. Thus it is said. This is the section on the life-continuum. Now follows the section on death. Therein, death (cuti) is the passing away of the life-continuum at the end of its duration. Its function is the relinquishing of the present existence. Thus it is said. This is the section on death. Now follows the section on the classification of consciousness by way of planes. Therein, the planes are the sense-sphere plane, the fine-material plane, the immaterial plane, and the supramundane plane. Consciousness is classified according to these planes. Thus it is said. This is the section on the classification of consciousness by way of planes. Now follows the section on the classification of consciousness by way of roots. Therein, the roots are greed, hatred, delusion, non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion. Consciousness is classified according to these roots. Thus it is said. This is the section on the classification of consciousness by way of roots. Now follows the section on the classification of consciousness by way of feeling. Therein, feeling is of five kinds: pleasant, painful, sorrowful, joyful, and neutral. Consciousness is classified according to these feelings. Thus it is said. This is the section on the classification of consciousness by way of feeling. Now follows the section on the classification of consciousness by way of association. Therein, association means the co-arising of consciousness and mental factors. Consciousness is classified according to its associated factors. Thus it is said. This is the section on the classification of consciousness by way of association. Now follows the section on the classification of consciousness by way of predominance. Therein, predominance refers to the dominant influence of certain factors over others. Consciousness is classified according to its predominant factors. Thus it is said. This is the section on the classification of consciousness by way of predominance. Now follows the section on the classification of consciousness by way of jhāna. Therein, jhāna consists of the factors of initial application, sustained application, zest, pleasure, and one-pointedness. Consciousness is classified according to the presence of these jhāna factors. Thus it is said. This is the section on the classification of consciousness by way of jhāna. Now follows the section on the classification of consciousness by way of path. Therein, the path consists of the factors of right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. Consciousness is classified according to its inclusion in the noble paths. Thus it is said. This is the section on the classification of consciousness by way of path. Now follows the section on the classification of consciousness by way of fruit. Therein, the fruits are the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship. Consciousness is classified according to its attainment of these fruits. Thus it is said. This is the section on the classification of consciousness by way of fruit. Now follows the section on the classification of consciousness by way of persons. Therein, persons are classified as ordinary worldlings, trainees, and those beyond training. Consciousness is classified according to the type of person to whom it belongs.

Thus it is said. This is the section on the classification of consciousness by way of persons. Now follows the section on the classification of consciousness by way of abhisankhāra. Therein, abhisankhāra refers to the volitional formations that propel beings into various realms of existence. Consciousness is classified according to the nature of these formations. Thus it is said. This is the section on the classification of consciousness by way of abhisankhāra. Now follows the section on the classification of consciousness by way of destiny. Therein, destinies are the various realms of rebirth such as hell, the animal kingdom, the realm of hungry ghosts, the human world, and the deva worlds. Consciousness is classified according to the destiny into which it leads. Thus it is said. This is the section on the classification of consciousness by way of destiny. Now follows the section on the classification of consciousness by way of spheres of mastery. Therein, the spheres of mastery are the various objects of meditative concentration. Consciousness is classified according to the sphere of mastery it pertains to. Thus it is said. This is the section on the classification of consciousness by way of spheres of mastery. Now follows the section on the classification of consciousness by way of the faculties. Therein, the faculties are faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, and so forth. Consciousness is classified according to the faculty it is associated with. Thus it is said. This is the section on the classification of consciousness by way of the faculties.
