The only distinction is that [the object] does not serve as an object by way of being the object of resultant kamma.
The sequence of objects for the fine-material-sphere functional consciousness regarding the five aggregates is exactly the same as what was stated for the wholesome objects.
Any further distinctions should also be understood according to the method stated for the sense-sphere functional objects. This also applies to the immaterial-sphere functional consciousness.

The state of being an object for those five groups is exactly as described. However, for the functional consciousness of the formless realm, only the first and third [jhanas] are the objects of the second and fourth [formless attainments]. 357–8.
Having thus shown the objects with the exception of materiality and Nibbāna, [the text now treats] the material object and the Nibbāna object.
In order to demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “matter has four origins” is commenced.
“Matter” refers to the aggregate of matter (*rūpakkhandha*), which is divided into twenty-eight types through the distinctions of primary elements (*bhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya*).

Although not every single instance of matter individually possesses all four origins, it is stated that “it has four origins” because the aggregate of matter as a whole arises from exactly these four origins.

"Of the fruition and functional [consciousness] pertaining to the sense sphere" means: of the resultant consciousness of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara-vipāka*) and of the functional consciousness of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara-kiriyacitta*). In that regard, first, for the wholesome [consciousness] of the sense sphere: at the time of performing meritorious deeds such as giving beauty and so forth;
at the time of comprehending beauty and so forth by way of impermanence and so on; at the time of the preliminary work and so forth for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*);

and at the time of relishing, delighting in, and misapprehending [objects], which pertains to the unwholesome [consciousness]. For the two types of direct knowledge, it refers to the supernormal power of transformation (*iddhividha*).

At the time of creating forms such as beautiful or ugly; at the time of recollecting past lives through the power of *pubbenivāsānussati*, by way of remembering, "In a previous existence, I was of such a complexion," and so forth;
at the time of seeing the beauty of beings passing away and being reborn through the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*); at the time of hearing sounds through the divine ear (*dibbasota*);
and at the time of knowing the future through the knowledge of the future (*anāgataṃsañāṇa*), by way of [knowing], "In the future, I shall be of such a complexion," and so forth.

At the time of cognizing: in the case of the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness and the two types of receiving consciousness among the sense-sphere resultants (*kāmāvacara-vipāka*), at the time of cognizing visible forms and so forth as appropriate;

in the case of the pleasant investigating consciousness, at the time of investigating and its subsequent registration (*tadārammaṇa*); in the case of the two types of equanimous investigating consciousness, at the time of investigating, its subsequent registration, and the registration of the sign of the deed (*kamma-nimitta*) or the sign of the destination (*gati-nimitta*);

in the case of the root-cause-accompanied resultant, at the time of the registration of the sign of the deed or the sign of the destination, and at the time of its subsequent registration; and in the case of sense-sphere functional states (*kiriyā*).
Furthermore, according to the method explained for the wholesome [states], it becomes the object of the eighth great functional consciousness (*kiriyacitta*),

of the smile-producing consciousness (*hasituppāda*) at the time of satisfaction thinking, "One gave such-and-such beauty and so forth," of the mind-door adverting consciousness (*manodvārāvajjana*) at the time of determining and adverting in the five doors and the mind door,
and of the five-door adverting consciousness (*pañcadvārāvajjana*) at the time of adverting in the five doors; thus, it is of fourfold origination.
Form (rūpa) is an object when it is concealed or massed together.

However, Nibbāna is the object for sense-sphere wholesome consciousness with three roots at the time of the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) purification, and at the time of the preliminary stages (parikamma) etc. of superknowledge (abhiññā) having Nibbāna as its object;
and it is the object for fine-material-sphere wholesome consciousness at times such as the recollection of cessation (nirodha) realized in a past existence.
In order to show that the object belongs to six groups— namely, the functional consciousnesses of the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere according to the method already stated,
as well as the wholesome states not included [within the mundane] and their resultant at the time of the path, its immediate fruition, and the enjoyment of the fruition— it is said,
"having Nibbāna as its object," and so forth. "Of both" means of the two kinds, namely those of the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere.
"Of various kinds" means of diverse types according to the method that will be explained in the twelfth chapter.

"The condition for the nine... etc., refers to all designations (paññatti) for sense-sphere wholesome, unwholesome, and functional consciousnesses—excluding the smile-producing mind-element—as well as for the two types of direct-knowledge consciousness;
and for the fine-material-sphere wholesome, resultant, and functional states, it refers to the kasiṇa-signs and so forth.

The designation of space is the object-condition for the first immaterial wholesome, resultant, and functional states; the three designations of non-existence are the object-conditions for the three [states] beginning with the third immaterial wholesome.
Thus, these designations serve as the object-condition for the nine groups.
Having thus shown which phenomenon is the object of which phenomenon by way of individual sections (uddhāra), [the text continues].

Now, in order to show how all types of consciousness arising in the four planes are associated with the six kinds of objects, the three verses beginning with “Two [types] have visible form as their object” are stated. Their meaning is exactly as explained above.

Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with “The first wholesome immaterial [consciousness],” although the method has already been explained below, it concerns the immaterial-sphere phenomena among the immaterial-sphere objects.

This was stated in order to clarify the various modes of occurrence according to the categories of the trainee (*sekha*) and the non-trainee (*asekha*). Regarding "of the wholesome": this refers to the wholesome consciousness of the second immaterial sphere belonging to both trainees and worldlings (*puthujjana*).

As for its result (*vipāka*), however, it can also be an object for those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), even while that result is occurring, because in their previous existence it had the sign of the kamma (*kammanimitta*) as its object.
It occurs in the immaterial realm with an extremely subtle state.
He said, "The first immaterial fruition," and so forth, because the life-continuum consciousness does not appear purified by meditation.
However, the first functional consciousness is not the object of the second immaterial wholesome consciousness, nor is it the object of the second immaterial resultant consciousness;
this is the grammatical connection. In that context, at the time when the taints are exhausted, for some wholesome [consciousness]...

Because it does not exist, it is said, "not of merit. Because the resultant consciousness of the base of infinite consciousness does not arise for one who possesses the functional consciousness of the base of infinite space, it is said, "not of result.

For one whose taints are destroyed, when entering the attainments for the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very life and for the sake of attaining the attainment of cessation, the first immaterial functional consciousness [arises] for the second...
He said, "The first is the functional consciousness," and so forth, because it becomes the object.

Having stated that it is "twofold," he spoke the words "wholesome [is the cause] of the wholesome" and "the functional is also [the cause] of the functional," etc., in order to show that very twofoldness and threefoldness.
That is exactly according to the method already explained. Likewise... may there be in the first immaterial-sphere consciousness.

The meaning is that, according to the method already stated, the object becomes twofold for trainees (*sekha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*), and threefold for those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).
374–5. “Whatever sphere of experience one takes as a basis” means whichever sphere among the spheres of form, the formless, Nibbāna, or concepts one takes as a basis.
“Whichever” refers to the immaterial phenomena. “Whoever” refers to a householder, a renunciant, or a youth. “It is said” (*kira*) expresses assent.
This [term] is connected with the phrase "one should enter" (*ottareyya*). "The further shore" (*pāra*) means the end.

Because this [Abhidhamma], due to its possession of the most subtle and profound method, cannot be crossed without difficulty by those who enter it according to reality, it is said to be "difficult to cross" (*duttara*), considering it to be hard to reach.
"Crossing" (*uttara*) means supreme. For because the *Abhidhammāvatāra* itself is supreme, its further shore—which is but a portion of it—is likewise supreme.
He is that person who has crossed over to the further shore of the entry into the Abhidhamma. "He crosses over indeed" means that he is certainly able to cross it; he is not unable to cross it.
Thus [ends the section] from the *Abhidhammatthavikāsinī*.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Classification of Objects in the *Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanā* is completed.
Chapter Seven.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Occurrence of Resultant Consciousness (Vipākacittappavatti-niddesa-vaṇṇanā) 376.

"By infinite knowledge" means by knowledge that occurs with an infinite object. "By the stainless" (*niraṅgaṇena*): here, lust and the other unwholesome states are called "stains" (*aṅgaṇa*) because through them individuals who possess them fall into a state of inferiority.
As it is said: "Lust is a stain, hatred is a stain, delusion is a stain; 'stain' is indeed a designation, friends, for evil, unwholesome states belonging to the sphere of desire," and so forth.

One who seeks (*esi*) or searches for qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) within his own continuum is a seeker of qualities (*guṇesī*); [he is addressed] by that seeker of qualities (*guṇesinā*). One who is devoted to compassion (*karuṇā*), or one who possesses it, is compassionate (*kāruṇika*);
[he is addressed] by that compassionate one (*kāruṇikena*). And here, by the phrase "with infinite knowledge" (*anantañāṇena*), he states the Blessed One’s omniscience;
by "without defilement" (*niraṅgaṇena*), his state of having exhausted the taints (*khīṇāsava*); by "seeker of qualities," his former conduct (*pubbacariya*); and by "compassionate,"...

The state of being endowed with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). By this much praise, he illuminates the Blessed One’s teaching of the result (*vipāka*) as being leading to liberation (*niyyānika*), and so forth.
For what is taught by one who is not omniscient does not lead to liberation; what is taught by one whose taints (*āsava*) are not exhausted is not manifest;
what is taught by one lacking merit does not take root; and what is spoken by one devoid of compassion does not bestow happiness. [This applies] to the Blessed One...
Furthermore, because he is omniscient, that which was taught by him leads to liberation; because his taints are exhausted, it is manifest;
because he possesses merit, it is firmly established; and because he is endowed with great compassion, it bestows happiness. "Born of mind" refers to the arising of resultant consciousnesses. 377–86.
Now, in order to show the ten types established in the commentary according to the matrix (mātikā) of the discourse on resultants:

“Twenty-nine types of kamma,” and so forth, was stated. Therein, because they serve as the fundamental cause for the discourse on resultants that has been commenced, the first determination made is of the twenty-nine types of kamma.

Once kamma has been discussed, since the resultants—which constitute the basis for the discourse on resultants—must also be discussed, the second determination is of the thirty-two resultants, expressed as: “Thirty-two resultants have been shown.”
It has been stated. Because the results of kamma are not seen in the [other] five doors, the third section—beginning with "In three...
and ending with "...are seen"—describes the doors of kamma and the doors of its results. In the context of discussing kamma and its results, the fourth section—beginning with "Wholesome...

and ending with "...various results"—is taught to show how a single kamma, depending on various conditions, produces manifold fruits, specifically regarding wholesome kamma of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).

The production of various fruits in both the course of existence (pavatti) and rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) has been stated. However, when this is said, those who do not understand that it was stated by way of the actual fruition (vipāka) obtainable in both the course of existence and rebirth-linking say:
"By the remainder of the fruition of that very same kamma."
“Having sacrificed a single flower, for eighty koṭis of eons,
I do not recall being born in an unhappy state.
Having grasped the meaning from such words based on the literal shadow of the phrasing, even for the volition that has already given rise to rebirth-linking, [there is no further...]
Thinking that they might imagine a rebirth-linking [to occur] through a single [kamma], the fifth [verse], beginning with “by one... pe ...

it is declared,” states the production of only a single rebirth-linking by means of a single kamma. Hearing of the occurrence of the fruition of various kammās within a single existence, those who do not understand the meaning of such statements as “Having seen the prince endowed with a hundred marks of merit,” [might think]: “By various kammās, there is only one [rebirth].”
"...there is a rebirth-linking"—thus they would think. This sixth section, "Various [karmas lead to] various rebirth-linkings," explains how various karmas give rise to various rebirth-linkings.

The continuity of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), which is dependent upon the heart-base, is cut off; yet, as it is being cut off, it does not cease abruptly.

Thus, when the vibration of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and the arrest of the life-continuum have arisen and ceased, she asks: “What is this?”
The functional mind-element (kiriya-manodhātu) arises, directing the stream of consciousness toward the object as if leading them forward;
immediately after that, one of the five sense-consciousness elements (pañcaviññāṇadhātu) arises, performing its respective function such as seeing;
immediately after that, the resultant rootless mind-element (vipākāhetuka-manodhātu) arises, receiving the very same object grasped by the preceding consciousness; immediately after that—
Apprehending that very same object, the resultant mind-consciousness element (vipākāhetuka-manoviññāṇadhātu) arises;
immediately after that, determining that very same object, the functional mind-consciousness element with roots (kiriyāhetuka-manoviññāṇadhātu) arises;

and immediately after that, whichever among the wholesome, unwholesome, or functional javanas of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) has obtained the necessary conditions, it arises directed toward that very same object.
Having become the impulsion (javana), it generally impels for seven times;

immediately after that, one of the eleven types of resultant consciousnesses with that same object arises twice—either as a registration (tadārammaṇa) or as an impulsion—according to the suitability of the karma, the object, the impulsion, the conditions, or the habitual practice;
immediately after that, there is a lapse into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
Standing here, the mango simile should be understood for the purpose of easily grasping this succession of consciousness.
How so? It is said that a certain man was sleeping with his head covered beneath a flowering mango tree;
then, one mango fruit, detaching from its stalk, fell to the ground with a "ṭha" sound, as if brushing against his ear-ornament.
It falls; he, awakened by its sound, removes the cloth from his head, opens his eyes, and looks out.
Then, stretching out his hand, he takes the fruit, crushes it, smells it, and having ascertained that it is ripe, he eats it.
Having relished what has entered his mouth along with the saliva, he sleeps once more just as before. In this regard, for that man—

The period of being possessed of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is like the time of sleeping at the foot of a mango tree; the moment the object strikes the sensitivity is like the falling of the mango fruit;
the moment the mind-element (manodhātu) turns back from the life-continuum is like the time of waking up by the sound of the fall;
and the moment the eye-consciousness performs its function of seeing is like the time of looking after having opened one's eyes.
The moment of receiving the object by the resultant mind-element (vipākamanodhātu) is like the time of grasping something after stretching out one's hand;

the moment of investigating the object by the resultant mind-consciousness-element (vipākamanoviññāṇadhātu) is like the time of crushing it after grasping it; the moment of determining it by the functional mind-consciousness-element (kiriyāmanoviññāṇadhātu) is like the time of smelling it;
and the moment of experiencing the flavor of the object by the impulsion (javana) is like the time of eating it.
The time of experiencing the object together with the phlegm as it enters the mouth is like the time of experiencing the object already experienced by the impulsion (javana) through its registration;
the subsequent falling asleep is like the time of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). In this way, the application of the simile should be understood.

Furthermore, what does this simile illustrate? It shows that the function of the sense-faculties (pasāda) is merely the striking against the object, while the activity belongs to the functional mind-element (kiriya-manodhātu).

The function of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is merely subsisting; the function of the five sense-consciousness elements is merely seeing and so forth; the function of the resultant mind-consciousness element is merely receiving (sampaṭicchana);
the function of the resultant mind-consciousness element is merely investigating (santīraṇa); the function of the functional mind-consciousness element is merely determining (vavatthāpana);
and the experiencing of the flavor of the object belongs specifically to the impulsion (javana), while the registration (tadārammaṇa) occurs by means of that [impulsion].
"Experiencing that which has already been experienced"—in this way, it demonstrates the mutual intermingling of phenomena by way of their functions.
Furthermore, although there is no directing agent who issues commands such as, "You be called adverting; you be one of the others, such as seeing;
you be called reception," the consciousness proceeds solely by virtue of the fixed order of consciousness (*cittaniyāma*).

This should be understood. However, that mental regularity (cittaniyāma), along with the regularity of the seasons (utuniyāma) and so forth, will be explained at the conclusion of the section on delimitation.
This, then, is the analysis of the occurrence of consciousness regarding a very great object.

As for a great object, however, because there is no arising of the registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa) in its case, when that object has come into range, according to the method already stated, [the process proceeds] up to the end of the impulsion (javana).

When process-consciousnesses arise, there is only a lapse into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). However, because the object’s lifespan is exhausted, even if the life-span remains for only the duration of a single consciousness-moment, the registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa) does not arise due to its weakness, like a man who is near death.
Furthermore, when registration arises, it necessarily arises twice and not just once; this occurs when only one consciousness-moment remains.

Furthermore, when that same object has arisen as a registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*), it does not arise for a second [registration consciousness] at the time of its arising because the first has already ceased.
For it is not the case that among two registration consciousnesses one has a present object and the other has a past object;
therefore, due to the non-arising of the second, the first also does not arise. However, in the *Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā*:

It has been stated that the registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa) occurs only once. In the *Paramatthavinicchaya* as well, having accepted that very position, it is said: "Once or twice, it takes that as its object.

However, in the *Abhidhammaṭṭhakathā*, after stating that "in the counting of the occurrence of consciousness, only two instances of the mental cycle appear in all cases," that [position] was not accepted; therefore, regarding a large object—

At the conclusion of the impulsion (javana), there is merely a lapse into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga); there is no arising of registration (tadārammaṇa). And because it is empty of such registrations, this stage is called the "fruitless turn" (moghavāra).

Since there is also an absence of the arising of impulsion when the object is limited (paritta), [this occurs] when the cognitive processes (vīthicitta) have arisen at the conclusion of investigation (santīraṇa).
Immediately following that, the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*) itself, having received repetition (*āsevana*), stands in the place of impulsion and proceeds for two moments;

thereafter, there is a lapse into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). It is impossible for it to turn back in the interim without reaching the determining consciousness, after having reached eye-consciousness and so forth.
However, because the object is very weak due to its short duration, the impulsion...
It does not arise. For when it arises, it arises only with a lifespan of seven consciousness-moments;

however, in that which has a lifespan of only a few consciousness-moments, the first impulsion (paṭhamajavana) itself does not arise. Since the others do not arise in the absence of that [first impulsion], there is no arising of impulsion with respect to a limited object (parittārammaṇa).
This second "futile section" (moghavāra) was stated in the Commentary. The author of the Sub-commentary (Ṭīkākāra) [explains as follows]:
However, not accepting it in that way, he formulates the second *moghavāra* differently. For it was said by him:
"Of the three *moghavāras*, the second *moghavāra* is to be grasped after investigation.

For if, in the section on dependence (*paṭicca-vāra*) and so forth within the anuloma-feeling-triad, [the statement] 'by way of repetition-condition (*āsevana-paccaya*), there are two [answers], excluding the path (*magga*), excluding the path-condition (*maggapaccaya*)... [is applied].

And it might be said that "there are two [types] in the case of repetition (āsevana)," whereby even the "vain section" (moghavāra) would be applicable. Furthermore, if even determining consciousness (voṭṭhabbana) were a condition of repetition, it would apply to both the wholesome and the unwholesome.

For there is no state not explicitly stated wherein a phenomenon that is fit to receive the condition of repetition becomes a condition of repetition for another phenomenon that is itself a condition of repetition. However, the status of determining consciousness as a condition of repetition for the wholesome and unwholesome...

It was not stated [there]. It is indeed rejected by the statement: "A wholesome state arises dependent on a wholesome state through the condition of non-repetition (*nāsevanapaccaya*); an unwholesome state arises dependent on an unwholesome state through the condition of non-repetition.

Even if it were argued that "this was said with reference only to those [mental states] of dissimilar feeling," even so, just as in the case of "adverting [is the condition] for wholesome [states],"...

It is stated that "aggregates are a condition for unwholesome aggregates by way of proximity-condition (anantarapaccaya)"; likewise, it could also be said that they are "a condition by way of repetition-condition (āsevanapaccaya).
If it is argued that this was not stated because of a difference in type (jātibheda), then one must surely say:

"Just as there is the status of being a repetition-condition for sense-sphere [states] toward form-sphere and other [higher] states despite a difference in plane (bhūmibhinna), so too would it exist despite a difference in type."

It might be that, by way of those of non-distinct birth (*abhinnajātika*), just as it is stated, "Adverting is a condition for root-cause-accompanied aggregates by way of proximity-condition (*anantarapaccaya*)," so too it could have been stated, "it is a condition by way of repetition-condition (*āsevanapaccaya*). But it was not so stated;
therefore, even in the triad of feeling, according to the abbreviated enumeration, [it is said]: "One [condition] is not-path by way of repetition-condition; one is not-path-condition..."

"In the case of repetition, there is one"—when determining [the relations] by this method of counting, since advertence lacks the status of being a condition of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*), the second "futile section" mentioned above should be examined and understood accordingly.
However, advertence is called "adverting" (*āvajjanā*) because it turns toward the cognitive process, the resultants, and the continuity;
thereafter, it is called "attention" (*manasikāra*) because it performs the function of the dissimilar impulsion (*javana*).
And having established it thus, in the *Paṭṭhāna* it is not stated that "determining (voṭṭhabbana) is a condition for wholesome aggregates by way of proximity-condition," etc.;

rather, it is simply stated as "adverting (āvajjanā). Therefore, since determining is unable to become the object-prenascence for four or five impulsion-moments, it becomes a condition for the adverting to visible forms and so forth.
"If it were not able [to do so], this would be its inherent nature; thus, it would be appropriate to show a second section on futility regarding the non-completion of the impulsion.
For this is the teacher’s intention: if even the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*) were to be a condition by way of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*), then just as it is said:
"In dependence upon a state associated with pleasant feeling, a state associated with pleasant feeling arises... [the same logic would apply].
In the positive-negative and negative-positive sequences, it is stated: “conditioned by repetition, not conditioned by the path,” and “pleasant...

[etc. ...not conditioned by the path, conditioned by repetition”; this is with reference to the consciousness that arouses laughter. Likewise, with reference to determining consciousness (voṭṭhabbana), it is stated according to the method previously explained:
“dependent on a state associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling,” and so forth.

This might be the reading. And if that were the case, then by way of counting according to the two instances, one would have to say: "In the case of the path, there are two [instances] by way of the repetition condition;

in the case of repetition, there are two by way of the path condition. However, it was not said thus; rather, it was stated: "In the case of the path, there is one by way of the repetition condition; in the case of repetition, there is one by way of the path condition.
Furthermore, if even the "determining" (voṭṭhabbana) were to be a repetition condition, then the second section on the floods (oghavāra) [would be inconsistent].

It might be so even in the previous instances. And if that were the case, it would follow that wholesome and unwholesome states [could be repetition conditions] for themselves, just as they are for others.
For there is no state that is not explicitly stated to be a repetition condition when it is fit to receive the status of a repetition condition;
this is because [the Sutta] has stated it exhaustively by saying, "The preceding wholesome aggregates," and so forth, including the *voṭṭhabbana* consciousness.

However, it was not stated [by the Blessed One] because there is no such statement as, "An indeterminate dhamma is a condition for a wholesome dhamma by way of the condition of repetition (āsevanapaccaya)," and so forth.
Not only was it not stated, but furthermore, [it was said]: "Dependent on a wholesome dhamma, a wholesome dhamma arises;
dependent on an unwholesome dhamma, an unwholesome dhamma arises," [referring to] wholesome and unwholesome dhammas such as contact (phassa) and the rest.
Having explained the arising of the wholesome and unwholesome by way of such conditions as co-nascence (*sahajāta-paccaya*),

it was specifically rejected with the words "not by way of the condition of repetition" (*nāsevanapaccayā*) because the first impulsion (*javana*) lacks the state of repetition due to its function of determining (*voṭṭhabbana*). Now, however,
there might be a synthesis here, since the state of being a condition of repetition is seen only for those states that possess the same feeling (*vedanā*).
This negation is made on the basis of wholesome and unwholesome states that have dissimilar feelings by way of registration (voṭṭhabbana). Even so,
just as it is stated that "adverting is a condition for wholesome aggregates and unwholesome aggregates by way of proximity-condition," so too,
by way of similar feeling, it should also be stated that [registration] is "a condition by way of repetition-condition."

It may be so. If it is argued that because registration (voṭṭhabbana) is of a different genus from the wholesome and unwholesome states, its status as a condition of repetition (āsevanapaccaya) for them has not been stated—then [we reply]:

Just as the state of being a condition of repetition is seen for sense-sphere states belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara) with respect to those of the fine-material and immaterial realms, despite being distinguished by way of plane, and just as it is seen for the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) and purification (vodāna) states despite being distinguished by way of lineage, so too should the status of registration as a condition of repetition be understood despite its distinction by way of genus.

There is no obstruction; moreover, for a great functional consciousness (mahākiriyacitta) accompanied by equanimity that has undivided feeling and undivided birth, just as it is stated that "adverting is a condition for the root-cause-accompanied aggregates by way of proximity-condition," so too it could have been stated that it is "a condition by way of repetition-condition," yet it was not so stated. Therefore, even in the triad of feelings...
The second "futile section" (moghavāra), which was stated by way of showing that determining (voṭṭhabbana) possesses the state of being a condition through repetition (āsevana-paccaya),
should be understood after investigation, because determining lacks the status of being a condition through repetition. However,

since there is no difference in meaning between determining and adverting (āvajjana), and since it has been stated that adverting is a condition for wholesome and unwholesome states by way of contiguity (anantara-paccaya), determining exists at the moment of arising.

It should be understood that this [consciousness] would function solely as an immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*) for the wholesome, unwholesome, and functional impulsion-moments (*javana*) of the sense-sphere, and not otherwise;
for at times such as fainting, near-death, or the onset of old age, the impulsion is incomplete and its momentum is weakened.
Regarding this, the Elder Master Dhammapāla has stated: "That which has attained the state of impulsion is like a flower from a tree whose roots have been severed."

Because it will be stated later as "viyā," there would otherwise be no functional (kiriyā) nature for the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*) occurring when the root of existence is not severed;
yet it is said: "At whatever time the mind-consciousness element arises—functional, neither wholesome nor unwholesome, and not the result of kamma—it is accompanied by equanimity.
Therefore, in the commentary, it says: "having stood in the place of javana."
The statement that [the consciousness] occurs twice at the place where the impulsion arises is said with the intention that it does not do so by way of being an impulsion itself.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction in saying "having obtained repetition" (*āsevanaṃ labhitvā*) or "repetition as if it were repetition" (*āsevanaṃ viya āsevanaṃ*).
For that which is expansive, its occurrence twice here constitutes its similarity to repetition. This is due to its expansiveness.
For it is said that this [impulsion] possesses the quality of originating a communication (*viññatti*).

Furthermore, although impulsion is expansive, because it does not occur many times and is thus weak, it would not function as a condition through repetition (*āsevana-paccaya*) in the primary sense; therefore, its status as repetition is not mentioned in this text.
However, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), it is mentioned figuratively (*pariyāyato*), just as it is in the case of resultant consciousnesses (*phala-citta*).

Regarding the phrase "a path-factor included in the path": although it is stated that "it is engaged for the fulfillment of the impulsion," because it is also stated that "it is unable to become a condition for the adverting consciousness and so forth," there is no distinction between this [fifth path-moment] and the first non-futile moment in terms of the occurrence of consciousness.
"Having come into the range of the eye" means having come into the range by way of being situated in a location suitable for the eye-door (*cakkhudvāra*).
"By that" refers to the functional mind-element (*kiriya-manodhātu*), because it is evident when the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) has ceased.
"Turned back" means turned away from continuing in a stream of consciousness, or transformed. The connection is with "arising among those that have arisen. "Gone" means ceased.

"‘That very same’ means the desirable object experienced by the impulsion (javana). ‘By that very same’ means by that sense-sphere wholesome consciousness which has ceased after having functioned as impulsion.
It is called ‘having that as its object’ (tadārammaṇa) because it occurs with respect to the very object grasped by the impulsion;
thus, just as in the case of terms like ‘Brahmā’s voice,’ it is ‘tadārammaṇa’ by eliding the middle term [of *tad-ārammaṇa*, meaning ‘that whose object is this’]."

[It is] so designated. "By way of similarity" means that although there is a difference in the object (*ārammaṇa*), there is a similarity by virtue of being accompanied by joy (*somanassasahagata*) and so forth.

The life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) that resembles the root is the "root-life-continuum. Even the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) is called "life-continuum" because it possesses the nature of the life-continuum, just as it is said:
"The root-conditioned life-continuum is a condition for the rootless life-continuum by way of proximity-condition (*anantarapaccaya*). In this context...
For if the very rebirth-linking consciousness were called "life-continuum" (bhavaṅga) during the course of existence (pavatti), there would be no distinction between them by way of their causes;
thus, one could not say, "A life-continuum with root-cause is a condition for a rootless life-continuum by way of proximity-condition.
Nor can it be said that this was stated with reference to a death-consciousness with root-cause and a rootless rebirth-linking consciousness.
It is understood that because it lacks the status of being a constituent of existence (*bhava*), the death-consciousness does not receive the designation "existence-factor" (*bhavaṅga*);
thus, it is known that the "root existence-factor with root-cause" mentioned there refers to the object-attaining consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*).
By stating "called 'object-attaining'" and then saying "it is called the 'root existence-factor'," it is indicated that both these names apply to this [consciousness].

392. "And that" means that registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*). "In this" refers to among these process-consciousnesses (*vīthicitta*). "Consciousnesses that enter into the count" means resultant consciousnesses that enter into the count. 394.
"Because they are not the same" means because they are not the same by way of being unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*).
396. The connection is: "The five preceding resultant consciousnesses, together with this one, become six. And here, it is according to the majority.

Because of the occurrence of joy with respect to a desirable object, the registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa) associated with joy is said to follow immediately after the impulsion (javana) associated with joy.
However, since impulsion possesses the function of grasping the object after having determined it, whereas fruition lacks that function,
even when impulsions associated with equanimity have occurred toward a desirable object, the registration consciousness remains associated with joy alone.

399–403. "In that door" means in that very eye-door (*cakkhudvāra*). "Feeling changes" means that even though the kamma was accompanied by joy (*somanassa*), because the object is of a neutral-desirable nature (*iṭṭhamajjhattatā*), the feeling of joy changes and becomes a feeling of equanimity (*upekkhāvedanā*).
Alternatively, although the resultant feeling below was of the nature of joy, due to the neutral nature of the desirable object, by way of that [object], [the feeling changes].
The meaning is that feeling undergoes transformation (*parivattati*).
The connection is with the words "when the impulsions have impelled" (*javanesu javitesu*). Alternatively, there is the reading: "in all four when they have impelled.

"They arise" means they arise by way of registration (*tadārammaṇa*). "By feeling" means by feeling acting as the instrument (*karaṇabhūtāya*). "Because of non-identity" means because of its lack of identity with the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi*).
“From the former” means from the fourfold set of object-attaining consciousnesses mentioned below. Alternatively, the construction is simply: “because they are not the same as the former.
When their state of being dissimilar to the former is stated, their state of being dissimilar even to the connection [between them] is also stated by implication;

thus the construction is that there are four named *paccavekkhaṇa* (reviewing) and the *bhavaṅga* (life-continuum) that follows them. By the word “and” (*ca*), the adventitious *bhavaṅgas* are included.

This shows that they also have those [objects] as their registration-objects (*tadārammaṇa*). Here too, because for the most part a javana accompanied by equanimity arises with respect to desirable-neutral objects, it is stated that the registration-impulsion immediately following the javana accompanied by equanimity is itself accompanied by equanimity;

however, according to the method explained below, there is also a registration-impulsion accompanied by equanimity when the javanas associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta*) and so forth have impelled.
The occurrence of registration consciousnesses dissociated from knowledge should be understood according to the method explained below.

Although the classification of "without effort" (asaṅkhāra) and "with effort" (sasaṅkhāra) was stated by way of the impulsion (javana), nevertheless, when conditions such as climate and food are weak, because the impulsion itself lacks the quality of being "without effort," it follows that at the conclusion of an "effortless" impulsion, the registration is also "without effort" and not "with effort. This is the rule regarding the condition.
However, even when the [mental] power is strong, because a javana with volitional effort (*sasaṅkhāra*) can arise through the force of others' encouragement,

there is no fixed rule that at the conclusion of a *sasaṅkhārika* javana the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) must necessarily be *sasaṅkhārika*, nor that at the conclusion of an *asaṅkhārika* javana it must necessarily be *asaṅkhārika*.
Therefore, at the conclusion of an *asaṅkhārika* javana, the registration consciousness may be either *asaṅkhārika* or *sasaṅkhārika*.
At the conclusion of the impulsion with volitional effort (*sasaṅkhāra-javana*), there occurs registration (*tadārammaṇa*) with volitional effort as well as without volitional effort (*asaṅkhāra*).
"These five" refers to the five resultants beginning with investigation accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā-sahagata-santīraṇa*), which have been described as having desirable-neutral objects.

"By the preceding seven" means one should designate them as occurring in the eye-door by way of the seven [resultants] beginning with eye-consciousness, which were described as having desirable objects; this is the intended meaning.
"By a single volition" means by a single unprompted (asaṅkhārika) volition accompanied by joy and possessing three roots.

The connection is that sixty resultant states thus arise. However, just as ear-consciousness and the others do not arise in the eye-door and so forth but arise only in the ear-door and so forth, so too [these resultants] do not arise in the five doors but [arise] only in the mind-door.
Since there is no arising of sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) resultant [consciousness], the occurrence of the resultant in the mind-door has not been mentioned. Alternatively,
by mentioning the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) that were already apprehended in the eye-door within the ear-door and so forth,
the method for including the mind-consciousness-element— previously apprehended in the five doors— within the mind-door is demonstrated.
This being so, there are sixty-seven resultant consciousnesses (vipāka) in all six doors. Alternatively,

although the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) that occurs in the five doors is also obtainable in the mind door, its non-inclusion here in the mind door serves as an illustration of the method for not including the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and mind-consciousness element that are obtainable in the ear door and so forth, even though they were included in the eye door.

Thus it is said; this being so, there are sixteen resultant [consciousnesses] in the five doors. And having established it thus, it was stated: "by way of inclusion of what has already been included," and so forth. 408–9. "By three resultants":
the connection is with the rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) bestowed by those three resultants which correspond to those three wholesome consciousnesses.
"In the pair accompanied by equanimity" refers to the two types of rebirth-linking associated with equanimity. Standing here, the simile of the waterwheel (nāḷiyanta-upamā) [is applied].

It should be understood. How so? It is said that at the time of pressing sugarcane, eleven oxen belonging to a certain village set out, and seeing a sugarcane field and knowing it was ripe, they approached the owner of the field and announced, "We are oxen for the press.
He replied, "I shall seek you out myself," and taking the sugarcane shed, he went along with them.
Having set up a sugar-cane mill there, they said, "We are eleven men; it is necessary for us to have one more. Take turns and provide one.
The sugar-cane owner, thinking, "I myself shall be the companion," filled the sugar-cane shed and became their companion.
Having each performed his own duties, when the sugarcane juice was boiled by the molasses-maker—

When the sugar was bound together and weighed by the owner of the sugarcane, and the portions had been distributed, they each took their own share, entrusted the hall to the owner of the hall, and having performed the work in four other halls in that very same manner, they departed.
In this context, the five sense-faculties (pasāda) are to be seen as like the five weaving-halls; the five objects (ārammaṇa) are like the five sugarcane fields.
The eleven resultant consciousnesses are like the eleven workmen carrying away the timber; the five types of sensory consciousness are like the owners of the sugar-cane plantation;

and the time when the twelve people—including the owner of the first plantation—gather together to take their shares of the produce is like the time when the eleven resultant consciousnesses gather together with the eye-consciousness.

The time when they become one at the eye-door with respect to a visible-form object and perform their respective functions is like the time when the master of a hall receives [tribute] in his hall; it is the non-transference of the door for the eye-consciousness,
just as the twelve [servants] who have performed their work together in the second, third, fourth, and fifth halls take their shares, so too it is for the eleven resultant consciousnesses.

The time when [the mind-element] acts together with body-consciousness as one at the body-door regarding the tangible object, performing its own respective function, should be understood as the non-transference of the door for body-consciousness, like the time when a master has already accepted [an offering]. 414.
*Assa* means "of this seed. *Hetupavattito* means "from the occurrence of conditions."

415. Now, since the occurrence of result for one who has taken a two-rooted rebirth-linking by means of a weak three-rooted kamma is identical to the occurrence of result for one who has taken a two-rooted rebirth-linking by means of a superior two-rooted kamma, setting that aside,
the passage beginning with “by a two-rooted kamma” is stated in order to show the occurrence of result specifically for one who has taken a two-rooted rebirth-linking by means of a two-rooted kamma.
418–9. Although javanas of the sense-sphere with three roots can arise for one whose rebirth-linking is with two roots, it is stated, “with joy...
[etc. ...in the case of two roots,” in order to show only those javanas that correspond to the karma.

Furthermore, even at the conclusion of a javana with three roots, the karma that provides the rebirth-linking is incapable of giving a result with three roots; thus, because there is no resultant mind with three roots taking that [rebirth-linking] as its object, [the javana is said to be with two roots].
And because the javana possesses the state of being double-rooted by way of the cause of similarity to the kamma, its object is likewise double-rooted. 424.
"These life-continuum processes" refers to these four root, adventitious, and back-life-continuum processes. "Eight indeed" means exactly eight. 426.

"By the ear, nose, and so forth" means by the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, and the rest. Here too, the mango simile is quite evident. [The same applies] by way of the simile of the machine-operator.

In this context, there are seven "driving-machines" (yantavāha); with these, having designated the eighth as the "hand-machine," the application should be understood according to the method already stated, making it the master of the [remaining] branches. 434–6. "Of one who has attained growth":
this refers to the state of being capable, after emerging from the mother's womb, of establishing oneself in restraint or non-restraint.

Regarding "one who has reached growth": although it was stated, "Of those with two roots... at the conclusion," in order to show that for one with a rootless rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), only a javana similar to the karma occurs; nevertheless, a javana with three roots also proceeds for them.
However, because the karma is incapable of yielding a rootless resultant even when the javana possesses two roots, it is said, "Rootless... is born."
443–8. Regarding the phrase “without a cause for rebirth-linking” (*ahetupaṭisandhi*) and so forth, the intended meaning has already been explained above.

Because a rebirth-linking consciousness that gives rise to rebirth in the woeful states does not produce an object inferior to that rebirth-linking itself, the text says “in a happy destination” (*sugatiyam*) in order to show the specific place where such a consciousness can occur;
the meaning is “in a happy destination of the sense-sphere. “By that” (*tena*) means by that resultant rebirth-linking which has arisen.
Having stated, "It is found in the four states of misery," the passage beginning with "The Elder [preaches] to those in hell" was spoken in order to demonstrate its specific scope.
"The Elder" refers to the Elder Mahāmoggallāna because he is well known for his journey through the hells. "Those in hell" (*nerayikā*) means those who exist in hell.
"He preaches the Dhamma" means that having fashioned a lotus in hell, he sits upon the pericarp of the lotus and preaches the Dhamma. "It rains" means...
This is stated by making the internal cause the meaning; the sense is "he causes it to rain. "Having seen the Elder" means because of seeing the Elder.
By this, he shows the reason for the arising of wholesome-resultant eye-consciousness due to the state of being a desirable object for the Elder, who possesses the complexion of an indranīla gem.
This same method applies to [the phrases] "having heard the Dhamma," and so forth. "Fragrance" means the fragrance produced by him.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated: “The fragrance of the robe of one sitting for his midday rest in a sandalwood grove.

“For those who smell” means for those who are smelling. “The two types of investigating consciousness” refers to the two types of investigating consciousness regarding extremely desirable or neutral odors and so forth.
By demonstrating the occurrence of wholesome resultant consciousnesses and desirable objects even in hell, their occurrence in the other three states of woe is also shown by implication.
450. "The restriction itself is the state of being restricted" means that even the consciousness having that as its object (tadārammaṇa-citta) is restricted by the impulsion (javana);

this is the meaning of the "stated restriction. However, "with reference to the wholesome" means it was explained in the Commentary with reference to wholesome impulsion, because—just as with the wholesome—there is no similar fruition for the unwholesome;
this is the intention. And here, immediately after wholesome impulsion, there is only the resultant consciousness with roots (sahetuka-tadārammaṇa).
This statement is made because the javana is "with cause" (sahetuka) by way of having a cause similar to the karma; thus, it is described in accordance with the javana.
However, it should not be said that, by way of being well-developed (paricita), that registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa) cannot be without a cause even through other karma.

For it is not only the karma that produces rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) which produces the registration consciousness; rather, other karma as well [produces it] from the registration consciousness that is to be brought about by the karma giving rebirth-linking.
"It also produces the unpleasant [result]. And immediately after an unwholesome javana, even a rootless "taking-that-as-an-object" (tadārammaṇa) occurs;

this is stated because it conforms to the javana by having a similar cause (kammasarikkhaka-hetuka). However, according to the method already explained, there is no such thing as a "taking-that-as-an-object" with roots.
456–7. Up to this point, according to the doctrine of the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷanāga, there are sixteen resultant consciousnesses together with the twelvefold path.

Having clarified this by means of both the *Ahetukavāda* and the *Mahādatta Thera’s* doctrine (resident at Moravāpi), and since there is no difference [in their views], that [latter] is not mentioned.

Instead, by way of the *Mahādhammarakkhita Thera’s* doctrine—which presents a synthesis based on wholesome, unwholesome, and functional states—the text says, "In a consciousness associated with joy," etc., in order to show the registration (*tadārammaṇa*) by way of the javanas that have been presented in combination. Somanassa...pe...

"Having impelled": when thirteen impulsion-consciousnesses associated with joy have impelled—namely, those wholesome, unwholesome, functional, and indeterminate states directed toward a desirable object.
"Should be sought... mental" (*mānasā*): according to the method explained below, only the five registration-consciousnesses accompanied by joy should be sought.
"Equanimity... having impelled": [this refers to] the wholesome, unwholesome, and functional [states].

When fourteen types of impulsion consciousness accompanied by equanimity have impelled, six [types of registration] are to be sought; that is, only those six accompanied by equanimity are to be sought.
Because those whose taints are destroyed have abandoned the perversions, functional impulsion accompanied by equanimity does not arise toward a desirable object;
therefore, when functional impulsions accompanied by joy have impelled, only registration accompanied by joy occurs.

It occurs. Since there is a state of joy (*somanassa*) regarding desirable and neutral objects, as well as undesirable ones and so forth, when functional impulsion moments accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā-sahagata-kiriya-javana*) have impelled, there is only an object-attending moment accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā-sahagata-tadārammaṇa*); this is the conclusion here.

However, for those in training (*sekhā*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*), because their perversions (*vipallāsa*) have not been abandoned, there is an impulsion accompanied by joy (*somanassa-sahagata-javana*) toward desirable-neutral objects and toward undesirable or undesirable-neutral objects.
Regarding the phrase "it arises": at the conclusion of a javana accompanied by joy, there occurs only a registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa) accompanied by joy;
it is not an absolute rule that there is none accompanied by equanimity. This should also be applied to desirable objects according to the method already stated. Therefore, this is said:
"The wholesome, the faulty, the imperturbable, the functional, and the javanas—these are limited."
“One among the five has that as its object; among those who are happy, it is according to what is appropriate.
‘The Pāpa, Kāmasubha, and Sōpekkhā [realms] have the impulsion of functional consciousness;
among those with equanimity, one among the six has that as its object, according to what is fitting.’”
458–62. Because those with two roots and those without roots are possessed of the obstruction of kamma-result (*vipākāvaraṇa*), there is no arising of jhāna at all for them;
thus he said, "by means of the three-rooted joy. "One fallen away from jhāna" means one who has fallen away from the mundane jhāna that had been produced.
"One full of regret" means one in whom regret has arisen, thinking, "The sublime state produced by great effort has been lost by me."
"What... pe ... mental?"—this is a question seeking permission; the meaning here is: "Does a mind having that as its object arise, or not?
Whether there be a lapse into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) or an object-mind (tadārammaṇa), what obstacle is there here? Thus he says, "It is prohibited in the Paṭṭhāna," and so forth.
Taking "prohibited" (paṭisiddhā) to mean a mere non-statement, he says "it is prohibited. If there were grief immediately after joy, [it would be so].
If, immediately after a state associated with displeasure (domanassa), a state associated with joy (somanassa) should arise, then—
just as it is said that "a state associated with pleasant feeling is a condition, by way of proximity-condition, for a state associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling"— likewise,
"a state associated with pleasant feeling [is a condition] for a state associated with painful feeling..."
It should be stated: "It is a condition by way of proximity-condition for painful feeling... pe... for pleasant feeling... pe... [it is] a condition.

Likewise, in the section on enumeration, with reference to the fact that [a state] associated with one feeling acts as a condition for that which is associated with the same feeling as itself, and for that which possesses the other two feelings, it should be stated: "nine in the immediate [condition]."

It might be so, yet it is not actually recorded thus in the Canon. However, regarding those states associated with the feelings of mental grief and mental joy, by means of the mutual and immediate conditions (*aññamañña-anantara-paccaya*), two counts are omitted and it is stated, "seven in the immediate.

Therefore, even though there is no explicit mention in the teaching according to the nature of things (*yathādhamma-sāsana*), it is as if they were prohibited because it indicates their non-existence;
thus it is said, "they are excluded" (*paṭisiddhā*). Or, [the phrase] "immediately after this" (*assa vā anantaraṃ*)...
The connection is with "the arising of displeasure" (*domanassassa uppatti*). "Its" refers to joy (*somanassassa*).

Having thus stated the reason for the absence of falling back into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), he says "sublime" (*mahaggata*) and so forth, further demonstrating the absence of that object at that time. It is prohibited in that very same context:
"A state with a limited object (*parittārammaṇo dhammo*) [is not a condition] for a state with a sublime object (*mahaggatārammaṇassa dhammassa*) by way of kamma-condition (*kammapaccayena*)."
Because there is no statement [in the texts] saying "it is a condition," it is prohibited right there in the *Paṭṭhāna*. "What indeed should be done? means what ought to be done.
The intention is that one cannot say "it is without consciousness" based on this much alone.

And here, only the joyless impulsion (*domanassa-javana*) with a sublime object (*mahaggatārammaṇa*) is stated by way of illustration; however, even in the case of objects such as the Buddha and so forth, which are desirable objects (*iṭṭhārammaṇa*), [the same applies].

When a javana of displeasure (domanassa) has occurred, for one who possesses rebirth-linking with joy (somanassa), there is no possibility of an object-receiving consciousness (tadārammaṇa) or a lapse into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).

464–5. Regarding the statement by the Teacher, “The roots are accompanied by equanimity,” because there is no occurrence of joy immediately following displeasure when the object is desirable, the challenger, pursuing the argument further, said:
“Is there adverting for it? The teacher, however, showing that there is no need to search for adverting here—since this consciousness arises even without it—said:
“There is none. Again, the challenger, unable to conceive of the occurrence of consciousness without adverting, said:
“How is it born? When this was said, the teacher [replied]: “What need is there for adverting here?”

Furthermore, in order to demonstrate that the claim "there is no occurrence of consciousness without an adverting consciousness" is not absolute, he says "of the life-continuum and the adverting [consciousnesses]," etc., showing the possibility of consciousnesses without an adverting consciousness; the intention is: what is the adverting consciousness for the life-continuum and the adverting consciousnesses?
Is it not simply non-existent? And is it not the case that the life-continuum and the adverting consciousnesses, at least, are inclined toward their respective objects?

Because they generally arise through habituation even without an adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*), he speaks the words beginning with "of the path" (*maggassa*) while again showing the types of consciousness that lack an adverting consciousness, in order to address the inquiry: "But how does this [resultant consciousness] arise?
"Of the path" means of the supramundane path-consciousness. "And of the immediately subsequent fruit" means of the fruit that follows immediately after the path.
The connection is: "What is the purpose of adverting? Thus, it does not exist; just as it does not exist for those [preceding moments], so too it does not exist for this one.

However, the teacher Ānanda states here that the noble path-consciousness and the fruition-consciousness immediately following the path—though they are similar to the preparatory and adverting consciousnesses in being accompanied by adverting—are cited merely as examples of arising despite the absence of adverting, on account of their arising in a state of inclination and so forth.
He praises them as having been "spoken. For this is his intended meaning:

if these [passages] were spoken with reference to the absence of adverting (āvajjana) that has Nibbāna as its object, then the *gotrabhū* and *vodāna* moments should have been shown, since by means of those alone the state of being without adverting for these [moments] is established.

Furthermore, at the time of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), [the text says]: "The conformity [consciousness] has a limited object or a sublime object; for the attainment of fruition..."

Because of the statement, “It is a condition by way of proximity-condition,” since the fruition-consciousnesses immediately following the Path (maggānantara) lack an adverting consciousness with the same object,
the fruition-consciousnesses of attainment would not [otherwise] need to be excluded.

However, although the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) and purification (vodāna) moments have practiced upon and are accumulated in relation to Nibbāna, they do not yet possess the quality of having practiced upon and being accumulated in relation to other objects.
The consciousnesses of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) are not included because, subsequent to the path-process, there is no preliminary work (parikamma) for that purpose.
Furthermore, the consciousness of the attainment of fruition immediately following conformity (anuloma) is something already practiced and accumulated;

it is not like the case of the path immediately following the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, where there is no preliminary work for that purpose. Therefore, it is indicated by the phrase "for one emerging from cessation."

467. Having asked, "What is its object? one might say that it has no object, just as one might say it lacks an adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*). To establish his own statement by demonstrating that state [of having no object], he says, "Without an object," and so forth.
"Whatever" means whatever previously familiar object it may have been directed toward. But was it not stated that it would have that as its object?

Since the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) takes only the object of the impulsion (*javana*) as its own object—otherwise, its status as a registration consciousness would be untenable—how can it be said that its object is limited (*paritta*)?
This is true; because the resultant consciousnesses of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara-vipāka-citta*) invariably have limited objects, it is not fitting for them to have sublime (*mahaggata*) objects.
Furthermore, the term "registration" (*tadārammaṇa*) is used here by taking the occurrence [of the consciousness] in the place where the registration occurs.

It is not stated [that it performs that function], because for it, the function of taking that as its object (tadārammaṇa-kicca) is impossible at that time. By what function, then, does this consciousness arise?

First of all, the function of taking that as its object does not exist due to the reasons already mentioned; nor does the function of investigating (santīraṇa-kicca), because it does not proceed in that manner.

It cannot even be said to have the functions of rebirth-linking or death. However, by process of elimination, since it serves as a constituent part of existence (bhava), it has the function of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
It would be appropriate [to say] that the very consciousness which has become the rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*); this is stated by way of the majority of cases.
Indeed, this same point was also demonstrated by the Elder Master Dhammapāla. 468–73.
Since no agent exists, how can there be a state of being with an opening (*sāvajjana*) for anyone whose occurrence is without an opening (*nirāvajjana*)?
In order to show that this is produced by the restraint of the mind with reference to the *codanā* (the prompting), it is said:
"And the regulation of season and seed," and so forth. "The regulation of season and seed" means both the regulation of season and the regulation of seed;

what is meant is the regulation of the intrinsic nature of the season and the regulation of the intrinsic nature of the seed. The state of being the regulation of karma and phenomena is simply the regulation of karma and phenomena (*kammadhammaniyāmatā*). "Simultaneously" (*ekappahārena*) refers to each respective...
Without exceeding the specific time for its season, [the fruit arises] at one and the same time. By the word "etc.
(*ādi*) in "fruit, flower, etc.," the inclusion of sprouts and so forth is intended. "Of all" means of all those things that produce fruit and so on at that particular time.
"The arising of fruits corresponding to each" means the production of fruits similar to their respective seeds; that is, the production of fruits in accordance with those various seeds.

The meaning is as follows: “The northern tip of the *kulattha* bean moving upward, the southern creeper avoiding the southern tree, the *sūriyāvatta* flowers facing the sun, and the *māluva* creeper moving toward the tree”—such things as these are all included herein.
“Chiddattaṃ” means the state of having holes, or simply a hole itself. “Bījajo” means...
The certainty of arising from the seed is "niyāma. It gives because it gives according to the certainty of its state as a condition for this or that [result].
This is the certainty in producing a fruit that is either similar to itself, like it, or unlike it. Furthermore:
"Neither in the sky, nor in the midst of the ocean..."
“Neither by entering a cleft in the mountains nor by going anywhere else in the world is there any place found where one,
while remaining there, could be freed from evil karma.”
In the introduction to this verse, it is related how a crow’s neck was caught as it flew through the air after a bundle of grass that had been set on fire rose up;
how a mariner’s wife was bound with a jar of sand around her neck and cast into the waters of the ocean;
and how the door of a cave where monks were dwelling was scorched by a falling mountain peak.
It should be understood that even the production of a result corresponding to a particular action is simply the fixed order of karma (*kamma-niyāma*).

"At birth" refers both to the seizing of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and to the emergence from the mother's womb; this is merely an illustration, since the shaking of the earth and so forth can also occur at such events as the full enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*) and the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakkappavattana*).
"Of the Bodhisatta" refers to the Bodhisatta in his final existence (*pacchimabhavika*). "The shaking of the earth and so forth."

The thirty-two portents, beginning with the shaking of the earth, are the specific signs. "And many other distinctions" refers to all the wonders that appeared at that time, distinct from the portents themselves.
Regarding "the arising of adverting and so forth": although there was no one to direct them by saying, "You be the adverting consciousness;
you be the seeing consciousness," and so on, they arose each according to their respective functions.

“Darkness in the heart” (*hadayandhakāro*) means darkness within the heart; the meaning is delusion (*sammoha*). Its “dispelling” (*viddhaṃsana*) is that which effects its abandonment; thus it is the “dispelling of the darkness in the heart.

“Exerted” (*payutto*) means one who possesses energy through an unremitting vigor until reaching final nibbāna without clinging (*anupādā-parinibbāna*). “Departure from the darkness of delusion” refers to arhatship.
Thus ends the commentary on the Exposition of the Occurrence of Resultant Consciousness within the *Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanā*, known as the *Abhidhammatthavikāsinī*.
Chapter Eight:
Explanation of the Miscellaneous Section. 475–6.
Now, for the purpose of making all the aforementioned types of consciousness clear:
“The Sutta, the doorkeeper,
the villager, the mango-eater,
the one born blind, and the cripple.”

“...the proximate cause in meaning.”—The section beginning with “Now then” is commenced in order to show the miscellaneous method (*pakiṇṇakanaya*) according to the matrix (*mātikā*) found in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
Therein, *manas* refers to consciousnesses (*cittānaṃ*). They also read it as *mānasa*, but that is not good. *Panthamakkaṭako* means...
The *uṇṇanābhi* (spider) is so named because it spreads its web in places where insects, beetles, and the like move about, thereby guarding their path.
The phrase "in the five directions" is stated by way of the five faculties (*pañcapasāda*), which are to be understood as the comparison.
"Therein" refers either to the path or, alternatively, to the middle of the web; "having spread out a thread" refers to the weaving of the web.
478–80. *Nti* refers to blood. In the suttas concerning the second and subsequent directions... [etc. ...the connection is with the word "struck.

The passage beginning with “The five faculties are to be seen” is the correlation of the similes. “The mind... like... means that the mind proceeding in dependence upon the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*) is to be seen as a monkey lying in the middle of a net.
"Stirring of the sensitivity" (pasādaghaṭṭana) means that which has stirred the sensitivity. "Turning back toward the life-continuum" (bhavaṅgāvaṭṭana) means turning back toward the life-continuum.
Since there is no such thing as a "functional process" (kiriyā) apart from a phenomenon (dhamma), the phenomenon itself is compared to the movement.

"Like following the thread" (suttānusāraṃva) means like proceeding according to the thread. Because it experiences the flavor of the object, the occurrence of the impulsion (javana) is [compared] to drinking broth.

These are stated by means of a simile. "The basis itself" means that whereas the preceding consciousnesses are dependent on the heart-basis (*hadayavatthu*), follow upon the sensitive matter (*pasādavatthu*), and have other objects, the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) is not like that.
It is explained that it proceeds entirely supported by the heart-basis alone, devoid of any other basis or object. "Reversion" refers to its returning once again to the state of the life-continuum.

Regarding the transformation: although there is a difference in terms of their intrinsic nature (*dhamma*) between the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*), and so forth, they are treated as a unity by way of the continuity of the stream;
thus, the application of the simile of the single monkey is stated.
486–90. *Opamma* is simply a simile (*upamā*). Thereafter, the connection is "consciousnesses from the basis of confidence. This is illustrated by this very simile.
"Each single object" (*ekkekārammaṇa*) means one of the five objects, such as visible form and so forth. "In all" (*sabbaso*) means in any of them, such as the eye and so forth; this is the meaning.
Now, in order to demonstrate that each single object enters the range of two [faculties] respectively, it is said: "Visible form in the sensitivity of the eye," and so on.
"A sky-goer" (*khaga*) is one who goes in the sky (*khe*); that is, a bird. "Of the branch-bearer" (*sākhino*) means of the tree.
"Of the visible form" (*rūpassa*) is a genitive case used in the sense of connection; it is connected with two things:
its striking [the sensitivity] and its coming into the range [of the sense]. "Of the sensitivity" (*pasādassa*) is a genitive case used in the sense of the object;

in terms of meaning, it is connected with "coming into the range. Through the object, and by the striking of the sensitivity even as it comes into the range, there occurs the movement of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
The meaning is: "approaching as if it were within range by way of being a condition. 494–5.
*Tato* means after the vibration of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). "Wholesome impulsion consciousness" refers to a wholesome impulsion consciousness of the sense-sphere.
By the word "or" (*vā*) in the phrase "or unwholesome," functional and indeterminate consciousnesses are also included. Here, one might ask: "But who is this?"
Does the impulsion determine [the result] by way of wholesomeness or unwholesomeness? It is through both appropriate attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) and inappropriate attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*).
For one in whom appropriate attention proceeds by way of the perfection of the four wheels, their adverting and determining are likewise appropriate;
for such a person, there is no arising of the unwholesome. But for one who, by the reverse of what has been stated...
When there is improper attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*), as well as improper adverting (*āvajjana*) and determining (*voṭṭhabbana*), no wholesome impulsion (*kusalajavana*) arises for that person.
Therefore, it should be understood that proper attention determines wholesomeness, while improper attention determines unwholesomeness.
However, functional impulsion (*kiriyājavana*) determines only Arahantship. Some [teachers]...
However, they say: "But functional impulsion (*kiriyājavana*) and attention (*manasikāra*) determine [the result].

For just as adverting (*āvajjana*) is a distinct condition for both the wholesome and the unwholesome, so too it is for functional impulsion. 497. Regarding the similes of the gatekeeper and so forth:
here, a certain king, having gone to his bed, is sleeping; his attendant [is at his feet]...
He sat massaging [the king’s] feet; a deaf doorkeeper stood at the door, and three attendants stood in succession between the bed and the door.
Then a man from the borderlands, taking a gift, knocked on the door;
the deaf doorkeeper did not hear the sound, but the foot-masser gave a signal, and by that signal the door—
Having opened it, he looked; the first doorkeeper took the gift and gave it to the second, the second to the third, and the third to the king, who then consumed it.

In this analogy, the impulsion (javana) should be seen as being like the king, the adverting consciousness (āvajjana) like the foot-massager, the eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa) like the deaf doorkeeper, and the receiving consciousnesses (sampaṭicchana-ādi) like the three doorkeepers.
The three process-minds are as follows: the striking of the sense-faculty by the object is like the knocking at the door by a border-dweller bringing a gift;
the turning back of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) by the functional mind-element (kiriyā-manodhātu) is like the time when the massage-man gives notice;
and the arising of eye-consciousness is like the opening of the door by a deaf gatekeeper upon receiving that notice.
The time when the function of seeing the object is accomplished is like the time when a gift is received by the first messenger;

it is the time when the resultant mind-element (vipākamanodhātu) receives the object. The time when the object is investigated by the resultant mind-consciousness-element (vipākamanoviññāṇadhātu) is like the time when the second messenger is given [the gift] by the first;
it is the time when the object is handed over by the second [element] to the third.

The time when the object is determined for the functional mind-consciousness element is like the first [moment]; the time when it is handed over to the impulsion by the determining consciousness is like the third [moment], when the gift is given to the king;

and the time when the impulsion experiences the flavor of the object is like the king’s time of enjoyment. This is the analogy of the gatekeeper. As for the question, "What does this simile illustrate?
and so forth, it should be understood according to the method explained under the analogy of the sugar-cane mill. Many...
Some village boys were playing with sand in the middle of the street when a kahāpaṇa coin struck one of them in the hand.
He said, "It has struck my hand; what indeed is this? Then one said, "This is white.
Another grasped it firmly along with the sand. Another said, "This is broad and square. Another said, "A kahāpaṇa."
"Bring it," she said. Then, having brought it, they gave it to his mother, and she placed it for him to work with.
In this regard, the activity of the mind should be seen as being like the time when many children are sitting down together while playing in the middle of an alleyway;

the moment the coin struck the hand is like the moment the sense-faculty (pasāda) is impinged upon by the object; and the moment he said, "What indeed is this?"— [The remainder of the passage describes the subsequent stages of the cognitive process.]

The time when the functional mind-element (kiriyā-manodhātu) seizes that object as its support is like the time when one says, "This is white," after the function of seeing has been accomplished by eye-consciousness;
it is like the time when the resultant mind-element (vipāka-manodhātu) receives the object, just as when one firmly grasps sand along with a clod of earth; [it is like saying] "It is broad."
The time when the object of the resultant mind-consciousness element (vipākamanoviññāṇadhātu) is investigated is like the time when it is said, "This is a square";
the time when the object of the functional mind-consciousness element (kiriyāmanoviññāṇadhātu) is determined is like the time when it is said, "This is a kahāpaṇa coin";
and the experience of the flavor of the object by the impulsion (javana) should be understood as being like the time when the child is brought before his mother—this is the simile of the village boy.
What does this simile illustrate? The functional mind-element turns back toward the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) without even seeing [the object];

the resultant mind-element receives it without even seeing; the resultant mind-consciousness-element investigates it without even seeing; the functional mind-consciousness-element determines it without even seeing;
