and the impulsion experiences the flavor of the object without even seeing. However, it is exclusively eye-consciousness that [sees].
It demonstrates that it accomplishes the function of seeing. The simile of the man blind from birth and the cripple will follow later.

Having grouped these many similes together and referred to them as "the gatekeeper simile and so forth," he says "by way of decisive support" (*upanissaya*) in order to clarify the state of being a decisive support in this context. "By non-confusion" means by way of not being lost.

And by way of being unimpaired by wind, bile, and so forth. For even when impaired by wind, bile, and so forth, the eye is indeed called "divided" because it fails to attain the state of being a condition for eye-consciousness;
yet, because it attains the state of being a support for the five faculties at the very moment of their existence, its non-division in terms of the moment is also logical.

This same method applies to the ear-sensitivity and the others as well. "By way of approaching the visible object-field" refers to [the case of] one standing at a distance, such as with crystal and so forth...
By the object's coming into the range of perception through its being situated in a location capable of serving as a condition for the arising of eye-consciousness in one who is present.
And by doing so, even that which stands at a distance or stands behind one is indeed said to have come into the range of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).
"Also by means of light as a support" means by means of a support known as light, which is capable of illuminating visible forms. In light...

And here, "having light as its support" means that light exists as a possibility, not because light is a supporting condition (*nissaya-paccaya*). "Mindfulness as the cause" means mindfulness itself is the cause;
it "occurs together with" that, hence it is "with mindfulness as its cause. By this, he shows that it is supported by light.
"By those who are united" means by those who are joined and become one, not by the absence of even one; such is the meaning.
“By means of the support of space” means by means of the support of space known as the ear-cavity. For this very reason, it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
“For auditory consciousness does not arise for one whose ear-cavities are closed. External space is also certainly intended;
for likewise, those standing outside do not hear when someone is speaking while sitting inside a house that has no openings. “By means of the support of air” means...
"By means of the air entering through the nostrils. "By means of water" means by means of the water-element consisting of saliva.

"By means of earth" means by means of the earth-element that serves as the basis for the sensitive part of the body (*kāyapasāda*). "Mind-consciousness" refers to impulsive mind-consciousness (*javana-manoviññāṇa*). "The mind...
should be understood" refers to the mind as the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*), as stated in the passage: "Because of the non-interruption of the mind."

This should be understood. Furthermore, even though it has ceased by way of death, it should be seen as being entirely broken apart, having proceeded merely by way of the occurrence of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and having entered a state of dullness, without attaining the status of a condition for the functional mind (kiriyāmayacitta).
This does not go everywhere because it is not obtained in the fourfold plane of existence (catuvokāra). Therefore he said: "But existence..."
“Fivefold existence” (*pañcavokāra*), and so forth. In this context, it is called "fivefold existence" because it is the sphere (*vokāra*) for the five aggregates (*khandha*).
For there exists a compound with a different referent (*aññapadatthasamāsa*) even when the case endings differ, such as "hair on the chest" (*urasiloma*).

Alternatively, it is called "fivefold existence" because it is differentiated (*vokarīyati*) by the five aggregates according to conditions. The phrase beginning with "In terms of meaning" (*atthato*) refers to the eye and so forth.
This was stated with reference only to the functions such as seeing, and not because there is any other qualification; therefore, no detailed analysis was given therein.
512–4. "All" means all without specifying the distinctions such as those belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) and so forth.

"Kamma" refers to volition (cetanā) that produces rebirth-linking, whether it is to be experienced upon rebirth (upapajjavedanīya) or to be experienced in a subsequent life (aparāpariyavedanīya). "Kamma-sign" refers to the object-base (vatthu)...

Having made it its object, at the time of accumulation, one accumulates karma; that [object] consists of requisites for giving and so forth, as well as requisites for killing living beings and so forth.

"The sign of the destination" (*gatinimitta*) refers to the sphere of form (*vaṇṇāyatana*) included within the state of existence to which one is to be reborn in another life. Furthermore, for one being reborn in the human world in a happy destination, this appears according to the color of the mother’s womb resembling a red woolen blanket;
for one being reborn in the world of the gods, [it appears according to the color of their celestial raiment].

It should be understood by way of the appearance of a pleasure grove or a *kapparukkha* tree; by way of the appearance of flames of fire and so forth for one being reborn in a miserable destination (*duggati*);
and by way of the appearance of being included within the fixed places where hungry ghosts and animals constantly roam among the realms of hungry ghosts and animals.
This description as "threefold" is stated according to what is possible; however, for those connected with the form and formless realms, there is only the sign of the deed (*kamma-nimitta*).
It has an object. For it is said that sublime resultant [consciousnesses] have exclusively objects similar to the kamma.
"Present or past" means present or past by way of moment. Therein, the sign of the destination is exclusively present;
the sign of the kamma is either present or past, while the kamma itself is only past. Future-object [consciousness].

However, because it has not come within the range of perception—like the sign of a present action or the sign of a destination—and because it has not been experienced—like the sign of a past action—it does not appear clearly;

thus, rebirth-linking, occurring as an extreme state of non-existence, is unable to arise by taking that [future object] as its object. Therefore, it is said: "There is no future. This applies to sublime (mahaggata) rebirth-linkings.
Because their objects are exclusively similar to the object of the kamma itself, and because— just like the kamma—

their objects are either past or "inexpressible" (anavyākata), no separate object is specified for them. In this regard, it should be understood that for the second and fourth immaterial rebirth-linkings, the object is exclusively past, whereas for the others, it is inexpressible.

517–20. Because great resultants (mahāvipāka) function only by way of the four functions beginning with rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), they proceed in the fine-material and immaterial realms solely as that specific resultant—namely, as rebirth-linking, life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and death—and because there is no object-receiving (tadārammaṇa) consciousness there, it is said:
"In the two [realms], the great resultants... Even though undesirable forms are impossible in the Brahma-world, having stood there, one [perceives them] here...

It cannot be said that unwholesome-resultant [consciousnesses] do not arise for those seeing an undesirable object; therefore, the three types of investigation (santīraṇa) are stated to exist even in the fine-material realm (rūpabhava).
For in the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*, the *Saccasaṅkhepa*, and other works, the occurrence of unwholesome-resultants in the world of form is shown with this very intention.
However, others [hold that] "the three types of investigation exist in the sense-sphere realm (kāmabhava), and in the fine-material realm..."
They say that the "two types of investigation" should be applied according to what is available.

"Even at times" means even when limited (paritta) javanas arise with limited objects. Having stated the reason for the absence of registration (tadārammaṇa) in both the material and immaterial realms by saying "due to the absence of seed," the phrase beginning with "the seed of rebirth-linking" was spoken in order to clarify that very point.
"Rebirth-linking itself is the seed," thus it is the "rebirth-linking seed. "Of that" means of that object [of the registration consciousness]. (521) Objection:
"If this is so, since eye-consciousness and the rest are also seeds for rebirth-linking in the sense-sphere realm, their absence there would follow";
raising this objection, he says "of eye-consciousness and the rest," etc. "Of the faculties" refers to the bases and doors of eye-consciousness and the rest.
Of the faculties such as the eye, etc. "By the power of their occurrence" means by the power of their presence there.
This is the intended meaning here: the eye and ear faculties, which serve as the bases for eye-consciousness and ear-consciousness, occur there;
thus, by the power of their occurrence, eye-consciousness and ear-consciousness occur. And when their occurrence exists...

Since the arising of a cognitive process (*vīthicitta*) is fixed, it is established that the functions of receiving (*sampaṭicchana*) and investigating (*santīraṇa*) can occur there, just as they do for eye-consciousness and the rest.
523–4. "Supramundane states" (*akāmāvacara-dhamma*) refers to sublime (*mahaggata*) and supramundane (*lokuttara*) states other than those of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
"Does not follow" (*nānubandhati*) means it does not continue. Regarding "the productive [consciousness]... follows": it is like one who, having gone out from a house, desires to go outside.
Just as a young child follows his own biological father or another relative who is like a father and desires his welfare by grasping his finger,
and not another such as a king’s officer, so too this [consciousness], because of its natural inclination to emerge from the object of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga),
[seizes] only its own producer— the first wholesome consciousness— or one similar to it, such as the second wholesome sense-sphere javana.
It follows after, and not another sublime or supramundane [state]; this is the meaning here. By the inclusion of the word "etc.
in the phrase "wholesome and unwholesome, etc.," the functional-inefficient (kiriyābyākata) is comprised. However, Master Ānanda, in the *Paṭṭhāna*, states:

"When the wholesome and unwholesome have ceased, the resultant arises as an object-condition"; thus, he maintains that the object-condition occurs only immediately after those phenomena that possess the nature of resultancy.
It has been said. For impulsion, being expansive, follows upon the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) like a river current following a boat;

however, because the functional impulsion (kiriyājavana) of one possessing the sixfold equanimity has a peaceful mode of occurrence, it does not follow [the life-continuum] like a leaf-boat following a river current—thus, he does not admit a registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa) immediately after the functional impulsion.
But the teachers beginning with the Elder Jotipāla maintain that even though it is possible for it to arise through some intention...

In some instances, non-mention is observed; for example, in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*’s exposition of the unwholesome (*akusala*), although the dominant factor (*adhipati*) is actually present, it is not mentioned.

Therefore, if the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) were to be mentioned immediately after the indeterminate (*abyākata*) javanas, one might think that it also occurs immediately after functional javanas (*kriyājavana*).
For this reason, the registration consciousness is not mentioned after functional javanas, but not because it is impossible [for it to occur].
And as for the leaf-boat shown here, it is not identical to that which is to be illustrated; for the turning and movement of ships and leaf-boats in a river current are dissimilar.

Thus, while it is logical that a ship follows the river current whereas a leaf-boat does not, here, however, it is the turning of both functional (*kiriya*) and impulsion (*javana*) consciousnesses toward the stream of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) that is intended.

They say: "It is not logical that there should be a lack of continuity for the former [the path]—on the grounds that its destiny is similar—and yet there should be continuity for the latter; therefore, this must indeed be investigated.
And just as this does not apply to sublime (mahaggata) and supramundane (lokuttara) states, so too when these sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) states...

When they proceed having the sublime (mahaggata) and unsurpassed (anuttara) states as their object, even those [sublime and supramundane states] do not follow after them; thus he said, "even mundane states of the sense sphere" (kāmāvacaradhammāpi), and so forth.

By the inclusion of the term "sublime," the supramundane (lokuttara) states should also be understood as being included here. With the word "and" (ca) in the phrase "those too" (te cāpi), the inclusion of those having supramundane objects is intended.
To the question "Why do they not follow? he replied, "Because of having a limited object" (parittārammaṇattā), and so forth. "Because of having a limited object" means:
This is because, according to the method explained below, the resultant consciousnesses of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara-vipāka) have exclusively limited objects (parittārammaṇa).
"Because it is not similarly familiarized" means that it is not familiarized in the same way as the impulsion (javana). This is what is meant:
just as a young child following his father or someone like his father [sees] only those things familiar to him, such as the door of the house, the interior of the street, or the crossroads.
It follows after that [object] which is within its range, but not one going to the forest or a realm of demons; likewise,
even when following after phenomena of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), it follows those phenomena only while they are occurring within a limited and familiar range,
and not when they are occurring in reference to sublime (mahaggata) or supramundane (lokuttara) phenomena.
527–32. Now, showing that this should be accepted on the authority of the *Aṭṭhakathā* rather than through logical argumentation, he says, "What is the use of that?
and so forth. Regarding "in the javana": this refers to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) javana.

The "registration consciousnesses"—those consciousnesses which have received the name "registration" (*tadārammaṇa*)—do not take up the state of registration; they do not proceed by way of being registration-consciousnesses.

This is the meaning. Alternatively, the meaning is that when the impulsion (javana) has impelled with reference to a name or a clan, the "registration" (tadārammaṇa) does not grasp—that is, it does not obtain—the object of that impulsion.
By the word "or" in the phrase "or in the realms of form and formlessness," it implies that "even when the impulsion has impelled, registration does not grasp [the object].
"With reference to a designation" (paṇṇattiṃ ārabbha) refers even to the realm of sense-desire (kāmabhava).
"Taking as its object" (*ārabbha*). "Having the three characteristics as its object" (*lakkhaṇārammaṇāya*) means having the triad of characteristics—impermanence and so forth—as its object;

the sense is "having powerful insight (*balavavipassanā*) as its object. Because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that "the three characteristics and the three designations (*paññatti*) are not found in the *Kusalattika*," due to the non-existence of the three characteristics as actual phenomena (*dhamma*), the objects of the insight that proceeds by taking them as its object [cannot be those characteristics].

[They] are not obtained. However, in the *Paṭṭhāna*, because of the statement: "Whether they be trainees (*sekha*) or worldlings (*puthujjana*), if they practice insight into the wholesome as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, then when the wholesome and unwholesome have ceased, the result arises with that as its object," it should be understood that the state of having that as an object (*tadārammaṇa*) is obtained for insight whose object is the aggregates.
Regarding "those fixed in falsehood" (*micchattaniyata*): "Which phenomena are fixed in falsehood?"

Regarding the passage beginning with "four types of consciousness-arising associated with views," this refers to those phenomena that proceed by way of a wrong grasp, having flashed forth as impulsions (javana).
But why is registration (tadārammaṇa) not obtained when they have thus flashed forth?
For, unlike determinate wrong view among sense-sphere resultants, the conceptualization of a self—such as "the self is annihilated" and so forth—[does not lead to registration].

Because they do not occur, when those [impulsions] have occurred through the influence of fixed wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*), the registration consciousnesses (*tadārammaṇa*) do not arise immediately following them;
however, when they have occurred through the influence of unfixed wrong view, it is not the case that the registration consciousness does not arise.
Alternatively, "in those fixed in falsehood" (*micchattaniyatesu*) means "in those objects whose intrinsic nature is fixed in a state of falsity."

Because one does not grasp the intrinsic nature (*dhammasabhāva*) of states fixed in falsehood (*micchattaniyata*), but rather grasps only the nature of being fixed in falsehood itself, and because its results (*vipāka*) are not manifest, object-conditions (*tadārammaṇa*) are not obtained with reference to that nature fixed in falsehood.
By the word "also" (*pi*), it includes those fixed in rightness (*sammattaniyata*); or else, by the phrase "with reference to supramundane states," it is implied.

Because they are already established [as included], they were not extracted separately. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, immediately after those fixed in falsehood (*micchattaniyata*), those fixed in rightness (*sammattaniyata*) are also extracted;
this is for the purpose of showing that, due to their mutual opposition and consequent strength, those fixed in rightness cannot serve as the objective basis (*ārammaṇa*) for the former.
This is just as [the latter] cannot be the basis for one whose nature is fixed in falsehood.

Because even for the resultant consciousnesses of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara-vipāka), which possess the nature of the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), the registration (tadārammaṇa) is not obtained when the impulsion (javana) occurs with respect to those analytical knowledges due to their non-manifest state; therefore, he said, "the analytical knowledges," and so forth.
"In the mind-door as well" means not only in the five doors, but also in the mind-door. "Of all" refers to those that are rootless (ahetuka), doubly-rooted (duhetuka), and so on.
Of all [these]. "In successive order" means according to the sequence stated below. 533.

"Is not found" means it is not found because the mind-door is non-resistant (*appaṭigha*). "From the life-continuum" means from the stream of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga-santāna*), or from its object. "Emergence" means the emergence of that [consciousness] when there is the life-continuum stream or its object.
535–6. "Seven for seven" means calculating seven for each one. "Fruitions of evil" means unwholesome fruitions (*akusala-vipāka*). "Of the twelve unmeritorious consciousnesses."

Having stated [the term], the expression "the ripening of evil" (*pāpapāka*) is used here according to the principle of a conventional designation (*saññā-sadda*), as in such passages as "this is the measure of the Sugata’s robe for the Sugata.

Having thus shown the occurrence of unwholesome results during the course of existence (*pavatti*), he now states "of eleven kinds," etc., in order to show their occurrence at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
This refers merely to the giving of a result during the course of existence by means of the volition of restlessness (*uddhacca-cetanā*).
He says, "having abandoned the mind of restlessness," because there is an absence of giving rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) [by such a mind]. What, then, is the reason here:

why does the doubt-accompanied [consciousness], though extremely weak due to its lack of resolve (*adhimokkha*), draw forth rebirth-linking, while the restlessness-accompanied [consciousness], though stronger than that due to its nature of resolve, does not draw it forth? It is because of the presence or absence of the nature of giving rebirth-linking. [The text continues: "Strong..."
For this investigation—"It draws [the rebirth-linking], but it does not draw when weak"—applies only to those states whose intrinsic nature is to give rebirth-linking.
However, for that which lacks the very nature of giving rebirth-linking, its state of strength is not a cause for drawing rebirth-linking.
But how is it to be known that "the state of giving rebirth-linking is absent in that which is accompanied by restlessness"?
Because they do not exist in the future among those states to be abandoned by vision (*dassanena pahātabba*). For unwholesome states are threefold:

those to be abandoned by vision, those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāya pahātabba*), and those that may be either abandoned by vision or abandoned by cultivation. Among these, the arising of consciousness associated with wrong view (*diṭṭhi*) and accompanied by doubt (*vicikicchā*) is called "to be abandoned by vision.
As it is said: "Which states are to be abandoned by vision? The four types of consciousness associated with the course of views (*diṭṭhigata*)."

“A state of consciousness accompanied by doubt. For these are called "to be abandoned by vision" because they are to be abandoned by the path of stream-entry itself, which receives the name "vision" from its first seeing of Nibbāna.

A state of consciousness accompanied by restlessness is said to be "to be abandoned by cultivation. As it is said: "Which states are to be abandoned by cultivation? That which is accompanied by restlessness..."
“a state of consciousness. For it is said to be “abandoned by development” because it is to be abandoned by the highest path.
Indeed, in the case of the three higher paths, [the knowledge] arises by way of development regarding that very object already seen by the first path; it does not see anything previously unseen.
Therefore, it is called “development. However, states of consciousness associated with grief but dissociated from views may be...
There may be states that are to be abandoned by vision and those called to be abandoned by cultivation. As it is said:

"The four types of consciousness-arising dissociated from views and accompanied by greed, and the two types of consciousness-arising accompanied by displeasure—these states may be abandoned by vision or may be abandoned by cultivation.
For these [first six], in their state of producing rebirth in the lower realms, they are abandoned by the first path; in their remaining states, [they are abandoned by the subsequent paths].
Because they are abandoned by the higher paths, they may be called "abandonable by vision" (*dassanena-pahātabba*) or "abandonable by cultivation" (*bhāvanāya-pahātabba*).
In this context, even that which is abandonable by vision is conventionally designated simply as "abandonable by vision" due to its commonality with what is abandonable by vision.
And if restlessness-accompanied [consciousness] were to provide rebirth-linking, then there would be unwholesome rebirth-linking.
Because [such a state] is impossible in a happy destination (*sugati*), one would have to grant that it exists only in the states of misery (*apāya*);

and if it were exclusively to be abandoned by vision, then, because the defilements leading to the states of misery would not yet have been abandoned, it would follow that those in training (*sekkhā*) could still be reborn in the states of misery.
But this is not tenable, as it contradicts such statements as: "He is liberated from the four states of misery and is no longer subject to falling into the lower realms."

Furthermore, if this [restlessness] were to be abandoned by vision, then it would have been stated in the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of the phrase "to be abandoned by vision" as "those to be abandoned by vision"; yet it was not so stated. Now, if it is argued that because "lust, hatred, delusion, and the defilements associated with them which lead to states of deprivation" are mentioned among those to be abandoned by vision, restlessness accompanied by agitation is also included therein; [we reply: no. Why? Because it is said: "Lust, hatred, delusion, and the defilements associated with them which lead to states of deprivation. Here, "associated with them" refers to those associated with lust, hatred, and delusion. But restlessness is not associated with lust, hatred, or delusion. Therefore, it is not included there. Consequently, since it is not included in the category of "to be abandoned by vision," it is established that restlessness is not to be abandoned by vision. Thus, the meaning of the sutta is fully explained. This concludes the commentary on the section concerning the defilements to be abandoned by vision. Now follows the commentary on the section concerning the defilements to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Regarding this, the following should be understood: first, the defilements to be abandoned by cultivation are indicated; second, the method for abandoning them is shown; third, the distinction between the two types of abandonment is demonstrated. First, the indication of the defilements to be abandoned by cultivation: "The underlying tendency to lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to ignorance, and the underlying tendency to the desire for existence—these, O bhikkhus, are the seven underlying tendencies. Among these, the underlying tendency to lust is the latent proclivity of lust toward objects of sensual pleasure. The underlying tendency to aversion is the latent proclivity of hatred toward disagreeable objects. The underlying tendency to views is the latent proclivity of the sixty-two views. The underlying tendency to doubt is the latent proclivity of doubt regarding the Four Noble Truths. The underlying tendency to conceit is the latent proclivity of the seven types of conceit. The underlying tendency to ignorance is the latent proclivity of ignorance regarding the Four Noble Truths. The underlying tendency to the desire for existence is the latent proclivity of craving for fine-material and immaterial existence. These seven underlying tendencies are the defilements to be abandoned by cultivation. Second, the method for abandoning them is shown: "And how, bhikkhus, is the underlying tendency to lust abandoned? By repeatedly practicing, cultivating, and frequently exercising the meditation on foulness, the underlying tendency to lust is abandoned... by repeatedly practicing, cultivating, and frequently exercising the perception of light, the underlying tendency to aversion is abandoned... by repeatedly practicing, cultivating, and frequently exercising the perception of impermanence, the underlying tendency to views is abandoned... by repeatedly practicing, cultivating, and frequently exercising the perception of suffering, the underlying tendency to doubt is abandoned... by repeatedly practicing, cultivating, and frequently exercising the perception of non-self, the underlying tendency to conceit is abandoned... by repeatedly practicing, cultivating, and frequently exercising the perception of peace, the underlying tendency to ignorance is abandoned... by repeatedly practicing, cultivating, and frequently exercising the perception of the repulsiveness of food, the underlying tendency to the desire for existence is abandoned. Third, the distinction between the two types of abandonment is demonstrated: "And what, bhikkhus, is the abandonment of the underlying tendency to lust? It is the destruction of lust, the abandoning of lust, the fading away of lust, the cessation of lust, the relinquishment of lust, the extinction of lust, the detachment from lust, the cessation of lust, and the path leading to the cessation of lust. This, bhikkhus, is called the abandonment of the underlying tendency to lust. And what, bhikkhus, is the abandonment of the underlying tendency to aversion? It is the destruction of hatred... [and so on for the others]... up to... the path leading to the cessation of the underlying tendency to the desire for existence. This, bhikkhus, is called the abandonment of the underlying tendency to the desire for existence. This is the distinction between the two types of abandonment. This concludes the commentary on the section concerning the defilements to be abandoned by cultivation. Now follows the commentary on the section concerning the defilements to be abandoned by higher knowledge (*ñāṇadassana*). Regarding this, the following should be understood: first, the defilements to be abandoned by higher knowledge are indicated; second, the method for abandoning them is shown; third, the distinction between the two types of abandonment is demonstrated. First, the indication of the defilements to be abandoned by higher knowledge: "The underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to ignorance, and the underlying tendency to the desire for existence—these, O bhikkhus, are the three underlying tendencies to be abandoned by higher knowledge. Among these, the underlying tendency to conceit is the latent proclivity of the seven types of conceit. The underlying tendency to ignorance is the latent proclivity of ignorance regarding the Four Noble Truths. The underlying tendency to the desire for existence is the latent proclivity of craving for fine-material and immaterial existence. These three underlying tendencies are the defilements to be abandoned by higher knowledge. Second, the method for abandoning them is shown: "And how, bhikkhus, is the underlying tendency to conceit abandoned? By repeatedly practicing, cultivating, and frequently exercising the noble wisdom of insight into phenomena, the underlying tendency to conceit is abandoned... by repeatedly practicing, cultivating, and frequently exercising the noble wisdom of insight into phenomena, the underlying tendency to ignorance is abandoned... by repeatedly practicing, cultivating, and frequently exercising the noble wisdom of insight into phenomena, the underlying tendency to the desire for existence is abandoned. Third, the distinction between the two types of abandonment is demonstrated: "And what, bhikkhus, is the abandonment of the underlying tendency to conceit? It is the destruction of conceit... [and so on]... up to... the path leading to the cessation of the underlying tendency to the desire for existence. This, bhikkhus, is called the abandonment of the underlying tendency to the desire for existence. This is the distinction between the two types of abandonment. This concludes the commentary on the section concerning the defilements to be abandoned by higher knowledge. Now follows the commentary on the section concerning the defilements to be abandoned by both vision and cultivation. Regarding this, the following should be understood: first, the defilements to be abandoned by both vision and cultivation are indicated; second, the method for abandoning them is shown; third, the distinction between the two types of abandonment is demonstrated. First, the indication of the defilements to be abandoned by both vision and cultivation: "The underlying tendency to lust for form, the underlying tendency to aversion toward form, the underlying tendency to views regarding form, the underlying tendency to doubt regarding form, the underlying tendency to conceit regarding form, the underlying tendency to ignorance regarding form, and the underlying tendency to the desire for existence regarding form—these, O bhikkhus, are the seven underlying tendencies regarding form to be abandoned by both vision and cultivation. Among these, the underlying tendency to lust for form is the latent proclivity of lust toward form. The underlying tendency to aversion toward form is the latent proclivity of hatred toward form. The underlying tendency to views regarding form is the latent proclivity of the sixty-two views regarding form. The underlying tendency to doubt regarding form is the latent proclivity of doubt regarding form. The underlying tendency to conceit regarding form is the latent proclivity of the seven types of conceit regarding form. The underlying tendency to ignorance regarding form is the latent proclivity of ignorance regarding form. The underlying tendency to the desire for existence regarding form is the latent proclivity of craving for fine-material and immaterial existence regarding form. These seven underlying tendencies regarding form are the defilements to be abandoned by both vision and cultivation. Second, the method for abandoning them is shown: "And how, bhikkhus, is the underlying tendency to lust for form abandoned? By repeatedly practicing, cultivating, and frequently exercising the meditation on foulness, the underlying tendency to lust for form is abandoned... by repeatedly practicing, cultivating, and frequently exercising the perception of light, the underlying tendency to aversion toward form is abandoned... by repeatedly practicing, cultivating, and frequently exercising the perception of impermanence, the underlying tendency to views regarding form is abandoned... by repeatedly practicing, cultivating, and frequently exercising the perception of suffering, the underlying tendency to doubt regarding form is abandoned... by repeatedly practicing, cultivating, and frequently exercising the perception of non-self, the underlying tendency to conceit regarding form is abandoned... by repeatedly practicing, cultivating, and frequently exercising the perception of peace, the underlying tendency to ignorance regarding form is abandoned... by repeatedly practicing, cultivating, and frequently exercising the perception of the repulsiveness of food, the underlying tendency to the desire for existence regarding form is abandoned. Third, the distinction between the two types of abandonment is demonstrated: "And what, bhikkhus, is the abandonment of the underlying tendency to lust for form? It is the destruction of lust for form... [and so on]... up to... the path leading to the cessation of the underlying tendency to the desire for existence regarding form. This, bhikkhus, is called the abandonment of the underlying tendency to the desire for existence regarding form. This is the distinction between the two types of abandonment. This concludes
"Is it possible to do so? No, because that [state] is described as being abandonable through cultivation (*bhāvanā*) by necessity.
Therefore, the very fact that it is not mentioned among those things to be abandoned by vision (*dassana*) establishes the absence of the giving of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
But is it not said in the *Paṭisambhidā-vibhaṅga*—?

“At whatever time an unwholesome state of consciousness has arisen accompanied by equanimity and associated with restlessness, having as its object a visible form… or… a mental phenomenon, or whatever else it may be directed toward—at that time there is contact… and there is non-distraction.
These states are unwholesome. Knowledge regarding these states is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā).”
“Knowledge regarding their ripening is the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā).

Thus, having extracted the arising of consciousness accompanied by restlessness, its ripening has also been extracted. How then can it be accepted that this [consciousness] lacks the giving of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi)?
This was not extracted with reference to the giving of rebirth-linking; rather, it refers to the ripening in the course of existence (pavatti-vipāka).
Having intended this. However, in the *Paṭṭhāna*:
“Conascent volition eradicated by vision is a condition, by way of kamma-condition, for mind-originated matter;
asynchronous volition eradicated by vision is a condition, by way of kamma-condition, for resultant aggregates and for kamma-produced matter.”
Having extracted only the state of being a conascent asynchronous kamma-condition for volition abandoned by seeing (*dassanena-pahātabba-cetanā*), the statement,

"Conascent volition abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāya-pahātabbā cetanā*) is a condition, by way of kamma-condition, for mind-originated matter," extracts only the state of being a conascent kamma-condition for volition abandoned by cultivation, but not its state of being an asynchronous kamma-condition.

Likewise, in the method of the opposite order as well—having extracted only the state of being a kamma-condition for that which is to be abandoned by seeing, [the text says]: “A state to be abandoned by seeing is a condition, by way of object-condition, for a state to be abandoned neither by seeing nor by development; likewise by way of conascence...
decisive support... pe... postnascence... and kamma-condition.”—[it continues:]...

“It is said: ‘A state to be abandoned by development (bhāvanāya-pahātabba) is a condition for a state not to be abandoned either by seeing or by development, by way of object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya), co-nascence... decisive-support... and post-nascence conditions. Thus, only the status of co-nascence and other such conditions is stated for a state to be abandoned by development, but not its status as a kamma-condition.
And there is no drawing forth of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) without a asynchronous kamma-condition; therefore, that [kamma-condition] does not exist [for it].”
In every respect, it is a rebirth-linking gift (*paṭisandhidāna*).

However, it is impossible to prevent its occurrence as a process-resultant (*pavattivipāka*), because in the *Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅga* the resultant of even those states accompanied by restlessness (*uddhacca*) is mentioned; furthermore, asynchronous kamma-condition (*nānakkhaṇika-kammapaccaya*) is mentioned there only with reference to rebirth-linking resultants.
And this being so, when certain teachers say: "The volition of restlessness yields both kinds of resultants... [they are correct].

If they were to say: "Just as in the case of the term 'states subject to result' (*vipākadhammadhamma*), where the word 'result' (*vipāka*) denotes the state of being liable to result, so too here, with reference to the liability to result in the case of those states accompanied by restlessness, it is said: 'knowledge of their result'," that should be regarded as merely their own dogmatic insistence (*abhinivesa-matta*). This is because the asynchronous kamma-condition (*nānakkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya*) has not been mentioned in the *Paṭṭhāna*. It should be understood that this is nothing more than their own subjective adherence.
It has been said: Just as, even though there is no state of resolving apart from the faculty of faith (saddhindriya),
the phenomenon of the faculty of faith is called "the state of resolving" by taking its specific capacity for resolving,
so too here, even though there is no state of being subject to fruition apart from the phenomena themselves, it is the very capacity of the phenomena to be subject to fruition [that is meant].
Having taken this up, its existence was stated. And if they were to grant that there is resultant [kamma] in the course of existence (pavatti), then just as it is said:

"A state associated with pleasant feeling is a condition, by way of kamma-condition, for a state associated with painful feeling, when occurring at different moments," and thus a kamma-condition at different moments is stated even with respect to the resultant in the course of existence, so too here the status of being a kamma-condition at different moments [would apply].
It might be said: "For there is no reason for not mentioning that which is obtainable. Therefore, even in the teaching according to the Dhamma, non-mention indicates non-existence itself.
Furthermore, if it were intended that restlessness-accompanied [states] give rise to a result in their active phase (*pavatti*), then [the text would have stated]:
"A state that is not acquired but subject to clinging is not a kamma-condition for a state that is acquired and subject to clinging."

The negation "it is not a condition" should not be made. For there is no other state that is neither-clung-to-nor-object-of-clinging (anupādinnupādāniya) which is incapable of being a condition for a state that is both-clung-to-and-object-of-clinging (upādinnupādāniya);
this [objection] is merely a verbal expression. For it has already been stated: "Having taken their status as being subject to fruition (vipākāraha), they are 'fruition' (vipāka)."

The statement "it is said" indicates the very existence of its result (vipāka). For when there is the state of being eligible for a result, there is no reason for it to be non-resultant (avipāka), as is the case with the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and so forth.

As for what was also said—"the non-mention of asynchronous kamma-condition (nānakkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya) indicates the state of being a result"—that too is not sound, because even that which is obtainable [as a condition] is not mentioned in some instances by anyone.

Because it was not stated [explicitly] due to the underlying intention (*adhippāya*). For instance, although the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*) is found in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, it was not mentioned there.

Therefore, if the status of being a asynchronous kamma-condition were stated with reference to the fruition occurring during the course of existence (*pavattivipāka*), then one might assume that it also gives rise to rebirth-linking fruition (*paṭisandhivipāka*);
thus, the status of being an asynchronous kamma-condition is established by way of the fruition occurring during the course of existence, even though it exists [in the case of rebirth].

"It was not said. However, as for that statement in the commentary which negates the kamma-conditionality of what is not-clung-to-but-favourable-to-clinging (anupādinnupādāniya) toward what is clung-to-and-favourable-to-clinging (upādinnupādāniya), that refers to superknowledge (*abhiññā*), wholesome states, and so forth;
therefore, on this basis alone, it is not possible to entirely negate the giving of result in the course of existence (*pavatti*) by restlessness-accompanied (*uddhacca-sahagata*) states.
Furthermore, as stated in the commentary: "And just as with the volition of superknowledge, so too with the volition of restlessness..."
It was stated, “In the formula ‘with volitional formations as condition, consciousness,’ this [volition] is to be excluded”; however,
that was said so that when restlessness-volition is demonstrated there, people might understand that just as other types of volition are a condition for both kinds of resultant consciousness—
namely, that of rebirth-linking and that of the course of existence— so too is restlessness-volition, and not because it lacks a resultant in the course of existence.
Ācariya Buddhamitta and others, however, divide the restlessness-accompanied [consciousness] into two types:
they describe one as giving both kinds of result and the other as being entirely devoid of result. Their analysis is as follows:

there is restlessness that is abandonable by cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and there is also that which is not abandonable by cultivation. Of these, that which is abandonable by cultivation occurs in the mental continuum of a trainee (*sekha*).

The other [unwholesome states] are those occurring in the mental continuum of worldlings (*puthujjana*). And the giving of fruit belongs only to that which occurs in the continuum of worldlings, not to the other.
For instance, even in the absence of the paths of seeing and cultivation (*dassana-bhāvanā*), there are certain worldlings and trainees (*sekha*) for whom such paths ought to arise;
at the time of their arising, the unwholesome states that can be abandoned by them are "to be abandoned by seeing" (*dassanena pahātabbā*).

They are called "to be abandoned by cultivation" (*bhāvanāyapahātabba*). However, because ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) lack the practice of cultivation, there is no consideration of what is to be abandoned by cultivation for them;
therefore, even though those [defilements] that are currently active cannot be abandoned by seeing (*dassana*), they are not called "to be abandoned by cultivation.
If they were so called, then some of those to be abandoned by seeing would become [identical to] some of those to be abandoned by cultivation.
Sometimes they may be conditions by way of the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), the predominance-condition (*adhipati-paccaya*), or the decisive-support-condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).

For there is no instance where, regarding one's own belongings, certain personality-beliefs (*sakkāya-diṭṭhi*) and so forth serve as conditions—by way of the object-predominance or decisive-support conditions—for some degree of desire-attachment (*chanda-rāga*) and the like directed toward the past and so forth at any time;
nor [is it stated] in the *Paṭṭhāna* that "those [states] to be abandoned by vision are conditions for those to be abandoned by cultivation..."

Since it is stated that "there is no condition for [them] by way of any condition," there is no method for abandoning unwholesome states occurring in worldlings (*puthujjana*) through cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

If the mere absence of such a statement were the authority here, then it would follow that there is likewise no method for abandoning unwholesome states occurring in the mental continuum of a trainee (*sekha*) through cultivation. But this does not follow; for those occurring in the mental continuum of a trainee—

Because they can be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā*). For that very reason, when the unwholesome states to be abandoned by vision have been abandoned by those in training (*sekha*) through some practice, they no longer serve as bases for gratification or delight.

Precisely because they have been abandoned, they do not give rise to mental joy (*somanassa*), which is their cause, nor to non-distraction, nor to mental grief (*domanassa*) or restlessness (*uddhacca*).
They do not become objects, object-conditions, predominance-conditions, or decisive support-conditions for those [defilements].
For noble ones do not, by relying on defilements already abandoned, give rise to lust, hatred, or agitation. And it is said:

"The defilements that have been abandoned by the stream-entry path—he does not repeat them, he does not return to them, he does not go back to them; thus he is 'Well-Gone' (Sugata). [Likewise] the once-returner... [and so forth]."

“...by the path of arahantship... [he is] the Sugata. However, regarding those things that can be abandoned by the vision of ordinary persons (*puthujjana*) and those that cannot be abandoned by vision, it cannot be said that they do not act as conditions for anything whatsoever. [For instance:
"One relishes and delights in a view; with that as the object, lust arises, a view arises, and doubt arises."
"Restlessness arises; taking doubt as its object, doubt arises; wrong view arises;
restlessness arises"—because it is stated here that wrong view and doubt have restlessness as their object.
For in this context, "restlessness" is said with reference to a mental state accompanied by restlessness, and not even to those [states] to be abandoned by vision.
[This refers to] restlessness (uddhacca) as a presently-arising mental factor. And having established this, in the exposition of the predominance condition (adhipatipaccaya), it is stated only thus:
“Valuing a view, one relishes it and delights in it; valuing that, lust arises, and a [wrong] view arises”;
it is not stated that “restlessness arises. Therefore, regarding the unwholesome states occurring in the continuum of a trainee (sekha):
Since those unwholesome states to be abandoned by vision do not possess the status of a condition for anything whatsoever within the mental continuum of worldlings,
it cannot be asserted that they are conditions for [other] states to be abandoned by vision; thus, the *Paṭṭhāna* does not extract [these states] as object,
object-predominance, or decisive-support conditions for states to be abandoned by cultivation occurring in the continuum of a trainee (*sekha*).
It establishes that those unwholesome states which are to be abandoned by seeing in the mental continuum of a worldling are, in fact, of a nature to be abandoned by cultivation;
it does not establish that those [unwholesome states] to be abandoned by seeing in the mental continuum of a worldling are of a nature to be abandoned by cultivation.

Therefore, although those states to be abandoned by seeing and cultivation cannot be defined as past and so forth, those among worldlings for whom such a state of non-arising (anuppattidhammatā) must be induced by those two [paths] are [the ones referred to].

Those that arise in the stream-enterer and are capable of being abandoned by vision are called "to be abandoned by vision" because of the expectation of the path of vision, even when they do not actually arise.

Those that arise in the trainees (sekha) and are capable of being abandoned by cultivation are called "to be abandoned by cultivation" because of the expectation of that [path], even when they do not actually arise.
However, those that arise in worldlings (puthujjana) and are incapable of being abandoned by vision—
According to the method explained below, [these states] are neither to be abandoned by vision nor to be abandoned by cultivation;
among them, those to be abandoned by cultivation do not produce a result because they lack their companions.

For thus, since they lack a companion that serves as a cooperative cause—namely, that which is reckoned as "to be abandoned by vision"—there is no asynchronous kamma-condition for the volition to be abandoned by cultivation.

It has been stated. However, for ordinary persons (puthujjana) who lack the vision and cultivation necessary to regard [objects] with detachment, it is impossible to deny that their own possessions give rise to resultants—because their desire, lust, and so forth toward those possessions, as well as the arising of consciousness accompanied by restlessness, remain unsevered;
thus, their companions (sahāya), namely the three fetters and the defilements associated with them, have not yet been exhausted. Therefore, regarding phenomena accompanied by restlessness...
"The result (vipāka) is stated in the Vibhaṅga.

If this is so, does it not follow that unwholesome states (akusala), which lack the quality of being abandoned by seeing or by cultivation because they have nothing further to be seen or cultivated, would have to be called "neither to be abandoned by seeing nor by cultivation"?

It does not follow; for wholesome states (kusala) and the rest, whose intrinsic nature (sabhāva) is not subject to abandonment, are [properly] described as "neither to be abandoned by seeing nor by cultivation."
Because they have been so stated, and because unwholesome states possess a nature opposed to what is not to be abandoned.

If this is so, does it follow that those [states] cannot be described within this triad? It does not follow, because the twelve types of unwholesome consciousness shown in the *Cittuppādakaṇḍa* are included under two terms.
For just as in the "Triad of Arisen" (*uppannatika*), all conditioned phenomena are included by way of their intrinsic nature (*dhamma-vasena*).
Because they are included by way of time, past states—even if not included by way of the [present] category—are not called "indeterminate" (*navattabba*);

for among those things included according to their arising as consciousness-moments (*cittuppāda*), there is no such thing as the indeterminate. Likewise, here too, because there is nothing indeterminate among those included by way of being consciousness-moments, they are not called "indeterminate.
For, in the case of the triads and dyads, there is absolutely nothing that is not included by way of the dhamma.

The offense of being "inexpressible" (*navattabbatāpatti*). For wherever there is any arising of consciousness that must necessarily be called "inexpressible," there exists for them a fourth category;

thus, as in the previously mentioned passages, even in that case, when the arising of consciousness is to be divided and classified, it is divided and classified by saying, "It may have an inexpressible and limited object," and so forth.
However, this is absent in the triad of arisen consciousnesses (*uppannatika*).
And here it is not stated in that way.

Alternatively, just as in the case of the fine-material element (rūpadhātu), because they share the same nature as those with resistance (sappaṭigha), it is said that "three great elements are with resistance," as it is said:
"For non-percipient beings, there is one great element that is non-demonstrable and with resistance"; so too for worldlings (puthujjana).

Since those states that exist while being active and possess a nature similar to those to be abandoned by cultivation may be called "to be abandoned by cultivation," there is no possibility of the undesirable consequence [of over-extension].

And this being so, even for worldlings, the desire-and-lust for one's own belongings and so forth—which exist while being active and are to be abandoned by cultivation—serve as the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for desire-and-lust for the belongings of others; and lust is likewise [a condition] for lust and views.
The meaning obtained here is that of the *adhipati-paccaya* (dominant condition).

For it is precisely for this reason that, in the exposition of the following passage—“A state to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāya pahātabbo dhammo*) is a condition, by way of decisive support (*upanissaya-paccaya*), for a state to be abandoned by seeing (*dassanena pahātabbassa dhammassa*); [namely,] as object-decisive-support (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*) and natural-decisive-support (*pakatūpanissaya*)”—the Blessed One, while explaining the states that function as the decisive-support condition for those states to be abandoned by seeing, stated: [the above].
“Natural strong-dependence (pakatūpanissaya): depending on a wish (patthana), one kills a living being... [and so on] ...one causes a schism in the Saṅgha.

Lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, and wish to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā) are related to lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, view, and wish to be abandoned by vision (dassana) by way of the condition of strong-dependence. Desire-lust for one’s own belongings and desire-lust for another’s belongings...”
“Desire-and-lust for one’s own possessions is a condition for desire-and-lust for the possessions of others by way of decisive support-condition”—
thus aspiration and the rest are demonstrated in the mental continuum of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).
In this way also, because there is no tangible object, the three great primary elements (*mahābhūta*) in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are not ultimately resistant (*sappaṭigha*).
Thus, while desire, lust, and so forth toward one's own belongings— which occur among worldlings (puthujjana) and are devoid of the meditation that should be looked upon—
are to be abandoned by meditation in the ultimate sense, the state of being a kamma-condition at different moments for those things to be abandoned by meditation has not been stated;
nor has it been said that "those things to be abandoned by vision are a condition, by any kind of condition, for those things to be abandoned by meditation."
It has been said: for those defilements that have conditions to be abandoned by seeing do not continue to arise after seeing has occurred.
However, in the case of restlessness-accompanied [defilement], which also has conditions to be abandoned by seeing, seeing has merely provided it with a deficiency of its companions;
no state of that [restlessness] has been rendered subject to non-arising by seeing. Therefore, it is to be abandoned exclusively by cultivation.

Therefore, since it is stated that [restlessness] has a single intrinsic nature by virtue of its association with agitation, the statement that it produces a result when accompanied by its associate—mindfulness—and the statement that it does not produce a result when it is absent, are not contradictory.
However, all of this is merely the "great-man-ism" (ahopurisikāra) of these teachers. Why?
Because it is stated that [restlessness] is to be abandoned exclusively through cultivation (*bhāvanā*). For it has been said thus:
The Blessed One said: “Which states are to be abandoned by development? A consciousness-arising accompanied by restlessness.

Now, if that which is accompanied by restlessness were not to be abandoned by development, then just as it was stated categorically in the *Atītārammaṇattika* that “there are none necessarily with a future object,” and then explained analytically, so too here it would have been stated categorically: “Those [consciousnesses] necessarily to be abandoned by development...”
Having stated "it does not exist," one would have to say: "It may be accompanied by restlessness; it may be abandonable by cultivation;
it should not be said that 'it is abandonable by vision' or 'it is abandonable by cultivation,'" and so forth. Yet, it has not been stated in that way.

Furthermore, the logical argument (yutti) stated as, "If those who are explaining that meaning were to say... and so on, is also illogical. Why? Because [it concerns] objects that are abandonable by vision.
Because lust, views, doubt, and restlessness are intended [to be included] by virtue of their respective states of being abandoned;

and as for the non-inclusion of restlessness in the exposition of the predominance condition— stated on the grounds that the arising of restlessness refers to a consciousness-arising accompanied by restlessness—
that too is not a valid reason, since there are other instances where the text is similarly incomplete.

Because it is seen as such. For instance, in the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of the statement, "A past state is a condition for a present state; a future state is a condition for a present state by way of object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*)," the knowledge of penetration of minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) is included;
yet, even though the knowledge of penetration of minds is found in the analysis of the statement, "A present state is a condition for a present state," [it is not included there].

It has not been accepted. Furthermore, as for the statement that [a defilement] abandonable by cultivation serves as an auxiliary cause for the giving of a result by one abandonable by vision, that too must be examined:

Does ignorance and so forth act as a cooperative cause for those abandonable by cultivation in the sense of being the basis for the capacity to give a result during the very moment of rebirth, just as it does for generosity, virtue, and so on; or rather...
Is it like a defilement (kilesa) in the giving of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) by karma? What is the point here?

If, first of all, the former method is taken, it follows that there would be a state of non-action for that which is to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanāya-pahātabba) within the continuum of a trainee (sekha);

for, in a continuum where the underlying tendencies (anusaya) of ignorance, conceit, and craving have been abandoned, it has attained a nature of non-resultation due to the deficiency of its companions, just like giving and so forth. If, on the other hand, the second [method] is taken, because of its being abandonable by cultivation...
It would follow that even what is desired [by some] must be abandoned through vision, because when rebirth-linking is given, there is no escaping the nature of leading to the states of misery;

therefore, the giving of result by restlessness-accompanied [kamma] must be accepted by us according to the method stated below, and not according to the words of anyone else. Those who follow the *Paṭṭhāna* should act accordingly.
537–8. "The two advertences go [to that]" means: because they merely perform the function [of adverting] and lack the giving of a fruit.

"Like a windflower" means like a vain flower; just as a flower produced on a tree that has first grown—even if its roots are not cut—does not produce fruit because it was not given fruit by previous [conditions], so too this [advertence] does not produce fruit even though the root of existence (bhava-mūla) is not yet severed.
The intention is that what has arisen in the continuum does not yield fruit by way of non-repetition (*anāsevanabhāva*).
"The state of impulsion (*javanatta*) is attained" refers to the eighteenfold consciousness unique to those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*). "By way of accomplishing its function" means:

while the root of craving for existence remains unsevered, it accomplishes the function of wholesome and unwholesome karma; or, by way of accomplishing the respective functions such as giving and so forth.
This is what is meant: just as a tree whose roots have been cut is fruitless, with the exception of the mere blossoming of its flowers, so too this [continuum],

because it proceeds within a mental continuity whose root— craving for existence (bhavataṇhā)— has been utterly severed, is indeed fruitless, with the exception of the mere accomplishment of its respective functions.
539–40. *Paṭicca* means having gone toward the causal phenomenon (*hetudhamma*), not setting it aside.
*Eti* means it proceeds; what is meant is that it persists, stands, or arises. For this term *eti* indicates proceeding in a sense common to both arising and persisting.
Thus he said: "Whether for persisting or for arising. For one particular condition [serves] for persisting...
Thus one is a benefactor, just as the posterior-arising condition (pacchājāta-paccaya) is; some [are benefactors] for arising alone, such as the immediate (anantara) and so forth;

some are benefactors for both, such as the root-cause (hetu) and others. Having thus shown the etymological meaning of the word "condition" (paccaya), he now says, beginning with "whatever phenomenon," in order to show the characteristic of a condition.
"Whatever" refers to the causal phenomenon (hetu-dhamma). "Of whatever" refers to the resultant phenomenon (phala-dhamma).

“Also for the sake of stability and arising” means for the purpose of stability or for the purpose of arising. Alternatively, “for stability” refers to the moment of stability (*ṭhitikkhaṇe*), and “for arising” refers to the moment of origination (*uppādakkhaṇe*).
There is a connection between the phenomenon that provides assistance and the phenomenon’s stability or arising.
By the word “assistance” (*upakāro*), he shows that which assists the functional capacity of the phenomenon. “Origination,” etc., [refers] to the condition itself.
This is the demonstration by way of synonyms. It is called *sambhava* (origin) because from it things come into being; likewise for *pabhava* (source).

It is called *hetu* (cause) because therein things grow (*hinoti*) and are established (*patiṭṭhāti*). Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the word *hi* should be understood here as having the sense of "establishing," just like the word "root" (*mūla*).
Alternatively, by means of this—acting as the basis for the action and bringing nourishment upward like a root does for a tree—the tree grows dependent upon that condition.
It is called a *hetu* (cause) because it goes toward its fruit and attains growth and increase. It is called a *kāraṇa* (reason) because it produces its own fruit.

It is called a *paccaya* (condition) because it is considered (*mato*) as such; thus, from the perspective of its origin, it is considered a "source" (*sambhava*) and so forth. What is meant is that these are identical in meaning;
their difference is merely in their verbal expression.

541–5. Having thus explained the meaning of all the conditions as they appear in the *Paṭṭhāna* by way of their common characteristics, the passage beginning with “But whatever state, such as greed,” etc., is stated here in order to show the specific nature of the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*) alone.

“In the sense of being a root” means in the sense of being a root defined as the accomplishment of the well-established state of the associated states. “Only six” refers to the state of being beneficial in the sense of being a root.
These six alone exist by virtue of their unique (āveṇika) nature. "By way of genus" means by way of the genus of the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
"Ninefold" means ninefold as the three wholesome roots, the three unwholesome roots, and the three indeterminate roots. Regarding the phrase "the establisher of phenomena...":
just as seeds such as rice and paddy are the establishers of the state of being rice and paddy, and blue and other colors are the establishers of the bases for the luster of gems and so forth.

Just as the light of sapphires and other gems establishes their own specific colors, so too the root-cause (hetu-paccaya), according to its respective nature, establishes the wholesome and other qualities of the states associated with it.

Thus, the meaning here is that the root-cause is that which establishes the state of being wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate for wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena, respectively.
"Some teachers" refers to the teacher Revata and his disciples and grand-disciples; thus he spoke with reference to them. Now...
Since the plural number is also appropriate when referring to many teachers, the phrase "some teachers" was stated specifically with reference to the teacher Revata.

"If this is so" means: if the state of being a root-cause (mūlaṭṭha) establishes the status of being wholesome and so forth, then it being thus, he said "in the material phenomena originating from that," meaning in the material phenomena originated by the cause (hetusamuṭṭhāna-rūpa), just as the mind is a condition for the material phenomena born of mind, so too are the states associated with it.

The meaning is as follows: "It does not succeed" means it is not established; what is meant is that the state of being a root-condition (hetupaccaya), as stated in the rule, "Roots are a condition, by way of root-condition, for states associated with roots and for the material phenomena originated by them," does not succeed.

Just as wholesome and unwholesome roots are insufficient to bring about the wholesome or other such qualities in the material phenomena originated by them, so too is the indeterminate (abyākata) root.

The reason is that it is not sufficient for the state of being indeterminate (abyākata) of the matter originated by those [roots]; for it is by its own intrinsic nature (sabhāva) that it is indeterminate—thus he said, “For it is not,” and so forth.
One might say, “If they do not establish the state of being wholesome and so on, then they would not even be conditions”;
therefore he said, “Not for them,” and so forth: “Roots [are conditions] for the states associated with roots and for the matter originated by them.”
Because of the statement, “it is a condition by way of root-condition,” the meaning is that those [factors] such as non-greed are indeed conditions for those material phenomena;
they do not fail to be so. 546–7. “Not to be gone to” means not to be understood. This is what is meant:

if wholesome and other roots were to establish the wholesomeness and so forth of the states rooted in themselves, just as they establish their own state, then [states] produced from wholesome or unwholesome root-conditions [would be problematic].
Material phenomena (*rūpadhammā*) might likewise be wholesome and so forth, or they might not be conditions for material phenomena as causes; yet neither of these two cases exists.
Therefore, it should not be understood that the "root-status" (*mūlaṭṭha*) is what establishes the wholesomeness and other qualities of wholesome states and the like.
Furthermore, if the state of being wholesome and so forth were dependent upon a cause, then the state of being indeterminate (*abyākata*) would also have to be dependent upon that same cause.

The indeterminate nature of rootless states would not be established. And if the state of being wholesome and so forth were dependent upon roots, then the state of being wholesome and so forth for those roots themselves would have to be independent.
If, on the other hand, even for those [roots] it were dependent on further roots, then in this way the unwholesome nature of a root associated with a deluded mind would not be established.
If that [unwholesomeness] of it were caused by another root, then the same would apply to the remaining roots as well.
It would have that [root] as its cause alone. And just as it is for the remaining roots, so too for the remaining associated states, it would have that [root] as its cause alone.

Now, if it were the case that the state of being wholesome and so forth belongs to the roots by their very nature, whereas for the associated states it is dependent upon the roots, then non-greed (alobha) might be either wholesome or indeterminate. For if it were wholesome by its own nature, then because of having that same nature—

It would not be indeterminate. If it were indeterminate, then because of having that same nature, it would not be wholesome, just as there is an absence of non-hatred in that which has the nature of non-greed.

Since, however, it exists in both ways, therefore—just as in the case of the associated factors such as faith and so on, which exist in both ways, you should seek their state of being wholesome and so forth as dependent upon causes rather than by way of intrinsic nature—so too should the wholesomeness and other qualities of the roots be understood.

It is to be sought as dependent on other factors, not by way of its own intrinsic nature. Furthermore, when that [nature] is being sought, it is dependent on such things as wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*);

thus, just as with the causes themselves, the state of being wholesome and so forth in the phenomena associated with the causes is dependent on wise attention and the like, not dependent on the causes alone.
For this very reason, he said:
“Monks, for one who attends appropriately (*yoniso*), unarisen wholesome states arise, and arisen wholesome states increase,” and so forth.
“By one who knows the proper occasion (*samayaññū*)” means by one who understands the Abhidhamma method.

“By accomplishing the state of being well-established” means by accomplishing the state of being properly established and firm in those phenomena that have oneself as their cause; for [phenomena] obtain causes and conditions...
States with roots are firm and well-established, like trees whose roots have grown deep; those without roots are not well-established, like moss from sesame seeds and the like.
"In all" means in every respect, including the sense-sphere realm and so forth.

550–1. Because mind-produced matter does not exist at the moment of rebirth-linking, [matter] exists as a condition only for those [mental states] associated with itself and for the matter produced by kamma (*kaṭattārūpa*).

Thus it is said: “for those... born together with itself. Furthermore, because they arise solely from the performance and accumulation of kamma, and not from causes such as a creator god (*issara*), these are called *kaṭattārūpa*, meaning matter produced by kamma.
"Meaning": *kaṭattārūpajātāni* means those material phenomena born of what has been done (*kaṭattā*) that have arisen and come into being.

"In the same way" means just as [the material phenomena] of what has been done arise in the case of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), so too [in this case]. By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and of those born of consciousness" (*cittajānañca*), the phrase "associated with itself" (*attanā sampayuttānaṃ*) is drawn in.

(553) Since supramundane resultant states do not occur by way of rebirth-linking, there is no state of being a condition for [material phenomena] originated by kamma; therefore, he says "of those born of consciousness," and so forth.
555. *Hetupaccayasambhavo*: a phenomenon produced by the condition of cause (*hetupaccaya*), or the mode of arising of phenomena that have arisen from the condition of cause.
*Sañjātasukhahetunā* means "by one who has produced knowledge" (*sañjātañāṇena*); the meaning is "by one possessing clear comprehension" (*sampajañña*).

For knowledge is called "having happiness as its cause" because of such statements as, "The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated; being concentrated, one understands things as they truly are. Thus, it is [called] *sañjātasukhahetu*.
“The benefit that exists in this very life,
and the benefit pertaining to the future—
through the realization of these benefits, the wise one,”
“He is called a wise man”—because of this initial statement, it is said that [he acts] for the sake of happiness, or as “the cause of happiness. 556.
One who is the lord of the world is a “world-lord” (*lokādhipati*); the meaning is: by the leader of the entire world. He is the master of those who are dependent on themselves.

As for "the dominant factor": by making desire the foremost, this means that when a state of consciousness arises having obtained the supporting condition of prior volitional formations—such as the thought, "What indeed is there that does not succeed for one who has desire"—desire functions as the foremost factor.
It proceeds while exercising control over the associated mental states, and the associated states proceed under its control.
Because it follows that [state] by way of being inferior and so forth, he says: “But having made desire the chief,” and so on.

“Having made it the leader” means having made it the precursor by way of its being co-nascent and preceding. “Desire as the dominant factor” (chandādhipati) refers to that very arising of consciousness;

it is called “desire as the dominant factor” by making it such that “desire is the dominant factor for this. “In the same way” refers to: “having made consciousness the leader... [up to] ... at the time.”
The method is exactly as stated in the passage beginning with “dominant by mind” (cittādhipati), and so forth. Regarding the phrase “in the remaining cases,” this refers to mind and the others.
Furthermore, it should be understood that these four do not function as dominants simultaneously, because time is restricted by the passage beginning with “desire... at the proper time.
And having established this, the *Paṭṭhāna* states: “Dominance by desire [is the cause] of those states associated with desire and of those things originated by them...”

In the passage beginning with "The [four] forms are a condition for [the four consciousnesses] by way of the predominance condition," the status of all four predominances as conditions is stated individually.
For if they were to function as predominance conditions at one and the same moment, then—

just as in the exposition of the root-cause condition where it is stated without distinction, "Root-causes [are conditions] for those associated with root-causes," and so forth, because the state of being a supportive factor in the sense of being a root exists— [the same would apply here].

Because two or even three roots can simultaneously function as conditions [for a single consciousness], if many [roots] were thus to occupy the status of "senior" (jeṭṭhaka) at one and the same moment, then even in the exposition of the predominance condition (adhipatipaccaya), it would have to be stated as: "The predominance [root] is [the condition] for those associated with the predominance [root]," and so forth.
However, since it is not stated in that way, but rather as: "The predominance of desire (chandādhipati) is [the condition] for those associated with desire," and so forth...
These four alone are stated by way of distinction; therefore, it should be understood that each individual dhamma serves as a predominance condition (adhipati-paccaya) within a single moment.
"In the sense of being foremost" means by way of preeminence.
"Those of good intelligence" (sumatino) refers to those who possess beautiful wisdom or right view; this is the meaning. Of them...
It awakens the mind; it causes one to awaken—thus it is "the awakening of the good mind" (*sumatimativibodhana*).

Those who possess a base mind, or for whom a base view is held, are "those of base minds" (*kumatino*), namely those with wrong views. Because it is their very mind and is conceived as being of the nature of mind, it is "the mind of the base-minded" (*kumatimati*), which is wrong view.
That very thing, by virtue of its similarity to fuel, is the "fuel"; and because it is like a fire to that [fuel], it is "base mind" (*kumati*)... [and so forth].

"Pāvakaṃ" means "extremely sweet," being sweet both through the essence of the meaning (*attharasa*), which is skillful and profound, and through the essence of the phrasing (*byañjanarasa*), which is perfectly pure and gentle.
"Avedi" means he knows it after having plunged into it. "Whoever" refers to anyone among the elders, novices, or those of middle standing.
"He knew the entire word of the Victor" means that, by attaining the capacity to grasp the entirety of the Victor’s word contained in the Three Pitakas, he understands it.
Thus ends the commentary on the Section on Miscellaneous Explanations within the *Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanā*, known as the *Abhidhammatthavikāsinī*.
Chapter Nine:
Explanation of the Description of the Condition of the Ripening of Merit (Puññavipākapaccayaniddesa) 560–1.

Because supramundane ripenings are not obtained within the discourse on the round of existence (*vaṭṭakathā*), it is stated that [these results] are "only mundane. The formations such as merit and demerit...
There are three formations: the formation of merit, the formation of demerit, and the formation of the imperturbable.
In this context, "merit" (*puñña*) is so called because it purifies one's own continuum by cleansing it of the fruits of demerit and of defilement and suffering;

or alternatively, it is merit because it produces a venerable fruit of existence. It is a "formation" (*abhisaṅkhāra*) in the sense of actively constructing its own fruit; thus, it is the "formation of merit."

It is "demerit" (apuñña) because it is the opposite of merit; and as stated by the method already explained, it is a "volitional formation" (abhisaṅkhāra), thus it is a "demeritorious volitional formation" (apuññābhisaṅkhāra).
