It is "imperturbable" (āneñja) because it does not waver or shake due to its extreme distance from the opposites of concentration; that which forms this is an "imperturbable volitional formation" (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra).

In this context, there are eight wholesome sense-sphere volitions (kāmāvacara-kusala-cetanā) that proceed by way of giving, virtue, and so forth, and those that proceed solely by way of meditation (bhāvanā).
The thirteen volitions consisting of wholesome volitions of the fine-material sphere are called the formation of merit (*puññābhisankhāra*).
The twelve unwholesome volitions occurring by way of killing living beings and so forth are called the formation of demerit (*apuññābhisankhāra*).

The four wholesome volitions of the immaterial sphere occurring only by way of meditation are called the formation of the imperturbable (*āneñjābhisankhāra*). Just as there are conditions for existence and so forth, so too [are there conditions] for those who...
The connection is that those [conditions] for the results (*vipāka*) must also be understood. However, some say that "those" refers to the formations (*saṅkhāra*);

that is not correct, because if that were so, there would be no restrictive statement following the non-restrictive designation "of which. 562. As to what those existences (*bhava*) and so forth are, he says:
"the three existences," and so on. Therein, by way of the sensual, fine-material, and immaterial [realms]...

There are three existences (*bhava*). By way of existence with perception (*saññībhava*), existence without perception (*asaññībhava*), and existence with neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññīnāsaññībhava*), as well as by way of one-aggregate existence (*ekavokārabhava*), four-aggregate existence (*catuvokārabhava*), and five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*), these three existences are fully subsumed right here. There are four modes of birth (*yoni*);

that is, the four classes of beings by way of egg-born (*aṇḍaja*), womb-born (*jalābuja*), moisture-born (*saṃsedaja*), and spontaneously born (*opapātika*). Among these, the class of beings produced in an eggshell is called the egg-born mode of birth. In the mother’s womb...

The class of beings born from a womb within water-lilies is called the moisture-born (*jalābuja-yoni*). The class of beings that arises by depending on the moisture of lotus calyxes, human wombs, filth, and so forth, is called the moisture-born (*saṃseda-jayoni*).

The class of beings that arises not having come from anywhere else, but appearing with all its limbs and members complete right there and then, is called the apparitional (*opapātika-yoni*). [These constitute] the five destinies (*gatipañcaka*).

This has already been explained below. Furthermore, the aggregates of consciousness that serve as the physical basis (*vatthu*) for rebirth-linking consciousness are called the "seven stations of consciousness" (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*).
These are sevenfold by way of diversity of body and so forth; thus it is said: "The stations of consciousness are seven. For this has been stated:
"Bhikkhus, there are these seven stations of consciousness. What seven? There are, bhikkhus, beings who are diverse in body..."
possessing diverse perceptions. Just as humans, some gods, and some beings in the states of deprivation—this is the first station of consciousness.

There are, monks, beings who are diverse in body but unified in perception, such as the gods of the Brahma-order who have first arisen; this is the second station of consciousness. There are, monks, beings...
“Beings with a single mode of body but diverse perceptions, such as the Ābhassara devas; this is the third station of consciousness.
There are, monks, beings with a single mode of body and a single perception, such as the Subhakiṇha devas;
this is the fourth station of consciousness. There are, monks, beings who, by completely transcending perceptions of form...”
With the subsiding of perceptions of resistance and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, [thinking] ‘space is infinite,’ they reach the base of infinite space;

this is the fifth station of consciousness. There are, bhikkhus, beings who, having completely transcended the base of infinite space, [thinking] ‘consciousness is infinite,’ reach the base of infinite consciousness; this is the sixth station of consciousness. There are, bhikkhus...
“Beings who, having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, thinking ‘there is nothing,’ have reached the base of nothingness—
this is the seventh station of consciousness. For here,
humans dwelling in immeasurable world-systems, sense-sphere deities, and [beings such as] Punabbasu, Mātupiyaṅkara, and Mātā are included.

The beings in the states of deprivation (*vinipātika*), the asuras who possess rebirth-linking through the ripening of wholesome karma, and the *vemanika* pretas—these are called "those with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions" because of the diversity of their material bodies by way of color and shape (such as long, short, thin, thick, black, or white) and the diversity of their rebirth-linking consciousness by way of being causeless, having two causes, or having three causes.
This is the first station of consciousness. Furthermore, the three classes of deities dwelling in the lower part of the first jhāna [sphere]... [who dwell] higher and higher...

Because they perceive diversity in the material body due to the inferiority of their own complexion and other qualities when compared to others, yet perceive unity through the consciousness that is the result of the first jhāna, they are called "those with diverse bodies and unified perception"; this is the second station of consciousness.
Furthermore, because the inhabitants of the four woeful states perceive diversity in the material body by way of complexion and shape, and perceive unity by way of unwholesome resultant perception...
And it should be understood that because they possess a single nature, they come together only in the second station of consciousness.

The three classes of gods dwelling on the level of the second jhāna are called "those with a unity of body and diversity of perception" because their physical bodies are identical in terms of color, shape, and so forth—due to the absence of distinction in the material body—and because their rebirth-perceptions differ according to the perceptions of the second and third jhānas in the fivefold system; this is the third station of consciousness.

Furthermore, the three classes of deities dwelling on the terrace of the third jhāna are called "those with a unity of body and unity of perception" because they are identical in their material bodies;
and according to the fivefold system, this is the fourth station of consciousness because of the unity of their rebirth-perception through the resultants of the fourth jhāna.
Then there are those dwelling in the Vehapphala realm and the five Pure Abodes, who [possess a unity of body] by way of the material body’s color and shape.
Because they are identical to the rebirth-linking perception by way of the perception that is the fruition of the fifth jhāna, they are included within the fourth station of consciousness itself.
The three stations of consciousness beginning with the base of infinite space are evident from the textual tradition alone.

However, non-percipient beings and those dwelling in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are included because of the subtlety of their consciousness, just as [the latter] is subtle compared to perception.
They are not included among the stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*), but because they are the dwelling places of beings, they are called "abodes of beings" (*sattāvāsa*).
Having done so, by combining those with the seven stations of consciousness, nine abodes of beings are stated.

563–4. Now, regarding the state of being a condition for the thirty-two kinds of resultant [consciousness] and the three types of formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*) within the existences (*bhava*) and so forth thus described:
In order to demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “In the sense-sphere, those known as meritorious volitional formations” is commenced.

“Of the nine resultant consciousnesses” refers to the nine resultant consciousnesses of a fortunate rebirth, categorized by way of being with or without roots. “By way of asynchronous... and conditions”:

because past wholesome or unwholesome kamma serves as a condition for the resultant states it is to produce within itself, it acts as an asynchronous kamma-condition (*nānakkhaṇika-kammapaccaya*); and for those very same [resultants]...
This is due to its being a powerful cause and by way of the decisive-support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*). For its status as a decisive support has been stated thus:

"Wholesome and unwholesome kamma is a condition for its result by way of the decisive-support condition. In all instances, the state of being a decisive support should be applied by way of powerful kamma;
for it is shown in the *Paṭṭhāna-vaṇṇanā* that weak kamma does not constitute a decisive support.
"Of five" means of the five [consciousnesses] by way of the wholesome-resultant eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, receiving-consciousness, and the two types of investigating-consciousness.
He says, "they do not exist at rebirth-linking," because of the absence of wholesome-resultant rebirth-linking in the miserable destinies (*duggati*).
Having thus shown the method of conditions according to the non-confusion between rebirth-linking and the course of existence (*pavatti*), he now [shows them] by combining them.

The phrase beginning with "honti" was stated in order to show this. It should be applied according to what is available: [these states] exist during the course of existence for sixteen [consciousnesses], and nine at rebirth-linking. 569–74.
"Meritorious formations in the fine-material sphere" refers to the five meritorious formations of the fine-material sphere, excluding the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).
But why are the direct knowledges excluded? Because they do not yield kamma-result; and furthermore, because their result...
It is because it is impossible, and not because of an absence of the inherent nature to produce a result (vipāka).

For if the volition of direct knowledge (abhiññā-cetanā) were to produce a result, then—since it is illogical for karma belonging to one plane to produce a result belonging to another plane—it would have to produce a result belonging to its own plane.
But would that [result] be produced with an object that is "not to be designated" (navattabbārammaṇa), or with an object such as the limited (paritta) and so forth? And in this regard, if first—

If it produces an object that is "not to be designated" (navattabba), that is not logical, because it has been shown that the resultant consciousnesses of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara-vipāka) invariably have the same object as their kamma,
and because the volition of direct knowledge (abhiññā-cetanā) itself has limited (paritta) and other such objects. If, on the other hand, it produces an object that is limited and so forth,
that too is not logical, because the resultant consciousnesses of the fine-material sphere invariably have objects that are "not to be designated."
For it is said in the *Cittuppādakaṇḍa*:

"The threefold sets of four jhānas of the fine-material sphere—whether wholesome, resultant, or functional—and the resultant of the fourth jhāna, namely the base of infinite space and the base of nothingness: these states are not to be described as 'having limited objects.'"
“‘Having a sublime object’ and also ‘having an immeasurable object.
Furthermore, the direct knowledges (abhiññā), which serve as the equipment for concentration and insight, are merely the benefits of concentration, similar to the fruit of concentration.
For each respective function desired—such as resolution, transformation, or hearing divine sounds—[is accomplished].
The volition of direct knowledge (*abhiññā-cetanā*) has as its fruit merely the production [of the state]. Therefore, he said: "When his mind is thus concentrated," and so forth.

Consequently, the volition of direct knowledge resembles the fruit of concentration but does not itself give a fruit; it lacks the arising of a result (*vipāka*), unlike the acquisition of conditions in that very existence which constitutes the benefit of giving and virtue.
However, some say: "[They are] powerful because of the attainment of repetition (*āsevana-lābha*) due to being of the same plane..."

They say: "The jhānas produce kamma-result because they exist as meditative attainments (*samāpatti*); however, although the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) possess the nature of jhāna, because that [result] is absent in them, they are merely adventitious with respect to their respective objects and are thus weak; therefore, they do not give rise to kamma-result.
And having established it thus, it was stated by the teacher Anuruddha:
“When association with equals is obtained, existing in great strength;
yet without obtaining such a cause, direct knowledge does not ripen.
This is not a valid reason, because it is stated that even in the case of limited jhāna, there is the giving of karmic result among the retinue of Brahmā and others without distinction.
For it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that a limited state does not give its result there merely by having been cultivated;
therefore, one cannot maintain that a jhāna gives its result only when it has been cultivated equally [with its result].

Furthermore, since mastery exists even in the case of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) through repeated preliminary work (*parikamma*), and since that [direct knowledge] possesses strength, it would indeed produce a result.
“Of the five resultant consciousnesses” means of the five fine-material-sphere resultant consciousnesses. “Non-meritorious formations” (*apuññasaṅkhārā*) means formations that are non-meritorious.
Alternatively, the word division is: “These are non-meritorious formations. “Of one” means of one unwholesome-resultant investigating consciousness.

“Of six” means of the six unwholesome-resultants, excluding the investigating consciousness. In the course of existence, they become conditions when undesirable visible forms and so forth have come into range.
This is the intended meaning. He says, "They do not exist at rebirth-linking," because there is no unwholesome-resultant rebirth-linking in a happy destination (*sugati*).
"Of four" refers to the four [consciousnesses] by way of unwholesome-resultant eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, receiving, and investigating.
Moreover, those [objects] are exclusively undesirable. And how could there be a connection with undesirable objects in the fine-material realm (*rūpabhava*)? To this he says:
“*So cā*,” etc. *So* refers to that very state of being a condition (*paccayabhāvo*). “*Kāmabhave*” is a qualification of undesirable forms and so forth, but not of the term “*upaladdhiyaṃ*.

Therefore he said: “*Aniṭṭha…pe… na vijjare*. However, some take it as a qualification of this very term “*upaladdhiyaṃ*,” [interpreting it as] “at the moment when Brahmās have come to the sensual existence (*kāmabhava*), there is no perception (*upaladdhi*) of form and so forth.”
They say: "Unpleasant... [and so on]... they do not exist there, because of the absence of any cause for mixed pleasure and pain in that which has become a basis for absolute happiness.

576. "Thus, first of all," etc., is the conclusion (*appanā*) of the very meaning already stated. By the word "and" (*ca*) in "yathā ca," the phrase "yesañca" is included. Similarly, here too, "te" (they) should be understood as being included by "tathā. 577–81.
From the point where a detailed exposition has been made, this is merely a brief indication starting from that state of existence (*bhava*).
Desiring to explain this, he said, “In that regard,” and so forth. “In that regard” (*tatra*) means among those [realms] such as existence (*bhava*).
“This” (*idaṃ*) refers to what is proximate and evident by way of being demonstrable. “Starting from the beginning,” however, means starting from existence.

“Without distinction” means that there are thirteen volitional formations of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) because there is no distinction between the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*). “In two existences” means in the existences of the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere. Of certain humans...
Because terrestrial deities also arise from egg-birth and womb-birth, it is stated with reference to them: “in the four... modes of origin (yoni). The phrase “in the diversities...

and stations of consciousness” is expressed as a non-elided compound (*aluttasamāsa*); the meaning is: “in the four stations of consciousness, namely, those characterized by diversity of body and diversity of perception,” and so forth.
“In the aforementioned manner” refers to the diversity of body and the rest; [this pertains] to the formation of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*).

Because among the twenty-one types of resultants (*vipāka*) belonging to the states of existence (*bhava*) and so forth, they do not serve as conditions for a single instance [of rebirth], but rather act as conditions for eight resultants during the course of existence (*pavatta*) alone—
without granting rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) within the realms of existence, modes of birth, destinations, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings included in the miserable destinies—

and because they act as conditions for sixteen resultants during the course of existence after granting rebirth-linking within those included in the happy destinies of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), and [those] included in the planes of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*).
It is said “as appropriate” because, having given rebirth-linking, it serves as a condition for ten types of resultant consciousness during the course of existence (pavatta).
582–3. The connection is with “in the sensual becoming” and “in the fine-material becoming. “In the three destinations” means in the three destinations excluding those of gods and humans.
“In one” refers to one station of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti) known as “diversity of body and unity of perception. In one...
In the single abode of beings known as "diversity of body and unity of perception.
584–6. In a single formless existence (*arūpabhava*). In a single womb: specifically, in the single womb of spontaneous birth (*opapātika-yoni*).

In the three stations of consciousness (*cittatthiti*): in the three stations of consciousness beginning with the base of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatana*). In the fourfold abode of beings (*sattāvāsa*).
In the fourfold abode of beings, beginning with the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana). "To be known... conditions":
the meaning is that formations (saṅkhāra) should be understood not only as the conditions themselves, but also as those things for which they are conditions. 587–90.
But has it not been stated that formations also serve as conditions for resultant states during both rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) and the course of existence (pavatti)? In that regard—

Rebirth-linking itself cannot even be understood [in this way]. For if it were said that the rebirth-linking consciousness comes here from a previous existence, that would not be tenable, because there is no movement of material or immaterial phenomena to another location even by the measure of a hair’s tip.
Nor is it tenable to say that it does not arise from the formations produced in the past existence, for that would entail the fault of being causeless.
With this intention, he who is challenging [the opponent] says: “Not of material and immaterial phenomena,” and so forth.
The Teacher, having accepted that intention and wishing to convince him, says: “There is none for the mind,” and so forth. Then, “without a cause” means without a cause therein; the meaning is:
without the craving for the formations of kamma that produce existence in the past, which serve as the object. “Having well-obtained conditions” means...
It has obtained its conditions through being perfectly complete by way of volitional formations (saṅkhāra) accompanied by their co-operative causes, such as ignorance (avijjā).

"Mere form and name" means that it is merely a phenomenon consisting of form and name, because there is an absence of a self, a soul, or anything else imagined by outsiders as a basis for designation.
Therefore he said, "And not a being," and so forth. It is called "passing on to another existence," etc., merely as a conventional expression (vohāramatta).
"It is said that one 'enters another existence. However, in terms of its actual meaning, the intention is merely the arising in the form of another existence through the convergence of conditions.

591. Now, beginning to clarify that process of rebirth-linking by way of the human rebirth-linking which is most evident, he says "That indeed," and so forth. "Sudubbudham" means extremely difficult to understand. Therefore, the ancients said:
"The being, rebirth-linking, and the mode of conditions— these are indeed difficult to discern."
“Four things are difficult to see, and they are very difficult to teach.
(592–3) “For one whose death is near” means for one whose death is imminent, whether due to the assault of another or through the exhaustion of the life-span and so forth.
“In the process of drying up” means gradually becoming parched, just like the successive development of the sense-bases of an embryo in the womb.
It is said that cessation also occurs gradually, as stated in the passage, "when the eye-faculty and so forth have perished.
However, some say this refers to "when the eye-faculty and so forth, which have arisen from various karmas, have perished. By the phrase "the heart... [and so forth]... what?
the fact that the body-faculty has ceased in the rest of the body is stated; thus, others maintain that even that which has arisen from a single karma perishes. But the teacher Ānanda says:
“In the *yamaka* (pairing): For whom the eye-base ceases, for him the mind-base ceases? Yes.
Or else, for whom the mind-base ceases, for him the eye-base ceases?
For those who are passing away with a mind but without eyes, the mind-base ceases, but for them the eye-base does not cease.”

Since it is stated in such passages as, “For those with eyes who are passing away, the mind-base ceases and the eye-base also ceases,” that the eye-base and so forth cease together with the death-consciousness, the faculties of the eye and so on do not perish prior to death.
However, with reference to their reaching a state of extreme weakness, the Commentary says, “when the faculties have ceased.”
This was stated with reference to cessation without remainder (anavasesa-nirodha), not with reference to death following the five-door javanas;
for even death immediately after the five-door javanas is shown in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). "In the mere location of the heart-base" means in the mere region of the heart-base.
For the body-faculty does not function depending upon the heart-base.

594–7. "Supported by the physical basis" (*vatthusannissita*) means that because the remaining faculties have ceased, it is supported solely by the heart-basis (*hadayavatthu*) due to its feeble state, which lacks the capacity to serve as a support for consciousness.
"Mind" (*citta*) refers here to the impulsion consciousness (*javana-viññāṇa*) that arises at that time, taking as its object kamma, the signs of kamma, and so forth.
Furthermore, for one being reborn in a happy destination (*sugati*), that mind is wholesome (*kusala*); in an unhappy destination (*duggati*), it is unwholesome.
It is unwholesome for one who is being reborn. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Bhikkhus, consciousness, while persisting, persists either clinging to the gratification in the sign or clinging to the gratification in the secondary characteristics.
If at that time one should die, it is possible that one will go to one of two destinations..."
“...he would go to a destination, either hell or the animal realm,” and so forth.
If this is so—[then consider: “In the case of a fortunate rebirth associated with knowledge, through which eight causes does such a rebirth arise?”
At the moment of impulsion (*javana*) of wholesome karma, three wholesome roots are co-nascent conditions for the volition (*cetanā*) born at that moment;

therefore, it is said that formations (*saṅkhārā*) have wholesome roots as their condition. At the moment of attachment (*nikanti*), two unwholesome roots are co-nascent conditions for the volition born at that moment; therefore, it is said that [formations] also have unwholesome roots as their condition.
Regarding "formations": at the moment of rebirth-linking, the three roots, being indeterminate, act as co-nascence conditions for the volition born at that moment;
therefore it is said, "consciousness has name-and-form as its condition, and name-and-form has consciousness as its condition.
But how is it shown that for one with a rebirth-linking in a happy destination, there are also two root-conditions at the moment of attachment? This is not so.

This was said with reference to the root-conditions associated with the javana-mind moments occurring at the time of death; however, it refers rather to the root-conditions associated with the javana-mind moments that arise by way of gratification, taking that performed deed as their object.

For even a deed that has been performed and accumulated is capable of producing its result only when it is gratified by craving. Some, however, [hold that this applies] to the state where [defilements] have not yet been abandoned at the time of performing the deed...
Some say that this was stated with reference to the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) within the continuum (*santāna*), meaning that at the moment of attachment there are two causes;
however, that is not tenable, because those [tendencies] cannot function as co-nascent conditions (*sahajāta-paccaya*).
The connection is: "The mind proceeds by taking as its object either merit or demerit previously practiced, or the sign of the deed (*kamma-nimitta*). Regarding "previously practiced":

"Previously practiced. For it is said: "Because of having been performed and accumulated. Or, with reference to the state of being repeatedly pursued by craving, it is called "previously pursued" (*pubbānusevita*).

They also cite the reading "gradually practiced" (*anupubbasevita*); the meaning is that it was practiced previously by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), that is, it was given as a rebirth-linking in the past. Furthermore, even that which has been given as a rebirth-linking in subsequent births...

It is not the case that it does not produce the result of the process [of rebirth]. By the mention of "merit and demerit," he shows the object of the rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) in happy or miserable destinies according to one's karma.
With the word "or" in the phrase "kamma or the sign of kamma," he includes the sign of the destiny (gatinimitta).
Among these, both the kamma and the sign of the destiny come within the range of the mind-door alone; however, the sign of kamma...
This applies even to the five doors. Having established this, rebirth-linking occurs even with an object apprehended through the five doors.
Others, however, explain that the sign of destiny (gatinimitta) is also obtainable through all six doors. Having established this, it is stated in the *Saccasaṅkhepa*:
"Rebirth-linking may occur at the five doors, even without [the direct presence of] karma, in the case of the two spheres."

However, because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that "the sign of the destination comes into the range of the mind-door," and because a five-door rebirth-linking with that as its object has not been shown, and because in the *Mūlaṭīkā* and other works it is said: "By the power of kamma,
the sense-sphere of visible form is presented [to the mind] at the mind-door alone, like one seeing a dream or like one possessing the divine eye..."
The teachers do not accept their statement because it was spoken with the restriction, “it goes.

Furthermore, in this context, the "sign of the kamma" (kamma-nimitta) should be understood as something present that enters the range of the five sense doors, appearing in the stream of objects at the time near death as something similar to the kamma performed;
otherwise, that very [kamma] would be what presents the object for rebirth-linking.
That very [kamma] would have to be the producer of rebirth-linking; for it is said, "Because of having been done and accumulated.

And at that time, the javanas occurring near the moment of death (cuti) would have to be the producers of rebirth-linking—not merely as proximate conditions to rebirth-linking, nor like those which do not present an object to rebirth-linking by saying, "In this [object], you must proceed. And at that time, regarding the rebirth-linking...

How could those [mental states] occurring in a single cognitive process (ekavīthi) be accumulated by action? How could they, being untouched by craving which consists of relishing, produce rebirth-linking?
And how could they not have results within the same cognitive process like mundane supramundane states?
"That consciousness" refers to that impulsion-consciousness (javana-viññāṇa), referring to the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-viññāṇa) by way of the principle of identity (ekattanaya).

It has been stated. For here, by way of the continuity (*santati*) of consciousnesses—namely, death-consciousness, rebirth-linking consciousness, and the consciousness immediately preceding them—the unity attributed to them is intended by the term "that consciousness.
[The phrase] "with its danger concealed by ignorance" refers to the craving for existence (*bhava-taṇhā*) that operates as a latent tendency (*anusaya*), which is associated with the mind.
Or [it occurs] when suffering and its dangers are concealed by ignorance. When such is the case, with respect to the object consisting of karma and so forth—

which serves as the basis for the arising of rebirth-linking consciousness— consciousness proceeds directed toward the place of rebirth-linking, being inclined, leaning, and tending toward it, precisely because craving has not been abandoned and because the preceding continuity has already undergone such a transformation.

He said: "Craving inclines it. But the "concomitant formations" (sahajā saṅkhārā) are the volition (cetanā) co-nascent with the javana-consciousness that is proximate to death, or alternatively, all [mental factors] beginning with contact (phassa).
"They hurl" means they function as the cause for the establishment of consciousness by way of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) upon that object, as if they were hurling it.
"That" refers to that consciousness. By saying "by the power of the continuity" (santativasā), he refers to that very same consciousness.

It rejects this false doctrine that "it runs on and transmigrates, and not another. For when there is a principle of diversity (*nānattanaya*), there is a principle of unity (*ekattanaya*) by way of continuity.

599. "...by way of object and so forth... it proceeds": it proceeds by way of conditions such as the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) and the support-condition (*nissayapaccaya*). How? In one whose death is imminent...
Indeed, by the power of karma, mind-door adverting consciousness arises directed toward an object such as karma, whose dangers are concealed by ignorance;
then, in the cognitive process proximate to death, due to the weakness of the physical basis and the sluggishness of its occurrence, four or five impulsion moments arise;
immediately following that, if there is registration, it occurs with that same object.

Or, when there is no [object], the death-consciousness arises by taking the object-field of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) as its support. They say that death occurs even immediately after the life-continuum.

But when the death-consciousness has ceased, that very same object—whether it be kamma, the sign of kamma, or the like—which has come into the range of the senses, is projected toward the object such as kamma by the conascent formations, with the power of the unabated defilements acting as the cause.
Just as one crossing a stream clings to a rope tied to a tree on the near bank and leaves behind the former support,
so too this consciousness— whether it experiences or does not experience the support arising from kamma produced by the subsequent state—
proceeds by means of conditions such as the object. In this context, the previous existence should be regarded as the near bank, and the tree standing there [is the rope].
The aggregates occurring in the previous existence are like the rope; the object of action and so forth is like the rope.
Some, however, say that the heart-base is like the rope, while others say that craving is like the rope. Consciousness is like the man;
the leaning of craving toward the object is like his grasping of the rope; and the formative forces of throwing are like the effort.
The death-consciousness is like the stepping-stone, and the world beyond is like the further shore.

Just as a man, when establishing himself on the further shore, whether he finds support by clinging to some tree on that shore or not, establishes himself solely upon the earth by means of his own bodily effort; so too is this.

Whether it is experiencing the support known as the heart-base—which is the bond for the individual existence in a future life—in the five-aggregate realm, or not experiencing it in the four-aggregate realm, that consciousness proceeds solely by means of objects and states associated with the support;
thus, it has not "come here," because it has arisen in this very same existence. From what [does it arise]? From karma.

[This refers to] the karma and so forth that produced one’s past existence. By the word “and so forth” (ādi), one should understand the inclusion of the formations that project [existence], the craving that functions by way of inclining [toward objects], the ignorance that conceals the danger regarding the objects such as karma, and the clinging and so forth that produce firm grasping.
In this context, “karma” refers to that which is to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*) and that which is to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparāpariyavedanīya*).

Or it is the kamma that produces rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). "Projecting formations" (*khipanaka-saṅkhāra*) refers to those formations co-nascent with the functional consciousnesses occurring near the moment of death, or the formations associated with the kamma that generates rebirth-linking, or according to some, the formations associated with the functional consciousnesses preceding that [rebirth-linking].

"Craving that proceeds by way of bending" refers to craving as it occurs in its state of underlying tendency (*anusaya*). This same method applies to ignorance (*avijjā*) which conceals the danger (*ādīnava*).

The objects such as *kamma* and so forth have already been explained previously. "Grasping that seizes firmly" refers to the clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*) and the rest, which function by way of seizing rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*) firmly, just as a snake seizes a frog.
Although there exists the relationship of condition and conditioned between echoes and the like, the continuity of the stream (*santānabandha*) is not manifest.
Without touching upon their state of unity or diversity, [the author], showing only the arising of causes from the future and the past, said, "And here," and so forth.

"Here" means in this section concerning death and rebirth-linking (*cuti-paṭisandhi*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in "echoes, lamps, seals, etc.," there is the inclusion of such things as the reflection of a face on the surface of a mirror.
"Without going elsewhere" means without reaching the location of the conditions for the sound and so forth.
This is what is meant: just as an echo does not reach the location of its origin but has sound as its cause;
a lamp [light] has another lamp or similar factors as its cause; a seal impression has the seal as its cause;

and the reflection of a face or similar object in a mirror or similar surface has that object facing it as its cause—since these do not exist prior to those causes—in the same way, this rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*) does not go to the place of its cause to have that as its cause.

It exists because it was non-existent prior to that; therefore, this [result] does not come here from a previous existence by way of its cause, as echoes and the like do from sounds and the like, nor does it arise without a cause from that [previous state], as echoes and the like do without sounds and the like.
Alternatively, "without going elsewhere" means that having been present previously in the location of the conditions, it does not go from there to another place.
They do not exist as conditions because they were non-existent prior to their arising; nor are they not conditions for sound and so forth. This should be applied in the same manner as stated above:

"There is no [identity] due to the continuity of the stream," meaning there is no oneness by way of the succession of the stream, because even within the stream, it is a different consciousness that manifests; nor is there difference, because [each moment] is distinct from the preceding ones.
Because the subsequent [moment] does not arise without the first-arisen phenomenon even at the time of arising, there would be no difference [between them], just as in the case of a lamp.
For even though the flame of a lamp is momentary, it is spoken of as "that very same [flame]" by taking recourse in the unity of the continuum (*santāna*), and it also accomplishes its own function.
By the phrase "when there is the binding of the continuum" and so forth, [it is shown that] in the binding of the continuum there is neither absolute unity nor diversity.
And he demonstrates that [the self] is not to be grasped, as well as the fault in grasping it. This is what is meant:

if, while there is a continuity of the stream, there were absolute identity, then because milk and curd would be non-different, and because the curd would not arise from itself independently, curd could not be produced from milk.
Furthermore, if, while there is a continuity of the stream, there were absolute difference, [the same fault would follow].

Because milk and curd are distinct, and because one thing cannot possess the state of being the owner of another merely by virtue of being its owner, a man who is the owner of milk would not be the owner of curd;
yet this is not seen to be the case in the world.
Therefore, since the delimitation of worldly convention occurs in this way, there is absolute unity, and also diversity.

Nor indeed should they be approached [as identical]. The intention is this: when identity is intended, one should not grasp [the subject] by way of the phenomena (*dhamma*), but rather by way of the continuum (*santāna*);
when difference is intended, one should not grasp it by way of the continuum, but rather by way of the phenomena. Therefore, the ancients said:
“In the investigation of oneness and otherness regarding the bond of the seen continuum...”
“Unity and diversity arise from the difference in moments.

Here, by the absolute negation of unity, the view that “pleasure and pain are self-made” is prevented; and by the absolute negation of diversity, [the view] that “pleasure and pain are made by another” is prevented.

607–9. Is it not the case? Or rather, the connection is: “Is it not beautiful? Is it not possible? Regarding “manifestation without transmigration,” this means being devoid of manifestation through transmigration.
Or, by way of non-transmigration, it means that [the result] manifests without having transmigrated.

"The arising of aggregates" (*khandhābhisambhavā*) means aggregates that have arisen; or alternatively, they are called "arising-grounds" (*abhisambhavā*) because karma arises within them—thus, the meaning is "aggregates that are the basis for the arising [of karma]. "Having ceased here" refers to that which has become the basis for the fruit.
Because it has ceased right here without going to another world. "From the arrival in another" means from not going to another world.
"Of that" means of the karma. "Of another" means of one other than the person by whom that karma was performed. "From another" means from something other than that karma which has been produced.
"This arrangement" means that there is no going from this world to another world; therein—
“Other aggregates arise”—this entire passage is according to the method already stated.
To clarify the meaning briefly stated as “In the continuity... [the] accomplisher,” the passage beginning with “But in one” was spoken.
“In one continuity” means: in that very collection of phenomena (*dhamma-puñja*) in which the kamma was produced.
The meaning [is as follows]: "Or it belongs to another... and so on... "it comes to be. In this context, the intention is that absolute identity and difference are both excluded.

Regarding the phrase "of this meaning": although the cause and the fruit are different in their essential nature (*atthato*), because they are connected by that very relationship of cause and fruit, that fruit should not be said to belong to another or to be other [than the cause]. This is the meaning of the statement. "Of seeds" refers to mango and citron seeds.
"Preparation" (*abhisaṅkhāra*) means the infusion of honey and so forth. "With honey and so forth" means with honey, the four sweets, liquid lac, and so on.
"Of that" means of that seed which has been infused. "Having first obtained the requisite condition" means having first obtained the condition for attaining the state of sweetness.
"At a later time" means at the time of the fruit. "And this too should be known in this way" means just as this [preceding example].
In this way, this too should be understood. This is what is meant:
just as when mango seeds and the like are planted after being treated with honey or the "four sweets," the taste of the fruit becomes sweet;
and when a citron seed is planted after being dyed with lac juice, the sour fruit becomes red; yet that seed neither performs the actual preparation nor reaches the place where the fruit grows.

Even though this is so, a specific fruit does not arise in the continuum of one seed from another seed, nor does it arise in another seed through the condition of volitional formation (*abhisaṅkhāra*).
In the same way, the karma produced within the aggregates that have arisen here in this world does not go to the next world.
Likewise, the resultant aggregates do not arise in a different continuum at a later time. Nor...
And they arise from the condition of other kamma.
For here, kamma is like a seed that has been prepared, or it is like the act of preparation itself;
the continuity of rebirth-consciousness and so forth for a being is like the continuity of sprouts and so forth from a seed. Of the sweet flavor produced therein—

Just as the existence of one who is attached to a vessel containing seeds arises from that very seed and from its own conditioning, so too should the existence of a sentient being who performs an action be understood to arise from that very action and from its own conditioning. 615. Regarding the phrase "in childhood... [etc.
...yielding fruit": this refers to the acquisition of knowledge and the training in crafts performed while in a child's body.

Furthermore, the application of medicine does not enter the aged body; nevertheless, the proficiency in knowledge, the mastery of craft, health, and so forth, resulting from that [application], exist in the aged body.
Yet these do not belong to anyone else, because they arise as similar [states] only within one included in that same continuum.
Nor do these [qualities] arise from any other source apart from the study of knowledge and so forth employed by the person who applied them.

Because [the cause] is absent when that [result] is absent, one should apply this principle here as well to the continuum (*saṃtāna*): whatever result there is, it belongs to nothing else, nor does it come from anything else.
By this, he demonstrates only the absence of the result when the formative forces (*saṅkhāra*) are absent; he does not intend to exclude other conditions.
Even though this is so—that is, even though there is manifestation without transmigration—and provided that the aforementioned faults have been avoided therein:
The meaning is: "even though it has been accomplished. "Existing" means existing and unceased, like the wick and oil of a lamp; this is the sense.
"Non-existing" means non-existing and ceased, like the death-consciousness of an Arahant who is free from the suffering of saṃsāra;
this is the sense. "At the moment of its occurrence" means precisely at the moment when the karma is occurring. Therefore he said: "And by that very cause, faith."
“Non-existent” means not having reached existence prior to the moment of its occurrence. “Ceased” means ceased after having passed through the three moments. Therefore he said:
“Prior to the moment of occurrence, or afterwards, it would be a permanent fruit.”
"Prior" means prior to the accumulation of kamma; this is stated by way of their commonality in non-existence. "Subsequent" means subsequent to the occurrence of the result. 619–20.
"Condition by way of what has been done" (kaṭattā-paccaya) means a condition precisely by virtue of having been done, and not by way of being present or absent.
Therefore he said: "Because of the having been done and the having been accumulated of wholesome kamma belonging to the sense sphere, the resultant eye-consciousness..."
"...arises," and so forth. If this were so, would even a deed performed by an Arahant become a *kaṭattā-paccaya* (the condition consisting in having been done)?

This is not the case. For just as when a tree has its roots cut, even a flowering blossom capable of producing seed does not yield fruit once the root has been severed, so too, for an Arahant, while the continuity of existence (*santāna*) still persists, [an action] does not produce a result once the root of the defilements (*kilesa*) has been completely cut off.
Kamma becomes incapable of yielding fruit at the very moment the root of defilement is severed. Thus the ancients said:
"This chariot of birth, mounted by foolish folk, has kamma and defilements for its wheels."
"One who destroys the wheel of defilements does not go along with the wheel of karma.

If it were a condition by way of having been performed (*kaṭattā*), it would be an obstacle that yields fruit eternally; therefore, he said "guarantee and so forth," etc. "Guarantee and so forth" means...
"By way of returning the original object, etc. By the inclusion of "etc.," the taking of goods with the thought "I will give the original object later," as well as the taking of a loan, are included.

This, however, is the intended meaning here: the existence or non-existence of acts such as acting as a guarantor is not a condition for the restitution, the giving of a replacement object, or the repayment of a loan; rather, it is merely a cause [for the initial transaction].
Nor does that [act] remain a condition for the giving away and so forth at all times, because once the giving away and so forth have been performed, it lacks the status of being a condition;
in the same way, regarding the production of the result, the existence or non-existence of the karma is not a condition, but rather it is merely the act of performing [the deed].
And when there is merely the act of performing, it is no longer a condition for those results that have already matured.

621. It is called *Paramatthappakāsana* because it elucidates the supreme, ultimate goal (*paramattha*). It is called *Pītibuddhivivaḍḍhana* because it increases rapture (*pīti*) and wisdom (*buddhi*), or rather, it increases wisdom accompanied by rapture.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Abhidhammāvatāra*, titled *Abhidhammatthavikāsinī*.
The commentary on the exposition of the condition consisting in the ripening of merit is finished.
Chapter Ten: Commentary on the Analysis of Matter.

622. *Ādimhi* means "at the beginning" [of the summary verse]. *Idāni* means "now," immediately following the analysis of consciousness and mental factors. *Vibhāvanaṃ* means the manifestation of the essential nature by way of exposition (*niddesa*) and further exposition (*paṭiniddesa*).
623. *Ruppati* means it undergoes change due to cold, heat, and so forth; or its meaning is that it is "assailed.

This undergoing of change is simply the arising of something dissimilar when conditions adverse to cold and so forth are present. For, having arisen from their respective conditions, [it does not remain as it was].
It is possible for those things established by their own nature (*ṭhitadhamma*) to be brought to change by something else;

therefore, "being affected" (*ruppana*) here should be understood as the very arising of dissimilar states in those things that arise subsequently—not as a transformation of a previously arisen material continuity (*rūpasantati*), but through the convergence of discordant conditions (*visabhāgapaccaya*).
And by taking it in this way, the doctrine of the transformation of the aggregates (*saṅkhārā*) becomes directly evident.
But is it not the case that even for immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*), a dissimilar arising is obtained when there is a combination of opposing conditions? True, it is obtained;

however, it is not more manifest (*vibhūtatarā*). For here, a "dissimilar arising" is intended in its most prominent sense, according to the principle of excellence, just as one says, "A maiden should be given to a handsome man."
If it is asked, "How is this known?"—it is from the mention of cold and so forth. For it has been said:
"And what, monks, do you call 'form' (rūpa)? It is called 'form,' monks, because it is afflicted (ruppati).
By what is it afflicted? It is afflicted by cold, it is afflicted by heat, it is afflicted by hunger, and it is afflicted by thirst."
“It is deformed; it is deformed even by contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things.
It is deformed, monks, therefore it is called ‘form’ (rūpa).
For here, the inclusion of cold and so forth indicates that the deformation of one who is touched by cold and so forth is most evident; therefore, that alone is intended here.

The term "grasped" (*gahita*) is for the purpose of making it known. Otherwise, since it would already be established by the general term "that which is disturbed" (*ruppati*), the inclusion of "cold and so forth" (*sītādi*) would be redundant.
If this is so, how can the designation "form" (*rūpa*) apply to the Brahma-world? For indeed, no specific kind of cold or other obstructive contact is found there. True;

nevertheless, even there, it does not transcend its essential nature of being subject to disturbance. For even that which is non-material (*arūpa*) does not transcend its essential nature of being subject to disturbance.

There is the designation "form" (*rūpa-saññā*). Just as even milk that has not been milked is called "milked" because it does not transcend its own nature, so too, although there is no specific obstructive contact such as cold and so forth there, there is indeed a supportive one.
For instance, the temperature-born form (*utu-rūpa*) exists among the Brahmās; therefore, since there is indeed "being affected" (*ruppana*) there, there is nothing [contradictory] therein.
"An obstruction to the designation 'form' (rūpa-saññā).
"It forms" (rūpayati) means that, while existing itself, it brings about a transformation in its own continuity.
Thus, by the previous analysis, the arising of transformation was shown as "being formed" (ruppana). But by this [present analysis], when opposing conditions assemble—
What is indicated by "being afflicted" (*ruppana*) is the state of being the cause for the production of something dissimilar within one's own continuity while [the cause] itself is still present.
In this position, there is no possibility of applying the conventional designation "matter" (*rūpa*) to that which is non-material (*arūpa*).

For it is only when [the cause] has ceased that it produces a non-material [effect] through conditions such as the immediately preceding condition (*anantara-paccaya*), not while it is still present. Regarding the word "matter" (*rūpa*) in the sense of undergoing transformation upon impact:
Some say that because there is no impact (*ghaṭṭanā*) among immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*), the designation "matter" (*rūpa*) does not apply to them.

Others hold that "impact" (*paṭighāta*) is what constitutes matter; according to their view, although the designation "matter" would logically apply only to material phenomena that possess resistance (*sappaṭigha-rūpa*), nevertheless, by way of a figurative expression for a part, the whole is also so designated, and thus all matter receives the designation "matter."
However, some here say: "It is stated as 'it forms' (*rūpayati*) by way of the sense-sphere of visible form (*vaṇṇāyatana*). For that [body], undergoing transformation of its appearance, "forms" it;

it manifests the state of being present in the heart. But since this is explained separately later in the exposition of the sense-sphere of visible form, there is no purpose for its detailed description here.
"Of beautiful form" (*surūpa*) means [endowed] with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the eighty minor characteristics, the fathom-wide aura, the jewel-garland, and so forth.
Because he is adorned, his physical body is beautiful; or, the word *rūpa* may signify intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), as in such passages as "that which in the world is a lovely form, a pleasant form.

Therefore, "surūpa" means one whose intrinsic nature is beautiful. By this, the beauty of the Teacher’s perfection of the Dhamma-body is also shown, as it illustrates his endowment with extraordinary and uncommon qualities such as the Ten Powers and the Four Grounds of Self-Confidence.

624. Regarding the phrase "due to the distinction between the primary elements (bhūta) and the derived matter (upādāya)": here, it is called *upādāyarūpa* because it exists dependent upon those [primary elements]; thus, the primary element (*bhūta*) is that which is derived from them.

Alternatively, the term *bhūta* here refers to the great primary elements themselves by means of the elision of the first part of the compound. Therefore, he says: "The great primary elements are fourfold.
That which is derived from the primary elements, and which does not itself derive from them or from anything else, is called *upādāya*.
And by defining it thus, there is no risk of the four great elements (mahābhūta) being classified as derived matter (upādāyarūpa), even though they arise in mutual dependence upon one another.
For those [elements] do not merely depend on one another; rather, they themselves are depended upon by derived matter.
Therefore, by the force of including the term "derived" (upādāya), there is no risk of the great elements being classified as derived matter. Now...

Or, because of the statement, “derived matter (upādāyarūpa) is that which is derived from the four great elements (mahābhūta),” the characteristic of derived matter is simply its dependence upon the four great elements, and not its dependence upon the three [other] elements and so forth;
thus, those [three] are not considered derived matter. “Derived from the elements and the derived” (bhūtopādāyaṃ) means by way of their distinction;
hence, “by way of the distinction between the elements and the derived. Since the word *bhūta* has both genders, he says “the great elements” (*mahābhūtā*).
In expressions such as “paṭisaṅkhā yoniso,” one should understand that there is an elision of the letter *ya* here [in the term *upādāyarūpāni*].
Now, what are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), how are they designated as "great elements," what are the derived forms (*upādāyarūpa*), and why are they called "derived forms"?
Keeping this inquiry in mind, he proceeds to clarify it in due order:
He said, “The earth element,” and so forth. “These four” means these four. “Mahābhūta” means that which is great (*mahā*) and has become (*bhūta*);
the meaning is: by the Perfectly Enlightened One (*Sammāsambuddha*), who has appeared in the world including the devas with greatness due to that great becoming.
Alternatively: “Time devours all beings... [and so on].
"Along with all those who have come into being, he who has become a devourer of beings cooks the cooker of beings."
Just as the word *bhūta* is used for "beings" (*satta*) in such contexts as [the phrase] "beginning with," here it refers to those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).

Thus, the meaning is "by a great being" (*mahābhūtena*), or alternatively, "by one who has great taints destroyed. For even one whose taints are destroyed is indeed called "become" (*bhūta*) because he has completely exhausted rebirth;
since he will not come to be again, he is called "become."

626. "The great elements have become manifest" means that they have become, arisen, and been produced as great elements by way of their constituent parts (*sasambhāradhātu*), both in the continuum of what is clung-to (*upādinnaka*) and in the continuum of what is not clung-to (*anupādinnaka*).
Regarding them in the continuum of what is not clung-to, it is said: "Two hundred thousand and forty nahutas—so much is this earth reckoned in terms of thickness."

By this method, "great manifestation" is explained. Even within the continuum of what is clung-to (*upādinnaka*), it should be understood by way of the bodies of fish, crocodiles, and tortoises measuring many hundreds of *yojanas*, as well as the bodies of devas, dānavas, and so forth.
For it has been said: "Bhikkhus, there are in the great ocean individual existences (*attabhāva*) measuring even a hundred *yojanas," and so on.
They are called "great beings" (*mahābhūta*) because they are great beings by virtue of displaying many extraordinary qualities and by virtue of being seen as many beings.

They are called "great beings" (*mahābhūtā*) because they possess great wonders; or, they are called "great beings" because they are great by their very nature as illusionists, *yakkhas*, and so forth.
Because these [four elements] are equal to them, they are "equal to the great beings.
For just as illusionists display water that is not a gem as a gem, or display clods of earth and the like that are not gold as gold, so too—

And just as they themselves, being neither spirits nor birds, manifest the state of being spirits and so forth, even so, while not being blue themselves, they manifest derived matter that is blue; while not being yellow...

[and so on] ...while not being white themselves, they manifest derived matter that is white. Thus, because of their commonality with the great elements of a magician, they are called "great elements."

And just as when yakkhas or great spirits seize someone, no location for them is found either inside the body or outside the body, yet they do not remain without depending on his various limbs and members.

For if they were situated inside the body, there would be no pervasion throughout the entire body; and if they were situated outside, then the wholesome or unwholesome action performed by one seized by a yakkha [would not be possible].

It would not belong to the *yakkha*. Furthermore, if they did not abide supported by each of its limbs, then when one possessed by a *yakkha* is struck, the arising of painful feeling in the *yakkha* would not occur, nor would there be the appearance of streaks on the body.
Since all this exists, therefore those [limbs] have no determinable location; in the same way, these [elements] are neither inside nor outside of one another.
They are found to exist, yet they do not stand without depending upon one another.

For if they were situated inside one another, they would be unable to perform their respective functions because of their mutual penetration. If, on the other hand, they were situated outside one another, they would be separate entities;
and if that were the case, the doctrine of inseparability (*avinibbhoga*) would be abandoned. Therefore...
"Points that cannot be specified. Because they are equal to the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*) in being non-perceptible entities (*yakkha*), they are "equal to the great primaries.
Furthermore, although these points cannot be specified, they assist the other three [primary elements] through their respective specific functions such as providing a foundation;
thus, acting as conditions by way of the co-nascent condition (*sahajātapaccaya*) and others, they exist only in mutual dependence upon one another.
Because they deceive by means of the unreal—that is, because they deceive beings through the unreal and untrue [attribution] of pleasing color, shape, and so forth, like female *yakkhas* and others;
and because great unrealities are found within them, they are designated as "great elements" (*mahābhūta*).
For just as female *yakkhas* and others [deceive] with pleasing colors such as black or brown, with shapes such as broad, stout, or emaciated, and with gestures of hands, eyebrows, and so on...
And just as they deceive beings by concealing their own terrifying nature and bring them under their control,

so too these [beings] conceal their own bodily characteristics such as harshness by means of a pleasing complexion in women, men, and others, by a pleasing configuration of limbs and members, and by a pleasing movement of hands, feet, fingers, and eyebrows.
They deceive foolish people; not allowing them to see their true nature, they bring them under their own control.

Regarding the phrases "the eye and the ear," etc., "form" itself is *rūpatā*. As for "the heart and its physical basis (*vatthu*) for the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element," it is called the "heart-basis" (*hadayavatthu*);
or, it is the "basis for consciousness in the heart," hence the "heart-basis. [The term is formed] by the elision of the first member of the compound.
“Basis” (vatthu) has been stated. Edible food itself is what constitutes the state of being food (āhāratā).

Although edible food was listed at the end in the description of matter (rūpaniddesa) in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, here it is listed immediately after the heart-basis for the purpose of showing the derived forms (nipphannarūpa) in a single location.
Those beginning with lightness (lahutā), namely softness (mudutā) and wieldiness (kammaññatā), are called “lightness and so forth” (lahutādayo).

Among those, there is this triad beginning with lightness (*lahutā*). Therein, the state of being light is lightness; likewise for softness (*mudutā*). That which is good for action is "actionable" (*kammañña*);

the state of that is "actionability" (*kammaññatā*). Because lightness and the others are themselves unmanifested, the qualification "of matter" (*rūpassa*) is employed to show that they are modifications of manifested matter.
"Twenty-four" is the delimitation by number; [this refers to] the powerful forms and so forth.
It has the sense of precluding. Regarding this, what ought to be said will be made clear later. "Depending" means depending indeed, and not even by way of support.
Because his mind has emerged from the four kinds of clinging (*upādāna*) due to being free from them, he is one whose mind is without clinging (*nirupādānamānaso*).

"631-2. *Patthaṭattā* means because of its extension (*puthuttā*). By virtue of that state of being extended (*puthubhāvato*), it is *puthavī*; through the method of etymology (*niruttinayena*), the derivation of the word *pathavī* as "the earth" (*pathavī eva*) is thus illustrated.
This, however, applies to the earth as a mass of material components (*sambhāra-pathavi*), for that is what has become extensive and spread out.

But with respect to the earth as a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa-pathavi*), it is *pathavī* in the sense of "spreading out" (*pathanaṭṭhena*), by way of being the foundation for co-nascent material phenomena."
"Appears" (*pakkhāyati*) means "manifests" (*upaṭṭhāti*). Alternatively, the former meaning [of "appears"] is also applicable by way of the earth of characteristics (*lakkhaṇapathavī*).

"From blowing" (*vāyanato*) means from moving; the meaning is that it causes the aggregate of the primary elements (*bhūtasaṅghāṭa*) to reach other locations by acting as the cause for their arising in different places.

"It heats" (*tejeti*) means it ripens or it settles; the meaning is that by its sharpness, it warms the remaining triad of primary elements. This is due to the requirements of the metrical composition of the verse.
And here, due to the elision of the word *iti*, it is stated simply as “it heats” (*tejeti*). It is the same in the case of “it pervades” (*āpeti*).
Therefore, that which heats is fire (*tejo*), and that which pervades is water (*āpo*)—this is what is meant. It pervades and extends to the limit of the material form that is to be protected;
thus, it is called the “function of binding. That which is pervaded is water (*āpo*). It is dried up and drunk.

Some say "it is the meaning. However, they maintain that this meaning is appropriate in terms of its constituent parts (*sasambhārāpe*), and it is indeed appropriate even in terms of its characteristic (*lakkhaṇāpe*).

For even that [characteristic] occurs as if being drunk by the other three elements through the mode of maturing and drying what is harsh. Or, it is called *āpo* because it nourishes (*āpāyati*); the meaning is that it causes growth or increase.
For such is its nature of causing full development (*paribrūhanarasa*). "Of those" refers to those previously mentioned.
“Of material phenomena derived from the primary elements (bhūta-upādāya-bheda-rūpa). I shall speak”—that is, I will explain. For what reason? He says:

“In [the exposition of] characteristics and so forth,” etc. The word *hi* has the sense of a cause (*hetu*). Since the phenomena (*dhamma*) will become manifest when their characteristics and so forth are known, the meaning is: “therefore, they are the causes for the manifestation of those [phenomena] hereafter.”

633–4. To resolve this objection—“Which, then, are those things called characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), functions (*rasa*), manifestations (*paccupaṭṭhāna*), and proximate causes (*padaṭṭhāna*), by knowing which the [other] phenomena will become clear?”—he says, beginning with “Or, the commonality (*sāmañña*)...”, while explaining the characteristics, functions, manifestations, and proximate causes according to their essential nature.

*Commonality* (*sāmañña*) is that which is shared, such as impermanence (*anicca*) and so forth. *Intrinsic nature* (*sabhāva*) is that which is specific to each phenomenon, such as hardness or the quality of touching and so forth.
*Asādhāraṇabhāvo*: the uncommon state. *Kiccaṃ*: the function, such as the function of supporting and so forth. *Sampatti*: the state of perfection.
For in passages such as "the fragrance has a delicious taste," because the perfection of the fragrance is expressed by the word "taste," perfection is called "taste.

*Phalaṃ*: the fruit existing as both co-nascent and non-momentary. *Upaṭṭhānanayo*: the mode of presentation to knowledge by way of being something to be grasped. *Āsannakāraṇaṃ*: the proximate cause, that is, the primary cause.
It is called a *lakkhaṇa* (characteristic) because one is characterized by it; it is "having hardness as its characteristic" (*kakkhaḷattalakkhaṇā*) because hardness is its characteristic.
But is it not the case that hardness itself is the earth-element? This is true.

Nevertheless, even though phenomena are undifferentiated insofar as they possess the status of being objects known or unknown through consciousness, this description is made by means of a distinction established through conceptual construction (*kappanā*). For in this way, there is an understanding of the specific meaning.

"Is" (hoti). Alternatively, it is called a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) because it is characterized (*lakkhīyati*); thus, the meaning here should be understood as: "the element that is characterized by being hard is the characteristic of hardness. The same method applies to the others as well.
"Having the function of supporting" (*patiṭṭhānarasa*) means having the activity of providing a basis for co-nascent phenomena.
Even for those not co-nascent, there is indeed the state of being a basis by way of their continuity (*santati*). For this very reason...
It is "manifesting as reception" because it presents itself to knowledge in the mode of receiving [the object].
By this, he shows that "manifestation" (*paccupaṭṭhāna*) here is used in the sense of function (*kicca*). As for the "footing" (*padaṭṭhāna*), he will explain all four together later.
It has "trickling" as its characteristic because, due to its state of fluidity, it has the characteristic of oozing. It has "nourishing" as its function toward co-nascent states.
Its function is to bring about a state of union without giving [the factors] away; for it is said that it shows their state of being satisfied.

Its manifestation is as a means of integration (*saṅgahapaccupaṭṭhāna*), because—like external water with bathing powder—it manifests by way of gathering together, not allowing the co-nascent states to be scattered.
Its essence is maturation (*paripācanarasa*), meaning its essence is to cause the state of being fully developed.
"Manifesting as the provision of softness" means that, like an external fire, it manifests as the provision of softness for the co-nascent phenomena such as the vital heat (*jatuloha*).
"Having the characteristic of distension" means having the characteristic of filling out. "Having the function of moving" means having the function of shaking.

"Projection" (*abhinīhāra*) is the state of being the cause for the arising of the three primary elements (*bhūta*) in another location, or else it is the carrying forth [of the result], like the sprout and so on from a seed. Each one... [and so on] ...should be understood accordingly.
The earth element has the other three elements—water and so forth—as its proximate cause; the water element has the other three elements—earth, fire, and so forth—as its proximate cause.
Thus, each individual element has the remaining three elements as its proximate cause.
For when this body is examined in the middle portion according to its height and circumference, it is seen to be pulverized into a mass of atomic particles.
The earth element may consist of as much fine dust as a single *doṇa* measure.
And this is held together by way of cohesion, so that it does not scatter, even when the water element is present in a quantity measuring half of that.
Furthermore, just as it does not reach a state of being moistened or slimy through the influence of the water element, which has the nature of trickling, so too is it sustained by the fire element.
However, so that it does not scatter by virtue of that [cohesion], it is made into a cohesive mass by the air element through its expansion.
Thus, even when reduced to fine dust, these flour-particles— having received conditions from the water, fire,
and air elements whose functions are binding, maturing, and moving— are moistened by moisture, matured by heat, and expanded by air.

It does not scatter or disintegrate here and there; and while not scattering or disintegrating, it assumes various distinctions of state such as the characteristics of male and female, and it manifests states such as minute, gross, long, short, firm, and hard.
Furthermore, the water element herein, which exists in the form of a viscous cohesion, is supported by earth, sustained by fire, and expanded by air.

It does not ooze, it does not leak, it does not flow out. Thus, being guarded by the three elements, not leaking and not flowing out, it demonstrates its state of being consolidated. For this [element] has the function of intensifying.
And herein, the fire element—matured by what is eaten, drunk, and so forth, consisting of the mode of heat, characterized by warmth—is established upon the earth element.
Sustained by water and distended by air, this body is maintained and it brings about excellence of complexion.
For, by properly digesting the food as it is consumed, it becomes the cause for the excellence of the nutritive essence (*rasa*) and so forth;
thus it maintains this body and brings about excellence of complexion. Indeed, [this occurs] through the support of karma, caused by clarity of mind.

Furthermore, the fire element (*tejodhātu*) is a specific condition for the perfection of color in the body, let alone for the excellence of matter produced by temperature (*utu*) and nutriment (*āhāra*).
Ripe by means of that [fire element], this body does not fall into a state of putrefaction.
And here, the air element (*vāyodhātu*), characterized by motion and distension, pervades the various limbs within the earth element (*pathavīdhātu*).
It is established. Just as it is not separate from its co-nascent states, so it is gathered together by the water element.
Just as the co-nascent states do not leak away, so it is sustained by the fire element.
Thus, being appropriately sustained by these three elements, it distends this body. And by that [distension], it is distended...
This body does not fall over; it stands upright. Thus, because each single element functions by way of the other three elements, it is said:
"And herein, each one should be understood as having the remaining triad of primary elements as its proximate cause.
Having thus shown the characteristics and so forth of the primary material phenomena together with their etymological explanations, the derived material phenomena are now [to be discussed].
Showing this, he says "it sees" (*cakkhati*), and so forth. Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, and considering that the word *cakkhati* can also have the sense of "discerning," it is stated:

"the meaning is 'it discerns'. Furthermore, "it sees" means that, as if indicating what is even or uneven, or as if speaking with clarity, consciousness becomes manifest. Alternatively, "it sees" means...
The meaning is that form, being presided over by consciousness, is as if it were relishing.
For this word *cakkhati* has the sense of "relishing," as in such expressions as "he relishes honey" (*madhuṃ cakkhati*) or "he relishes the sauce" (*byañjanaṃ cakkhati*). Indeed, this has been said:
"The eye, Māgaṇḍiya, delights in forms, rejoices in forms, and exults in forms. And he will say later: "It has the function of attracting among forms."

If this is so, does it not follow that since the ear and the other [faculties] also possess the quality of finding gratification in sounds and so forth—according to such statements as, "The ear, Māgaṇḍiya, delights in sounds"—they too must be designated by the term "eye"?
It does not follow, because the term is used in its conventional sense (*nirūḷha*).
For this word "eye" is conventionally established for the visual organ alone, just as words like "lotus-born" are established for lotuses and the like.

635–6. Even in the section explaining the eye and visible form (*cakkhurūpa*), everything that comes under the general term "eye" is presented in its various divisions by saying, "In this context, the eye... and so forth. "In this context" (*tattha*) means in that explanation of the eye.

"By way of the division into wisdom and flesh" (*paññāmaṃsappabhedato*) means by way of the distinction between the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*) and the eye of flesh (*maṃsacakkhu*). "In this context" (*tattha*) refers to those two kinds.
"In the eye": "consisting of wisdom" means it is wisdom itself. "By names" is connected with "fivefold by names.
To the question "By which names?", he says: "the qualities of a Buddha," and so forth.
Therein, "by the names 'Buddha-eye,' 'Dhamma-eye,' and 'Universal-eye'" refers to these names. "By the names 'Knowledge-eye' and 'Divine-eye'" refers to those names as well. "In due order" means:
According to the sequence already stated. "Nānatta" means diversity or distinction. "Me" means from me, or the meaning is "my word.
"Nibodhatha" means understand or know.
637. In that context: "Bhikkhus, while surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, I saw beings with little dust in their eyes..."
Showing that what is described in the passage beginning with “one of great defilement, with sharp faculties” is called the Buddha-eye, he says:

“In the underlying tendencies and latent dispositions,” and so forth. Therein, “in the underlying tendencies and latent dispositions” means in both the underlying tendencies (*āsaya*) and the latent dispositions (*anusaya*) of sentient beings; the meaning is that [the eye] operates therein.
Therein, it is called an *āsaya* because the mind comes and rests (*seti*) there, like a tiger’s lair (*byagghāsaya*). For just as a tiger, for the sake of its prey...
Even after having departed, it returns again and lies down in the very same dense forest; for that reason, that place is called its "abode.
In the same way, wherever the mind, though active elsewhere, returns and lies down, that should be understood as its abode.
Furthermore, it is fourfold by way of the view of eternalism and so forth. For this has been said:

“Eternalism and annihilationism views, as well as conformable patience, and that knowledge which is according to reality—this is designated as ‘disposition. The discussion on latent tendencies (*anusaya*) will follow later.
Regarding the “superiority and inferiority of the faculties”: this refers to the five faculties beginning with faith.
Regarding "sharpness and softness": the faculty is sharp because it has reached the highest degree; it is soft because it has not reached that highest degree.
Furthermore, this Buddha-eye should be understood as being the first two among the six unique knowledges (*asādhāraṇañāṇa*).
638. Regarding "below... pe ... perceiving": [this refers to] "on that very seat, the dustless, stainless Eye of Dhamma arose."

Thus it was stated above that knowledge in the three paths is designated as the "Dhamma-eye. As for "knowledge of omniscience," this refers to the knowledge characterized as the state of being all-knowing (*sabbaññubhāva*).
For that [knowledge] is called the "state of omniscience" because it serves as the basis for the application of the designation "all-knower" (*sabbaññū*) and for the function of the intellect.
"The eye of universal vision" refers to that which sees everything completely and from all sides by way of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth.
It should be understood that in the sense of seeing, he is the "all-around eye.
For this very reason it was said: "There is nothing here in this world unseen by him, nor anything unknown or not comprehended."
“The Tathāgata has directly known all that is to be known;
therefore, he possesses the universal eye.
