(Dhp 182) Regarding the phrase “the eye that arose,” it is said to have come down [in the tradition] as that knowledge: “Bhikkhus, ‘This is suffering’—this was not heard by me before... (SN 22.57).

The "eye of knowledge" (*ñāṇacakkhu*) is that which has arisen in various suttas as "the eye arose regarding phenomena, knowledge arose," occurring in twelve modes through the three turnings regarding the four truths, such as "suffering is to be fully understood; it has been fully understood.
Furthermore, that which [is expressed as] "I saw, monks, with the divine... [is the divine eye].

To show that the wisdom associated with the consciousness of direct knowledge (abhiññā) termed the fifth jhāna—as described in the passage beginning with "with the purified eye"—is what is called the "divine eye" (dibbacakkhu), the words "born of the consciousness of direct knowledge" and so forth were stated.

Furthermore, regarding this, the first and third knowledges are exclusively of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). However, the teacher Ānanda has stated that the fourth [knowledge] is also of the sense-sphere, just like the preceding two.

Others say that it is also appropriate to call the eye of knowledge "the insight-knowledge of the noble path. However, it appears more fitting to call it "the knowledge of the reviewing of insight together with the supreme path.
(640–4) Having thus shown the divisions of the eye of wisdom, [the author] now shows the divisions of the fleshly eye as well.

“‘The fleshly eye,’ and so forth, has been stated. Regarding ‘together with its constituent parts’ (*sasambhāra*): the ‘constituent part eye’ (*pasādacakkhu*) and the ‘fleshly eye’ (*maṃsacakkhu*)—by way of these two, they are called ‘constituents’ (*sambhārā*) because they are brought together by them;
these are the components. Furthermore, these should be understood as the material continuities (*rūpasantati*) arising from the four [great] primaries that serve as their support.
Together with the constituents is ‘with its constituents’ (*sasambhāra*). And [this refers to] that which is with its constituents...”
The connection is: "it is called a lump of flesh. The connection is: "below the bone of the eye-socket" means it is demarcated by the bone situated below the eye-socket.
"Above" means above the eye-socket. "On both sides by the corners of the eyes" means by the corners of the eyes on both sides of the eye-socket.
"Internally by the brain" means inside the eye-socket.
"With the brain remaining" means that it is bound together with the brain inside by means of the cords of sinews (*nahārurajjūhi*).
"The entire world" refers to the whole world of foolish worldlings (*bālaputhujjana*). "That" refers to that lump of flesh.
"Like a lotus petal" means like the petal of a blue lotus due to its broad, expansive blueness. "He knows" means he perceives. The eye.
"It is not called that" means that when it is apprehended in such a way, it is not what is called "the eye. If one asks, "What then is it?
he says: "It is called its basis. "Its" refers to that intended ultimate-sense eye. "But this," however, is the conclusion. 645–7.
Furthermore, as for that composite eye, those constituents by which it is composed [should be understood] both by their specific nature and by their enumeration.
And in order to demonstrate this, the passage beginning with "color and odor" was stated. "State" (bhāva) refers to the female state in a woman and the male state in a man;
it is the state that is currently present. "Origin" (sambhava) refers specifically to the water element as the source of origin.
"Shape" (saṇṭhāna) refers to the sense-sphere of visible form (vaṇṇāyatana) as it is perceived through its respective shape among the great elements arranged in those various ways.

The separate mention of "origination" (sambhava) and "shape" (saṇṭhāna), even though they are not distinct entities from the water element (āpodhātu) and the color-base (vaṇṇāyatana), is because such states—whether existing as such or not—as well as the water element and so forth, are found within the aforementioned lump of flesh.
For when the water element and the color-base proceed by way of a continuum, their particular stages are termed "origination" and "shape. "Ten" refers to the four [elements].
The elements and the visible forms and so forth dependent upon them—these ten. The qualification "arising from four [causes]" is included for the purpose of specifying the internal causes;
what is meant is that they arise from all four causes.

(648) The eye... and so forth... up to life itself—these are exclusively kamma-born; and since the preceding ones arise from four causes, there are forty-four material phenomena (*rūpa*). This is the meaning: there are forty-four material phenomena.
649–52. "By way of these material phenomena" means by way of the fourteen material phenomena mentioned in brief, or the forty-four in detail.
"Composed as a whole" (paripiṇḍita) means gathered together from all sides.
Where there is white, black, red, earth, water, fire, and air—this [body], however, is so called because of its abundance of phlegm (semha).
It is white because of the predominance of bile; it is black because of the predominance of blood; it is bloody-red because of the predominance of blood;

it is parched because of the predominance of earth; it trickles because of the predominance of water; it burns because of the predominance of fire; and it flickers because of the predominance of wind.
This is what is proclaimed and elucidated by the wise, such as the Buddhas and others, as the "eye of constituent parts" (sambhāracakkhu) due to its possession of constituent parts.
"Dependent on this white" (*ettha sito*) means it is supported by the eye together with its constituent parts, being dependent upon them. Therefore he said, "bound to this.
Regarding "the clarity of the four primary elements" (*catunnaṃ bhūtānaṃ pasādo*): clarity (*pasāda*) is the nature of the lucidity of the four primary elements;
thus the reading "by means of its white circle" (*setena maṇḍalena assā*) is appropriate. However, in the manuscripts they write, "but in her two white circles" (*sete tu maṇḍale tassā*).

Regarding the phrase *kaṇhamaṇḍalamajjhe*: here too, although one should have said “in the middle of the black circle” (*kaṇhamaṇḍalassa majjhe*), the case ending has been elided for the sake of metrical convenience—as in the case of “the fourth [dhyāna]” (*catutthadū*) and so forth—and thus it is stated as *kaṇhamaṇḍalamajjhe*.

For in this way, both the meaning and the grammatical construction become perfectly appropriate. Indeed, even in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), it says: “of that which is surrounded by a white circle... (*setamaṇḍalaparikkhittassa*).
"In the middle of the black circle," it is said. However, others, taking the reading exactly as it stands, connect it thus:
"In the white circle in the middle of that eye together with its constituent parts which is completely surrounded, [and] in the middle of the black circle.
"In the visible circle" means in the visible circle that serves as the location for the arising of the bodily configuration of those standing directly in front.

"Having become a support... and so forth... "having rendered assistance by means of the four elements that serve as its own basis—possessing the functions of supporting, binding, maturing, and moving—just as a prince is supported by the four nurses whose functions are holding, bathing, adorning, and fanning.
"By temperature, mind, and so forth" refers to the three—temperature, mind, and nutriment—that originate the continuity.

And here they say that temperature and nutriment included within other groups are intended. "Preservation by means of vitality" means being protected by the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) which is itself dependent upon the four elements; for such is its characteristic of preserving matter born of karma.

By the phrase "by color, odor, taste, etc.," the word "etc. includes nutritive essence (*oja*); alternatively, the reading is "by color, odor, taste, and nutritive essence. And they establish the basis and the door.

It establishes its status as a basis (*vatthu*) and a door (*dvāra*) according to what is appropriate. For it establishes the status of being a basis for eye-consciousness by way of being its support (*nissaya*), and its status of being a door by way of being the gateway for its occurrence.

However, for the [mental states] beginning with the receiving consciousness and ending with those having that same object, because they do not depend on that [eye], it establishes only their status as a door, not their status as a basis. "With a measure equal to the head of a louse" means...
The meaning is that it is marked by a surface-measure equal to the head of a louse, or that it stands in a place of a measure equal to the head of a louse.
It "stands" in the sense that it pervades the seven layers of the eye-films (paṭala), remaining like oil poured upon seven cotton-pads.
By doing so, the fact that the eye consists of many components is established. Even when [the eye] is afflicted, the removal of the films [is possible].

For indeed, the eye exists. And just as the eye [exists], so too its four supporting elements and the seven ocular membranes—such as vitality, color, and the rest—should be understood as existing only by pervading [the eye] and functioning inseparably.

"It was said" means it was said by the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta). In the phrase "he perceives visible forms," the letter *m* serves to facilitate the euphonic junction (*sandhi*) of the words.
This is as in such expressions as “the ascetics and recluses [are] mutually [dependent]” (*aññamaññaṃ samaṇamacalo*). Alternatively, *manu* means “mortal” (*maccu*).

Although the eye does not see form, what indeed sees it? It is consciousness alone which is dependent upon it. For just as in such expressions as “the beds are making a noise,” where the activity of that which is supported is figuratively attributed to the support itself because such conventional usage is possible, one says, “he sees by means of the clarity of the eye” (*cakkhupasādena passati*).
It has been stated. Indeed, it was with this very intention that the Elder Ācariya Jotipāla also said this. This is the definitive conclusion here:
does the eye see the form, or rather, does consciousness? What is the point here? If the eye were to see, then even one possessing another consciousness would see with the eye.
Or if it were consciousness, would it not see even what is screened by a wall and so forth, because of its non-obstructive nature?
This is not a fault. For one who holds the view that "the eye sees," it is not the case that the entire eye sees;
rather, it is only that which is presided over by consciousness (viññāṇa) that sees. Furthermore, for one who holds the view that "consciousness sees," it is not the case that all consciousness sees;
rather, it is only that which is dependent on the eye, and that does not arise with respect to what is obstructed. Where there is light...

Where there is an obstruction by walls and the like, [visual consciousness] does not arise; however, where such an obstruction is absent—as in the case of crystal, clouds, or a layer of mist—it certainly arises even when the object is screened off.
Therefore, because it has not arisen, one does not see what is screened off. This alone is the definitive conclusion:
that visual consciousness sees. For that is its function of seeing. If this is so, how is it [said] "by means of the eye"?
"Having seen a form": the intended meaning here is "by means of that [eye] acting as the instrument.
Alternatively, an action dependent on a support is expressed by the name of that support, as in "the beds are making a noise. "Resembling the head of a louse" means similar to the head of a louse;
what is meant is that it is the size of a louse's head. This is stated with reference to its place of residence, but not with respect to its own [actual] size.
By way of measure: for that [materiality] is indeed exceedingly subtle by measure, having the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) as its limit.
However, this [consciousness-originated materiality] occurs in a location the size of a louse's head.

And not only this alone, but all materialities with universal bases (*sabbatthānika-rūpa*) occur there as well. And this, when being produced there, is produced only after filling that location. By way of forty-nine groups (*kalāpa*).

And it proceeds simultaneously because material phenomena have a lifespan of seventeen mind-moments, and because kamma-born material phenomena arise during each of the three phases of every single consciousness-moment. 657.
Regarding the statement "it hears, therefore it is the ear": here, does the ear hear, or is it consciousness? This is to be understood according to the method explained below.

It should be applied according to the circumstances. "Thickly covered with fine tawny-colored hairs" means accumulated within the ear canal along with its constituent parts by fine hairs of a tawny color.

"In a place shaped like a finger-ring" refers to the region of flesh shaped like a finger-ring. "Of the aforementioned kind" refers to those [faculties] whose functions consist of sustaining and so forth.
"Being maintained by vitality" (āyu) refers here to [the faculties] such as color-form (vaṇṇa) and the rest.
"Surrounded" (parivārita) should be understood as being connected [to the preceding]. "It stands" (tiṭṭhati) means it stands filling that location in the manner previously described.
The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated. "It smells" (ghāyati) means it takes up fragrance. "It tastes" (sāyati) means it experiences flavor.
Regarding the phrase "it summons life" (jīvitam avhāyati): because swallowing is rooted in the apprehension of flavor, the flavor of swallowing serves as the cause for life.
"Life": it calls out because of its inclination toward that [life]; thus, it is as if it is calling out.

"In a place shaped like the tip of a lotus petal" means in a location having the shape of the upper part of a lotus petal cut in the middle. "Of stains" refers to the stains of the defilements (*kilesa*) and so forth, as well as the tainted phenomena (*sāsava-dhamma*) which are the objects of those stains;
these arise from karma produced by the root-cause of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) in those who have attained the state of unsurpassed excellence.
Among the specific conditions for sensual lust (*kāmarāga*), among the nose, tongue, and body, it is the body in particular that serves as a condition associated with the taints (*sāsava*);
therefore, it alone is called their "home. For it is by means of it that beings, relishing the pleasure of touch, even engage in sexual intercourse.
Alternatively, the four aggregates based on the physical faculty of the body are specifically "stains" because they serve as powerful causes for sensual lust and the like.
This "source" (*āya*) of theirs is called the "body" (*kāya*). In the phrase "in this body," it means in this body together with its constituent parts.
For that too is called a "body" because it is the source (*āya*) of the foul things such as hair, filth, and so forth.

By the words "as far as there is anything clung-to (*upādinnaka*)," he indicates the absence of the sensitive matter of the body (*kāyapasāda*) in the tips of the hair, the tips of the nails, and so on. By the phrase "like oil in a cotton pad," he...

...a state of uninterrupted continuity. Furthermore, these [faculties] such as the eye, because they are inclined toward their respective domains of form and so forth—just as snakes, crocodiles, birds, dogs, and jackals are inclined toward their respective domains known as anthills, water, the sky, villages, and charnel grounds—should be viewed accordingly.
For, due to its uneven disposition, the eye is like a snake that delights in the holes of an anthill;
due to its inclination toward hollows, the ear is like a crocodile that delights in water-hollows; and due to its inclination toward space, the nose is...
The eye is like a bird that delights in the cloudless sky; the tongue is like a village-dwelling dog because of its inclination toward the village;

and the body is like a jackal that delights in a raw charnel ground because of its inclination toward what is clung-to (*upādinnaka*). It is stated [in the text] "due to an uneven inclination" (*visamajjhāsayatāya*) with reference to the fact that the eye has an uneven inclination.
Or else, the eye of a person possessing eyes has an uneven inclination by way of their own disposition (*ajjhāsayavasena*). This same method applies to the remaining [faculties] as well.
Regarding the phrase "having seen... [the marks]": here, "desirous of seeing" (*daṭṭhukāmo*) means one who wishes to see; the state of being that is "desire to see" (*daṭṭhukāmatā*).

This is a designation for craving for form (*rūpataṇhā*). Furthermore, it is twofold: manifest and unmanifest. Its nature is a yearning rooted in ignorance that conceals the danger (*ādīnava*) in the future regarding the eye and so forth.
Among these, this [craving] which thinks, "Such and such a thing is subtle and capable of perceiving objects... [is the manifest].
They are evident as having arisen either before or after the accumulation of karma with the thought, "May there be an eye. However, for one who performs karma—
either by aspiring for the excellence of a complete sense base (*paripuṇṇāyatana-bhava-sampatti*) without specifying a particular faculty,

or by performing it without such aspiration through the persistence of craving therein— the latent tendencies (*anusaya*), due to their state of being unabandoned, serve as the diverse causes consisting in the efficacy of that karma.

It is unmanifest. That [unmanifest] is twofold: that which has as its cause (nidāna) and its decisive support (upanissaya) the desire to see—that very same kamma—and that which has that as its origin (samuṭṭhāna), are thus "originated by kamma whose cause is the desire to see" (daṭṭhukāmatā-nidāna-kamma-samuṭṭhānāni).
The clarity (pasāda) of such primary elements (bhūta) is the "desire to see"... [etc. ...the clarity;

it has that as its characteristic (lakkhaṇa), or it is characterized as being thus, hence it is "characterized by the clarity of the primary elements originated by kamma whose cause is the desire to see."
And here, for those born from a womb, it should be understood that either the karma that provides the rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) or another [karma] produces the eye and other faculties.

However, for those of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*) who are produced with fully developed sense bases at the very moment of rebirth-linking, it should be understood that the very same karma which generates the rebirth-linking produces the entire individual existence (*mattabhāva*) in its fullness. But how can this be by means of a single karma?
Is there a distinction among the eye and other faculties as they arise? Yes, because their causes are different.

For craving—which consists of the aspiration for this or that state of existence—being itself diverse in form due to its longing for the sense bases included within those respective existences, establishes a corresponding diversity in the karma that produces those various existences by way of being their decisive support (*upanissaya*). Consequently, through the possession of such capacity, that [karma] is endowed with specific distinctions.
It produces a fruit that appears as if it has assumed many forms and possesses many distinct intrinsic natures;

yet here, this capacity should not be understood as something other than the nature of being capable or incapable. This point should be accepted because a single action, having acquired specific distinctions through particular causes, possesses the capacity to produce a distinguished fruit, and because it serves as the cause for the production of sixteen or more types of results.
Even in the world, it is observed that a single grain of rice is the cause for the production of both full and incomplete grains.
But what is the use of this investigation into logic? This should not even be investigated.

For the fruit of karma, such as the eye and so forth, and the ripening of karma, are entirely within the range of the Buddhas' knowledge alone, and not within the range of others, because they lie beyond the scope of mere reasoning. Therefore, by the Blessed One:

Having shown the danger with such words as, “The ripening of kamma is inconceivable; it should not be speculated upon. Whoever should speculate upon it would partake of madness and frustration,” [the Buddha] rejected [speculation].

Regarding the phrase “in forms, the function of drawing in”: the drawing in belongs to the person, or rather to the consciousnesses such as adverting, by virtue of their attaining a state of being inclined toward that [object].
It is the state of being a cause. It has the state of being a support as its manifestation because it functions as a dependence-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*).
For even though visual consciousness sometimes arises in dependence on light and so forth, at the moment of its arising, it arises only in dependence upon the eye.

Here it may be asked: among the forty-nine eyes that come into existence at the time of the arising of visual consciousness—whether they have short, very short, or medium life-spans—[which one is the support?]
What is it that experiences the state of being the support for eye-consciousness? It is said:
At the moment of arising of the rebirth-linking consciousness, the second bhavaṅga arises depending upon the pre-arisen, established, and pre-existent basis (vatthu);
together with that [second bhavaṅga], depending upon the pre-arisen, established, and pre-existent basis that has arisen [simultaneously].
The third life-continuum (bhavaṅga) arises; in this manner, the occurrence of consciousness should be understood to continue for as long as the lifespan lasts.

According to the method stated in the *Niddesa* on the Knowledge of What is the Path and What is Not the Path: when the eye, having struck a visible form, becomes the support for consciousness after one mind-moment has passed, then, due to the preceding life-continuum consciousness acting as the immediately preceding condition (*anantara-paccaya*) among two flickerings of the life-continuum—
The meaning of "arising together" (*saha-uppanna*) has been stated here in the Sihaḷa-ṭīkā [Commentary] on the *Visuddhimagga*.
However, the Elder Dāṭhānāga, who resided at Mūlagāma in Taḷāka, stated:

"The eye arises together with either the adverting consciousness or the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), which serves as its immediate condition (*anantarapaccaya*). This is poorly stated; for if that were the case, in another instance...
It would follow that when [the door] is struck, it becomes the support for another eye-consciousness;

and in that case, even that which has arisen together with the thirteenth consciousness, starting from below the movement of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) through the third and fourth [consciousnesses], would become a support.
But this should not be said, because [it is only] for certain process-consciousnesses (vīthicitta) arising from the third and fourth consciousnesses onward [that this applies].
It does not become a door because it has already ceased; for the door-state of the mind-door is seen only when it has ceased.

If it is argued that—on account of such statements as "the second bhavaṅga arises depending on the physical basis (vatthu) arisen at the moment of the arising of the rebirth-linking consciousness"—"what is intended by 'support' is that which has passed away by even a single citta-moment," then this too [would be] one that has passed away by a single citta-moment.

Regarding the statement "it is logical as a support" (*nissaya*): if this were so, then the expression "by means of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) which has become its immediately preceding condition" would be logical;
for by that, it would have been admitted that "even two thought-moments past can be a support.

Therefore, it appears that this is not the Elder’s intended meaning. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "transcending one thought-moment," [it refers to] a single thought-moment that has not yet passed.
This is stated for the purpose of demonstrating its strength by showing that it lasts beyond a single moment of consciousness due to its weakness;

it is not, however, because there is an absence of a supporting condition (*nissaya*) for those [moments] that have passed through two, three, or four moments of consciousness. And having established this, it was said by the Venerable Ācariya Dhammapāla Thera:

"The reception-mind and the others [that follow] are near to death; beyond that, because the matter born of karma (*kammaja-rūpa*) does not arise, [the rebirth-linking mind] exists in only one [moment]."
"occur in the heart-base (hadayavatthu). Therefore, one should not consider that to be the Elder’s own considered opinion.
Among the many co-nascent translucent elements (pasāda), is there only one support, or are they all [supports]? Has it not been stated:
"Previously, even a single eye was a condition for visual consciousness"? But which [text] is that? It is that which states: "Whichever among them is most prominent..."

Having offered [this] which is worthy of being struck against by forms (*rūpa*). However, in the *Visuddhimagga-Ṭīkā* (Sīhaḷa-saṃvaṇṇanā), after stating, "All [the bases] indeed serve as supports," it raises the following objection:

"If that is so, then just as in the expression 'dependent on the eye and forms, visual consciousness arises' (*cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ*), there is the plural form 'forms' (*rūpe*), should one not likewise employ the plural form 'eyes' (*cakkhūni*)?"

In order to purify that [misconception], and to refute the erroneous view that "only a single consciousness arises supported by the two types of sensitivity (pasāda) which depend on the two physical eyes along with their material bases," the Blessed One did not use the plural number, but rather stated:
"The visible-object base is a condition, as an object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya), for the eye-consciousness element and for those mental states associated with it..."
It is stated that "the singular number is used in the sense of a general category (*sāmañña*), as in [the phrase] ‘condition’ (*paccayo*) and so forth.

However, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla, not accepting that very statement from the Sinhalese commentary (*Sīhaḷa-saṃvaṇṇanā*), said: "Even a single eye is a condition for consciousness, but visible form (*rūpa*) is manifold because of the distinction in its modes of being a condition. And it has been stated by us below in exactly the same way.
"Vibhāvita" (discerned): "Seeing... the proximate cause" means that those primary elements (*bhūta*) from which this sensitivity (*pasāda*) arises are themselves its proximate cause.
The meaning for the sensitivities of the ear and so forth should also be construed according to the method explained in the description of their characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), etc.
658. "Some": certain among the Mahāsaṅghikas. "The predominance of fire, etc., in the eye, etc. refers to the [predominance] of the primary elements that serve as their support.

Showing that there is a predominance of those [elements], he says, "of those with fire as the predominant factor," and so forth. Therein, "of those with fire as the predominant factor" means that although the four elements are equal in terms of their measure (*pamāṇa*), fire is predominant in terms of its function (*kicca*). The same applies to the others. Regarding "space... the rest":

the sensitivity (*pasāda*) of the elements with space as the predominant factor is the ear; of those with air as the predominant factor, it is the nose; of those with water as the predominant factor... [the tongue].
The meaning is that the tongue and the body consist of earth as designated by the term "tangible objects.
659. To those who speak thus, he asks what their answer is, saying: "But they," and so forth. He says, "Bring a sutta," meaning:
this matter cannot be accepted on the basis of your mere word alone; rather, bring a sutta that elucidates it.

For when a sutta has been brought forward, the intention is: "Having examined whether its meaning is of interpretable sense (*neyyattha*) or of definitive sense (*nītattha*), if this meaning can be understood by means of it, we shall accept it. [The phrase] "even a single sutta...
even a little" means that even while searching for a sutta here and there, one will certainly find at least a single verse-line of a sutta that elucidates that meaning.
For they will certainly not perceive it, because there exists no such discourse (suttanta) within the word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Piṭakas. 660.

If it is argued that although this meaning is not seen by way of a discourse, it is nevertheless seen through logical reasoning (yutti), [the author] says "If there were a distinction," etc., to show that even that is not the case.
For if there were a distinction among the primary elements (bhūta), how could confidence (pasāda) arise?
"It would neither exist nor not exist; what is the reason for this? He says: "For the clarity of equal primary elements has been elucidated by the ancients.
Because the clarity of equal primary elements alone has been elucidated by the ancients, and not that of unequal ones.

For it is due to the hardness of a mass where the earth element is predominant, the trickling of a mass where the water element is predominant, and the combustibility of a mass where the fire element is predominant [that such distinctions are made].
Furthermore, because the aggregate of the air element (*vāyodhātu*) is excessive, the sensitive matter (*pasāda*) is unable to become established within them;
therefore, the sensitive matter would arise only for those [elements] that are equal in their function, and not for those that are unequal.
661–2. If this is so, how is there a distinction among the sensitive matters? To this he says, "Therefore," and so forth. Because it is in the manner described...
There should be no distinction among the primary elements (*bhūta*) that serve as the basis for the translucent organs (*pasāda*).

Therefore, having completely and in every way abandoned this conceptualization of distinction—such as "this [element] is deficient" or "this is excessive"—among those elements that are the supports for the translucent organs, one should understand that the distinction among the translucent organs arises from the distinction in their respective kamma.
Just as, although there is no distinction among the primary elements, their visible forms, tastes, and so forth, are mutually dissimilar.

In this way, the eye and the other [faculties] are also mutually distinct even in the absence of any difference in their constituent elements (*bhūta*). This specific distinction, moreover, is to be understood through the particularity of karma.

For even a single act of karma, when it has resulted in the aspiration for a physical existence possessing the five sense bases, is distinct and unique to each [individual] due to its specific capacity as the cause for the distinctions of the eye and so forth. Indeed, not...
By whatever specific quality it is a condition for the eye, by that same quality it is a condition for the ear, because it has attained the status of a different faculty.

From the statement, “At the moment of rebirth-linking, sublime volition is a condition for the kamma-produced material phenomena by way of kamma-condition,” it is understood that at the moment of rebirth-linking,
a single volition serves as the kamma-condition for all kamma-produced material phenomena that exist at that time.
For when there is the arising of faculties through various volitions at that time, the *kaṭattā-rūpa* (matter produced by past action) would be reached by both limited and exalted kamma;
yet, it is established that a single rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is not produced by multiple kammic acts. Thus, it is proven that the arising of multiple faculties occurs through a single kamma.
The statement, “Indeed, there is no distinction among them due to a distinction in the primary elements (*bhūta*),” is spoken as a conclusion.

663. Thus, in order to show that even among these [types of consciousness] which are distinguished by the particularity of their kamma, there is this further distinction regarding the grasping of the object, it is said:
“In this way, among these...,” and so forth. “Grasping what is not reached” (appattagāhaka) means grasping what is not attained;

for consciousness arises with respect to objects such as visible form precisely upon its own support, without adhering to anything other than that support, because it serves as the cause for the arising of consciousness. Some, however, maintain that even this [consciousness] is “only grasping what is reached” (sampattaggāhaka).
They say this, but it is not correct, because consciousness arises even when the object is at a distance or larger [than the sense organ].
For if the eye and ear were to grasp only an object that has reached them, then regarding visual objects such as stars situated at a distance separated from the eye-organ,
or the lunar disc and so forth which are larger in size than their respective supports, and regarding auditory objects [grasped] by the ear-organ...
Furthermore, consciousness would not arise in relation to sound-objects (saddāyatana) that are produced in distant locations—

such as the sounds of the stomach or joints, those separated by layers of skin and so forth, or broad sounds such as the roar of the ocean— because the body-faculty and other faculties, which grasp objects through direct contact,
are not observed to function in such a manner.

And here one might say: "Since the functioning of a sense-faculty occurs externally to its physical basis (*adhiṭṭhāna*), it grasps whatever extent of an object falls within its reach, pervading that very mode of apprehension;

therefore, this reason—that consciousness arises because of the presence of an object at a distance or one that exceeds [the size of the faculty]—is unproven. That is not so, because the sense-faculty does not arise outside of its physical basis.
Thus they are non-existent [outside their bases]. For the sense-faculty (indriya) functions only in its own base (adhiṭṭhāna), since we observe the application of its functions there.
If it were to function outside of this, then even when the base is covered, there would be the grasping of objects;
therefore, because the eye and ear grasp objects that do not reach them only while remaining in their respective bases, this is not unestablished: "there is an interval" and "it is superior."
"And because it is the cause for the arising of consciousness. Therefore the ancients said:
"Even when engaged with all objects of experience, that which is seen among the splendors of form—the consciousness of discrete and manifold parts—is an obstacle to the grasping of the whole."

The meaning of this is as follows: when there is equality—whether in terms of connection (*saṃbandhe*) or contact (*ghaṭṭane*)—with respect to the engagement with the objects (*gocare*) of all [the sense bases] such as the eye, beginning with visible forms (*rūpa*) and so forth, because they accomplish a single function;

then, regarding those objects that are visible forms and sound-bases (*rūpa-saddāyatana*), which have become the domain [of perception], and which are separated from the eye and so forth both by distance and by being obstructed by something else, and which are large in measure—[this consciousness] arises.
That consciousness which is the visual consciousness is an obstacle to the apprehension of what is present—that is, to the grasping of what is proximate—by the eye and the ear.
Furthermore, if the eye were an apprehender of what is present, it would see even the color situated within its own orbit.
Likewise, it would see the collyrium in the eyelids, the color of the eye at the base of the eyelashes where they are touched, and even the applicator-stick of collyrium.
If it were to grasp [objects] from afar, this would not be seen; therefore, it grasps only an object situated in the very place where its support resides.

If the ear-base (*sotāyatana*) were also a grasper of what has arrived, then the sound-base (*saddāyatana*) produced by mind (*cittasamuṭṭhāna*) could never be an object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) for ear-consciousness (*sotaviññāṇa*).
For there is no arising of mind-produced things outside [the body].

And in the *Paṭṭhāna*, it is stated without qualification that "the sound-base is a condition for the ear-consciousness-element by way of object-condition," thus expressing the fact that sound is the object of ear-consciousness.

Furthermore, if the ear were a grasper of what is in contact, then because it would have to grasp [its object] only within the location of its own sense-field, there would be no determination of direction or place for sound, just as there is none for odor.
In this way, for a sound-shooter who shoots an arrow by following the sound, the arrow would fall upon his own ear;
therefore, the sound, remaining right where it arose, enters the range of the ear.
If this is so, how is it that the sounds of washermen and others situated at a distance are heard only after a long time? [This is due to] their not grasping [the object] upon arrival.
Is it not the case that there ought to be hearing simultaneously by those situated at distant and near locations?
This is not so, because of the difference in the apprehension of sound according to its degree of manifestation for those who are distant and near.

For just as in the case of the sound of speech, there is the apprehension of specific syllables and their non-apprehension by those distant and near respectively, due to the difference in the apprehension [of the sound] according to its degree of manifestation; so too, in the case of the sound of a washerman or others, for one who is near...
From the beginning until the end, as the sound gradually becomes manifest, and at the end of the distance— or even in the middle—
when it has become manifest through its accumulation, there arises for those who grasp the certainty according to how it is manifested the conceit,

"I heard quickly" or "I heard after a long time," due to the specific grasping by the mind-door impulsion (manodvārika-javana) that occurs subsequent to the ear-consciousness process (sotaviññāṇa-vīthi). This is the occurrence of ear-consciousness.
However, in both cases, because the sound reaches the range of hearing at the very moment it exists while situated in the place where it has arisen.
If there is no propagation of the sound through a series of material elements (bhūta-paramparā) in all directions, how can an echo arise?
Even a sound situated at a distance becomes a condition for the arising of an echo elsewhere and for the movement of vessels and other objects.
It should be understood as being like an iron hook for the movement of iron.
As for the rest... "the grasper": furthermore, the remaining triad of sensitive organs consisting of the nose, tongue, and body is a grasper of what is encountered;
this is because, by way of its support and by itself, it serves as the cause for the arising of consciousness in relation to an object that is already in contact with its own support.
Odors and tastes are cognized only as they are conjoined with their respective bases—the bases of the nose and the tongue—along with the odor-bases and taste-bases themselves.
And the tangible, which consists of the three primary elements, is cognized only as it is conjoined with the body-base. Regarding the phrase "undergoing a change of color":
this refers to the arising of an unattractive color due to causes such as bile (*pitta*) and so forth, by way of a transformation of the color.
"Arising": it makes manifest the state that has entered the heart—that is, the intention (ajjhāsaya) residing in the mind.

"Manifests" means it makes it clear like a physical form (rūpa); the meaning is that it displays it as if it had a tangible shape. For since verbal roots have many meanings, the word *rūpa* here should be understood in the sense of "making manifest.
The connection is: "That [intention] is the form (*rūpa*). It is the resistance within the eye, or of the eye.
"Having this as its characteristic" means having the characteristic of impinging upon the eye. The same applies to "having the characteristic of impinging upon the ear," and so forth.

Here, "impinging" (paṭihanana) refers to the mutual orientation toward one another of the sense object and the sense faculty, and their standing in a suitable location, considering it to be like a physical impact (paṭighāta).
Just as there is a shaking of a weak person when an impact occurs, so too [is there a reaction] when there is this orientation toward the sense object.
When there is the possessor of the object, the basis-form which is connected with it, and the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) supported by that, there occurs a vibration.
That [vibration] occurs either of the form within the eye, or of the eye within the form. Therefore he said:
"In whatever invisible and impinging eye, visible form—both visible and impinging—is struck; or in whatever invisible eye..."
"Is there resistance in the resistant form that is with visibility? and so forth. Being an object (*visayabhāva*) is the state of being an object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccayatā*).

Regarding the phrase "manifested as the state of being a sphere of activity (*gocarabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāna*)," here, "object-ness" (*visayatā*) is the state of not being otherwise; "sphere of activity" (*gocarabhāva*) is the abundance thereof.
This is the distinction between an object (*visaya*) and a sphere of activity (*gocara*). It "sounds" (*saddāyati*), meaning it is uttered, or by its own conditions.
The meaning is that it is brought to a state perceivable by the ear. It perfumes itself, thus it is "fragrant" (*sugandha*);
or it makes itself known as "foul-smelling" (*duggandha*). Therefore, he said, "it indicates. 664.
The faculty of a woman alone is the "female-faculty" (*itthindriya*). Just as the faculties such as the eye belong to a man as well, [so too does this faculty belong to a woman].
This is not so. However, this [faculty] occurs invariably only in a woman; therefore, it is called the "female faculty" (*itthindriya*).

The same applies to the male faculty (*purisindriya*). The state of being a woman is "femaleness" (*itthibhāva*); it is called "femaleness" because by means of it the mind becomes a woman, or because it is the designation for a woman.
"Arising at rebirth-linking" (*paṭisandhisamuṭṭhita*) means arisen precisely at the moment of rebirth-linking, by means of the rebirth-linking consciousness.
It arises simultaneously [with the faculties]. By this, he indicates its non-manifestation—except for the transformation of gender (liṅgaparivattana)—just like the eye-faculty and the others.
As for "this female characteristic (itthiliṅga) and so forth," this refers to the female characteristic and so on that have become the fruit of the faculty.

By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (ādi), there is a grouping of the female sign (nimitta), female gestures (kutta), and female deportment (ākappa). Among these, the clarity or lack of clarity of the hands, feet, and so on [is included].
Shape is the female characteristic. For the shape of the hands, feet, neck, chest, and so forth of women is not like that of men.
Thus, their lower body is slender while their upper body is thick; their hands and feet are small, as is their mouth;
the flesh of their breasts is thick; they lack beards and have prominent teeth; and there is the wearing of hair-bands and garments.
The female sign (*itthinimitta*). Even in childhood, playing with dolls, pestles, and so forth, and spinning thread with cotton wool—this and the like are "female gestures" (*itthikutta*);
the meaning is "female activity. The "female attire" (*itthākappa*) consists of such modes as walking with an unsteady gait and so forth.
For even when seeing a man who is unsteady, a woman stands, lies down, sits, eats, and consumes food just like a woman.
They say this. However, having stated that this exposition of the female gender and so forth is unwholesome (*akusala*), the teachers explain it in another way as well.

How? The female organ is the "female gender" (*itthiliṅga*); the intention for sexual intercourse is the "female sign" (*itthinimitta*); the lack of clarity in walking, moving about, and so forth is "female gesture" (*itthikutta*); and the female physical form is "female appearance" (*itthākappa*).
And here, "intention" (*adhippāya*) refers to craving for sexual intercourse with a man.
For that [natural characteristic] indeed functions as more constant and powerful among them;
therefore, because it serves as the sign for the perception "this is a woman," it is called the "female sign" (*itthinimitta*).

Although the signs of artificiality (*kutta*) and imitation (*kappa*) are also included within the very category of signs for the perception "this is a woman," nevertheless, because they are mentioned separately, it is intended that only the natural characteristics (*sara*) function as the sign.
665. But is this female sex organ and so forth produced at rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) in the same way as the femininity faculty (itthindriya)? To this he says:

"Precisely dependent on the femininity faculty," and so on. For although the female sex organs and such arise through their respective conditions such as karma, they generally come into being in a continuum that is already accompanied by the femininity faculty, appearing in those various forms.
And because they do not exist in other places, they are said to "arise dependent upon the female faculty" (itthindriya) with reference to their being cultivated by that state.
Having established this, he will later say: "The female... [etc. ...is manifested as the state of being a cause.
It is precisely through this dominant state (adhipatibhāva), termed "the state of being a cause," that its status as a faculty is stated in the context of the faculties.

This is because [the mind] does not produce the material phenomena of the female gender-sign and so forth in the continuum in any other way, but rather because of the presence of conditions such as the faculties;

however, it does not act as a support or a preserver for the material phenomena within that same group (*kalāpa*)—as the life-faculty does for its own group—or for the material phenomena of other groups—as nutriment does for other groups.

And this being the case, its status as a faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*) and its status as a presence-condition (*atthi-paccaya*) and non-disappearance-condition (*avigata-paccaya*) are like those of the life-faculty and nutriment.

And these are not mentioned in the Pāḷi. Since femininity and so forth are dependent upon other conditions, therefore, even in material phenomena produced by mind or by karma—such as a corpse or a painted image—that same shape is seen wherever its predominance exists.
Furthermore, although these arise in dependence on the female faculty, they do not arise at the moment of rebirth-linking for those in the womb; they arise only during the course of existence.
Therefore he said: “In the course of existence...
[etc. ...in rebirth-linking. (666–7) However, for moisture-born and spontaneously born beings, something arises together with the female faculty at the very moment of rebirth-linking itself.

The word *ca* (and) is used in the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of another statement; it should be understood as having the meaning of “whatever. This is because, among the forms such as gender (*liṅga*) and so forth—
Among forms, the form-base (rūpāyatana) is cognizable by the eye; therefore, he says, "The female gender-mark and so forth are cognizable by the eye.
However, since those other than these are, as the case may be, cognizable by the ear and cognizable by the mind, he says, "or not.
The aforementioned conceptual proliferation (papañca) should also be applied to the male faculty (purisindriya) according to what is possible; this is an extended application (atidesa).
While speaking, he said, “This very one,” and so forth. Regarding the phrase “the rest as well”: someone might occasionally think that this refers only to what has been stated thus far;
therefore, he said, “in the case of the male faculty. “Of the first eon” means of the humans belonging to the first eon.
For when those who had passed away from the Ābhassara world and were reborn here, after the lapse of a long period of time, [they began to consume] gross food.
When urine and feces had formed within them, their wound-openings burst open for the purpose of their discharge;
thus, the male-nature of the man and the female-nature of the woman became manifest.

For, by the power of the access-concentration (upacāra-jhāna) that had occurred in previous existences, as long as the force of the suppression of sensual lust within the continuum of beings has not subsided, so long do those things which serve as the proximate cause (upanissaya) for powerful sensual lust [persist].

The female and male faculties appeared. However, when, due to their interruption, powerful sensual lust finds an opportunity, then those [faculties], supported by that [lust], arise within the continuum of beings.
668. "From another time" means after the first aeon. Regarding the phrase "in the course of existence... revolves": it is as in the case of the son of the merchant of Soreyya.

The intended meaning is "transforms. By the word *api*, it is indicated that just as with a bhikkhunī, there is a transformation during the course of existence for a bhikkhu who had undergone rebirth in the Vinaya account of the first *pārājika* offense. As it is said:
"Now at that time, the female characteristic appeared in a certain bhikkhu; and at that time, the male characteristic appeared in a certain bhikkhunī."

However, one for whom neither of these two has arisen at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) is called "one without faculties" (abhāvaka); it should be understood that for such a person, there is no arising of the faculties even during the course of existence (pavatti).

Reflecting on this inquiry—"What is the cause for the production of both of these, and for their destruction, from which they arise and by which they are said to revolve?"—he said: "By great evil karma," and so forth.
In this context, "by a great [power]" means by the great force of a karma such as adultery. It is by way of a bad deed that serves as the decisive support (*upanissaya*).
The phrase "only by a great wholesome [deed]" is stated with reference to a happy destination; however, in an unhappy destination, both [sexes] arise solely through unwholesome karma.
(670) Since the physical mark (*liṅga*) necessarily perishes when the faculties (*indriya*) perish, he said: "the female mark perishes."
But here the intended meaning should be understood as follows: Of these two, the male faculty is superior and the female faculty is inferior.
The disappearance of the male faculty occurs through great unwholesome karma, while its arising occurs through great wholesome karma;
the disappearance of the female faculty occurs through weak unwholesome karma, and its arising likewise [occurs through weak wholesome karma].
Through weak wholesome karma, however, both [the faculties] disappear in an unhappy destination,
and their re-arising occurs only through unwholesome karma. If, in a happy destination, even the female faculty is produced by wholesome karma alone,
how then is it that after committing the act of adultery and being cooked in hell, one becomes a woman five hundred times in the human world due to that very evil deed?
Is this not a contradiction because of such statements as “it is produced”? This is not a contradiction, because it is stated by way of the result of outflow (nissanda-phala).

For instance, even when a kamma is capable of producing the male faculty (purisindriya) at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), its capacity may sometimes be obstructed by a powerful evil deed, such as adultery with another’s wife;
in that case, due to its inability to produce its own male faculty, only the female faculty (itthindriya) [is produced].

It produces [the male faculty]. However, during the course of existence (pavatti), due to its own powerful state, it may—having warded off unwholesome karma such as adultery which serves as a decisive support (upanissaya) for the female faculty—beginning from rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), give rise to the male faculty.

Yet, at times, its capacity might be obstructed by karma such as adultery that has gained strength through the arising of a sense of harmony; in such a case, due to its own weakness, the male faculty [may not arise].

It does not produce [the male faculty], but produces only the female faculty. Thus, because the female faculty is produced by means of the kamma that has adultery with another's wife and so forth as its decisive support (*upanissaya*), it is said that the female faculty was produced by that [kamma].
671–2. But when that kamma again attains strength—either through the recovery of harmony [of conditions] or through the exhaustion of other evil kamma—
If that [organ] had existed, then upon its disappearance, one would produce the male faculty (*purisindriya*) according to one's own strength, as if striking a tree with a blow;
however, the female faculty (*itthindriya*) does not arise because of the absence of its own cause.

Even in the case of the production of both, because of the production of dissimilar faculties, from the moment of the stability of the seventeenth consciousness prior to that, the respective kamma that originates them [continues].
It does not produce that respective faculty. Together with the seventeenth consciousness, it ceases along with the preceding consciousness because of the arising of a dissimilar faculty.
For if it were to arise even after the seventeenth moment of consciousness, the other would not arise;
this is because the simultaneous arising of two [such moments] within a single continuum is not admitted. Therefore, indeed: "For one who..."
Or, when the male faculty arises, does the female faculty arise for that person?”—in this question, a negation was made with the word “no.
And having done so, he will say: “Even for one who possesses both sexual characteristics,” and so forth.
Furthermore, when one [faculty] has ceased, the signs and so on connected to it cease after a few days; once those have ceased, the others [gradually] follow.

"The teachers say they are born [as such]. Because one possesses both kinds of sexual organs—namely, the karma that produces the female sign and the karma that produces the male sign—one is called 'ubhatobyañjano' (a hermaphrodite).
The phrase 'tassāpi' ('even for him') shows that even for one who possesses both kinds of sexual organs, there may be only a single faculty; how much more so, then, for the other?"

But surely, since there are two kinds of sexual characteristics (*byañjana*), there ought to be two faculties (*indriya*) as well; for those characteristics arise in dependence upon their respective faculties?

True, they do arise. In this case too, for one who possesses both female characteristics, the female faculty (*itthindriya*) arises in dependence upon which the female sign (*itthinimitta*) persists for as long as life lasts;
and for one who possesses both male characteristics, the male faculty (*purisindriya*) [arises in dependence upon which the male sign persists].
It is only the male characteristic; the other [the female characteristic], however, does not arise for him from the cause of the female faculty (*itthindriya*) or the male faculty (*purisindriya*).

To show by what reason that [other characteristic] exists, the inquiry "this being so" (*evaṃ sante*) was made, and the resolution beginning with "nor is there non-existence" (*na cābhāvo*) was stated.
"This being so" means when only one faculty is present. "Nor is there non-existence" refers to that which, depending upon [the presence of the other], [arises].

It arises; because of its absence, there is an absence of female characteristics in one who possesses both sets of male characteristics, and an absence of male characteristics in one who possesses both sets of female characteristics—this is the meaning.
"And its non-existence would not occur" means that the non-existence of the second set of characteristics would not occur.
"That is not the cause of the characteristics" means that this faculty is not the cause for the second set of characteristics. Why? Because it is constant.

Because of their absence. For when a lustful thought arises in a hermaphrodite woman, at that time the male characteristic becomes manifest while the female characteristic remains concealed and hidden; likewise for the other in the case of the former.
And if their faculty were the cause for the second characteristic, both characteristics would persist at all times.
But it does not remain; therefore, this should be understood: "That is not the cause for its manifestation. If one asks, "What then is the cause?
he says: "The cause for that... [etc. ...is the cause. In that context, "accompanied by kamma" means accompanied by the kamma established in a previous existence that produces the sense faculties.
"A mind of lust" means [lust] of a woman for a man, or of a man for a woman.
Or, a mind of lust for sexual intercourse may arise. When that has arisen, it is manifest; when it has subsided, it is concealed.

Since this person possesses only one sex organ, therefore a hermaphrodite with female characteristics conceives a fetus for another’s sake, and also causes another to conceive for their own sake. For, by virtue of possessing the female faculty (*itthindriya*),...
One takes [the embryo] oneself; one causes another to take it by performing an act of violence upon others.

A *purisobhatobyañjanaka* (a hermaphrodite with male characteristics) causes another to take an embryo by performing an act of violence upon others, but because he possesses the male faculty (*purisindriya*), he does not himself conceive an embryo.
For when the female faculty (*itthindriya*) exists, the female marks and so forth arise, and when those exist, there is the manifestation of being "female."
Therefore, he said that its function is to make [the object] known, stating: "Its function is to manifest as 'female.

Furthermore, both types of this faculty pervade the entire body just like the bodily intimation (*kāyapasāda*); yet there is no confusion between it and the bodily intimation, due to their difference in characteristic and their difference in support. 673.
Its characteristic is the preservation of co-nascent material phenomena so that they may proceed through the three moments.

Thus, its characteristic is preservation (*anupālanalakkhaṇa*). Since the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is exclusively born of kamma, the fact that those [material phenomena] which must be preserved are also born of kamma is established by the very mention of "co-nascent" (*sahaja*);

therefore, the term "born of kamma" was not used [again]. Even though the kamma-born material phenomena last for only their own respective three moments, it is precisely by being the cause for their continued occurrence that the life-faculty is their preserver. Hence he said: "Its function is to make them occur."
And here, "maintaining" (pavattana) means their sustaining, establishing, and having a cause for persistence according to the method already stated.

For it is not possible for karma alone to be the cause for the persistence of those things born of karma, just as nutriment and so forth are not the causes for those born of nutriment and so forth. Why is that?

Because of its non-existence at that moment. For karma, having ceased, becomes a condition for materiality; consequently, the materialities originated by it are like the corpse of one whose parents have died.

Sons, such as those of a junior father, exist in dependence on another support—that is, the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*)—and apart from that life-faculty, there is nothing else capable of sustaining them; therefore, that [life-faculty] alone is their "function of maintaining.

However, things born of nutriment (*āhāraja*) and so forth proceed independently of others, like sons who have a living father, by means of their own respective conditions. For nutriment and the rest [proceed] by themselves...
Having arisen at the very moment of their existence, material phenomena persist solely through the maintenance and occurrence of those [conditions];

therefore, the factors arising from them do not depend on the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) for their support. The remaining [phenomena] also persist only by way of their respective conditions and do not await any other cause for their stabilization.
Furthermore, even that which is kamma-originated acts as a sustainer from the very moment of its arising; it is that which maintains those things to be sustained.
The primary cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) of this [mental body] consists of the co-nascent elements that must be maintained; thus it is called "having the elements to be maintained as its primary cause.

674. Regarding the "mind-consciousness element" (*manoviññāṇadhātu*): excluding the mind-consciousness element that is the resultant of the formless realm (*arūpāvacara-vipāka*), the remainder is the mind-consciousness element.

Therefore he said, "in the five-aggregate plane" (*pañcavokāre*). In the five-aggregate plane, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness elements depend upon whatever material form (*rūpa*).

The connection is that those [bases] which proceed are called "the bases" (*vatthu*). Furthermore, the qualification "in the fivefold existence" (*pañcavokāre*) is made by way of the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*);
however, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) does not exist at all in the fourfold existence (*catuvokārabhava*).

Although the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*) is not mentioned in the canonical text (*pāḷi*), its existence should be understood both through scripture (*āgama*) and through logical reasoning (*yutti*). In this regard, first, as for the scripture: [The text continues with the scriptural citations.]

“The material form depending upon which the mind-element (manodhātu) and the mind-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu) occur is a condition, by way of support-condition (nissayapaccaya), for that mind-element, that mind-consciousness-element, and for the mental states associated with them”—such is the statement from the *Paṭṭhāna*.
However, the reasoning should be understood as follows:

the two elements have as their support derived matter that is fully developed (nipphanna-upādāyarūpa) because, in the five-aggregate existence (pañcavokārabhava), their occurrence is bound up with matter. For whatever has its occurrence bound up with matter [is so supported].
That [support] is seen as the support for each respective derived form (nipphanna-upādāyarūpa), such as the eye-consciousness element.

In this regard, it is not logical that the visible-form base (rūpāyatana) and so forth, nor nutritive essence (ojā), serve as their support, because they are observed to function even outside of what is bound to the sense faculties (indriya).

Nor is it logical that the female faculty (itthindriya) and male faculty (purisindriya) are their support, because they are absent even in the continuum of those devoid of both sexes (abhāvaka-santāna).

Because of the observation of two elements. Since the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) also possesses another function characterized by simultaneous preservation, it is not logical for it to be their support.
For that [life-faculty], being occupied with its other function, is unable to serve as the support for these two;

therefore, by process of elimination, it should be understood that there exists a support for them called the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*). Let the heart-base be the support for the two elements for now.
This consists of both the physical basis (*vatthu*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
It should be understood that this is produced by kamma, has a specific function, and exists as a single entity located in the region of the heart. How is this known? It is said:

because it serves as the physical basis for consciousness, it is produced by kamma, just like the eye-sensitivity. For whatever matter serves as the physical basis for consciousness is produced by kamma, just as the clarity of the eye is.

Therefore, because the specific function [of the heart] is performed by making it the bone, attending to it, and focusing the entire mind upon it, it is understood that this [consciousness] abides there due to the exhaustion of the region of the heart as one thinks something. As the teachers have said:
"Because it is the product of kamma and serves as the basis for existence, it has a fixed function like the eye."
"And through reflection, with their chests heaving, they remain there, having understood.

If there exists what is called the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*), which serves as the support for the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*), why then was it not mentioned in the section on materiality (*rūpakanda*)?
Is it not the case that there is no reason for not mentioning something that actually exists? No, there is no such reason, because other reasons exist.

What, then, is that reason? It is the difference in teaching. For while visual consciousness and the others have exclusively the eye and so forth as their bases, mental consciousness does not in the same way have the heart-basis as its base in all cases, since it has that as its base only in the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*).
And it is precisely by way of exclusive dependence that the teaching of the bases proceeds: "There is material form that is the basis for visual consciousness... [and so on].
Because it is distinguished by its dependence on eye-consciousness and so forth— as in the passage beginning, "There is matter that is not the basis for eye-consciousness"—

and because when the pairs (duka) and so on are stated according to that [heart-basis], such as "There is matter that is the basis for mind-consciousness," the corresponding object-pairs and so forth do not occur; for there is no [matter]...
If it were possible to say, "There is a mental consciousness object;
there is matter that is not a mental consciousness object," then the dyads of bases and objects would have different scopes, and the teaching would not be of a single flavor.
Yet, the Blessed One’s intention was to teach a teaching of a single flavor; therefore, the heart-base was not mentioned therein, not because it cannot be found.
For this is the nature of the Blessed One: that even when it is possible to teach a discourse with a single flavor, there may be no inclusion of certain factors.

Thus, in the *Nikkhepakanda* as well, because it is not spoken of through the classification of consciousness-arising (*cittuppāda*), one cannot say "initial application (*vitakka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*)" in the response to the term "without initial application and without sustained application" (*avitakkāvicāra*); yet [these] are present in the response to the term "without initial application, with sustained application only" (*avitakkavicāramatta*).
Vitakka was not extracted [from the compound]; otherwise, it would have had to be stated as "vitakko ca.
Because it carries [the mind] upward as if lifting it by way of being its support, it has "lifting up" (ubbāhana) as its manifestation.
Regarding the four kinds of nutriment, since the context here concerns form (rūpa), the nutriment of physical food (kabaḷīkāra-āhāra) is to be understood; thus he says, "as nutriment."
“Edible food. In this context, it is called *kabaḷīkāra* because it is made into mouthfuls (*kabaḷa*).
It is called *āhāra* because it is taken in; the meaning is that it is swallowed after being made into mouthfuls. This was stated in order to show the food together with its physical basis.

However, here it is the nutritive essence (*ojā*) of edible food that is meant by the term “food. Therefore he said, “by whatever nutritive essence,” and so forth. And that [essence] has the nature of nourishing matter and provides support and strength.
There is one specific distinction: it consists in the carrying of nutritive essence (ojā) that follows from limb to limb and is dependent upon the primary elements.

Since internal nutriment produces material form only after having obtained external nutriment as its condition, this [internal nutriment] also "carries" material form by way of being its decisive support (upanissaya).

Thus it is said: "It carries the material form consisting of the octad with nutritive essence as the eighth. That which has nutritive essence as its eighth member is called "the octad with nutritive essence as the eighth."

"By whatever vitality": by whatever vitality known as *ojā*—reckoned as such because it generates material form immediately after its own arising—which resides in the substance of rice, boiled milk-rice, and so forth;
"wherever": in whichever country, city, and so on. The intention is that it is called "edible food" (*kabaḷīkāro āhāro*) because it has that [substance] as its basis.

676. If it is asked, "What then is the function of the physical basis (vatthu), and what is that of the nutritive essence (ojā)?"—showing that the function of the physical basis is the removal of danger and the function of the nutritive essence is preservation—it says, "food, drink, and so forth," and so on.

"It carries the fire born of karma" means it takes up the heat born of karma. For if the physical basis, such as boiled rice and so forth, were absent within the belly, the heat born of karma would arise and [consume] the derived matter known as the lining of the stomach.
He seizes [the being]; he causes [the being] to say, "I am hungry, give me food. At the time of eating, having released the covering of the belly, he seizes the non-clung-to (anupādinnaka) object;

then the being becomes one-pointed. For just as a shadow-demon, seeing someone who has entered the shade, seizes them, binds them with a divine chain, and rejoices in his own abode, [so too does he seize the being] when it comes at the time of hunger.
It bites the head; having been bitten, it cries out. Hearing that cry, if other people also come, it seizes each one as they arrive, devours them, and rejoices in its own abode.

In the same way, whatever object there is—food, drink, and so forth—the heat born of karma seizes it, digests it, and takes it back again to the lining of the stomach. Therefore, food, drink, and the like...
When the *vatthu* has entered its own membrane of the abdomen, it takes hold of the acquired body (*upādinnakāya*) and, having released it from there,
carries it into its own presence by way of causing itself to be grasped. "Entirely" means that the *vatthu*, when devoid of nutritive essence (*ojā*),
is unable to sustain life or the kamma-born elements.

677. “Nutritive essence” … [as before] … “the cooker”: the intention is that while the nutritive essence is able to sustain life, it is not able to carry the kamma-born heat because the stomach is not full. “Manifesting as support”:
it manifests as support for this body precisely by way of carrying the eightfold materiality consisting of nutritive essence. “By the body” means by the material body. “Its own state” means—
"Making known one's own intention" means making others understand.

"In accordance with the apprehension of the body" means by means of recollecting the mind-door javanas—termed "definitive apprehension"—which occur immediately after the eye-door javanas that consist in the apprehension of the color residing in the vibrating body;
the meaning is that they follow immediately upon those [eye-door javanas]. For when an object such as a visible form has entered the avenue of the five doors, according to the conditions...
After a wholesome or unwholesome impulsion has arisen and the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) has subsided, a mind-door impulsion arises taking that same object and then the life-continuum subsides;
again, having determined the object at that very same door, an impulsion arises and the life-continuum subsides.
Therefore, immediately after two successive impulsion-moments occurring following a visual-door impulsion—

When the mental-door impulsion-series (manodvāra-javanavīthi) has already occurred during the third instance and has thus been grasped, then by means of that [series] acting as the instrument (karaṇa), the state is cognized by the impulsion itself at the mental door during the fourth instance.
By this, the verbal noun derivation (karaṇasādhana) of the word "viññatti" is stated.
However, by the phrase "by oneself," etc., its status as an object derivation (kammasādhana) is expressed.

Having thus shown the occurrence of the word *viññatti* (intimation) in two types of agents, he now states the sutta beginning with “restraint by body” (*kāyena saṃvaro*) in order to show the *kammadhāraya* compound [of *kāya-viññatti*] together with the word *kāya*.
He does so while demonstrating that the conventional term “body” (*kāya*) applies both to the physical body and to intimation.

[The phrase] “because it is the cause for making known one’s intention through bodily movement” means: because it exists as the cause for making known one’s intention by means of the moving body acting as the instrument.
The connection is: "bodily intimation" (*kāyaviññatti*) means "intimation by way of the body" (*kāyena viññatti*). This, however, is the meaning here:
because it is the cause of the bodily movement that constitutes intimation, one takes the "body"—defined as that bodily movement—as the cause for knowing the intention;
thus, since intimation is grasped as the instrument for making known the intention, it is said: "one intimates the intention by means of the body. Likewise...

Having apprehended the movement of the body, because it is apprehended through intimation (viññatti) as being caused by that [movement], and because it is itself known by means of the body, it is therefore called "bodily intimation" (kāyaviññatti), in the sense of "intimation by means of the body. 678.
"By the air-element born of mind" means by the air-element originated by the consciousness that sets in motion such actions as approaching. "The state of alteration of form" (ākāravikāratā).
The modification is the state of having a shape. Of what, then, is that the "modification of shape"?

It belongs to the mind-born great elements (mahābhūta) that have wind as their predominant factor, by virtue of their functional capacity. What is that capacity? It is the state of being a cause for motion, the state of being mind-born, and the state of being derived matter (upādāyarūpa).
Alternatively, the connection is: "the modification of shape belonging to the wind element born of mind. For it is not only the genitive case [that indicates possession].
It is not only in dependence on the connection with motion, but also in dependence on the connection with the alteration of shape.
If this is so, how can intimation (viññatti) be derived matter (upādāyarūpa)?

For, by the statement "produced by mind and born of the element," intimation would result in being merely the alteration of shape belonging to the air-element; and derived matter does not depend upon a single primary element.
Is there not a statement that "derived matter (upādāyarūpa) exists [as] the four great elements"? This is not a fault;
for the state of being a modification of the four applies to even one among the four, like property held in common by four people.

Alternatively, a group in which the air element (*aniladhātu*) predominates is here called "the air element," because of the conventional designation applied when that [element] is predominant, just as [a group] is designated by the predominance of the constituent element (*sambhāradhātu*).

There is the conventional designation "earth"; therefore, there is no contradiction in calling the single mode of transformation of the mind-born great elements—when the air element is predominant—"bodily intimation" (*kāyaviññatti*).
Furthermore, its predominance should be understood in terms of functional capacity (*sāmatthiya*), not in terms of physical magnitude.

Otherwise, their state of inseparable coexistence (*avinibbhogavutti*) would be untenable. For predominance occurs by way of its own superior function, through which it proceeds in distinction from the others.
It exists. Furthermore, it is predominant by virtue of its capacity, because it conforms to its cause. For the cause is the consciousness that initiates the forward movement and so forth;

since that consciousness has the intrinsic nature of an intention toward motion, it is logical that the air element alone should be predominant in the group of material phenomena arising from it as they conform to it.

However, some take the view that "it is the air element itself that undergoes a change of shape"; according to their opinion, [the air element] would possess the status of derived matter (*upādārūpa*).
This is poorly formulated. For it cannot be said that the modification of one thing constitutes the derived matter (upādārūpa) of four others.
To the question, "What kind of modification is this? he says: "It is the cause for the movement of co-nascent matter.

In this context, "co-nascent" means co-nascent with itself. Since the movement of matter born of temperature, mind, and nutriment occurs only through its connection with mind-born matter, [it is so described].
It is like dry cow-dung balls and the like thrown into the current of a river; however, as for movement by way of intimation (*viññatti*), it is the movement of that which is born of mind alone.

Therefore, it is said: "of that which is co-nascent. "Of matter" means of the material body (*rūpakāya*). "In movement" refers to the state of being moved, which consists of stiffening, supporting, and moving.
For even stiffening and so forth are [included] because they are directed toward movement.
"Moving" is appropriate [as the definition]. "Causes" means those that have become causes, having become cooperative conditions (*sahakārīkāraṇa*). What is expressed by this much?
That which is called "bodily intimation" (*kāyaviññatti*) is neither the body of matter (*rūpakāya*) as it is actually quivering, nor is it the quivering air-element;
rather, it is a modification of the body of matter consisting of an exertion (*ussāhana*), like that of one lifting a large rock with all one's might at the time of grasping it.
What is meant is that a single modification of form, which is obtained by way of being a condition for vibration, is called "bodily intimation" (*kāyaviññatti*).
