But is there not some modification distinct from the appearance of the vibrating color and so forth, whose apprehension occurs immediately after the apprehension of that color?
How, then, is this known? It is known from the apprehension of the underlying intention (*adhippāya*). For [intimation] does not exist in those things devoid of the modification of intimation.
It is observed that in cases such as the shaking of a tree, there is the apprehension of intention; it is likewise observed in cases such as the movement of the hand.
Therefore, one must certainly accept this: that there exists some modification distinct from the mere appearance of trembling and so forth, which serves as the indicator of intention.
Furthermore, a cause that makes something known makes its object known only when it has itself been apprehended, not merely by virtue of its existence.
The apprehension of modification is also established by inference immediately after the apprehension of the color that is to be made known. For they say:
"Sounds that have not yet attained the status of being objects do not convey meaning."
"Things do not become manifest merely by their existence;
they become manifest when they are known.
If the apprehension of modification alone is the cause for the apprehension of intention, why is there no apprehension of intention in the case of those for whom the convention has not been grasped?

Is it not so? It should be understood that not only the apprehension of change (*vikāra*) is the cause for the apprehension of the intended object, but rather, the apprehension of a previously established relationship (*sambandha*) must also be seen as its decisive support (*upanissaya*).

For instance, when one sees signs of water such as the horns of cows and the like left behind at a watering place in the forest, there arises immediately thereafter—though its immediate antecedent is not consciously perceived—a cognition [of water].
Just as one perceives the mode of cognition that recognizes the accompaniment of water in gośīrṣa sandalwood and the like,
thereby knowing "there is water here," so too, having grasped the appearance of quivering, there occurs in the mental-door process—

occurring immediately thereafter and with its immediate antecedent unperceived— the grasping of a purposive modification accompanied by the supporting condition (upanissaya) of the previously grasped connection.
681–2. It is logical that the air element, accompanied by intimation and transformation, acts as the cause for the movement of co-nascent matter.
To resolve the objection—“Does the air element move all co-nascent matter?”—it is said: “But having obtained support,” and so forth.
“Support” (*upatthambha*) means that which supports; the meaning is “the supporting condition. In the course of a single adverting consciousness (*ekāvajjana-vīthi*)...
This is said with reference to the cognitive process (javana-vīthi) of the mind-door, because the process of the five doors lacks the capacity to originate intimation (viññatti).

The phrase "by the six preceding consciousnesses" connects to the idea that [the bodily formation] receives support from the air element (vāyodhātu) originated by the six preceding impulsion moments (javana) among the seven.
However, some versions of the manuscript read "originated by the air element."
Having seen the reading, they take it as an instrumental noun (*bhāvasādhana*) and connect it thus: "having obtained support produced by the air element arisen from the six preceding consciousnesses.
Regarding the phrase "because it is accompanied by intimation" (*viññattisahitattā*):

the meaning is that, being itself accompanied by intimation, it causes the co-nascent matter born of consciousness to move toward another location by acting as its cause; other [matter] does not do so.

This, however, is the intended meaning here: just as, for example, when a cart is to be pulled by seven yokes, only the oxen yoked to the seventh yoke move the cart once they have received support from the oxen yoked to the six yokes below;
whereas those yoked to the first yoke and so forth merely provide stability and maintenance, acting as their supports—exactly so [is it in this case].
The air element produced by the seventh impulsion, having received support from the air element produced by the six preceding impulsions, moves the mind-born matter.
However, those produced by the first impulsion and so forth merely provide stabilization and maintenance, acting as its supports.
And here, "movement" refers simply to arising in another location from the location where it has already arisen.
Because there is not even a hair’s breadth of movement among phenomena (*dhamma*), otherwise phenomena would lack non-agency (*abyāpāratā*) and momentariness (*khaṇikatā*).
But how is it that this [consciousness] acts as the cause for the arising of co-nascent material phenomena (*sahajarūpa*) in another location?
Just as co-nascent material phenomena arise elsewhere from the place where they were established by the material phenomena produced by the preceding impulsion (*javana*) and so forth.
Thus, it should be understood that their very arising together with those [other elements] constitutes the state of being the cause for arising in another location.
Now, since the apprehension of the manifest intimation (*viññatti*) is stated immediately after the apprehension of the appearance of vibration,

and because it is specified as being "accompanied by manifest intimation," does this mean that the air element (*vāyodhātu*) is accompanied by a transformation only when it is associated with the mode of motion?

It is not the case that these [bodily formations] are devoid of informative intimation (*viññatti*) and transformation, even though they are unable to move by acting as the cause for arising in another location;

for, by merely performing the functions of stiffening and supporting, the air element (*vāyodhātu*) originated by the first impulsion (*javana*) and subsequent moments is indeed accompanied by informative intimation and transformation.

This is because a transformation consisting in the state of being directed toward a particular direction occurs when one intends to perform such actions as advancing after having gone in that direction. For [the formation] coexistent with the intention...
They declare that intimation is a modification. For it was by that very Blessed One said: "What is that material form which is bodily intimation?
It is the stiffening, the rigidity, the state of being rigid of the body—whether of one with a wholesome mind... or of one with an indeterminate mind—when moving forward... or stretching out;
it is the intimation, the making known, the state of having been made known."
"This is that form which is bodily intimation"—thus, the mode of being a condition for stiffening and supporting is called "bodily intimation.
And by defining it in this way, the statement that even the adverting of the mind-door (manodvārāvajjana) originates intimation becomes well-founded.
683–4. That modification of the mode [of the body] which is the condition for the impact of the acquired earth element born of consciousness—this is...
The connection is: "vocal intimation is to be understood. Therein, "born of mind" means originating from the consciousness that sets in motion the differentiation of speech.
"In the impact of the appropriated" means in the function termed "impact" upon the locus of syllable-production, which is designated as an aggregate of appropriated [matter];
the meaning is "of the impact. "Condition" means being its concomitant cause. "A single modification of mode" means...

The meaning is this: it is a specific variety of formal alteration (ākāra-vikāra-visesa) which, being distinct from the tangible derived matter (*upādinnarūpa*) that is struck, and from the earth element itself that strikes, is a type of matter characterized by the condition of striking that is derived from the earth element.

Regarding the term "of the earth element" (*pathavidhātuyā*), the genitive case should be understood according to the method explained in the *Kāyaviññatti* under the heading "dependent on both relations," and so forth.

However, this is the distinction: whereas in that case [the mind] is apprehended immediately after the apprehension of the appearance of the vibrating object, here it should be understood as being apprehended immediately after hearing the sound being heard.
And because the sound arises simultaneously with the impact due to the absence of rigidity and so forth, the method beginning with "but having obtained support" does not apply here.

For "striking" (ghaṭṭana) is indeed found even in the first impulsion and subsequent moments. Therefore, he said: "by reason of sound. Now, what is the difference between striking and movement (calana)?
Striking is the state of the groups of primary elements (bhūtakalāpa) arising in closer proximity to one another due to a specific condition;

movement is the successive production of even a single [element] in a different location. This is the distinction between them. Here, the similes of the cow's head and so forth [are to be understood].
These [terms] should be applied according to their possibility. *Sāva* means that very same intimation (*viññatti*) due to the word *saha*.

*Sakyakulindunā* means by one who, in the sense of illuminating the Sakyan royal family—which is like the perfectly pure expanse of the sky—acts as its moon; or alternatively, *indu* means "one who exercises supreme sovereignty" (*paramissariyaṃ karoti*).
Since the word *indu* denotes the highest [status], the meaning is "by the most eminent of the Sakyan clan."

685. Now, if it is argued that while intimation (*viññatti*) indeed consists of sound, there exists a sound born of consciousness (*cittaja*) that is non-intimating (*aviññattika*), [the author] says "sound is not born of consciousness" and so forth, demonstrating that such a thing does not exist.
"The impact of intimation" (*viññattighaṭṭana*) means the impact of the earth element conditioned by intimation.
By the phrase "by the very impact of the elements" and so forth, he supports the point already stated. For it is by the very impact of the elements...

The sound arises, and not without it; this is the meaning. And by this [passage], those who say—on the grounds that the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* states "the sound produced by the diffusion of applied thought (*vitakkavipphāra-sadda*) is not cognizable by the ear-sense"—that the mind-originated sound produced by the diffusion of applied thought arises even without intimation (*viññatti*), because of the statement:
"That which is the intimation and the making known by that speech," [are refuted]; for [if it were so], it would follow that it is not cognizable by the ear.
He rejects their assertion that "manifestation does not arise together with sound, and for that very reason, there is also a set of nine sound-elements produced by mind.

Indeed, this is also rejected by the compilers [of the commentaries], who considered it contradictory to the position of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* (Great Commentary), which holds that sound itself exists but is not cognizable by the ear.
However, the teacher Ānanda, without rejecting the position of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*,...
In this context, he explains the underlying intention (*adhippāya*). How so? According to the Sutta:

"Having heard with the divine ear the subtle sound produced by the movement of the tongue, palate, and so forth, which arises from applied thought (*vitakka*) and is co-nascent with intimation (*viññatti*), one points it out";

and according to the Paṭṭhāna, the status of being an object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) for ear-consciousness is stated with reference to gross sound. It is with this underlying intention that [the author speaks] of the sound resulting from the diffusion of applied thought (*vitakkavipphārasadda*).
"Being cognizable by the ear-consciousness" has been stated.
(686–7) "By way of making known" means because it is the cause for making one's intention known through the sound of speech.

"Cognizable by oneself" means because it is to be cognized by oneself either through the apprehension [of the object] or by means of the sound of speech. "Of that" refers to the word *viññatti*. "The occurrence of two factors" [refers to the following].
"It makes known" is *viññatti*; "it is made known" is *viññatti*. Thus, its occurrence or production is in the sense of either the cause or the object.
But is this twofold intimation produced by consciousness, or is it produced by karma and so forth? To this he says: "The two kinds of intimation," and so on.
"Like the eight material phenomena" means like the eight material phenomena found within their respective groups (*kalāpa*).
Because the two types of intimation (viññatti) are spoken of together, sound is not found in the material group (kalāpa) co-arising with bodily intimation;
therefore, even though it is present in the material group of vocal intimation, that is excluded and only "eight" are stated.
By way of grasping the aforementioned transformation, the intention of the possessor of that [intimation]—namely, "this person wishes to do this"—is [discerned].
It is said to "make known" because its function is to manifest the intention.

Because it is a transformation of the air element (*vāyodhātu*) which is the cause of bodily movement, it is said to have "the manifestation of the cause of bodily movement" as its proximate cause (*paccupaṭṭhāna*).
It is said to have "the mind-originated air element as its proximate cause" because the air element possesses a predominance of activity.
"Manifesting as the state of being a cause for vocal sound" means, according to the method already stated, that it manifests as the causal state for the sound born of mind known as vocal sound.
However, some here [argue] that because it is stated to be "the condition for impact," the arising of sound occurs immediately after the impact.
They say: "Having been grasped, the earth element arisen from consciousness performs merely the function of striking the clung-to [body];

at the very moment of being struck, the sound that arises is produced solely by temperature (utu). However, because it has consciousness as its condition, it is called 'arisen from consciousness' in a figurative sense.
According to their view, sound born of consciousness (*cittaja-sadda*) cannot be established; therefore, one should not accept this.
It should be understood that, just as a sound arises within the water itself at the time of heating water, so too,

at the very moment the earth element originated by consciousness (citta-samuṭṭhāna-pathavī-dhātu) arises after striking the clung-to (upādinnaka) matter, a "bhūtika" sound arises as the ninth factor within that same group (kalāpa). Therefore,
even the sound originated by consciousness arises only by way of vocal intimation (vacī-viññatti), such as the sound of snapping one's fingers and the like.
However, because there is an absence of vocal intimation (*vacīviññatti*), it is produced solely by temperature conditioned by mind (*cittapaccayautusamuṭṭhāna*).
688. Because there is no plowing (*viggaha*), it is not plowed; since one is unable to plow or cut it, it is "space" (*ākāsa*);
he said, "it is called space because it is not plowed," and as for what that is, he said, "the opening (*vivara*) of forms," referring to the ear-cavity and other such forms.
The meaning is "it enters within. By this, he refers to the cloudless sky (*ajaṭākāsa*). However, by the phrase "that which is... the delimitation," he refers to the space intended here;
that, by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhī*), is called "space" (*ākāsa*).
It is "delimitation of form" (*rūpapariccheda*) because it delimits forms, or because it is itself delimited by them, or because it is the mere delimitation of those [forms].

"Having that as its characteristic" means it has the characteristic of delimiting material form (*rūpaparicchedalakkhaṇo*). For this [space] acts as if it were delimiting each respective cluster of material form.

Therefore, it is said: "Its function is to manifest the boundaries of material form. The meaning is that its task is to distinguish them thus: "This is the lower limit of material forms; this is the upper limit.
In terms of its actual essence (*atthato*), however, because it is merely the delimitation of material forms—
Having been sacrificed [into the fire], it is grasped; therefore it is said that "matter has the characteristic of appearing as a limit. Here it is asked:

when delimiting this matter, does one delimit it from a group (kalāpa) produced by four causes, or from many groups produced by a single cause, or rather from a single group produced by a single cause, or from a single instance of matter?
It should be understood as being from a single group produced by a single cause.
For if one delimits [matter] from a group arising from four [causes], or from many groups arising from a single cause,
then it would follow that either the state of being touched is what is delimited, or else it would result in the non-separability of material phenomena belonging to different groups,

just as with those belonging to a single group. Alternatively, if one delimits it from each individual material phenomenon, then [the same consequence follows] even for the material phenomena belonging to a single group.

There might be the undesirable consequence of their existing in mutual separation, as is the case with various groups of material qualities (*rūpa-kalāpa*); however, both of these [consequences] are unwanted.
Therefore, it should be understood that [space] delimits each individual group from the group that arises alongside it.
Its manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*) is the state of being untouched, or the state of having gaps and openings; thus, it is said to have "the state of being untouched as its manifestation."

Or it is said that its manifestation is the state of having gaps and openings. In this context, since there is a delimitation of the primary elements within a particular group (kalāpa), and because they manifest by way of not being in contact with one another, its manifestation is the state of non-contact.

For even though the elements belonging to one group are indeed in contact with those belonging to other groups due to their nature as a single, solid mass, [they are considered non-contacting in relation to their own specific boundaries].
Nevertheless, because they are distinct from one another in terms of their intrinsic nature (*dhamma*), they remain unmixed.

That which is their distinctness—their mutual non-mixture—is "delimitation" (*pariccheda*). Like [the elements] with respect to other primary elements (*bhūta*), it is not actually in contact with them;
otherwise, there would be no delimitation, because those primary elements would attain a state of pervasiveness. For non-pervasiveness is indeed non-contact.
Therefore the Blessed One said in the exposition of this [space]: "It is untouched by the four great elements.
Alternatively, its state of having "non-contact" as its manifestation is stated because it presents itself through the mutual non-intermixture of the elements within the same aggregate;
and its state of having "cavity and aperture" as its manifestation is stated because it presents itself as the state of being a cavity and aperture by way of ear-holes, mouth-cavities, and so forth.

It has been stated: for when there is a delimitation of matter (*rūpa*), there is the state of having openings and fissures. It is said that "it has its proximate cause in delimited matter" because it is obtained precisely where those matters are delimited, by way of their being delimited.
689–91. Regarding the exposition of the triad of lightness, malleability, and wieldiness of matter: these are the lightness of matter, the malleability of matter, and the wieldiness of matter.
The intention is that this is stated now when the exposition of this triad of lightness of matter (*rūpalahutā*) has arrived.

"In the same manner as stated above" means that just as it was said regarding the immaterial [aggregates'] lightness and so forth—"lightness of the body is lightness of the body" (*kāyalahubhāvo kāyalahutā*)—and so on, following that very method, the modifications of matter should also be understood by way of their connection with matter, such as "the lightness of matter is lightness" (*rūpassa lahubhāvo lahutā*). The lightness of matter...

Lightness (*lahutā*) has the characteristic of the subsiding of the state of heaviness in matter; its function is the crushing out of heaviness; it is manifested as non-slowness; its proximate cause is light matter.
Plasticity (*mudutā*) is the softness of matter; it has the characteristic of the subsiding of the state of rigidity in matter;
its function is the crushing out of rigidity; it is manifested as non-opposition to all activities; its proximate cause is plastic matter.
The workability of matter is *kammaññatā*. Its characteristic is the subsiding of the state of unwieldiness of matter;
its function is the crushing out of unwieldiness; it is manifested as a state of adaptability for bodily activities; and its proximate cause is workable matter.
The meaning here should be understood according to what has been stated by us in various places. These three, moreover, [are called] "modes" because they are states of transformation of matter.
To show that they are called "transformations of matter" (*rūpavikārā*), it is said: "The three... [etc. ...by one who discerns.
Furthermore, these arise respectively from causes opposed to the disturbance of the elements that produces rigidity of matter;

from causes opposed to the disturbance of the elements that produces hardness; and from causes opposed to the disturbance of the elements that produces a state of non-conformity with bodily activities of material forms.

This should be understood. In this context, "disturbance of the elements" (*dhātukkhobha*) refers to the provocation of wind, bile, and phlegm, or the state of transformation of the elements such as taste and so forth;
although stated in two ways, it should be seen as meaning, in substance, the transformation of the earth element and the others themselves.
"Adverse conditions" refers to unsuitable climate, food, and a distracted mind; and that is mentioned because it serves as a specific condition for those respective transformations.
But in general, they are conditions for all [mental states], for they never abandon one another.
Since their diversity is difficult to discern when they do not abandon one another, the passage beginning with "Of these" was stated in order to clarify that.

The connection is: "The illustration is according to the sequence. For a healthy person is the illustration for lightness (*lahutā*), and well-massaged skin is the illustration for malleability (*mudutā*).
[The text compares] wieldiness (*kammaññatā*) to well-polished gold.

Now, while it may be appropriate here to cite the healthy person as an illustration because his continuum is bound to the sense faculties (*indriya*), how can this apply to well-massaged skin and well-polished gold?

For lightness and the other qualities do not occur in a material continuum that is not bound to the sense faculties, due to the absence of conditions that counteract the disturbance of the elements (*dhātu*).

It is true that this is merely an illustration of a form similar to softness and wieldiness; however, it is not what is intended here, because its intrinsic nature (sabhāva) is not that of softness and wieldiness as understood in this context.
If this is so, how is it that lightness and so forth are attributed to cotton wool and the like? There is no such thing as lightness and so forth in an ultimate sense (paramattha) there;
rather, the conventional designation of "lightness" and so forth is applied to them simply because of the absence of the causes for heaviness and the like.
It is not able to perform its function because it is entirely dependent on present conditions;
otherwise, buoyancy and the other qualities would have to exist at all times. It has the characteristic of non-sluggishness, which means the characteristic of lightness.
Its function is the dispelling, casting off, and removal of heaviness; thus, it has the function of dispelling heaviness. For although this—

It is not able to dispel the heaviness of material phenomena (*rūpa*), but because it is a transformation of light material phenomena that are the opposite of heavy ones, it is said, by way of a figurative expression—as in the cases of "birth produces it" and so forth—that "it dispels heaviness.

For when this [lightness] exists, there is simply a lack of heaviness in those material phenomena that have arisen. This same method applies to malleability (*mudutā*) and wieldiness (*kammaññatā*). As for mental buoyancy (*cetasika-lahutā*) and the others:
However, it should be understood that because they function as the destroyers of their respective opposing unwholesome states (*akusaladhamma*),
their specific functional capacity is established in a non-figurative sense precisely due to their nature as mere modifications.
"Manifesting as a quick revolution" means a non-sluggish revolution, like the successive shifting and turning of a person who is neither dull-witted nor diseased.

The meaning is "presenting itself. Because it is perceived right there as a state of change in whatever material form possesses lightness (*lahutā*), it has light material form as its proximate cause (*padatthāna*).
The same applies to the others. "Non-hardness" (*athaddhatā*) means the absence of rigidity.

Because it presents itself by its own softness, being non-opposed in all functional activities, it has non-opposition as its manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*). For that which is soft is [non-opposed] in some cases...
It is not contradictory. In all three instances, the letter *a* has the sense of opposition (*paṭipakkhattha*).

Some say that because they originate as the opposites of the causes for sluggishness and so forth, lightness and the other qualities [are called "non-sluggishness," etc.]. Others, however, say that it negates the state of being a sentient being (*satta*).

Its characteristic is the state of adaptability (*kammaññabhāva*), defined as suitability for the activities to be performed by the body; thus, it is "characterized by adaptability suitable for bodily activities."
"Unwieldiness is called 'weakness,'" thus wieldiness is said to be manifested as the state of non-weakness.

692. Regarding "the accumulation of material phenomena" (*rūpānam ācaya*) and so forth: that which is the initial accumulation (*caya*) of derived material phenomena, or the gathering (*caya*) of them from various sources according to their respective conditions—as if they have come from here and there—is the first arising and the growth of material phenomena termed "accumulation" (*upacaya*). This is what is meant by "accumulation."
In the summary [uddesa], it is stated as "upa-ññattaṃ" and "upa-sittaṃ," because the prefix *upa-* is seen there to have the sense of "successive" (*paṭhamūpari*).
However, that which is the continuous succession of those very same material phenomena—their occurrence by way of uninterrupted connection—is called "continuity" (*santati*).
For at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), it is called "accumulation" (*ācaya*) due to the state of accumulation consisting in the arising of matter and so forth; thereafter, until—

The seventeen moments of consciousness are called "accumulation" (*upacaya*) because of their state of increase. For at that time, there is only the accumulation of matter through karma, consciousness, and temperature, and not its diminution.
Alternatively, from the arising of nutriment-born matter until the arising of the eye and other sense organs, it is called "accumulation";
beyond that, however, until the end of death, it is called "continuity" (*santati*). And having established it thus—
“Whatever is the accumulation of the sense bases (*āyatana*), that is the growth of matter (*rūpa*). Whatever is the growth of matter, that is the continuity of matter.

Having stated in the commentary on this passage—which was spoken for the purpose of showing that there is no difference in meaning between growth and continuity—that “accumulation means arising, growth means increase, and continuity means occurrence,” [it continues]: “On the riverbank...”

An analogy has been stated: "Just as the time when water begins to rise in a well-dug pit is like the arising of accumulation (ācaya); the time when it is full is like the increase of accumulation (upacaya);
and the time when it flows over and continues is like the occurrence of continuity (santati).

And here, by the use of the plural form in the expression "the accumulation of material forms" (rūpānam ācayo), it is shown that what is called "arising" (uppāda) refers to those things that are currently arising.

It is a modification (*vikāra*). And since there is this state of being a modification, it is demonstrated that because of the distinctness of the various phenomena (*dhamma*) that possess modification within oneself, even for many material phenomena (*rūpa*) arising at a single moment, the state of their arising as modifications occurs individually and not as a mere aggregate.

Furthermore, such an arising belongs not only to material phenomena; rather, the arising of immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) [is also like this], [as is the case] for both material and immaterial phenomena.
It should be understood as aging, impermanence, and the lightness, softness, and wieldiness of form.

(693) Regarding "the form of birth," the intention [of the commentators] in the *Aṭṭhakathās* is that it refers to both [aging and impermanence], because they both have the intrinsic nature of the arising of form.
If this is so, why was it stated separately? Because it was taught by the Blessed One in that very way. And why did the Blessed One [teach it thus]?
"It was taught in such a way," he said, beginning with "because of the diversity of modes" (*ākāranānattā*). The diversity of modes has already been explained below.

The first arising of a syllable is its accumulation (*upacaya*); its repeated arising is its continuity (*santati*). In this way, it should be understood for material phenomena (*rūpa*) arisen from the three [other] sources as well;
thus they describe their diversity of modes. "According to the disposition of those to be trained" (*veneyyānaṃ vasena vā*)—at that time, it is said...

When the listeners have thus understood, the thought arises: "This 'birth' (jāti) is the source of all phenomena, yet it itself is not born from anything, just as 'primordial nature' (pakati) is for the proponents of primordial nature. Dispelling their misconception, [the text states]:
"'Birth' is nothing other than the very arising of material form (rūpa) existing by way of a continuous process of accumulation; it is simply that which is so designated. And that...

The teachers maintain that [the Buddha] teaches by dividing [growth] into two—namely, accumulation (*upacaya*) and continuity (*santati*)—in order to show that whatever arises obtains the designation "born" only through its conditions.
"From the prior end" means from the prior portion, that is, from the state of the future. Arising (*uppāda*) refers to material phenomena as they are currently arising.
It is said to have "the function of causing emergence" because it is as if it causes [the object] to emerge from the future moment.
It is said to have "the manifestation of handing over" because it is grasped as if handing it over [with the thought], "Receive these material phenomena.
Its manifestation as a state of fullness should be understood by way of the meaning that "accumulation" (*upacaya*) is a subsequent piling up.

Just as that which has reached the moment of arising is called "arisen" by virtue of its causal condition in the initial action (*ādikamma*), so too that which has entered the moment of arising is called "accumulated.
Thus it is said: "having accumulated matter as its proximate cause" (*upacitarūpapadaṭṭhāna*).
"Characteristics of occurrence" (*pavattilakkhaṇa*) should be understood as the occurrence of material phenomena that are proceeding by way of continuous arising.

"Having the function of continuous succession" means having the activity of continuous succession by way of preceding and succeeding moments. For if there were no arising, there could be no continuous succession by way of preceding and succeeding moments.
Because it must be grasped as non-interruption precisely due to its nature of continuous succession, it is said to "have non-interruption as its manifestation.
It is said to "have continuous succession of material form as its proximate cause" because it is perceived in material forms that are joined together by way of preceding and succeeding moments.
694. *Jīraṇa* means the state of being worn out; the meaning is the loss of the state of novelty.
Among material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*), this [aging] is manifest because changes such as brokenness and so forth are seen in the teeth and other parts;

the other [aging], however, is unmanifest due to the absence of such visible changes. Granted, even among material phenomena, momentary aging (*khaṇikajarā*) is indeed concealed, which is what is called "incessant aging" (*avīcijarā*).
However, in order to show that aging is thoroughly concealed in non-material phenomena (arūpadhammā), it is stated without qualification that "it is manifest in material phenomena.
Furthermore, the transformation consisting of brokenness and so forth does not exist in momentary aging (khaṇikajarā). The ripening of matter is the aged state of material phenomena;
since the destruction of that which has reached aging is inevitable, it is said that [aging] "has the function of bringing [them] near," meaning its task is the bringing near of destruction.
The meaning is as follows: "Even when its own-nature has not departed" means even when the own-natures such as agreeableness or hardness have not departed;

for while it is called "aging" at the moment of its persistence, the phenomenon does not abandon its own-nature at that time. "The state of being new" is the stage of arising; since it is apprehended by way of the departure of that [newness], he said:
"It has the manifestation of the departure of the state of being new. "Like the state of being old in rice" means even when the state of being rice has not departed.
It causes the departure from the state of being new, like the agedness of rice. While the agedness of rice removes all states [of the grain], this [aging] removes only the state of arising.
It is characterized by breaking up on all sides and in every way; thus it has "dissolution" as its characteristic.
That which is called "permanent" (*nicca*) is stable (*dhuvam*); however, matter (*rūpa*), because of its momentary destruction, is not permanent and is therefore "impermanent" (*anicca*).

Its state is impermanence (*aniccatā*). Furthermore, because that [impermanence] causes matter that has reached the stage of stability to seem as if it is sinking away through the very process of its dissolution, it has "sinking" as its function (*rasa*).

And since it is apprehended precisely in the form of exhaustion and passing away due to the state of breaking up, it is said to have "the manifestation of the state of exhaustion and passing away. Exhaustion (*khaya*) means destruction by way of gradual sequence, like the wick of a lamp.
They say that "decay" (vaya) is simultaneous cessation, like [the extinguishing] of oil.

696–7. "From a collection" means from a heap. "Some" refers to the inhabitants of Abhayagiri. Those whose habit is to speak of "torpor-matter" (middharūpa), or those for whom there is such discourse, are called "proponents of torpor" (middhavādino).
As for what is called "torpor-matter," it is torpor that arises from three origins: temperature, consciousness, and nutriment.
“Name-and-form”: the connection is that these are to be rejected. To the question of how they are to be rejected, he says: “The Sage,” and so forth.

There are no hindrances because, through the path of stream-entry, the hindrance of doubt is abandoned; through the path of non-returning, the hindrances of sensual desire, ill will, and restlessness-and-worry are abandoned;
and through the path of arhatship, the hindrances of sloth-and-torpor are abandoned. This is the intended meaning here: if sloth...
Form would be something that should not be abandoned. The aggregate of form is to be directly known, to be fully understood;
it is not to be abandoned, not to be developed, and not to be realized. "Which phenomena are to be abandoned neither by seeing nor by cultivation?
The wholesome in the four planes, the resultants in the four planes, the functional-inindeterminate in the three planes, and form."
And because of the statement, “Nirvana and these states are not to be abandoned either by seeing or by cultivation,” there is an absence of abandonment regarding material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*).
This being the case, its status as an hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*) would be contradicted, since hindrances must be abandoned.
For it is not the case that when hindrances are not to be abandoned—
“The doubt that I previously had, you who possess the eye have explained it to me;
truly, you are a sage, a perfectly awakened one;
there are no hindrances in you.”—This praise of the Blessed One by way of the abandoning of the hindrances would be appropriate. If it were so [stated]: “Form, monks, is not yours...”
Is it not the case that the fact that form (rūpa) is to be abandoned is also made known by such statements as "Abandon that"?

No, because what is intended there is the abandoning of the desire and lust (chandarāga) directed toward that object. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, whatever is the subduing of desire and lust for form, that is the abandoning of it.
Nor can it be said that this [principle] does not apply here as well, since it is precisely by way of the abandoning of the desire and lust directed toward that object [that form is abandoned].
It is stated [that sloth and torpor are not form] because it is a statement establishing [the point], and because the abandoning of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and so forth is not intended there;
therefore, since it would contradict statements such as "there are no hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) for you," sloth and torpor are not form.

However, if another [opponent], due to a firm and deluded adherence, [claims that] the abandoning of the hindrances occurs precisely through the abandoning of the desire and lust (*chandarāga*) directed toward them...

“Intended” means that one might establish one’s own position; in order to refute that, he says “the hindrance of sloth and torpor,” etc., bringing forward again the statement regarding its association with the hindrance of ignorance.
The connection is: “both the hindrance of sloth and torpor and the hindrance of ignorance are associated with the hindrance. This...

It is stated: “Because of the statement ‘conjunction with four,’ conjunction is obtained only among immaterial phenomena (arūpadhamma) with one another, not among material phenomena (rūpadhamma) with one another, nor between the material and the immaterial;

therefore, if torpor (middha) were material, it would not deserve that statement regarding conjunction. Now, it might be argued: “In this context, the expression ‘as far as obtainable’ can be understood.”
This is as in such passages as, “gravel and pebbles, and schools of fish, whether moving or stationary,” and so forth.

For just as in such passages as, “gravel and pebbles, and schools of fish, whether moving or stationary,” the movement [is attributed] to the gravel and pebbles by way of reference to the schools of fish—
since movement is not possible for the gravel and pebbles themselves— and the standing is by way of reference to both, so too is the case with "as it is obtained" (yathālābha).
Is it that here too, the term "associated" (*sampayoga*) is used with reference to both torpor and restlessness, while the term "hindrance" (*nīvaraṇa*) is used with reference to both?

That too is not so, because the nature of matter (*rūpa-bhāva*) has not yet been established. For if the nature of matter were established, then—due to its impossibility [in the case of torpor]—the application [of the term "hindrance"] would be appropriate according to what is available.
By this much alone, although the immaterial nature of torpor (*middha*) is established, just as in the expression "a double bond is a firm bond,"...
"Thus, being established by many suttas, it becomes unassailable. Quoting from the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of the passage in the *Paṭṭhānapakaraṇa*—"Dependent on a state that is an hindrance...

[etc. ...by way of condition"—and bringing forward even the arising in the formless existence (*arūpabhava*), which is stated therein as "in the formless [existence]... [etc. ...arises," he says: "In the Great Treatise, the *Paṭṭhāna*," and so forth.
This is because states such as craving for jhāna (*jhānanikanti*) are, in their essential nature (*dhammata*), greed and the like.
Because it is not distinct from the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*) and the others, it is stated as “the hindrance of sensual desire,” and so forth.

Here one might object: “In such passages as ‘Monks, these five hindrances are obstructions (*nīvaraṇa*’), because sloth-and-torpor (*thina-middha*) is mentioned together with them as being of the nature of a hindrance, it is also stated here together as ‘the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor’; moreover, in the formless realm (*arūpa-bhava*), it is only sloth [that is absent].”
"Does sloth and torpor arise? This is not sound, because remorse is not included [in that list].
For if inclusion here were to occur merely because something was included in one [list], then remorse—which is mentioned there as being included in one [category]—could also have been included here;
yet this is not the case, because it is stated specifically as the "hindrance of restlessness. Therefore, it is not [included].
"It is possible to ward off his rebirth in the formless realm. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), [it is meant]:

"Monks, this entire mass of unwholesomeness is these five hindrances. Having abandoned these five hindrances—because of the abandoning, the vomiting out, the release, the relinquishing, and the relinquishment of that sloth and torpor, he is free from sloth and torpor... [and so on]. Tenena... [By this...]
"It is called 'free from sloth and torpor' because this mind cleanses, purifies, thoroughly cleanses, liberates, releases,
and completely liberates itself from this sloth and torpor"— this is how he includes such passages from the Canon.
Even if there were two kinds of torpor— material and immaterial— the immaterial kind is taught among the hindrances (nīvaraṇa).
Is it not form? That too it is not, because there is no specific designation. For *middha* (drowsiness) was not taught among the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) by way of distinction—as in:
"Bhikkhus, whatever is *thina* (sloth), that too is a hindrance; whatever is *middha*, that too is a hindrance;
'sloth-and-drowsiness' is a hindrance"—but rather because it was stated without distinction. Therefore, regarding the twofold nature of *middha*:
Even by such a supposition, it is not possible to deny its status as an hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*).

For one could indeed say that even that torpor (*middha*) which is imagined to be distinct from the immaterial (*arūpa*) is an hindrance because its intrinsic nature is torpor, just like the other hindrances.
If you do not accept that torpor has a material nature (*rūpabhāva*), how can the Blessed One experience sleep? Is it not torpor?
Is it not established that sleep exists because it is stated in the *Vibhaṅga* as “sleep, drowsiness,” and so forth? This is not so;
for just as with the feminine gender and so on, the cause of sleep—namely, *middha* (torpor)—is analyzed by way of the state of sleep itself.

If it is asked, “Even so, since the cause of sleep (*middha*) is absent, how can there be sleep for the Blessed One?”—it cannot be said that he has no such sleep, [as the Buddha] says: “I recall... [and so on].
However, Aggivessana, from such statements as “...I slept during the day,” it follows that the Blessed One’s sleep was not due to *middha* (drowsiness), but rather due to bodily illness;
yet one cannot say that the Blessed One lacked that [bodily illness], because of his statement: “My back is aching, I shall stretch it.
Nor should this be understood as an absolute restriction, namely, that “only *middha* [is meant].”
"Because of sleepiness. Therefore, there is another cause for sleepiness as well. What is it? It is physical illness;
thus, it should be understood that the Blessed One’s sleep was not caused by torpor (*middha*).
698. "Having shown the absence of each individually" means having shown the state of non-existence of each one, beginning with the air element.

But how is that to be demonstrated? He says, "By the air element," and so forth. Therein, what is called "bodily power" (kāyabala) is, in its actual sense, a specific mode of manifestation of the air element, because it is the state of its expansion. Since the ignorant call this "power," it is said:
"When the air element is apprehended, the material quality of power is indeed apprehended. Its origin is in the realm of desire (kāmadhātu) for certain beings.
The specific mode of occurrence of the water element that serves as the condition for the maturation of the faculties is what is meant by the phrase "the produced matter of the water element.
The connection is: "what has been grasped is indeed already included [within what was previously mentioned].

There is no arising of matter apart from accumulation (upacaya) and continuity (santati), and there is no such thing as "birth" (jāti) other than the state of arising itself; thus it is said: "the matter of birth [is comprised] within accumulation and continuity. This applies even to matter originated by kamma.
The proximate cause of disease is the disturbance of the elements (dhātukkhobha) arising from unwholesome conditions; this is even more so for other types of suffering.

In its actual sense, this occurs only during the moments of the maturation, subsistence, and dissolution of material phenomena (rūpadhamma). Therefore, it is said: "the form of disease is included by means of decay (jaratā), impermanence (aniccatā), and so forth."
699–704. They are called "origins of matter" (*rūpasamuṭṭhāna*) because matter arises and is born from them.

As to what those are, he says: "the temperature, consciousness, nutriment, and kamma. Regarding the phrase "nutriment is a cause of matter," the word "iti" (thus) should be supplied here; thus, kamma, temperature, consciousness, and nutriment—these are the causes of matter.
"Causes of matter" means conditions that generate matter. Therefore, he says: "by these very [factors]," and so forth.
Those which have only one single origin are "single-origin" (*ekasamuṭṭhāna*). Is it not the case that there is no arising of a conditionally arisen phenomenon from a single condition?
True, there is not; however, the intended meaning here is "from among the conditions that produce matter.
The eight faculties are the five beginning with the eye, the pair of female and male faculties, and the life faculty—thus making eight faculties.
The two types of intimation are by way of bodily and vocal intimation.

"By two" means that for some it is by consciousness (*citta*), and for others by temperature (*utu*); thus, by two. For two conditions do not exist as causes for one and the same thing at one and the same moment.

The same applies to the remaining cases. Regarding temperature, nutriment, and so forth... "produced" (*kata*) refers to each being produced by three: by temperature, by nutriment, and by consciousness.

It is said: "And the four elements" refers to the four great primary elements (*mahābhūta*). For these are called "elements" (*dhātu*) in the sense of being devoid of a sentient being and devoid of a soul.
"Four existences" (*catubbhava*) means they arise from the four [causes] beginning with kamma. "Two" refers to aging and impermanence.
Now, including those arising from mixed origins as well, the numerical limit of those things produced by their respective conditions is [to be understood].

To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “by kamma” was stated. Therein, twenty [factors]—the eight faculties, the pure octad (suddhaṭṭhaka), continuity (santati), accumulation (upacaya), and space (ākāsa)—are born of kamma (kammaja).
Seventeen [factors]—the two types of intimation (viññatti), sound (sadda), the triad of lightness and so forth (lahutādi), and the eleven beginning with the pure octad—are born of consciousness;
the meaning is that they are “born of mind” (cetasā jātā). Sound, the triad of lightness and so forth, and the eleven beginning with the pure octad—these five and ten [make fifteen].

Fifteen [factors] arise from temperature (*utu*). The triad of lightness (*lahutā*) and so forth, along with the pure octad (*suddha-aṭṭhaka*) and others—eleven in total—arise from nutriment (*āhāra*).
Together with aging (*jaratā*) and impermanence (*aniccatā*), they become sixty-eight; such is the connection [of the text].
Having stated, “Aging... arisen,” he then provides the reason for that by saying, “Of what has been born,” and so forth.

It has been stated. In that context, "because of the ripening and breaking of what is born" means: because of the ripening of a phenomenon that has already arisen due to aging (*jaratā*), and because of the breaking [of it] due to impermanence (*aniccatā*).
This is what is meant: aging and impermanence belong to a phenomenon that has already arisen, not to one that is currently arising.
For if they were to belong to what is currently arising, then even those two would have the designation of "being born."

It would be appropriate [to say] that they would arise. However, regarding a phenomenon that has already arisen, it is fitting to say that these [factors] do not arise from its birth onwards, because of their own subsequent occurrence.

But if someone were to argue, "What contradiction is there even in their being born?", then, in order to refute that mistaken grasp, he said, "They would be born," and so forth. Let it be granted that they too have a distinction of maturation; even then, what...
Regarding the contradiction, he says “for not,” and so forth. The connection is “the ripening does not ripen,” by which it is shown that it does not break up;
for the breaking up of that which has ripened is certain. Or, in the phrase “nor does it break up even when there is breaking,” the state of ripening is likewise stated here.
For that which is unripened does not break up; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of non-difference between arising and breaking up. There is none.
He stated this by summarizing the very point already explained—that there is no cooking or breaking apart of those various stages of ripening.

What, then, has been said up to this point? If aging and impermanence were to arise through some condition, then that which has arisen would necessarily possess aging and dissolution; thus, those [stages] would indeed have aging and impermanence, but they do not.
And yet these are perceived. Why? Because aging does not age or break apart by means of another aging, nor does disintegration disintegrate or age by means of another disintegration;
otherwise, that aging would itself age and break apart by means of another aging and disintegration, and that disintegration would age and break apart by means of another aging and disintegration.
"It breaks up" means that it would follow that there is no stability;
this is what is being stated. 709–10. "Of that which is born," etc., is the conclusion. Alternatively, it is the setting aside of the result of the objection to be stated further on.
"It might be somewhere," etc., is the apprehension of a supreme [alternative]. "In this case" refers to this [position]: "The two—decay and impermanence—are not cooked."
In the context of the phrase "nor does it break," the word *iti* in the expression "the accumulation of matter" (*rūpassūpacayo*) has the sense of "beginning";
thus, the meaning is by means of the statement "the accumulation and continuity of matter. The connection is: "Let there likewise be ripening, and let there likewise be breaking apart.
However, the intended meaning here is as follows: just as in the description of matter arising from karma and so forth, [it is asked] "What is that matter... [and so on].
What is appropriated (upādinna)? The eye-base …pe… the body-base, the femininity-faculty, the masculinity-faculty, the life-faculty,
or whatever other matter there is produced by karma, such as the visible-form base …pe… the tangible base,
the space-element, integration of matter, continuity of matter, and physical nutriment— thus [it is said] regarding integration and continuity.
Because it has been demonstrated [as such], it is shown that birth arises even in the absence of a subsequent birth.

Likewise, aging and dissolution must be accepted as the process of growing old and breaking up even in the absence of subsequent aging and dissolution; otherwise, the very state of birth would itself be subject to dissolution.
711. “And not even... and so forth is a rejection of the opponent’s view based on mere suspicion.
If it is not to be understood that [the dharma] is born, then why was it stated thus in the *Niddesa*? To this he says: “Of that which is being born,” and so forth. This is what is meant:

even though there is no actual birth (*jāti*), because there is the state of manifestation for those phenomena that are in the process of being born, there is the conventional designation of that [birth] as their condition.
"It is called 'birth' there [in that context], but not in the ultimate sense (paramatthato), because it arises [only conventionally].
For birth is merely the manifestation of that which is being born; therefore, this is proving the unproven by means of what is itself unproven.
With the words "In that context" (*tattha*) and so forth, he again raises the suspicion of [the opponent's] ultimate view and refutes it. In that regard, of those phenomena...

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: whatever is birth (jāti) necessarily receives the designation "having that as its condition" (tappaccayatta) and the conventional term "arising" (abhinibbatti).
"Tathā" means "just as it necessarily receives [them], so [it is here]. For the pronouns *yaṃ* and *taṃ* possess an inseparable relationship.
"Having those phenomena as its condition" is *tappaccayā*; the state of being that is *tappaccayattaṃ*; and the designation occurring by way of that state is *tappaccayattavohāro*.

The meaning is: "that conventional designation (vohāra) such as the state of being a condition for karma. "Conventional designation of arising" (abhinibbatti-sammuti) means the conventional designation occurring by way of arising, [expressed as] "it arises" or "it is born.
"Originating from karma, etc. (kammādi-sambhava) means originating from the four conditions beginning with karma. The connection is:
"due to the absence [of these factors] at the moment of the manifestation of the power of the productive conditions. This, however, is the meaning here:
—Regarding those conditions for the production of material phenomena (*rūpa*) which have not ceased their activity toward their arising:

with reference to the state of being obtained as a modification by the phenomena (*dhamma*) that are then being born, at that moment characterized by the condition and the efficacy of the function, "being born from a condition" (*jātattaṃ paccayato*) is admitted by way of the person to be trained (*vineyyapuggala*). From that...
Because it is not apprehended either before or after, and having established this, it is said: "But it is obtained through birth.

However, because aging and dissolution are obtained at the moments of stability and dissolution subsequent to the moment of the power of their conditions, it is not possible to grant [the same status] to them in that way;
the intention is that this conventional expression is obtained through birth. The two verses beginning with "The conventional expression of being conditioned by that... [follow].
This was stated by way of conclusion. 718–9.
Now, what is the use of this scratching of the neck? Has it not been said by the Blessed One in the Sutta:
"Bhikkhus, aging-and-death is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen"? Therefore, how can it be said that [aging] is decay?
If someone were to say that impermanence does not arise from anything at all, the passage beginning with “It is ‘impermanent’” was stated in order to show their thought and refute it.
To the question “Why should this not be said? he replied, “For that is a teaching by way of a method (pariyāyadesanā).

In order to clarify its nature as a teaching by way of a method, the passage beginning with “of things that are impermanent” was stated. By the word “thus” (tathā), the term “conditioned” (saṅkhata) is included.
720–3. By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "impermanent and conditioned," [the text] includes "dependently arisen.
This is the intended meaning here: because aging and death are the nature of impermanent and conditioned phenomena, they occur when those [phenomena] exist and do not occur when they do not exist.
For that which is unborn does not age or break up; therefore, with reference to its dependence on birth, it is said: "aging and death..."
It is stated in the Sutta by way of a figurative expression (*pariyāya*) that "it is conditioned, dependently arisen, and for that very reason impermanent.

Just as, although intimation (*viññatti*) and so forth do not originate from the mind in an absolute sense, they are said to have the status of originating from the mind because they are modifications produced by the mind;
so too, the status of lightness (*lahutā*) and the other [characteristics] as being born of the mind and so forth should be understood merely as a figurative illustration.
Because it is so desired. In the direct sense (*nippariyāyena*), there are exactly eighteen derived material phenomena (*nipphanna-rūpa*) originating from karma and the other [causes].
"The three" refers to the triad of characteristic-materiality (*lakkhaṇa-rūpa*) consisting of birth, aging, and dissolution.
"Like a sky-flower" means like a flower in the sky; just as a sky-flower does not exist at all because it has never been born, so too is this [unproduced materiality].

The meaning is "it does not exist. "Constant like the unconditioned" means that just as the unconditioned *nibbāna* is permanent and stable because it is unconditioned by anything, so too this [space] is constant and eternal because it is unconditioned by anything.
"But neither of these" means that both of these do not exist, being like a flower in the sky, and yet they are not unconditioned like *nibbāna*.

This is the meaning. "Existing dependent on a support" means that for those things being born, ripening, or dissolving, their existence is bound to the supports of birth and so forth by virtue of their nature as mere states of being born and so on. To substantiate this very dependence on a support, it is said:
"In the case of earth and the rest," etc. This, however, is the summary of the meaning here: [the dependence] of the supports, such as earth and the rest...
When these states exist, the triad beginning with birth is discerned; therefore, they do not not exist. And because they are not discerned when those [states] are absent, they are not permanent.
It should be understood that it was precisely to refute this very adherence that the Blessed One spoke of birth four times and of aging-and-death by way of the formula beginning with "impermanent."

724–5. As for the term "produced" (*nipphanna*): they are called "produced" because they must be apprehended by way of their own specific intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), such as hardness and so forth, after transcending states such as delimitation—as in the cases of "delimitation of matter," "change of matter," or "characteristic of matter"—or because they are produced directly, without figurative usage, by conditions such as kamma.
Conversely, those that are the opposite of these are "unproduced" (*anipphanna*).
Having heard that "the [three characteristics] are unproduced," another person, wishing to bring about an undesirable consequence, says, "If they exist," and so forth.

With the words "Of those very [characteristics]," however, he rejects that [position]. A bodily modification is called bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*); a verbal modification is called verbal intimation (*vacīviññatti*);

a fissure, an aperture, is called the space element (*ākāsadhātu*); the state of lightness is called lightness (*lahutā*); the state of malleability is called malleability (*mudutā*); the state of wieldiness is...

Workability (*kammaññatā*) is called "origination" (*nibbatti*); accumulation (*upacaya*) is called "growth" (*pavatti*); continuity (*santati*) is called "duration" (*thiti*); the mode of decaying is called "aging" (*jaratā*);

and the mode of non-existence after having been is called "impermanence" (*aniccatā*). Thus, because these very eighteen derived material phenomena are themselves modifications, they are both "derived" (*nipphanna*) and "conditioned" (*saṅkhata*).
How then could those [three unconditioned phenomena] be called "unconditioned" (*asaṅkhata*) on account of being modifications of those very same material phenomena?

They explain the meaning by connecting the phrase as follows: "If the produced forms that serve as the support for unproduced forms are conditioned (saṅkhata), then how can those [unproduced forms], which are their modifications, be called unconditioned (asaṅkhata)?
According to their intention, it should be understood that in the phrase "nipphannā ceva," the particle *ca* is established through grammatical tradition (*āgama*).

726–7. "The female state... [etc. ...is described" is the establishment of the result (*phalaṭhapana*). "This being so," and so forth, is the objection (*codanā*). "But another... and so forth, is the resolution (*parihāra*).
In that context, regarding the statement "the unity of the sensitive matter of the eye and the body arises":

because the state of the sensitive matter of the body exists within the sensitive matter of the eye, and the state of the sensitive matter of the eye exists within the sensitive matter of the body, there is the manifestation of the tangible object for the former, and for the other...
"And the appearance of form occurs" means that there would be a unification of the sensitivity of the eye and the body; this is merely an illustration.
For, according to the method already stated, the ear-sensitivity, body-sensitivity, and so forth, likewise possess unity alone. 728–30.
"But one does not exist in another" refers to their occurrence except by way of mutual inseparability.
One material form does not exist in another material form from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*), because they belong to different aggregates by virtue of having distinct bases.

For the sensitivity of the eye is dependent on the primary elements produced by kamma rooted in the desire to see, whereas the sensitivity of the body is dependent on the primary elements produced by kamma rooted in the desire to touch.
"Unmixed" means unconfused. If this is so, does it mean that the body-base and so forth do not exist everywhere? That too does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Indeed, it is not possible to point out their difference by separating them; therefore, to demonstrate this, it was said:

"by way of mutual inseparability," and so forth. [The phrase] "because they proceed... by way of mutual inseparability" means because they proceed as non-disjoined through the mode of mutual inseparability from the continuity [of the stream].
However, the meaning is not "by way of inseparable materiality" (*avinibbhoga-rūpa*), for [this does not apply to] the sensitivity of the eye or the body.
It is possible to speak of these inseparable material phenomena belonging to a single group (*ekakalāpa*) as being in different locations.
Just as it is said that visible form, taste, and so forth are mutually pervasive because they cannot be separated, yet in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*) there is no taste within visible form;

for if there were, the apprehension of taste would occur simultaneously with the apprehension of visible form. In the same way, this applies to the body-base (*kāyāyatana*) and the others in the ultimate sense.
It does not exist everywhere; however, no one who knows the proper occasion can specify a particular location by saying, "This is here" or "That is there.
In the phrase "there is bodily serenity," the word *iti* has the sense of "therefore. That is why he said, "therefore.
"Thus declared" means that it is declared as being present in all locations (*sabbaṭṭhānika*).
"731–2. 'Also by way of characteristics, etc. means also by way of the characteristics, functions, manifestations, and proximate causes as previously stated.

'The shadows of the banners... have gone' means that the shadows of the banners—which consist of five colors such as blue and so forth, made of threads of five colors—have each attained the state of being a simile (upamā-bhāva) for those [five aggregates] according to their respective single color; this is the meaning. However, some [read] 'chāyā'..."
"These have a likeness," they say; "likeness" (*chāyā-upama*), the state of having that likeness is "likeness-likeness" (*chāyā-upamatā*); these phenomena have reached that state.
However, this was likely said by them thinking that the shortening [of the vowel] occurs here through a *bahubbīhi* compound in the sense of "having reached the likeness-likeness.
But for the sake of the metrical composition of the verse, it should be understood as a shortening. In the cases of "the fourth [duty]," etc.,...
Indeed, by showing even the elision of case endings (*vibhattilopa*), the Teacher does not show concern for mere phonetic forms (*byañjana*) in such instances.

As for what is said by those who do not wish to connect the preceding word "of them" (*tesam*) with the subsequent word "of phenomena" (*dhammānam*)—namely, [the phrase] "having reached diversity" (*nānattam samupāgatam*)—that must certainly be connected here, even against their will. Not...
"Indeed, he does not look upon those who have fallen into diversity.

Furthermore, even if they were to imagine the reading "those who have fallen into diversity" (*nānattaṃ samupāgatā*) there, let their satisfaction be granted by imagining a reading that is not even seen in the manuscripts.
However, the intended meaning here is as follows: just as when five-colored banners are gathered together and raised up...

Just as shadows, though appearing as if joined together, are nonetheless unmixed with one another, even so these material phenomena existing in all places, though they appear as if joined together, are nonetheless distinct in their intrinsic natures and unmixed when considered according to their specific characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*).
For even those existing within a single group (*kalāpa*) are distinct in their intrinsic natures according to their characteristics; how much more so then those existing in different groups?
733. That which is bound to the world by its own conditions is called "mundane" (*lokika*); the state of being such is "mundanity" (*lokikatta*).

It is a "cause" (*hetu*) because by means of it the aggregate of associated states goes forth (*hinoti*) and becomes established; thus, greed and so forth, as well as non-greed and so forth, are causes in the sense of being supportive.
That which is not such a cause is "not-a-cause" (*nahetu*). That which is conditioned by its own conditions is "conditioned" (*abhisaṅkhata*).
It is conditioned (*saṅkhata*). They flow (*savanti*) up to the peak of existence (*ābhavagga*) or until the stage of change-of-lineage (*agotrabhu*), thus they are *āsava*s;

that which is "with *āsava*s" is *sāsava*; the meaning is that it is to be latched onto by the *āsava*s. "Dependent on conditions for its occurrence" means that because its activity is contingent upon its respective conditions, it is said to be "possessing conditions" (*sappaccaya*); this is merely an illustration. Because it belongs to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), because it is rootless (*ahetuka*), and because it is dissociated from roots (*hetuvippayutta*).
It is of one kind for such reasons as being subject to fetters, subject to ties, subject to clinging, subject to floods, subject to yokes, subject to hindrances,
being defiled, being adhered to, being non-mental, being dissociated from consciousness, not belonging to the fine-material sphere,
not belonging to the immaterial sphere, not being included within the [three] planes, not leading to emancipation, and being impermanent. Thus it is of one kind.

734–8. Having thus shown the singlefold method, he now begins the internal dyads and so forth with the words "internal and external" (*ajjhattika-bahiddhā*) in order to show the twofold method and others included by the word "etc. (*ādi*). Therein, first, regarding the internal dyad:

that in which the conceit "I am" (*ahaṃ-māna*) is placed is the self (*atta*), that is, personal existence (*attabhāva*); because it proceeds with reference to or directed toward that self, [it is called "internal"].
"Internal" (*ajjhattika*) means those phenomena bound to the sense-faculties, existing within them, or existing within oneself (*attani*).
Granted, there are other things produced internally as well; however, by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhī*), only the eye and so forth are called "internal.
Alternatively, it is like saying, "If we did not exist, you would be like a mere log of wood."
Because they are exceptionally beneficial to the personal existence (*attabhāva*), these alone specifically receive the designation "internal.

Regarding "faculties" (*indriya*) and "non-faculties" (*anindriya*): they are "faculties" in the sense of sovereignty (*ādhipacca*), while the remainder are "non-faculties" due to the absence of that quality.

Among them, the five beginning with the eye are faculties because they exercise sovereignty over the visual consciousness and so forth, by following their state of being keen or dull; as for the pair consisting of the female faculty and the male faculty—
It should be understood that [the female faculty] acts as the cause for the state of being female and so forth, while the life-faculty acts to maintain co-nascent material phenomena.
It is "gross" because it must be apprehended through impact by way of the relationship between object and subject; it is "subtle" because it is the opposite of that.
"Clung-to" (*upādinnam*) means grasped by kamma; for that which is produced by kamma is, as it were, grasped by that kamma with the thought, "This is my fruit."
Eleven... [etc. ... "With resistance" (*sappaṭigha*): because it is not cognizable by eye-consciousness and because it lacks the quality of being visible, it is "invisible" (*anidassana*);
however, because there is mutual impact through their striking against one another, it is "with resistance. By negating both of these, it is "invisible and non-resistant" (*anidassana-appaṭigha*).
"Born of kamma": herein, that which is exclusively originated by kamma consists of nine types—the eight faculties and the physical basis (*vatthu*).

Form. And that which is the elevenfold form produced by kamma among the elevenfold forms produced by the four origins—thus, all twenty kinds [of form] are "born of kamma" (kammaja) because they arise from kamma.

For whatever has been born, is being born, or will be born, all that is called "born of kamma," just as [the milk already drawn] is called "milk" (duddha). That which is other than kamma is "non-kamma" (akamma).
“Born from non-action” means born from that which is not action; here, the negative particle *a-* has the sense of "other. Therefore he said:

“born from conditions other than that. The meaning is: born from conditions other than action—namely, from temperature, consciousness, and nutriment. The terms “born of consciousness” (*cittaja*) and so forth could have been included by following the same pattern already stated, but they were not shown.

"In the tetrad of the seen, it is to be regarded as 'the seen' (*diṭṭha*). That which is the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*)—that which one has seen, that which one will see, that which one sees, and that which one might see—all that is called "the seen," because it does not transcend its own nature, just as in the term "the desirable" (*iṭṭha*).

This same method applies to the heard (*suta*) and so forth. What is called "the seen" is the sphere of visible form, because it is cognizable by eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*). What is called "the heard"...
The sound-base (saddāyatana) is so called because it is to be cognized by ear-consciousness.

That which is called "the sensed" (muta) refers to the triad of odor, taste, and tangible bases, because they are to be grasped by reaching or contacting them, or because they are connected with the sensitive organ (pasāda). For this reason, these are said to be objects apprehended through direct encounter.
That which is called "the cognized" (viññāta) is the remainder, because it is to be cognized solely by mind-consciousness.

"Both door and basis": because they serve as the gateway for the occurrence of visual consciousness and so forth—which depend upon themselves—as well as for the occurrence of the receiving-consciousness and so forth—which depend upon others—they are both "door" (*dvāra*) and "basis" (*vatthu*). As for "being merely a door and not a basis":
it is "merely a door" because it serves exclusively as the gateway for kamma; [this refers to] the arising of consciousness that depends upon it.

Because it is non-existent, it is not a base (*vatthu*). Being a base itself, it is not a door (*dvāra*), because the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) have it as their support; thus it is only a base.
Like the eye and so forth, it is not a door because there is no door for the occurrence of those [consciousnesses] that depend on another.
The remaining twenty-one kinds of matter, by way of the opposite of what was stated, are neither doors nor bases. This refers to the fourth tetrad.
In the tetrad of bases (*vatthu-catuṣka*). The "third term" refers to the phrase: "being only a base, it is not a faculty.
739–40. The connection is "again, fivefold. It is explained as "fourfold" precisely because it originates from four [bases].

The sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) is "to be cognized by eye-consciousness" because it is to be grasped by that [consciousness], but not because it is to be cognized by eye-consciousness alone.

For this is cognized both by the adverting consciousness and so forth, and by the impulsion consciousnesses functioning through the mind-door. This same method applies to those things cognizable by the ear and so on.

However, that which is cognizable by mind-consciousness is to be known solely by mind-consciousness; for the eye-consciousness and the others do not arise with respect to anything other than visible form and the rest.
"By way of the division of bases and non-bases" means by way of the division of the six bases and the non-base. The pentad beginning with visible form is cognizable by the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
Because the mind-base (*manāyatana*) is not material and because a portion of the mental-object-base (*dhammāyatana*) is material, it is said: "It is elevenfold by way of the division of bases.

(743–5) This is because there is no arising of matter in the immaterial realm (*arūpabhava*), and because the non-percipient realm (*asaññībhava*) is included within the fine-material realm (*rūpabhava*).

It was stated: “In the two realms of existence, kāma and rūpa. Regarding the phrase “excluding the earth-dwellers,” this refers to the exclusion of the earth-deities (bhummadeva), because when categorized by their mode of birth (yoni), they are similar to human beings.
“The first three” refers to the egg-born (aṇḍaja), the womb-born (jalābuja), and the moisture-born (saṃsedaja) modes of birth.

For these are not found among the aforementioned divisions [of the fine-material realm], and by the negation of those, the final mode of birth, the spontaneously born (opapātika), is thereby permitted.

"In terms of meaning, it is already implied. In this context, because even the "outgrowths" (*ussada*) are included under the term "hell," even insects and small creatures in the Great Avīci Hell are born only after their bodies have first increased in size.

Since the *nijjhāmataṇhika* ghosts are constantly afflicted by illness and lack sensual desire, they do not undergo conception; therefore, the egg-born (*aṇḍaja*) and womb-born (*jalābuja*) modes of birth do not exist there.
Some say that because it is burning, an embryo does not take root in the womb.

Furthermore, because those being reborn must undergo great suffering due to the power of their evil karma, they must possess a large body; thus, even the moisture-born mode of birth (saṃsedaja-yoni) is not possible for them.
This is because their bodies are scorched by the flames of fire at the time of rebirth, and therefore [they cannot find] flowers and the like in moist places.
Some say that because there is no possibility of birth from moisture, moisture-born beings (*saṃsedaja*) do not exist at all;
therefore, they maintain that for them, the only mode of birth is the apparitional (*opapātika*). Now, what is the distinction between the moisture-born and the apparitional modes of birth?
A moisture-born being first arises with a small body depending on the interior of a lotus or similar environment, and grows gradually. The other, however, [arises] wherever—
He is reborn there, appearing with a body of definite proportions, like a youth sixteen years of age, with all his limbs and members fully developed.

Regarding the "remaining three destinations": excluding the divine destination and the hellish destination, among the remaining three—namely, those designated as human, peta, and animal—some humans are indeed egg-born, such as the Elder Kuntaputta and the Elder Dvebhātika. Some...
There are also moisture-born beings, such as the brahmin Pokkharasāti and others who were born within the interior of a lotus;

some are also spontaneously born, such as the courtesan Ambapālī and others. Furthermore, the remaining "withered-thirst" (nijjhāmataṇhika) pretas, all quadrupeds, winged creatures, long-lived beings (dīghajāti), and all other animals—these constitute the four modes of birth.
