746–7. One who lies in the womb (*gabbha*)—that is, in the mother’s belly—is called *gabbhaseyyaka*. That very being, by virtue of being attached to form and so forth, is the "womb-dwelling being" (*gabbhaseyyakasatta*). Of that womb-dwelling being:
"thirty forms" refers precisely to the thirty kamma-born material phenomena (*rūpa*), by way of the decads of the body, sex, and physical basis.
For at that time, there is no mind-born material phenomenon, because the rebirth-linking consciousness lacks the capacity to originate matter.

Nor is it temperature-born, because of the absence of a previously arisen temperature. For temperature produces matter that has reached its proper stage, and nutriment-born matter is absent in that body because of the lack of ingested food;
therefore, at the moment of rebirth-linking, only the thirty types of matter produced by kamma arise, which are collectively called "embryo-matter" (*kalalarūpa*).

And those [drops], having been placed by Jātiuṇṇā into the shoulder-blade of one person from whom the oil had been extracted and poured out, become clear, limpid, and like drops of pure oil, merely the size of a drop remaining at the tip. As it has been said:
"Just as a drop of sesame oil..."
Like the unclouded cream of ghee, such is the resemblance of its color;
it is called the *kalala*.

By the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "only those possessing intrinsic nature" (*sabhāvasseva*), he demonstrates the impossibility of the thirty material phenomena in one who lacks intrinsic nature, because of the absence of the tenfold set of material qualities (*bhāvadasaka*) in such a person.

Therefore, he said: "In one lacking intrinsic nature... by way of the physical basis of the body. Some maintain that by the phrase "of those lacking intrinsic nature and those born from a womb," he shows that this is not the case for those of apparitional birth (*opapātika*).
However, having previously spoken of those of apparitional birth who possess intrinsic nature, [the author] uses this to exclude them from the present context.

It should be understood that the phrase "of beings who have not yet entered the womb" (*abhāvagabbhaseyyakasattānaṃ*) is what is intended. Since egg-born beings were already included by the previous mention of "those dwelling in the womb," their separate mention here should be understood according to the principle of "the cow and the bull" (i.e., mentioning the general and the specific), and not for the purpose of excluding the state of non-existence (*abhāvakabhāva*) for them.
Otherwise, the statement regarding the twenty types of material phenomena would be contradicted.
Furthermore, the status of non-existence here should be understood according to the context of egg-born beings (*aṇḍaja*).
For it is not possible to bring the word "non-existence" (*abhāva*), which has become a compound with the word "womb-dweller" (*gabbhaseyyaka*), into this context.

748. Regarding the phrase "by including what was already included, they become eleven," this means that among the material phenomena (*rūpa*) included in one group, [they are counted again] in another group...

By way of non-inclusion, there is the pure octad; thus, for one who is without sex (abhāvaka), eleven material phenomena arise at the moment of rebirth-linking: life, body-integration, and the physical basis.
However, for one with sex (sabhāvaka), there are twelve material phenomena, being the same as the former plus one of the two sexual characteristics.

This is the method applied to those groups of material phenomena occurring at the moment of rebirth-linking that have been mentioned and will be mentioned, by including what was not previously included.
This same method should be understood regarding the apprehension of form.
Now, although it was stated, "In all the decads," how are those decads to be known? To this he says, "By the life-faculty," and so forth.
"Pure octad" refers to the four great elements and the color, odor, flavor, and nutritive essence dependent upon them.

The pure octad is unmixed with life-faculty and the rest. Indeed, these same eight, because they occur in some cases as inseparable, are called "inseparable material phenomena" (*avinibbhoga-rūpa*); at least one such group is called a "kalāpa.
However, the Elder Ācariya Jotipāla, having stated that "ten material phenomena—both produced and unproduced—that exist in inseparable association constitute one kalāpa," said:
Furthermore, for the purpose of clarifying that same point, this was said:
“Existing inseparably, possessing four kinds of single characteristics;
or, among those [eight] produced entities, excluding the characteristic of the body.”

750. *Kāyadasaka*: This is called the "body-decad" because the body is the tenth member therein; or alternatively, it is a decad characterized by the uncommon body. This same method applies to the eye-decad and the others. *Pariyāpuṭaṃ* means known, or rather, explained. 752–3.
Because seventy material phenomena are obtained at all times—both during rebirth-linking and during the course of existence—among the deities of the sense-sphere, it is said:
"Seventy material phenomena are constant. For they never possess deficient faculties, nor do they ever become non-existent [in those respects].

If it is said, “Is the Dhamma called a sense-base (āyatana)? [and one answers] “Yes,” then even though smell and taste lack the status of being sense-bases [independently], some status as a sense-base must be predicated of them.

And if, like the status of earth and so forth, they were to have some intrinsic nature (sabhāva) other than the status of tangible objects, then they would be included within the sense-base of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana).
However, if their status as a sense-base exists only in virtue of their being the natures of smell and taste...

And since it is the case that "it is odor and it is a base, thus it is the odor-base; it is taste and it is a base, thus it is the taste-base," this [definition] is already established, and the status of these as odor-base and taste-base cannot be denied.

In the Pāli, it is stated: "The five sense bases appear" and "the six sense bases," and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "three nutriments":

“...the non-arising of the nose-faculty.

However, the Elder Jotipāla and others state: “It is said that thirty material phenomena arise for one born of moisture who is blind from birth, deaf, and lacking a nose-faculty or being a neuter, by way of the tongue-decad and the body-base-decad; this does not refer to a being of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*). And in the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga* commentary...”
Because it is stated “at the moment of rebirth,” this method is set forth specifically with reference to a being of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*). And in the *Yamaka-aṭṭhakathā* it is said:
“In the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is no spontaneously born being who is without the nose. If there were such a one, one would have to say that for him eight bases (*āyatana*) appear.
Furthermore, in the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga*: “At the moment of rebirth in the sense-sphere realm...”

In the explanation of such passages as “For some, eleven bases (āyatana) appear,” the term “spontaneously born (opapātika) petas” and so forth is used exclusively; the term “moisture-born (saṃsedaja)” is not mentioned.

It should be understood that this was stated by including moisture-born beings who possess complete bases within the category of spontaneously born beings. For it is said thus in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā):
They say: "Moisture-born beings are described as being included among the spontaneously born (*opapātika*) by virtue of their having complete sense bases;
or rather, it is said 'of the spontaneously born' in order to show that all [beings] with complete sense bases are included within the primary mode of birth.
Therefore, they maintain that there is no contradiction with the Canon (*pāḷi*).
But others say: "There is no spontaneously born (opapātika) being in the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu) who is without a nose.

If there were, it would have been said that for some eight bases (āyatana) manifest. This [statement] was made with reference to moisture-born spontaneously born beings among humans, who possess all their bases complete.
However, because there exist certain noseless insects, this was said with reference to moisture-born spontaneously born beings in the woeful states."
They say this. According to the opinion of Ācariya Ānanda and others, that [position] is indeed subject to refutation.
757–8. "In between the maximum and the minimum" means in the middle of the maximum limit stated as "seventy" and the minimum limit stated as "thirty.
... "Accordingly... for one who is discerning": for example, sixty [years] for one born blind.

The meaning is that the arising of material phenomena (rūpa) should be understood by way of the mutual dependence of complete sets of material phenomena— such as the absence of the eye-decad in one who is blind, the absence of the ear-decad in one who is deaf,
and the absence of both the eye-decad and the ear-decad in one who is both blind and deaf— and so forth according to this method. As for what remains to be said here, it has already been stated.

759–60. Having thus shown the occurrence of materiality at rebirth-linking within the three realms of existence, the passage beginning with “twenty-seven kinds of materiality” is now stated in order to show its occurrence during the course of existence.

For in the case of a sense-sphere being with complete sense bases—provided there is no impairment of the sensitive organs such as blindness or deafness—there are twenty-seven kinds of materiality present from the seventeenth consciousness prior to the death-consciousness until that moment.

Material phenomena proceed [in this way]. However, for one whose sense bases are incomplete—such as one born blind—the decrease and increase of material phenomena should be understood according to the method explained above.
[An objection is raised: "But do not only twenty-eight material phenomena proceed in the sensual realm?
To this, he says: "Because of their non-proceeding," and so forth.

"The nose... [etc. ...do not exist": because they have become dispassionate toward the sensitivities that grasp odors and so forth by means of the cultivation of detachment from sensual desire (*kāma-virāga-bhāvanā*), the triad beginning with the nose does not exist.
However, because they have not become dispassionate toward the eye-faculties for the sake of supreme vision and so forth, those [faculties] arise for them.
The two [mental] faculties do not arise because they are the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for sensual lust (*kāmarāga*). Some [teachers say...]
However, as for those who say, "The triad of lightness and so forth is also absent in the fine-material existence because there is no disturbance of the elements that causes stiffness and so on;
for when such a disturbance of the elements exists, there must be its opposites, namely lightness and so forth," that is not a valid reason.

For the arising of a state opposed to something does not depend upon the presence of an opposing factor that is to be pacified. If it were so, [the triad would be absent] even in the occurrence of functional consciousnesses with roots.

There would simply be an absence of bodily lightness and the other [three characteristics]; therefore, only five material phenomena do not arise for non-percipient Brahmas, while the remaining twenty-three material phenomena do arise.

For non-percipient Brahmas, however, fifteen arise, excluding thirteen material phenomena—namely, the five sensitive organs, the two sexual characteristics, the heart-base, the two modes of intimation, and the triad of lightness and so forth.
761. "Four continuities" refers to the fourfold continuity of material phenomena by way of the four conditions. "In the case of [certain] forms there are three continuities":
because Brahmās lack food, there is an absence of nutriment-born materiality; thus, there are three continuities. "Two continuities":

because of the absence of both mind-born and nutriment-born materiality, there are two continuities. "Externally, one continuity": because all three—kamma-born and the others—are absent, there is only the temperature-born continuity.

762–4. Having thus stated the numerical delimitation of material phenomena in rebirth-linking and the course of existence, the passage beginning with "When matter is being produced" is now stated in order to show the sequence of their arising therein.
"Of all" means of all beings belonging to the sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere existences.
Regarding the phrase "but at the moment of rebirth-linking," the words "there is a triad of decads" are to be supplied as the remainder of the text. Therefore he said:

“*Yathevā*,” etc. Although the triad of decads was mentioned previously at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), it is stated again here to show the specific distinction beginning with the words “*tañca kho sandhicittassā*.
Because the material qualities born of kamma arise in the three moments of consciousness, he says “*tathevā*,” etc.
“Thirty, thirty each” means thirty material qualities born of kamma for each [moment].

The Master Ānanda, however, said: "There is no moment of stability for consciousness, and since there is no arising of material phenomena at the moment of their dissolution, even those material phenomena produced by the four causes occur only at the moment of the arising of consciousness.
For he stated this in the *Cittayamaka*: "Furthermore, that which here was called the 'moment of stability of consciousness' must be examined as to whether it exists or does not exist."
For in the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of the phrase "arisen and arising," it is stated only as much as: "at the moment of dissolution (*bhaṅgakkhaṇa*), it is arisen but not arising";
it is not stated as "at the moment of stability (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*) and at the moment of dissolution.
Likewise, regarding the phrase "not arising and not arisen," it is stated only as much as: "at the moment of dissolution, it is not arising but not non-arisen."

It was not stated, nor was it stated, "at the moment of presence and at the moment of dissolution. Thus, regarding the complete answer to the question, "neither ceased nor ceasing," after saying "at the moment of arising and as future," there is no mention of "at the moment of presence";
and in the section on the time that has passed, after saying "at the moment of dissolution, consciousness has transcended the moment of arising," there is no mention of "at the moment of presence."
The absence of speech indicates the absence of a moment of duration for consciousness. For even in the Sutta, it is said: “The alteration of that which has endured is discerned.
Since there is no alteration of that very same single [moment], one cannot say that the continuity which is discerned as altering is not the duration of the stream.
That which exists is "enduring" when it possesses those two moments. And herein, as for the mind...
The arising of matter at the moment of cessation has been stated, and that must be investigated. Why? Because it was stated:
"Is it the case that for whom the truth of origination ceases, for him the truth of suffering arises? [The answer is] "No.
Furthermore, it cannot be understood that this denial was made with reference to mind-originated matter alone, because there is no specific context concerning mind-originated matter.

For this is the Master’s intention: by not mentioning the "moment of presence" in the sections on the arisen and the arising, and so forth, he demonstrates that there is no such thing as a moment of presence for consciousness.

Indeed, no reason is seen for omitting something that is obtainable in the Abhidhamma, which is the teaching according to the true nature of phenomena (*yathādhamma*). It is not merely that it is not mentioned in the Abhidhamma.
It indicates the state of the mind at the moment of its persistence; moreover, the Sutta-pāḷi has come down as: "In that which persists, alteration is discerned.

Alteration means a difference between the preceding and succeeding states. Furthermore, in whatever manner a phenomenon arises, does it perish in that same manner, or does it perish in another manner? If it perishes in that same manner, then...
There is an arising for the sake of aging. Since it has become otherwise, it is simply something else; thus, in every respect, there is an absolute absence of a moment of persistence.
And if matter were to arise at the moment of the mind’s dissolution, it could not be said "no" by classifying it as the truth of suffering;
yet it has been stated [otherwise]. Therefore, it is understood that "there is no arising of matter at the moment of the cessation of the mind."
However, this is not acceptable to the elders Ācariya Jotipāla and Dhammapāla. They maintain:

"Even though they share a single basis, the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*) is distinct from the moment of cessation (*nirodhakkhaṇa*). For the moment of arising is defined in relation to the state of arising, while the moment of cessation is defined in relation to the state of cessation.
And since the state of cessation is different from the state of arising, [they are distinct] even within a single [entity]."
And since phenomena must be accepted according to their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), otherwise it would follow that one phenomenon arises while another ceases;
thus, just as there must be a state of cessation, so too must there be a state facing cessation, which is both stability (*ṭhiti*) and aging (*jaratā*). This is what must be admitted.

If this is so, why is the moment of duration (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*) not mentioned in the Canon (*pāḷi*)? It should be understood that the way the Canon proceeds is by way of demonstrating the underlying method (*naya*) in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained (*vineyyajjhāsayānurodha*).
For even the teaching of the Abhidhamma sometimes proceeds in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained;

for example, the arising of material form (*rūpassa uppādo*) is taught by dividing it into "accumulation" (*upacaya*) and "continuity" (*santati*). This is also the case in the teaching of the dyads such as "associated with a cause" (*hetusampayutta-duka*).

And here [these cases] should be illustrated. Furthermore, in the answer to the question beginning with "Or for whom," one may say "No" with reference to the immaterial world (*arūpaloka*) or to mind-originated matter (*cittasamuṭṭhānarūpa*).
For this is the nature of the *Yamaka* (Pairs) teaching, namely, its application according to what is possible.
Alternatively, by the principle of proximity (*paccāsatti*), that truth of origin which ceases is that by which the truth of suffering is to be produced.
Regarding that which is designated as matter dependent on the mind and mental factors, there is no arising of it at that time; thus the answer is "no.

This is not because of a denial of all matter, for they say that therefore it is not possible to deny the production of matter at the moment of the mind's persistence or at the moment of its dissolution.

As for the material phenomena born of temperature (*utu*), they arise from the moment of the presence-phase of the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*) onward, by way of groups of eight and nine.

For, within the kamma-born material phenomena that have arisen at the moment of rebirth-linking, the temperature element—which arises and ceases simultaneously—reaches its location and, during its presence-phase, produces eight material phenomena; therein, the temperature element that has arisen...
At the moment of the dissolution of the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*), there arises the first life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) consciousness at its moment of arising;
thus, by such means, an octad arises. Occasionally, at the time of the manifestation of sound, a nonad arises together with that sound.

And as for the mind-born material phenomena (*cittajarūpa*), from the moment immediately following the rebirth-linking consciousness—that is, starting from the first life-continuum consciousness—the [material phenomena] produced by those consciousnesses that generate matter arise.
They arise by way of the octad at the moment of arising, and by way of the nonad of sound and so forth at the time of the manifestation of sound and so on.
However, those born of nutriment arise after the lapse of one or two weeks.
But is it not the case that nutriment produces matter through the condition of ingested nutriment; and how can there be ingested nutriment for one lying in the womb? It is from the mother’s food.
For what is eaten by the mother performs the function of food for the body within the womb, like an ointment. Thus said the ancients:
"Whatever food, drink, and meal his mother eats,"
“By that [food] he sustains himself there,
the man while still within the mother’s womb. Therefore,
when the body is sustained by the food swallowed by the mother, the internal nutritive essence (ojā), having obtained its requisite conditions, produces material form (rūpa).
The eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body faculties arise later, after having passed the stage of the five sensitive organs (*pasāda*), in the seventh week;
Ācariya Ānanda stated that they arise in the eleventh week. This is the method for the manifestation of matter among those born from a womb.
For those of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*) as well, seventy material phenomena produced by kamma arise at the very moment of the arising of the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*).
In the same way, at the moments of its subsistence and dissolution,

the occurrence of the matter produced by kamma and that produced by temperature for beings belonging to the sense-sphere existence and for the fine-material Brahmās— whether at their maximum or minimum levels—
should be understood according to the method already stated, namely "seventy, seventy," and so forth, as appropriate. However, nutriment-born matter arises first of all for those of the sense-sphere.
It arises at the time of swallowing one’s own saliva when it has reached the mouth. For those Brahmās who possess perception (*saññī*), that [saliva] is entirely absent.
And for those without perception (*asaññī*), there is no such thing as nutriment born of mind (*cittaja*) or nutriment born of food (*āhāraja*); this is the distinction.

Furthermore, among these material phenomena (*rūpa*) thus arising, that which has arisen at the moment of the mind’s arising takes as its primary object the mind that arose simultaneously with itself.
Having done so, that which arose at the moment of the cessation of the seventeenth consciousness ceases at the moment of the presence of the eighteenth;
that which arose at the moment of the dissolution of the eighteenth ceases at the moment of the presence of this [nineteenth];
and thus, from the moment of arising until the moment of cessation, down to the seventeenth consciousness prior to the death-consciousness, it ceases accordingly as appropriate.

"It proceeds by way of the four continuities and so forth. However, for one who is near death, beginning from the moment of stability of the seventeenth consciousness prior to the death-consciousness (*cuti*), karma-born matter (*kammajarūpa*) no longer arises.
If it were to arise, death would not occur because the karma-born matters would not have been severed.
For it is only when there is a total cessation of karma-born matter that one is said to be "dead. Indeed, it has been said:
“When vitality, heat, and consciousness leave this body,
then it lies cast away like a useless log. With the seventeenth [moment of consciousness],
that which arose together [with the life-continuum] ceases along with the death-consciousness, and nothing else arises.

"Through the exhaustion of the life-span, through the exhaustion of karma, through the exhaustion of both, or by some external intervention"—thus, according to the commentary, death occurs only for materiality born of karma, even when that which is born of nutriment and that which is born of consciousness are present. That [death] does not arise for one whose life-force has departed.
However, materiality born of the physical elements continues to proceed. The same applies to those born of moisture; but as for those of spontaneous birth (opapātika), [it is different].
Because there is no casting off of the body, that [process] does not proceed either.

(765–6) It is "impermanent" (*anicca*) because it possesses arising and passing away, and thus is neither eternal nor stable; or alternatively, it is "impermanent" because, due to its constant momentariness, it is not to be approached as "eternal" (*nicca*) by way of such views as eternalism.
For this destruction, being independent of any cause other than the producing conditions— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
It is momentary at every instant. It is impermanent because it is devoid of lasting substance. It is non-self in the sense of being subject to lack of mastery.
It is a "mass of suffering" (*dukkhakkhandha*) because it is a heap or collection of sufferings due to its oppression by arising and passing away, and because it is the basis for suffering.
Furthermore, such a mass is unmixed with pleasure; thus he said "entire" (*kevala*). Or else, because there is no form whatsoever that has the nature of pleasure, it is "entire" in its totality.
It is called "the mass of suffering" (*dukkhakkhandha*) as stated in the phrase "and the entire mass of suffering.

It is viewed as a disease because it must be maintained by conditions and because it is the root of disease. For it should be regarded as a disease insofar as it must be sustained by appropriate conditions, like a chronic illness;

for a chronic illness is a "disease" (*roga*), while other ailments are "afflictions" (*ābādha*). And this [mass of suffering] is like a primary disease among the secondary diseases that follow it, such as the diseases of the defilements (*kilesa*).

It should be regarded as a disease by way of its fundamental nature. It should be regarded as a boil because it is associated with the sting of suffering, because it drips with the impurity of the defilements, and because it is swollen, ripened, and burst by way of arising, aging, and dissolution.

For it is joined with the "breaking" (rujjanena) known as the threefold suffering—namely, the suffering of suffering, the suffering of formations, and the suffering of change—according to the appropriate object.

And it should be regarded as a "boil" (*gaṇḍa*) because it flows with the impurities of defilements such as lust through its association [with them], because it comes into being without having previously existed, because it is bloated at the moment of its arising, and because it successively reaches a state of ripening and bursting through aging and dissolution.
It is "other" (*para*) by virtue of not being subject to one's own will and being uncontrollable; for just as another person, when falling, [cannot control] another...

It does not come under one's control; thus, because it cannot be made subject to one’s will through such states as beauty or pleasure, and because it cannot be governed—being "uncontrollable" (avasavattanato) in the sense that it is impossible to command it with such injunctions as "do not grow old" or "do not die"—it should be regarded as being "external" (parato) due to its state of being uncommandable.
It is "dissolving" (palokato) because of its crumbling away through sickness, aging, and death, and because of its inherent instability. This [is] by means of sickness and so forth...

It should be understood as "perishing" (*palokato*) because it breaks up and disintegrates in various ways, or because of the specific sense of "dissolution" (*abyāsanattha*) inherent in the word *loka* when it enters into this context, given its general meaning of ruin.
"Desire" (*chanda*) refers to desire that functions through the mode of attachment (*rajjana*).

(767) "By the General of the Dhamma" (*dhammasenāpatinā*): he is the General of the Dhamma because he is the leader and guide of the army of the Dhamma; this refers to the Elder Sāriputta. "By him who has welfare as his aim" (*hitatthinā*): one for whom welfare (*attha*) is considered as benefit (*hita*) is "one who has welfare as his aim"; by such a person. "Attentively" (*sakkaccā*): being untiring in the tasks of learning, memorizing, and so forth.
Thus ends the explanation of the Analysis of Matter in the *Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanā*, titled *Abhidhammatthavikāsinī*.
11. The Eleventh Chapter:
Commentary on the Description of Nibbāna.

768–9. The connection is as follows: "Nibbāna," which was listed immediately after "form" at the beginning, [is what is treated here]. The connection is: "I shall explain its analysis according to my ability."
"From existence to existence" means from one state of becoming (*bhava*) to another state of becoming, whether that becoming be small or great.

"Because of weaving together" means because of stitching together. For craving, by virtue of being the leader of *saṃsāra*, stitches together existence after existence—from one state of becoming to another—and like a tailor, it performs the work of sewing together existences that are small or great according to happy or miserable destinies. "Because of having departed" means by way of dissociation.
Because it has emerged [from suffering]. It is "deathless" (amata) because it is the opposite of death, or because it is like the deathless.

It is the "supreme happiness" because it has emerged from all suffering. It is the "tranquility of all formations" (sabbasaṅkhārasamatha) because by means of it all formations (saṅkhārā) are stilled, calmed, and brought to the state of non-arising.
All acquisitions (upadhī)—such as the aggregates (khandha), the substrates of existence (ūpadhi), and so forth—as well as all calamities, are relinquished.

By this [phrase], "the relinquishing of all acquisitions" is meant. Because, by resorting to that, craving—divided into sensual craving and so forth—comes to total destruction, fades away, and ceases, it is therefore called the "destruction of craving," "dispassion," and "cessation.
Furthermore, it is called "obstruction" (*rodha*) because beings, bound by the shackles of the defilements, are obstructed therein; this is a designation for *saṃsāra*.
"Departed from that" refers to cessation (*nirodha*).
770. "Attainment" refers to penetration by means of the Noble Path through practice corresponding thereto.

It has the characteristic of peace because it is the condition for the pacification of all suffering through the state of the destruction of lust and so forth, and because it is free from the fever of the defilements.
It has the characteristic of not abandoning its own nature because it does not waver; its function is to provide reassurance.

For it stands as a source of reassurance for a weary traveler wandering through a perilous wilderness devoid of food, drink, and the like—just as a forest edge or a body of water appears to one exhausted by wandering—so too does it stand for the Fully Enlightened Buddhas amidst the great terror of suffering that transcends the path of words.
For the practitioner who has grown weary from wandering through the wilderness of saṃsāra and has entered the path of practice appropriate to that state,
this [sign] produces supreme relief at the very moment it is seen, because it has never before been seen even in a dream throughout beginningless saṃsāra.
Because it is apprehended without being grasped as a solid entity due to its variegated nature as the sign of the aggregates, it is said to have the "signless" as its manifestation.
Because it presents the means of escape from all that is conditioned (*saṅkhata*), it is "presented as the escape" (*nissaraṇapaccupaṭṭhāna*).

Having thus shown the characteristics and other attributes of Nibbāna, he now says "here it is said," etc., while avoiding the position of the caviller (*vitaṇḍavādin*) by maintaining that [Nibbāna] exists in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*) except as a mere designation (*paññatti-matta*); for how [could it otherwise exist]?

To show that this is indeed an adherence, he said: "Of the sectarians... [etc. ...because it leads away. "By means of practice appropriate to each" means by means of right practice consisting of virtue, concentration, and wisdom.

For just as only those Noble Ones who have attained the knowledge of others' minds know the supramundane minds of others—and among them, only an Arahant knows the minds of all—so too is Nibbāna [known] by means of the right practice consisting of virtue and the rest.
It should not be said that it "does not exist" because it is apprehended by means of a skillful method (*upāya*), since it is apprehended by the Noble Ones (*ariya*).
For just as it cannot be said that the sun and other such objects do not exist simply because they are not seen by those born blind or those with ophthalmia,

since their existence is established by the fact that they are within the range of experience for those with sight— so too, this [Dhamma] cannot be said to "not exist" merely because it is not seen by the foolish worldling (*bālaputhujjana*).
It should not be said [that it is not so]. However, because it appears as a mere portion of the noble ones' eye of wisdom, one must absolutely accept that "Nirvana exists.
This is the intended meaning here. Now, the connection is: "And [the view] that Nirvana is merely the destruction of lust and so forth.
The connection is: "It was shown by the Venerable... [etc. ...Thera. [This refers to] the discourse illustrating the destruction of lust and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "of interpretable meaning" (*neyyattha*), having made a negation by saying "that is not so" according to the intended sense (*adhippāya*), this must be accepted categorically;
otherwise, if the meaning of the scripture were taken according to the literal expression (*yathāruta*), many faults would arise.
To demonstrate those [faults], he said, "Even of arahantship," and so forth. This was stated by that very Venerable Thera Sāriputta when he was questioned about arahantship.

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). "According to your opinion" means according to your own inclination, which prattles on by merely citing the canonical text (*pāḷi*) without investigating the logical consistency (*yutti*) of the Teaching. And yet, this is not tenable; such is the intended meaning.

It is not tenable for the supramundane fruit-consciousness (*lokuttara-phala-citta*) to result in the mere destruction of lust and the other defilements, because that supreme fruit consists of four aggregates (*khandha*), as stated in the Canon.

Because it has been handed down. Therefore, for one who expresses [a view] merely by looking at the Pāḷi without investigating the logical consistency (yutti), there is the consequence of an undesirable conclusion.
"By the shadow of the phrasing" means by the mere shadow of the word-meaning, which is incapable of withstanding scrutiny.
"Of both" refers to the two suttas handed down respectively by way of Nibbāna and by way of Arahatta. "Meaning" (attha) refers to the intended meaning (adhippāyattha).
But what is that meaning? He says, “For one who...,” and so forth. The destruction of lust and the other defilements means the non-arising and cessation of lust and the rest.

Although that Dhamma is itself indestructible, because it serves as the decisive support (upanissaya) for the destruction of lust and the others, it is spoken of by way of a metaphorical designation (upacāra) as “the destruction of lust and the others, Nibbāna.
This is just as in expressions such as “ginger is fever” or “sugar is phlegm,” which are stated by way of a metaphorical designation of the fruit [for the cause].

Regarding the connection: Nibbāna, which serves as the object for the path that brings about the non-arising, cessation, and destruction of the defilements, can be described in terms of its actual meaning as "the decisive support (upanissaya) for destruction.
Therefore, it is said: "Because it is the decisive support for destruction. By the metaphorical designation of "destruction" (*khayopacārena*):
this means by way of applying the name of its own effect—namely, destruction—to itself; that is what is expressed. The cause of aging...

"Tipusa" is called "jarā" (old age), and sugar, which is a cause of phlegm (*semha*), is called "phlegm. "At the end of destruction" means at the conclusion of the complete exhaustion of lust and the other defilements.

Alternatively, "destruction" (*khaya*) refers to the Path—as in expressions such as "knowledge of destruction"—and it is called "destruction" by way of metaphorical designation because it arises at the end of that [Path], namely at the conclusion of cessation; or it is so called by way of proximity.
"All foolish worldlings" refers to all such beings as dogs, jackals, and so forth;

they too would have attained [the destruction of the defilements], because even for them there exists the destruction of lust and the other defilements by way of moments. And if that were the case, the implication is that the practice of the path would become purposeless.

"Because of the multiplicity of the destructions of lust and so forth" means that just as there are many instances of lust and the other defilements, so too there are many instances of their destruction.
Because of its multiplicity due to the state of having various modes. For if this were so, the destruction of lust would be "lust-destruction," but not [the destruction] of hatred and the rest;

likewise for the destruction of hatred. Thus, there would be a different destruction of lust, a different destruction of hatred, and a different destruction of delusion—meaning three *nibbānas* consisting of the destruction of the three unwholesome roots—and four [nibbānas] consisting of the destruction of the four clingings, and so forth; thus they would be many.
[The states] are indeed called *nibbānas*. Now, in order to show the defects included by the word "beginning" (*ādi*), it is said:

"the characteristic of the conditioned" (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇa*), and so forth. Because of the statement: "Bhikkhus, there are these three characteristics of the conditioned for the conditioned: arising is discerned, passing away is discerned, and the alteration of that which stands is discerned," destruction, which is reckoned as "passing away" (*vaya*), is a characteristic of the conditioned.
It has been stated that "it would follow that Nibbāna possesses the characteristic of the conditioned.
Because of the statement, "Bhikkhus, aging-and-death is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen," he says, "included within the conditioned.
And whatever is included within the conditioned, like other conditioned phenomena, is impermanent and exists in dependence on conditions.
He said: "It is impermanent because it is included within the conditioned (*saṅkhatapariyāpannattā*). For it has been said: "Impermanent indeed are all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*).
What is meant by this much? If, for the sake of fulfilling your own wish, you were to say that destruction is Nibbāna, [we reply:

because the unconditioned would then possess the characteristics of the conditioned, and because being the opposite of the conditioned would imply its inclusion within the conditioned, it would consequently exist at all times.
It is said that this would entail the impermanence of what is permanent, and the suffering of what is supremely blissful.

Having thus far shown the defect of cessation-by-destruction (bhaṅgakkhaya) as being *nibbāna*, he now states, "If cessation (*khaya*) were *nibbāna*," etc., in order to negate the existence of that [defect] in cessation-by-non-arising (*anuppādakkhaya*). [This refers to] that which serves as the immediate condition (*anantarapaccaya*) for the first path.

Knowledge is called "change-of-lineage" (gotrabhū). That which precedes the remaining paths is called "cleansing" (vodāna). That which precedes the attainment of fruition is called "conformity" (anuloma).
However, because that [conformity] has only formations as its object, it is not included here. "O gentle-faced one" is a word of conciliation addressed to another.
By the present-tense designation "they are ceasing," he asks about the state of currently ceasing. This same method applies to the others as well. "Having considered" means...
Having investigated, the intention is: "Speak with mindfulness as the primary concern, by way of not contradicting the reply given by you to the question, 'Is the lineage (gotrabhu) ... [etc] ...
the door?'—'I say it is simply the destruction of lust and the other defilements. This refers to the lineage, the purification of the lineage-consciousness, and the path.
He spoke thus because at the moment of the lineage, there is no non-arising or cessation of the defilements.
"‘Lust and the other defilements will be exhausted’—this refers precisely to the fruit-consciousness that arises at the time when the defilements have been exhausted.
‘Not seeing an object’ means not seeing the object that ought to be mentioned for the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) and subsequent states;
or alternatively, it means not seeing a condition to be grasped even though the status of being an object exists for others."
“Moreover,” and so forth, is another way of refuting that Nibbāna is a state produced by cultivation through the non-arising and cessation [of defilements].
The statement, “the meaning is ‘it is produced’ (uppādīyati),” is said with the intention that, upon the arising of the Path, the destruction of the defilements is also called ‘produced.
For otherwise, there is no such thing as the ‘arising’ of destruction. Alternatively, [it refers to the verse]: “Surely he... will become unsurpassed.”
Having shown the fault in regarding both the cessation of the momentary and the cessation of non-arising as being Nibbāna by means of this brief argument,

[the author] now points out the undesirable consequence that would follow if the path were also considered to be Nibbāna on the grounds of its commonality with such terms as "destruction of lust" (*rāgakkhaya*), etc., simply because the word "destruction" (*khaya*) is used as a designation for the path—
as it is in expressions like "knowledge of destruction" (*khaye ñāṇa*). And if that were the case, it would lead to an unacceptable conclusion.
Anticipating this objection, he says, "Furthermore," and so forth. For if that were the case, the phrase "it is produced" would refer exclusively to the Path.

If it is here suspected that the consequence of the Path being identical with Nibbāna might follow, then one must state the fault that the change-of-lineage (gotrabhu) would consequently have the Path as its object.
This is true; however, even by this much, it is possible to refute the opponent's argument.

The effort was made to show the distinction between [the two types of] relinquishment. "By means of practice corresponding [to the goal]" means by means of the practice of conformity (*yathānuloma-paṭipatti*), which consists of a succession of purifications of the skin. 771.
"One who has faith" means one whose faith is awakened; one who is endowed with unshakable faith that has entered the Path; [faith] that has entered the Path.
Indeed, even when one endowed with such qualities creates the form of a Buddha in the sky and says, "The self is permanent, happy, and eternal," he does not believe it, just like Sūrambaṭṭha.
"Grateful" (akataññū) means he knows Nibbāna, which is uncreated (akata).

"One who has severed the bond" (sandhicchedo) refers to the severing of the bond of rebirth through the cutting off of craving—the evil that links existence—and thus the state of having severed further rebirth in existence.

He remains having exhausted rebirth. "One whose opportunity is destroyed" means that because rebirth has been exhausted, his scope for future existence has been eliminated, as he is no longer seen anywhere in the world of space.
"One who has vomited out" means that because there is no attachment to anything, his craving has been discarded.
"The supreme person" means a person distinguished by being the foremost object of offerings in the world including the devas.
"Difficult to penetrate" means difficult to pierce through and difficult to attain. They are "to be escaped from" because they are to be relinquished;
that is, renunciation (*nekkhamma*). The connection is: "this is the escape from sensual desires. In this context, "escape from sensual desires" means the departure from sensual desires;
or alternatively, it is that by which or in which they escape—that is, they depart.

The meaning is: escape, the place of escape from sensual desires, and the means of escape. "Renunciation" (*nekkhamma*) refers here to the first jhāna, for that has emerged from sensual desires and is thus taken as "renunciation.
However, in other contexts, even going forth (*pabbajjā*) and so on are called "renunciation. For it is said:
“Going forth, the first *jhāna*, Nibbāna, and insight (*vipassanā*);
all wholesome states (*kusala-dhammā*) are called ‘renunciation (*nekkhamma*).
The formless is the base of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatana*). “Bhūta” means existing; the meaning is the five aggregates (*khandha-pañcaka*). “This has come to be (*bhūtamidan’ti*),”...
In such passages as "Sāriputta, I do not perceive [anything else]," the pentad of aggregates is called "the real" (*bhūta*).
That which has arisen equally and correctly in dependence upon its own causes is "dependently arisen" (*paṭiccasamuppanna*). [The phrase] "the first...

might exist" refers, by way of being the escape from the conditioned, to the non-existence of *nibbāna*—which is described as being in grammatical coordination with that [escape]—and thus, in due order, to the escapes from sense-desire and form.
Otherwise, even the first jhāna and the base of infinite space would result in non-existence. Now, in order to demonstrate the intended meaning through scripture, it was said:
"But not destruction," and so forth. [The passage] "There is... well-furnished" implies:
"There is no escape from sensual pleasures in the world; what is the use of seclusion? Thus [he spoke].
When [the Buddha] was being obstructed by Māra, the Elder Āḷavaka spoke these words while establishing [the existence of] Nibbāna:
“There is... it is well-touched. “Well-touched” (*suphusita*) means thoroughly touched; what is meant is that it has been realized.

The four terms beginning with “unborn” (*ajāta*) are synonyms for one another. Alternatively, unlike feeling (*vedanā*) and the other aggregates, it is not subject to the combination of causes and conditions.
That which is not born and does not arise from the assemblage of causes is "unborn" (*ajāta*).

That which has not come into being, has not appeared, and has not arisen by itself without a cause is "unbecome" (*abhūta*). Thus, because it is unborn and unbecome, and because it is not made by any cause whatsoever, it is "unmade" (*akata*).
Furthermore, the states of being born, having become, and being made belong only to conditioned phenomena such as form and the rest, and not [to this].
It is called "unconditioned" (*asaṅkhata*) for the purpose of showing that Nibbāna has an unconditioned nature.

Alternatively, "conditioned" (*saṅkhata*) means that which is made by conditions having come together and combined; that which is not thus conditioned, and which is devoid of the characteristics of the conditioned, is "unconditioned.

Thus, when the state of being produced [by causes] has been negated through these various reasons, the *pakati* (primordial matter) of the proponents of *pakati*— [The remainder of the sentence is cut off in the source text.]
It might be suspected that this was produced by a single cause; therefore, to show that it was not made by anyone, it is called "unmade" (*akata*).
Likewise, even though it is without conditions, it might be suspected that this has appeared as a self-existent entity;
to preclude that, it is called "unbecome" (*abhūta*). And this is its state of being unconditioned, unmade, and unbecome.
It is called "unborn" (*ajāta*) to show that it is, in every respect, of an unborn nature (*ajāta-dhamma*).
In the phrase "the unconditioned" (*asaṅkhataṃ*), the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning.
By this [it is implied]: "If, monks, this unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned were not, there would be no escape for the born... [and so forth].

“An escape from what is born, become, made, and conditioned would be discerned. But because, monks, there exists the unborn, the unbecome, the unmade, and the unconditioned, therefore an escape from what is born, become, made, and conditioned is discerned.
Such scriptural passages as these are included [in this context]. Hence he said: “In many discourses (suttantas), by means of the Dhamma, for the world with its devas...”
He is the Lord of Dhamma (*dhammasāmī*) because he is the master and lord who teaches the Dhamma according to his wish for the world.
The meaning of the word *Tathāgata* has already been explained above. He is the *Sammāsambuddha* because he has perfectly and fully awakened to all phenomena (*sabbadhamme*) by himself;
or, he is the *Sammāsambuddha* because he has woken up by himself through the departure of the sleep of delusion, or because he has blossomed through his own intelligence.

Regarding "the triad of limited states": this refers to the triad of limited states presented by way of the categories of "limited states, exalted states, and immeasurable states. Regarding "because of the consequence of having an indeterminable object":

because of the contingency that they would belong to the side of having an indeterminable object. Therefore he said, "they would fall on the side of having an indeterminable object. Regarding "the jhānas of the triads and tetrads of the fine-material sphere":
this refers to the jhānas of the triads according to the fourfold method, and [the jhānas] according to the fivefold method.

Regarding the fourfold jhānas: because they proceed by taking even limited objects (paritta) and so forth for the sake of attaining the state of direct knowledge (abhiññā) through wholesome functional states (kusalakiriyā), it is said that "they are the result (vipāka) of the fourth jhāna.
Therefore—both on account of the reasoning already stated and on account of the Pāḷi—what more can be said?
Insight-knowledge (vipassanāñāṇa) has conditioned phenomena as its object; furthermore, when it has reached the state of conformity (anuloma), it [overcomes] the defilements (kilesa).
It abandons them by way of a factor of that [attainment], but it is not able to abandon them by way of complete eradication (*samuccheda*).

Likewise, wholesome knowledge such as the first jhāna, which has conventional truth (*sammutisacca*) as its object, abandons defilements only by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*), not by way of eradication.

Thus, regarding the abandonment of defilements by way of eradication, there is no power in knowledge that has conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*) as its object or conventional truth as its object.
Because those [fetters] are not capable [of being abandoned], the noble path-knowledge that effects their abandonment must have an object that is the opposite of both of them;
and that is Nibbāna alone. Thus the Ancients said: “Knowledge which has the conditioned as its object, or indeed has a concept (paññatti) as its object;”
"One does not destroy that object by [committing] evil, having accepted something other than it. Regarding "due to the absence of the intrinsic nature of form":

by this it is shown that just as the intrinsic nature of material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*) is their susceptibility to change (*ruppana-sabhāva*), and their possession of resistance (*paṭighātavatā*), their existence as a cluster, and their connection with a location are their intrinsic natures;
so too, for Nibbāna, there is no resistance anywhere, nor is there any spatial limitation (*sappadesatā*).
And he shows that it does not exist [in such a way]. For Nibbāna cannot be pointed out as being "in such a direction" or "in such a location.

"Because of the absence of proliferation (*papañca*)" means because of its non-existence by way of not persisting together with the proliferations of craving, conceit, and views, and because it is the condition for their absence.
Indeed, craving, views, and conceit are called "proliferations" because they cause beings to proliferate within saṃsāra.
772–5. Having thus established Nibbāna through both reasoning and the Suttas, the passage beginning with “the ultimate, the infinite” is now stated for the purpose of demonstrating its synonyms.
In this context, it is called “the end” (*anta*) because it is the final limit of the process of saṃsāra.

They say that by this term, the Nibbāna-element without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*) is expressed; however, the Nibbāna-element with residue (*sopādisesa-nibbānadhātu*) is also applicable here.
They also read it as *akatanti*. Its meaning is the same as what was stated above. It is *ananta* (infinite) because it lacks arising and passing away.

It is *santa* (peaceful) because it lacks the fever of the defilements (*kilesa-pariḷāha*) and the agitation of the defilements (*kilesa-kkhobha*). It is *apalokita* (illuminated) because it lacks darkness (*paloka*).

It is *paṇīta* (sublime) because it brings no satiety. It is a *saraṇa* (refuge) because it destroys all suffering. It is *khema* (secure) because it is free from fear, being unassailed by the thieves of the defilements. It is so because it wards off all calamities.

It is a refuge (*tāṇaṃ*) because it is a fit place to take shelter from the suffering of birth and so forth that pursues one. It is a sanctuary (*leṇaṃ*) because it provides peace for those who practice accordingly, serving as a supreme support.
It is auspicious (*sivaṃ*) because it is free from all oppression.

Even for those lacking the necessary spiritual predisposition (*upanissaya*), having heard [the Dhamma] directly from the mouth of the Omniscient One, [one should understand it] by setting aside [worldly concerns] on account of its qualities.
It is subtle because it is difficult to penetrate by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). It is truth (*sacca*) because of its non-erroneousness.

It is the destruction of suffering (*dukkhakkhaya*) because it brings about the complete exhaustion of all suffering. It is without taints (*anāsava*) because, due to its excellence in brilliance, it is impossible for the four taints (*āsava*) to function by taking it as an object, just as flies cannot alight upon a red-hot iron ball.
Furthermore, it renders even the teaching of the Great Compassionate One free from the burden of effort.
It is "difficult to see" because it is hard to penetrate; it is "supreme" because it is distinguished by the quality of being unconditioned even among supramundane phenomena;
it is "the further shore" because it has become the bank of the great ocean of saṃsāra; it is "non-manifest" because it is not within the range of either the fleshly eye or the divine eye;
or it is "non-manifest" because of the absence of any simile that could serve as a manifestation.
It is "constant" (*dhuva*) because its nature is not subject to change. Precisely for that reason, it is an "island" (*dīpa*) because it is the supreme refuge.

It is "free from affliction" (*abyāpajjha*) because it is devoid of the oppression of disease and so forth; for that very reason, it is "without calamity" (*anītika*). It is "without a substrate" (*anālaya*) because it lacks a substrate of craving (*taṇhālaya*).

It is the "footing" (*pada*) because it constitutes the unconditioned portion within the conditioned and the unconditioned, or because it is the supreme refuge. It is "immortal" (*accuta*) by virtue of its indestructibility. It is "indestructible" (*akkhara*) because it does not perish and does not decay.
It is *vimutti* (liberation) because it has emerged from the conditioned. It is *mokkha* (release) because it is the cause for release from the bondage of existence.

(776–7) *Evaṃ* means in the manner already stated. *Viññāya* means having understood by way of study and inquiry. *Adhigamūpāyo* refers to the three trainings which serve as the means for penetration.
*Kātabbo* means it should be practiced. *Saddhābuddhikaraṃ* means that which produces and increases faith and wisdom. *Tathāgatamate* means in the word of the Buddha contained in the Tipiṭaka.
Or, regarding the four truths: it is "born of wisdom" (*paññāsambhava*) because it is produced by wisdom, or because its origin is wisdom;
that very thing is "serenity" (*sampasādana*), which is resolute confidence (*adhimuccana*) in the Buddha and others; that which produces this is "that which produces serenity born of wisdom.
"Possessing beautiful meaning and phrasing" (*atthabyañjanasālinam*) means endowed with extremely sweet meanings and phrases, or possessing the essence of meaning and phrasing.

Alternatively, the meaning is obtained by changing the letter *ra* to the letter *la*. Those who know the essence (*sāra*) are "knowers of the essence" (*sāraññū*); to cause them to be amazed is "the amazement of the knowers of the essence" (*sāraññuvimhāpana*).
"Finality" (*niṭṭha*) means the conclusion; the intention is that it is the final Nirvana without clinging (*anupādāparinibbāna*), rooted in what consists of hearing (*sutamayamūlaka*).
Thus [ends] the *Abhidhammatthavikāsini*.
The commentary on the Description of Nibbāna in the *Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanā* is finished. Chapter Twelve.

Commentary on the Exposition of Designations (*Paññatti-niddesa-vaṇṇanā*): "At this point" means at the conclusion of the exposition of the phenomena as they were previously listed. "Only this much" means only the mind, mental factors, matter, and Nibbāna.

"Because they are to be designated" means that, unlike ultimate phenomena (*paramattha-dhamma*), which are known by virtue of their own respective intrinsic natures (*sabhāva*), these are not known by way of their own individual essences, but rather through worldly convention (*lokasaṅketa*).

Because it is being made known (*paññāpiyamānattā*). As for "because of making known" (*paññāpanato*): it is because of making known by way of revealing phenomena that exist and do not exist according to the ultimate sense (*paramattha*).

Therein, by the phrase "because of being made known," it is said that *upādāpaññatti* (derived designation), which constitutes a designation of meaning (*atthapaññatti*), is expressed as a grammatical object (*kamma-sādhana*) in the sense that "it is made known (*paññāpetabbato*)," i.e., it is made known in the manner of a designation. By the phrase "because of making known" (*paññāpanato*),...

It is called a "conceptualization" (*paññatti*) because it makes known or informs by way of a mode; thus, it should be understood as a "conceptualization as a name" (*nāma-paññatti*), which serves as its designator by way of the agentive instrument.

In the *Paṇṇattiduka-niddesa*, the "conceptualization based on the aggregates" (*upādā-paññatti*) is stated by the four terms beginning with "calculation" (*saṅkhā*), while the "conceptualization as a name" is explained by the six terms beginning with "name" (*nāma*); such is the opinion of the teachers.

Because it was desired, it was said, “Therefore it was said,” and so forth. “Of those various phenomena” refers to the wholesome, unwholesome, and other phenomena mentioned previously in the Abhidhamma matrix (mātikā).
“Designation” (saṅkhā) is the state of being designated as “I” and “mine,” and so on.
“Conventional term” (samaññā) is the state of being known by way of linguistic convention. “Description” (paññatti) is the state of being described in many ways by way of non-confusion.
“Vohāra” (conventional usage) means being spoken of by making [the meaning] manifest, or being employed by way of verbal expression.
“Nāma” (name) is that which bends toward the object. That, moreover, is twofold according to its derivation as *anvattha* (corresponding to the meaning) or *ruḷhi* (conventional).

It is fourfold according to the classification of names: common, qualitative, eulogistic, and accidental. “Nāmakamma” (naming) is the act of naming. “Nāmadheyya” (designation) is the establishing of a name; “nāmadheyya”...
"Vā" means the name of the best. "Nirutti" is the speaking of a meaning by extracting it through the medium of syllables. "Byañjana" is making [the meaning] manifest.

"Abhilāpo" is the act of expressing. "Aham" refers to one's own continuum of aggregates (khandhasantāna), which is distinct from form and the other [sensory objects], and which has become the object of the intellect characterized by the conceit of "I."

He speaks of "derived designation" (*upādāpaññatti*) as that which is designated as being neither identical to nor different from its basis, and thus indefinable. Therefore he says, "‘I,’ indeed," and so forth.
Having shown the arising of derived designation with the words, "'I'... having made [it]," he clarifies it by means of the passage beginning with "as.

Since "convention" (*samaññā*), "designation" (*paññatti*), and "usage" (*vohāro*) are synonyms for "such a reckoning" (*evaṃ saṅkhā*), it is therefore stated: "Now, it is a designation because of the act of designating," and so on.

"Born in accordance with that" (*tajjā*) means it has arisen as something corresponding to that; the meaning is that it is a designation (*paññatti*) occurring by way of conformity to the intrinsic nature (*dhammasabhāva*) of things, rather than existing merely through worldly convention like a non-existent designation.

Since the designation of a name (*nāmapaññatti*) also occurs in dependence upon and based on the cause known as the "meaning of the word," it receives the conventional term "derived designation" (*upādāpaññatti*); thus, it too has the designation of being a derived designation.
It has been stated thus. For the author of the *Gaṇṭhipada* also, with this very intention, explains "designation based on a cause" (*upādāpaññatti*) as follows:
a designation possessing a cause (*upādānavatī paññatti*) is designated by taking hold of and depending upon a causal object;

indeed, every variety of designation falls under the category of "designation based on a cause" according to this characteristic. For it is said that there is no designation whatsoever that does not depend on a cause.
"Designation by comparison" (*upanidhāpaññatti*) is a designation that occurs by taking into account—that is, in relation to—a single opposing designation.
By the mention of "eye" and "ear," he shows the internal bases (*ajjhattikāyatana*); by the mention of "visible form" and "sound," he shows the external bases (*bāhirāyatana*).

By the mention of "earth," "fire," and "air," he shows the tangible base (*phoṭṭhabbāyatana*) in its various divisions. By this very same [method], [he also shows] the base of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*).
It should be understood that the division of what is currently being obtained has been shown.
This is because a designation such as "earth" is established by taking the name of one [instance] within the earth consisting of constituent parts and referring to the collection itself;
and a designation such as "jar" is established by taking the names of all [instances] among the collections of phenomena and referring to the collection itself.

It is made known; therefore, it is said: “of one,” and so forth. Therein, because earth and the rest become manifest when they are made known by taking the name of one individual and referring to the collection, the phrase beginning with “how” was stated in order to show the other [the method] while setting that aside.
This is called “designation of a collection” (samūha-paññatti) because it makes known a collection. Among the directions, space, and so on, by the mention of “direction” (disā)—
By taking the revolution of the moon and sun as its basis, it demonstrates the designation of the directions, such as the east and so forth, which is made known.
By the inclusion of "space," it demonstrates the designation of space, such as wells, caves, and so on, which is made known by depending on phenomena that do not touch [one another].

By the inclusion of "time," it demonstrates the designation of time, such as forenoon and so forth, which is made known by depending on the revolution of the moon and other such factors. By the inclusion of "signs" (nimitta)...

By the mention of "externally," it shows the external sphere of earth and so forth, as well as the kasiṇa-signs and so on, which are designated in dependence upon internal distinctions of meditative development (*bhāvanā*).

By the mention of "non-existence" (*abhāva*), it shows the designation of non-existence (*abhāvapaññatti*)—the object of the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*)—which arises in dependence upon the base of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatana*) meditation, whose nature is the non-occurrence [of the former] through the power of meditative development. By the mention of "cessation" (*nirodha*),...

It shows that the designation of cessation (*nirodha-paññatti*) is designated in dependence upon the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*) which has been suppressed by the power of meditation (*bhāvanābala*).

By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), it includes such characteristics as impermanence (*anicca-lakkhaṇa*), which are designated in dependence upon this or that phenomenon and possess the intrinsic nature of exhaustion and so forth.

For even that [designation] is indeed a designation of a non-aggregate (*asamūha-paññatti*), because—like the directions, space, and so on—it is not designated in dependence upon a collection of phenomena (*dhamma-samūha*).

This [designation] is twofold as a derivative designation (*upādāpaññatti*). Because a designation based on that which arises (*tajjāpaññatti*) is included within the derivative designation itself—as it occurs without abandoning the literal meaning of the words—it is said that "it illuminates an existing ultimate reality.
And having established this, it is stated further on that "even the six types of designations are subsumed under this very [category].
"Existing" (*vijjamāna*) means being apprehended by way of its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
“Non-existent” means not being found by way of intrinsic nature, setting aside worldly convention. “Merely a name” means possessing only a name.

“Immediately after the impulsion of the ear-door” means [by consciousness] that arises immediately after the cognitive series of the ear-door impulsion which has present sound as its object, and the cognitive series of the mind-door impulsion which follows it and has past sound as its object.
For the cognitive series of the mind-door javana (manodvāra-javana-vīthi) is also included here by that very term, as it occurs immediately after the ear-door javana.

"By means of a previously grasped convention" means by means of a convention previously grasped through the apprehension of the relationship between a word and its meaning, such as: "This is the meaning of this [word]," or "This is the designator of this [meaning].
"By which" refers to that designation (nāma-paññatti) acting as the instrument. [It is] by the mind-door javana-consciousness.

"By that which has become the agent": either by the mind-door impulsion-consciousness acting as the instrument, or by whichever designation of name (nāmapaññatti) has become the agent—this is the meaning.
"It is made known" means that the two-fold class of objects, according to conventional and ultimate reality, is made known—that is, it is explained. Thus say the ancients:
“That by means of which meanings are understood beyond that itself—this should be known as ‘conceptualization’ (paññatti), fashioned by worldly convention.
In which cognitive process (javana-vīthi) is this [concept] understood?
It is understood in each instance for one who hears a sound such as “pot,” and so forth.
The teachers maintain that with respect to sound, there are two rounds of impulsion (javana) each based on present and past objects; following that, one round based on the collection of sounds;

and then one based on the designation of names (nāmapaññatti). Thus, immediately after the cognitive process (vīthi) of impulsion having the collection of sounds as its object, the designation of names becomes manifest, and thereafter comes the comprehension of the meaning.

The connection is: "with reference to which the method of the sixfold set was stated. "Thus, of those that do not exist" means of those that do not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*).
"In any manner whatsoever" means in some way, either from the perspective of ultimate reality or from the perspective of worldly convention (*lokasaṅketa*).

"Of those that are not apprehended, such as the fifth truth, etc. refers to the fifth truth, space, and so forth. By the inclusion of the word "etc.," the eighth factor of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) and others are intended.

It includes. "Of the 'ordinary person' and so forth" refers to the "ordinary person," "doer," "experiencer," "self," "person," and so on, which are conceptually constructed based on the common state of being a sentient being, silver, or gold, and the size of the natural thumb and so forth.

By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (ādi), it includes such things as sky-flowers. It is a designation for what does not exist based on what does exist, [derived] from things existing in the ultimate sense.

Because a person (puggala) is designated even though they do not exist by way of the [three] knowledges and so forth. The meaning in the remaining cases should also be understood according to this same method.
"In this very context" means precisely within the designation based on the aggregates (upādāpaññatti).
"Just as one might take water with the tip of a blade of kusa grass and measure the water in the ocean..."
"Thus human sensual pleasures [are inferior] in the presence of divine pleasures.

Because of this statement, it is said that "human [pleasures]... are indeed inferior when compared with the prosperity of a wheel-turning monarch and the prosperity of the devas in the human world. "Mānusaka" means existing in the human world. And the phrase "the ultimate goal exists" (*paramattho ca vijjatī*) is an elliptical addition to the text.
778. The third alternative does not exist because it is not found. For this has been stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*:
“The Perfectly Awakened One, the best among speakers, has proclaimed two truths:
the conventional and the ultimate; a third is not found.

“He does not waver in the doctrines of others” means that he does not waver, does not tremble, and does not shake when confronted with the doctrines of other sectarian teachers, such as those who propound the existence of a primal person (*puruṣa*) and so forth, or when faced with their signs (*nimitta*).
Thus ends the commentary on the Exposition of Designation within the *Abhidhammāvatāra-saṃvaṇṇanā*, titled *Abhidhammatthavikāsinī*.
13. The Thirteenth Chapter:

An Exposition on the Penetration of the Agent (Kārakapaṭivedhavaṇṇanā) "Shown" means demonstrated by way of enumeration, exposition, and so forth. "Wholesome and so forth" refers to the wholesome and unwholesome. Of these, however—

The connection is with the word *na niddiṭṭho* (not specified). Just as the term "agent" (*kārako*) was mentioned previously, even though "experiencer" (*vedako*) was not explicitly stated, because of his own [the opponent's] tenet that "the self is the agent and the experiencer," it was said: "for that agent and experiencer.

The intention is that there would also be an absence of wholesome and unwholesome states; otherwise, one would incur the fault of [denying] causes (*ahetuka-dosa*). Their functioning is dependent upon those wholesome and unwholesome states.
"These" refers to those whose existence is dependent upon them. "Of these" refers to the wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth.

"Therefore" means that in the absence of an agent, there would be an absence of both the wholesome and unwholesome states, as well as their respective results. "Futile" means that even after teaching, there would be no one to be enlightened; thus it is futile.
Having stated, "This is not futile," the subsequent statement, "It is purposeful," is made for the sake of ensuring the listener's firm conviction. For even in the world...
"They employ such conventional expression, thinking: 'It is exactly thus, and not otherwise,' and so forth. "Therein" means: in the apprehension that the self exists even in the absence of an agent.
"Favoring" (anurodha) means: partiality toward what is agreeable. "Here" means: in the apprehension that wholesome states and so forth exist even in the absence of an agent.
"Opposition" (virodha) means: aversion.

Having thus established through reasoning the existence of wholesome states and so forth even in the absence of a creator, [the author] now says "But furthermore" (*athāpi*) and so on, in order to establish it by means of an illustration well-known in the world.
"But furthermore" (*athāpi*) means even in the absence of a creator. By the mention of "earth," he indicates the earth-element (*pathavī-ja*).

Likewise, by the mention of "water," he indicates the water-element (*āpo-ja*). "Fire" (*tejo*) refers to the fire-element (*tejodhātu*), which is twofold according to its cold and hot natures. "Season" (*utu*)...

The seasons beginning with winter. By the inclusion of the word "beginning" (*ādi*), seeds and so forth are comprised. The productive condition is the cause (*hetu*), while the sustaining condition is simply called a condition (*paccaya*);
thus he says, "by the combination of cause and condition. For it has been said: "The cause is that which brings about the fruit; the condition is that which sustains it.
Having thus established the occurrence of wholesome and unwholesome states even in the absence of an agent, he now [addresses] the self (*attā*) as imagined by others.
In order to refute that [position], the passage beginning with “But even if here...
has been commenced. Granted, the self is merely imagined through a view external to wisdom; however, the other person thinks, “I imagine it by means of wisdom.
Therefore, according to that person’s own tenet, it is said, “imagined by wisdom. We shall first examine that; so let this [objection] stand for now, even in the absence of an agent.
The investigation into the existence or non-existence of wholesome states and so forth means, first of all, "we shall examine that very self.
With the intention of pointing out a fault here, he asks without granting a formal admission, saying, "What is the fault here?
The meaning is: "What is the defect in [the view] that it is either conscious or unconscious? The other [responds]: "In both cases, there is indeed a fault."
For that which is an insentient self is not an agent or an experiencer, just like a wall, a tree, and so forth.
To show that the absence of agency and experience is established by inference—namely, "this self is insentient"—the passage beginning with "If it were insentient" was stated.
"Inseparable" (anañño) means inseparable by way of non-distinction; otherwise, the very statement "it is sentient" would be untenable.

"Co-existent" means that there is no other [entity]; thus, there would be the destruction of the self as well, just as when one among inseparable material phenomena is destroyed, the other is also destroyed.
The intention is that even consciousness is not destroyed, just as when one among inseparable material phenomena is not destroyed, the other is also not destroyed.
Having stated the reason, “Because of the non-otherness of volition (*cetanā*),” he said “Because of the nature of volition,” and so forth, in order to substantiate that very point.
Having heard that “if there were no self (*attā*), there would be no destruction even of volition,” the opponent remains speechless;
with the intention that there is no specific cause for the destruction of volition [other than the self], he said, “But if [it is argued] that volition itself,” and so forth. The self alone...
"Let it perish; let the volition remain. For what purpose would there be attachment to oneself when there is no cause for distinction?
The intention is: "What opposition is there to the volition? "The promise is lost" means the promise previously given has fallen away.
"If that does not happen"—that is, if, when one's own destruction occurs, there is no non-destruction of the volition—because of the non-difference between the volition and the self.
Because it would follow that if volition were destroyed, the self (*attā*) itself would also be destroyed, your proposition that "the self does not perish" is inferior.

"Contrary to the manner stated" means contrary to the manner already described. The meaning is: your intention might be that even when volition is destroyed, the self does not perish, whereas even though the self is not destroyed, volition does perish. The self...
"Let it perish; let volition remain"—the intention is that both [the self and volition] must possess an identical capacity for application (*samānayogakkhema*) in another state.
"You are inferior to your own assertion" means that volition alone perishes, while the self does not perish; you are merely inferior to your own assertion.
"In this world" refers to the other side. "Made by distinct characteristics" means made by mutually dissimilar and differentiated characteristics.
"Produced in a different place" means produced in a distinct location. "Jātavedo" (the one born of what is born) means that which is felt or known; this is a designation for fire.
"While being burned" means while being cooked after having been placed on a hearth. "A single part of these" refers to those things whose locus of occurrence is one;
the state of being such is "particularity" (*ekadesattaṃ*).

"Because of inseparability" means that although there is a distinction in terms of their characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), they are not separated by way of location (*ṭhāna*) because they are not dissociated;
thus, "inseparability" is stated as a synonym for "being in one place. "That is incorrect" means that it does not cohere with the statement, "there is no single location for both.
"The admission is inferior" means that if the previous admission is authoritative, then this [present] admission...
It is inferior. Or else, the meaning is that if this [self] is the measure, the other is inferior.

Alternatively, because the self, through the diversity of its own parts within volition, reaches a state of being non-volitional, the promise previously given by you—that "the self is conscious"—is lost;
thus the meaning here should be understood.
