“Making [it] ‘the self is insentient’ means: having established that the self is devoid of consciousness. ‘Because of the fault stated previously’ refers to the fault stated at the beginning with the words, ‘If it were insentient,’ and so forth. ‘Therefore’ means: because, when examined in this way, [the self] is found to be incapable of withstanding scrutiny;

therefore [this is said]. 779. ‘If it were thus’—the connection is as follows: if, in the ultimate sense, there is no agent of wholesome and unwholesome deeds nor any experiencer of their results, then, such being the case, for what reason was it spoken by the Blessed One?”

"Sandhāvati" means it wanders through the cycle of existence (*saṃsarati*). Because pleasure and pain—which are results (*vipāka*)—have as their condition the wholesome and unwholesome kamma performed by oneself, they are said to be "performed by oneself"; thus it is stated: "Pleasure and pain are self-made. 780.
"Has entered into the cycle of existence" refers to:
"The succession of the aggregates (*khandhā*), And of the elements (*dhātu*) and sense-bases (*āyatana*);..."
“The continuity being uninterrupted is called ‘saṃsāra.
Thus, one has entered upon the cycle of existence—which proceeds by way of days and the sequence of the aggregates as described—by means of its repeated occurrence.
“Suffering is his great terror”: for this being who has entered into saṃsāra, suffering such as birth and so forth is a great terror.
The meaning is "leading to great fear. "Opapātiko" means one who is being reborn.
(781) "The five aggregates are indeed a burden": the five aggregates, beginning with form, are of the nature of a burden;
what is meant is that they are like a burden placed upon the head. "The bearer of the burden" is the person who carries that burden of the five aggregates. "The taking up of the burden" is...

The taking up of the burden of the five aggregates by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). "Laying down the burden" is the laying down of the burden by means of final *nibbāna* without clinging (*anupādā-parinibbāna*), through bringing about the state of no longer having to take it up again.
(782) "That" refers to wholesome and unwholesome kamma. "One's own" means dependent upon oneself.
783. “Of one person” is the connection [of the phrase]. “In one eon” means in a single eon (*kappa*).
784. “Lacking faith,” etc., has its meaning explained below.

Having stated, “And that is according to conventional designation (*sammuti*), not in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*),” the following passage beginning with “Has it not been said by the Blessed One” is intended to establish that very point.

It has been said: regarding the verse beginning with “Is there, then, a being? (*kiṃ nu satto*), although it was spoken by the Elder Nun Vajirā, because it was spoken according to the very intention of the Blessed One, it is considered as having been spoken by the Blessed One;
thus it is stated, “This too was spoken by the Blessed One. “‘Is there, then, a being?’—thus he answered”:
among form, feeling, and so forth, what indeed do you grasp as a “being” or a “person”? (*kiṃ nu satto puggalo*)?

786. "Aṅgasambhāra" means in the assembly of parts such as the wheels and so forth; the meaning is: in the bringing together of the parts such as the wheels and so forth. "Sadda" (sound) refers to conventional expression (*vohāra*).
"Tasmā" means because the Blessed One has thus stated that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*), there is no being;
therefore. The meaning is: one should not rely on the mere word while abandoning the intended meaning. "Daḷhamūḷhaggāhī" means one who grasps [the teaching] while being profoundly deluded.
Even when the reason has been shown, grasping by way of not relinquishing is "firm grasping. Grasping by way of being incapable of even seeing the reason is "deluded grasping.
He said, "And one should not... [etc. ...be so," meaning that one should not be such a person.
"Of the Sutta passages" refers to those discourses that exist in both ways, according to their interpretable meaning (*neyyattha*) and their definitive meaning (*nītattha*).
The intention is that two truths have been taught according to the needs of those individuals who are to be trained.

For those who attain distinction through the teaching of conventional truth (*sammuti*), he teaches by way of conventional truth; and for those who [attain distinction] through the teaching of ultimate truth (*paramattha*), he teaches by way of ultimate truth.
Just as a teacher skilled in local dialects [teaches] the youths living in various regions...
"In each respective language. Regarding "conventional truth" (*sammutisacca*) and "ultimate truth" (*paramatthasacca*):

here, such things as "person," "being," "woman," "man," "kshatriya," "brahmin," and "deity"—though non-existent from the perspective of ultimate reality—are conventional truths because they exist as such by virtue of the conventions established in the world.
The aggregates (*khandha*), elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), and so forth, exist only by way of ultimate reality.
Suchness is the ultimate truth. Therefore, the teachers of the commentaries said:
“The conventional expression is true, being the cause for worldly consensus;
The expression of the ultimate is true, being the cause for the actual state of phenomena.”
“Therefore, for the Teacher, the Lord of the World,
who is skilled in conventional usage, no false speech arises when he employs conventional designations.
(787–8) For one who contemplates this text constantly and perpetually, supreme wisdom is thereby accomplished.
It attains a state of expansion. It draws out and removes intense mental distress (*cittasantāpa*), thus it is "drawing out" (*adhinīhara*).

It effects the destruction of doubt (*vimati*), perplexity (*vicikicchā*), or delusion (*moha*) by way of being their decisive support (*upanissaya*), thus it is "the destroyer of doubt" (*vimativināsakara*). It is "pleasing" (*piyakara*) because it increases the mind through its excellence in both meaning and phrasing.
It "shines forth" (*vikasati*), that is, it glows (*dibbati*). "Here" (*idha*) means in this teaching (*sāsana*) or in the Abhidhamma.
Thus ends the commentary on the "Penetration of the Agent" in the *Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanā*, titled *Abhidhammatthavikāsinī*.
14. The Fourteenth Chapter:
Commentary on the Exposition of the Development of Fine-Material-Sphere Concentration (Rūpāvacara-samādhi-bhāvanā-niddesa-vaṇṇanā) 789.
Having thus shown all phenomena in brief by way of both the ultimate and conventional meanings, [the author] now...
Since a son of noble family who desires the goal must, through familiarity gained by means of grasping, delimiting, and so forth,
apply himself single-mindedly to meditation regarding those [objects], he begins to show the method of meditation in brief, saying "the method of meditation," and so on. Therein,
"the method of meditation" refers to the method of mundane and supramundane meditation, the sequence for the increase of wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*).
*Attha*: It brings and leads to welfare pertaining to both the present life and the future life; thus it is a "welfare-approach" (*hitānaya*), and that is the welfare-approach.

They honor it, or honoring it. Because it brings happiness to beings through instruction regarding the purposes of both the present life and the future life, it is a "happiness-approach" (*sukhānaya*), and that is the happiness-approach.
Or, the construction may be: "I explain the supreme, or the supreme approach to cultivation."

790. The connection is: “The knowledge and vision that is superior to the qualities of human beings. In this context, the “qualities of human beings” refers to the ten courses of wholesome action (*kusalakammapatha*), which constitute the natural qualities of human beings. That which is “superior to those” is the knowledge and vision consisting of the sublime (*mahaggata*) and supramundane (*lokuttara*) states.
For these are called “knowledge” (*ñāṇa*) in the sense of knowing, and [they are called] “vision” (*dassana*) in the sense of seeing as if by direct perception.
And "vision" is what is intended. Or, the phrase "of those superior to ordinary men" is connected according to its literal position.
The meaning is: of those superior to foolish men—namely, both the meditators and the Noble Ones. 791.
By the words "of suspicious conduct," etc., the purpose of purification of virtue is shown. Therein, it is to be remembered with suspicion (*saṅkāya saritabbo*).

"His conduct is suspicious" (*saṅkassara-samācāro*): it is conduct that should be approached with suspicion, such as when, upon seeing some base deed, one thinks, "This must have been done by so-and-so," or when seeing others whispering about something, one thinks, "Having learned of this or that impropriety of mine, they are whispering.
Such is the conduct to be approached with suspicion.

The meaning is as follows. To clarify this very point regarding one who is immoral (*dussīla*), it is said: "devoid of virtue" (*sīlavajjita*). Alternatively, "immoral" means one whose virtue is corrupted, or whose virtue has fallen into a state of breach and so forth.
"Devoid of virtue" means entirely lacking in virtue in every respect. "There is no jhāna" means that even mundane jhāna is absent; how then could there be the Path?
That is to say, how could there be the supramundane Path, and for what reason would supramundane states [arise]?
The meaning is that only the cause is found.
792. It is called *cāritta* because they move about (*caranti*) by means of practicing that virtue in its fulfillment.

It is called *vāritta* because one protects (*tāyati*) or guards oneself by means of it, or because it protects oneself from what is prohibited (*vārita*). That which has been declared by the Blessed One as "this is to be done" [is *cāritta*].

The fulfillment of the training rules as they have been prescribed is called "conduct" (cāritta). The non-performance of that which has been prohibited by the rule "this should not be done" is called "restraint" (vāritta).

Regarding the terms "without breach" and so forth: if, among the seven classes of offenses, one has broken a training rule, one's virtue is said to be "breached," like a garment with a hole; the opposite of that is [virtue without breach].
"Without breach" (*acchidda*). That which is broken at the beginning or the end is called "fragmentary" (*khaṇḍa*), like a garment torn at its edges;

other than that is "unfragmented" (*akkhaṇḍa*). It is "unfragmented" by way of performing [the action] in due order; or alternatively, there is the reading "unfragmented and without breach" (*akkhaṇḍamacchidda*) by way of not transgressing the sequence.
By the inclusion of the term "without flaw" (*akammāsa*), "unsullied" (*asabala*) is also expressed, [referring to the absence of] both sulkiness (*sabala*) and flaw (*kammāsa*).
Because the breach is of a minor nature; for such is the distinction between them.

One whose two or three training rules have been broken in succession is called "speckled" (*sabalā*), like a cow that is speckled with various colors such as black or red due to a patch of dissimilar color appearing on its back or belly.
One whose [rules] have been broken at intervals is [called "speckled"] at those intervals.
That which is like a cow variegated with spots of dissimilar color is called "speckled" (*kammāsa*).

But that which is not of such a kind is called "unspotted" (*asabala*) and "unspeckled" (*akammāsa*). By the term "blameless" (*anindita*), he includes its being praised by the wise and the free, its being untainted, and its being conducive to concentration.
In this regard: "By means of this virtue, or vow, or holy life, may I become a deva..."
"Or by some other deity"—thus it is called "free" (bhujissa) because it is not clung to by craving and is liberated from the slavery of craving;

for in the world they say one who is not a slave is "free. Because it is fulfilled with the aforementioned qualities, it is "praised by the wise" (viññuppasaṭṭha), being laudable by the Buddhas and others who are wise.
Because it is not clung to by craving or views, that which partakes of stability is called "not clung to" (aparāmaṭṭha). [This refers to] the jhānas and so forth...
It is called "conducive to concentration" because it is capable of serving as a condition for the attainment of distinction.
"The bliss of seclusion" refers to the bliss of seclusion from both body and mind, as well as from material possessions.

For even in the case of one who possesses virtue, the bliss of physical seclusion—such as when dwelling in empty huts and the like—is specifically characterized by suffering if terrifying objects and so forth come within range of his perception; whereas for one who is immoral, this is likewise the case.

"Through clear comprehension. "The unsurpassed ornament": because it is the cause for attaining a splendor that is not shared by anyone else among gods, Brahmās, kings, royal ministers, and so forth, it is a distinguished ornament that is peerless.

"The jewel": because it generates a delight even more distinguished than the Wheel-Jewel and others of the universal monarchs, it is the unsurpassed jewel. For while the Wheel-Jewel and the rest generate only the delight associated with the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), this [jewel] generates even that which is associated with the turning away from the cycle (*vivaṭṭa*).

It is called *janetī* because it specifically generates delight. It is a *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling gem) because it produces the attainment of whatever one desires, and thus it is equal to a *cintāmaṇi*.
It is a *yāna* (vehicle) because it is a vehicle for crossing over the wilderness of *saṃsāra*. It is *sītala* (cool) because it brings about a state of coolness in the mind.

It is a "washing away of the stains of the defilements" (*kilesa-mala-dhovana*) because [it cleanses] the turbidity of the defilements, which is difficult even for the Ganges, Yamunā, and other rivers to purify.
“Washing”: it is the root of all virtues; that is, it is the root of all mundane and supramundane virtues.
The scriptural passage beginning with, “Established in virtue, what further root of wholesome states is there? And virtue that is thoroughly purified,” serves as the illustration here.
It is the destroyer of the power of defilements because it destroys the strength that serves as the basis for the transgression of those defilements.
Therefore, because virtue is endowed with such benefits as these, it possesses a twofold characteristic:

it has the characteristic of concentration (*samādhāna-lakkhaṇa*) because it accomplishes the non-distraction of bodily action and so forth through such means as downcast eyes and silence; and it has the characteristic of a foundation (*patiṭṭhāna-lakkhaṇa*) because it serves as the root of wholesome states.
Alternatively, it has a twofold nature by way of right conduct (*cāritta*) and restraint (*vāritta*).
*Attha*: one who desires welfare (*attha*) by way of wishing for the benefit of another is called *atthakāma*. One whose virtue (*sīla*) is dear is called *piyasīla*.
798–9. The connection is: "The obstacle (*palibodha*) must be severed. But how many kinds of obstacles are there, and what is their nature?
To this he says, "There are ten obstacles," and so forth; the intention is that [this] was stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. Therein:
"Abode" refers to anything from a single small room up to an entire monastic complex;
for one whose mind is bound to it, that is an impediment, but not for another. "Family" refers either to a family of kinsmen or a family of supporters;

for one who dwells in close association with them, that is an impediment. "Gain" refers to the four requisites; these too are impediments only for one who has expectations regarding them. "Group" refers to a group of those specializing in the Suttas.

Or a group of those specializing in the Abhidhamma. These are obstacles for one who has not yet found an opportunity for the practice of the ascetic’s duty (*samaṇadhamma*) through the granting of recitations and inquiries.

"Work" refers to new construction; for one doing it, there is an obstacle in every respect, as he must know what has been obtained or not obtained from carpenters and others, and must exert himself regarding what has been done or left undone.
"Traveling" refers to the difficulty of dispelling the mind when it is set on going along a road.

That is an impediment to the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*). Regarding "relatives": since the term "family" here includes the family of relatives, it should be understood that each individual relative is included here.
However, those who are teachers (*ācariya*) or preceptors (*upajjhāya*) and so forth in the monastery, or mothers and so forth at home, are impediments when they are ill.
"Affliction" (*ābādha*) refers to any kind of disease; when it causes pain, it is an impediment. "Literary work" (*gantha*) refers to the preservation of the scriptures (*pariyatti*).

That is an impediment for one who is constantly occupied with recitation and other such duties. "Supernormal power" (iddhi) refers here to mundane supernormal power; for that is difficult to maintain and is broken by even a slight lapse.

However, this [impediment] is an obstacle to insight (vipassanā), not to concentration (samādhi), because [insight] is to be attained once concentration has been reached. "Those" refers to those impediments.
"Having completely severed obstacles": here, the first [obstacle] is by means of a mind free from longing for that [place];
the second, by not associating [with others]; the third, by abandoning places where gain and honor arise and going elsewhere;
the fourth, by completing the work on the texts as it was begun, or by taking up another [text]; the fifth, by [completing] the task as it was begun...
The sixth [duty] is by way of completing [the task], or by way of entrusting it to the Saṅgha and others; the seventh is by going and investigating the matter;
the eighth is by attending to [him] and restoring his kinsmen to their normal state, or by providing medicine, or by the resolution of energy;
the ninth and tenth are to be terminated by remaining uninvolved in those matters. "He should be approached" means the procedure for approaching him wherever he dwells.
The procedure for one who approaches [the teacher] should be understood according to the method explained in the *Visuddhimagga*.

Hereafter, in order to avoid excessive length in the text, we shall set aside the detailed exposition found in the *Visuddhimagga* and provide merely a commentary on the meaning of the words. Regarding the phrase "of the meditation subject" (*kammaṭṭhānassa*):
here, it is so called because it is the basis for the occurrence of the work of yoga (*yogakamma*), and because it is the work of successive cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
And it is a meditation subject by way of being its cause. Furthermore, it is twofold: universal and portable.
Among these, loving-kindness, mindfulness of death, and the perception of foulness are called "universal meditation subjects" because they must be cultivated and desired in all circumstances.
Any meditation subject whatsoever that accords with one's temperament is a "portable meditation subject" because it must be constantly carried about.
This is the name. To show that one who gives these two kinds of meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) is a "giver of meditation subjects," and that such a person should also be sought after, it is said:
"Beloved and venerable," and so forth. "Beloved" means he is to be loved by beings because of his perfection of virtue and other qualities.
"Venerable" means for that very reason he is to be respected; he should be regarded with reverence, like a stone parasol.
"Bhāvanīyo" means one who is to be respected. "Vattā" means one whose habit it is to speak by way of admonition and exhortation even upon seeing some form of indolence.
"Vacanakkhamo" means one who is patient with questioning; having been questioned, he remains unshaken—this is what is meant by being patient with discourse.
"And one who can deliver profound talk" means that, without engaging in frivolous talk (*tiracchānakathā*), he speaks in connection with the ten bases of discourse (*dasakathāvatthu*).
"How does he speak only what is profound? means he does not direct one toward what is improper—that is, he does not urge one toward that which is harmful and unfit for practice.
"Endowed with such qualities as these": by the word "etcetera" (ādi), he indicates the possession of qualities such as perfection in faith.
"At the proper time" means at a time suitable for both himself and his teacher.
“Having performed the duties” means having performed the duties toward the teacher as prescribed in the Khandhaka according to whether the teacher is junior or senior.
Now, in order to show the procedure for how the teacher should act, it is said, “By him also,” and so forth. “By him also” means by the one who gives the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
“Having known the temperament” means that one who possesses the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) [should know] his mental disposition.
Or, having observed the redness of the heart, one should question the other with such words as, "What is your temperament? Which mental states do you frequently manifest?
and so forth; having thus understood that person's temperament, the teaching should be given in accordance with it.
One can also understand the temperament of some individuals from their posture and other signs, but that is not entirely definitive. [Regarding] "temperament..."
Having stated "having known," [the question arises] what that is and how many kinds there are; thus he says: "This temperament, however, is by way of lust, hatred, and delusion," and so forth.

It is called a *carita* (temperament) because it moves (*carati*) within the continuum (*santāna*) due to its state of being predominant; it refers to lust and the other defilements which are liable to arise in the continuum when there is no cultivation of their opposites.

805. "By way of the mixed method" means by way of association and by way of their inclusion within a single continuum; these are the various combinations of them. "They become sixty-four"—[this is the number].
“Seven [types] for each triad beginning with lust, and seven for each triad beginning with faith;
in the case of the roots consisting of one, two, or three, there are seven times seven through combination.
When these nine sets of seven have been stated, they amount to sixty-four when divided as appropriate along with the sixty-three views. Thus it was said by the Elder Upananda:
“Greed, hatred, and delusion; by greed and also by aversion;
together with greed and delusion, and delusion and aversion.
‘The triad of greed and so forth is one,’ thus there are seven triads beginning with greed.”
Faith, understanding, and reasoning—along with faith and understanding.
“Reasoning by means of faith, and also reasoning by means of understanding;
the triad of faith and so forth, as one, constitutes the seven triads beginning with faith.”
“The triads beginning with lust, divided according to one, two,
and three [factors] respectively, should be combined as appropriate with faith,
wisdom, and applied thought. Thus, there are three sets of seven for each of the single-rooted and double-rooted [types].”
In each of the seven [sections], there is one; that should be known as the "seven-sevens.
Faith together with lust, and wisdom together with that very same [lust];
likewise, reasoning with that, and faith and wisdom together with that.
“By that [method], one should apply it to faith and intention, and also to wisdom and intention;
having combined them with that very same method, one should apply it to the conceptualization of faith and wisdom.
And likewise, according to the method for the root of lust, one should set forth a single heptad.”
Faith together with hatred, and wisdom together with that very same [hatred].
By that very means there is reasoning, and by that both faith and wisdom;
by that there is the application of faith, and also the application of wisdom.
“Having mixed together by means of that very [method],
faith, understanding, and thought, as well as the method for the root of hatred—
one should point out one heptad. Faith along with delusion, and understanding along with that very same [delusion];”
By that very means there is reflection, and by that, faith and understanding.
By that very means there is the application of faith and the application of understanding;
having mixed together the reflection on faith and the reflection on understanding by that very same means.
“In the method beginning with Delusion as the root, one set of seven is indicated;
likewise in the method beginning with the Single Root—thus those three sets of seven should be known.
Having combined them with passion and hatred, as well as faith and wisdom with those same two.”
By those [factors] there is intention, and by those there is faith and wisdom.
Through those two— faith-intention and wisdom-intention—
combined together, there is the conceptualization of faith and wisdom.
“One should point out one set of seven concerning the overcoming of lust and hatred;
then, having combined them with lust and delusion, [another] with faith and those same [two], and with wisdom.
With those [three], there is the application of thought; with those [three], faith and wisdom; and with those [three],” [it is said].
The application of faith by means of those [qualities], and also the application of wisdom.
By combining these two alone, one should designate a single set of seven:
the conceptualization of faith and wisdom, as well as the removal of lust and delusion.
“Having committed [wrong] through lust, hatred, and delusion, [one acts] through those very same faith and wisdom;
through those [same factors], there is the formation of intention, and through those, both faith and wisdom.
Through those, there is the formation of intention by faith, and also the formation of intention by wisdom.”
By mixing those very same [factors] with faith, understanding, and applied thought,
one should point out a single set of seven for each of the methods of hatred and delusion.
Thus, in the method of the two roots, that triad of sets of seven should be known.
“By means of lust, aversion, and delusion, there is faith and likewise by those same [factors] there is wisdom;
by those there is intention, and by those there is both faith and wisdom.
By means of those there is the intending of faith, and also the intending of wisdom.”
Having combined those very same [categories] with faith, understanding, and thought,
one should point out a single sevenfold set within the method of the three roots.
Thus, it should be understood that there are sixty-three [factors] in the nine sevenfold sets.
"And there are indeed sixty-four [types] even by way of view"—so say some.

(806–7) But has it not been stated that "one should give [the meditation subject] after knowing the temperament"? With reference to this inquiry—namely, which meditation subject is suitable for which temperament—it was said [previously] after showing the meditation subject suitable for each respective temperament; then, for him...

The passage beginning with "And the foul" (*asubhā ca*) is commenced in order to show the classification [of meditation] by way of: enumeration, bringing about absorption, the differentiation of jhānas, transcendence, increase and non-increase, object, plane, grasping, condition, and distinction. Therein, the ten kinds of foulness are:
the bloated (*uddhumātaka*), the livid (*vinīlaka*), the festering (*vipubbaka*), the fissured (*vicchiddaka*), the gnawed (*vikkhāyitaka*), the scattered (*vikkhittaka*), and so forth.

The ten [meditations on foulness]—the bloated, the livid, the festering, the cut-up, the gnawed, the scattered, the hacked and scattered, the bleeding, the worm-infested, and the skeleton—and likewise mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati) make eleven;
these are suitable for one of lustful temperament because they serve as the means for suppressing lust.

And here, by the inclusion of "foulness" (asubha), the meditation subject preceded by concentration that takes that as its object is included. The same applies to the remaining [temperaments] as appropriate.

It should be seen. Because they have immeasurable beings as their object, they are called "immeasurables" (*appamaññā*); this is a designation for the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), namely loving-kindness (*mettā*), compassion (*karuṇā*), gladness (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekkhā*).

Furthermore, together with the four colored kasiṇas—the white kasiṇa, the blue kasiṇa, the yellow kasiṇa, and the red kasiṇa—they constitute eight, because they serve as the means for suppressing hatred.
And because its object is non-resistant, it is conducive to one of a hateful temperament (dosa-carita).
808. Regarding the phrase "and it is a single [object]," here "single" refers to the recollections (anussati);

the meaning is that it is one among the recollections, not with reference to those of deluded temperament (moha-carita) or discursive temperament (vitakka-carita), since for them other [objects] conducive to their own temperaments are also available. That... [etc.]... is what is meant.
However, for one of deluded temperament (*mohacarita*) and one of discursive temperament (*vitakkacarita*), it is conducive because the mind becomes established through the power of counting.

809–11. Regarding the phrase "the former... for embodied beings": this first set of six recollections (*anussati-chakka*)—namely, recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of virtue (*sīla*), recollection of generosity (*cāga*), and recollection of the deities (*devatā*)—is, according to the sequence of the Canon, for one of faithful temperament (*saddhācarita*).
"Conducive" means suitable by way of being highly beneficial. "Mindfulness engaged in death and peace" means mindfulness applied to death and to peace;

thus, what is meant is "recollection of death" (*maraṇānussati*) and "recollection of peace" (*upasamānussati*). "Perception based on nutriment" means the perception of repulsiveness regarding nutriment.
"Analysis of elements" means the analysis of the four elements. "For a person of intellectual temperament" means for a being whose character is dominated by wisdom.

"The remaining kasiṇas" refers to the earth, water, fire, air, light, and space kasiṇas, which are the remainder after the four color kasiṇas suitable for one of hating temperament have been mentioned;
thus, these six together with the previous four make ten that are the direct opposites of this [temperament].
Because there is no distinction to be grasped as "unsuitable" for this [temperament], they are described as being suitable for all temperaments, such as those dominated by greed and so forth.
812. "Because of being an absolute opposite" means that for those of a lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*) and so forth, the meditation subjects such as the foul (*asubha*) are direct opposites.

"Because of being highly suitable" means that for those of a faithful temperament (*saddhācarita*) and so forth, the meditation subjects such as the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*) are highly suitable.
Thus, by way of being direct opposites and by way of being highly suitable, all of this is individually conducive to them.

It was stated [in that way], but not because it is unsuitable for the other. For there is no such thing as a development of the wholesome that does not suppress lust and the like, or that does not assist faith and the like. Thus, in the Meghiya Sutta:
"Four things are to be further developed: the meditation on the foul is to be developed for the abandoning of lust; loving-kindness is to be developed..."
“For the abandoning of ill will, mindfulness of breathing should be developed; for the cutting off of applied thoughts, the perception of impermanence should be developed;
for the uprooting of the conceit ‘I am,’ the perception of non-self should be developed.
Thus it is said that four states are to be developed for each single purpose. Likewise, in the Rāhulovāda Sutta: “Loving-kindness, Rāhula...”
By such statements as “Develop meditation,” seven subjects of meditation have been taught;
yet neither the Venerable Meghiya nor the Elder Rāhula possessed all four temperaments, nor did they possess every type of temperament.
Therefore, it is said that one should not adhere to the mere literal expression, but rather seek the underlying intention in every case.
813–4. Although the numerical limit of the meditation subjects can indeed be known by the method already stated, it cannot be easily understood because of their intermixture;

therefore, in order to show their numerical limit both collectively and individually according to their types, the passage beginning with "All meditation subjects" was stated. "Forty" is indicated from the Pāḷi, and from the Commentary.
And having combined them, one should define them as "forty-four. How so? "The ten kasiṇas... [and so on] ...perception and nutriment.
Regarding "the ten foulness-recollections," the word "ten" should be applied to each individually: "ten foulnesses, ten recollections.
The ten foulnesses have already been explained below. The six mentioned here as "the first group of six recollections" are the recollection of death and so forth.
Mindfulness directed to the body, mindfulness of breathing, and mindfulness of peace—these are the ten recollections (*anussati*).

"The analysis of the four elements" refers to the discernment of the four elements, beginning with earth. In the phrase "perception as nutriment," the letter *ga* has been elided for the sake of metrical composition;

thus, perception pertaining to nutriment is expressed as "the state of nutriment-perception" (*āhāratā-saññā*). Alternatively, nutriment itself is the "state of nutriment" (*āhāratā*), and [perception] pertaining to that is what is meant.
And this perception is called "nutriments" by way of metaphor; the meaning is "perception of repulsiveness in nutriment.
815–6. Is jhāna produced in all these meditation subjects? Yes, access-jhāna is produced in all of them, but absorption-jhāna is not produced in some; therefore, some [subjects] yield only access.
Some produce [access concentration], while others produce even absorption. To explain how this is to be understood, he says: "Among these," and so forth.
"Bringing about access only" means *upacārāvahā*; here, a restrictive sense (*avadhāraṇa*) should be understood, as in the case of the words "expectant" (*apekkho*) and so on.

Among those, excluding mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*) and mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*), there are the remaining eight recollections (*anussati*), such as the recollection of the Buddha, as well as perception (*saññā*).

"And definition" (vavatthāna): these ten [factors] are said to lead to access concentration (*upacāra*) in the absence of a specific development, because they possess various modes, profundity, and the nature of intrinsic phenomena (*sabhāva-dhamma*).
Having thus shown them by way of leading to access and absorption (*appanā*), he now shows them by way of the classification of jhānas, beginning with "those that lead to absorption."
It has been stated. "Possessing four jhānas" means they possess the fourfold fine-material-sphere jhānas according to the fourfold method;
the meaning is that they serve as the object for each one of those [jhānas]. However, according to the fivefold method, they should be understood as "possessing five jhānas.
"Consisting of the first jhāna" means they serve as the object for the first jhāna alone, because the other [jhānas] have the state of repulsiveness [as their object].

They do not become objects [of the higher jhānas]. For even with respect to a repulsive object, one enters the first jhāna by the power of applied thought (vitakka), like a boat crossing a river with a violent current by means of the power of an oar.
However, because those [higher factors] are absent, one does not enter the remaining [jhānas] in those [objects].
819. "Carrying three jhānas": according to the fourfold method, it carries three jhānas; however, according to the fivefold method, it carries four jhānas.
For loving-kindness (mettā), compassion (karuṇā), and gladness (muditā) do not possess the fifth jhāna because they take as their object only those states associated with joy (somanassa).
Indeed, when loving-kindness and the others have reached absorption (appanā), they do not proceed without joy. "The fourth sublime abode (brahmavihāra)" is the connection [with the preceding].

It is called a sublime abode because it is the abode of the sublime (brahmānaṃ uttamānaṃ vihāro), or because it is an abode that has become sublime (brahmabhūto vihāro); this [fourth] is by way of the cultivation of equanimity (upekkhā).
It pertains to the fourth jhāna. Furthermore, it enters only that tetrad of jhānas obtained by way of loving-kindness (mettā) and so forth, and not the other.
Why? Because it is the outflow (nissanda) of loving-kindness and the rest.

For just as the formless attainments (āruppa) are the outflow of the kasiṇas, and as the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is the outflow of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), so too equanimity (upekkhā) is the outflow of loving-kindness and the rest. The formless [attainments]...
“Belonging to the fourth jhāna”: this is stated because even the formless attainments (āruppa) are considered subdivisions of the fourth jhāna itself by way of the equality of their factors (aṅga).

Having thus shown [the jhānas] by way of the classification of jhānas, it was further stated, “by way of the object and the factors,” etc., in order to show them again by way of transcendence (samatikkama).
“Transcendence of the object” and “transcendence of the factors” refer to the objects and the factors that are to be transcended.
The transcendence by way of mastery is twofold. Is it found as twofold in all cases? No, he says: “Transcendence of the object...
[and] transcendence. For in the four formless attainments, there is only transcendence of the object;
having transcended one or another among the nine objects—with the exception of the space kasiṇa—there is the base of infinite space, and likewise the base of infinite space and the others.

Because one must transcend [the lower stages] to reach the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*) and so forth, there is no "transcending of factors" (*aṅgātikkama*) in the formless realms;

for all four [formless attainments] are identical in terms of their factors. "Transcending of jhāna-factors" (*jhānaṅgatikkama*) in the fine-material sphere refers to the transcending of the jhāna-factors such as applied thought (*vitakka*) in the meditation subjects belonging to the fine-material realm, and this is stated according to what is actually obtainable.
In those possessing the first jhāna, both types [of transcending] are present.
There is no "surmounting" [of the hindrances] mentioned here, because the surmounting of the hindrances is common to all eight attainments and thus was not included.
Having thus shown it by way of surmounting, he said, "The ten kasiṇas," etc., in order to show it again by way of extension and non-extension.
Among these forty meditation subjects, only the ten kasiṇas are to be extended.
"And not... [as in the text]... the foul and so forth. As for the remaining [meditations], such as the foul and so forth, they should not be expanded.

Why? Because they appear only in a limited mode, and because they lack further benefit. For instance, the ten kinds of foulness and mindfulness occupied with the body appear only in a limited mode, since they are limited by their own respective locations. Even when expanded, only a heap of corpses appears.
There is no special benefit [in this]. For even when those [objects] are not expanded, there is indeed the suppression of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*).
If this is so, does it not contradict the statement that the jhānas based on the foul (*asubha*) have an immeasurable object? It does not contradict it.

For one person grasps the sign (*nimitta*) in a bloated corpse or a skeleton that is large, while another grasps it in one that is small; it is by way of this method [that the contradiction is resolved].

For some, the jhāna has a limited object; for others, it has an immeasurable object. Or rather, the state of having an immeasurable object is stated with reference to one who would extend it without seeing this absence of benefit. Even the sign of the breath (ānāpānanimitta) appears delimited by the tip of the nose, the mouth, or other such points;
and even when one extends it, only a mass of air is extended. Although it may appear as a ball of cotton-wool or the like, [it remains so].

For the sign is merely the size of a winnowing basket; likewise, for one who increases even the sign of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), it would increase only to the size of a heap of grain, and there would be no purpose served by that.
Therefore, neither of these two should be increased.
As for what was said, "He dwells having pervaded one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness," and so forth—that too refers to the mode of comprehension (*pariggaha*).
This was stated, not by way of increasing the sign (*nimitta*). In the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), there is no counterpart sign at all;
so what could be increased? However, the fact that their objects are "immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*) should be understood here simply by way of having encompassed [them].

Among the immaterial-sphere objects, space should be brought to mind solely by way of the removal of the kasiṇa, because it is merely the clearing away of the kasiṇa; beyond that, for one who increases it...
There is nothing at all; consciousness cannot be expanded because it is a dhamma with its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*).

Only the preliminary work (*parikamma*) can be expanded. The departure from consciousness is merely its non-existence. Even the object of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception cannot be expanded because it too is a dhamma with its own intrinsic nature;
therefore, those [objects] also should not be expanded. The immensity of the objects of the formless attainments lies in the space cleared by the vast kasiṇas.
They should be understood according to their occurrence. Furthermore, the recollections of the Buddha and so forth should not be expanded because they are signless (*animitta*).

For it is the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*) that would be expanded, and these [recollections] lack such a sign; therefore, these thirty meditation subjects beginning with the foul (*asubha*) should not be expanded, because their location is delimited, because there is no further purpose, and because they do not expand.

822–3. Having thus shown [the objects] by way of their increase and non-increase, the passage beginning with “There are ten kasiṇas” is commenced in order to show them again by way of their objective supports (*ārammaṇa*).
“They become objective supports consisting of counterpart signs (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*): these twenty-two, having become counterpart signs, serve as objective supports.
“The rest”: the remaining eighteen would not be objective supports consisting of counterpart signs.
824–5. Now, in order to show [the subjects] by way of plane, it is said: “The foulnesses,” and so forth.
They do not occur among the devas because of the absence there of foul things and of repulsive food.

For even the fivefold skin, though occurring there, does not appear in a repulsive aspect due to divine power. Because of the absence of inhalation and exhalation in the Brahma-world, “mindfulness of breathing”...
And so it was said, beginning with "and. For because there is no purpose produced by the power of jhāna, there are no in-breaths and out-breaths in the Brahma-world.

Now, in order to show [the objects of meditation] by way of grasping, the passage beginning with "the fourth" was stated. Therein, regarding the phrase "the fourth... must be grasped by what is seen":
excluding the air-kasiṇa, the remaining nine kasiṇas and the ten foulness subjects—these nineteen [are to be grasped].
They are to be grasped—that is, apprehended—by means of the visible object itself acting as the instrument. Thus it is said in the Commentary:
"They are to be grasped by what is seen; the meaning is that in the preliminary stage, the sign of these [parts] is to be grasped by looking with the eye.
(828–31) And even when there is mindfulness directed to the body—that is, even in *kāyagatāsati*—only the pentad of skin (*tacapañcaka*) is seen.

What is to be grasped is by what is seen; the rest here is by what is heard. Here, in this context of mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*), the rest—the fivefold excrement and so forth—is to be grasped by what is heard. Thus, mindfulness directed to the body is to be grasped by means of both what is seen and what is heard.

Because the in-breath and out-breath that touch the upper lip, the nose-tip, and so on, is to be grasped, it is said: "Mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*) is here illustrated by what is touched."
Because the wind must be apprehended here by way of perceiving the moving color in the bowls of the *ucchusasa* (candala) and others, and by way of bodily contact, it is said:
"Only the wind kasiṇa is apprehended here by what is seen and touched. They are not to be taken up from the very beginning;
that is, they should not be established by one who is a beginner in the sense of commencing the development of meditation, as is the case with the three lower divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*).
Because it is impossible to achieve the fine-material-sphere fourth jhāna within the kasiṇas without first attaining it.
Having thus shown [the classification] by way of inclusion, the passage beginning with “Among these meditation subjects” is now stated in order to show it by way of condition.
Therein, regarding the phrase “among these meditation subjects,” the objects and the jhānas are to be understood here according to what is appropriate for each.
It should be understood. Because it is impossible to remove the space-kasiṇa, it is said, "without the space-kasiṇa.
Having attained and remained in three jhānas for each of the [first] three divine abidings—loving-kindness and so forth—the fifth jhāna arises by way of the divine abiding of equanimity;
thus it is said, "the three divine abidings," and so on. Of the two impulsion-moments of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception...
It is said, “the fourth immaterial attainment,” and so forth, because it touches cessation immediately after [the third].
“Conditions for insight, the excellence of existence, and happiness” means that they serve as conditions for insight, for the excellence of existence, and for dwelling in happiness in this very life.
836–9. Having thus shown the classification of meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) that arose incidentally, the teacher again [explains] the method of practice to be undertaken.
To demonstrate this, it was said: “Having taken up a meditation subject,” and so forth. “Living nearby” means living in the same house or the same monastery as the teacher.
“Should be told” means that after hearing of his progress again and again, it should be reported.
In the phrase “at every moment of his arrival,” the *sa-* is merely for the purpose of euphonic junction (*padasandhi*); the meaning is “at each successive moment of his arrival. Alternatively:
It should be told at the very moment someone has arrived. For in such instances, the meaning is obtained through the force of repetition (*āmeḍita*) itself.
Indeed, it would not be logical to say that it should be told at that moment for one who has arrived only once, and should not be told thereafter.
"Neither too brief nor too detailed" means that, having avoided what is overly condensed or overly prolix, it should be of a measure that allows for easy memorization.

It should be told. However, if he has already mastered the meditation subject by nature, or has gained proficiency through recitation or mental attention, then one or two sessions should be given to him after having him recite it in the teacher’s presence.
Having thus shown the procedure for the teacher’s practice, [the text continues] with the meditation subject that has been grasped.
Showing the further procedure to be performed by that yogi, he said, "By that too," and so forth.
"A well-swept place" (*sammaṭṭhāna*) means that place where one who has been struck is appeased; it is called a "well-swept place" because it is like a well-swept area.
For just as when a well-swept place is taken up, a person's enemy is unable to overcome him, so too with the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
When it is grasped, sensual lust—known as the "adornment of the mind"—is unable to overcome the person possessing it and bring them under its own power.
Therefore it is said: “Like a well-swept place, thus ‘well-swept’. It overcomes the mind, thus it is the “mind-adorned” (manobhū);
[the phrase] “of that mind-adorned one. ... [omitted] ... “avoided by eighteen... etc.
“The Great Abode, the New Abode, the Abode of Old Age, and the Roadside;
the Tavern, the Leaf, the Flower, the Fruit, and the Desired;
the City, the Wood, the Field, the Dissimilar, and the Port.”
“A border region where it is difficult to find a friend, where no true companion is to be found.
Having understood these eighteen states, a wise person should avoid them from afar,
just as one would avoid a path beset with dangers.

When it is said to be "free at all times from the eighteen faults of a dwelling," the term "suitable" (*anurūpa*) means that if a place is possessed of even one of these eighteen faults, it is called "unsuitable";
by the absence of those [faults], it is favorable to one's own practice of yoga (*yogakamma*).
For monasteries such as the Mahāvihāra are not favorable to the practice of yoga; therefore, first, regarding the Mahāvihāra, by means of performing the observances (*vatta*) and so forth—
It becomes an obstacle. However, where everything has already been completed and there is no further disturbance from others, even a great monastery (*mahāvihāra*) of such a kind is suitable.
In a new monastery, much new construction work must be done; therefore, in the absence of any other favorable circumstance, it is unsuitable.
Likewise, a dilapidated monastery is [unsuitable] because it requires extensive maintenance.
It is an obstacle to the meditation subject. A monastery dependent on a road is one that is crowded day and night by travelers.
A "soṇḍī-vihāra" is one where there is a stone lotus-pool called a *soṇḍī*;

many people gather there for the sake of drinking water, and likewise at a monastery possessing leaves, flowers, and fruits for those same purposes. One who dwells in a monastery that is desirable and esteemed by the world—
"Many people come thinking, 'He is an arahant. Even in a monastery situated near a city, there is the coming into range of discordant objects of perception and so forth.

In one situated near timber, there is discomfort due to wood-gatherers and the like. In one situated near a field, there is discomfort right in the middle of the monastery due to the threshing of grain and so forth.
And even in one inhabited by persons of a discordant nature, there is the need for preventing quarrels and the like."
They criticize [these places]: in a location dependent on a port, there is discomfort due to people arriving frequently by boat;
in a location dependent on a border region, people have little faith in the Buddha and his disciples;
and in a location dependent on a frontier between two kingdoms, when a dispute arises between the two kings, they seize a bhikkhu wandering for alms in both territories, thinking, "This is a spy."
They might subject one to imprisonment and the like; furthermore, there are unsuitable dangers such as those from non-human beings (amanussa).
If there is no one who has dwelt with virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitta) to dispel the doubts that have arisen, there is indeed great harm. Therefore, these dwellings are also unsuitable;
thus, having avoided such a dwelling, one should dwell in a suitable one free from the aforementioned faults.
To show that the suitability of that monastery should be understood in this way, the passage beginning with "from the village" was spoken.

"From the village" means from the village serving as the alms-resort (*gocara*). "Not too far" means it is not too distant because it lies within half a *gāvuta* on this side of the alms-resort village.
"Not too near" means it is not too close according to the latter measurement, being five hundred bow-lengths (*dhanus*) from the alms-resort village. By this—

It shows the perfection of coming and going. Furthermore, a lodging situated neither too far nor too near to the village used as the alms resort—specifically in the northern or southern direction—is particularly characterized by the perfection of coming and going. Here, being neither too far nor too near is mentioned merely as an illustration.
Moreover, because it is stated that [the lodging] is "endowed with five factors," this implies, along with being neither too far nor too near, [the other three factors].
The possession of five factors should be understood by combining these four qualities, beginning with being uncrowded during the day. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“And how, bhikkhus, is a lodging possessed of five factors? Here, bhikkhus, a lodging is not too far [from a village], nor too near;
it is well-served for coming and going; it is uncrowded during the day and has little noise at night.”
It is free from noise, and free from the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and creeping reptiles;
moreover, while dwelling in that lodging, the requisites of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick arise without difficulty;
furthermore, in that lodging there dwell elder bhikkhus who are learned, masters of the tradition, and bearers of the Dhamma.
Those who are masters of the Vinaya and masters of the Mātikā approach them from time to time and inquire about the meaning of questions, saying:

"Venerable sir, what is this? What is the meaning of this? Those venerable ones reveal to him what has not been revealed, clarify what has not been clarified, and dispel his doubt regarding various points that are grounds for uncertainty.
“Monks, it is in this way that a lodging possesses five factors.
Herein, the first factor is accessibility due to being neither too far nor too near;

the state of being uncluttered, quiet, and undisturbed by noise is due to the absence of crowds of people during the day, the absence of the sound of people’s chatter at night, and the absence of the clamor of people’s assemblies at all times.
The second [reason] is the absence of dangers such as gadflies and mosquitoes; the third is the easy acquisition of requisites such as robes and almsfood;
and the fourth is the fact that it is a dwelling place for elders endowed with qualities such as great learning—one should dwell in a monastery endowed and possessed of these five factors.
840-1. Having first mentioned the great impediments such as dwelling and so forth, the minor impediments are now presented;
in order to show their specific nature and the manner of severing them, the passage beginning with "Long hair" is stated.
The construction is: "That bowl must be well cooked."
"In a secluded place" means in a location remote from people. "Avoiding... [and so on] "...blood": these are the four defects of the *kasiṇa*;
therefore, one should avoid such clay. "Fine" means smooth, having had the grass roots, gravel, and sand removed, and being well-kneaded.
"The color of dawn" means resembling the dawn; the meaning is that it has the luster of the color of dawn. Or even externally...
“Such a place” means even outside the monastery, in a secluded spot at the edge of the dwelling.
“Portable” means that which is fit for being carried about after having been gathered up. “Remaining where it was made” means that which stays exactly where it was fashioned.
847–50. “By way of measure” means by the measure that will be explained below. “Having pounded it round” means having made it circular and then pounded it.
That refers to a piece of leather, a bamboo mat, or a cloth strip. "Kaṇṇika" means like a *kaṇṇikā* (a circular ornament);

by its roundness, it is said to have the shape of a lotus *kaṇṇikā*. Therefore he said, "even. Or there is the reading "kaṇṇikāsama. "Vidatthicaturaṅgula" means a measure of one *vidatthi* plus four *aṅgulas*.
Indeed, referring to this very measure, it is said in the Commentary: "in the size of a spoon..."
"Or the size of a shallow bowl," it is said. "Turning away" means Nibbāna.
For even when performing the preliminary work for a kasiṇa, one does not stop at just that much, but strives specifically for the sake of Nibbāna.

"Making it level like the surface of a drum" means having struck it with the hand, making it level like the surface of a drum by the absence of any unevenness or depressions. "Having swept that place" refers to the spot where one sits.
He gazes at the kasiṇa; if that place is dirty, he should sweep it. "Having bathed" means having bathed for the purpose of removing bodily fatigue.

851–2. "In a space within arm's reach of that kasiṇa-maṇḍala" means in a space at a distance of two and a half cubits from the spot where that kasiṇa-maṇḍala is placed; [this refers to] the middle between the kasiṇa-maṇḍala and the seat.

It means it is prepared having made the measure of the reach of the hand (*hatthapāsa*). "High by four finger-breadths" means being high by four finger-breadths; that is, it means having legs four finger-breadths high.
For to one sitting at a distance, the *kasiṇa* does not appear clearly;
to one sitting closer, the defects of the *kasiṇa*, such as the hands, fingers, and feet [of the preparer], become apparent. [If it is] higher...
Furthermore, when sitting, one must bend the neck to look [ahead]; otherwise, the knees are strained at a lower level.
Therefore, one should sit on a stool with legs a span and four finger-breadths high, at a distance within arm's reach.
Since among the four postures, lying down belongs to the side of indolence, while standing and walking belong to the side of agitation, sitting—
However, because it belongs to the side of non-languor and non-agitation, and because the posture is peaceful, it is said "having sat down";
the meaning is: having folded the legs crosswise so that the thighs are bound together on all sides.
To show the manner in which the sitting becomes comfortable for one who sits, it is said "having set the body straight"; that is, having established the upper part of the body upright.
The meaning is: having set the eighteen vertebrae edge-to-edge. For when one is seated in this way, the skin, flesh, and sinews do not sag;
thus, those pains that would otherwise arise moment by moment due to their sagging do not arise.
When they do not arise, the mind becomes one-pointed and the meditation subject does not fall away. Then...
And it attains growth, increase, and expansion through successive stages of distinction. Now, showing the method for grasping the object, he said:
"having placed mindfulness before the face" (*katvā parimukhaṃ satiṃ*); the meaning is: having established mindfulness directed toward the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
For here the prefix *pari-* has the same sense as the prefix *abhi-*, or else, by means of the prefix *pari-* in the sense of proximity, [it refers to] the face.
The meaning is: "having established mindfulness in close proximity. As it is said: "This mindfulness is established, well-established, at the tip of the nose or on the sign of the mouth.
Therefore it is called: 'having established mindfulness facing the opening' (parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā). Alternatively: "‘Parī’ has the sense of encompassing;
‘mukhaṃ’ has the sense of an outlet; ‘sati’ has the sense of establishing. Therefore it is called ‘parimukhaṃ’."
Because of the word "sati" (mindfulness), the prefix *pari-* in words such as *pariṇāyikā* (leader) has the sense of "encompassing" (*pariggaha*).

Because of the word *mukha* in phrases such as *suññatavimokkhamukha* (the door to the liberation of emptiness), it has the sense of "exit" (*niyyāna*). Thus, having established mindfulness that encompasses the exit, it is said:
"having established mindfulness and circumspection in every way, which is grasped without confusion and abandoned confusion."

853–5. "Having seen the danger in sensual pleasures" means having reflected upon the danger in both objective sensual pleasures (*vatthukāma*) and defilement-sensual pleasures (*kilesakāma*) by way of such passages as, "These sensual pleasures are like a skeleton of bones, insofar as they are devoid of sustenance.

"Having seen renunciation as security" means having seen renunciation as secure, [thinking]: "Renunciation is the escape from sensual pleasures; renunciation is the means for transcending all suffering. Thus...
"Renunciation" refers to the meditative absorption (jhāna) together with its preliminary stages, Nibbāna, and insight (vipassanā);
or, having seen all wholesome states as secure and fearless, one becomes one who has conceived a longing for them—this is what is meant. "Supreme...
[the Triple Gem]" means that by recollecting the qualities of the Triple Gem—the Buddha and the others—one generates powerful rapture and gladness. "A partaker... [and so forth].

"Having released" means: "By means of this practice of renunciation followed by all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and noble disciples, I shall certainly and entirely partake in, and become a recipient of, the bliss born of seclusion of mind and so forth"—thus, by seeing the benefit in the practice, one exerts the highest and greatest effort toward that object. By way of manner...
"By an even [gaze]" means by a mode of looking that is neither too wide-open nor too dim, which is termed "neither too wide-open nor too dim.
For if one looks with eyes too wide open, the eye becomes fatigued as if one were staring intently at an extremely subtle and indistinct form;
and because it reveals its own inherent nature, the circle [of the eye] becomes overly prominent. Likewise...
If one attends to it according to its color or its characteristic marks, the sign does not arise for him.
Furthermore, for one who opens the eyes too little, the visual object appears indistinctly, as if looking with the "elephant's gaze" (gajanimīlaka).
Due to this slackness of effort in seeing, the mind falls into lethargy and becomes sluggish; thus, in this way too, the sign does not arise. Therefore, just as on the surface of a mirror...
When grasping the sign of the face, one does not open the eyes too widely there, nor too narrowly; rather, one grasps it with an even manner.
In the same way, it should be developed by grasping with an even manner, such as not opening [the eyes] too widely and so forth.
"Grasping the sign" means grasping with the mind the sign perceived by the eye in the earth-kasiṇa.
856–7. Now, in order to show the method for grasping the sign (*nimitta*), it is said: "The color should not be looked at," and so forth.

"The color should not be looked at" means that the dawn-like color present there in the earth-kasiṇa (*pathavīkasiṇa*) should not be contemplated; for if one attends to it by way of its color, it becomes a color-kasiṇa (*vaṇṇakasiṇa*).
Furthermore, what has already been grasped by visual consciousness cannot [be grasped again].

To prevent [misunderstanding], it is not said here "it should not be looked at," but rather—as in the cases of "it is to be examined by the mind" and so forth—the term "examining" (pekkhana) is used in the sense of mental reflection. Regarding the phrase "the characteristic is not to be seen":

that which is the characteristic of hardness of the earth element there should not be brought to mind; for if that were brought to mind, the meditation subject of the elements (dhātu-kammaṭṭhāna) would be lost.
"Because it is grasped. "But without abandoning the color" means that because it must be grasped after having been seen, one does not abandon the color.

For, by way of its predominance (*ussada*), the mind [is directed] toward a conceptual phenomenon (*paṇṇatti-dhamma*); thus, due to the excess of the earth-element's functional capacity, the conventional designation "earth" is applied to the earth together with its constituent parts (*sasambhāra-pathavī*).

Toward that conceptual phenomenon designated in dependence upon the earth together with its constituent parts—just as the reflection of a face appears on the surface of a mirror—[the mind is directed].
Having fixed the mind as if it were [an object]... "With one-pointed mind" means that, not allowing the mind to scatter again toward various objects, one becomes single-minded.

Regarding the phrase "saying 'earth, earth' thus," the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla stated that at the time of the first attention (*paṭhamasamannāhāra*), there might even be some vocal expression (*vacībhedo*).
858. If the mind is to be established in mere conventional usage, let it be that the earth should be brought to mind by way of its synonyms;
what fault is there? Showing this, he said, "The earth, the ground," and so forth. Alternatively, does meditation occur only when the name "earth" is stated, or even when another term is used?
To answer this, he said, "The earth, the ground," and so forth. It is also permissible to recite only one [synonym].
Among these, it is permissible to choose whichever one comes to one through its own familiarity or abundance and speak of that alone.
Although this is indeed permissible, nevertheless, because the name "earth" (pathavī) is the most well-known,
the teachers maintain that it should be developed as "earth, earth" precisely according to what is most familiar.

859–60. “Having opened [the eyes]... pe... for so long”: this means that for as long as the learning sign (*uggahanimitta*) has not arisen in the manner about to be described, one should open the eyes for a short time, look at the circle of earth by way of grasping the sign, and then close the eyes again for a short time;
in this way, even for a hundred times, a thousand times, or more than that.
"Having opened [his eyes], that yogi should advert": the meaning is that he should direct his attention to it in the same manner as it was perceived when looking at it. 861–3.
"But it comes into the range of vision": the construction is that if it enters the domain of the javanas of the mind-door, then that acquired sign (uggaha-nimitta) is said to have arisen.
If, even regarding the acquired sign, there is a disk of earth...

If one develops [the meditation] without looking, the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*) will not arise. And because it is impossible not to look in the sense of being close [to the object], it is said:
"One should not sit," and so forth. The connection is: "by one sitting as is convenient, or by one developing [it] as is convenient.
864–5. Regarding "prolixity... washing": elsewhere than the place where one is sitting due to some necessity such as urination, etc.
When one has gone out and returned to sit down again, the feet must be washed. For if one steps onto the lodging with unwashed feet, there is an offense;
and if one were to wash the feet at every single moment, it would be a source of excessive trouble. Therefore, for the sake of avoiding that, two sandals should be desired.
Even if they have many soles, they might still produce sound, and sound is a thorn to meditative absorption (*jhāna*).
Therefore it is said, "having a single floor. Likewise, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "And a walking staff (kattaradaṇḍa) should be desired for the purpose of warding off dangers.
"By some unsuitable thing" means by any one of the unsuitable things to be mentioned later among the unsuitable conditions such as the dwelling place (*āvāsa*).
"That place" refers to the location where the kasiṇa-maṇḍala is situated. "Taking that, he purifies it" means [he purifies it] according to its original state.
"Having grasped the learning-sign again" means having produced it again.
"Seated comfortably on a chair" means having returned to one's dwelling place and being seated comfortably on a chair according to the prescribed method.
"Should be developed" means that sign should be increased by means of attention. "Should be brought to mind" means correctly...

It should be brought to mind or properly recollected. "Struck by reasoning" means that the meditation subject should be struck and repeatedly beaten by right intention—associated with the mind of development—which, under the name "reasoning" (takkā), functions through the activity of striking and beating as it proceeds again and again;
for when attention has attained strength, its frequent application [is required].
The meaning is "it should be set in motion.
"He desires that" means he desires to attend to that sign. "Doing thus" means doing the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) in such a way as to strike it with reasoning.
It refers to one who applies himself in such a manner that the development brings about successive stages of distinction.
When, however, one practices in this way and the faculties such as faith become very clear and sharp, then— due to the distancing of states such as lack of faith—

the factors of jhāna belonging to the sense-sphere, such as applied thought (*vitakka*), manifest in great numbers, supported by the seven powers that have attained exceptional strength. And from that, those [factors] which are the direct opposites of them...
Sensual desire and the other [hindrances], together with the evil states associated with them, become distant. Therefore it is said: "They are suppressed...

even the five hindrances. "The meditator becomes concentrated...": by means of the access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) that has arisen in that meditator by taking the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) as its object, both the mind and the counterpart sign become concentrated through the access jhāna. The counterpart sign also...
It arises because access concentration (upacāra-jjhāna) cannot exist without it.
871–4. "Of this" refers to the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta). "Of the former" refers to the learning sign (uggaha-nimitta). "From the bag" means from the bag for the mirror.
"Like a crane near water" means like a crane near a cloud; for she is exceedingly pure due to the blueness of the cloud.

When it appears, then "it appears to him"—this is the connection. Thus, by means of the similes such as the surface of a mirror, he shows that the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) is much more purified and subtle than the learning sign (uggaha-nimitta). Therefore he said, "even more than that.
In the learning sign, defects of the kasiṇa such as finger-marks, footprints, handprints, and so forth, are apparent; but this [counterpart sign], according to the method already stated...
The meaning is that it appears even a hundredfold and a thousandfold more purified than that.
The phrase "possessing a subtle shape" and so forth is stated because it lacks a substantial (ultimate) nature.

For if it were such [as those things], it would be cognizable by the eye, gross, accessible to comprehension, and subject to the three characteristics; however, it is not like that. But if this [consciousness] does not possess shape and so forth, [how can it be seen?]

To the question, "In what way is it the object of jhāna?", he said: "The manifestation... [etc.]... for us. Therein, "produced by wisdom" (*paññaja*) means produced by the wisdom consisting in development;
what is meant is that it is merely the act of perceiving by means of the wisdom of development. For there is no arising from anywhere of a dharma that lacks intrinsic nature (*asabhāva*).
Therefore he said: "It is merely the mode of manifestation consisting in development," belonging solely to one who has attained concentration.

The meaning is that, through the power of a specific mode of meditation, there arises by means of that very meditation a mere appearance consisting of that [object], produced by the excellence of that meditation.
(875–8) The intention is that once [the hindrances] have been suppressed and settled, no further effort need be made for that purpose.
For as soon as the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*) arises, access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*) directed toward it suppresses the hindrances.
It arises. "The defilements have subsided" means that the remaining defilements associated with them have settled properly;
the meaning is that they have been stilled. When "access concentration" (*upacāra-samādhi*) is mentioned, it follows by implication that there is another kind of concentration as well;
to show this, the passage beginning with "but by two aspects" was stated. "By two aspects" refers to the distancing from the opposites of the factors of jhāna.

These two reasons are: [the attainment of stability] and the attainment of the state of being firm. Now, in order to demonstrate those reasons by way of the stages of concentration (*samādhi*), it is said:
"At the moment of access," and so forth. "At the moment of access" means on the plane of access, in the stage of access.

"In the acquisition of that" means in the stage of attainment (*adhigama-avasthā*), which is the acquisition of that absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*) for the sake of which one has practiced this path.
To explain how one attains concentration on the level of access (*upacāra-bhūmi*) and how one does so on the level of absorption (*appanā-bhūmi*), he says:

"By the abandoning of the hindrances," and so forth. At the moment of access, although the factors of jhāna (*jhānaṅga*) are not yet more distinct or have reached a state of loftiness (*mahaggata-bhāva*), the mind is concentrated through the suppression (*vikkhambhana*) of those states that are their opposites; this is also the case at the stage of attainment (*paṭilābha-bhūmi*) regarding those [factors] that have reached absorption.
The meaning is that concentration is attained through the manifestation of the jhāna factors.
879–80. Regarding the phrase "the factors... nor yet": at the moment of access (upacāra), the factors are neither firm nor have they reached the power of full development;
this is the meaning. "Appanāya" means at the moment of absorption (appanā). "Therefore" means because the factors arise as firm.
Therefore, regarding the statement that "the absorption consciousness (appanā-citta) continues even for a day": just as a strong man might stand up from his seat and remain standing for a whole day,
even so, when absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi) has arisen, the jhāna-consciousness— having once interrupted the flow of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga)—
continues for the entire night or day solely by way of a succession of wholesome impulsion-moments (kusalajavana).

The meaning is as follows: By stating that "it can continue for even a whole day once absorption is reached," it is shown that this is not the case during the moment of access concentration (*upacāra*).

For in that stage, because the factors [of absorption] have not yet fully arisen, just as a young child, when picked up and set standing, falls back to the ground again and again, so too the mind at times takes the sign as its object and at times sinks back into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).

"By that very same cross-legged posture" means: by means of that very cross-legged posture—in its capacity as an instrument (*karaṇa*) or as a cause (*hetu*)—having expanded that sign (*nimitta*) which he attained while sitting.
For the expansion of the sign is appropriate on the level of access concentration (*upacāra-bhūmi*).
"Like the womb of a wheel-turning monarch" means like the womb of one possessing merit who is destined to become a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*). Decline (*parihāni*).
"There is no loss" means that for one who has attained access concentration (*laddhūpacārajjhāna*), there is no falling away.

For as long as the sign (*nimitta*) is not lost, the jhāna having that as its object remains unlost; however, when the sign is destroyed through a lack of protection, even the jhāna already attained perishes, because its existence is dependent upon it.
Therefore he said, "In protecting," and so forth.
885. "Abode" (āvāsa): That abode where, for one dwelling there, a sign that has not yet arisen does not arise, or one that has arisen perishes;
where mindfulness that has not been established does not become established, and an unconcentrated mind does not become concentrated—this is an unsuitable abode.
Therefore, when there are many dwellings in a monastery, one should [examine] three [qualities] in each one.
Having stayed for three days, one should abandon that place where the mind is not one-pointed and dwell instead in its opposite.
"Gocara" means a village for alms; it is unsuitable if it is too far from or too near to the lodging, or if it is located in the eastern or western direction where alms are difficult to obtain.
"Bhassa" refers to unsuitable talk included within the thirty-two types of frivolous conversation.
For that [sign] leads to the disappearance of the sign. "A person" refers to one who indulges in frivolous talk, a person devoid of virtues such as moral discipline;
one by relying upon whom the unconcentrated mind does not become concentrated, or the concentrated mind does not become firm—such a person.
For he makes it turbid, just as muddy water makes clear water turbid. "Food."

However, sour food may be unsuitable for one person, while sweet food is unsuitable for another. Likewise, a cool temperature may be unsuitable for one, while a warm temperature is unsuitable for another.
Therefore, whatever food or temperature does not provide comfort to one who partakes of it, that food and that temperature are unsuitable.
As for the posture: among standing, walking, and so forth, whichever is conducive to the concentration of this person whose mind is unconcentrated—

If a certain posture does not conduce to the stability of the concentrated mind, this is an unsuitable posture; therefore, one should examine it for three days—just as one would an abode—and then avoid it.
"One should resort to the seven suitable things" means that, by way of the opposite of what was stated above, one should resort to the seven things beginning with a suitable abode.
In this context, "suitable for talk" refers to that which is based on the ten bases of discourse; even that should be spoken in moderation.

"Practicing in this way" means practicing by avoiding the seven unsuitable things and cultivating the seven suitable things in the manner described, for one who is abundant in the cultivation of the signs.
