...is called "shifting of the object" (*ārammaṇasaṅkantikatā*). This refers to the attainment of each individual kasiṇa among all the kasiṇas.
Having attained the first jhāna in the earth kasiṇa, the second in the water kasiṇa, the third in the fire kasiṇa, and the fourth in the air kasiṇa;
then, having removed the blue kasiṇa, the base of infinite space; from the yellow kasiṇa, the base of infinite consciousness; from the red kasiṇa...

The base of nothingness [arises] from the white kasiṇa, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception [arises] from that; thus, the surmounting of both the factors and the objects is called the "transition of factors and objects.
Having defined the first jhāna as five-factored, one defines the second as four-factored and the third as three-factored.
The fourth [jhāna] has two factors: the base of infinite space... pe ...the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Thus, the defining of merely the jhāna factors is called "defining the factors. Likewise, the defining of merely the object, such as "this is the earth-kasiṇa" or "this is the water-kasiṇa," is called "defining the object. There is also the defining of both the factors and the object.
"Some maintain" means that because this is not mentioned in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), it certainly cannot be that bliss of meditation (*bhāvanāsukha*).
However, among those who have attained the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*), only one in a hundred or a thousand is able to tame the mind by means of these fourteen modes.
"Tamed" means tamed by means of the fourteen modes. "Concentrated" means concentrated by means of the concentration of the fourth jhāna.

"Pure" (*suddha*) means either by way of the removal of hindrances, or by way of the presence of the purity of mindfulness accomplished through the equanimity that is neither concerned with nor opposed to [the object].

"Utterly purified" (*pariyodāta*) means utterly purified precisely because of its stainlessness, like gold that has been polished; it is said to be "luminous. Alternatively, [it may be explained as follows:]
"Pure" means it is so stated by virtue of being free from the agitation of applied and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*).

"Without blemish" refers to those conditions for the attainment of jhāna—such as the thoughts occurring in the manner of, "One endowed with concentration like mine ought to be such as this," or "Oh, would that the Teacher himself were to teach the Dhamma to the monks after repeatedly questioning me! and so forth.
"Free from blemish" (anaṅgaṇe) means by virtue of the absence of evil desires and their range.

"Undefiled" (anupakkilese) means that because of the departure of those things called defilements (upakkilesa)—namely, lust and so forth in the sense of being defiled by approaching [an object]—or because of the removal of the mental defilements mentioned in such passages as, "Covetousness is a defilement of the mind; ill-will, anger...
and so on, it is "free from defilement. "Become pliant" (mudubhūte) means by way of bringing about a state of proficiency.
"Because it is well-developed, it has become pliant"—this means it has attained mastery (*vasibhāva*).
For a mind that has attained mastery is called "pliant," just as leather that has been thoroughly rubbed down or lac that has been well-processed is said to be pliant.

"Wieldy" (*kammanīya*) means, precisely because of its pliancy, that through its attainment of the state of the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), it is capable of action; that is to say, it is fit for the performance of psychic powers such as transformation (*vikubbanā*), and so forth.
It becomes pliant. For a mind that has become pliant is capable of action, like well-refined gold;

and both of these states arise precisely because of its being well-developed. As it is said: "Bhikkhus, I do not see even a single other thing that, when developed and cultivated in this way, becomes so pliant and workable as the mind, bhikkhus."
"Steadfast" (*ṭhita*) means established immovably among these qualities such as purity; or it means established having discerned a state of excellence through the perfection of cultivation.
"Unshakable" (*acala*) means unshakeable precisely because of that steadfastness; what is meant is that it has reached imperturbability (*āneñjappatta*).

Alternatively, it is "steadfast" because it remains under its own control through softness and wieldiness; it is "unshakable" because, being embraced by faith and the other [faculties], it cannot be shaken by lack of faith and the like.
Regarding the phrase "endowed with eight factors": by not taking stability and immovability separately, "concentrated" (*samāhita*) is treated as a single factor.
However, when those two are taken separately, since qualities such as "perfectly purified" constitute factors of the concentrated mind, one does not include "concentrated" as a factor;
rather, it is the state of being endowed with the eight factors beginning with "perfectly purified."
It should be understood. "For the modes of supernormal power" (*iddhividhā*) means for the sake of the categories of supernormal power, or for the classification of supernormal power.

In terms of its meaning, however, the "modes of supernormal power" refers to the knowledge of direct higher knowledge (*abhiññāñāṇa*) which serves as the condition for various manifestations, such as one person becoming many.

"He directs" (*abhinīharati*) means that for the sake of attaining direct higher knowledge, he withdraws the preliminary-work mind from the kasiṇa object and sends it toward direct higher knowledge. "Supernormal transformation" (*iddhivikubbaṇaṃ*)...
Here, it is called *iddhi* because it succeeds (*ijjhati*); that is to say, it is accomplished and obtained.
For whatever is accomplished and obtained is said to "succeed. As it has been said:
"If one who desires sensual pleasures succeeds in that... and so forth.

The transformation by means of supernormal power (*iddhi*)—the act of abandoning one's natural appearance—is "transformational supernormal power" (*iddhivikubbana*). This is stated because this [power] is the predominant factor among the various types of supernormal powers (*iddhi*).

Alternatively, it is "transformational supernormal power" in the sense that it is both supernormal power and transformation. The separate mention [of these two] should also be understood for the very reason already stated.
1052–4. To show the method by which that [attainment] is to be accomplished, it is said: “the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge,” and so forth. Herein, some say:
“Having entered the four jhānas in succession and having emerged from the fourth jhāna”; but that is incorrect.
For the taming of the mind is for the purpose of entering [jhānas] according to one’s wish; thus, it is the fourth jhāna itself [that serves as the basis].

And it is based on the [fourth] jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), not the others. Regarding "a hundred... pe ... a mind": if one desires a hundred, one forms the preliminary mind (*parikamma-mānasa*) by thinking, "May I become a hundred, may I become a hundred";
if one desires a thousand, one does so by thinking, "May I become a thousand, may I become a thousand.

"Preliminary mind" refers to the sense-sphere consciousness (*kāmāvacara-citta*) that arises after emerging from the foundational jhāna (*pādaka-jjhāna*), proceeding with the thought, "May I become a hundred," and so forth.
And the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā-pādaka-jjhāna*). "Direct knowledge" (*abhiññā*)... [etc. ...

Here, the initial attainment of the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge is for the purpose of stabilizing the preliminary consciousness (*parikamma-citta*); the subsequent attainment is for the purpose of seizing the peak of power of the determining consciousness (*adhiṭṭhāna-citta*). "He determines" (*adhiṭṭhāti*):
having adverted to the object with the mind, immediately after that, following the three or four preceding access-consciousnesses (*pubbabhāga-citta*), [he determines].
"Resolution" (adhiṭṭhāna) is so named because it is the act of resolving by means of the knowledge of direct higher power (abhiññāñāṇa) through the determination of what has arisen;
the meaning is that one brings about certainty. For in all contexts, "resolution" refers to the knowledge of direct higher power.

1055–7. "With the counterpart sign as object" means having the counterpart sign as its objective support. Here, the preliminary (parikamma) stages have various objects, whereas the stages of mental absorption (satārammaṇikāni) have a single object.

Herein, among these preliminary exercises (parikamma) and resolutions (adhiṭṭhāna), the preliminary mental states—which are sense-sphere consciousnesses occurring with the thought "May I be hundredfold," having a hundred as their object—become objects of a hundred for each individual consciousness because they proceed individually with the thought "May I be hundredfold.
The same method applies to the objects of a thousand and so forth. "And the consciousness of that resolution" refers to that [consciousness] of the hundredfold and so on.
There is also the mind of resolve (*adhiṭṭhānacitta*). Furthermore, their state of being a hundredfold is by way of color, not by way of the designation of a "being" (*sattapaññatti*).
For while form may be displayed as a hundred or a thousand, it is not the designation that is so displayed.

And here, if one produces a hundred [images] of blue color alone, then even though there is diversity in the color due to its various successions, each one is a single unit because of its unity as "blue."
All the preliminary consciousnesses take as their object [the sign] appearing entirely blue.

However, if there is a multiplicity of preliminary consciousnesses with various colors and various functions, each one takes as its object a single color and a specific function within those various colors.
But the consciousness of resolution takes as its object the commonality of the color.
Even after taking up the preliminary object, it produces one possessing various colors because the domain of supernormal power (iddhi) possesses inconceivable potency.

The inclusion of the word "like" (*viya*)—as in "like the absorption consciousness" (*appanācitta*)—is stated because of the similarity between the direct-knowledge consciousness (*abhiññācitta*) and the jhāna consciousness at the moment of their first arising, not because that [direct-knowledge consciousness] itself constitutes absorption.
For that very reason, it is distinguished by the inclusion mentioned previously.
"Accompanied by the fourth jhāna" means possessing the fine-material-sphere (rūpāvacara) fourth jhāna; it is associated with that. If this is so, one might ask:
"What is the distinction between the fourth jhāna and this [state]? To this he says: "The distinction lies in the preliminary work (parikamma).

For here there is no other distinction apart from the distinction in the preliminary work. By the inclusion of the term "grasping," the three or four impulsion-moments (javana) occurring in the stage prior to absorption (appanā) are also included.

Or, by including what was not previously mentioned, the preliminary (parikamma), access (upacāra), and conformity (anuloma) stages, the final one being called "change-of-lineage" (gotrabhū), and so forth, are all the same as the rest.
Therefore it is said: "The rest here is the same as before. This concludes the commentary on the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power (iddhividha-ñāṇa).
1058. The divine ear (dibbasota): [It is] that of deities, which—unobstructed by bile, phlegm, and so forth—is capable of apprehending objects even at a distance.
It is "divine" (dibba) because it is equal to the divine ear-faculty, because it is obtained by way of the divine abiding, and because it itself is supported by the divine abiding;
it is "ear" (sota) in the sense of hearing and because it performs the function of the ear, being similar to it.
"This" (idaṃ) means that which was mentioned in the summary as "the divine eye and ear"—that is the meaning of "this."
1059–64. Because one first adverts to a gross sound and afterwards to a subtle sound, he says, "both gross and subtle.

Indeed, for the purpose of gaining proficiency, one should first, in the forest, beginning with the sounds of lions and so forth, advert to all sounds in their proper sequence starting from the gross and proceeding to the subtle; likewise in the eastern direction and so on.
In all directions, one should attend to the sign of sound (saddanimitta) of both gross and subtle sounds.
Those sounds become evident even to his natural mind, but they are especially evident to his preliminary-work mind (parikammacitta).
"Of him" means of that yogi. "The sign of sound" refers to the aforementioned sign of either a gross or a subtle sound.

"Taking up each [sound] in turn" means the coarse and subtle forms that are being apprehended. "Directing the mind" means directing the mind with the preliminary (parikamma) consciousness, thinking: "In this direction, this sound is coarse or subtle.
"Among sounds" means among those sounds—whether coarse or subtle—which have become the objects of the preliminary consciousness. "One or another" refers to whichever [sound] it may be.
Frequent attention proceeds by way of performing the preliminary work (*parikamma*); that is one sound.

If even the consciousness of direct knowledge (*abhiññā-citta*) takes as its object only that very same object grasped by the preliminary work, then what is the distinction between that [consciousness] and this [preliminary consciousness]? It is said:
the preliminary consciousness grasps the mere sound because it grasps what has not been heard before, whereas the consciousness of direct knowledge [grasps it] even though it has not been heard.
"Grasping by way of hearing" means that one grasps [the object] precisely because it serves as a condition for the awakening to the meaning through the act of grasping;
this is the distinction between these two. "Skilled in what has been heard" means expert in the scriptures (*pariyatti*).

1065–6. "Firmly established" means having attained firmness; the sense is that it has reached a state of strength. That which is to be increased is the object of the foundational meditative absorption (*pādakajjhāna*).
"How much? he asks, and replies with "That which has entered within this," and so forth.
For when one enters the foundational jhāna while attending to the kasiṇa sign as its object, thinking, "May it pervade this much space," the kasiṇa sign remains pervading that much space.
Having emerged from that attainment, even without entering the foundational jhāna again, [he can still direct his mind].
Even though there are many varieties of sound, he adverts to them because of his well-developed meditation.

Therein, immediately after the adverting consciousness has arisen directed toward any particular sound, four or five impulsion moments arise; among these, the last is the supernormal power consciousness (*iddhicitta*).
Thus, having adverted to as much of the sound as he desires that has reached him, by means of the knowledge of direct higher knowledge (*abhiññāñāṇa*)—
He knows. However, by one who has not thus expanded the kasiṇa-sign, the basic jhāna must indeed be attained once again.
For he hears that sound occurring at that place only after attaining the basic jhāna, emerging from it, and then hearing with an abhiññā consciousness.

It is for this very reason that it is said: "It is said with reservation: '...he hears by means of the object of the basic [jhāna]... One who possesses the power of supernormal success (iddhividha-lābhī)...
However, unlike those who have attained the remaining higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), this [iddhi] is not accomplished by merely taking existing sounds and so forth as its object;

rather, because it involves the creation of adventitious forms, one must enter the foundational jhāna twice in every respect before accomplishing it. Furthermore, the mention here of "one or two finger-breadths" is made with reference to subtle sounds.
"Listening": having thus delimited [the sounds] again and again through hearing, one becomes an adept (abhiññā) who has mastered them;

then, listening to what is emitted, one hears it. "Even individually": even when sounds such as those of conchs, kettledrums, and small drums arise together from all quarters up to the Brahma-world, making a single tumultuous noise, one desires to define each one separately according to its specific source.
When it exists, one is indeed able to discern each sound individually, thinking, "This is the sound of a conch, this is the sound of a drum, this is the sound of a small drum," and so forth.
This concludes the commentary on the knowledge of the divine ear (dibbasotañāṇa). 1069–73.
Regarding *cetopariya*: it is called *pariya* because it goes to the mind; it knows by delimiting [the state of mind] through such factors as being with lust (*sarāga*), and so forth.
Meaning. For those verbal roots whose meaning is "going," their meaning is also "understanding. *Cetopariya* means "belonging to the mind" (*cetaso pariyam*).

That which exists in the mind is "mental" (*mānasam*), which is to say, knowledge (*ñāṇa*). Since it is both the "pervading of the mind" (*cetopariya*) and "mental" (*mānasa*), it is called "knowledge of the pervading of minds" (*cetopariya-mānasa*).
"By means of the divine eye alone" means by means of the divine eye as its decisive support (*upanissaya*); for that [divine eye] is the preliminary work (*parikamma*) for its arising.
Therefore, because this [knowledge] proceeds by means of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*) alone, it is said "therefore.

The connection is: "having seen with the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhuñāṇa*), which has received the conventional designation 'divine eye' due to its similarity to the divine [eye] and other such qualities.

"The heart" (*hadaya*) does not refer to the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*), but rather to the lump of heart-flesh (*hadayamaṃsapesi*), which is externally shaped like a lotus bud and internally resembles the fruit of the *kosātakī* plant.
It is so called because the blood now being described rests supported by it.
The heart-base, however, functions supported by this blood. "Having seen the blood" means having seen the color of the blood;
for even with the divine eye, only color is seen. For that very reason, because it resembles the [physical] eye, it is called "the eye. "Of another" means...
[It is] of another. For just as that which is not another is the self (attā), so too that which is not the self is another.
But how can the mind of another be known by seeing the color of blood with the divine eye? To this he says: "Endowed with joy," and so forth.
"Blood" means red, having a color like that of the *nigrodha* fruit. "Black" means having a color like the *jambu* fruit. "Resembling sesame oil" [is the description of its clarity].
By this, he expresses the state of being serene.
But how is it that when the mind is accompanied by joy and so forth, the blood born of karma (kammaja) attains various colors?
Although the primary elements (bhūta) supported by the heart-base (hadayavatthu) are indeed born of karma, that blood itself is exclusively born of karma.
There is no fourfold continuity of matter (*catusantatirūpa*) there either, because it is not found there. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:

"Having seen the color of another's heart-blood, one discerns: 'This matter is originated by the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*), this is originated by the faculty of grief (*domanassindriya*), and this is originated by the faculty of equanimity (*upekkhindriya*).
Thus, even in that case, whatever is not mind-born (*acittaja*)..."

Is it not the case that there should be no occurrence according to the aforementioned classification of colors? It must be so, because the remaining material phenomena of the continuity follow along with them.

For just as, in the case of walking and other such activities, mind-born material phenomena are followed by temperature-born, kamma-born, and nutriment-born material phenomena—otherwise, the body’s arrival at another location would not even be possible—so too here, the mind-born material phenomenon is followed by the remaining material phenomena of the continuity.
It follows accordingly; and at times of faith or anger, it should be understood that the very occurrence of a change in the color of the eye is the illustration of that meaning.
Therefore, it is well said: "The blood may be red," and so forth. Having seen the blood of the heart...
First, having seen the blood by means of inferential knowledge (*anumāṇañāṇa*), one should resolve: "It must be made to reach strength. It must be made to attain the state of strength.

For a yogi wishing to arouse the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) must, while being a possessor of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), first—according to the method explained below—make the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) endowed with the eight factors and capable of being directed toward its goal, and then increase the light.
By means of the divine eye, through seeing the color of the blood existing in dependence upon the flesh-muscle of another’s heart,
one determines that person’s mind— by way of grasping the method— as being "accompanied by joy," or "accompanied by grief," or "accompanied by equanimity";
then, having entered the foundational jhāna and emerged from it, [one contemplates] "this person’s mind..."

One should perform the preliminary work [with the thought], "I know. Having repeatedly entered and emerged from the foundational jhāna for a hundred times or a thousand times, one should proceed in that very same way.

As he proceeds in this manner by means of the divine eye through the method of seeing the color of the blood in the heart and so forth, there arises at that time the determination: "Now, the knowledge of penetration of minds will arise. This is what is established as occurring then.
Taking that mind as its object, mind-door adverting consciousness arises, followed by three or four sense-sphere impulsion moments.
The fourth or fifth moment is the superknowledge-consciousness (abhiññā-citta) belonging to the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara).

In this context, the knowledge associated with that absorption-consciousness (appanā-citta) is the knowledge of penetration of others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa). For it is there [in that state] by means of this [knowledge]—
Once the preliminary work has been done, that [knowledge] proceeds by penetrating and distinguishing another's mind directly,
just as the knowledge of the divine eye perceives visible form and the knowledge of the divine ear perceives sound. Beyond that, however,
there occurs the determination of sensual-sphere consciousnesses as "with lust" and so forth, just as there is the determination of colors such as blue and so on.
1074–5. Furthermore, the method for stabilizing this knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) once it has been attained is exactly like the method for its attainment;
that very [method] has been shown here by the Teacher. The passage beginning with "When thus stabilized" and so forth demonstrates the benefits of stabilization.

The phrase "all of it indeed" should be connected with both terms—"sense-sphere consciousness" and "the mind in the fine-material and immaterial realms"—referring to the fifty-fourfold [consciousness].

The meaning is that it understands each and every instance—namely, sense-sphere consciousness, the fifteen fine-material-sphere consciousnesses, and the twelve immaterial-sphere consciousnesses—according to their individual classifications such as "with lust" and so forth.
This discussion of direct knowledge (abhiññā) is given from the perspective of an ordinary person (puthujjana);

therefore, supramundane consciousness is not mentioned here. For even that [supramundane consciousness] is understood by a higher noble one, or by a similar noble one, regarding a lower or a similar [consciousness].
Furthermore, one knows the mind of an equal or inferior level, but an inferior person does not know the mind of a superior one.
Just as this is so, likewise a worldling who has not formed a mental resolve regarding the immaterial-sphere jhāna, or even a trainee (sekha), does not know an immaterial-sphere mind.

However, by way of one who possesses the eight attainments, the knowledge of the immaterial-sphere mind is stated here. An Arahant, moreover, even without having formed a mental resolve regarding the immaterial realm—
Because the ignorance that conceals those [past lives] has been destroyed, he knows them as well. This concludes the commentary on the knowledge of penetration of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa).

1076–7. "Former abodes" (pubbenivāsa) refers to the dwellings lived in previous past births, which occurred within one's own continuum and were experienced through the cultivation of objects by means of one's own and others' consciousnesses.
For even those aggregates experienced by the consciousness of others have indeed been dwelt in previously.
"Herein": "past lives" (pubbenivāsa) is what is meant. However, those [recollections] such as the recollection of the breaking of the cycle of rebirth (vaṭumaka) are the domain of the Buddhas alone.

Knowledge that reveals past lives in their specific forms is "knowledge of past lives" (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa). "By that": by means of that knowledge. "Recollection of them" (tadanussati): the recollection of those past lives.
In the three lower jhānas, the body and mind are [suffused] with joy and bliss respectively, as appropriate.

He said, "The four jhānas should be attained for the sake of consolidation," beginning with the words "But as for the jhānas. Otherwise, it might have been stated that one should attain only the foundational jhāna.
The sitting posture in which one begins the recollection while seated is the very last sitting posture mentioned here.
1078–80. From that time onwards... [etc. ... "in due order" means that everything done in previous births and so forth in that existence is included;
thus it shows, individually by way of day and night and so on, that "everything should be brought to mind," and so forth.
"Done during the day or at night" refers to the sequence in reverse order, beginning from the very last sitting down—namely, the arranging of the seat and the entering of the lodging.

One should review all that was done during the entire day and night. "What is to be reviewed? means that whatever task was performed in the interval between those times, all of that is to be reviewed in reverse order.

This much is evident even to the ordinary mind, but it is especially evident to the preliminary-work mind (*parikamma-citta*). However, if anything therein is not evident, [one should review it again].
Again, having entered the foundational jhāna and emerged from it, one should advert [to the object];
by this much, it becomes as clear as a lamp when lit. For entering the foundational jhāna is like a whetstone for a knife; it brings about the sharpening of mindfulness and wisdom.
Therefore, through that entry, these two reach the highest degree of refinement. In the former...
"Becoming" means [arising] in the preceding existence immediately after this present existence.
"Name-and-form that has been produced" means name-and-form produced by its own conditions. "Well" means it should be adverted to thoroughly and without omission;
for a bhikkhu who has performed the preliminary work for this direct knowledge is able [to accomplish it] at the very first attempt.
Having dispelled the rebirth-linking [consciousness], one must make name-and-form the object at the moment of death;
even if one is unable to do so, one should not abandon the task but should repeatedly attain the foundational jhāna itself, and having emerged from it, one should advert to it again and again.
And while adverting, one should first advert to form and afterwards to name.
"It should be adverted to" (āvajjitabbaṃ), so say the teachers. Others, however, speak in the opposite way.

In this regard, the knowledge that occurs by taking as its object everything from the time of one's last sitting until the moment of rebirth-linking does not count as the "knowledge of recollecting past lives" (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa), because it lacks the quality of having phenomena from previously lived births as its object; rather, that is merely preparatory knowledge (parikammañāṇa).

But when, having passed beyond the moment of rebirth-linking, mind-door adverting arises taking as its object the name-and-form that arose at the moment of death, and when that [adverting] has ceased, absorption consciousness arises in the manner already described;
the knowledge associated with that is called "knowledge of recollection of past lives. Therefore he said, "But when... and so forth.

Here it is asked: Does the single consciousness of direct knowledge (abhiññā-citta) take all the mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa) occurring at the moment of death as its object, or does it do so by means of different [moments of] consciousness?
What follows from this? If it is by one alone, then there is a discernment in an indistinct form, like that of someone looking at a cloth from a distance.
And if it is by different [moments], then there must be separate attainments of the foundational jhānas and so forth.

"Is it necessary [to do so]? There is no fault in either case. Because the domain of supernormal power (*iddhi*) is inconceivable, one who perceives name-and-form with even a single mind of direct knowledge (*abhiññā-citta*) sees it only as determined form, not as undetermined form;
or else, having first entered the foundational jhāna and emerged from it, one sees it with a concentrated mind through the preliminary work (*parikamma*) performed.

Because it has already occurred, one simply adverts to and takes as an object [the attainment] again, without having to enter it once more. This concludes the commentary on the knowledge of recollecting past lives.

1086–8. Regarding "the divine eye" (*dibbacakkhu*): it is called "divine" because it resembles the divine, because it is to be acquired by means of the divine abidings (*dibbavihāra*), and because it itself is supported by the divine abidings;
or else, it is "divine" due to its great radiance and other such qualities. It is like an "eye" in the sense that it sees forms.

The eye. For just as the physical eye (maṃsacakkhu), when presided over by consciousness, functions as if it were announcing what is even or uneven, this [divine eye] performs the function of the eye even more excellently than that;
thus it is "divine" (dibba) because it is both divine and an eye, and it is "the divine eye" (dibbacakkhu).
By means of that divine eye. "Having the kasiṇas as its object" means having the kasiṇas as its object by way of all eight kasiṇas.

"Having made it capable of being directed" means: having made it capable of being directed—that is, fit to be sent and worthy of being sent—toward the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*), by means of the fourteenfold taming of the mind and by bringing about its endowment with the eight factors.
The phrase "the fire... or the kasiṇa should be made near" is to be supplied to the text. "Should be made near" refers to the arising of the knowledge of the divine eye.

It should be made proximate and causal; that is to say, having made the access concentration (upacāra-jjhāna) more proficient therein, one should expand it, make it capable of appearing at the desired moment, and then establish it.
"In this" refers to this sphere of seeing forms with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu).
It is "described as the best" because the light kasiṇa (āloka-kasiṇa) alone has the nature of emitting radiance.
It is explained that they are "distinguished" because they are superior to others by virtue of producing light. 1089–90.
"Having produced": having produced [the counterpart sign] by means of the production of access concentration (upacāra-jhāna), according to the method stated in the description of the first jhāna.
For with the arising of access concentration, there is the arising of the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta). This is because the foundational jhāna (pādaka-jhāna) exists already.
By way of absorption (appanā), it is unable to radiate light by its own power merely through its occurrence, nor is it able to make it stable as it has been extended;
however, the preliminary work (parikamma) is capable of doing both.
Therefore, one should develop it only on the level of access (upacāra); thus he said, "on the level of access," and so forth. "The level of access" means:
And here, it should be understood that the preliminary consciousness (*parikamma-citta*) is precisely that which functions by way of making the light stable.

"Absorption" (*appanā*) refers to absorption by way of *jhāna*; for absorption by way of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) is not accomplished by one who has not performed the preliminary work. Therefore he said: "dependent on the foundational *jhāna*.
"Dependent on the foundational *jhāna*" means it has the foundational *jhāna* as its object; it does not [refer to] the divine eye.

It has the preliminary work as its support and the preliminary work as its object; and if that were so, the intention is that the seeing of forms would not occur due to the absence of the expansion of light. 1091–3. "Within... [and] in existence":

one should see only those things belonging to the category of form that are included within existence (*bhava*), and not those outside it, because the latter serve as causes for the arising of distraction.
The intention is that it must be seen with the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*). For even when light is projected, it does not come within the range of the physical eye (*maṃsacakkhu*).

Indeed, the time for the preliminary work (*parikamma*) passes away in the meantime; here, "preliminary work" refers to access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*) having the aforementioned kasiṇa as its object.
That [access concentration] does not occur while one is seeing what has become form (*rūpagata*); rather, the seeing of what has become form occurs by means of the light of the kasiṇa.

And the light of the kasiṇa [is absent] by way of the preliminary work (*parikamma*); thus, neither of these two occurs due to the non-occurrence of the preliminary work. Therefore he said, "The light, too," and so forth.

When that [light] has disappeared, even what belongs to the realm of form (*rūpagata*) is no longer seen; for one who sees what belongs to the realm of form, the turn for the preliminary work has passed.
However, for one intent on the preliminary work, there arises knowledge with the kasiṇa as its object, and thus what belongs to the realm of form is seen.
To the question "How should one proceed?", he says "By that," and so forth. "In this way, by successive order" means:
having repeatedly entered the foundational jhāna and emerged from it, one should frequently pervade [the mind] with light.
"The light becomes firm" means that the light within the mind should become long-lasting; and when that is the case, even for a very long time therein...

One sees only that which has become form (*rūpagata*). Therefore it was said: "There is light here," and so forth. Showing that this meaning should be clarified by the simile of the grass torch (*tiṇukkūpamā*), he said:
"By a grass torch," and so forth. It is said that once, at night, a certain man set out on a path by means of a grass torch;
that grass torch of his went out, and then the level and uneven parts of the ground were no longer discerned by him. He [then] placed that grass torch on the ground...
Having blown on it, he lit it again; it flared up and produced a light far greater than the previous light.
As he repeatedly extinguished and relit it in this manner, the sun eventually rose.

When the sun had risen, [thinking] "there is no further need for the work of the torch," he discarded it and continued on for the rest of the day. In this context, the light of the torch is like the light of the *kasiṇa* during the stage of preliminary practice (*parikamma*).

Just as when a lamp is extinguished there is no seeing of even or uneven forms, so too, for one who contemplates visible forms, when the light disappears due to the lapse of the preliminary-work stage, there is no seeing of visible forms;
just as striking a lamp [to relight it], so too is the repeated attainment of the basic jhāna;
and just as striking the lamp produces a light greater than the previous light, so too for one performing the preliminary work again, there is a more powerful pervasion of light.
Just as the rising sun remains pervading the extent of the area it has reached once its light has become firm, so too does the vision remain after having spread over the extent it has increased;
and just as one might travel for even a whole day after discarding a torch, so too does one see forms for even a whole day with the firmly established light after the burning light has increased.
To this extent, there is both the preliminary work consisting of various acts of adverting and the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*).
Since the order of their arising has not been shown, the phrase beginning with “the order of their production as well” was stated in order to demonstrate that.
Because it follows the method explained below, it is indeed easy to understand. Regarding the phrase “those four or five,” some manuscripts write this;
however, the correct reading is “three or four.”
1100. Therein, "the mind that accomplishes the aim" means the mind which has become the accomplisher of the aim because it accomplishes whatever aim one has set out to achieve.

For when that [mind] has arisen, even things that are not within the range of the physical eye—such as what is inside the belly, what is supported by the heart-basis, what is supported by the surface of the earth below, what is behind walls, mountains, or enclosures, and what is in other world-systems—[become visible].
This visible form comes into the range of vision; it is as if being seen by the physical eye.
And it is that very same form which is capable of being analyzed according to its own nature, just like eye-consciousness.

However, this is not the case for the preliminary-stage consciousnesses that function by way of adverting and preparatory work; for even when they take an object, they do not analyze it as it truly is.
“...just as the mind-moments of adverting, receiving, and so forth, proceed.

(1101–2) But surely there are two types of direct-knowledge knowledge (*abhiññā-ñāṇa*), namely the knowledge of the future (*anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance according to karma (*yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa*);
why then are they not shown here? To this he says: “Of the knowledge of the future,” and so forth. The divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*) succeeds separately.
Due to the absence of preliminary work (*parikamma*), these [knowledges] are acquired as attendants to the acquisition of the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*) itself.

For this very reason, they are called its "adjunct knowledges" (*paribhaṇḍa-ñāṇa*). Just as the girdle-regions (*mekhala-ṭṭhāna*), which occupy the position of attendants to Mount Sineru, are called "adjuncts" because they are established by its establishment, so too are these [knowledges] [established] by the establishment of the divine eye.
It should be understood that his peripheral powers (*paribhaṇḍāni*) are accomplished.

Let this be so for now; however, why was the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings (*cutūpapātañāṇa*) not shown? To this he said, "The knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings as well," and so forth.
For it is the very knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhuñāṇa*) that, by discerning form at the moment of death and at the moment of rebirth, functions with respect to passing away and rebirth.
It is called "knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings" (cutūpapāta-ñāṇa); at the time of discerning the remaining forms, it is called "the divine eye" (dibba-cakkhu).

Therefore, in the ultimate sense, it is one and the same knowledge designated by two names; however, the "divine-eye knowledge" and the "knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings" differ only in their phrasing.
In some places, "mind-made knowledge" (manomaya-ñāṇa) is also mentioned as a separate direct-knowledge (abhiññā) knowledge.
In terms of its meaning, this is simply the knowledge of the various supernormal powers (*iddhividhañāṇa*).
This concludes the commentary on the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhuñāṇa*). 1103. "Here" means in this teaching. "By this treatise" means by this treatise named *Abhidhammāvatāra*.
Thus ends [the section] from the work titled *Abhidhammatthavikāsinī*.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Higher Knowledges in the *Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanā* is finished.
Chapter Seventeen.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Objects of Direct Knowledge (Abhiññārammaṇaniddesa) 1104–5. Regarding the five beginning with the modes of supernormal power (iddhividha):
“The modes of supernormal power, the divine ear, The knowledge of others’ minds;”
“Recollection of past lives and the divine eye—thus [they] are fivefold.

Thus there are five that have been mentioned. However, these are called the “seven direct knowledges” because knowledge of past lives is included within the knowledge of recollecting past abodes, and knowledge of the mind-made body is included within the knowledge of the various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*). Knowledge of past lives refers to [knowledge of] others’ present existence...

Knowledge of the object of the active consciousness from the moment of rebirth-linking until its conclusion. Knowledge of the mind-made (manomaya-ñāṇa) is the knowledge of the various supernormal powers (iddhividha-ñāṇa) proceeding by way of the manifestation of a mind-made body and so forth.
Now, beginning to show that [knowledge] for the sake of non-confusion regarding the determination of the objects of these super-knowledges (abhiññā-ñāṇa), he said "of the seven," etc.
"The four triplets of objects" refers to the triplet of limited objects (parittārammaṇa-ttika) and the triplet of path-objects (maggārammaṇa-ttika).
The triad of past objects and the triad of internal objects—these are the four triads of objects.
Regarding the word "here" (*ettha*), does it refer to the triads or to the objects? What is the point here? If it refers to the triads, that is incorrect;
for direct-knowledge knowledges do not occur within the [other] triads. If it refers to the objects, that too is incorrect; for there is no other...
"Having designated one [object], it is appropriate to take up another. "Let it be as you wish. Let it be for the triads first;

has it not been stated that 'the knowledges of direct knowledge (abhiññā-ñāṇa) do not occur among the triads'? This is not a contradiction, because by the designation "triads," only the objects are being taken.
Or alternatively, let it be for the objects; has it not been stated, "having designated one..."?
"It is improper to refer back to something else"—this too is not a fault for the very reason already stated.

1107–10. "In the seven [categories] beginning with the limited (paritta)" means: although there is no difference in the objective basis (vatthu), there are seven divisions of objects beginning with the limited, which are distinguished by way of the differences in plane, time, and continuity, and by way of the objects being limited, sublime (mahaggata), past, future, present, internal, and external.
Because the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power (*iddhividhañāṇa*) lacks the path as its object (*maggārammaṇatā*), the triad of having the path as its object is not found here.
"Desiring to go with an invisible body by making the body dependent on the mind" is the connection [of the sentence].

And "making the body dependent on the mind" means bringing about a state of movement in the body that corresponds to that [mind], by way of the body's becoming invisible and possessing a swift motion like it. Just as the mind...
It is seen that there is swift movement; likewise, having made the body invisible and moving swiftly, one desires to go to whatever place is desired—this is the meaning here.
“By means of the mind” (*cittavasena*) implies the remainder of the reading: “one transforms by means of a magnified mind” (*mahaggata-citta*).
Therefore he said: “He places it upon a magnified state of mind. For, having entered the foundational jhāna and emerged from it...
One performs the preliminary work (*parikamma*) with the thought: “May this body become invisible like this mind and move swiftly.

Having performed the preliminary work, one enters absorption again, and upon emerging, performing the preliminary work in the same way, one takes up the body and mounts it upon the sublime mind that serves as its basis (*pādakacitta*), making it as if it were of the same nature (*taggatika*), so that it becomes invisible and moves swiftly.

It acts. However, for the sake of swift movement, it should be understood as reaching the desired place in just a few thought-moments (*cittavāra*), rather than in a single thought-moment (*ekacittakkhaṇa*)—unlike those who have not developed the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), whose progress is slow.
As it is said: "Bhikkhus, I do not see even a single thing that revolves so swiftly as this, bhikkhus, namely, the mind."

For here, since material phenomena (rūpadhamma) are already included by the very mention of "others," it is not tenable for the occurrence of matter to be based on moments of consciousness (cittakkhaṇa).
Furthermore, wherever phenomena arise, they disintegrate right there;
nor is it possible for anyone to alter the characteristics of phenomena through the power of psychic potency (iddhibala). [Thus,] the material body [is governed] by way of consciousness.

For one who applies [the meditation] to the jhāna based on the body, the body itself is the object; thus he says, "from having the body as its object," meaning that the color-form (vaṇṇa) within the body is the object.

Regarding the phrase "making the mind dependent on the body": here it should be understood that the mind does not make the body appear slow, as the body itself is slow, but rather it merely causes the state of appearing slowly.

1112–3. When it makes the future or the past its object: when those who resolve upon the future—such as the Elder Mahākassapa and others in the case of the great treasure-store of elements—make the future their object;
and when, at the time of transforming the mind by means of the body, they make that very same basis-jhāna which has long since ceased their object, they make the past their object.
At that time, it has a past object and a future range; however, the present is its range because the present material body is made its object.

For even when one is creating elephants and so forth by supernormal power, although the preliminary work has a future object, the consciousness of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna-citta*) has only a present object.
This is just as the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*) has the access sign (*upacāra-nimitta*) as its object.
The object of that [consciousness] becomes manifest simultaneously with it. 1114–5.
Regarding “the body... might”: when one transforms one’s own body by means of the mind, it is because one takes the internal body as the object;
when one transforms one’s own mind by means of the body, it is because one takes the mind as the object.

By means of the word *vā* (or), in the sense of including what has not been explicitly stated, it may have an internal object (*ajjhattārammaṇa*) because, at the time of manifesting one's own form as a youth and so forth, the body itself is made the object.
"In the seeing of external forms" (*bahiddhā rūpadassane*) refers to the time of seeing external forms such as elephants, horses, and so on. 1116–8.
"In the present and the limited" (*paccuppanne paritte ca*): this is an analysis of the specific characteristics [of the divine ear]. For the divine ear has only the present as its object.
Sound is the object, and it is limited by its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). Regarding "of the sound in the womb": this refers to the sound of wind within the womb.

However, in that case, when there is the hearing of the sound of insects, the object is exclusively external. They say that even when one who has attained mastery hears the sound produced by the expansion of his own thoughts, the object is internal;
however, that [sound] does not allow the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) to proceed beyond the eleventh moment of the life-continuum consciousness.
It is appropriate that [the mind] remains in this state precisely as one who has attained mastery by virtue of the capacity for adverting after emerging from the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
The phrase "and of another's sound" is to be connected [to the preceding]. For it is not only upon hearing the sound from another's belly that there is an external object;
rather, it is also upon hearing the sound produced by another's mind.
"Regarding 'in the case of the limited, etc. (parittādīsu): this refers to the limited, sublime, and measureless objects;
the path, the past, future, and present objects; and external objects. 'Of the limited' (parittānaṃ) refers to sense-sphere consciousnesses.

'Of the intermediate' (majjhimānaṃ) refers to the fine-material and immaterial-sphere consciousnesses, which are designated as 'intermediate' because they exist between the limited and the measureless. And their being 'intermediate' is by way of the teaching, not by way of intrinsic nature."

Regarding the statement "in knowing the path-consciousness" and so forth, this was said with reference to the position of the Great Commentary (Mahā-aṭṭhakathā), which holds that the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa) knows only the mind of another and does not know the remaining three aggregates. This is the intended meaning here:
because the knowledge of others' minds knows only the mind, it does not have the Path as its object; for it knows the consciousness associated with the Path.
However, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that taking the Path as an object is permissible by way of a figurative method (*pariyāya*). But since it is stated in the *Paṭṭhāna*:

“Wholesome aggregates are related to the knowledge of supernormal powers, the knowledge of penetration of minds, the knowledge of recollection of past lives, the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their deeds, and the knowledge of the future, by way of the object condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*)”—therefore, all four aggregates can be the object of the knowledge of penetration of minds.

Consequently, the status of having the Path as an object is obtained in the literal sense (*nippariyāya*) itself; this is the definitive conclusion of the authors of the Compendium (*Saṅgaha-kārā*) on this point.
1123–5. He knows the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa) as it occurs within the past seven days and likewise within the future seven days.

However, from that point onward, everything occurring from the moment of rebirth-linking up to the end of rebirth-linking, and from the moment of death up to the end of death, is the domain of the knowledge of past lives (atītaṃsañāṇa) and the knowledge of future lives (anāgataṃsañāṇa); it is with this intention that he says "in the past," and so forth.
“Knowledge of the past and future minds of others is possible, but it is not possible for the present mind,” he asks with the words, “And how, moreover...,” and so forth.

The other [the respondent], in order to show where it is possible, first analyzes the present and says, “The present is said to be threefold,” and so on. [These are] by way of moment, continuity, and duration.
"Present by moment," "present by continuity," and "present by duration"—thus it is stated in three ways according to moment (*khaṇa*), continuity (*santati*), and duration (*addhā*).
"Attained in three moments" means included within the triad of moments consisting of arising, presence, and dissolution.

"Beginning with the present moment" means that the word "moment" (*khaṇa*) and so forth refers to the present; thus, it is called "present by moment. "Included in one or two turns of continuity" means...
In this context, for one who has been sitting in darkness and has gone to a place of light, the object does not yet become manifest;

rather, until it becomes manifest, the continuity of material form (rūpasantati) or immateriality (arūpasantati) occurring during that interval should be understood as "one or two moments of continuity" (ekadvesantativārā).
Likewise, for one who has wandered about in a place of light and entered a small inner room, the material form does not immediately become manifest.
It continues until that [sound] becomes manifest; in this interval, one should understand there to be one or two hundred vibrations, as if for one who had already been sitting there.

Furthermore, having stood at a distance and seen the hand-movements of washermen and others, or the hand-movements of striking bells, drums, and so forth, yet not yet hearing the sound, in the interval until one hears it, there are one or two hundred vibrations.
"should be understood"—thus, first of all, do the elders who are reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya say.

However, the reciters of the Saṃyutta Nikāya, having stated the two continuities—namely, the continuity of form and the continuity of the formless—[explain] that for one who has stepped into water, [the continuity lasts] as long as the line made by the water where he stepped upon the bank has not subsided;
and for one who has come from a journey, as long as [the heat] in the body...
The state of being smoke does not subside; for one who has entered the womb after coming from the heat, the state of darkness does not disappear until [the end].
When one attends to the meditation subject within the womb and looks out by opening the window during the day, the flickering of the eyes does not subside;
this is called the continuity of form (*rūpa-santati*). [It lasts for] two or three impulsion-moments (*javana-vāra*).

Having stated, "It is called the immaterial continuity," and further stating, "Both of these are indeed what is called present-by-continuity (santati-paccuppanna)," they thus speak of only one single instance of continuity.

In that regard, according to the reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya, because for some it becomes clear even when [the process] is rapid, they have also employed the term "one" in the phrase "one or two instances of continuity.
However, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla [states]: "That which is originated by elements, etc., whose intrinsic nature is extremely subtle..."
Or it should be understood as one, two, or up to twenty times,” so it was said.
1127–8. “Delimited by a single existence” means a collection of phenomena delimited by way of rebirth-linking and death within a single existence, included within that one existence.
Referring to this, it was said: “Friend, both the mind and the mental objects—both these are present.”
"And if consciousness is bound to desire and lust for that present [object]," and so forth.

Here, "present by way of continuity" (*santatipaccuppanna*) is what appears in the commentaries on the Abhidhamma, while "present by way of duration" (*addhāpaccuppanna*) is found in the Suttas. "Some" refers to the inhabitants of Abhayagiri.
"And just as," etc., is the illustration of their simile here: a single flower [is attached] to its own stalk to one [person].
The connection is: "it pierces the stalk. Regarding the minds of the multitude...

it pierces [them] such that, without making a distinction like "past mind," "future mind," "this person's mind," or "that person's mind," when the minds of the multitude are adverted to as a single mass with the thought "I know another's mind," then at the moment of arising, one mind [knows] the mind of one [person].
The meaning is that it penetrates [the object] exclusively either at the moment of stabilization (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*) or at the moment of dissolution (*bhaṅgakkhaṇa*).
To show that their statement is incorrect, it was said: "By which one adverts," and so forth.

For even if one were to advert for a thousand years in this manner, there would be no coexistence of the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*) and the impulsion consciousnesses (*javana*) upon a single object; and as for the consciousness of direct knowledge (*abhiññācitta*), [it is likewise].
If one knows the present momentary state, one knows it only as it occurs together with the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*) upon a single object, and not otherwise;
therefore, because those two—the adverting and the impulsion (*javana*)—cannot exist simultaneously on a single object, that [position] is untenable.
If it is asked, "Let it be so; what fault is there here?", he says: "Of the adverting and the impulsion," and so forth. Therein:

Any place other than the cognitive series of the path and its fruits is an undesirable location. For in the cognitive series of the path and its fruits, diversity of object is desirable because the formations are the objects of adverting and the other [mental states], while Nibbāna is the object of change-of-lineage and the others; elsewhere, however, it is undesirable.
Therefore, the charge that there is the fault of adverting and impulsion falling upon different objects in an undesirable location is inappropriate—such is their statement.
The intention [of the commentator] is that it is explained as "inappropriate" in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). 1133–4.
If this is so, how is it that the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) has the present as its object? To this he says, "Therefore," and so forth.
Because it has been explained as inappropriate in this way, therefore. "From a single impulsion-moment" (*javanavārato*) means by way of a single impulsion-moment. However, this...
This was stated for the purpose of showing the present by treating it as light immediately after the momentary present;

however, that consciousness which occurs during the time measured by a second impulsion-series (javana-vīthi) relative to the past and future from the perspective of the currently occurring impulsion-series is all called "continuity-present" (santati-paccuppanna) in the Commentary.
Therefore, the phrase "from the occasion of the impulsion" refers to the second impulsion-occasion.
"It should be illustrated" means that it is not [illustrated] by the entirety of the present; this is the intended meaning. This has been explained in the *Saṃyutta-aṭṭhakathā*.

Herein, the passage beginning with "This is the illustration" is an explanation of the mode of occurrence of the supernormal power consciousness (*iddhicitta*) by way of illustrating the fact that the impulsion phase (*javanavāra*) belongs to the duration-present (*addhā-paccuppanna*).
1139–41. Having included even the present by way of continuity (*santati*) within the present by way of duration (*addhā*), he said:

“...the end of the duration... and so forth. However, Master Ānanda [notes] that nowhere in the Canon is it stated that the term "present" as it occurs in the Abhidhamma matrix (*mātikā*) has the meaning of both the present by way of duration and the present by way of continuity;
therefore, by way of the commonality of being consciousness, the mind that adverts is what has become manifest.

One adverts to the presently existing consciousness; and the preliminary exercises proceed by taking that variously existing consciousness as their object through the commonality of its nature as consciousness, serving as the preliminary work for the knowing of that consciousness.
However, the knowledge of penetration into others' minds arises in the same single moment as the presently existing consciousness which it penetrates.
In this regard, because it is grasped as a single unit by way of the continuity of the stream...

The acts of adverting and so forth occur within the very same consciousness; and that consciousness which is discerned by the knowledge of penetration into others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa) is that very same consciousness.

Therefore, because they occur in an identical mode, there is no diversity of objects in an undesirable sense; thus, one maintains that this [knowledge] has a present object only by way of the present moment (khaṇapaccuppanna).
"The others" refers to the acts of adverting and the preliminary (parikamma) consciousnesses. At the eye-door...
"Consciousness" means eye-consciousness.

Regarding "in the eight [types of objects] such as the limited (paritta)," this refers to the eight types—limited and so forth—as stated in the case of the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa), with the present object excluded and the "indeterminate" (navattabba) object included. In the passage "In the past... [etc. ...or even the fruit," here:

"By oneself" (*attanā*) is merely an illustration. By means of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa*), one also recollects a path developed by others and the fruit realized [by them].

Or, by the particle *vā* in the sense of including what is not explicitly stated, the meaning should be understood as follows: "the path developed by oneself and the fruit," or "the path developed by others and the fruit. And so it is said in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*):
“By oneself, and by others, when recollecting the path cultivated and the fruit realized. However, the word *eva* is used merely for the purpose of completing the meter.
In the phrase “or even the fruit,” the word “cultivated” (*bhāvita*) should not be connected [to the fruit];
for the fruit is not something to be cultivated, but rather something to be realized. In the phrase “recollecting the path by oneself,” [the same applies].
Or it should be connected with the phrase "developed by others. "Absolutely" means necessarily.

(1148–50) Now, are not the knowledge of penetration of minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) and the knowledge of the destiny according to deeds (*yathākammūpagañāṇa*) also exclusively those whose objects are past?
What, then, is the difference between their objects and that of this [knowledge]? To this he said: "The knowledge of penetration of minds... and so forth. "Even though... is this [phrase].
The collection of particles, or a single particle, should be understood as occurring in the sense of "approaching" when there is no mention of a specific distinction.
"Atha kho" (but then/however) marks the commencement of the mention of a specific distinction. "Cittameva" (the mind alone)—this has already been examined previously.

"In the past, merely volition"—this too was stated just as before with reference to the doctrine of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. For therein, regarding the knowledge of rebirth according to karma (*yathākammūpagañāṇa*)...
Only volition itself is the object, not consciousness nor the other mental states;
for this reason, it is said that "knowledge of rebirth according to karma" takes only past volition as its object.
However, according to the scriptural passage shown below, all four aggregates are the object of knowledge of rebirth according to karma.

This is the conclusion of the compilers: "There is nothing that is not its range" means that there is no aggregate (khandha), nor anything connected to the aggregates—such as name, clan, and so forth—that is called "not its range.
For the intention is that among past aggregates and things connected to the aggregates, all have the same destination as the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa).

1151–2. Regarding "recollection of one's own aggregates" (*attakkhandhānussaraṇa*): this refers to the time of recollecting one's own aggregates. Regarding "recollection" (*saraṇe*)... [and so on] ...regarding "the range" (*gocara*):
when recollecting the name, clan, and so forth—according to the method beginning with "In the past there was the Blessed One Vipassī;

his mother was Bandhumatī, his father was Bandhumā"—as well as the sign of the earth and so forth, it has an object that is not to be defined (*navattabbārammaṇa*). Thus, it is called "having a range that is not to be defined" (*navattabbagocara*).
For this was stated by way of the triads of limited objects and past objects;
however, by way of the triad of internal objects, when the dhammas that serve as the object of the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*) jhāna are its object, it has an "indeterminable" object;
at other times, when the object is a designation (*paññatti*), it has an external object. And here, "name and clan" refers to that which is bound up with the aggregates (*khandha*).
The meaning of a phoneme is established by convention, not the phoneme itself. For the phoneme is limited because it is included within the sense-base of sound (*saddāyatana*).
As it has been said: "The analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*) has a limited object.
1154. Regarding the supernormal power of the divine ear: because it takes as its object present and limited material form, therefore...

It has a present object and a limited object; and in the case of seeing the physical form within one's own belly, or seeing the blood residing in another's heart, it has an internal object and an external object.
Regarding the eight [knowledges] beginning with the limited, this refers to those mentioned for the knowledge of recollecting past lives, excluding that which has a past object.

Including that which has the future as its object, there are eight [knowledges]. By the phrase "knowing that it will arise," etc., he refers to the knowledge of the aggregates that are about to arise.

For the future is not outside the range of the knowledge of the future (*anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa*). Indeed, regarding those phenomena connected with the future aggregates and their constituents, that knowledge shares the same scope as the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*).

1163. *Jānane nāmagottassa* means at the time of knowing the name, clan, and so forth, according to the method beginning: "In the future, a Perfectly Enlightened One named Metteyya will arise; his father will be named Subrahmā, and his mother will be named Brahmavatī. 1164–5.
*Pañcasu parittādīsu* means in the five [categories] by way of limited, exalted, past, internal, and external objects. *Kāmakammassa* means of karma belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).

"1169. *Vividhatthavaṇṇapadaṃ* means endowed with words of various meanings and words of phonetic expression (*byañjana*). The word division is: *madhurāttham atinīharanti* and *madhurāttham atinīharañca*.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Abhidhammāvatāra*, titled the *Abhidhammatthavikāsinī*."
The commentary on the exposition of the objects of direct knowledge is finished. Chapter Eighteen:
The Commentary on the Exposition of Purification of View.

1170–2. Now, since a bhikkhu who possesses a more stable development of concentration—having thus attained its benefits by way of direct knowledge—must develop wisdom, and because it is in this way that wisdom becomes more stable in every respect and reaches the peak, he begins the exposition of the method for its development, saying: "But as for concentration," and so forth.

"What is wisdom? is a question regarding its essential nature (*sarūpapucchā*). "What is its meaning? asks: what is the meaning of this term "wisdom"? The intention is: upon what denotable object (*abhidheyyattha*) does the word "wisdom" depend? 1173–4.
"Wisdom, insight-wisdom"—this shows precisely that wisdom which is intended here; elsewhere, however, it is of many kinds.
There is a differentiation of wisdom. "Associated with a meritorious mind" means conjoined with a wholesome (kusala) state of consciousness.
Here, by the term "merit" (puñña), both types of the indeterminate (abyākata) are excluded; likewise, it refutes the wrong view that occurs in the form, "there is defilement.
By the term "insight" (vipassanā), all other wholesome wisdoms occurring on the basis of such things as the doctrine of the ownership of one's actions (kammassakatā) are excluded. Knowledge (jānanā).
When it was said, "or by way of mode," one should attend to the inquiry: "What is this so-called knowing by way of mode?

In order to show that knowing by way of various modes is distinguished from the modes of perceiving (*sañjānana*) and cognizing (*vijānana*), he poses a question out of a desire to explain: "What is the distinction, what is the difference, between perception (*saññā*), consciousness (*viññāṇa*), and wisdom (*paññā*)?

He then provides the answer beginning with "Of perception, consciousness, and wisdom... Even though they are equal in being modes of knowing, that is, even though they are identical in their mode of cognizing the object.
1175. "Merely perceiving" (*sañjānanamattam*) means knowing by taking as a sign of perception (*saññānimitta*) an object—whether it exists or does not exist—such as "blue," "yellow," and so forth.
For this [perception] has the function of making that [sign] a condition for further perceiving.

By the word "mere" (*matta*), in the sense of excluding qualifications, it excludes the modes of cognizing (*vijānana*) and fully understanding (*pajānana*); and by the particle "only" (*eva*), [it excludes] even at any time this [latter mode].
One determines that those specific qualities do not exist at all. Therefore, he says: “the penetration of the characteristics,” and so forth.

Because one is unable to effect the penetration of the characteristics—namely, “impermanent, suffering, non-self”—and is unable even to perform the function of consciousness, how could perception perform the function of wisdom? Thus, it is said that it is unable to effect the penetration of the characteristics.
It has not been stated that it is unable to lead one to the path.
However, consciousness, when occurring with respect to an object, does not function there solely by way of perceiving blue, yellow, and so forth as perception (saññā) does;
rather, it functions precisely by knowing the specific qualities such as impermanence therein, as well as other similar distinctions.
He says, "But consciousness... and so forth, because it occurs. But how does consciousness penetrate the characteristics?

By the path shown by wisdom. For when insight that takes the characteristics as its object occurs after having penetrated the characteristics many times, insight can arise even with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge due to the proficiency gained through familiarity.
Just as, when reciting a well-mastered text, even the sections that have been learned by heart are not clearly perceived;
and the phrase "to penetrate the characteristics" is said with reference to making the characteristics the object of cognition, not to the act of penetrating itself.
"Having ascended" means having begun by way of the sequence of knowledge of arising and passing away, etc., in order to reach the path.
Consciousness (*viññāṇa*) is unable [to do so] because its intrinsic nature is non-awakening. "In the manner stated" means in the manner stated regarding consciousness.

For that [wisdom] both knows the object and penetrates its characteristic. Moreover, by its own unique power not shared by others, it is able to bring about the path. And their knowing of the object is like the knowing of a coin by a foolish village money-changer.

It should be understood as follows: Suppose a heap of kahāpaṇa coins is placed on a money-changer’s board, and three people—a young child who has not yet developed the understanding of commerce, a villager, and a money-changer—are looking at it.
Of these three, the young child knows nothing more than the mere appearance of the kahāpaṇas—whether they are variegated, multicolored, long, short, square, or round. "This... [he thinks].
He does not know that it brings enjoyment and utility to human beings and is regarded as a jewel.
A village dweller knows both of these things, yet he does not know the distinctions such as, "This is clever and of great value; this is counterfeit; this is of medium value; this is of low value.
A money-changer knows all those varieties; and knowing them, he knows them even by merely looking at them.
Even upon hearing the sound of it being struck, smelling its scent, tasting its flavor, or holding it in the hand, one knows:
"It was made in such-and-such a village, town, city, mountain, or riverbank," or "It was made by such-and-such a master.
In this context, perception is like the sight of a coin by a young child whose intellect has not yet developed conventional linguistic usage.
It grasps the object as a mere lump without making a distinction, because it apprehends the mode of appearance of the object only by way of its being blue and so forth;
consciousness should be regarded as like a villager’s sight of a coin, owing to its capacity to grasp only certain particular features,
whereas wisdom should be regarded as like a money-changer’s sight of a coin, owing to its capacity to grasp everything without exception.
1178–80. “Penetration of individual essence” (*sabhāvapaṭivedhana*): one’s own nature, or a common nature, is the individual essence (*sabhāva*).
Its penetration—by way of full understanding as the known and full understanding as investigation—is the penetration of the specific and general characteristics of phenomena.

It has the function of shattering that which conceals the aforementioned individual essences of phenomena, just as the light of a lamp dispels external darkness that conceals pots, cloths, and so forth.
For the light of knowledge arises only by dispelling the darkness of the heart; thus it is said:
"Its essential function is considered to be the destruction of the darkness of delusion. Precisely for that reason, it stands present in the manner of non-delusion regarding all phenomena;
or, being itself the cause, it establishes non-delusion as its fruit; thus it is said: "It has non-delusion as its manifestation."

Since it is insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*) that is intended here, concentration (*samādhi*) is its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*). For this reason, he says "because of its immediate cause being concentration," based on the Sutta passage: "One who is concentrated understands things as they really are" (*samāhito yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti*). 1181–2.
What is called the penetration of the individual essence of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*) is the unique characteristic of wisdom; there is no differentiation of it by means of that [penetration].

He says, "It is called manifold by way of its characteristics," because it is obtained [in various ways]. The world (*loka*) is said to be the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) in the sense of breaking up and disintegrating.
Because they are included within that, or because they are known therein, they are called worldly (*lokika*). Because they are not included therein, they are supramundane (*alokika*).
To the question, "Which among these are worldly and which are supramundane? he says, "By the worldly," and so forth. [This refers to] the arising of wholesome worldly states of consciousness.

"Associated with the path" means connected with a mundane path. More specifically, however, the term "path" is used because wisdom—which occurs in its totality as associated with the path comprised by the fourfold purification beginning with purification of view—also occurs in its individual parts;

or else, it is used because the designation "path" applies to each factor individually, such as right view and the rest. They are "supramundane" (*lokuttara*) because they have transcended (*uttarā*) the world (*loka*). They are also supramundane...
For [these states] associated with the path are to be developed, and they are indeed obtained at the conclusion of insight (vipassanā);

thus, there is no contradiction in including the supramundane (lokuttara). Therefore, he said, "by the supramundane," and so forth. By the inclusion of the phrase "consisting of what is heard, etc.," he includes that which consists of mental development (bhāvanāmaya).
1183–5. "By one's own reflection" means by means of one's own reasoning in establishing various blameless purposes, rather than through the instruction of another.
"Without relying on one's own power of ingenuity. "By one of vast wisdom" (*bhūripaññena*) means by one of great wisdom; the sense is: by one whose wisdom is as expansive as the earth.
"But having heard from another" means having heard the instruction from another. "And accomplished through what was heard" is a qualifying term that includes the sense of the cause;
the meaning is: because it is accomplished through what was heard. "Because it is accomplished through what was heard... [and so forth].
Or the reading is “vā. “Yathā vāpi tathā vā” means whether having heard it from another or not having heard it.

“Attainment of absorption” (appanāpattā) is stated in order to show that this is the culmination reached through development consisting in meditation; it does not mean, however, that only those [levels] reaching absorption constitute development consisting in meditation.
Furthermore, these three kinds of wisdom should be understood according to the text as follows:
“In this context, what is wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmaya-paññā*)? It is that which, regarding fields of work established by yoga,
or fields of craft established by yoga, or branches of knowledge established by yoga, consists of the conviction that one’s own actions are one’s own property (*kammassakatā*),

or that which conforms to the truth, such as the conviction or view that ‘form is impermanent,’ or that ‘feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent’— whatever such conformable inclination or view there may be.”
One acquires inclination, joy, vision, and the acceptance that arises from reflecting on the Dhamma without having heard it from another;

this is called wisdom consisting in reflection (*cintāmayā paññā*). In that regard, what is wisdom consisting in hearing (*sutamayā paññā*)? … [as before] … one acquires it after having heard it from another; this is called wisdom consisting in hearing.
Furthermore, all wisdom of one who has attained meditative absorption is wisdom consisting in cultivation (*bhāvanāmayā paññā*).”
And here, although the wisdom consisting of reflection and that consisting of hearing are described by way of the sense-base of action and so forth as being exalted and supramundane respectively,

and the wisdom consisting of cultivation is also described [in those same terms], what is intended here is the wisdom conforming to the truths consisting of reflection, which is found only in two types of Bodhisattvas in their final existence, and the remaining great wisdom found in those who have fulfilled the perfections.
