Wisdom consisting of what has been heard that accords with truth is intended here; even though it reaches the supramundane absorption, it is specifically wisdom consisting of meditation (*bhāvanāmaya-paññā*) that is meant.

Regarding the "tetrad of analytical knowledges" (*paṭisambhidā-catukka*): this is by way of the tetrad of analytical knowledges known as the analysis of meaning (*attha*), phenomena (*dhamma*), language (*nirutti*), and eloquence (*paṭibhāna*).
But if wisdom consisting of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*) is intended here, why are the analytical knowledges mentioned? [Because they belong] to those who practice insight.

When the various classifications of wisdom (*paññā*) are being demonstrated for the sake of proficiency in knowledge, the wisdom of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā-paññā*) is mentioned here for two reasons:

either because there is a desire to speak of it, or because the wisdom of the analytical knowledges is the fruit of insight (*vipassanā*), or because, within the context of mundane and supramundane wisdom, one wishes to mention the wisdom of the analytical knowledges as that which must be attained together with supramundane wisdom.
Regarding the phrase "knowledge regarding meaning, phenomena, and language": "meaning" (*attha*)...

"Knowledge of meaning is the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā); knowledge of the Dhamma is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma (dhammapaṭisambhidā); and knowledge regarding the expression of the terminology therein is the analytical knowledge of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā).
Thus it is said. This refers to the triad of knowledges differentiated according to the three [categories] beginning with meaning.

Regarding "in all three": this means by way of the objective field, function, characteristic, flavor, manifestation, proximate cause, plane, and so forth, in respect of the three aforementioned analytical knowledges.
When one takes these as an object and reviews them, thinking, "These knowledges indicate this meaning," there is knowledge that has reached such differentiation;
or, it is knowledge among the three kinds of knowledge by way of the limited (*paritta*), the sublime (*mahaggata*), and the measureless (*appamāṇa*).

For even the analytical knowledge of the object (*paṭisambhidā-ārammaṇa*) is itself the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*). And for this very reason, in the Suttanta-bhājaniya portion of the Pāḷi, it is called "knowledge among knowledges."
And in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated without qualification: "For one who reviews knowledge by taking all-pervading knowledge as its object, there is knowledge that has reached differentiation.
And this being so, even though the analytical knowledge of the sublime (*mahaggata*) is absent, the analytical knowledge of language (*nirutti-patisambhidā*) has a limited object (*parittārammaṇā*);
the other three analytical knowledges may have limited objects, may have sublime objects, or may have—

Regarding the phrase "having an immeasurable object," the fact that the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*) can also have a sublime object (*mahaggatārammaṇa*) is stated in the *Pañhāpucchaka-pāḷi*.
However, in the *Abhidhammabhājanīya*, it says:
"At whatever time a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen, accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge..."
Whether it be a visible-form object …pe… or a mental-object (dhamma) object, whatever [object] he has taken up, at that time there is contact …pe… there is non-distraction.
Whatever other immaterial states (arūpino dhammā) exist at that time, these states are wholesome (kusala).
Knowledge regarding those states is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhammapaṭisambhidā). Knowledge regarding their result (vipāka) is the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā).
“The knowledge regarding the expression of the language by which those phenomena are designated— that is the analytical knowledge of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā).

The knowledge by which one knows those knowledges, thinking, ‘These knowledges illuminate this meaning’— that knowledge regarding those knowledges is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā).”
Because the teaching proceeds by way of the sequence of the arising of consciousness (cittuppādakkama), the reading is made with remainder.

For the teaching in the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya proceeds without leaving out any of the meanings included within the arising of consciousness; it does not, however, refer to all that is knowable (sabbañeyya).

Thus, according to the statement regarding the object as it has been shown, it says, "by which knowledge one knows those knowledges," but this does not deny that [that knowledge] has other objects as its objective support. This is because of the nature of the teaching.

Because it is not subject to alteration. And having established this, regarding that *nibbāna*, it is stated that the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*)—even in the future—cannot be said to have a past object, a future object, or a present object; thus, the fact that the analytical knowledge of meaning has *nibbāna* as its object is expressed.
And here, "meaning" (*attha*) is, in brief, a designation for cause and fruit.
For because the fruit of a cause is realized, attained, and reached by following the cause, it is therefore called "meaning" (*attha*).

Furthermore, "phenomenon" (*dhamma*) is, in brief, a designation for a condition. For because it sustains, causes to proceed, or holds that which is to be reached, it is therefore called "phenomenon. "Etymology" (*nirutti*) refers to the fundamental language of sentient beings.
The Māgadhī language is that in which the teaching of the Buddhas occurs. "Patisambhidā" (analytical knowledge) refers precisely to the three types of knowledge mentioned above;
for this is stated in the Abhidhamma: "Knowledge regarding suffering... [and so on]... knowledge regarding its result is the analytical knowledge of meaning," and so forth.
However, since this is merely a summary of the meaning, it becomes clearer when explained by way of its detailed classification; therefore:
Having summarized that, the passage beginning with “whatever has arisen by way of conditions” is commenced in order to show its meaning and so forth through its classification.

“Whatever has arisen by way of conditions” means whatever has arisen from conditions such as causes (hetu) and the rest. However, what is intended here is only that which is understood by following the cause, thinking, “this has been produced from that”; likewise, those things consisting of the fruits of the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Resultants are understood by way of the presence of non-functioning; the remaining functional states that are not resultants are understood by way of the presence of non-resultant activity;

the unconditioned, being the escape, is understood by way of the presence of extinction (nibbāna); and the ultimate phenomena such as the aggregates, which constitute the meaning of the Buddha’s word, are illustrated by this [term].
Thus he said that it acquires its conventional designation for its meaning only when it is understood according to the canonical text.

“Whatever has arisen by way of conditions,” and so forth. In this context, cause and fruit, as well as the meaning of what was spoken, are understood through their respective dependence on causes and their dependence on the words spoken;
thus, they are the meaning in a figurative sense (*pariyāyato*). The remainder is understood solely by way of their own respective individual natures;
thus, that is the meaning in the non-figurative sense (*nippariyāyato*). Therein, the figurative meaning is stated according to the Suttanta-bhājaniya, while the non-figurative meaning—

It should be understood as being by way of the *Abhidhamma-bhājaniya*. "Spoken" refers to the Dhamma of the Pāḷi. The remainder should be understood by applying the method explained under the fivefold meanings (*pañcaka*) as appropriate.
And herein, Nibbāna is the meaning that is to be attained; the spoken meaning is the meaning that is to be made known; the other is the meaning that is to be produced.

"Meaning" (attha) is threefold. It should be understood that there are three kinds of meaning: the path is the cause that brings about [the goal]; what has been spoken is the cause that makes known; and the other is the cause that produces.
Furthermore, here the status of "dhamma" is not predicated of functional states (kiriyādhamma) because they lack fruition (avipāka).
If this is so, should their status as "meaning" (atthabhāva) not also be denied, since they are not fruitions? No, because they exist as things arisen from conditions (paccayuppanna).

If this were so, would it follow that even wholesome and unwholesome states possess the status of "existence" (atthabhāva), since they too are produced by conditions? This is not a fault, because it has not been denied.
However, because the result of maturation (vipāka) is manifest due to its being the primary cause, their status as "phenomena" (dhammabhāva) alone was stated; [one might object:

"But for functional states (kiriya), since they serve as conditions, would they not also incur the status of 'phenomena'? This is not a fault, because it has not been denied. [This applies] to the connection between karma and its fruit.
Furthermore, it should be understood that because the state of being a cause is absent, the state of being a phenomenon (dhamma) is not tenable.

Moreover, for one who reflects merely upon wholesome and unwholesome states, as well as resultant and functional states, without making such a distinction as "this is a condition" and "this is the conditioned," the analytical knowledges of phenomena and meaning do not arise;
therefore, their nature as meaning and phenomena must be stated.
1189. "Sabhāvaniruttī" means non-perverted terminology (*aviparīta-nirutti*).

"Non-perverted terminology" refers to the Māgadhī language, which is described as a linguistic expression that is always fixed in its specific relation to the comprehension of each respective meaning and is never deviant.
For that [Māgadhī] is always fixed in its specific relation, whereas other languages change over time.
As for its meaning, the teachers say that it is a designation of names (*nāmapaññatti*). As they have said:
"The Magadhan language is etymology; in meaning, it is the conventional designation of names.
However, others say: if natural etymology were of the nature of a designation, then in that case, the designation itself would have to be expressed.

If one were to fall into the position that there is no "expression" (*abhilāpa*), then it would be impossible to state: "In that regard, knowledge of the expression of the terminology of phenomena is the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*).
For "expression" means that which is to be expressed. Indeed, there is nothing else to be expressed or uttered apart from speech.
Now, if what is to be expressed—that which is to be made known—is by means of terms such as "contact" (*phassa*) and so forth, then in that case...
Since even the eight categories of meaning (attha-dhamma) must be made known, it follows that they too possess the nature of language (nirutti). Furthermore, because the Commentary states:

"‘Contact’ is a term for its own intrinsic nature (sabhāva-nirutti); ‘contacts, contacts’ is not a term for its own intrinsic nature," it is thus shown that a sound accompanied by modification through intonation (viññatti-vikāra) is language.
For one who reflects upon that sound which is a term for its own intrinsic nature, making it the object [of consciousness]...

Because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "The knowledge that has reached the distinctions within that discourse of unsurpassed terminology is the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*);

thus, this analytical knowledge of language is said to have sound as its object, not a conceptual designation (*paññatti*) as its object," the analytical knowledge of language occurs in the mind-door subsequent to the cognitive process of ear-consciousness which has the sound of language as its object. And having established it thus: "The analytical knowledge of language..."
They say that the statement, "it has a limited object," is thus justified. However, the teachers beginning with the Elder Ācariya Jotipāla have said:
"The statement that 'the analytical knowledge of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā) has a present object' was spoken with reference to the subsequent cognition that grasps a present sound;
and this being so, [one might object] that while one thing has a present object, another thing [of the same type] would also have a present object."

It is said that one "attains" it; however, just as the knowledge of the divine ear (*dibbasotañāṇa*) is the condition for the determination of the distinctions between sounds such as those of humans, and thus makes manifest each respective sound, so too, when the knowledge that has the present sound of expression (*nirutti*) as its object and is the condition for the determination of expressions according to their true nature (*sabhāva*) and lack of true nature (*asabhāva*), and which makes them manifest, is called the "analytical knowledge of expression" (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*), there is no contradiction with the Canon (*pāḷi*). That [knowledge] [takes] that sound of expression according to its true nature...
Nor can it be said that one cannot describe [the knowledge] as "reviewing by making [sound] the object," for it is indeed reviewing the present sound-object.

For that knowledge arises precisely as something that analyzes the conventional terminology (nirutti), because it functions as the cause for determining the various distinctions immediately after the review of each respective sound; thus, it arises as something that breaks through and penetrates that terminology.

"And it is also included within the classification. (1190) "Threefold" means that this follows the very method already explained below. "Contemplating" means contemplating by way of non-delusion, thinking: "These knowledges illuminate this meaning.
But is it not the case that even these three knowledges do not transcend the intrinsic nature of things and phenomena?
Among the knowledges, there is the knowledge that constitutes the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*) and the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*).
Why, then, is it stated separately as "among those... [it is] reckoned"? It is because what is intended is the knowledge occurring within the three knowledges that have objects.
For that knowledge which has another knowledge as its object proceeds precisely by penetrating even that object through non-delusion.
This is what is called here the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*). And having established it thus, it was said: "These knowledges illuminate this meaning.
However, the knowledge that has mere knowledge as its object is itself the analytical knowledge of meaning (*attha-paṭisambhidā*).
And although this analytical knowledge occurs in relation to knowledges that possess objects, it clarifies the distinction between those objects through the three preceding knowledges alone.

How is this so? Just as a learned man who is incapable of teaching the Dhamma, though he knows the Dhamma that must be spoken by a preacher of the Dhamma, yet the actual delivery of the teaching is the domain of the preacher alone—so too should this be understood.
Furthermore, regarding these [three knowledges], penetration occurs through non-delusion at the moment of the path for the three trainees (sekkhā) and the one beyond training (asekha).
Also by way of making the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) its object. For it possesses the nature of both the path and the fruit.
And this being so, it is both mundane and supramundane, while the remaining three are exclusively mundane. Thus said the ancients:
"The acquisition of these [three] occurs through non-delusion at the moment of the paths of the trainee and the adept."
"Knowledge of meaning as it is found is twofold, but that which is with taints is [only] knowledge.
(1191) Now, in order to show that these four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) attain clarity through five aspects, the passage beginning with "the scriptures" (*pariyatti*) is commenced.
Therein, "the scriptures" (*pariyatti*) refers to the thorough mastery of the Buddha’s word, including both the canonical texts (*pāḷi*) and the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
“Paripucchā” means asking in order to know thoroughly and completely the analysis of the word-meanings and the meanings of the difficult points (*gaṇṭhipada*).

“Listening” (*savana*) is the grasping by way of ear-consciousness, having made it a matter of bone—that is, having applied oneself with earnestness. “Attainment” (*adhigama*) is the arising of the path.

However, in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), it is stated: “Attainment is the arising of the path of Arahatship. This refers to the progression through the various distinctions on the stage of the trainee (*sekha*).
This was said by considering that [the knowledge of] one's own domain has a limited scope, whereas [the knowledge of] the plane of the Asekhas has a vast scope;

or rather, it was said specifically with reference to their preeminent attainment. For even for those who have reached these [lower stages] as trainees (sekha), there is an attainment of clarity through the reaching of Arahatship.
However, just like prior application, the attainment of Arahatship is also a condition for the clarity of the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) in an Arahat. It is not otherwise.

The phrase "it occurs" should be connected to the causality of the purification of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*)—both those of the trainee (*sekha*) and the adept (*asekha*)—as appropriate for each of the five.

"Former application" (*pubbayoga*) refers to the exertion in insight meditation (*vipassanā*) within the dispensation of previous Buddhas, ranging from the stage of one who has "gone and returned" (*gatapaccāgata*) up to the vicinity of the "conformity" (*anuloma*) and "clan" (*gotrabhu*) stages.
And herein, both the former application of attainment and the present application cause the unarisen to arise and the arisen to be maintained.
It should be understood that while these [factors] make it clear, the remaining ones are conditions for its state of being very clear.
Having thus shown the classification of wisdom by way of its singlefold nature and so forth, the passage beginning with "How should it be developed?
is now commenced in order to clarify the method of development. In this regard, since by means of this wisdom the phenomena such as the aggregates...
Regarding these stages (*bhūmi*): the two purifications, namely purification of virtue (*sīlavisuddhi*) and purification of mind (*cittavisuddhi*), constitute the root;

the five purifications—purification of view (*diṭṭhivisuddhi*), purification by overcoming doubt (*kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi*), purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path (*maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhi*), purification by knowledge and vision of the way (*paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi*), and purification by knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassanavisuddhi*)—constitute the body.
Therefore, among those states that have become the stages...

The passage beginning with “In the aggregates, etc. is commenced in order to show that [the meditation] should be developed by one who, having cultivated familiarity with knowledge through the means of learning and interrogation, has perfected the two purifications that serve as the foundation, and is now perfecting the five purifications that constitute the body [of the path].
“In the aggregates, etc. means in the various categories such as the aggregates, bases, elements, faculties, dependent origination, and so forth. And “in those that serve as the ground” means...
In those things which serve as the basis for the arising of knowledge through the apprehension of the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and so forth.
"Purity of virtue" and "purity of mind" refer to purity of virtue and purity of mind, which constitute the root.

For when there is purity of virtue and purity of mind, this wisdom is said to be "root-born," but not when they are absent. The five beginning with "purity of view" are the "body" because they are to be developed.

There are five [purifications], beginning with purification of view. For these five purifications—beginning with purification of view—which occur as a continuous stream of this wisdom, should be understood as the "body" by way of characterizing the whole through its parts, being like the feet, hands, and head [of that body].
"By that wisdom" means by the wisdom that occurs regarding phenomena such as the aggregates, etc., through study, questioning, and so forth.
"From birth and so forth" means from birth, aging, death, and the rest.
Having stated that "it should be developed," it is now explained that because wisdom increases only through the growth of the body known as the five purifications—
which is firmly established upon the roots known as purification of virtue and purification of mind within the planes of the aggregates and so forth— [the development of wisdom follows].

It is called "name" (nāma). Therefore, in order to show one aspect of the aggregates and so forth, which serve as the ground for insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*), the passage beginning with "And form" (*rūpañca*) was stated.
"Therein" (*tattha*) means within those five aggregates. "Whatever" (*yaṃ kiñci*) is an expression used to include everything without exception.
By the phrase "past, future, etc.," that very same [form] is shown by including it within the eleven bases (*okāsa*). By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), the present is included.

1197–1200. Regarding the terms "inferior" (*hīna*) and so forth: it is "inferior" because it is originated by unwholesome (*akusala*) kamma, and "exquisite" (*paṇīta*) because it is originated by wholesome (*kusala*) kamma.
Alternatively, it is "inferior" insofar as it is a cause for the arising of unwholesome results, and "exquisite" in the opposite sense.

It is "distant" by way of subtle material phenomena (*rūpa*) and so forth that are difficult to grasp, and "near" by way of the others; such is the meaning to be understood through these and similar terms. "Having made all that into one" refers to [the matter] divided by distinctions such as the past and so forth.

Having grasped all that together as a single unit by means of the intellect through its nature as a mass of form (*rūpa-rāsi*), it is called the "form aggregate" (*rūpakkhandha*) in the sense of being a "mass," just as in the expressions "great mass of water" and so forth. For it is said in the Sutta: "having gathered that together and condensed it.
This same method applies to the "feeling aggregate" (*vedanākkhandha*) and the others as well. However, within each individual instance of feeling and so forth, [it is like] the ocean...

It should be understood that the word *khandha* (aggregate) occurs by way of conventional metaphor (*ruḷhī*), because—as seen in expressions such as "I have seen [it]"—the designation for the whole is applied even to its parts.
The connection is: "whatever has the characteristic of being felt. The state of being the feeling-aggregate (*vedanākkhandha*) belongs to feeling itself.
A detailed exposition on the classification of feeling into past, future, and so forth should be taken from the *Visuddhimagga*.
“Having the characteristic of volitional formation (abhisaṅkhāra-lakkhaṇa)” is said thus because the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) has volition as its primary factor;
it means that its characteristic is the piling up or the collecting together of associated states upon an object.
Alternatively, because it is said that “they form the formed (saṅkhataṃ abhisaṅkharonti),” its intrinsic nature is the act of forming so that one’s own fruit becomes properly accomplished.
This is the meaning. Furthermore, this applies by way of wholesome and unwholesome volition (cetanā).

Having thus shown, even partially, those phenomena that constitute the ground for insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā), [the author] now—without repeating the purification of virtue (sīla-visuddhi) and purification of mind (citta-visuddhi) since they were explained previously—will demonstrate the purification of view (diṭṭhi-visuddhi), which is the starting point for the cultivation of wisdom.
The passage beginning with “the four great elements” has been commenced. And by a practitioner desiring to accomplish that,
although the analysis of name-and-form must be established either by way of the determination of the four elements, or by way of the twelve bases, or by way of the five aggregates,
or by way of both these condensed categories, or by way of the jhāna already attained— by whichever particular means it may be done—
Because an exposition of the detailed analysis would lead to excessive prolixity, the analysis here is shown solely by way of the aggregates as they have been realized.
"By means of eighty-one types of consciousness" refers to the eighty-one mundane types of consciousness.

Supramundane consciousnesses, however, do not come within the range of discernment for either the practitioner of bare insight or the practitioner of serenity, because they have not yet been attained. "The four formless [realms]..."

"Aggregates" (khandhā) refers to the four formless aggregates. Matter (rūpa) has the characteristic of being "malleable" (ruppana), because it undergoes change when brought together with opposing conditions such as cold and heat.
Name (nāma) has the characteristic of "bending" (namana), because it bends toward its object.
"Grasps" (parigaṇhati) means that one grasps after having delimited [the object] by means of wisdom (paññā) which performs delimitation.
1206–9. Regarding the phrase "the twin trunk of the palm tree": this refers to a twin palm trunk produced from two seeds that have become one.
For even though those twins belong to distinct continua, they appear as if non-distinct; likewise are material and immaterial phenomena.

Since its twofold nature is already established by the very expression "name and form" (*nāmañca rūpañca*), the statement "he defines it in two ways" refers to [defining] that which is distinct from name-and-form.
It is for the purpose of showing the non-existence of anything else. For that very reason, he said: "By name and by form," and so forth.

Because it is not determined as being merely name-and-form, and because the distinctions such as the continuity and the compactness [of the aggregates] have not been made, the delusion that occurs through the grasping of a collection as a single entity—without any underlying adherence—is "delusion regarding a being" (*sattasammoha*).
It is for the purpose of destroying—that is, for the purpose of suppressing—that [delusion]. "By means of many suttas" means...

“By ‘yathā hi’ and so forth,” it refers to this [passage] shown here, as well as to many other discourses (suttanta) such as: “Mahāli, if this form were the self, then this form would not lead to affliction,” and so on.
“That” refers to that name-and-form (nāmarūpa).

"1210–2. *Aṅgasambhārā* means: because of the collection of parts, for that cause, and for that reason—without abandoning that [collection]—while that very thing exists; this is the meaning. *Saddo* means conventional designation (*vohāro*). *Khandhesu* means:
while the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*) exist, without abandoning them, there is the conventional designation "a being.
This is what is meant: just as in the case of the collection of parts such as the axle, wheels, felloes, and spokes..."

Just as when various parts are gathered together into a single mass and established in one place, there is the mere conventional designation "chariot," yet upon examining each individual component, no such thing as a "chariot" exists in the ultimate sense; even so,
when the material and immaterial phenomena designated as the aggregates of clinging proceed by way of a continuum, there is the notion of a "being," a "person," or a "living soul."

Or it is merely conventional usage; for when each individual phenomenon is investigated from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramattha*), there is no so-called "being" (*satta*) that serves as the basis for the grasping of "I am" or "I," but there exists only mere name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
For one who sees in this way, that vision is indeed "seeing things as they really are" (*yathābhūtadassana*), which is called the purification of view (*diṭṭhivisuddhi*).

Anticipating the inquiry, "If there is no such thing as a sentient being (satta), how then can the purposeful functions of going and so forth be accomplished by mere name-and-form (nāmarūpa) alone?", he says, "Just as...
and so forth. Herein, the summary of the meaning is as follows:
Just as a wooden machine, being lifeless—devoid of a living soul—due to the absence of a living soul operating within it, is for that very reason devoid of volition (nirīhaka).

It is devoid of activity; nevertheless, through the conjunction of wood and rope and by way of specific conditions, that wooden machine moves and stands, appearing as if it were possessed of life and agency, accomplishing functions such as going.
Likewise, although this name-and-form is indeed soulless and effortless, nevertheless, due to the specific conditions produced by their mutual interaction—
"In conjunction, it appears as if living, active, going, and staying. (1213) "Truly" means from the perspective of reality;
that is to say, from the standpoint of the ultimate truth (*paramattha*).
This name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is conditioned, empty of a soul (*jīva*) and so forth, like a machine. This name-and-form, conditioned by causal factors, is empty like a machine.
Or [it is] a connection. "A mass of suffering" means a heap of suffering due to constant affliction.
"Similar to grass and wood" means equal to grass and wood because of the emptiness of a self.
1215. "Yamaka" means a pair. And that state of being a pair is by virtue of mutual dependence; thus he said, "both are dependent on one another."
For this very reason, when one [of the two] is destroyed, both are destroyed.
Indeed, there is never a case in the five-aggregate existence where matter ceases through death while the immaterial does not cease, or where the immaterial ceases while matter does not cease.
However, in the one-aggregate and four-aggregate existences, the reason for their occurring without depending upon one another is as follows:

"This has already been explained below. Furthermore, this analysis is by way of conditions alone; the meaning is that with the cessation of conditions, there is the cessation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
"Conditions" means those things that have become conditions; even though they serve as mutual conditions for one another, when one ceases, both indeed cease.

1216–9. They "deprive of luster" (nittejjanti) that which is devoid of luster and lacking in majestic power. To show where it is that they deprive something of its luster, the text says, "he does not speak," and so forth.

For otherwise, it would be impossible to say that a name is deprived of luster in acts such as inspiring confidence or encouragement, nor can it be said of matter in acts such as supporting or binding.
Precisely for this reason, after stating, "in the same way, matter is also deprived of luster," [the text continues].
“It is said: ‘I am eating’ … [and so on] … ‘it is not found.
By the passage beginning with ‘dependent upon mind,’ the lack of intrinsic power in both mind and matter is further elucidated through the method of contrast (*vyatireka*).
For matter proceeds in activities such as going while dependent upon mind, and mind proceeds in activities such as seeing while dependent upon matter.”
Furthermore, their mutual dependence demonstrates that each is individually incapable of accomplishing its own function;
for in this way, the emptiness of self and the absence of agency in name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) become even more clearly evident.

But how can there be efficacy when those things that are individually incapable possess efficacy upon coming together? Even in the case of non-causes, efficacy arises through their combination despite their lack of harmony.

Because it would result in the fallacy of being causeless. Having taken to heart the objection that "even a hundred or a thousand people who are individually unable to see cannot see when combined," he said, "But of this... and so forth.
For even by means of a simile, a matter not yet established must be proven. Therefore he said: "I shall give you a simile; for here, by means of a simile, some wise men..."
“...understanding the meaning of what has been said. Now, here is the simile of the man blind from birth and the cripple:
Suppose a man blind from birth and a cripple both desired to set out for a certain direction. The man blind from birth said to the cripple:
“I am indeed able, sir, to perform with my feet whatever must be done on foot, but I have no eyes by which to see.”
“...might see the level and the uneven. The cripple said this to the man blind from birth:
“Friend, I am indeed able to do with my eyes what must be done with eyes, yet I have no feet by which I might go forward or back.
Delighted and joyful, the man blind from birth mounted the cripple upon his shoulders; the cripple [proceeded] for the man blind from birth.
Sitting upon the shoulder, he said: "Release the left, take the right; release the right, take the left.
In this regard, even one blind from birth, lacking luster and weak, cannot go by his own power; likewise, a cripple in a chair cannot go by his own power.
Yet, it is not that their movement does not proceed by depending on one another. Even so...
Even name, being devoid of its own energy, does not arise by its own power, nor does it proceed in those various activities;
even form, being devoid of its own energy, does not arise by its own power, nor does it proceed in those various activities;
yet their arising or proceeding does not occur without depending upon one another. Thus said the ancients:
“They are not born by their own power,
nor do they endure by their own power;
they follow under the sway of another’s dhamma.”
“Conditioned things arise as weak by their own nature.
They arise from external conditions, originate from external objects,
and are brought forth by external phenomena through the conditions of those objects.”

1222–3. Now, in order to clarify that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) likewise lacks mastery over itself, even in the case of the simile of the boat and the rudder, the two verses beginning with "Just as" (yathā hi) were spoken.

Therein, "relying upon" (nissāya) means having established oneself [upon]. "They go" (yanti) means they move. "Relying upon men" means depending on men such as the steersman and the laborers who act as guides;
for it is not through their own actions—such as seizing the oars, adjusting the rigging, or pouring water—that the boat moves.

Just as one reaches a desired destination without a boat, yet both [the boat and the passenger] travel upon the ocean by depending on one another, so too name-and-form proceed by depending on each other; this is the intended meaning.

1224. "Having dispelled the perception of a being" means having removed the grasping at a self within the five aggregates, which has been cultivated since beginningless time according to the methods already described.

Having suppressed [the defilements]... it is called "name" (*nāma*). Thus, by way of clearly discerning their characteristics in every respect—stating, "This is name; such is the extent of name, no more than this.

This is form (*rūpa*); such is the extent of form, no more than this"—this demonstration of the actual nature of those things is called "purification of view" (*diṭṭhivisuddhi*) by the Buddhas and others, because it purifies the stain of the view of self (*attadiṭṭhi*).
This is the meaning. It should be understood that this is not called only "purification of view," but it is also to be known as a designation for the "determination of name-and-form.
"From birth and so forth" means from suffering such as birth, aging, sickness, and so on. As it is said: "Birth is suffering;
aging is suffering; sickness is suffering; death is suffering; and not obtaining what one desires is suffering."
"That too is suffering; in short, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering. "The two extremes" refers to the two extremes known as eternalism and annihilationism.
Alternatively, it refers to the two extremes consisting of the absolute existence of a being and its non-existence.
For, since a being is not found in the ultimate sense, the notion that "a being exists" must indeed be rejected; it is only by way of worldly convention [that such a term is used].
"Because it is not apprehended, even the notion that 'it does not exist' must be avoided"—this is how it connects with "it makes [the mind] exceedingly pure.
"Stains consisting of views" means stains known as views. They bring about destruction, total exhaustion, and suppression without remainder.
For it is because it purifies the stains of views that it is called "purity of view."
Thus ends the commentary on the Exposition of Purification of View within the *Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanā*, known as the *Abhidhammatthavikāsinī*.
19. The Nineteenth Chapter:
Explanation of the Description of Purification by Overcoming Doubt (Kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhiniddesa-vaṇṇanā) 1227.
Because it has been shown as the objective domain for the purification of view (diṭṭhivisuddhi) just described, [the word] "of this" (etassa) refers to that.
It was stated [thus], not for the sake of distinguishing it from something else, because there is nothing other than that.

Whether the application of insight (*vipassanā*) occurs internally or externally, once the goal is accomplished, all name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is encompassed without exception by way of its characteristics.
Having known the "cause-condition" (*hetupaccaya*), that is, having grasped the cause-condition; "for the purpose of grasping the cause-condition."
This has been stated. For it is because of the discernment of conditions that he attains the overcoming of doubt throughout the three periods of time.
"Having overcome" means having transcended; the meaning is "having suppressed.
That knowledge, being thus departed and having attained mastery like a jhāna, occurs in the continuum of the practitioner by way of continuity; therefore, it is said to be "steadfast."
1229–30. "Of name-and-form... ... "Having adverted": just as a skilled physician, having seen a disease, searches for its origin;
or just as a compassionate man, seeing a young child lying on his back in the middle of a carriage road, adverts to the child's parents, thinking, "Whose child is this?"; even so...

What is the cause of name-and-form (nāmarūpa), or what is its condition for existence? It cannot be without a cause, because otherwise it would follow that everything exists everywhere, at all times, and for everyone alike;
nor can it have a creator god (issara) or similar entity as its cause, because apart from name-and-form itself, no such creator god or other entity exists.
As for those who claim that the creator god and so forth are merely name-and-form itself—for them, [the question remains] regarding that name-and-form designated as a "creator god" and so on...
Because it would follow that [nāma-rūpa] lacks a cause, there must be causes and conditions for it;
thus, the meaning is: "Having adverted to the causes and conditions of name-and-form, thinking, 'What indeed...'"?

Having first done this much, for one who discerns the causes and conditions of this name-and-form, the discernment of the condition for form is easy because of its grossness and its manifest nature; therefore, the discernment of its condition comes first.
Showing that this must be done, he said, "Of the material body," and so forth.

In that regard, just as the discernment of conditions for name-and-form serves to exclude the doctrines of no-cause or irregular causes, so too it should be undertaken to exclude delight in various things by means of bringing about disenchantment and dispassion;
thus, to show this by way of the thirty-two aspects, he said, "Head-hairs, body-hairs," and so forth.
1232–3. Ignorance... [and so on] ... "He is dead": ignorance, craving, clinging, and kamma—these four kinds of phenomena are the cause (*hetu*) of this aforementioned material body;
the meaning is that the fourfold nutriment is the condition (*paccaya*).

Now, with reference to the objection as to why the former is the cause and the latter the condition, [the author] says "producer" (*janaka*), etc., and [explains] this according to worldly convention.

To demonstrate this capacity, the passage beginning with "of the cause and the sprout" was stated. In that context, these qualifying terms—“producer” and “sustainer”—are included within the meaning of “cause”;
what is meant is that they function as producers and sustainers. Here, “producer” means that which brings about origination.
By this, it is shown that ignorance and the other factors are causes of the material body because they are its specific (asādhāraṇa) causes, just as a seed is the cause of a sprout.

"Being a protector" means being a supporter. By this, however, it should be understood that nutriment is shown to be a condition by way of its status as a common cause, just as earth, water, and so forth are for a sprout. 1234–7. "These...
have been explained": thus these five states beginning with ignorance [have been explained] as causes and conditions according to their respective roles.
She has gone. Just as a mother is a support (*upanissaya*), so too is ignorance:
by way of concealing the faults existing in the various states of existence (*bhava*), craving by way of longing, and clinging (*upādāna*) by way of firm grasping.

Thus, being the causes of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) and becoming, they are "formative" (*abhisaṅkhārika*) because they are the proximate causes for the desire for existence through their function as generators and companions; or rather, they are the supports, just like a mother.

They serve as decisive supports (upanissaya). Just as a father is called the "progenitor" because he produces the semen from which a son arises, so too is karma called the "progenitor" because it brings about the arising of a being.

Just as a nurse is the one who nourishes and sustains a newborn boy, so too is nutriment the one that develops and sustains the body once it has arisen; thus it is said: “The nurse... [and so on]... would come to be.”

Granted that ignorance and the other factors are also conditions for the mental body (*nāmakāya*), nevertheless, the phrase beginning with "the eye" was stated in order to show the method of discerning its conditions in a more manifest manner.
Therein, in the expression "the eye and," the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of conjunction;

by it, all internal conditions such as the adverting of consciousness (*āvajjana*) and so forth, which serve as conditions for eye-consciousness, are included. [The others are] visible form and light alone.

Furthermore, by the word "and" (*ca*), it includes other external conditions just as external form is a condition of object for eye-consciousness and light is a condition of decisive support (*upanissaya-paccaya*). "Dependent upon" (*paṭicca*) means having obtained that which has become a condition.

By this, [it is shown] through the modes of support (*nissaya*), pre-existence (*purejāta*), faculty (*indriya*), dissociation (*vippayutta*), presence (*atthi*), and non-disappearance (*avigata*) in relation to the eye.
It shows that visible forms and light function as conditions—according to their respective possibilities—as object, decisive support, prenascence, presence, and non-disappearance conditions;
and for the others included under "sound," it shows their state of being conditions by way of proximity and so forth, and co-nascence and so forth.

By the word "and so forth" (ādi), one should understand the inclusion of ear-consciousness and the rest together with their conditions, just as in the case of contact and the rest. Thus, all [this] leading up to the stage of comprehension...
The name is comprised together with its condition. Therefore he said: "He discerns the condition for the mental body.
(1238–40) "Having seen" means having seen the present occurrence. By the phrase "likewise in that way," it is not merely the state of having conditions that is referred to;
rather, by whatever kinds of conditions—such as ignorance and so forth—it occurs now, by those very same kinds it occurred in the past as well.

It should be understood that "occurs" (*pavattati*) also implies being accompanied by conditions (*paccaya-sahita*). "In the past" (*pubbante*) refers to the portion consisting of the continuity of past aggregates.
"Come in five ways" (*pañcadhā-āgatā*) refers to: "Did I exist in the past? Did I not exist in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having been what, what..."
"Did I exist in the past?"—thus [these views] have come down or occurred in five ways. Regarding the "future":
in the future, within the series of aggregates, they are proclaimed in five ways as follows: "Shall I exist in the future? Shall I not exist in the future?"
"Shall I indeed exist in the future? How shall I indeed exist in the future?
Having been what, what shall I indeed become in the future?"—thus it is stated in five ways.
1241. “In the present period as well” means in the period beginning with the present rebirth-linking and ending with death.
By the mention of “period” (*addhāna*) here, he refers specifically to the constituent part that is the present aggregates;
for there is no such thing as time apart from those [aggregates]. Thus, it is described as being sixfold.
“Am I indeed? Or am I not indeed? What indeed am I? How indeed am I? From where has this being come, and to where will it go?”—thus it is said to be sixfold.
Because the word *sabba* (all) is used even in a partial sense—as in such passages as “All tremble at punishment”—the term *anavasesā* (without remainder) is stated even after saying “all.
This is because there is no remainder (*avasesa*) or residue (*avasiṭṭha*) left of her.
"Without remainder": this means that even by way of a single doubt, all sixteen kinds [of doubts] have been left without exception.

"Is abandoned": it is abandoned by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*). Granted, through the purification of view (*diṭṭhivisuddhi*) alone—by not seeing a being apart from mere name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)—doubt regarding the present has indeed been abandoned; however, by the abandoning of doubts concerning the past and the future...
It is stated right here in order to show the complete abandonment of doubt regarding the present.
Alternatively, it is stated here because the investigation of the doubt concerning the conditions for the occurrence of impersonal name-and-form in the present takes place right here.

Or rather, this is a praise of the statement regarding the abandonment of doubt about the present, just as [the abandonment] of things already abandoned in the paths of stream-entry and so forth is praised.

And there is the statement regarding the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*) and so forth, beginning with "the abandoning of the five lower fetters" (*pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahāna*).

1242. "Also by way of kamma and its result": in a previous kamma-existence, delusion is ignorance (*avijjā*), the accumulation is volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*), attachment is craving (*taṇhā*), the approaching is clinging (*upādāna*), and volition is becoming (*bhava*); thus these five factors exist in a previous kamma-existence.
Here, with respect to the conditions for rebirth-linking: here, rebirth-linking is consciousness; descent [into the womb] is name-and-form;
sensitivity is the sense base; what is touched is contact; and what is felt is feeling—these five phenomena have as their condition the karma performed previously in this very existence of rebirth.
Here, due to the ripening of the sense bases, delusion is ignorance... [and so on] ...volition is becoming—these [are the factors].
"Five factors are conditions for rebirth-linking in the future within the process of kamma-existence"—this is said with reference to the rounds of kamma and its result (*kammavaṭṭa-vipākavaṭṭa*).
Herein, it should be understood that the round of defilements (*kilesavaṭṭa*) is also included within the round of kamma itself by virtue of being an associate of kamma. 1243.
Regarding the term "to be experienced in the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*): here, "the present life" (*diṭṭhadhamma*) refers to that which is directly perceived, namely, the present.
The personal existence (*attabhāva*); therein, the karma whose fruit is to be experienced is that which is to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*).

But by the power of karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*), in subsequent lives (*aparāpariyavedanīya*), or as having been experienced (*ahosikamma*)—the term "upapajjāparāpariya" is stated by means of the elision of the latter member of the compound. Therein, having arisen immediately after the present existence...
Kamma whose fruit is to be experienced upon rebirth is *upapajjavedanīya*.
Other kamma whose fruit is to be experienced in some other state of existence—other than the present life—in any particular personal existence whatsoever, is *aparāpariyavedanīya*.
Kamma that can be described as "the kamma existed, but its result did not exist; it exists [now], and it will exist [in the future]" is *ahosikamma*.

The first impulsion volition (paṭhamajavana-cetanā), having attained a state of strength through its invincibility by opposing factors and through the excellence acquired via specific conditions, proceeds with particular intensity due to the influence of a corresponding prior karmic formation (pubbābhisaṅkhāra).

It is called "to-be-experienced-in-this-life" (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya) because it yields its fruit within that very same existence. For, in the manner described, it is powerful within the stream of the impulsion consciousness.

Because it occurs through the influence of assistance or non-assistance toward those endowed with specific qualities, and because it lacks the result of repetition (*āsevana*), its ripening is slight;
thus, unlike the other two types of karma, it does not depend on the cessation of the active continuum nor on the acquisition of a physical location.
Consequently, it yields only a result of occurrence and ripening—like a mere flower—in this very life, and it does not grant a result accompanied by roots (*sahetuka*).

However, it might also lead to the drawing forth of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). "Being unable to do so" means that the giving of the result (*vipākadāna*) by karma occurs only through the convergence of other conditions such as the physical basis (*upadhi*) and its application; therefore, because those [conditions] are absent, it is unable to give its result in that very same existence.
Regarding the phrase "karma that has been" (*ahosikamma*) … pe … "result": here, the term "karma that has been" (*ahosi kamma*) is to be understood as separate words.
It should be applied thus: "There was karma, but there was no fruition of that karma; there was karma, but there will be no fruition of that karma;

there was karma, but there is no fruition of that karma. In this context, the first [statement] is said with reference to karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*) and karma to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*) that has passed its own respective time. For that [karma], both the time of the action and the time of its fruition have elapsed.

It receives that designation because it has passed away; the second [statement] is said with reference to the yet-to-come attainment of Arahantship, concerning kamma performed in previous births that is to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparāpariyavedanīya*) and whose result has not yet been given;

the third, however, concerns kamma performed in the immediately preceding birth that is to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*), as well as kamma performed in past births by an Arahant that is to be experienced in a subsequent life.
It has been stated. However, others say: "This was stated by dividing a single past kamma into three types with reference to the absence of its result (vipāka) throughout the three periods of time.
"Accomplishing the purpose" means that which brings about the purpose of giving and so forth, or killing and so forth. As to what that is, he says: "the volition of the seventh impulsion."

For that volition which brings about determination, having acquired its specific distinction in the manner described, becomes a condition for the continuity of kamma-result (vipākasantāna) immediately following rebirth-linking.
Being thus conditioned as an immediate antecedent condition, it yields its result in the immediately succeeding existence;
this is called "to-be-experienced-upon-rebirth" (upapajjavedanīya). And here, by way of common usage, it is referred to as "the seventh impulsion-volition."

Thus it was said. However, during the occurrence of retrospection, mastery, and so forth, even the fifth [jhāna] and others may arise. Regarding the phrase "gives fruition": having given rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), it gives the fruition of the course of existence (pavatti);
but there is no case where it gives the fruition of the course of existence without having first given rebirth-linking.
For the teachers maintain that the immediate succession of death is the opportunity for [kamma] to be experienced upon rebirth. But once rebirth-linking has been given, even after hundreds of births—
It gives result in the course of existence (*pavatti-vipāka*). Therefore the Blessed One said: "Having given a gift to an animal, a hundredfold merit is to be expected.

Regarding the phrase "of both... it gives": because they lack the aforementioned causes, the five volitions (*cetanā*)—not having attained the state of being experienced in the present life or in the next rebirth (*diṭṭhadhamma-upapajja-vedanīya*)—since their nature of giving a result is not cut off, whenever they find an opportunity, they give the rebirth-linking result (*paṭisandhi-vipāka*).

Or it gives result in the course of existence (*pavatti*). By the phrase "when there is the occurrence of saṃsāra," he illuminates that in the absence of the occurrence of saṃsāra, it stands on the side of "lapsed" action (*ahosikamma*), because there is no opportunity for it to ripen.
Having thus first shown the fourfold [classification] by way of the time of giving result, he now [shows it] by way of the method of giving result.
In order to show its fourfold nature according to its function (*kicca*), the passage beginning with "heavy" (*garuka*) was stated.
Therein, "heavy" means that which is highly blameworthy and of great power—a karma that cannot be obstructed by any other karma. "Frequent" (*bahula*) means that which is performed repeatedly;
even if done only once, it is that which has been habitually cultivated. "Proximate" (*āsanna*) means that which is recollected at the time close to death.

And what is "done" (*kata*)? "Kamma that has been done" (*kaṭattā-kamma*) refers to that kamma which is to be called simply "done" because it has not reached the state of being weighty (*garuka*) and so forth.

In this regard, whether it be wholesome or unwholesome, among those that are weighty or not weighty, only that which is weighty—such as the kamma of matricide and the like, or sublime (*mahaggata*) kamma—ripens first. Likewise, among those that are frequent or not frequent, that which is frequent...
Whether it be virtuous conduct or unvirtuous conduct, that very same [kamma] ripens first.
Among those deeds performed far or near, one is reborn by means of whichever was recollected at the time of death; there is nothing further to be said regarding what was done when death was imminent.
However, "completed" kamma (*kaṭattā-kamma*), having been repeatedly habituated, draws forth rebirth in the absence of the aforementioned types. Thus...
That which is weighty (*garuka*) ripens first of all; for it is described as "weighty. In the absence of the weighty, that which is habitual (*bahulīkata*) ripens;
in its absence, that which is proximate (*āsanna*); and in its absence, the "projecting karma" (*kaṭattā-kamma*). Thus it is said: "Karma performed in previous births ripens.

(1245) That which produces the continuity of resultant [consciousness] by way of giving rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and so forth is the "productive" (*janaka*). [It is also the producer] of the continuity of pleasure and pain.

Or it is that which sustains the continuity of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) by acting as a cause for its prolonged persistence. Therefore he said: "It sustains pleasure and pain; it causes them to proceed for a duration.

When pleasure and pain are occurring, it gradually obstructs and oppresses them through the onset of conditions such as frequent illness. Therefore he said: "It oppresses and obstructs pleasure and pain."

"It does not allow the course [of the result] to proceed. Likewise, it is "interruptive" (*upacchedaka*), "obstructive" (*paṭibāhaka*), and "injurious" (*upaghātaka*) by way of preventing the occurrence of the ripening of opposing kamma. Therefore he said: "having obstructed its ripening.
"Form and the immaterial resultant aggregates" refers to the resultant aggregates of both form and the immaterial; for even the form born of kamma is designated by the term "resultant" (*vipāka*).
"It exists" refers to what was stated as "the aggregates that are the result of form and the formless.

"By another kamma" means when rebirth-linking has been given by another kamma—whether wholesome or unwholesome—that has become the agent, and the resultant [state] has been produced. Therefore he said, "when the resultant has been produced.
They say "when the resultant has been produced" with reference to the resultant of the course of existence (*pavatti-vipāka*). [This refers to] the pleasure and pain that arise.
"It supports" means that wholesome supporting kamma, being wholesome itself, supports the pleasure arising from another wholesome kamma by way of warding off its opposite;
unwholesome [supporting kamma] likewise supports the suffering arising from another unwholesome kamma. And while thus providing support, it persists for a long time.
It is said that it "sets in motion" (pavatteti) in the sense that it "sets in motion the course" (addhānaṃ pavattetī). It "afflicts" (upapīḷakaṃ) the arising pleasure and pain;

that is, while being unwholesome, it afflicts the continuity of pleasure by providing the causes for obstacles such as disease to one who is happy, and while being wholesome, it [afflicts] the continuity of suffering by providing the causes for pleasure such as medicine to one who is suffering from disease and so forth.

It oppresses that which is about to cut off [the life-faculty]. However, some say: "Even though it does not produce the cause for pleasure or pain, by obstructing the process-result (*pavattivipāka*) of the kamma that gives rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the kamma that itself yields its own result is 'obstructive kamma' (*upapīḷaka-kamma*).
But if that were the case, it would have to be said that only the kamma giving rebirth-linking is "productive kamma" (*janaka-kamma*).

Furthermore, it follows that there is a distinction between this [kamma] and the obstructing [kamma]. If you argue that it is because this [kamma] is an obstacle to rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi-vipāka), we say no, because it was stated without qualification.
As for the objection raised when it is said, "having destroyed weak kamma":
"Since that [weak kamma] has already been established and has already ceased, how can this [strong kamma] be its destroyer?"—[this objection is addressed as follows:]
Showing that what is called "the destruction of karma by means of intent" (sandhāya) is indeed the warding off of its result, he said:
"having warded off its result. And that warding off is the making of an opportunity for the arising of one's own result; thus it is said:
"he makes an opportunity for his own result. Karma for which an opportunity has been made for ripening is indeed said to be "ripened" (vipakka).
He said, “It becomes thus... pe ... it is called ‘arisen’.
The obstructive [kamma] cuts off the result of another, but does not itself give its own result;
however, the destructive [kamma], having cut off the weak kamma, produces its own result—this is the distinction between them. Some say...
However, other teachers maintain that there is yet another method for classifying karma as "productive" (janaka) and so forth. How so?

That karma which, when performed, results in the arising of resultant states and the materiality of the kamma-produced aggregate during both rebirth-linking and the course of existence, is "productive.

On the other hand, that karma which, when performed, serves as a condition for the non-occurrence of obstacles or interruptions to the desirable or undesirable fruit produced by another [karma]—[is termed "supportive"].

When there is the arising of an accessory condition (*upabrūhaka-paccaya*), those [karmic results] become nourished and maintained for a longer duration in accordance with the generative power (*janakānubhāva*);

that is the supporting condition (*upatthambhaka*). That which, being antagonistic, afflicts the wholesome or unwholesome fruit produced by the generative [kamma]—by way of signs such as the disharmony of the elements of disease—is the obstructing condition (*upapīḷaka*). Furthermore, by whatever kamma, through the efficacy of the generative [kamma],...
Even though it is capable of being maintained for a very long duration, it is impaired and interrupted by the arising of conditions that cut off its fruit;

thus, it is called "destructive. And here, some explain the wholesome nature of the second [action] by way of its leading to freedom from illness and long life, and the unwholesome nature of the latter two by way of their leading to much illness and short life;
however, [this does not apply] to beings such as the Nāga Bhūridatta and others, because from this...

Since there exist kamma that supports, oppresses, and destroys the unwholesome ripening of hungry ghosts (petas) and those in the woeful states who have not been provided with the means of subsistence,

the wholesome or unwholesome nature of these four [types of beings] is not contradicted. Although both the interval between kamma and the interval between its ripening are manifest in their true essence only to the Buddhas through their knowledge of kamma and its ripening— for this is a unique quality of the Buddhas— [the classification remains valid].
This is uncommon among disciples, but it should be understood in part by one who possesses insight (vipassaka).
For one who does not know [it] in its entirety, the discernment of conditions (paccayapariggaha) is not fulfilled; therefore, with reference to such discernment, the words "Thus, this...
and so forth were spoken. In whatever manner name-and-form (nāmarūpa) proceeds in the present time through such conditions, in that very same manner it proceeds in the other [times] as well.
"In two time-periods" (*addhadvaye*): this was said beginning with "Just as this... in order to show how that same method applies to the past and the future.
This is because the censure is intended to demonstrate that even in the three time-periods there is only action, non-action, and the fruit thereof. The passage beginning with "Thus, both action...
is stated by way of a conclusion to the very same meaning already expressed. "For one who thus regards it... is abandoned": for one who views it in this manner... [is abandoned].
That doubt which, concerning the past and so forth, occurs in the manner of "Did I exist?

and so on, is abandoned. Once that doubt has been abandoned, in all states of existence, modes of birth, destinies, stations, and abodes of beings, there appears only mere name-and-form proceeding by way of the connection between cause and fruit.
For this very reason, he said: "By way of the connection between cause and fruit," and so forth.
When an action accomplished through giving and so forth proceeds within the totality of causes, the designation "agent" is applied to the mere cause;
thus it is said: “Beyond the cause, he does not see a cause. The connection is: “He does not see a ripener... nor a perceiver.
“Ripener” (*pāka*) means the experiencer of the result (*vipākavindaka*). Not seeing [an agent] in this way, [he understands]: “When there is a cause, there is an agent.”
When there is the occurrence of karmic fruition, the wise designate "the experiencer" by mere conventional usage.
Thus one sees with right wisdom. "Pure phenomena" means phenomena unmixed with any being or person.
"In this way" means that this kind of seeing is right seeing; the meaning is that it is unerring seeing.

1249. Regarding "the seed, the tree, and so forth": just as from a seed comes a tree, and from a tree a seed, so too, when searching for a succession of causes, there is no prior limit to the continuum of the seed and the tree because it is beginningless;

likewise, when searching for the sequence where result arises conditioned by karma and karma arises conditioned by result, there is no prior limit to the continuum of karma and result because it is beginningless.
It is not discerned. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), it includes such sequences as: "the hen from the egg, from the egg the hen, again from the hen the egg," and so forth.
1250–3. Regarding the future cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*):
just as in the past, so too in the future period, there is the succession of the aggregates (*khandha*), and so on.

"When the aforementioned saṃsāra exists, non-occurrence is not seen. This means that when one investigates the succession of effects in the future—thinking "from karma there will be fruition, and from fruition there will be karma"—for one whose fetters (*saṃyojana*) are not yet exhausted, the non-occurrence of karma and its fruition is not seen;
rather, they simply continue to occur. In saṃsāra, which proceeds by way of the connection between cause and fruit, [the beginning] "before... [is not seen].
By the statement, “No limit is discerned,” the absence of a cause is expressed; by the statement, “The cessation of activity is not seen,” the absence of an end to the result is expressed.
“This matter” refers to the matter stated in the passage beginning with, “There is no doer of karma.
“Not self-dependent” means not having mastery over oneself; the meaning is that they are dependent on wrong adherence. “Mutually contradictory” means...
Views that are mutually contradictory, or views that conflict with one another.
It is "profound" because it is the domain of profound knowledge; likewise, it is "subtle. It is "empty" because of the emptiness of beings and the emptiness of mutual intrinsic nature.
It is called "condition" because it is the condition for name-and-form, and by the penetration of that condition alone, everything is penetrated.
1254–6. "There is no kamma in the result" means that there is no kamma persisting within the result, just as dust and the like do not persist on a wall or similar surface.
"There is no ripening in the kamma" means that likewise there is no ripening persisting within the kamma.
To clarify this very point by way of a simile, it was said: "Just as [there is none] in the sun," and so forth. "In the gem" refers to the sun-crystal (sūriyakanta-maṇi). No...
"Outside of them, that exists"—having said this, [it is shown that] outside of those [three causes], that fire does not exist.

"By means of the fuel" means by means of the three conditions, such as heat and so forth, when they have come together. Although the passage beginning with "Not within the action" was already explained below in terms of its meaning, it should be understood that it is stated again for the purpose of concluding the simile.
1257–8. If cause and fruit were mutually devoid of one another, how could the fruit be produced from the cause? To this he said: “But it is by depending on karma.
Not only is the fruit of karma empty and devoid of an agent, but all categories of phenomena (dhamma) are likewise devoid of a doer;
to demonstrate this, the verse beginning with “There is no god here” was spoken. [The phrase] “by means of the causal equipment of conditions” refers to...
Because a single cause does not produce either a single or multiple fruits, it is "the sign of the rooting out of causes" (*hetusamūhanimitta*);
or, since "provision" (*sambhāra*) is a designation for conditions, the meaning is "the sign of the causal condition" (*hetupaccayanimitta*). 1259.
Having crossed over the time-periods, they are free from doubt: having crossed over the sixteenfold doubt regarding the three time-periods. Not only this...
He abandons the sixteenfold doubt, and furthermore, he also relinquishes the eightfold doubt that occurs in the manner beginning with, "he doubts the Teacher.
For here, by "doubt," mundane phenomena—which serve as the objects of doubt regarding the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the training—are intended.
Indeed, defilements cannot arise with reference to supramundane phenomena.
They are able [to discern]. "The past" (*pubbanta*) refers to the past aggregates (*khandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*); "the future" (*aparanta*) refers to those yet to come;
"the past and future" (*pubbantāparanta*) refers to both of these, or alternatively, to the present continuum (*addhā-paccuppanna*) because it is connected to both parts.

By the inclusion of "dependently arisen phenomena," the eighth object of doubt—the mere name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-matta*)—is grasped; however, by the inclusion of "specific conditionality" (*idappaccayatā*), its condition is grasped.
Since it has been grasped, when the sixteen-based doubt is abandoned, the eight-based doubt becomes truly baseless.
And with the abandonment of these, even the sixty-two types of views are suppressed, because they are associated with views through their association with doubt.
For just as a view is completely eradicated only together with doubt, so too is doubt.
When suppressed, it is suppressed together with the view itself.
For the doubt regarding the sixteen bases—which proceeds in the manner of "Did I exist in the past? and so forth—is based upon the adherence to a self;

that very doubt is what is described as having the prior limit and so forth as its object, as well as the sixty-two types of views which have the adherence to a self as their basis, and those associated with them which have the Buddha and others as their objects.
"Arisen" means having arisen and being established.
1260–2. "Known as the 'Crossing of Doubt'" means it is known as the crossing of doubt because of the overcoming of the aforementioned doubts.
It is not only known as the "Crossing of Doubt," but it is also called "knowledge of the stability of phenomena," "knowledge according to reality," and "right vision."

This has been stated. Herein, they are called *dhammas* because they are maintained (*dhāriyanti*) by their own conditions. It is called *ṭhiti* (stability) because the fruit remains therein, depending on it for its existence;
thus, the stability of *dhammas* is *dhammaṭṭhiti*, meaning the conditions that are *dhammas*.

Alternatively, *dhamma* means cause—as in such terms as "analytical knowledge of *dhammas*" (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*)—and thus *dhammaṭṭhiti* refers to the nature of the stability of the cause. From the perspective of the *dhamma*...
And since there is no other intrinsic nature (sabhāva), the conditionality of conditioned phenomena is "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa).
Knowledge of the things as they truly are—namely, the impermanence and so forth of formations as they truly are—is "knowledge of things as they truly are" (yathābhūtañāṇa).
"Seeing rightly" is right vision (sammādassana). "Having gained a footing" means that the footing in the Teaching is the Noble Path (ariyamagga). This...
However, although he has not yet attained that [fruit], because he stands in the practice of the means for attaining it, he is as if one who has gained a firm footing;

thus he is called "one who has gained a footing. For this very reason, the minor stream-enterer (cūḷaka-sotāpanna), being endowed with mundane virtue, concentration, and wisdom, is certain—just like a stream-enterer—and destined for a happy destination, even though he does not penetrate further.

The "one who has entered the stream" (sotāpanna) is one for whom the states of deprivation, the miserable destinies, and the fallen realms have been exhausted. Alternatively, he is "one who has gained a foothold" through the attainment of purification by overcoming doubt.
For, by seeing name-and-form together with their conditions, the thorn of wrong view is properly struck out;

having discarded the theories of no-cause and irregular causes, and knowing the occurrence of phenomena according to their respective conditions, his faith is established in the Teaching, and thus he is "one who has gained a foothold."

It is called "name" (*nāma*). Through the discernment of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-vavatthāna*), one understands the truth of suffering (*dukkha-sacca*); through the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*), the truth of the origin (*samudaya-sacca*);

and subsequently, by means of the method of mental attention to impermanence and so forth, having directly known (*abhiññā*) the truth of the path (*magga-sacca*), one sees the state of suffering in its occurrence.
Then, seeing that its cessation consists in non-occurrence, because of being single-mindedly inclined toward that cessation, even by means of the mundane [path]—
Because he has realized the four noble truths through knowledge, he is incapable of rebirth in the states of misery (apāya) and is capable of rebirth on the plane of a stream-enterer (sotāpanna);
thus he is called a "minor stream-enterer" (cūḷasotāpanna), as it is said: "For the stream-enterer is minor.
Therefore—because this knowledge possesses such great benefit—one who is wise is endowed with the wisdom that regards his own welfare.
Therefore he said, "one who desires welfare.
Thus ends [the section] from the *Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanā*, titled *Abhidhammatthavikāsinī*.
The commentary on the description of purification by overcoming doubt is finished.
Chapter Twenty:
The commentary on the description of purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path.

1263. Now, the sequence for the exposition of the purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path—which was listed immediately after the purification by overcoming doubt—has been reached.
However, that [purification] occurs when the adventitious defilements such as the "aura" (obhāsa) arise;

and since these aurae and so forth arise in the knowledge of arising and passing away (udayabbaya-ñāṇa), and the knowledge of arising and passing away arises when there is insight into the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa-vipassanā);

And for him, the comprehension by groups (kalāpasammasana) is the beginning. For that is easy for a beginner to comprehend because it proceeds by way of defining phenomena after summarizing them according to their distinctions such as past and so forth;
therefore, in order to show that one should first apply oneself to that very practice and accomplish it in due order, [the text] says: "By means of comprehension by groups alone," and so forth.
It has been undertaken. Alternatively, there is the comprehension of groups (kalāpasammasana) between the two purifications;

however, that must be included within one of the two purifications. Since it constitutes the beginning of the knowledge of what is the path and what is not the path (maggāmaggañāṇa), its inclusion right there is appropriate;
thus, with the desire to include it in this very place, it is said: "by means of the comprehension of groups alone," and so forth. However, some [teachers]...

Since "comprehension by groups" (kalāpasammasana) is not included even within the single purification [of purification of view], they describe the practice of insight (vipassanācāra) without mentioning it. By means of comprehension by groups alone— that is,
by way of defining phenomena that are divided into categories such as past and so forth,

either by grouping them together or by comprehending those groups— one should apply oneself to the insight of the knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path (maggāmaggañāṇadassanavipassanā).
Alternatively, by way of expressing the instrumental case in the sense of the locative, the meaning is: "The practice of comprehension by groups (kalāpasammasana) is to be undertaken.

Although it was stated that "the practice is to be undertaken by means of comprehension by groups alone," it has not been shown here in order to avoid prolixity in the text; rather, it should be understood from the *Visuddhimagga*. 1264.

"Of a presently arisen phenomenon" refers to either a present phenomenon in terms of continuity (santati-paccuppanna) or a present phenomenon in terms of the moment (khaṇa-paccuppanna). From the beginning...
However, the arising and falling away of the momentary present are difficult to discern;
therefore, one should first practice the contemplation of arising and falling away by way of the continuity present.
"Arising" refers to both the initial manifestation and the momentary manifestation of the two types of the present. "Alteration" means destruction.

1265. "Contemplation is also knowledge": that contemplation of both arising (*udaya*) and passing away (*vaya*) is taught as knowledge by the Perfectly Enlightened One, the possessor of excellent knowledge. Herein is the canonical text:
"How is it that wisdom regarding the contemplation of the transformation of presently arisen phenomena is knowledge of the contemplation of arising and passing away?
Form that has been born is present; its characteristic of production is arising; its characteristic of transformation is passing away."
“Contemplation is knowledge. Feeling that has arisen... perception... formations... consciousness... the eye that has arisen... up to... existence that has arisen is present;
its characteristic of production is arising (*udaya*). Its characteristic of transformation is passing away (*vaya*). Contemplation is knowledge.
Herein, the statement “the vision of arising is for the very purpose of the vision of exhaustion” is said to show that the vision of passing away is primary.
