Having stated, "wisdom in the contemplation of change," it was further said, "knowledge in the contemplation of rise and fall," because that vision of passing away is preceded by the vision of arising. 1266–8.
"Prior to its arising" means prior to its birth; "of what has not yet arisen" is what is meant. "Accumulation" (nicaya) means a heap.
Or rather, it does not exist from which [place] it could come, because that which is arising has not yet acquired its own-being and is therefore non-existent in every respect.

Therefore he said, “As it thus arises,” and so forth. Having stated, “As it thus ceases,” and so forth, he shows that just as these phenomena do not exist in every respect in the future period, so too in the past period; for they are indeed non-existent.

The simile of the lute is introduced in the Commentary at this point in order to clarify—by means of a partial illustration—the meaning contained in the whole: that there is an arising of material and immaterial phenomena when causes and conditions coincide, and that once arisen, they reach a state of total non-existence.
With the intention that this [simile] should also be brought forward here, he says: "In this regard, the simile of the lute," and so forth.
"Of this meaning" means: in the elucidation of this meaning—that there is indeed no arising of things that do not exist, and that what has arisen lacks existence thereafter.
"The simile of the lute" refers to a simile presented by way of a lute. That, moreover, should be regarded as follows:
just as when a lute is being played, there is no accumulation of the sound prior to its arising, nor is there [an accumulation] while it is arising...
It comes from accumulation. There is no going to the cardinal or intermediate directions for that which is ceasing, nor does what has ceased remain stored anywhere;
rather, depending upon the lute, the playing of the lute, and the appropriate effort of the person, it arises having not been, and having been, it passes away.
In this same way, all phenomena—both material and immaterial—arise having not been, and having been, they pass away.
1269–70. Having thus shown, in brief, the method of attention to rise and fall, [the text] further explains, in the analysis of this very knowledge of rise and fall:
"With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form"—thus one sees the rising of the aggregate of form in the sense of the arising of conditions;
and "with the arising of craving... with the arising of kamma... with the arising of nutriment, there is the arising of form"—thus [one sees it] in the sense of the arising of conditions.
One sees the arising of the aggregate of form; even while seeing the characteristic of production, one sees the arising of the aggregate of form.
Seeing the arising of the aggregate of form, one sees these five characteristics.

One sees the passing away of the aggregate of form in the sense of the cessation of conditions, thinking: "With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of form. [And so on: "With the cessation of craving... etc.

“From the cessation of karma... [and so on] ...from the cessation of nutriment comes the cessation of form”—thus one sees the fall of the aggregate of form in the sense of the cessation of conditions.
One who sees the characteristic of change also sees the fall of the aggregate of form;
seeing the fall of the aggregate of form, one sees these five characteristics. Likewise: “From the arising of ignorance comes the arising of feeling.”
One sees the arising of the aggregate of feeling in the sense of the arising of conditions: "With the arising of craving...
[and so on] ...with the arising of action... [and so on] ...with the arising of contact, there is the arising of feeling.
One sees the arising of the aggregate of feeling by seeing its characteristic of being produced; one sees the arising of the aggregate of feeling.
Contemplating, he sees these five characteristics. By way of the cessation of conditions—“with the cessation of ignorance...

[and so on] ... with the cessation of craving... [and so on] ... with the cessation of karma... [and so on] ... with the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling”—he sees the passing away of the aggregate of feeling.
Even while seeing the characteristic of change, he sees the passing away of the aggregate of feeling; of the aggregate of feeling...
When we observe these five characteristics, we see them in the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness just as we do in the aggregate of material form.
However, this is the distinction: for the consciousness aggregate, in the place of contact, one observes "the arising of name-and-form" and "the cessation of name-and-form.
Thus, by observing the rise and fall of each individual aggregate, there are ten characteristics for each, making fifty characteristics in total.

Based on those [statements], the passage beginning with "of that very knowledge" is commenced in order to show, by way of both conditions and moments, the method of attention in detail: "In this way too is the arising of form; in this way too is the passing away of form; in this way too form arises; in this way too form ceases.
Therein, "from the arising of ignorance" means from the production of ignorance, from its existence.

The meaning is as follows: Arising, which is the opposite of cessation, constitutes the state of existence; therefore, when ignorance established in a previous existence is present, there is the origination of form—that is, the arising of form—in this present existence. This is the meaning. Regarding those things included by the word "etcetera":
"From the origination of craving comes the origination of form; from the origination of kamma comes the origination of form; from the origination of nutriment comes the origination of form."
Likewise, in the passage on the vision of passing away—“With the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of form; with the cessation of craving... with the cessation of kamma...

with the cessation of nutriment comes the cessation of form”—and so forth, it should be understood that by means of the three factors beginning with ignorance, their cooperative causes, namely clinging and the rest, which belong to the past, are also included.
Among the conditions for the process of existence (*pavatti-paccaya*), because physical nutriment (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*) is the most powerful, it alone is taken up as "from the arising of nutriment.
However, when that is taken, temperature and consciousness are also necessarily included by virtue of their commonality as conditions for the process of existence;

thus, it should be understood that the demonstration of the arising of matter produced from the four [nutriments] has already been clarified through its conditionality. [This occurs] only when accompanied by the decisive support (*upanissaya*) of ignorance and craving.
The physical body arises through kamma; and in the absence of the craving for existence, which has ignorance as its proximate cause, birth itself would simply be impossible.
Just as ignorance and craving are the proximate causes for material form (rūpa), so too should they be understood for feeling (vedanā) and the other aggregates.

Nutriment, however, is the sustainer of material form once it has arisen, because edible food (kabaḷīkāra-āhāra) is intended here—or perhaps because the teaching was given according to the specific context.
Or, the inclusion of "nutriment" is by way of an inclusive description. Regarding "the cessation of ignorance":

through the non-arising cessation of ignorance by means of the knowledge of the supreme path, there is the non-arising cessation of future form, because of its non-existence in the absence of conditions. This same principle applies here as well to the statement, "With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of kamma.
Regarding "the cessation of nutriment": this refers to the absence of physical nutriment (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*), which is a condition for the process of existence. "The cessation of form" [follows].
There is an absence of the material form originated by that [contact]. The remainder should be understood according to the method explained below.
However, this is the distinction: because of the statements, “One who is touched feels; one who is touched perceives;

one who is touched intends,” and “With contact as condition, there is feeling; feeling born of eye-contact; perception and volition,” contact is the cause of the aggregates of feeling, perception, and mental formations.

The condition for occurrence and the cessation of those [factors] through their cessation: in the *Mahāpadāna Sutta* and the *Mahānidāna Sutta*, as well as in the Abhidhamma section on the mutual condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*), it is stated that "consciousness has name-and-form as its condition" (*nāmarūpapaccayā viññāṇaṃ*). Thus, name-and-form is the condition for the occurrence of consciousness, and through their cessation, there is the cessation of that [consciousness].
This is expressed in such passages as, "With the arising of contact, there is the arising of feeling," and so forth.

1271. In the observation of the arising of the aggregate of form as "ten, ten," there are these five characteristics: the characteristics of being conditioned by the existence of these four conditions—namely, ignorance, craving, kamma, and nutriment—and the characteristic of the production of form.
In the observation of its fall, there is the non-arising and cessation of the four conditions beginning with ignorance, and [the cessation] of form.
“Momentary cessation” (khaṇanirodho) and so forth—these five characteristics constitute the ten characteristics of the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha).
Likewise, there are forty characteristics for each of the four aggregates beginning with feeling (vedanākkhandha); thus, there are fifty characteristics in total.
Therefore, it is said: “fifty characteristics. Furthermore, the meaning of “characteristic” (lakkhaṇa) for those four conditions is their existence.
"And non-arising and cessation": by these eight, the arising and passing away of form and so forth are characterized;

for the arising of form and so forth is characterized by the presence of the four conditions, their passing away by non-arising and absolute cessation, while origination and transformation are indeed the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṅkhata-lakkhaṇa*). "He contemplates phenomena" refers to form and so forth.

One contemplates phenomena as possessing arising and passing away. Regarding this, some first say: "The vision of the arising and passing away of the immaterial aggregates is by way of the temporal sequence (*addhā*) and the continuity of moments (*santati*), not by way of the single moment (*khaṇa*).
According to their opinion, there would be no vision of arising and passing away from the standpoint of the moment at all.

Others, however, say: "By means of the vision of arising and passing away from the perspective of conditions, without touching upon the distinctions of past and so forth, [one sees them] as common to all."
The claim that “one sees the occurrence and availability of feeling through conditions such as ignorance, but not its arising;
and in the absence of ignorance and so forth, one sees its non-occurrence and unavailability, but not from the perspective of the moment of dissolution;
for in seeing rise and fall, one sees the arising and dissolution of present phenomena,” is incorrect. For it is by way of continuity (*santati*) that material and immaterial phenomena—
For one who is attending to rise and fall, when the development gradually reaches its peak,
the rise and fall appear moment by moment due to the attainment of a sharp and keen state of knowledge.
For this person, first attending to rise and fall from the perspective of conditions, subsequently attends to the conditioned phenomena beginning with ignorance.

Having let go [of the coarse] and grasped the aggregates that possess arising and passing away, he attends to their arising and passing away even in terms of the moment, by way of seeing their arising and passing away from the perspective of their conditions.
When his knowledge becomes sharp and clear, then material and immaterial phenomena appear as they arise and break up moment by moment. By means of that—
It is said: “In this way there is the arising of form,” and so forth. Therein, “in this way there is the arising of form” means that by the method thus stated, through the origination of ignorance...
[and so on] ...through the origination of craving... [and so on] ...through the origination of karma... [and so on] ...even through the origination of nutriment, there is the production of form.

“In this way there is its passing away” means that by the very same method thus stated, through the cessation of ignorance... [and so on] ...through the cessation of craving... [and so on] ...through the cessation of karma... [and so on] ...through the cessation of nutriment, there is the passing away of form.
"Non-arising" (*anuppāda*) is this detailed attention by way of condition. "In this way matter also arises":
in this way, even matter originating from kamma—matter originating from nutriment, temperature, and consciousness—arises, appears, and is produced.
"In this way matter passes away": even matter originating from kamma—matter originating from nutriment, temperature, and consciousness—passes away in this way.
"It ceases" is the detailed attention from the perspective of the moment. Therefore it was said:

"Thus, here, by way of conditionality, there is rise and fall from the perspective of the moment. All phenomena become manifest; that is, these phenomena, having not been, come to be, and having been, they pass away.
Just as in the present, so too in the past and future—this is the method for [understanding] phenomena of the past and so forth.
For one who sees both the arising and the passing away in two ways, the distinctions of the truths, dependent origination, the method, and the characteristics become manifest.

For such a person, whose true nature of all phenomena has thus become manifest, formations appear as ever-new, thinking: "In this way, indeed, these phenomena that have never arisen before now arise; having arisen, they cease. And not only are they ever-new, but...
They appear as things that endure for only a very brief time—like a line drawn with a stick on water, like a mustard seed placed on the point of an awl, or like a flash of lightning.

Therefore he said, "Like lines of sticks on water," and so forth. Although only the lines of sticks on water and the others were shown for the purpose of demonstrating a progressively more extremely brief duration, nevertheless, it was the slow cessation itself that was demonstrated.
This is because the cessation of formations is even more rapid than that.

For it is said that the cessation of material form is swifter than the clashing of the sharp edges of the hoofs of celestial youths, who, delighting in the act of running, dash headlong against one another from above and below;
how much more so, then, for immaterial phenomena. It is not only those things that endure for a very brief time that appear thus.

Then, thinking "even though it is without core, it appears to be so," he said "the plantain tree" and so forth. In that context, a firebrand being whirled in a circular form is itself the "firebrand-wheel" (*alātacakka*).
Illusion (*māyā*) refers to such things as the "net of Indra" produced by the power of spells and medicinal herbs.
"To this extent" means from the application of the comprehension of the aggregates (*kalāpasammasana*) onwards, up until the penetration of arising and passing away (*udayabbaya*).

The method of development has been commenced; thus far, even the comprehension by groups (*kalāpa-sammasana*) through this procedure of development is merely a preliminary exercise (*parikamma*) for the arising of the knowledge of rise and fall.
The connection is: "the knowledge that sees rise and fall. And as for the characteristics... [omission] ...it stands:

having penetrated the fifty characteristics in this manner—that what is subject to decay arises, and what has arisen meets with decay— *Note: The ellipsis indicates the omission of intermediate text regarding the contemplation of the three characteristics.*
[The state] is established. Now, because that which has just arisen has not yet attained strength, he says "tender" (*taruṇa*).
Insight (*vipassanā*) in the primary sense is obtained by the contemplation (*sammasana*) that proceeds by way of the comprehension of aggregates (*kalāpasammasana*) and so forth.
He says "and for whom," etc., because [insight] is obtained only by that which proceeds by way of the contemplation of rise and fall (*udayabbayānupassanā*) and so forth.
1278–80. Now, showing that ten imperfections of insight (*vipassanupakkilesa*) arise for one who is practicing insight by means of this "young" insight (*taruṇavipassanā*), he says:
"Of insight," and so forth. "By this" refers to the young insight consisting of the contemplation of rise and fall (*udayabbayānupassanā*);

it does not refer to the young insight consisting of the contemplation of dissolution (*bhaṅgānupassanā*), nor to that consisting of the contemplation of disenchantment (*nibbidānupassanā*), and so on.

The meaning is "by powerful insight" (*balavavipassanāya*). For at that time, the defilements of insight (*vipassanūpakkilesā*) do not arise. In the phrase "of the one who possesses insight" (*vipassakassa*), the particle *eva*—meaning "only"—is indicated by elision;
thus it means "of the one who possesses insight alone. For this very reason, he will later say, "of one who has attained penetration," and so forth.

They are called "defilements" (*upakkilesā*) because they defile insight by serving as the basis for the grasping of views and other such errors. "Attained" refers to the penetration of the fruit of the Four Noble Truths.
Because he has attained penetration (*sampattapaṭivedha*) and is one among those such as stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), it says "of the stream-enterer and others.

Furthermore, the word *api ca* has the sense of a conjunction for what is about to be said. And this was stated by way of a description of the highest limit (*ukkaṭṭhaniddesa*), because [the fetters] do not arise even for one who has reached powerful insight (*balavavipassanā*).
Or else, the phrase "of one who has attained penetration" was stated with reference to one who has reached powerful insight; he too—
For indeed, because one stands in a place near to the attainment of penetration (*paṭivedha*), it is called "penetration already attained.

And this being so, the word *api* has the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) as stated. Alternatively, the word *api* has the sense of the conjunction of what has been stated, while the word *ca* has the sense of the conjunction of what has not been stated;
by this, the laying aside of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) is included. Having begun insight (*vipassanā*)...
Even for one who has fallen into an intermediate cessation, the defilements of insight do not arise.
"One who has practiced wrongly" means one who has practiced in whatever way through a failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*) and so forth; the meaning is one who has engaged in a censurable practice.
Alternatively, "one who has practiced wrongly" refers to one whose practice is devoid of the absence of right practice known as the cultivation of insight (*vipassanābhāvanā*).
1281. Indeed, it is the practice of insight (vipassanā) together with its requisites that constitutes right practice in the preliminary stage;
any other is wrong practice. For this very reason, on the side of purification, it is said: "of one who has practiced rightly.

And since that [right practice] occurs even for one who has laid down the burden, in this context even one who has set aside the meditation subject is included by this very term. Thus: "of one who has practiced rightly."
This applies to one who has practiced correctly according to the method explained below, and not to one who has practiced wrongly or who has abandoned the burden.
"Devoted to yoga" means one whose habit is to apply himself to meditation through appropriate application or knowledge.
Since that state of being devoted to yoga can also occur by way of serenity (samatha), he says "only for one who constantly practices insight (vipassanā)" in order to exclude that. "Arise" means...

Here too, the word *eva* (only/just) should be connected [to the verb]; thus, the meaning is that they do not arise. Otherwise, the very knowledge of what is the path and what is not the path (*maggāmagga-ñāṇa*) would be impossible.
The phrase "it is said" (*kirā*) refers to oral tradition. Furthermore, it should be understood that this oral tradition has come down precisely through the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
As it is said: "How is the mind seized by agitation regarding phenomena (*dhammuddhacca*)? When one attends to [phenomena] as impermanent, a radiance (*obhāsa*) arises..."
Thinking "light is a phenomenon," he adverts to the light; from that arises distraction and restlessness.

With a mind agitated by that restlessness, he does not understand, as it really is, the appearance of things as impermanent. He does not understand, as it really is, their appearance as suffering... [and so on] ...or their appearance as non-self.
Likewise, when attending to them as impermanent, knowledge arises... [and so on] ...joy, tranquility, and bliss.
“Resolution, exertion, establishment, equanimity, and attachment arise. One adverts to attachment, thinking, ‘This is a state.
From that comes distraction and restlessness. With a mind agitated by that restlessness, one does not understand, as it really is, the appearance of things as impermanent;
one does not understand, as it really is, the appearance of things as suffering... [and so on] ...one does not understand, as it really is, the appearance of things as non-self.”
1282. Now, in order to clarify the true nature of those [signs] such as the illumination, and to show the manner in which insight becomes defiled when they arise, it is said:

"Of insight," and so forth. The "illumination of insight" is a radiant material form (*rūpa*) produced by the mind of insight and produced by the temperature (*utu*) belonging to one's own continuity (*sasantati*). Among these, that produced by the mind of insight...
The body of the yogi remains radiant; having released the other body, it pervades everywhere according to the power of his knowledge.
This is perceived by him alone, and he sees even material forms in the space touched by that light.

Regarding this, they say it must be investigated whether he sees while seeing with eye-consciousness (*cakkhu-viññāṇa*) or with mind-consciousness (*mano-viññāṇa*). Thus says the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla.
However, it was said: "It appears as if reasonable to say that, like one who has attained the divine eye, that [object] is cognizable solely by mind-consciousness. 1283–4.

Regarding the statement, "One who has reached the path and reached the fruit thinks, 'I am'": this refers to the fact that even though one has not yet reached the path, one thinks, "Indeed, no such radiance has ever arisen for me before;
surely I have reached the Noble Path and realized the fruit," thus taking hold of what is not the path.

He grasps it as “the path. But for one who grasps in this way—that is, for one who grasps what is not the path itself as “the path”—the very course of insight (*vipassanāvīthī*) is called “overstepped,” because the practitioner has let go [of the practice] due to the overweening conceit (*adhimāna*) that thinks, “I have attained the path.
There is also a reading *vipassanāvīthinti*; for one who grasps in this manner—
The meaning is that insight (vipassanā) has then truly "ascended the path.
"That bhikkhu sits relishing the very light" means that the bhikkhu, having abandoned the insight he had undertaken, sits relishing the light itself through either greed or wrong view.
Furthermore, for some bhikkhus, this light extends only as far as the place where they sit cross-legged.
It arises illuminating: for some, the inner chamber; for some, the outer chamber; for some, the entire monastery;
for some, a *gāvuta*, half a *yojana*, a *yojana*, two *yojanas*, or three *yojanas*;
and for some, creating a single light from the surface of the earth up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma-world, just as fish and turtles [are visible] within a *yojana* of the ocean.
They appear; thus they arise. But in the case of the Blessed One, it arose illuminating the ten-thousandfold world-system.
1285. "Insight-rapture" (*vipassanā-pīti*) is rapture associated with the mind of insight. The minor and other types have already been described below;
this fivefold rapture arises in succession as the path of insight-contemplation of rise and fall has entered its course.
However, when it reaches the head, there is only the pervading joy (*pharaṇā-pīti*) together with the knowledge of rise and fall (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*).
For even at times other than the moments of access and absorption, there is indeed pervading joy. Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: "It arises filling the entire body. 1286–7.
Regarding the phrase "for the meditator... they come to be": for that meditator in whom this serenity (*passaddhi*) has arisen, during his night-quarters...
The meaning is that for one sitting in the daytime resting place, both body and mind become tranquil; there is no distress.

Since the six pairs beginning with tranquility (passaddhi) are mutually conjoined, he said "and they are light," etc., showing all of them by way of demonstrating their function—namely, that when tranquility has arisen, the others have also indeed arisen.
And here, by the mention of "body" (kāya), it should be understood that the material body (rūpakāya) is also included, and not merely the triad of aggregates beginning with feeling (vedanā).
For bodily tranquility (kāyapassaddhi) and the others are the removers of distress and so forth even for the material body.
"They become wieldy" means that they are not only wieldy, but also perfectly clear and straight; however, because these two are inseparable, both are implied.
It was not stated separately because the state of tranquility (*passaddhi*) and so forth of body and mind occurs precisely through the destruction of the remaining defilements (*saṃkilesadhamma*)—

such as restlessness (*uddhacca*), sloth-and-torpor (*thinamiddha*), views (*diṭṭhi*), conceit (*māna*), the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), lack of faith (*assaddhiya*), deceit (*māyā*), and hypocrisy (*sāṭheyya*)— which serve as the causes for their lack of tranquility and so forth,
since at that time the arising of the consciousness of insight (*vipassanā*) proceeds by way of their dismantling.
1288–90. It belongs to humans (*manussa*), thus it is human (*mānusī*); that is, the pleasure and delight of sensual desire appropriate for humans.
Because it does not transcend being experienced by such distinguished humans, it is also included as divine pleasure (*dibbarati*).

Or, because it resembles human [pleasure], divine pleasure is "human" (*mānusī*); because it transcends that, it is "not human" (*amānusī*), meaning non-human; that is, "non-human" (*amānusiṃ*). "An empty dwelling" (*suññāgāraṃ*)...
Whatever secluded lodging there may be, or even insight (vipassanā) itself— because it is empty of permanence and so forth, and because it serves as a basis for the happiness of the practitioner—
it receives the designation "an empty dwelling" (suññāgāra). Through the disappearance of those defilements that prevent the settling of the mind,
and through a bhikkhu’s seeing the terror of cyclic existence with a peaceful mind by means of right knowledge...

For those people who possess correctly undertaken insight and who contemplate and comprehend material and immaterial phenomena by way of the contemplation of their arising and passing away, there arises a delight known as the joy and happiness of insight—a delight that is superhuman because it is the objective domain of such individuals. This is the summary meaning of the verse here.

The second verse, however, is spoken specifically with reference to the knowledge of arising and passing away (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*). In that context, "from whatever" means from whatever form or from whatever formless state.
1291. "Knowledge and the rest" refers to the seven beginning with knowledge and faith.

They are to be understood by way of insight (vipassanā) according to the method already stated—that is, following the manner in which it was said: "Knowledge is insight-knowledge; faith is the faith associated with the mind of insight," and so forth.
In this context, "knowledge" is like a discharged thunderbolt for one who weighs and examines material and immaterial phenomena by way of contemplating their rise and fall.
A state that is free from agitation, sharp, heroic, and exceedingly clear arises. For by means of this, the yogi thinks, "I have attained the Path.
Faith (*saddhā*) is a powerful faith consisting of an extraordinary clarity of the mind and mental factors due to the removal of the turbidity of the defilements;
it is not, however, faith that functions as a mere conviction in the results of karma or in the Triple Gem. It is also well-established (*sūpaṭṭhitā*).

The immovable [knowledge] arises, resembling the king of mountains. And when this has arisen, whatever place he reviews, that very place enters into his knowledge of rebirth according to karma (*yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa*), which has become its surrounding ornament by plunging into and leaping across it.
Because the other world is its object, and because the sphere of visible forms (*vaṇṇāyatana*) has passed away, the other world is the domain of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).
It appears as if through mindfulness. Pleasure, however, arises as exceedingly refined, suffusing the entire body.
When that has arisen, the whole body becomes pervaded and nourished by the exceedingly refined material qualities (rūpa) originated by it.
Equanimity, moreover, consists of both equanimity of insight (vipassanupekkhā) and equanimity of adverting (āvajjanupekkhā). Therein, because of its nature of investigating and scrutinizing—

Insight-equanimity (*vipassanupekkhā*) is that which abides in a state of neutrality while investigating mental formations (*saṅkhāra*). In terms of its actual meaning, however, it is simply the equanimity of onlooking (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*) occurring in that manner.

The feeling associated with the mind-door adverting consciousness (*manodvārāvajjana-citta*) is called "adverting-equanimity" because it functions as a neutral observation during the act of adverting.
This twofold equanimity arises at that time; for indeed, in that [moment]...
At that time, equanimity regarding insight (vipassanupekkhā), which maintains neutrality toward the arising and passing away of all formations, arises powerfully;
so too does the equanimity of adverting at the mind-door.

For as he adverts to this or that object, it proceeds with a sharpness like a loosened thunderbolt or like a red-hot iron arrow leaping from its quiver. His energy, moreover, is neither slack nor over-exerted.
While grasping at the associated states from the side of the defilements and the side of indolence, there arises a state that is poorly grasped;
and there arises a subtle and peaceful aspect, which creates a basis for attachment toward insight adorned with light and so forth, and which functions with excessive intensity in meditation.
This [aspect] is not even fit to be regarded as a defilement. And just as it is with the light, so it is here.
Likewise, when any of these other [factors] have arisen, the practitioner perceives: "Indeed, never before has such rapture arisen in me;
never before have such serenity, knowledge, faith, mindfulness, bliss, equanimity, energy, or inclination arisen;
surely I have attained the path and its fruit. As he perceives thus, his insight is said to have entered the path.
He sits relishing those very [defilements]. Furthermore, these imperfections of insight (vipassanūpakkilesa) generally arise in those who have attained serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā).
Because the defilements have been suppressed by meditative attainment (samāpatti), they do not manifest; consequently, he gives rise to the thought, "I am an Arahant.
1292–3. Regarding the basis for the imperfection: in the ultimate sense, view, conceit, and craving are here the imperfections; of these...
It is by way of its object (*vatthu*) as the place of arising, not by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), because it is unwholesome.
However, just as with the aura and so forth, attachment (*nikanti*) also serves as the basis for the grasping of views and the like; thus, its status as an object is indeed appropriate.

For one who adverts to this or that [aura, etc.], meditation declines; that is to say, for one who adverts to this or that aura and so forth, through the influence of views, conceit, and craving, [the thought arises]: "This is mine..."

For one who applies the apprehension of "illumination" and so forth, the development enters the cognitive process (*vīthi*) and revolves. One who has heard little is called "one of little learning" (*appa-suta*).
However, when illumination and the rest arise for one who is "learned" (*bahu-suta*), he reflects: "This illumination has arisen for me;
moreover, it is impermanent, conditioned, dependently originated, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation."
Or, if the illumination were the self, it would be fit to be grasped as "self"; however, this which is non-self has been grasped as "self. Therefore, he contemplates it thus:

"In the sense of being subject to lack of mastery, it is non-self; in the sense of not existing after having come to be, it is impermanent; in the sense of being oppressed by arising and passing away, it is suffering," and so forth.
Contemplating in this way, he disentangles the tangle of defilements regarding the illumination and the other phenomena.
Phenomena are not the path; rather, insight-knowledge that has entered the right course and is freed from defilements is the path.
Thus, one distinguishes between what is the path and what is not the path. Therefore it was said: "All [states] such as illumination," and so forth.

Knowledge regarding the path and the non-path is "knowledge of the path and the non-path" (*maggāmagga-ñāṇa*); what is meant is the purification by knowledge and vision of the path and the non-path (*maggāmagga-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi*). For the attainment of this purification by knowledge and vision of the path and the non-path...
And by that yogi, the determination of the three truths has been accomplished. How so?

First, through the purification of view (*diṭṭhivisuddhi*), by means of the determination of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the determination of the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) is accomplished. Through the purification by overcoming doubt (*kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi*), by means of the discernment of conditions (*paccayapariggaha*), the determination of the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*) is accomplished. For in the method of the Abhidhamma, all defilements...

Kamma is the truth of origination, and through the determination of the right path within this purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path, there is the truth of the path.
For by determining the path that serves as the means to that [cessation], the [truth of cessation] is indeed determined as well.
Thus, first of all, the definition of the three truths is accomplished by mundane knowledge alone.

Thus ends the commentary on the section explaining the Purification by Knowledge and Vision of What Is and What Is Not the Path, within the *Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanā* titled *Abhidhammatthavikāsinī*.
Chapter Twenty-One: Explanation of the Description of Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Way (Paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhiniddesavaṇṇanā) 1298.
"By means of eight knowledges" means by means of the eight knowledges beginning with the knowledge of arising and passing away (udayabbayañāṇa). Of the conduct of insight...
The knowledge of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa*) at the point of reaching the summit is insight that has reached its peak.

Its reaching the summit, however, occurs by way of the eight knowledges beginning with the knowledge of arising and passing away; thus he said, "by way of the eight knowledges. The ninth is the knowledge in conformity with the truths.

Thus, these eight—beginning with the knowledge of arising and passing away—and this ninth knowledge are called the "knowledge and vision of the way" (*paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana*). One proceeds [by means of it].

This is called the "Noble Path" because it is the way of practice; and it is called "knowledge and vision" in the sense of knowing the arising and passing away [of formations] and in the sense of seeing them directly.
To show those knowledges according to their specific nature, it is said: "eight knowledges," and so forth. Among these, there is the knowledge of the contemplation of arising and passing away.

Although it is the foundation for the full understanding by scrutinization (*tīraṇapariññā*), nevertheless, in the sense already stated, it is indeed also the knowledge and vision of the way (*paṭipadāñāṇadassana*);
therefore, that too is mentioned here. In the other case, however, it was said with reference to what has merely arisen and is not yet proficient.

For when it is not yet proficient, it serves as the basis for the full understanding by abandoning (*pahānapariññā*) through the accomplishment of the abandonment of the perception of permanence and so forth. Since, by the attainment of that [proficiency]—
Among the eighteen great insights (*mahāvipassanā*), some are indeed already attained.
For without the penetration of the rise and fall through direct experience, the mere investigation of the general characteristics cannot result in the supreme abandonment of opposing factors.
And if there is no abandonment of opposing factors, how could knowledge and the other qualities possess an unimpeded momentum like a diamond, or possess such qualities as sharpness and clarity?
Therefore, knowledge of rise and fall that has reached a state of proficiency should be regarded as belonging exclusively to the side of full understanding by abandoning (*pahānapariññā*).

1300–2. Regarding "in dissolution" (*bhaṅge*): it is "dissolution" because of the dissolution of formations. It is "fear" (*bhaya*) because one who sees things as they really are fears this. The phenomena of the three planes (*tebhūmakadhammā*) are that which is feared;

when these appear as fearful, the knowledge that grasps the mode of what is to be feared is "knowledge of fear" (*bhayeñāṇa*). For it is thus called "knowledge of the appearance as fear" (*bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇa*).

It is called [that]. One who desires to be liberated is "one desirous of liberation" (*muccitukamyam*); this refers either to the mind or to the person. The state of being such is "desire for liberation" (*muccitukamyatā*).

Since that, however, is simply knowledge, it is said: "Knowledge is desire for liberation. Furthermore, knowledge that occurs in the mode of reflective contemplation is "knowledge of contemplation by reflecting" (*paṭisaṅkhānupassanā-ñāṇa*). That which occurs by way of viewing formations with equanimity through a state of detachment—

Knowledge is the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa*). However, the description here uses a *visandhi* (extended euphonic) construction for the sake of the metrical structure of the verse.
It is called "conformable to the truths" (*saccānulomika*) because, by the removal of the coarsest of the obscurations to the truths, it is conducive to the penetration of the truths.
Thus he says: "This is the knowledge conformable to the truths; it is called 'conformity' (*anuloma*)."
1303. If it is asked: "Since the knowledge of rise and fall has already been established previously, for what purpose is there further application to it?

It is for the purpose of clearly discerning the characteristics of impermanence and so forth. For the knowledge of rise and fall, having been defiled below by the ten imperfections, was unable to discern the three characteristics according to their actual nature; [only when] freed from those imperfections...
However, if he is able [to do so], then for the purpose of discerning the characteristics, he should again apply himself to that very same object.

Yet, because he does not attend to the characteristics of arising and passing away, and because they are concealed by the continuity of the stream and the density of the postures, those characteristics do not become manifest.
Therefore, by attending to arising and passing away and stripping away the continuity, he should discern the characteristic of impermanence as constant oppression.
Having grasped the postures, having disclosed the characteristic of suffering, having analyzed the elements and performed the resolution of the compact,
and having observed the characteristic of non-self, one should repeatedly contemplate formations as "impermanent,
suffering, and non-self. As he thus weighs and examines them, when the entire range of formations appears to him with lightness, [he realizes...]
Due to the sharpness of his knowledge, the object appears as if it were breaking apart, with distinctions such as its arising being concealed;
his knowledge becomes established precisely at the moment of dissolution. At that time, the insight-knowledge called "contemplation of dissolution" (bhaṅgānupassanā) has been attained.
As he cultivates that very contemplation of dissolution—which has the cessation of formations as its object—when, amidst all states of existence, modes of birth, destinations, stations, and abodes...
Because formations have the nature of breaking up, they appear as a great terror, like ghosts, demons, and the like;
at that time, his knowledge of the appearance of fear has been attained. But does this knowledge itself feel fear? It does not fear. For it [knows]:
"Past formations have ceased; present ones are ceasing; future ones will cease."

It is merely a matter of investigation; however, because it involves grasping all conditioned phenomena—which have fallen into calamity—as being manifestly fearful, it is called "knowledge of the manifestation of fear.
When one cultivates that knowledge of the manifestation of fear, [one perceives] no refuge whatsoever among the conditioned phenomena within all states of existence.
Neither a shelter nor a refuge is perceived; rather, formations appear as nothing but a danger, like an enemy with sword raised.
As he thus perceives only the danger in formations, the knowledge of danger (*ādīnava-ñāṇa*) arises.
While he is thus seeing all formations as dangerous, when [he applies it] to those included within the three realms of existence...
Disenchantment arises, weariness settles, and he gains delight in the state of peace that is dissociated from all conditioned phenomena;
at that time, the knowledge called "contemplation of disenchantment" has arisen for him.

When, through this knowledge of disenchantment, his mind no longer clings even to a single conditioned phenomenon as he becomes disenchanted with all conditioned phenomena, [he is liberated] from everything.
From the contemplation of formations, a desire to escape arises like that of a frog who has fallen into the mouth of a snake;
at that time, the knowledge called "desire for deliverance" (muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa) has arisen.

When he thus becomes unable to perceive all formations under the aspects of permanence, pleasure, beauty, and self, then—in order to provide the means for deliverance—by means of [contemplating] impermanence, non-finality, and so forth...

When one comprehends the entire range of conditioned phenomena by superimposing the characteristic of impermanence through their constant oppression and so forth, the characteristic of suffering through their state of being afflicted and so forth, repulsiveness through their lack of intrinsic worth and so forth, and the characteristic of non-self through their emptiness and so forth, there arises the knowledge called "contemplation of reflection" (*paṭisaṅkhānupassanā-ñāṇa*).
By means of that, regarding those conditioned phenomena thus comprehended, [the realization occurs]: "This is empty of a self or..."
By means of the passage beginning with “or as belonging to a self,” emptiness is described through its divisions, such as the two-pointed [emptiness] and so forth;

that should be discerned. When one has thus seen it as empty and, having applied the three characteristics, is investigating, then—having abandoned both fear and delight—equanimity becomes established toward all conditioned phenomena, like a man who has relinquished his wife, and the mind [withdraws] from the three realms of existence.
When it does not extend further, then the knowledge called equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa*) has arisen for him.

However, as long as this does not see Nibbāna, it remains indifferent even while investigating formations, relying again and again upon formations—even those undesirable—just like a crow searching for food in a pit, though it sees no other direction. Therefore it was said: "But among these knowledges," and so forth.
1306. *Vipassanā*... [as before] ...is called "leading to emergence" (*vuṭṭhānagāminī*).
Because it has reached the peak (*sikhā*), that is, the highest state, it is "reached the peak. It goes toward emergence, thus it is "leading to emergence.

For "emergence" refers to the Path because of its emerging from both the external sign to which one is attached and from what occurs internally; since it goes toward that, it is "leading to emergence."
The meaning is that it "joins with the Path.

(1307) *Taṃ* refers to that knowledge of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa*), which is called "insight that has reached its culmination" and "knowledge in conformity with the truths" (*saccānulomañāṇa*).
*Āsevantassa* means of one who practices, develops, and cultivates it repeatedly by way of comprehension (*sammasana*).
For him, conviction through resolve will arise as more powerful by way of cultivation; energy will be well-sustained and capable of dispelling opposing factors;
mindfulness will be well-established through its orientation toward the object;
and the mind will be well-concentrated due to the preponderance of tranquility and bliss. Thus, it becomes a condition for the arising of conformity-knowledge.
The equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā), which is capable of becoming [the path], arises with sharp intensity.
1308–12. Contemplating impermanence and so forth through one aspect—such as "impermanent" and so on—it proceeds seven times and then ceases;
having entered the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), it is said to have "descended. After that, it is considered a turn of the life-continuum.

"By the method employed in equanimity towards formations" means by the very method employed in equanimity towards formations through taking the object as impermanent and so forth, not by the method of comprehension (*sammasita*).

Therefore he said: "Impermanent... performing... "Having caused the subsidence into the life-continuum" means having brought about the turning back of the life-continuum, not allowing the mind to proceed by way of the life-continuum. "The preliminary work" refers to the path.

Because it performs the preliminary work (*parikamma*) and acts as a condition for reflection (*paṭisaṅkhāraka*). "Access" (*upacāra*) is so called because it is near to the Path (*magga*), or because it moves in its vicinity.
1313–6. He himself states its conformity (*anuloma*) by means of the words "of the preceding," and so forth.

For this [knowledge] occurs with reference to formations (*saṅkhāra*) by way of the characteristic of impermanence (*anicca-lakkhaṇa*) and so on; thus, "it is indeed the knowledge of rise and fall (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*) regarding those very phenomena that possess rise and fall."

“Indeed, it was only in that which is subject to arising and falling away that he saw the contemplation of arising and falling; indeed, it was only in that which is subject to dissolution that he saw the contemplation of dissolution;
indeed, it was only in that which is fearful that the contemplation of fear appeared as fear;

indeed, it was only in that which is fraught with danger that the contemplation of danger saw the danger; indeed, it was only in that which is to be disenchanted with that the knowledge of disenchantment became disenchanted.”

And because these eight knowledges have performed their task, it is as if they were saying in substance: "Indeed, the knowledge of desire for deliverance has become desirous of deliverance precisely regarding that which must be delivered";

"Indeed, the knowledge of reflection has reflected precisely upon that which must be reflected upon"; and "Indeed, equanimity regarding formations has become equanimous precisely toward that which must be treated with equanimity."
It conforms because it has the function of comprehending the three characteristics in all forms of insight;
likewise, because the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment on the higher noble path are to be attained by means of that very method.
For indeed, if conformity knowledge did not proceed by way of suppressing the defilements that obscure the coarse truths, change-of-lineage knowledge would not arise.
When change-of-lineage knowledge has not yet arisen, path-knowledge does not arise;
therefore, because it conforms to the preceding and succeeding stages, it is "designated as 'conformity' (anuloma).

For that very reason—namely, by way of conformity with the lower knowledges and because it conforms to the higher factors conducive to enlightenment—it is called "knowledge of conformity to the truths" regarding the truth of the path.
Because it is conformable (*anulomika*). "Leading to emergence" (*vuṭṭhānagāminī*) means [it is] insight leading to emergence that has conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) as its object.
"The end" (*pariyosāna*) means the prior limit. For among the insights having conditioned phenomena as their object, this is specifically called "insight leading to emergence.
However, that which has the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) as its object goes to, or reaches, emergence—which is the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*)—in its entirety.
For even more specifically, it deserves to be called "insight leading to emergence"; thus he said, "the knowable in all its aspects," and so forth.
1317–8. "Praised" means lauded;
it is so called because it seeks out the great aggregates of virtue and the rest, which have the Noble Path as their foundation.

"By the Great Seer, the Fully Enlightened One, through seeking. "Peaceful" means due to the state of having calmed the defilements (*kilesa*). "Yoga" means meditation (*bhāvanā*) or application to meditation.
Thus ends [the section] from the *Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanā*, titled *Abhidhammatthavikāsinī*.
The commentary on the description of purification by knowledge and vision of the way is finished.
Chapter Twenty-Two:
The commentary on the description of purification by knowledge and vision.

1319–21. Now, having reached the exposition of the purification by knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassanavisuddhi*), he first shows which knowledge arises immediately after it by saying, "From this point onwards," and so forth. "From this point onwards" means above this knowledge of conformity (*anulomañāṇa*).
"Because it is the object for adverting" means that, like the functional mind-element (*kiriyamanodhātu*) performing the function of adverting, it serves as the object for the Path.
Because it stands at the stage of adverting (āvajjana), it is indeed not included [in the path], owing to the absence of the characteristics of both kinds of purification.
Nevertheless, since it is the culmination of insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā), it belongs to the side of insight;

thus he says, "It is insight because it has fallen into the stream of insight. By this, he shows its classification under the purification by knowledge and vision of the way (paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi).

1322. Among worldlings (*puthujjana*), that which pertains to them is "worldling-like" (*pothujjanika*). That very lineage (*gotta*)—the designation "worldling" unmixed with the noble ones (*ariya*)—is the "worldling-lineage" (*pothujjanika-gotta*).

For a common designation among those born of the same lineage is called "lineage" (*gotta*); it is so called because it protects (*gaṃ tāyati*) one's intelligence and because it protects the name by virtue of its exclusive scope.
The word "or" (*vā*) is used to introduce an alternative meaning that will be explained later.
The connection is with "change-of-lineage" (*gotrabhū*) because it proceeds having overcome [the lower stage].

Nibbāna is called "lineage" (*gotta*) because it protects and causes the arising of the cognition "it is noble" (*ariya*) and of the corresponding designation; this is the intended meaning. "From that" means it arises from that lineage as its object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*).
Here, the word "iti" should be understood in the sense of a reason. Therefore, the meaning is: "It is change-of-lineage because it arises from that."
1323–5. *Ñāṇadassanavisuddhi* itself is *ñāṇadassanasuddhika*.
There is no other thing whatsoever that must be done by that bhikkhu in order to accomplish it—this is the connection. If one asks why there is nothing else, he says:
"For that which... and so forth. When it is asked, "Which indeed?", because the inquiry "How? has arisen, [he replies] "up to the end of the anuloma" (*anulomāvasānaṃ*).
With the words beginning "No," he establishes that point.

1326–7. Furthermore, when the gross obscurations concealing the truths have been removed by these three kinds of conformity-knowledge (anulomañāṇa) according to the strength of his own capacity, his mind does not leap forward into any state of conditioned formations (saṅkhāra).
It does not cling; like water on a lotus leaf, it recoils and rolls away.
All objects consisting of signs and all objects consisting of occurrences appear as obstacles.

Then, when all objects consisting of signs and occurrences have appeared as obstacles, immediately after the second or third knowledge of conformity (*anuloma-ñāṇa*), there arises the knowledge of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū-ñāṇa*).

It arises. Therefore he said, "Of that," and so forth. "Initial adverting" (*paṭhamāvajjana*) as well as "initial attention" (*paṭhamābhogā*)—thus, initial adverting is that which constitutes initial attention.

For here the suffix *-tā* is used in its own sense (as a nominalizing suffix). In this context, adverting should be understood by way of the turning of the stream of consciousness, while attention should be understood by way of its own act of attending.

1328–33. *Anantarādīhi*: by way of the six conditions, namely, proximity (*anantara*), contiguity (*samanantara*), repetition (*āsevana*), decisive support (*upanissaya*), absence (*natthi*), and disappearance (*vigata*). *Muddhaṃ*: that which has become the summit. Because it arises only once due to its absolute certainty, and because there is no returning, it is *anāvatta* (non-returning).
*Anāvajjanampi cā ti*: even while being without adverting (*anāvajjana*). *Saññaṃ datvā viya*: as if having given a sign, "thus..."
It is as if one were giving a signal, saying, “Arise! *Anibbiddhapubbaṃ* means never before pierced or split open. *Viddhaṃsentova* means while destroying or causing its destruction.
*Jāyati* means it is produced or brought into being. And here they bring this simile:
it is said that a certain archer, having had a hundred wooden shields set up at a distance of eight usabhas, covered his face with a cloth, fastened his arrow, and [prepared to shoot].
He stood at the edge of the target circle; another man, having aimed the target circle, would give a signal with a staff when the board was facing the archer.
Without letting go of the signal from the staff, the archer would discharge his arrow and pierce through a hundred boards.
In this context, the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) is like the one giving the signal with the staff, and the archer is like [the practitioner].
Just as piercing a hundred wooden planks without letting go of the perception of the target-stick, path-knowledge—
without letting go of the perception given by change-of-lineage knowledge— takes Nibbāna as its object and pierces through those aggregates of greed,
hatred, and delusion that have never before been pierced or shattered.

1335–8. *Anāmatagga*... [etc] ... *mahodadhin*: the great ocean of the suffering of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), which has produced births from the eighth existence onwards and whose limit is unknown.
"All enmities and fears" refers to the five enmities, such as the taking of life, and the twenty-five great fears.
"Many benefits" refers to the benefits such as faith established in the Triple Gem.
“By the first path” means by the first path known as the stream-entry path (*sotāpatti-magga*). This concludes the commentary on the knowledge of the first path.
1339. “Immediately after that” means right after that. “Two or three” means two fruition-consciousnesses (*phala-citta*) for one of non-sharp wisdom, and three for one of sharp wisdom. 1340–3.
Having stated, “They speak without knowing,” the passage beginning with “Of one” is spoken in order to show the reason for that.

By the phrase "the fifth path-consciousness," through the very indication of the absence of a sixth, the doctrine of the Elder Godatta—who asserts that there is "one fruition-consciousness"—is also refuted.
(1344) "Up to this point" means by the mere arising of the fruition immediately after the arising of the first path. [Thus, one is called] a stream-enterer.
"He is called" means that he is called the second noble person, the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*).

Even if he should become greatly negligent by resorting to occasions for negligence such as the sovereignty of the gods or the sovereignty of a universal monarch (*cakkavatti*), he is capable of making an end of suffering after wandering and transmigrating only seven times at most within the happy destinies of the sense-sphere realm. As it has been said:
“Even if they are exceedingly heedless,
they do not enter upon an eighth existence.
However, the teachers maintain that there is no such fixed rule regarding the realms of form and the formless.
1347. By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "fruits, etc.," he includes such things as the abandoned defilements.

Thus, first he reviews the path, thinking: "Indeed, by this path have I come"; then he reviews the fruit, thinking: "This benefit has been gained by me"; then he reviews the abandoned defilements, thinking: "These very defilements have been abandoned by me."
Then he reviews the defilements to be abandoned by the three higher paths, thinking, "These indeed are the defilements remaining for me.
Finally, he reviews the deathless Nibbāna, thinking, "This Dhamma has been penetrated by me as an object.
Thus, there are five kinds of reviewing knowledge for a stream-enterer. And just as it is for the stream-enterer, so it is for the once-returner and the non-returner as well.
However, for an Arahant, there is no reviewing of remaining defilements. Thus, all nineteen kinds of reviewing knowledge are accounted for.
Therefore he said: “The reviewing knowledges are nineteen. (1348–50).
To show those [states] by way of which these knowledges occur, he said: “The path and the fruit,” and so forth.
This is merely the highest limit. For even for those in training (*śaikṣa*), the reviewing of defilements already abandoned may or may not occur;
for not everyone is capable of it therein. It was for this very reason that Mahānāma asked the Blessed One:
"What indeed is that state not yet abandoned within myself, by which at times even states of greed (*lobhadharma*) seize my mind?"

"Abiding," and so forth. "He undertakes yoga": either sitting on that very same seat, or at another time, he applies himself to the yoga of insight for the sake of attaining the second stage—known as the path of the once-returner—which brings about the attenuation of sensual lust and ill will.
Its status as "second" should be understood both in terms of the sequence of the teaching and in terms of its actual arising.
Furthermore, it is called "ground" (*bhūmi*) because those associated states exist therein by way of being its support;

or alternatively, because even though they share the same supramundane nature, it itself becomes manifest, unlike Nibbāna which does not become manifest, and for that reason it too is called "the ground.
It "polishes with knowledge" means that, having brought about a greater sharpness of the faculties in their respective modes, [it polishes] the powers and the factors of enlightenment.
Having established the three characteristics in their most distinct state, he polishes them by means of investigation.
Therein, he "turns over" by moving his knowledge back and forth. Therefore it is said: "He enters the path of insight.

"In the manner stated above" means precisely in the manner stated for the arising of the knowledge of rise and fall (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*) and so forth. "Immediately after the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhu*)"—
Here, it is called "change-of-lineage" (gotrabhū) because it is like the change-of-lineage [of the noble path].
For the knowledge that precedes the first path is called "change-of-lineage" in the primary sense, because it overcomes the lineage of the worldling and establishes the lineage of the noble ones;

this [knowledge], however, is called "change-of-lineage" in a secondary sense because it resembles that. Furthermore, it is so called because it takes as its object a certain defilement-purification and absolute purification.
And it is called "purification" (*vodāna*). Therefore, it is said in the *Paṭṭhāna*: "The conformity [knowledge] is a condition for purification by way of the immediately preceding condition.

Furthermore, because in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* it is stated: "Eight states of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhu*) arise by way of concentration, taking the sense of overcoming arising and so forth as their basis;
ten states of change-of-lineage arise by way of insight," and so forth.

It has come down by way of the lineage-follower (*gotrabhū*) alone; therefore, it is said here as well that it is "immediately after the lineage-follower," taking it as having become [realized] from Nibbāna, which is designated as the lineage (*gotra*).
Commentary on the Knowledge of the Second Path.

1355–7. *Yaṃ* means because. *Sakideva* means only once. *Imaṃ lokaṃ āgantvā* (having come to this world)—by this [phrase], among the five types of once-returners (*sakadāgāmī*), [the first type is indicated].
Having excluded four, only one is included here. For some, having attained the fruit of a once-returner (sakadāgāmiphala) right here, attain final nibbāna right here;
some, having attained it here, attain final nibbāna in the world of the gods; some, having attained it in the world of the gods, attain final nibbāna right there;
and some, having attained it in the world of the gods, are reborn here and then attain final nibbāna—these four are not included here.
But he who, having reached this [state], dwells in the world of the devas for the full span of his life, and having been reborn here, attains final Nibbāna—only this one is included here.
"One who makes an end" means one who would make an end of suffering; or, "one who makes an end in existence," meaning one who makes an end of existence.
This is to be connected with "for the attainment of the third stage. "For the abandoning of ill-will and sensual lust": [this is the meaning].
For the sake of abandoning without remainder those very fetters that were attenuated by the path of the once-returner. This concludes the commentary on the knowledge of the third path. 1363–7.

He is called a non-returner (*anāgāmī*) because he does not return to the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) by way of rebirth-linking. Therefore it was said: "He attains final nibbāna right there. "Right there" means:
whether in the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*) or elsewhere, wherever he has arisen, right there he attains final nibbāna. His nature is such that he does not return.
Therefore, because there is no further return to this world by way of taking rebirth from that world, it is of a nature not to revert;

however, one may still come for the purpose of seeing the Buddha, seeing the Elder, or hearing the Dhamma. "For the abandoning of attachment to the fine-material realm and so forth" refers to the five higher fetters (uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana), namely:
attachment to the fine-material realm, attachment to the immaterial realm, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance.
"For the sake of abandoning without remainder. "For destruction" means for ruin. This is the commentary on the knowledge of the fourth path. 1371–4.

"A great one whose taints are destroyed" (mahākhīṇāsava) is a term of constant veneration due to his great majesty; it is not a term used with reference to a specific person, as in the case of "Mahāmoggallāna.
For there is no such thing as a "lesser one whose taints are destroyed" (cūḷakhīṇāsava). He has attained his own goal, his personal aim.
“Anuppattasadattha” means one who has attained his own welfare (*sadattha*) by means of this [path]. And “own welfare” (*sadattha*) should be understood as *arahatta* (Arahatship).

For that is called “own welfare” because it is one’s own welfare in the sense of being bound up with oneself, in the sense of not abandoning oneself, and in the sense of being one’s own ultimate goal.
“Khīṇasaṃyojana” means one for whom the ten fetters of existence (*bhavasaṃyojana*) have been exhausted.

One who is worthy of offerings is called *dakkhiṇeyya*. "All four" refers to the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*), the path of once-returning (*sakadāgāmi-magga*), the path of non-returning (*anāgāmi-magga*), and the path of arhatship (*arahatta-magga*).
"By one desiring purity" means by one wishing for their own purification. One whose wealth is austerity is a "wealthy in austerity" (*tapodhana*); [it is] by such a person.
Thus ends the commentary on the Exposition of Purification by Knowledge and Vision, within the *Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanā* entitled *Abhidhammatthavikāsinī*.
23. The Twenty-third Chapter: Commentary on the Discussion of the Abandoning of Defilements (Kilesappahānakathā). 1375.
Now, for the purpose of understanding the power of this very purification by knowledge and vision of the fourth path-knowledge:

In order to show which phenomena are to be abandoned by which [factors], as well as their abandonment and the functions such as full understanding (*pariññā*) at the time of realization (*abhisamaya*), the passage beginning with "Among these, by which...
which phenomena" is commenced. "Which phenomena" refers to those phenomena that are defilements (*saṃkilesadhamma*).
Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth, in the sense of binding and fettering, the aggregates (*khandha*) bind other aggregates; karma binds beings through its fruit; or suffering binds beings.
The fetters (*saṃyojana*). They are defilements (*kilesa*) in the sense of obstructing associated states, in the sense of afflicting them, and by way of their being thoroughly corrupted.
They are "states of falsehood" (*micchatta*) because they proceed in a false and perverted manner through such means as dogmatic adherence.
They are "worldly phenomena" (*loka-dhamma*), "phenomena included within the world," or "phenomena that do not cease when the world-process exists."
The worldly conditions (*lokadhammā*). The state or activity of stinginess is *macchariya*. They are called *vipallāsas* (perversions) in the sense of being inverted.

They are called *ganthas* (bonds) because they bind both the mental body (*nāmakāya*) and the physical body (*rūpakāya*). They are called *agati* (wrong paths) because they are not to be traveled by the Noble Ones, or because they are an improper destination.

They are called *āsava* (taints) because they flow out; that is, from the peak of existence (*bhavagga*) to all realms of the world, or from the stage of the lineage-determining knowledge (*gotrabhū*) toward all phenomena.
The meaning is that they proceed by pervading; or, they are called *āsava* because they flow toward the suffering of *saṃsāra*.

Alternatively, they are called *āsava* because they flow through the gates of restraint and non-restraint, such as the eye and so forth, into the continuum of sentient beings, just as pus flows from a wound. Or, they are called *āsava* because by means of them, minds flow toward sense objects.
They are called *ogha* (floods) because they are like floods in their capacity to cause one to reach the great ocean of *saṃsāra*. According to the method explained below...
They are called *yojanā* because they are joined [to objects]. They are called *nīvaraṇāni* (hindrances) because they obstruct the attainment of the specific mundane and supramundane qualities.
They are called *parāmāsā* (misapprehensions) because, having transcended the true nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena such as impermanence, they grasp them as being otherwise than their true nature.

They are called *upādānāni* (clinging) because they seize upon the object violently, like a snake seizing a frog. By virtue of not being abandoned, they persist within the continuum of sentient beings, like the poison of a rat.
They are called *anusaya* because they arise having obtained a corresponding cause (*anurūpa-kāraṇa*). They are "stains" (*mala*) in the sense that they cause the mind to become soiled.
And since they are unwholesome kamma and are paths to the miserable destinies (*duggati*), they are "unwholesome courses of action" (*akusala-kammapatha*).

However, in this context, it should be understood that those which have not yet attained the status of a course of action are included by virtue of their essential nature. A "mental arising" (*cittuppāda*) is so called because the mind arises therein.
A "mental-constituent aggregate" (*cetasikarāsi*) which is also an unwholesome arising of consciousness (*cittuppāda*) is thus called an "unwholesome arising of consciousness" (*akusalacittuppāda*).

Because they exist as the uppermost portion beyond the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), because they are to be abandoned after reaching the third path, and because they are to be cultivated [only] above it, they are "higher" (*uddhambhāga*);

namely, the fine-material and immaterial existences (*rūpārūpabhava*). They are "fettering to the higher" (*uddhambhāgiya*) because they are beneficial to those [existences], insofar as they connect one to the aggregates and so forth that arise therein.

"These very fetters" refers to the higher-fettering fetters (*uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana*). They are called "lower-fettering" (*adhobhāgiya*) because they pertain to the lower portion—the realm of sensual existence (*kāma-bhava*)—due to its being the lowest section relative to the realms of form and formlessness;
or because, since the defilements that arise therein have not been abandoned, they must be severed prior to the attainment of the third path.
These fetters are beneficial (i.e., conducive) to those [lower realms], hence they are called "lower-fettering fetters."

Among these ten, however, the fetter of fine-material existence, the fetter of immaterial existence, and the fetter of sense-sphere existence are in substance nothing other than greed (*lobha*). The personality-belief and the adherence to rules and observances are likewise just views (*diṭṭhi*). Therefore, in terms of actual phenomena (*dhamma*), there are seven fetters.
Wrong intention, wrong effort, and wrong concentration are designations for the applied thought, energy, and concentration that function in such a manner.
The three beginning with wrong speech are volitions (*cetanā*) that function in such a manner. Wrong mindfulness, moreover, is a state of consciousness (*cittuppāda*). Wrong knowledge...

Delusion (*moha*) is that which has proceeded in such a manner. Wrong liberation (*micchā-vimutti*) is the false grasping that occurs in regard to the "worldly monuments" (*lokathūpika*) and so forth, taking them to be liberation.

"By way of metaphorical designation of the cause" (*kāraṇūpacārena*) means by applying the name of the cause to the effect, such as saying "gain is caused by gain" or "loss is caused by loss. "Grasping at worldly conditions" (*lokadhammaggaṇa*) means grasping by means of the inclusion of worldly conditions.

"Stinginess regarding residence" (*āvāsamacchariya*) refers to stinginess with respect to a dwelling, or stinginess caused by a dwelling. The same applies to stinginess regarding families (*kulamacchariya*) and so forth.

In this context, "dwelling" (*āvāsa*) refers to monasteries and the like. "Family" (*kula*) refers to both the family of supporters and the family of kinsmen. "Gain" (*lābha*) refers specifically to the acquisition of the four requisites.

"Beauty" (*vaṇṇa*) refers to both the beauty of the physical body and the beauty of virtuous qualities. "Dhamma" refers to both the scriptural tradition (*āgama*) and spiritual realization (*adhigama*).
The term "three" is stated without breaking down the categories; however, when they are broken down, there are twelve.
Covetousness and ill will should be understood as bodily ties because they proceed by way of assailing and attacking.
Adherence that proceeds toward a groundless object in the form, "Only this is true, all else is false," is adherence to the view that "this alone is the truth.

Here, the bodily tie of adherence to rules and observances and the bodily tie of adherence to the view that "this alone is the truth" are in fact just views in their actual meaning; therefore, there are three bodily ties in terms of their constituent phenomena (dhamma).

“Lust, hatred, delusion, and fear”: this is stated because they are causes of going astray (*agati*). For going astray consists in doing what should not be done and not doing what should be done by means of lust and the rest.

Among the taints (*āsava*), sensual lust and lust for existence are, in meaning, greed; thus, in terms of phenomena (*dhamma*), there are three taints. “Of those very same” refers to sensual lust and the rest.

For these, like a flood (*ogha*), cause one who has fallen into them to enter the ocean of the states of loss (*apāya*); they do not allow one to lift up the head from the suffering of saṃsāra; and they join the aggregates and so forth with further aggregates and so forth.

"Grasping at sense-pleasures and so forth" refers to grasping at sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*), grasping at views (*diṭṭhupādāna*), grasping at rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*), and grasping at a doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*). Herein, grasping at views and the others are simply those very views as they occur; grasping at sense-pleasures is greed. Thus, in terms of their intrinsic nature (*dhamma*), there are two types of grasping. Regarding "underlying tendencies of beings":
here, if they are called "underlying tendencies" because they lie latent within the continuum of a being in the sense of being unabandoned, why are only these six mentioned?
Is it not the case that other defilements also exist in an unabandoned state? We do not [define them] merely by the fact of being unabandoned.
We speak of "latent dispositions" (*anusaya*); however, latent dispositions are defilements that have become firmly rooted by virtue of their state of being unabandoned.
And their "becoming firmly rooted" should be understood as their unique, specific nature not shared with others.

For it was by the Tathāgata, who knows the specific nature of phenomena, that these alone were called latent dispositions; namely, sensual lust itself is the latent disposition of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*). The same applies to the rest. Others [say]:

However, having stated the etymological definition as "the underlying tendency (*anusaya*) of sensual lust," etc., some explain that the *anusayas* are the seeds of sensual lust and so forth—the power produced by defilements within the personal existence (*attabhāva*) that gives rise to further defilements.
The refutation of their view is not presented here because it would lead to prolixity (*papañca*).

The taking away of life is "killing" (*pāṇātipāta*). In conventional usage (*vohārato*), "living being" (*pāṇa*) refers to a sentient creature; in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*), it refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). In that [life-faculty]...
Taking life is the volition of killing that originates from an application which severs the life-faculty in a living being while perceiving it as such.
Taking what is not given is the volition of theft that originates from an application which takes another’s property while perceiving it as such.

Sexual misconduct is the volition of transgressing against a place where one should not go, proceeding through the door of the body out of a desire for what is not the true Dhamma. [Regarding] a non-existent matter...
False speech is the volition that originates the effort to communicate something in such a way as to misrepresent the facts to another who desires to know them.
However, only that which causes a breach between others constitutes a course of action (*kamma-patha*); the other is merely a deed (*kamma*).
Malicious speech is the volition that originates an effort to cause a breach between others, arising either from a defiled mind with the desire to divide them or from the desire to please oneself.
That [unwholesome bodily action] also constitutes a course of kamma only when the two [parties] are divided.

Harsh speech is an exclusively cruel volition that originates from the application of means to cut off another's life. Idle chatter is defiled volition originating from the application of means to communicate what is meaningless.
However, that becomes a course of kamma only when it is understood by others. Covetousness has the characteristic of longing for another's property with the thought, "O, may this be mine!"
Covetousness (*abhijjhā*). Ill-will (*vyāpāda*), characterized by mental malice, is the thought: "Oh, may this being perish!

Wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*), characterized by distorted vision, consists of such modes as "there is no giving," and so forth. And herein, the division into courses of action (*kamma-patha*) occurs only through the views of nihilism, causelessness, and non-action.
Among these, killing and the rest are threefold bodily action alone; they arise only through the doors of body and speech.
It does not occur at the mind-door. Likewise, the fourfold bodily action beginning with false speech is exclusively verbal action;
