however, the threefold mental action beginning with covetousness is exclusively mental action. That [mental action] occurs in all three doors. It has already been stated that even when occurring through other doors, they do not abandon their respective names.
As for their nature, here the first seven are of the nature of volition (*cetanā*), while the other three are associated with volition.

They are to be seen. However, the distinctions regarding their great faultiness, slight faultiness, application, and so forth, should be understood according to the method explained in various places.
"These" refers to these knowledges of the path. "According to what is possible" means in accordance with each respective path.

"Leading to the states of deprivation" (*apāyagamanīya*) means those by which one goes to the states of deprivation. "The rest" means those not leading to the states of deprivation. "Gross" refers to [the defilements abandoned] by the third path.
They are gross in comparison to the state that is to be abandoned. Therefore, he said: "The subtle ones are to be destroyed by the knowledge of the third path.

The connection is that they are subtle forms of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and ill-will (*paṭigha*). By the restriction "only those to be destroyed by the knowledge of the fourth path," he excludes their being destroyed by the first path and so forth.
For there is no state of lust for the fine-material realm (*rūparāga*) and so on that leads to the states of misery, such that they would have to be destroyed even by the first knowledge.

However, wherever the word *eva* (only) is not used for emphasis—wherever it will be stated that "this or that is subject to destruction by the second knowledge," or "subject to destruction by the third knowledge," or "subject to destruction by the fourth knowledge"—it should be understood that in each such case, having already had its state of leading to states of deprivation destroyed by the preceding knowledges, it becomes subject to destruction by the subsequent knowledge. Therefore, greed... [and so on].
Regarding the phrase "those to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge" (*catutthañāṇavajjhā*): here, greed and the other [defilements] are indeed also to be abandoned by the lower paths.
"In him" (*yassa*) refers to the retinue.
The connection is: "perverse perception and mind regarding suffering as pleasure" (*dukkhe sukhanti saññācittavipallāsā*).
Regarding "the wrong courses are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the first path":

although desire and the rest are of the nature of craving and so forth and are therefore to be abandoned by the higher paths, nevertheless, because the performance of what should not be done and the non-performance of what should be done—which are rooted in them—lead to the states of misery (apāya), they are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the first path.
As for the remorse consisting of regret concerning wholesome and unwholesome deeds done or left undone, that is to be abandoned here by the third knowledge.

It has been said. However, regarding the remorse mentioned in the statement, "One incurs an offense through being overcome by remorse," it was with reference to that specific kind of remorse that the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā* states, "Remorse and doubt are abandoned by the path of stream-entry.
Therefore, this intended meaning (adhippāya) of these two statements should be understood. In other similar instances as well, it is only the intended meaning [that must be discerned].
It is to be sought [through investigation], not to be accepted based on contradiction.

Or rather, the fact that remorse (*kukkucca*) is censurable by the first and third knowledges is stated with reference to the abandoning of gross and non-remaining [remorse]. As for that which arises in an Arahant:
"He did not accept [the alms-food], being remorseful, thinking, 'The Blessed One has prohibited eating alms-food from a lodging-house after having stayed there repeatedly.'"
Worry that has arisen is not an hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*). For no hindrance arises in an Arahant;

rather, what resembles a hindrance is called "disciplinary worry" (*vinaya-kukkucca*), which consists of a state of inquiry as to whether something is permissible. That is merely a mental state occurring in such a way.

The underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) of sensual lust and ill-will are accompanied by residual attachment and are to be abandoned by the third knowledge; however, the fact that their coarse forms are to be abandoned by the second knowledge is according to the method already explained below.

And here, by the inclusion of "unwholesome states of consciousness" (*akusalacittuppāda*), it should be understood that hypocrisy (*makkha*), flattery (*palāsa*), deceit (*māyā*), fraud (*sāṭheyya*), obstinacy (*thambha*), and impetuosity (*sārambha*) are also included.
1376. "With this or that": with this or that particular killer. But do these [states] kill these phenomena in the past and the future, or rather in the present?
What follows from this? If they were to kill them in the past and the future, they would be fruitless.

One exerts effort. Why? Because at that time, those things to be abandoned do not exist. If [the effort is directed] toward the present, even then it is fruitless because the things to be abandoned coexist with the effort.
Or, if abandonment were somehow possible, it would follow that the cultivation of the path is defiled, since the things to be abandoned and their abandoner would exist simultaneously?
This is true; however, for those who [hold that] by means of the path...

Defilements that are bound to arise inevitably when their causes are encountered because they have not been eradicated are said to "slay" those [causes] in the future by inducing in them the state of non-arising for their own production. 1377–82.

Regarding the functions such as full understanding: there are four functions by way of full understanding (*pariññā*), abandoning (*pahāna*), realization (*sacchikiriyā*), and development (*bhāvanā*).
“Stated” means as stated in such passages as “Suffering is to be fully understood,” and so forth, and “He who, monks, sees suffering,” and so forth.
“At the moment of the realization of the truths” means at the moment of penetrating the four noble truths.
“According to their true nature” means by way of their non-perverted nature. Having said, “They are to be known,” [one asks]: how, then, are they to be known?
"How indeed can four functions occur simultaneously for each single knowledge?

For nothing such is seen in the world, nor is there any scriptural authority [for it]"—bearing this objection in mind, he first shows the manner of their knowing by means of a simile, saying "For a lamp," and so forth. "Vidaṃseti" means "it shows. "Pariyādiyeti" means "it exhausts."
"By the clear realization of full understanding" means by penetration characterized as knowing through complete delimitation.

"He clearly realizes" means he penetrates by way of non-delusion. "Precisely by the clear realization of abandonment" means he clearly realizes precisely through non-delusion by way of penetration characterized as abandonment consisting in eradication.
"By the method of development" means by way of being a co-nascent condition and so forth.
By means of the method of realization through cultivation (*bhāvanābhisamaya*).
For path-knowledge realizes by way of penetration—termed the cultivation of the Noble Path—which arises from the prior cultivation of the path consisting of right intention and so forth;
thus, it penetrates the Eightfold Path without delusion. For that [knowledge], while destroying delusion regarding associated states, also destroys its own delusion.
"Cessation" means Nibbāna. "Realizes" means he penetrates it by way of making it directly manifest.

"He realizes cessation" means that through the penetration of the object, he penetrates the single Truth of Cessation; and through the penetration of non-delusion, he penetrates all four Truths by means of path-knowledge.
Having thus elucidated the single penetration by way of reasoning, the passage beginning with "And it is said" is stated in order to establish it through scripture as well.
For the knowledge of one possessing the path—referring to one who possesses the vision of a single truth—is described in the passage:
"Friend, whoever sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
This was stated by the Venerable Gavampati Thera in order to establish that point through an investigation into the state of possessing the vision of the other truths.

Otherwise, if there were a gradual realization (*kāmābhisamaya*), since what was previously seen would not be seen again, the vision of suffering and so forth for one who sees the origin and the rest could not be spoken of again.
Now, however, making a correlation with a simile here, he said:
“Lamp,” and so forth. Because it is the cause for the absence of dependence, the lamp is similar to the full understanding of suffering (*dukkha-pariññā*).

Because it destroys opposing factors, it is similar to the destruction of darkness through the abandoning of the origin (*samudaya-pahāna*). Because it nourishes the light of knowledge, it is similar to the manifestation of light through the cultivation of the path (*magga-bhāvanā*).
In that same way, according to each respective path, there is the realization (*sacchikiriyā*) of cessation (*nirodha*).

Likewise, the phrase "the exhaustion of the moisture of the defilements occurs" expresses, by way of metaphorical usage of the cause, the similarity between the realization of cessation and the exhaustion of moisture.
(1385–6) Showing that same meaning through another simile, he said: "Rising," and so forth. "Illuminates" means makes manifest.
"It strikes back" means it allays. Here too, just as the sun illuminates forms, so does path-knowledge fully understand suffering (*dukkha*).
Just as it destroys darkness, so does it abandon the origin (*samudaya*).
Just as it displays light, so does it develop the path by way of being a co-nascent and other conditions. Just as it allays cold...
Thus, the application of the simile should be understood as follows: one realizes cessation (*nirodha*), which is the subsiding of all the distress and fever of the defilements (*kilesa*).

(1388) "He attains" (*appeti*) means he reaches. Because, through the full understanding of suffering (*dukkhapariññā*), there is the state of transcending the near shore of the personality-view (*sakkāya*), it is similar to abandoning the near shore;

because, through the cultivation of the path (*maggabhāvanā*), there is the carrying of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*), it is similar to carrying a load. Up to this point...
The benefit shown here is that which proceeds from the destruction of various defilements through the development of wisdom (*paññābhāvanā*).
However, it should also be understood that the attainment of the Noble Fruits (*ariyaphalasamāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) are also its benefits.
These, moreover, should be understood in brief as follows: "The attainment of the Noble Fruits" refers to each of the four respective fruits...
There is absorption in cessation for the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very life, which is the noble fruit.
For all four types of noble persons enter into the attainment of their respective fruits.

However, some say that "only non-returners and arahants enter into it because they have brought their concentration to perfection"; that is not a valid reason, for [the ability] to enter into the attainment one has personally acquired [is what matters].
This is because there is nothing further to be done for the sake of fulfilling concentration.

For even an ordinary person whose defilements are not entirely severed is able to attain the mundane meditative absorptions (lokīyasamāpatti) they have previously acquired; how much more so, then, for noble ones (ariya) who have eradicated certain defilements?
However, those in higher stages do not enter into lower stages—even those previously attained—because they have become a different type of person (puggalantara).

Because of having approached [the higher state]. For, through the eradication of the defilements of karma and the cessation [of rebirth], there is for a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) an approach to the status of another person—such as a once-returner (sakadāgāmī)—just as there is for worldlings;

and because supramundane wholesome states yield immediate fruit, one who has gone from a lower to a higher stage is like one who has gone to another existence. Thus it is said of each respective noble one...

Each respective fruit is like the life-continuum (bhavaṅga); therefore, because it has subsided through the attainment of the state of another person, there is no entering into the attainment of a lower fruit by one who has attained a higher one.
However, one who has attained a lower fruit does not enter the higher one because it has not been reached.
Thus, all four types of persons enter only their own respective fruits. That...

However, a noble disciple who wishes to attain [this attainment] should, having gone into solitude and withdrawn into seclusion, contemplate formations by way of their arising and passing away and so forth.

For him, as he practices progressive insight into the process of occurrence, immediately after the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) which has formations as its object, his consciousness enters into cessation by way of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti).
And herein, because of the mind’s inclination toward the attainment of fruition, even for one still in training (sekkha)—
Only the fruit arises, not the path. For the practice of insight that brings about the Noble Path is indeed different from that which brings about the attainment of the fruit.

Thus, on the course of the Noble Path, the conformities of knowledge (*anuloma-ñāṇa*) arise as being conducive to the path, having reached the highest perfection among mundane knowledges by the exceptional shattering of the gross aggregates of greed and so forth that have not been previously pierced.

In the cognitive process of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), however, because those respective defilements have been eradicated by their respective paths, these [jhānas] arise without concern for suppressing defilements;
they arise having merely reached the stage of preparation for the noble ones' possession of the bliss of the fruition-attainment.
Thus, there is no possibility of emergence from them for anyone. Since this is so for them...
It should be understood that the final [consciousness], having emerged from the sign of formations (*saṅkhāra-nimitta*), would serve as the immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*) for the Path;
and for that very reason, the knowledge that serves as the immediate condition for the attainment of fruition (*phala-samāpatti*) has formations alone as its object, not Nibbāna.
Furthermore, when the period delimited by the continuity of its occurrence—due to the influence of previous formative forces (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra*)—has passed away, [the attainment occurs].
Emergence from that [attainment] should also be understood by way of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).

However, the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is the non-occurrence of consciousness and mental factors through the successive cessation [of the mental process], occupying the position of the third and fourth fruits.
For it is only non-returners and arahants who, by means of the total eradication of sensual desire and the other [fetters], [enter] into concentration...
They attain cessation because they are endowed with the fruit of serenity through its fulfillment.
For this occurs only for one who possesses the two powers by way of the simultaneous development of serenity and insight;
therefore, an Anāgāmī or a Khīṇāsava who desires to attain it and has obtained the eight attainments should go into seclusion and dwell in solitude.
Having entered the first jhāna and emerged from it, the formations therein should be contemplated as impermanent, suffering, and non-self;

then, having entered the second, third, and fourth jhānas, the base of infinite space, and the base of infinite consciousness, and emerged from them, the formations therein should likewise be comprehended; then, having entered the base of nothingness and emerged from it—

Four preliminary duties must be performed: (1) the removal of various items tied up [with the body], (2) the honoring of the Saṅgha, (3) the summoning of the Teacher, and (4) the determination of the duration of the journey.
In this regard, beds, chairs, and so forth, which have been separated from the body, must be disposed of within seven days in such a way that they do not go to waste.
The formal resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) consists in not disturbing what has been bound in various ways. Regarding the body, there is no separate function of formal resolution.
However, when the Saṅgha wishes to perform some formal act, such as a motion (*ñattikamma*), it honors the Saṅgha by making a prior mental application (*pubbābhoga*), thinking:
"I shall rise as soon as they call me. And the Teacher [said]: "In the laying down of training rules (*sikkhāpada*) and so forth, until I..."
"Before he calls me, I shall emerge"—this is the preliminary mental application regarding the Teacher's summons.
The delimitation of the duration is the observation of one's own life-force as being capable of continuing for within seven days.
Having thus performed the preliminary duties, one should attain the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Then, after passing over one or two thought-moments,
He becomes mindless, he touches cessation; then, according to his determination, he will emerge from that cessation by means of either the third or the fourth fruit.
Thus, this twofold attainment is the benefit of supramundane wisdom (*lokuttara-paññā*).
[The phrase] "by one who has crossed over the world with its devas, or by one who has crossed further" refers to the Supremely Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*) by means of the supramundane.

The connection is with "the cultivation of wisdom" (*paññāya bhāvanā*). "Cultivation of welfare" (*hitabhāvanā*) refers to this cultivation of wisdom which discerns welfare in both this world and the next.
"Accompanied by happiness" (*sukhasaṃhita*) means accompanied by happiness due to such qualities as having lush shade and water.

"Welfare" (*hita*) means beneficial for spiritual practice (*yogakamma*). "Supreme" (*uttama*) means most exalted; the intention is that it is pre-eminently lofty and powerful. "Free from agitation and trembling" (*aviggahakampada*).
"Does not give resistance and motion" means it is "without resistance and motion.
Thus [ends] the commentary on the *Abhidhammāvatāra* named *Abhidhammatthavikāsinī*.
The commentary on the Discussion of the Abandoning of Defilements is finished.
Chapter Twenty-Four: Commentary on the Exposition of Conditions.
1395. Now, in order to show the method of their conditionality (*paccaya-vidhi*), the passage beginning with "of those which" (*yesaṃ*) is commenced.
A *paccaya* is that depending upon which (*paṭicca*) this fruit comes, proceeds, persists, or arises. A *hetu* is that wherein it goes forth (*hinoti*) or is established (*patiṭṭhāti*).
Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the word *hi* should be understood as having the sense of "establishment," just like the word *mūla*.

Or, it is called a *hetu* (cause) because by means of this—acting as the basis for kamma and carrying nourishment upward like a root—the tree reaches its fruit dependent upon that [root] and attains growth.
It is a *hetu* in the sense of being a root, and a *paccaya* (condition) in the sense of being helpful; thus it is a *hetupaccaya*.
The meaning is: a condition that is a cause, or a condition by way of its causal state.

The same should be understood regarding the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) and the others. This [consciousness] is a condition for matter originated by kamma during rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), for matter originated by consciousness during the course of existence (*pavatti*), and for conascent mental states in both instances.

By the phrase "all mundane and supramundane," it is included under the term "mundane" because even conceptual designations (*paññatti*) are known in the world; thus, among the sixfold division beginning with matter, [it is classified as such].
This shows that among the phenomena designated as conditioned and unconditioned, there is no phenomenon that does not serve as an object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*).

For this very reason, it is stated indeterminately as "taking whatever phenomenon [as an object]. Now, one might ask: since it is said "whatever phenomenon," does this not mean that designations (*paññatti*) are not included?
This is not a fault, because the word *dhamma* here refers to the knowable (*ñeyya*). [The word] "taking" (*ārabbha*)...
"Having supported," means "having grasped. "They arise" is merely an illustration; for they not only arise but also persist by taking that as their object.

Just as a weak man stands up and remains standing by leaning on a staff or a rope, so too do mental states (citta) and mental factors (cetasika) arise by supporting themselves upon objects such as visible form.

And they remain. A state that is beneficial by virtue of its preeminence is the predominance condition (*adhipatipaccaya*). "By virtue of its preeminence" means by way of being foremost (*pamukhabhāvena*).

For a state that serves as the counterpart to those things dependent upon itself is called "predominance"; thus, it functions for them by way of being foremost. "Predominance of desire" (*chandādhipati*)...

Because of such statements as, "States associated with desire (chanda) and the material phenomena co-arising with them are a condition for those [states] by way of the predominance condition (adhipatipaccaya)," it is said, "In this context, 'co-nascent predominance' (sahajātādhipati)," etc., showing that the four factors beginning with desire are co-nascent predominances for co-nascent mind and matter.

Furthermore, the statement, "For one who possesses desire, what action indeed does not succeed? refers to the decisive support (upanissaya) consisting of prior volitional formations (purimābhisaṅkhāra).

When a thought-moment arises having been obtained, desire and the other [mental factors] function as the primary and preeminent factors, bringing about the associated states and the material phenomena originated by them, and doing so under their own control;
and they themselves proceed according to those [states], following after them in their inferiority and so forth. Therefore, they are "predominance conditions" (adhipati-paccaya), but not—
On one side: for when the mind proceeds having made desire (*chanda*) its burden and desire its chief, then desire alone is the dominant factor (*adhipati*), not the others.

This same method applies to the remaining factors as well. Indeed, their status as dominant factors arises from their proceeding by overcoming those things that would otherwise obstruct their own occurrence. They are "the rest" because they lack the quality of being worthy of such esteem as has been described for those [three].
And because it is stated that there is the state of being an object-predominance condition (*ārammaṇādhipati*) precisely for that which is treated with reverence. For this has been said:

"Whatever mental states—whether consciousness or mental factors—arise by treating a certain phenomenon as reverent, those phenomena are a condition for those respective phenomena by way of the predominance condition.
In that context, "by treating as reverent" means either by way of respectful esteem and honor, or by way of relishing.

Or it is that which should be received as heavy and weighty, having been treated with respect. For an object worthy of esteem becomes a condition for the relishing, the reviewing, the path, and the fruit—which are inclined, directed, and bent toward it—as if bringing them under its own control.
Therefore, this should be understood as the predominance condition (*adhipati-paccaya*), because it is helpful by way of being the counterpart to those things dependent on itself.
It obstructs, thus it is *antara*; the meaning is "an interposer. That for which no such interval exists is *anantara*.
That very [condition] is the *anantarapaccaya* (proximate condition); the intended meaning is a phenomenon that assists by way of being proximate.
"Immediately ceased" means that immediately after its own cessation, it serves as the arising-condition for the emergence of a corresponding state of consciousness.
Those material phenomena that have ceased immediately after being in the preceding moment do not constitute a condition by way of contiguity (*anantarapaccaya*).
A phenomenon that assists by way of immediate succession is a condition of contiguity (*samanantarapaccaya*); likewise, the term "condition of contiguity" is also [defined] thus.
Apart from the mere prefix, there is no difference here at all: whatever is a condition of contiguity is itself a condition of contiguity.

For the state of being capable of producing [a result] immediately after the preceding and succeeding [moments], due to their state of arising without interval, is "proximate conditionality" (*anantarapaccayatā*).

Because there is no shape—as in the case of material aggregates—and because there is no simultaneous location for the condition and the conditioned, there is no distinction such as "this is above, below, or across that";
thus, by bringing about its own unity as it were, through a state of perfect immediate succession...
The capacity to produce [a state] is the condition of immediate succession (*samanantara-paccayatā*);

therefore, although there is no difference in terms of the phenomenon itself, their separate teaching was given by taking the distinction based merely on the phrasing and meaning according to the persons to be trained.

As for the opinion of some teachers that "it is the condition of immediate succession because of the immediacy of the object, and the condition of immediate proximity because of the immediacy of time," that—starting from "from cessation... [is refuted].

This is rejected by such statements as: "For one emerging from the attainment of fruition, the wholesome *nevasaññānāsaññāyatana* is a condition by way of immediate-proximity condition (*samanantara-paccaya*)," and so forth.
A co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*) is a phenomenon that assists by way of simultaneous arising, just as a lamp is for light.

Furthermore, this [conditioning] is threefold: "mental states and mental factors [are related] to one another and to co-nascent material phenomena; the great elements [are related] to one another and to derived material phenomena;
and at the moment of rebirth-linking, the physical basis and the resultant [states] are related to one another. Therefore, it is said: "mental states and mental factors," and so forth.
Indeed, even that which is stated in the Pāḷi as being sixfold by way of the immaterial aggregates and so on—
That which was stated is also included right here. As for the absence of the state of being a co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*) among the remaining material phenomena here,
between the physical basis and the occurrence of immaterial phenomena in both cases, and among the derived material phenomena and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*),
this should be understood as the non-possibility of a specific capacity for the state of being a condition.
A phenomenon that assists another phenomenon which assists itself by way of its arising or its stabilization is the mutuality condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*).
This state of being an assistant should be understood as existing through the very fact of mutualness, not by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta*) and so forth.
For even while being a co-nascent condition or the like, something may still be a mutuality condition for another.

There is no mutual conditionality between mind and mental factors on the one hand, and mind-born matter on the other, nor between the great primaries and derived matter, because such a relationship does not exist.
As it is said: "The four formless aggregates are a condition for one another by way of mutual conditionality; the four great primaries... [and so on]...

at the moment of descent [into the womb], name-and-form are a condition for one another by way of mutual conditionality. However, regarding the phenomena arising from conditions, the Teacher [states]:
Because it is stated without distinction as being "thus a mutual condition" (*aññamaññapaccaya*) due to its being spoken of without being grasped [as a separate category],

the supporting condition (*nissayapaccaya*) is a phenomenon that assists by way of being a foundation (*adhiṭṭhānākāra*), like the earth for trees and so forth, and by way of being a support (*nissayākāra*), like cloth and so forth for paintings and the like.
"Bases of matter" (*vatthurūpa*) refers to [the heart-base] as the foundation for the seven consciousness-elements.
The material bases (*vatthurūpa*) are conditions by way of support (*nissaya-paccaya*). The primary elements (*mahābhūta*), mind, and mental factors are mutually [supportive];

likewise, the primary elements are the support for derived matter (*upādārūpa*). Mind and mental factors are conditions for co-nascent material phenomena by way of being their support, because they depend on them for their existence;
since they are supported by their own fruit and are not rejected, they are called "support" (*nissaya*).
Just as *upāyāsa* (despair) is an intense form of *āyāsa* (exertion), so too *upanissaya* (decisive support) is an intense form of *nissaya* (support); the meaning is that it is a powerful cause.
Therefore, a phenomenon (*dhamma*) that assists by way of being a powerful cause should be understood as the *upanissaya-paccaya* (decisive support condition). This is threefold:
objective decisive support (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*), proximity decisive support (*anantarūpanissaya*), and natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*). Thus he said, "Objective," and so forth. Therein—
“Having given a gift, having undertaken virtue, and having performed the Uposatha duty, one esteems it and reflects upon it;
having esteemed wholesome deeds performed in the past, one reflects upon them; having emerged from jhāna, one esteems the jhāna and reflects upon it;
those in training esteem the change-of-lineage (gotrabhu) and reflect upon it; they esteem purification (vodāna) and reflect upon it; those in training...”

“Having emerged from the path, they esteem the path and review it”—in such a manner, the object-strong-dependence (ārammaṇūpanissaya) has been analyzed without making any distinction from the object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati).
Therefore he said: “The object-strong-dependence is simply the object-predominance. Although no distinction was made, [the two are not identical].

Although they are thus distinguished, there is nevertheless this difference between them: whatever object the mind and mental factors arise by treating as important, that object is necessarily a "strong object" (*balavārammaṇa*) among their objects.
Thus, in the sense of being merely treated as important, it is the "object-predominance" (*ārammaṇādhipati*);
and in the sense of being a strong cause, it is the "object-strong-dependence" (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*). In this way, their distinction should be understood.

The proximity-decisive-support condition (*anantarūpanissaya*) is also explained—without making any distinction from the proximity condition (*anantarapaccaya*)—in such a manner as: "Preceding wholesome aggregates are a condition for subsequent wholesome aggregates by way of the decisive-support condition.
Therefore, it is said: "But the proximity-decisive-support is simply the proximity condition. Even though this is so...

The "proximate condition" (*anantara-paccaya*) is so called by way of the arising of a suitable consciousness immediately following itself; the "proximate decisive support condition" (*anantara-upanissaya-paccaya*) is so called by way of a powerful cause—it is in this way that their distinction should be understood.
"Natural decisive support" (*pakatūpanissaya*) is the decisive support by its own nature alone, devoid of any other condition.

What is meant is that there is a certain kind of decisive support (upanissaya) which is distinct and separate from the object-condition (ārammaṇa) and the proximity-condition (anantara). Alternatively, it is called "natural decisive support" (pakatūpanissaya);

here, "natural" (pakata) refers to the prefix *pa-*, which indicates that the state has been produced within the mental continuum by virtue of its capacity to bring about its own fruit, and that it has been cultivated. Therefore—

The meaning is that natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*) consists of either that which has been produced within one’s own continuum—such as bodily pleasure, pain, faith, virtue, and so forth—or that which has been cultivated—such as climate, food, and so forth.

Furthermore, "cultivation" here is twofold: cultivation by utilization and cultivation by object. By establishing it in this way, the status of decisive support is also obtained for things yet to come.

[This applies to] bodily pleasure... and so forth... and that which... *Note: The ellipses (... and "yo ca" indicate that the passage is an excerpt from a larger text, likely the *Paṭṭhāna-Atthakathā*.*

In this context, bodily pleasure and pain are the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for lust, faith, and so forth; weather, food, and so forth are the decisive support for mental concentration and so forth;

and faith, virtue, and so forth are the decisive support for faith, virtue, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), whatever arises depending upon whatever is included as being the decisive support-condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for that respective thing.
For this is the Great Authority regarding conditions (*paccaya-mahāpadesa*). Thus it is said:
Regarding "the decisive support condition" (*upanissaya-paccaya*):
A pre-arising condition (*purejāta-paccaya*) is a phenomenon that, having arisen earlier than the conditioned state, assists it by way of its continued presence.
And since this [condition] consists only of material phenomena, it applies only to immaterial phenomena. Therefore he said: "It is called the 'base-pre-arising' (*vatthu-purejāta*)," and so forth.

And just as here the term "bases of material form" includes the heart-base as well, so too by the inclusion of the phrase "visible forms, etc.," it should be understood that mental objects (dhammārammaṇa) are also included. But is it not the case that only the five sense objects are presented as pre-existent conditions (ārammaṇapurejāta)?

True, they are presented as such; however, in the section on questions (pañhāvāra), it says: "Whether they be trainees (sekha) or worldlings (puthujjana), [they perceive] the eye as impermanent... [and so forth].

Since the passage beginning with "insighting into [them] as suffering and non-self" includes present eye-sense and so forth without distinction, it is impossible to deny that a mental object (dhammārammaṇa) possesses the status of an object-prenascence condition (ārammaṇapurejāta). This is also established by the sense of the matter itself:
"Whatever present object the mind seizes upon when it functions at the mind-door, that is its object-prenascence condition."

"...occurs. Herein, the fact that bases and objects act as a support by way of their prior-arising aspect—without becoming a support through the specific qualities of dependence, objective support, or mode—is what constitutes their status as a "prior-arising condition" (purejāta-paccaya).
This is its distinction from their status as conditions of dependence (nissaya) and objective support (ārammaṇa).

The postnascence condition (*pacchājātapaccaya*) is a phenomenon that assists previously arisen material phenomena by way of providing support, just as the volition (*cetanā*) of a vulture chick has a craving for food. For, through the nutriment of mental volition (*manosañcetanāhāra*), the state of being a cause for the persistence of the continuum—

which would otherwise fail to persist without the subsequently arisen consciousness and mental factors— is the assistance rendered by the subsequently arisen consciousness and mental factors in their capacity as postnascent conditions.

The state of being a postnascent condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*) is distinguished by its dissociated mode (*vippayutta-ākāra*) and so forth; thus, the supportive efficacy of all conditions should be understood as being distinguished from the modes of other conditions.

However, because it is stated [in the Paṭṭhāna] that "postnascent states of consciousness and mental factors are a condition for this prenascent body by way of the postnascent condition," it is said to be of one kind; hence he says, "consciousness and mental factors."

Repetition (*āsevana*) is that which grasps the state of being of the same genus (*sajātīyatā*) by means of its own quality of being distinguished by a superior state of proficiency and strength—just as a preceding knot [strengthens] a subsequent knot through its state of being wholesome (*kusala*) and so forth.
Therefore, only those phenomena of the same genus are the repetition-condition (*āsevanapaccaya*) for one another.
For phenomena of a different genus do not [strengthen] those of a different genus by means of the quality of repetition, characterized as a state of proficiency and strength.
They are unable to cause their own [mental states] to take up that [state], nor do they themselves take it up from there.

However, because those immediately preceding states consist of both mundane wholesome and unwholesome [states], as well as non-attentional functional impulsions (*kiriyajavana*), he said, "excluding the two types of adverting," and so forth.

Furthermore, based on the statement, "There is one [condition] for repetition (*āsevana*) by way of path-condition (*maggapaccaya*)," it is only the smile-producing consciousness (*hasituppāda*) among the rootless functionals (*ahetuka-kiriya*) that possesses the nature of repetition.

The two types of adverting consciousness do not constitute a condition by way of repetition (*āsevana-paccaya*). Even supramundane wholesome consciousness does not acquire the quality of repetition because it precedes a fruit of a different class.
Resultant indeterminate consciousness likewise does not do so, as it proceeds by the force of karma;
having reached the state of fruition, being transformed by karma and impelled by the momentum of karma, it proceeds as if it had fallen, maintaining its own intrinsic nature.
Having been grasped and having been cultivated, it does not produce another result, nor does it arise by taking up the power of a previous result.
For although supramundane resultant consciousness arises by way of impulsion, it takes up the quality of repetition (āsevanaguṇa), yet it does not cause another to take it up.
As for what was said by the teacher Dhammapāla Thera, "There is no impulsion apart from repetition," [it refers to this].
That which was stated should also be understood as being said "by way of the majority"; otherwise, it would follow that the Teacher failed to consider the specific rule.
For it is likewise stated in the *Paṭṭhāna-aṭṭhakathā*: "But there is no such thing as a supramundane condition of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*).
This is because the path does not take the change-of-lineage state as its repetition, owing to their difference in nature by way of plane and so forth.
Because it is not intended [here]. For it is stated in the *Paṭṭhāna*: "The state of lineage (*gotrabhu*) is a condition for the path by way of the condition of repetition;
purification (*vodāna*) is a condition for the path by way of the condition of repetition.
It is an assistance to co-nascent states and to those occurring at different moments, by virtue of being the activity of accumulation (*āyūhana*) characterized as the application of consciousness.
Dhamma is a kamma-condition. For "kamma" is said to be volition (*cetanā*), and that consists of the activity of exertion.

It is "co-nascent" (*sahajāta*) because it arises together with the conditioned state; it is "not of the same moment" (*nānakkhaṇika*) because it exists at a different moment from the conditioned state. The connection is: "volition, whether mundane or supramundane, is co-nascent.
That [volition] is a condition for those things called co-nascent and for the material phenomena originated by them; the other [types of kamma] are...
However, it should be understood as referring to resultant and kamma-produced matter (*vipākakaṭattārūpa*).

"Wholesome and unwholesome volitions associated with the taints" (*sāsavakusalākusalacetanā*) refers to wholesome volitions of the sense-sphere, fine-material, and immaterial spheres, as well as unwholesome volitions, which act as supportive conditions by way of performing the function of differentiating the continuity of resultant and kamma-produced matter as it proceeds within a continuum distinguished by its own arising upon the convergence of other conditions. For it is by way of such a function that—

Their occurrence is due to their being active, not otherwise. However, the other [mental factors], while occurring by way of the activity of accumulating for co-nascent states, should be said to be supportive.

By the restriction here, however, one excludes kamma such as covetousness associated with volition (*cetanā*), because—even though they possess the nature of resultant phenomena—they do not share the same essential nature as those factors excluding volition. Anāsava...pe...

By the term "condition" (*paccaya*), he shows merely a distinction from mundane wholesome volition (*lokiyakusala-cetanā*), not an absence of asynchronous kamma-conditionality (*nānakkhaṇika-kammapaccayatā*).
And having established this, it is stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*):
"But immaterial-sphere volition and supramundane volition, having arisen and ceased, are conditions for their respective resultant aggregates by way of asynchronous kamma-condition."

Only non-material phenomena (arūpadhammā) that assist in producing a state of effortless tranquility in the co-nascent mind and matter (nāmarūpa) by virtue of their own effortless and tranquil nature are the resultant condition (vipākapaccaya). Therefore, it is said: "resultant consciousness and mental factors.

For these, being unachievable through effort and arising merely from the performance of karma, possess an effortless and tranquil nature; however, this is not the same as the tranquility consisting in the subsiding of the defilements (kilesa).
Indeed, because they are characterized by an effortless and peaceful state, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and other such states are difficult to discern.

Even in the five sense doors, it is understood that the apprehension of visible forms and so forth occurs only through the activity of the impulsion (javana) consciousness. However, the resultant states consisting merely of the adverting, receiving, and investigating moments are indeed difficult to discern.

The nutriment condition (āhāra-paccaya) is an assistance to both the material and immaterial realms by way of providing support; for even though it possesses the quality of producing, its function is specifically that of supporting.
The primary function of nutriment is to generate; yet even while generating, nutriment generates only by way of supporting through non-interruption.

Thus, its very state of being a support is its state of being nutriment. In this regard, edible food supports only the material body, whereas the remaining three support both the material and immaterial bodies.
For these [three] are not merely causes for the non-interruption of mental phenomena (nāmadhamma), but also—
It is a condition for the material phenomena produced by kamma at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), and also for those born of consciousness during the course of existence (*pavatta*).

It is the faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*) in the sense of sovereignty (*ādhipacca*), which consists in making itself conform to the states arisen through its own conditions in their respective functions. For it overcomes those things that would obstruct the occurrence of the states acting as dominant conditions (*adhipati-paccaya-dhamma*).

The sense of predominance (*adhipati-ṭṭha*) is the state of being weighty by way of continued occurrence. Furthermore, regarding the functions of seeing and so forth of the faculties: [this occurs] through eye-consciousness and the rest; in living, through matter born of karma;
and in the states of being happy and so forth, through immaterial phenomena that are themselves living and happy and so forth; in resolve, exertion, establishment, non-distraction, and understanding;

in the process of knowing "I shall know the unknown" and in the state of one who has already known—thus, [the predominance of the faculties occurs] through those co-nascent with faith and the rest. Thus...

The specific function of the faculties (*indriya*) is simply this: in their respective functions, the mere state of being followed by phenomena such as the eye and so forth, through conditions such as the eye and so forth, constitutes the sovereignty (*ādhipaccaṭṭha*) of those faculties.
This alone is their distinction. By the inclusion of the "group of seven material [faculties]," he indicates the five beginning with the eye, as well as the pair of female and male faculties.
Furthermore, having grouped the life-faculty together with the immaterial life-faculty, he includes it under the term "life."
It is grasped. In this way, there are twenty-two faculties (*indriya*).

The faculty that occurs with the thought, "In beginningless *saṃsāra*, I shall know the Dhamma of the Four Truths not yet known and not yet realized, or indeed Nibbāna itself," is the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*);
it is the knowledge of the first path. The faculty of one who understands—that is, one who knows without overstepping the boundary seen by the first path—is the faculty of "knowing" (*aññindriya*).
The faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*) refers to the six types of knowledge from the fruit of stream-entry up to the path of arhatship.
The faculty of one who has already known (*aññātāvindriya*) is the faculty of one for whom the task is completed regarding the four truths; it is the knowledge of the fruit of arhatship.

Although this was included by way of the "group of seven material phenomena" (*rūpasattaka*) with reference to its status as a faculty in the first sense, it is mentioned again here because, in some respect, it lacks the quality of being a contributing factor (*upakārakatā*).
In order to show that the female and male faculties (*itthi-purisindriya*) are not included here, the phrase beginning with "among those" (*tesu*) was stated.

For although these [faculties] generally follow along with the gender-mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, they do not follow as conditions due to their status as causal factors; this is the meaning already expressed.

By approaching through the contemplation of the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*) and the contemplation of characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*), the contemplation of the object constitutes the condition for jhāna.
And since that [mental formation] is the specific individual nature of applied thought (*vitakka*) and the others, he said, "the condition for jhāna," and so forth.

Furthermore, it should be understood that these are conditions for the material phenomena produced by kamma (*kaṭattārūpa*) at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), for the mind-born material phenomena (*cittajarūpa*) during the course of existence (*pavatta*), and for mental states (*nāmadhamma*) in both cases.
Their quality of being an assistance to co-nascent phenomena is in the sense of leading away from a happy destination, from an unhappy destination, from the wholesome, or from the unwholesome.
Regarding the conditionality of the path (*maggapaccayatā*), since that [conditionality] belongs to right view and the other factors, he says "the path-condition" (*maggapaccayo*) and so forth.

By the inclusion of "intention" (*saṅkappa*), he shows both right intention (*sammāsaṅkappa*) and wrong intention (*micchāsaṅkappa*). The same applies to the remaining factors as well. For wrong intention and the others are factors of the path to the states of deprivation (*apāya*);
and herein, wrong mindfulness, wrong speech, and so forth, as well as volition (*cetanā*), are the mental arisings occurring in such a manner. This too [is included] in the condition for jhāna.
It should be understood as the condition for those very things that have arisen by way of conditions.

Although they are distinct in the ultimate sense, their status as associated conditions consists in their being helpful through the characteristic of association—defined as simultaneous arising and so forth—as if they had attained a state of unity.
And this applies only to mental phenomena (nāmadhamma), not to material phenomena (rūpadhamma); thus he says, "associated condition," and so forth.

The state of being a dissociation condition (*vippayuttapaccaya*) is the quality of being helpful through the attainment of diversity by way of being dissociated—that is, through the state of non-association—even though [the factors] are conjoined by way of mutual relationship and are equal.
And that [dissociation] belongs only to the bases (*vatthu*), and to mind and mental factors (*cittacetasika*). Thus he said, "The dissociation condition," and so forth.

For the six bases [are related] to the seven consciousnesses respectively, both at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and during the course of existence (*pavatta*), as well as to mind and mental factors.
It is a dissociation condition for the material phenomena produced by kamma (*kaṭattārūpa*) at the moment of rebirth-linking, and for those originated by consciousness during the course of existence.
The phrase "bases arisen prior" is stated specifically with reference to the bases such as the eye;

however, the heart-base is obtained as both a co-nascent condition and as a condition at the moment of rebirth-linking, because it functions as a condition even then. For this has been said in the analysis of the co-nascent [condition] under the indeterminate category:
"At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant indeterminate aggregates are related to the kamma-produced material phenomena;

aggregates are related to the physical basis, and the physical basis is related to the aggregates, by way of dissociation condition. Likewise, it is stated specifically in the case of eye-consciousness and so forth that "subsequently arisen consciousness and mental factors" [are related], because of such statements as:
"Conascent wholesome aggregates are related to mind-originated material phenomena by way of dissociation condition," and so on.

However, they can also be found as co-nascent [conditions]. And having established it thus, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "The dissociation condition is threefold, by way of being co-nascent, prenascent, and postnascent.

Yet, although this is a material phenomenon (*rūpadhamma*), it does not serve as a condition for another material phenomenon, because there is no possibility of association (*sampayoga*) between them.
For those mental phenomena (*nāma*) such as the eye and so forth, which proceed as if emerging from within, and the material phenomena, exist only in dependence upon the mind.
When [mental states] are arising, there is a suspicion of association; therefore, their state of being dissociated conditions is stated.

However, there is no suspicion of association between material phenomena and material phenomena. Furthermore, for mental states that arise in dependence upon a physical basis, the object is merely the sphere [of experience];
thus, there is also no suspicion of association between them. By virtue of existing with a present intrinsic nature, for such [a state]...

The state of being an assistant through the act of supporting the phenomenon (dhamma) is "presence-condition" (atthipaccayatā). For even though they possess the quality of producing [an effect], the function of presence-conditions is preeminently in maintaining [the effect];
thus, their role as supporters is taken into account. And since these are specifically the material life-faculty (rūpajīvitindriya) and so forth, he says, "the presence-condition," and so on.
For the material life-faculty [supports] the kamma-born material phenomena (kaṭattārūpa), and edible food [supports] this [body].
For the body, the pre-arisen objects are the "presence condition" (*atthipaccaya*) for mind and mental factors;

these are the phenomena mentioned under the "support condition" (*nissayapaccaya*), as well as the phenomena arising through that same condition mentioned in that very context. Regarding the phrase "phenomena mentioned under the support condition," this refers to the inclusion of the physical basis (*vatthurūpa*), the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), mind, and mental factors by virtue of their common nature as phenomena, and not exclusively those that function specifically as a support condition. This also includes post-arisen mind and mental factors.
Because the pre-arisen body is specified as a condition in the section on questions.

Furthermore, since there is no status of "presence-condition" (*atthipaccayatā*) for Nibbāna—which exists at all times—because it assists through its mere presence only those things that do not assist by their very existence;
or because the state of being an assistant is incompatible with the assistance rendered by the absence of those things associated with arising and so forth.
Regarding the conditionality of presence (*atthipaccayatā*), there is no contingency of that [condition] being a condition for itself.

In the case of "the condition of absence" (*natthipaccaya*) and so forth, the state of being a proximate condition (*anantarapaccayatā*) consists in being an auxiliary factor either by mere immediate succession or by way of determining the mind.
When a collection of phenomena such as contact (*phassa*) and the rest is occurring, because a second [moment] is absent, those [phenomena] do not obtain an opportunity for their own persistence.
The state of being a condition by way of absence (*natthipaccayatā*) is the quality of being helpful by providing space for the mind and mental factors that are arising immediately thereafter.

The state of being a condition by way of disappearance (*vigatapaccayatā*) is the quality of being helpful through the state of having disappeared—that is, through not occurring—by not departing from its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

However, in terms of meaning, no distinction is stated between these two, because both possess the status of being phenomena that function as immediate conditions (*anantarapaccaya*); they differ only in their intrinsic natures.

The distinction between these conditions should be understood as follows: although there is no difference in the phenomena themselves, the state of being an assistance (*upakārakatā*) constitutes the conditionality of presence (*atthipaccayatā*), while the state of being an assistance by way of not having passed away [due to cessation] constitutes the conditionality of non-disappearance (*avigatapaccayatā*).

For it was after knowing in every aspect the specific capacity of phenomena that the Blessed One taught the twenty-four conditions; thus, through faith in the Blessed One, one understands: "These phenomena are indeed distinct in this way."

Having generated knowledge consisting of what has been heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*), one should apply oneself to the realization of that [truth] by means of knowledge consisting of reflection (*cintāmaya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*). Although the efficacy of the Dhamma is without distinction,
it should be understood that the condition mentioned previously is stated again in another way according to the individuals to be trained in various ways—
just as, for example, after stating the "pair of rootless states" (*ahetukaduka*), the "pair dissociated from roots" (*hetuvippayuttaduka*) is stated.

Because the great elements (mahābhūta) are mutually co-nascent conditions for one another and for derived matter (upādārūpa); because the great elements are mutual mutual-dependence conditions for one another and support conditions for derived matter; because edible food is the nutriment condition for this body;
and because the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) is [the condition] for the great elements, for derived matter, and for matter produced by kamma (kaṭattārūpa).
There is the conditionality of non-existence and dissociation; therefore it is said: "Materiality is a condition for materiality... [etc. ...in seven ways.
In the cases of "materiality for the immaterial," etc., one should apply the conditions after having carefully examined the phenomena arising from those conditions as explained below.

As for "there is no case where materiality is a condition for both materiality and immateriality," this means that even though materiality, acting as a co-nascent condition, is a condition for both the pair of materiality and immateriality...
It is stated thus because it is considered "not yet come" by way of its status as a condition (*paccayabhāva*).
When all conditions are brought together— namely, the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) and the decisive support-condition (*upanissayapaccaya*),

the kamma-condition (*kammapaccaya*) consisting of conascence and asynchronous volition, and the presence-condition (*atthipaccaya*) which is divided into conascence, prenascence, postnascence, and so forth— all of them [are included].
Showing that conditions are, in brief, only fourfold, he says: "But all these," and so forth.
Thus ends [the section] from the *Abhidhammāvatārasaṃvaṇṇanā* named *Abhidhammatthavikāsinī*.
The commentary on the Exposition of Conditions (*Paccayaniddesa*) is finished.
Commentary on the Concluding Discourse (1400–2):
One whose mind (*mati*) is beautiful (*sundara*) because its range is unimpeded regarding all phenomena is "Sumati"; [the text refers to] that Sumati.
He awakens the investigation of the Blessed One’s intention and the movement of his knowledge; thus, he is "the awakener of the investigation of the excellent mind.
Those whose minds are conflicted are "doubtful" (*vimatino*); the meaning of "conflicted minds" is "contradictory views. He destroys their delusion; thus, he is "the destroyer of doubt and delusion.
Since [he was] by name the bhikkhu Sumati, and out of respect—that is, through great honor and the request for his esteem—...
Having been requested, and always being properly humble, this *Abhidhammāvatāra* has been composed by me. For it is thus:
"The cultivation of the virtuous, the manifestation of welfare through the revelation of welfare, and that which always brings satisfaction"—this is the construction [of the verse].
(1403–14) Regarding the phrase "inappropriate" (*ayutta*) or "contradictory" (*viruddha*): here, "inappropriate" means that which is contrary to the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
They say that what is contrary to the Pāḷi is "contradictory" (viruddha). And the meaning of "modes of expression" (byappathānaṃ) is "paths of speech. "Threefold" means there are three types:
one mode of expression is perfect in sound but not perfect in meaning; one is perfect in meaning but not perfect in sound; and one is perfect in both—this is the sense.
"Welfare alone is the goal" means it has welfare as its purpose (hitattha); he desires that for himself.
One who desires his welfare. "Kelāsasikhara" means the peak of Mount Kelāsa;

for it is the great silver peak, the preeminent among the eighty-four thousand peaks of the Himavat, which is adorned with palaces that are entirely white and shaped like that [mountain]. By "Kaṇhadāsa":... [end of fragment]
By the lay follower (upāsaka) of such-and-such a name. In the "Eastern Palace" (Pācīnapāsāda), that is, in the palace situated in the eastern quarter.
This is the *Abhidhammāvatāra*. Here ends the commentary on the *Abhidhammāvatāra*, titled the *Abhidhammatthavikāsinī*.
The Concluding Discourse:
In the delightful city of Pulatthipura, by the sovereign of the city,
the king Parakkamabhuja of mighty arms;
He dwells in the Jetavana monastery which he caused to be built,
delightful with its beautiful halls, excellent ponds, and groves, frequented by those who delight in perfected virtue, self-control, restraint, and tranquility.
Honored by the hosts of virtuous disciples,
he attained the revered status of an *ācariya* among many works such as the words of the Lord of Sages, esteemed by the wise.
And here, indicating his power of knowledge through the commentary on the Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā and other works,
beginning with the *Sāratthadīpanī*, which is the essence of sweet meaning—
Delighting the virtuous through her eloquence,
she took pity upon him— upon the Elder Sāriputta,
that mine of essential qualities firmly established.
He who, dwelling as a resident of the Nandipariveṇa monastery, attains sublime delight in the teaching of the Supreme Victor—
he accomplishes no small benefit for his listeners.
Renowned by the name uttered by Sumaṅgala,
he has composed this *Abhidhammatthavikāsinī*,
which elucidates [the Abhidhamma] and is endowed with sweet meaning.
The Commentary on the *Abhidhammāvatāra* is completed.
